docs.title: Initial Access — Master Reference
docs.text:
About this page

Built on the Initial Access chapter of CRTO (Certified Red Team Operator) study material, then expanded with per-version Windows 10 / 11 patch status (22H2 · 23H2 · 24H2), realistic viability, and the latest evasion trends, OPSEC, and Blue Team / DFIR detection strategy. The emphasis is on mechanics, patch constraints, and detection/defence rather than weaponization.

Structure (four parts)

  • Part 1 — Phishing taxonomy & host-based payloads (DLL Side-Loading, .NET AppDomainManager)
  • Part 2 — Installer and Office payloads (MSI, Excel Add-In, code-signing policy changes, GadgetToJScript droppers)
  • Part 3 — Evolution of triggers and anti-sandbox (Batch tricks, LNK vulnerabilities and patches, GrimResource/MSC)
  • Part 4 — Containers (MotW bypass matrix) & Delivery (HTML/SVG Smuggling, site cloning) + current trends

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• 1. Overview & phishing payload taxonomy
  • 2. Payloads — DLL Side-Loading / AppDomainManager
  • 2.3–2.6 Installer · Office · code signing · droppers (Part 2)
  • 3. Triggers — Batch / LNK / GrimResource (Part 3)
  • 4. Containers — MotW bypass matrix (Part 4)
  • 5. Delivery — HTML/SVG Smuggling · site cloning
  • 6. Appendix — 2025~2026 current initial-access trends

docs.title: 1.1 A modern definition of Initial Access
docs.text:
Initial Access (MITRE ATT&CK: TA0001) is the tactic of establishing the first foothold inside a target network. Attackers do sometimes exploit externally exposed servers (VPNs, web servers) or carry out supply-chain compromises, but the most common and effective route is still social engineering via spear phishing.

In the past it was enough to email a report.exe or a macro-laden .doc. Against a modern layered defence (email sandboxes, MotW, EDR, ASR rules) those are blocked instantly. Today's operator therefore has to combine several techniques into a multi-stage infection chain that disrupts automated analysis by security products and slows down reverse engineering by the DFIR analyst.

docs.title: 1.2 The five components of a phishing package
docs.text:
The payload taxonomy formalised by security researcher Mariusz Banach gives the most standard framework for designing an initial-access package:

DELIVERY( CONTAINER( TRIGGER + PAYLOAD + DECOY ) )
Component Role Traditional (past) Modern red-team trend (present) 1. Delivery The means of getting the package past perimeter security (firewall, web proxy, email gateway) to the victim Direct email attachment, plain HTTP download link HTML Smuggling, SVG Smuggling, abuse of legitimate cloud storage (OneDrive, SharePoint), messenger (Teams) phishing 2. Container A compression/disk format that bundles the files (trigger, payload, decoy), eases delivery, and blocks MotW (Mark-of-the-Web) propagation or adds encryption .zip, .rar .iso, .img, .vhd/.vhdx, .wim, .7z, WebDAV shares 3. Trigger The file the victim directly interacts with (double-click) after opening the container, kicking off payload execution .exe, Word/Excel macros (.docm, .xlsm) .lnk (shortcut), .bat/.cmd, .msc, legitimately signed executables (LOLBin / side-loading hosts) 4. Payload The malicious code that actually runs on the victim (or a dropper/loader that fetches the final payload) A single malicious .exe, a PowerShell one-liner Malicious .dll (for side-loading), .xlam, encrypted shellcode files (.bin, .dat), .NET assemblies 5. Decoy A benign file shown right after the trigger fires, so the victim believes they opened a normal document None (nothing happens, or a fake error window) A legitimate .pdf, .xlsx, .docx that fits the pretext perfectly (must keep the same format as the trigger's icon)

docs.title: 1.3 A real attack chain (Case study: Lumma Stealer campaign)
docs.text:
A representative chain showing how real threat groups combine the components to evade security products:

[Victim: downloads a file disguised as a PDF from a website]
       │
       ▼
┌───────────────────┐
│  1. Trigger       │  A Windows shortcut (.LNK) disguised with a PDF icon runs
└─────────┬─────────┘
          │ (invokes)
          ▼
┌───────────────────┐
│  2. LOLBin (1st)  │  wmic.exe or mshta.exe connects to a remote server (80.76.51[.]231)
└─────────┬─────────┘
          │ (download and run)
          ▼
┌───────────────────┐
│  3. Dropper (2nd) │  Obfuscated JavaScript (.js) -> calls an obfuscated PowerShell script
└─────────┬─────────┘
          │ (unpack and run hidden)
          ▼
┌───────────────────┐
│  4. Final Payload │  Lumma Stealer (Kompass-4.1.2.exe) runs
└─────────┬─────────┘
          │ (obtains C2 address - Dead Drop Resolver technique)
          ▼
┌───────────────────┐
│  5. C2 comms      │  Parses an HTML tag ("actual_persona_name") on a Steam community
└───────────────────┘  profile page, decrypts the real C2 domain, then communicates

Update note — per-version Windows validity of this chain

  • WMIC: On Windows 11 (22H2 and later) and upcoming Windows Server, wmic.exe has been removed from the default install (deprecated / removed on demand). Putting wmic in a trigger chain will therefore fail against a current Windows 11 target.
  • mshta.exe and JavaScript: These are the top target of default detection rules in modern EDR (e.g. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) and of ASR (Attack Surface Reduction) rules. Modern operators therefore favour DLL side-loading (below) over script engines.

docs.title: 2. Payloads in detail (and brought up to date)
2.1 DLL Side-Loading (DLL side-loading & abuse of WinSxS)
Core idea (DLL Hijacking vs. DLL Side-Loading)
docs.text:
When a Windows application (.exe) runs and the absolute path to a required dynamic-link library (.dll) is not hard-coded, Windows searches folders in a fixed order (the Standard DLL Search Order):

  1. The directory the application (.exe) is in (most important ⭐)
  2. The system directory (C:\Windows\System32)
  3. The 16-bit system directory (C:\Windows\System)
  4. The Windows directory (C:\Windows)
  5. The current working directory

  6. Directories listed in the PATH environment variable

  7. DLL Hijacking: When an already-installed program looks for a DLL that doesn't exist (NAME NOT FOUND), the attacker plants a malicious DLL in a path the standard user can write to (e.g. a sub-folder on PATH). Mostly used for privilege escalation and persistence.

  8. DLL Side-Loading: Optimised for initial access. A legitimately signed .exe (from Microsoft or another trusted vendor) is bundled in the same folder (inside the container) with a malicious .dll named exactly like the one that .exe loads. By search-order rule 1 (the application's own directory), the signed .exe loads the malicious .dll sitting beside it the moment it runs.

docs.title: Why target C:\Windows\WinSxS?
docs.text: Executables in the default system folders (System32 etc.) have been hardened over successive patches so they only search safe paths (their own folder, the GAC, and so on). But C:\Windows\WinSxS (the Windows Component Store) is a huge warehouse that keeps pre-patch, older binary versions for application compatibility (side-by-side assemblies) and update rollback. In other words, a vulnerable, pre-patch version of a genuinely Microsoft-signed binary that is fixed in the main OS can still be sitting inside WinSxS.

docs.title: [Analysis guide] Identifying a vulnerable binary in WinSxS
docs.text:
Step 1. Observe the behaviour of the current binary (ngentask.exe) — Run the current ngentask.exe from its default path and watch it with Sysinternals Process Monitor (ProcMon).

  • ProcMon filters:
    • Process Name is ngentask.exe
    • Path ends with .dll
    • Result is NAME NOT FOUND
C:\Users\Analyst> C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\v4.0.30319\ngentask.exe

Result: You see DLLs it can't find, but it only searches inside C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\... and the GAC (Global Assembly Cache) — it never looks in external folders, so hijacking is hard.

Step 2. Find an older ngentask.exe in WinSxS — Use PowerShell to search for older versions kept inside the WinSxS directory.

PS C:\> Get-ChildItem -Path C:\Windows\WinSxS -Recurse -Filter ngentask.exe | Select-Object -ExpandProperty FullName

C:\Windows\WinSxS\amd64_netfx4-ngentask_exe_..._4.0.15805.0_...\ngentask.exe
C:\Windows\WinSxS\amd64_netfx4-ngentask_exe_..._4.0.15805.285_...\ngentask.exe
...

Step 3. Run the older version and check its search order — Run the older binary and watch ProcMon again. The older version follows the standard search order to find mscorsvc.dll and tries to load it from the current working directory (NAME NOT FOUND). That location is the spot vulnerable to side-loading.

docs.title: [Advanced] Higher-reliability side-loading concepts for real operations
docs.text:
Beyond simply firing from DllMain, two concepts matter for reliability and success rate in a real engagement:

  1. DLL Proxying / Forwarding: When the legitimate program loads the DLL and immediately calls a specific export, a replacement DLL that lacks that export causes the program to crash — the victim notices, and a crash dump lands in the EDR telemetry. A proxy DLL (e.g. SharpDllProxy) forwards the program's legitimate function calls to the real system DLL (C:\Windows\System32\...) so the program keeps running normally while the malicious code runs on a background thread.
  2. Third-party signed binaries: When a Microsoft default binary (e.g. ngentask.exe) runs from an unusual path (e.g. Downloads), modern EDR gets suspicious. Operators therefore increasingly use older signed executables from NVIDIA, Adobe, Cisco, VLC, etc. as the host — third-party programs legitimately install in many locations, so they evade path-based heuristics far better. (Reference database: HijackLibs.net)

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text: Independent of DLL search order, every application written in the .NET Framework has an official feature to specify the AppDomainManager it will use at startup. The technique: create a .NET assembly (DLL) that inherits from System.AppDomainManager, then use an environment variable or a .config file to tell a legitimate .NET executable "load this DLL as your manager when you run."

docs.title: [Concept example] Structure of a custom AppDomainManager
docs.text:
Step 1. .NET Framework class library (PoC only — just shows a MessageBox)

using System;
using System.Windows.Forms;

namespace AppDomainHijack
{
    // A public class that inherits from AppDomainManager
    public sealed class DomainManager : AppDomainManager
    {
        // Override the method called automatically when the domain initialises
        public override void InitializeNewDomain(AppDomainSetup appDomainInfo)
        {
            // PoC — in a real engagement a loader would go here; this document is for understanding the mechanism
            MessageBox.Show("Hello World", "Success");
        }
    }
}

Step 2. Place a legitimate .NET binary and the DLL in the same folder — Pick one of the signed .NET executables shipped with Windows (e.g. ngentask.exe, dfsvc.exe, UEVAppMonitor.exe) and put the compiled DLL beside it. The assembly name specified in the config/environment variable must match the actual DLL filename for it to load.

Step 3. Choose a trigger (two options)

  • Option A — environment variables (mainly used from a batch file or LNK trigger):
PS C:\> $env:APPDOMAIN_MANAGER_ASM  = 'AppDomainHijack, Version=1.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=null'
PS C:\> $env:APPDOMAIN_MANAGER_TYPE = 'AppDomainHijack.DomainManager'
PS C:\> .\ngentask.exe
  • Option B — application config file (.config) (cleanest for container packaging ⭐): Put a text file named after the executable with .config appended (e.g. ngentask.exe.config) in the same folder, and running just the .exe works without any environment variables.
<configuration>
  <runtime>
    <appDomainManagerAssembly value="AppDomainHijack, Version=1.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=null" />
    <appDomainManagerType value="AppDomainHijack.DomainManager" />
  </runtime>
</configuration>

docs.title: [Compatibility & patch matrix] Part 1 assessment
docs.text: Technique Target OS / framework compatibility Impact of recent patches (Win 10 / Win 11 23H2~24H2) Real-world viability & OPSEC tips WinSxS-based DLL Side-Loading All Windows versions (Win 10 / Win 11 / Server) The WinSxS structure is retained at the OS level. However, modern EDR detects a default system binary running from an unusual path behaviourally. [High — but change the host] Using a third-party legitimately signed executable as the host instead of a Microsoft default gives a high success rate even on current Win 11 + EDR. AppDomainManager Injection .NET Framework (v2.0 ~ v4.8.1) only (built into every Win 10/11) Does not work on apps built on .NET Core 3.1+ or .NET 5~9 (use DOTNET_STARTUP_HOOKS instead). ETW records the .NET assembly-load event to EDR. [Medium-high — still strong] The .config method leaves no script on disk, so it resists static detection. But the DLL's code must avoid AMSI/ETW via obfuscation and dynamic API calls (D/Invoke).

docs.title: [Blue Team / DFIR] Detection and defence
docs.text:
1. Detect OriginalFilename mismatch in the PE header (Sysmon Event ID 1 & 7): Even if an attacker renames ngentask.exe to PDFViewer.exe, the PE header's OriginalFilename still reads ngentask.exe. EDR alerts when the current filename differs from the header name, or when a file that should live in System32/Framework64 runs from Downloads or a mounted virtual drive (D:\, E:\).
  2. Watch for abnormal .config creation and unsigned DLL loads: Monitor *.exe.config creation via Sysmon Event ID 11 (FileCreate), and track events where a signed Microsoft binary loads an unsigned DLL.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Windows Installer (.msi) stores the files needed for installation and the per-step actions in an internal relational database (a set of tables). In the taxonomy it can therefore act as both a Container and a Trigger/Payload.

  • Packaging structure: Visual Studio's 'Setup Project' lets you place target files into Program Files, the desktop, etc., and manipulate file properties to rename on drop (TargetName) or hide (Hidden: True).
  • Abusing Custom Actions: The main reason MSI is risky is Custom Actions — the ability to hook arbitrary executables (.exe), DLLs, or scripts (.vbs, .js) into the install/commit/rollback/uninstall steps.
  • Disguise: Attackers enable the Run64Bit property, pass legitimate-looking arguments like /install /quiet, and fill in a legitimate Manufacturer and ProductName so it looks like normal software in Control Panel and in its install path.

docs.title: Recent patches and constraints
docs.text:
1. Parent-child process behaviour detection (EDR): In the past msiexec.exe executed the payload in the background and evaded ordinary AV. Today, modern EDR (MDE, CrowdStrike, etc.) on Win 10/11 classifies msiexec.exe spawning an unsigned binary or a script engine (wscript.exe, powershell.exe, rundll32.exe) as high risk and blocks it immediately.
  2. UAC / admin rights: Configuring the MSI to drop into C:\Program Files triggers a UAC elevation prompt for a standard user. If the victim lacks local admin, the install fails — so real threat groups modify the MSI tables for a per-user install (%LocalAppData% paths) that needs no elevation.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Ordinary macro documents (.docm, .xlsm) are blocked from running macros by the MotW tag applied on download and by Office's Protected View. This technique bypasses that by combining an Excel add-in (.xlam) with Office's Trusted Locations.

  • The Trusted Locations gap: For files opened from certain folders registered in the Trust Center, Office skips security checks and enables macros immediately:
    • %ProgramFiles%\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\XLSTART\ (not writable by a standard user)
    • %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Excel\XLSTART\ (writable by a standard user ⭐)
    • %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Templates\ (writable by a standard user)
  • Auto-run mechanism: The XLSTART folder auto-loads every workbook/add-in (.xlam) in it each time Excel starts, with no user consent. A .xlam containing an Auto_Open() subroutine copied there runs its macro on the next launch — so it doubles as a persistence technique.

docs.title: Recent patches and constraints
docs.text:
1. Blocked by ASR (Attack Surface Reduction) rules: Even if you strip MotW via a container and auto-run through XLSTART, Defender ASR (if enabled on Win 10/11 Enterprise) blocks the post-macro steps. (Key rules: "Block all Office applications from creating child processes", "Block Office applications from creating executable content", "Block Win32 API calls from Office macros".)
  2. Tighter control of Excel 4.0 (XLM) and XLL: Besides VBA-based .xlam, C/C++ DLL add-ins (.xll) were heavily abused — but recent M365 updates greatly strengthened blocking of internet-sourced add-ins and AMSI's runtime memory scanning of macros.

docs.title: 2.5 Code signing and the shift in the SmartScreen trust model
Core idea
docs.text:
Code signing adds a digital signature to an executable or installer to assure the publisher's identity and file integrity. Microsoft Defender SmartScreen treats signing as a key trust signal; signed files trigger far fewer (or no) warnings and fare better in static AV/EDR verdicts.

  • Standard vs. EV certificates (as the course describes):
    • Standard: Signs the file, but SmartScreen warnings still appear until the certificate has built up global download reputation.
    • EV (Extended Validation): Issued after strict vetting; historically earned instant SmartScreen trust on first use, fully removing the 'Unknown Publisher' warning.
  • How attackers obtain certificates: Signing under their own company name gets them identified and revoked immediately, so they set up shell companies or steal other companies' certificates leaked in public repos, buckets, or forums.

docs.title: [Essential update] The upheaval in code-signing and SmartScreen policy (2023~2026)
docs.text:
This is where the course and today's environment diverge most.

  1. Hardware token (HSM) storage mandated (CA/Browser Forum rule change): Since June 2023, even Standard code-signing certificates are no longer issued as .pfx/.p12 files. All private keys must live only in a physical hardware token (FIPS 140-2 Level 2 or higher) or a cloud HSM (Azure Key Vault, AWS KMS). This sharply reduced "steal a .pfx and sign locally" attacks, shifting the threat toward hijacking cloud CI/CD signing permissions.
  2. EV's 'instant SmartScreen bypass' privilege removed: After a surge of EV abuse via shell companies, Microsoft overhauled the SmartScreen scoring algorithm. On current Win 10/11, an EV signature no longer grants instant reputation, and warnings persist — regardless of EV status — until reputation is established from file/signer history and distribution volume.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
A dropper is an intermediate program that doesn't expose the final payload in the container, but hides it in its own embedded resource and either writes it to disk or downloads it at runtime.

[How a GadgetToJScript-based dropper works]

1. Build .NET DLL (C#)        2. Serialize & convert to script     3. Runs on victim PC
┌──────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────┐    ┌────────────────────────┐
│ MyDropper.dll        │    │ GadgetToJScript tool     │    │ Double-click dropper.js│
│  └─ Embedded Resource│ ──>│  └─ Build .NET gadget    │ ──>│  └─ wscript.exe runs   │
│     (http_x64.exe)   │    │  └─ Base64 encode (to JS)│    │  └─ Deserialize in mem │
└──────────────────────┘    └──────────────────────────┘    └───────────┬────────────┘
                                                                        │
                                                                        ▼
                                                            ┌────────────────────────┐
                                                            │ C# constructor auto-runs│
                                                            │  └─ Drops/runs EXE under│
                                                            │     C:\ProgramData\...  │
                                                            └────────────────────────┘
  • Reflection and resource extraction: The executable is embedded as a resource in a C# library, and the class constructor reads it into memory via Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly().GetManifestResourceStream().
  • Choosing a drop location (OPSEC): Dropping into %TEMP% or the home directory gets detected immediately. So droppers create a sub-folder under C:\ProgramData\* — a standard path that even a standard user can write to and create folders in.
  • Turning it into a script with GadgetToJScript: A compiled .NET DLL can't run by itself, so GadgetToJScript abuses .NET deserialization to convert the assembly into .js/.vbs/VBA/HTA script. When the victim runs the .js (wscript.exe), the object deserializes in memory and the dropper code in the constructor executes.

docs.title: Recent patches and constraints
docs.text:
1. AMSI fully integrated: When wscript.exe/cscript.exe runs a .js/.vbs, the engine hands the plaintext to AV via AMSI right before execution. The serialized gadget patterns GadgetToJScript produces now have signatures in every commercial AV/EDR, so without obfuscation/AMSI bypass they're blocked on run.
  2. Retirement of .NET BinaryFormatter: BinaryFormatter deserialization is disabled by default in recent .NET due to its risk, and even on 4.8.1 the EDR's ETW telemetry watches in-memory Assembly.Load in real time.
  3. Win 11 restrictions on JScript/VBScript: To curb legacy-script-engine infections, Microsoft is restricting WSH and VBScript defaults or removing them as optional features (FOD).

docs.title: [Compatibility & patch matrix] Part 2 assessment
docs.text: Category / technique Target OS / environment Impact of recent patches Blue Team detection focus Windows Installer (.msi) All Windows versions (built-in msiexec.exe) UAC prompt when targeting Program Files. EDR behavioural detection when msiexec.exe spawns an abnormal child process. Sysmon ID 1: parent msiexec.exe with a child that is unsigned or runs from C:\ProgramData. Static analysis of the MSI CustomAction table (Orca). Excel Add-In (.xlam) MS Office (2016/2019/M365) XLSTART is still a Trusted Location. But ASR, when enabled, blocks macro-driven process creation and Win32 API calls. Sysmon ID 11: real-time monitoring of new files in %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Excel\XLSTART\ and AddIns (top-priority rule). Code Signing (EV cert) All Windows versions (SmartScreen) HSM storage mandated, reducing cert leaks. EV instant-bypass privilege removed (merged into reputation). Even for signed binaries, cross-check certificate issue date, unfamiliar publisher name, and first-seen prevalence in the org. GadgetToJScript (.js/.vbs dropper) .NET Framework 4.8.x (built into Win 10/11) AMSI and .NET ETW detect serialized gadget patterns with high probability. Drop-.exe-then-Process.Start is weak against EDR. Detect wscript.exe/cscript.exe loading .NET CLR DLLs (clr.dll, mscoree.dll) in memory (Sysmon ID 7). Watch for new executables under C:\ProgramData.

docs.title: Triggers (initial execution & anti-sandbox)
docs.text: A trigger is the file the victim first interacts with (usually a double-click) after mounting/extracting a container. Its goals are to disguise itself as a familiar file to avoid suspicion, and to run the payload and a benign decoy at the same time in the background.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
A text script format that runs commands sequentially through cmd.exe (.bat, .cmd, .btm).

  • Hiding the window: @echo off at the top plus > nul 2>&1 on commands hides stdout and stderr.
  • Env-variable anti-sandbox trick: To evade automated AV emulators/sandboxes, the batch checks whether it was launched by a real double-click or by an analysis CLI, by comparing environment variables.
[How environment variables differ by launch method]

1. User double-clicks in Explorer:
   • %cmdcmdline% : C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe /c ""C:\Users\Victim\Desktop\test.bat" "
   • %~f0         : C:\Users\Victim\Desktop\test.bat
   ▶ %cmdcmdline% contains %~f0 (the script path) -> proceed as normal

2. A sandbox/analyst runs it from an already-open CMD:
   • %cmdcmdline% : "C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe"
   • %~f0         : C:\Users\Victim\Desktop\test.bat
   ▶ %cmdcmdline% does NOT contain the script path -> treat as analysis, exit immediately

In short, it pipes %cmdcmdline% to find /i "%~f0" to search for the current batch path, and if no match (||) it exits immediately, defeating programmatic automated analysis.

docs.title: Recent patches and constraints
docs.text:
1. Can't change the default icon (social-engineering limit): .bat/.cmd can't carry their own icon resource and always show the default batch icon. Used alone they're easily spotted, so they're mostly a 2nd-stage script invoked hidden by a .lnk or another trigger.
  2. EDR command-line auditing and AMSI: Every child process spawned via cmd.exe /c has its full command line recorded to the security log (Event ID 4688, Sysmon ID 1). Modern Defender/EDR also detect obfuscation patterns (e.g. substring tricks like %var:~0,1%) statically and dynamically.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
The .lnk (Shell Link) binary format is the most widely used deceptive trigger in initial access.

  • Extension hiding via NeverShowExt: Even with 'Show file name extensions' enabled, the .lnk extension is never displayed, thanks to the registry NeverShowExt attribute. Naming a file report.pdf.lnk makes it appear as exactly report.pdf.
  • Icon disguise and compound commands: Using the WScript.Shell COM object, the target (TargetPath) can be set to %COMSPEC% (cmd.exe) while the icon (IconLocation) is overridden with an Edge (msedge.exe, 13 — the built-in PDF icon) or Excel (EXCEL.EXE, 0) icon.
  • Driving hidden files: If a payload inside the container (e.g. macros.xlam) has the hidden attribute, the .lnk's Arguments can xcopy /H it into %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Excel\XLSTART\, clear the hidden attribute with attrib -H, and open the decoy (sales.xlsx) — all in a single click.

docs.title: Recent patches and constraints
docs.text:
1. Stronger SmartScreen/MotW checks (CVE-2022-44698, CVE-2023-36025, CVE-2024-21412 patches): There used to be bugs where a .lnk with MotW bypassed SmartScreen, but concentrated patching means current Win 10/11 builds strictly check the target path and arguments of an externally sourced .lnk.
  2. explorer.exe → cmd.exe/powershell.exe process-tree detection: When a .lnk click launches cmd/powershell, the parent is recorded as explorer.exe and the command line shows &&, start, xcopy, etc. That is a basic block/alert condition in modern EDR and ASR.
  3. Current trend (LNK + LOLBins/side-loading): Instead of putting the heavily detected cmd/powershell directly in TargetPath, operators now point it at a legitimately signed executable (a DLL side-loading host) hidden alongside in the container, skipping the script-interpreter call entirely.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Discovered and named 'GrimResource' by Elastic Security Labs in 2024, this abuses the .msc (Microsoft Saved Console) format — the settings file for the Windows management console (mmc.exe).

[GrimResource (.msc) execution flow]

[Victim: double-clicks a malicious .msc file]
       │
       ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. mmc.exe runs (auto-elevating)                        │
│    └─ If a local admin, gains High Integrity            │
└───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                            │ (parses the .msc internal XML)
                            ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. Triggers an XSS flaw in apds.dll (StringTable abuse) │
│    └─ Loads a URL-encoded XSL stylesheet (xsl.loadXML)  │
└───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                            │ (invokes the XSLT script engine)
                            ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 3. Runs embedded VBScript / JScript                     │
│    └─ WScript.Shell or a DotNetToJScript payload        │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • XSS and XSLT execution via apds.dll: A .msc is essentially XML text. By manipulating its StringTable section the technique triggers an XSS flaw in the Windows help library apds.dll, loading a URL-encoded XSL stylesheet (VBScript/JScript inside an ms:script tag) as xsl.loadXML(unescape(...)) to run arbitrary code.
  • Auto-elevation benefit: mmc.exe is an auto-elevating binary per its manifest, so if the victim is in the local admin group, the payload runs at High Integrity (admin) right at initial access.

docs.title: [Essential update] GrimResource patch status and constraints
docs.text:
1. Officially patched by Microsoft (doesn't work on current builds): After disclosure, Microsoft patched the root cause in regular updates (e.g. late-2024 cumulative updates) so mmc.exe/apds.dll won't process abnormal external resources or inline scripts. On patched Win 10 (22H2) and Win 11 (23H2/24H2) it no longer works.
  2. Thoroughly detected by EDR: An office user running a .msc is itself unusual, and mmc.exe loading apds.dll then spawning a child process (cmd.exe etc.) or loading the .NET CLR is blocked immediately by major EDR.

docs.title: [Compatibility & patch matrix] Part 3 assessment
docs.text: Trigger format Target OS Impact of recent patches Blue Team / DFIR detection focus Batch (.bat, .cmd) All Windows versions The %cmdcmdline% trick can still evade older sandboxes. But modern EDR sandboxes simulate the Explorer click event and defeat it. Event ID 4688 / Sysmon 1: cmd.exe with find /i + env-variable combos. Block batch files running from ISO/archive mount paths (D:\, E:\, %TEMP%). Shell Link (.lnk) All Windows versions (Explorer native) NeverShowExt extension hiding is identical on all versions. CVE-2023-36025 / CVE-2024-21412 patched many SmartScreen-bypass bugs. Alert when a .lnk's Target points at a system interpreter (cmd, powershell, mshta, rundll32). Extract timestamps and the attacker's MachineID/MAC artifacts from inside the .lnk (DFIR). MS Saved Console (.msc — GrimResource) Unpatched Win 10/11 only Patched on current cumulative updates — no longer works. Directly affected by the gradual VBScript deprecation. Sysmon ID 7 (ImageLoad): mmc.exe abnormally loading apds.dll, mshtml.dll, vbscript.dll, jscript.dll in sequence. Static detection of apds:// or loadXML strings in the .msc XML (YARA).

docs.title: [Blue Team / DFIR deep dive] LNK forensic artifacts (OPSEC)
docs.text:
When you create a .lnk with PowerShell (WScript.Shell), Windows writes the creating computer's NetBIOS hostname, volume serial, and even MAC address into the .lnk binary structure (the DistributedLinkTrackerBlock in the ExtraData block).

  • Defender (DFIR) view: Analysing a recovered .lnk with LECmd (Eric Zimmerman's tool) can pin down the attacker's build-environment computer name and timestamps.
  • Operator (OPSEC) view: When creating a .lnk for a target, strip the metadata (TrackerDataBlock) with a tool or build it in a disposable clean VM, to avoid leaking internal infrastructure details.

docs.title: 4.1 Mark of the Web (MotW) — structure and role
docs.text:
MotW is a security identifier that Windows (or a browser/mail client) automatically attaches to files downloaded from the internet or an untrusted zone.

  • NTFS Alternate Data Stream (ADS): NTFS can store hidden extra streams alongside a file's main data (:$DATA). On download, the browser creates a Zone.Identifier ADS recording the origin.
PS C:\Users\Analyst\Downloads> Get-Content -Stream Zone.Identifier .\test.pdf

[ZoneTransfer]
ZoneId=3
ReferrerUrl=https://.../test.pdf
HostUrl=https://.../test.pdf
  • ZoneId meanings: 0 Local Machine · 1 Local Intranet · 2 Trusted Sites · 3 Internet (applied to external downloads) ⭐ · 4 Restricted Sites

With a ZoneId=3 tag, the file Properties window shows a "this file came from another computer and may be blocked" warning; Windows forces SmartScreen on executables and applies Protected View (blocking macros) to Office documents.

docs.title: 4.2 Purpose and packaging of containers
docs.text:
1. Bundling and hiding multiple files: Dependencies like the trigger (.lnk), payload (.dll/.xlam), and decoy (.pdf/.xlsx) are bundled into one package. A tool like PackMyPayload with its -H option sets the hidden attribute on inner files so the victim sees only the trigger when they open the container.
  2. Blocking MotW propagation: The container itself (e.g. test.iso) carries MotW (ZoneId=3) as a download, but the traditional core trick was to launder (strip) MotW by exploiting the gap where older archive/mount tools don't copy the Zone.Identifier stream to the individual inner files on extraction.

docs.title: 4.3 [Essential update] Per-format MotW propagation patch status (Win 10 / 11)
docs.text:
The course says mounting a .iso/.img removes MotW from inner files — but this is the area that changed most dramatically due to Microsoft patches.

Container format Native Windows support Past behaviour (per course) Current OS behaviour (Win 10 22H2 / Win 11 22H2~24H2) Current viability .iso, .img (optical disc image) Yes (double-click mounts a virtual DVD) ISO internals are ISO-9660/UDF, not NTFS, so no ADS → inner-file MotW disappears. [Patched — CVE-2022-41091 etc.] If a mounted ISO/IMG original has MotW, the kernel driver auto-inherits MotW (ZoneId=3) onto all files inside the mounted virtual drive. [MotW bypass gone] Still usable to bundle and hide files, but no longer works for MotW laundering. .vhd, .vhdx (virtual hard disk) Yes (double-click mounts a virtual disk) Recognised as a separate local disk, so MotW didn't propagate — a popular bypass. [Patched] Like ISO, a VHDMP driver update propagates the original VHD's MotW onto files inside the mounted volume. [Low] VHD mounts in a normal office environment raise immediate EDR alerts. .zip (standard archive) Yes (built into Explorer) Explorer extraction propagated MotW, but 7-Zip/WinRAR extraction dropped it. [Hardened] Explorer still propagates. Current WinRAR and 7-Zip (with the option on) were patched to propagate MotW on extraction too. [Medium] Less for MotW bypass, more as a password-protected ZIP to evade static scanning at the email gateway — still widely used. .7z, .rar, .tar, .gz Yes (built in since Win 11 23H2 ⭐) Not natively supported before — couldn't open without a separate archiver. [Big Win 11 change] Since Win 11 (23H2+), open-source libarchive is built into Explorer, so these extract natively without extra software. [High — new research target] Early libarchive integration had bugs that dropped MotW on certain formats (CVE-2024-21410 etc.); an ongoing patch target. .wim (Windows Imaging) Partial (openable with 7-Zip etc.) Usable for file packaging. A normal user can't mount it with a double-click; only viable where a third-party archiver is installed. [Low] Low usability, so only for limited targets.

docs.title: Delivery (perimeter bypass & payload delivery)
docs.text: Delivery is getting the finished package (container) past the target's layered perimeter (firewall, email gateway, web proxy, network sandbox) to the victim endpoint undetected.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Traditionally you host a malicious file on a web server and get the victim to click a download link — but then the packet's MIME type and the file's binary body are exposed to the web proxy/security appliance and blocked. HTML Smuggling combines HTML5 (the download attribute) with JavaScript (the Blob API) to assemble the file directly in the victim's browser memory, generating no binary-transfer traffic on the network.

[Traditional download vs. HTML Smuggling network traffic]

❌ Traditional download:
[Attacker web server] ─(HTTP: application/octet-stream + malicious binary)─> [proxy/firewall] 💥 blocked

✅ HTML Smuggling:
[Attacker web server] ─(HTTP: text/html + ordinary text/JS string)─> [proxy passes] ─> [victim browser]
                                                                                │
                                                        ┌───────────────────────┘
                                                        ▼
                                             [JS runs inside the browser]
                                             1. Decode Base64/encrypted string (atob / Web Crypto API)
                                             2. Convert to Uint8Array, build a Blob object
                                             3. Create a hidden <a> tag and auto-click to drop the file locally

Flow: ① encode the container (e.g. .iso/.zip) as Base64 and embed it as text in a JS variable in the HTML → ② the proxy sees only plain text (HTML/JS) and passes it → ③ in the browser, decode with atob(), convert to Uint8Array, and build a Blob → ④ create a local object URL with URL.createObjectURL() and auto-click a hidden <a> to drop the file into Downloads.

docs.title: [Advanced] Detection by modern appliances, and evasion
docs.text:
• Detection today: Modern email gateways and NGFWs flag HTML Smuggling statically when they see combinations of atob, Uint8Array, Blob, msSaveOrOpenBlob, createObjectURL, and they can decode Base64 strings themselves.
  • Evasion: ① Instead of plain Base64, encrypt the payload (e.g. AES-GCM) and decrypt at runtime in the browser with crypto.subtle.decrypt() — without the key the appliance can't tell what the file is. ② Obfuscate the key API strings, or split the payload into chunks pulled from external JSON / image metadata and reassembled, to evade static signatures.

docs.title: 5.2 SVG Smuggling
docs.text:
SVG is an XML-based text image format, and the standard allows a <script> tag with executable JavaScript directly inside the image.

<svg width="100" height="100" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" stroke="black" stroke-width="4" fill="none" />
  <script>
    // The moment the SVG opens in a browser, inner JS (e.g. HTML Smuggling logic) runs — PoC
    alert('Hello World');
  </script>
</svg>
  • Delivery/execution advantage: Many organisations block .html/.htm attachments, but .svg is classified as an image and often passes the filter. On Windows the default handler for .svg is Microsoft Edge, so a victim who double-clicks the "image" opens Edge and the hidden JavaScript runs.

docs.title: 5.3 Cobalt Strike Site Clone & Drive-By Download
docs.text:
Instead of standing up Apache/Nginx and planting smuggling code, this uses the Cobalt Strike C2 framework's built-in web server and Site Cloner to quickly build a phishing site and drive-by download.

Setup outline: ① Host File uploads the package to the team server's web server with a realistic-looking Local URI and a typosquatted domain → ② Clone Site clones a real site and sets Attack to the malicious file URL (cloning a login page can also log keystrokes) → ③ a size-0 invisible <IFRAME> is injected at the bottom of the cloned page so merely visiting triggers the download.

<IFRAME SRC="http://.../GPU-Z.2.22.0.exe?id=null" WIDTH="0" HEIGHT="0"></IFRAME>

docs.title: Recent patches and OPSEC (important ⭐)
docs.text:
Applying the course's Cobalt Strike lab as-is will mostly fail or be blocked immediately.

  1. The end of HTTP (port 80) and mixed-content blocking: Modern Chrome/Edge warn on plain-HTTP sites and silently block an HTTPS page's hidden HTTP <iframe> auto-downloading an executable as an 'insecure download' / 'drive-by'. A valid SSL/TLS cert (Let's Encrypt etc.) on HTTPS (443) is mandatory.
  2. Team-server fingerprinting and mandatory redirector: Cobalt Strike's built-in web server has distinctive HTTP response headers / default error pages, so Shodan/Censys or threat intel exposes the team server IP immediately. Never expose the team server directly — put an Apache/Nginx or Cloudflare Workers redirector in front to filter and forward only legitimate traffic and hide the infrastructure.

docs.title: Appendix. 2025~2026 current initial-access trends
docs.text: Beyond file-based phishing, the three techniques most actively used by current operators and real threat groups (APT, ransomware):

docs.title: 6.1 Device Code Phishing & AiTM (MFA-bypass phishing)
docs.text:
• Background: With cloud migration (Microsoft 365, Entra ID) and MFA adoption, stealing cloud session tokens has exploded as an initial-access path, over running malware.
  • AiTM (Adversary-in-the-Middle): A reverse-proxy phishing framework like Evilginx intercepts the session cookie (ESTSAUTH etc.) the moment the victim completes MFA on a fake login page, neutralising MFA.
  • Device Code Phishing: Abuses the OAuth 2.0 device-authorization flow used for smart-TV/IoT login. The attacker first requests a code, then tells the victim to "go to Microsoft's official auth page and enter this code." The victim enters it on Microsoft's genuine domain, bypassing proxies and phishing detection, and the attacker's tooling (TokenTactics etc.) receives the access and refresh tokens the moment auth completes.

docs.title: 6.2 Microsoft Teams (external tenant) phishing & ClickFix
docs.text:
• Teams phishing: With email gateways now so strong, attackers impersonate internal helpdesk via Teams (external-tenant chat is allowed by default) to message victims directly with malicious links/payloads.
  • ClickFix: A technique surging recently. A fake prompt ("to view this document you need to update / prove you're not a robot") instructs the victim to paste a clipboard-loaded, obfuscated PowerShell/Mshta command into Win + R and run it themselves. Because a command the user types into Run never goes through download (MotW) or email-attachment checks, it fully bypasses perimeter security.

docs.title: 6.3 Edge-device zero-days & abuse of remote RMM tools
docs.text:
• Edge-device exploits: Instead of phishing, attackers hit vulnerabilities in exposed enterprise VPN/firewall/file-transfer appliances (Ivanti, Fortinet, Palo Alto, Citrix) to plant web shells/backdoors on EDR-less Linux appliances and pivot inside.
  • Pushing legitimate RMM installs: Since custom C2 beacons risk EDR detection, initial access increasingly drops a fully legitimate, signed commercial RMM installer (AnyDesk, ScreenConnect, Atera, Action1) and has the victim run it, then takes the foothold over a legitimate remote-control channel.

docs.title: [Final summary] Blue Team / DFIR initial-access defence checklist
docs.text:
Defence layer Techniques addressed Actionable defence & detection 1. Network & browser HTML/SVG Smuggling, Drive-by, AiTM/Device Code phishing Block .svg, .iso, .img, .vhd, .lnk, .msc outright at the email gateway and web proxy. Enterprise browser policy (GPO/Intune) to block auto-downloads of executables on non-work sites. FIDO2 phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys / hardware keys) + conditional access (login only from registered devices). 2. OS & container ISO/VHD mount, LNK/BAT/MSC triggers, ClickFix (Win+R) GPO to disable auto-mount handlers for .iso/.vhd and centrally collect Microsoft-Windows-VHDMP-Operational (Event ID 1, 12). Monitor registry RunMRU for powershell/mshta/cmd/curl typed directly into Win+R (ClickFix). 3. Endpoint & process DLL Side-Loading, AppDomainManager, MSI/XLAM/RMM abuse Enable Defender ASR rules broadly (block Office child processes, restrict WMI/PsExec, etc.). Use WDAC or AppLocker to block unsigned binaries and unapproved RMM in user-writable paths (C:\ProgramData, %APPDATA%, %TEMP%). Hunt for signed binaries whose OriginalFilename differs from the process name, or that load unsigned DLLs from unusual paths (Sysmon ID 7).

This page is a personal reference re-organised from CRTO study notes, for Blue Team / DFIR learning (detection and defence).

docs.title: Persistence — Master Reference
docs.text:
About this page

Built on the Persistence chapter of CRTO (Certified Red Team Operator) study material, then expanded with per-version Windows 10 / 11 behaviour, why some legacy techniques are now dead, and the latest EDR/DFIR detection matrix. As with the rest of this handbook, the emphasis is on mechanics and detection artifacts — what the operator touches and what it leaves behind — rather than weaponization. Examples stay at the conceptual level (registry paths, flow diagrams), not working malware.

Structure (three parts)

  • Part 1 — Concept, OPSEC principles, and user-land persistence (Registry Run keys, Startup folder, Scheduled Tasks)
  • Part 2 — Advanced evasion persistence (COM Hijacking, WMI Event Subscription, Windows Services)
  • Part 3 — System hooking, modifying existing resources, and application-level persistence (LNK tampering, IFEO/SilentProcessExit, Winlogon, ServiceDll hijacking, Office/PowerShell/dev-tool persistence, RID hijacking)

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• 1. Overview & OPSEC principles
  • 2. User-Land persistence
  • 3. Advanced evasion persistence (Part 2)
  • 4. System hooking & modifying existing resources (Part 3)

docs.title: 1. What persistence is, and the operator's principles
1.1 What is persistence?
docs.text: Persistence (MITRE ATT&CK: TA0003) is the tactic of keeping the access to a target that was hard-won through initial access. It means planting a backdoor or auto-run trigger around the system so that the operator's C2 beacon comes back and recovers the connection even after the victim shuts down (reboot), logs off, or the running process crashes.

docs.title: 1.2 Three design principles for persistence
docs.text:
1. Privilege level matters: The techniques available differ completely depending on whether you currently hold standard-user (Medium Integrity) or local-admin (High Integrity) rights. Right after initial access you usually have standard-user rights, so user-land persistence comes first.
  2. Separate payload from trigger (OPSEC): Registering a blatant command like powershell.exe -enc ... or an unsigned malicious .exe directly in a persistence location (e.g. a registry Run key) gets caught in seconds by AV and by a Blue Team Autoruns review. The DLL side-loading and .NET AppDomainManager techniques from Initial Access should be combined with the persistence trigger so it looks like a legitimate program auto-starting.
  3. Resilience and cleanup: Running too often generates excessive network traffic and process-creation logs, which get detected. Using a too-common default path, on the other hand, makes removal easy.

docs.title: User-Land persistence
docs.text: When you don't have local-admin rights yet (before UAC), these are the core techniques to re-run a payload at reboot or re-logon within the current logged-in user's context.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Windows automatically runs programs registered under certain registry paths when a user logs in. A standard user can't modify the system-wide HKLM (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE), but can freely modify the current-user hive, HKCU (HKEY_CURRENT_USER).

  • Key registry paths:
    • HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run (runs every time the user logs in)
    • HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce (runs once at next login, then the value is auto-deleted)
    • (Admin required) HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run (runs for all users at login)
[Registry Run key flow]

[User logs into Windows]
       │
       ▼
[userinit.exe -> explorer.exe initialises]
       │
       ▼
[Reads HKCU\...\CurrentVersion\Run]
       │
       ▼
[Runs the registered value: e.g. C:\ProgramData\LegitApp\Updater.exe]
       │
       ▼
[DLL side-loading fires -> loads malicious DLL in the same folder -> C2 reconnects]

docs.title: Recent behaviour and constraints (Win 10 / Win 11)
docs.text:
1. Task Manager / startup-app notification: On Win 10/11, adding a new entry under HKCU\...\Run can raise a system-tray toast ("a new startup app was added"), and it shows up in the Task Manager → Startup apps tab.
  2. Real-time registry monitoring by EDR: Every commercial EDR and Microsoft Defender statically/dynamically scans the target file the instant a value is written to a CurrentVersion\Run key (Registry Value Set). Pointing a dropper or C2 beacon .exe directly here is a non-starter — it must point at a legitimately signed binary (a DLL side-loading host) or a benign routine that hides a script.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Similar to Run keys, Windows Explorer (explorer.exe) auto-runs every file or shortcut (.lnk) in certain special folders when it starts.

  • Key paths:
    • Current user only (standard-user writable): %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup (full path: C:\Users\<Username>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup)
    • All users (admin required): C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp
  • Operation: Rather than dropping an .exe directly in this folder, the usual approach is to hide the real payload (e.g. a DLL side-loading package) deep inside %LocalAppData% or C:\ProgramData, and place only a shortcut (.lnk) pointing to it in the Startup folder.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text: • Highly exposed: The Startup folder is the first path Blue Teams and AV check. A Sysmon Event ID 11 (FileCreate) for a file whose path contains \Start Menu\Programs\Startup\ is a default alert in almost every SOC.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
The Windows Task Scheduler runs programs at a certain time or on a certain system event. Many assume admin rights are required, but a standard user can create a scheduled task that runs under their own rights.

  • Trigger constraints by privilege:
Trigger type Privilege needed Notes / usefulness Specific time / periodic (daily, weekly, every X hours) Standard user The safest to use. E.g. run at 9:30 AM (arrival time) or hourly so the beacon revives if it dies. On idle Standard user Runs while the user is away from the keyboard — hard to notice. At logon Admin recommended (standard user possible in limited cases) A full user-logon trigger generally requires High Integrity. At startup Admin (High Integrity / SYSTEM) Runs as SYSTEM during boot, before user login.
  • How it works: Tasks are registered via schtasks.exe, PowerShell's New-ScheduledTask cmdlet, or the Task Scheduler COM object (Schedule.Service). Once created, the task definition is stored as an XML file under C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\, with cache info in the registry at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache\.

docs.title: Detection and OPSEC
docs.text:
1. Avoiding schtasks.exe process-creation detection: Running schtasks.exe /create ... from the command line records the full command line in the process-creation log (Event ID 4688, Sysmon ID 1), exposing it to EDR immediately. Modern tooling (e.g. Cobalt Strike BOFs) therefore calls the COM API (ITaskService) or RPC (ATSvc / ITaskSchedulerService) in memory to register a task quietly, without spawning a process.
  2. Windows Security log (Event ID 4698): Even if the schtasks.exe execution is hidden via COM/RPC, the Task Scheduler service itself records Security log Event ID 4698 (a scheduled task was created) and Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational Event ID 106 when a new task registers. So instead of an odd name like Updater or Maintenance, the key is masquerading — matching the names and folder structure of existing legitimate Microsoft or Chrome/Edge update tasks.

docs.title: [Part 1 summary] User-Land persistence comparison
docs.text: Technique Privilege Trigger Main artifacts Stealth Registry Run Keys (HKCU\...\Run) Standard user At user login (when explorer.exe starts) Registry value change (Sysmon ID 13); exposed in Task Manager "Startup" tab ★★☆☆☆ (very common and well known; must combine with DLL side-loading) Startup Folder (...\Programs\Startup) Standard user At user login .lnk or file creation in the folder (Sysmon ID 11) ★☆☆☆☆ (directly exposed on the filesystem; very high detection rate) Scheduled Tasks Standard user or admin Time/periodic, idle, logon, startup, etc. XML under C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\; Security Event ID 4698 / TaskScheduler ID 106 ★★★☆☆ (very useful when created via COM/BOF and masqueraded as a legitimate task)

docs.title: Advanced evasion persistence
docs.text: User-land registration under Run keys or the Startup folder is easily exposed to a Blue Team scan (e.g. Autoruns). To evade static checks by AV/EDR, operators hijack the OS's own legitimate internal components or management features.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Windows COM (Component Object Model) is the core architecture that lets software components talk to each other and share functionality. Many legitimate applications and system services call objects with a specific COM class ID (CLSID) when they run.

  • CLSID resolution order: When Windows requests a COM object by CLSID, it consults the current user's registry path HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID before the system-wide HKCR (HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT) or HKLM.
  • Hijacking structure: If a legitimate program frequently calls a unique CLSID at boot or on a specific event, the operator manually creates HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID\{target-CLSID}\InprocServer32 (or LocalServer32) and sets its value to the path of a malicious payload (or a side-loading DLL) instead of the legitimate DLL.
[When a legitimate program runs]
       │
       ▼
[Calls a specific CLSID object] ──> [Searches HKCU (user registry) first] ──> [Finds the attacker's malicious DLL path]
                                                                                       │
                                                                                       ▼
                                                         [Malicious DLL force-loaded inside the legitimate program]
  • Choosing a target: A good target is a COM object that a background app auto-started at login (e.g. a OneDrive settings utility, a taskbar notification program) tries and fails to load (NAME NOT FOUND) right after boot — the beacon revives naturally without crashing the system.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text: • EDR mechanism: Modern EDR monitors and blocks, in real time, the creation of new keys under HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID or modification of a child InprocServer32 value to point at an abnormal path (.exe, .dll) or a script handler.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) is a powerful built-in framework for querying and controlling management information. Its event subscription feature lets you auto-run a specified payload (Consumer) when a condition (Event) is met — "at a certain time" or "when a certain process runs."

  • Three core components of WMI persistence:
    1. __EventFilter (condition): Defines which system event to react to (e.g. 180 minutes after boot, or when a certain admin tool runs).
    2. __EventConsumer (action): Defines what to do when the condition is met. Usually a CommandLineEventConsumer to quietly invoke a specified command or script.
    3. __FilterToConsumerBinding: Binds the filter and the consumer together.
  • Fileless storage: WMI objects don't exist as .exe files on disk; they live inside the WMI repository database (C:\Windows\System32\wbem\Repository\OBJECTS.DATA). File-scan-based AV doesn't easily find them.

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
• Local admin required: Creating or modifying a WMI event subscription needs local-admin (High Integrity) or SYSTEM rights by default. (It can't be created with the standard-user rights you have right after initial access.)
  • DFIR strategy: Enumerate all registered filters and consumers with PowerShell (Get-CimInstance -Namespace root\subscription -ClassName __EventConsumer), or detect creation of a script-bearing WMI consumer via Sysmon Event ID 19, 20, 21 (WMI monitoring).

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
Using a Windows service that runs continuously in the background is a traditional and reliable system-persistence technique.

  • Privilege and operation: Registering a new service requires local-admin or SYSTEM rights. Once registered, it's started by Scm.exe (Service Control Manager) at boot (Automatic start type), regardless of whether a user logs in.
  • OPSEC: Name and describe the new service like a legitimate Microsoft one (e.g. Windows Update Medic Service), and point its binary path (BinPath) at a disguised path and a DLL side-loading host.

docs.title: [Part 2 summary] Advanced evasion persistence comparison
docs.text: Technique Privilege Storage (artifacts) AV/EDR detection difficulty Notes / limits COM Hijacking Standard user or admin HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID\ Moderate–High Loads via a legitimate program even with no malicious file on disk. Requires analysis to choose a target CLSID. WMI Event Subscription Local admin required (High / SYSTEM) WMI repository (OBJECTS.DATA) High (fileless) Hidden inside the DB rather than as a file, evading static scans. But admin rights are a prerequisite. Windows Services Local admin required (High / SYSTEM) Registry HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\ Low–Medium Always runs at boot, but easily exposed in Autoruns or service tools, so masquerading is essential.

docs.title: System hooking, modifying existing resources & app-level persistence
docs.text: Creating a new file or registry key is easily caught by security event logs and EDR. A skilled operator instead quietly modifies settings, shortcuts, services, or business apps that already exist on the system.

docs.title: 4.1 Tampering with existing shortcuts (.lnk) and StartIn directory hijacking
Why modifying beats creating
docs.text:
Creating a new .lnk in the Startup folder runs once at boot but is immediately caught by Blue Team monitoring (Sysmon Event ID 11). Modifying a browser (Chrome, Edge) or messenger (Teams, Slack) shortcut already pinned to the desktop or taskbar — which the victim clicks voluntarily every day — avoids the boot-time auto-run scan entirely.

  • Key target paths (standard-user writable):
    • Desktop: %USERPROFILE%\Desktop\
    • Taskbar pinned icons: %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Internet Explorer\Quick Launch\User Pinned\TaskBar\
[Two approaches to tampering with an existing .LNK, and the OPSEC difference]

Approach A: Directly altering the TargetPath (old approach — high detection risk ⚠️)
  • Before: "C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe"
  • After:  "C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe /c start payload.exe && start chrome.exe"
  ▶ Problem: creates an explorer.exe -> cmd.exe process tree, a flashing black window, and EDR command-line detection.

Approach B: Altering the working directory (StartIn) + DLL side-loading (modern OPSEC ⭐)
  • TargetPath: "C:\...\App.exe" (kept as the original! no command-line change!)
  • StartIn   : "C:\Users\Victim\AppData\Local\CustomFolder\" (a folder hiding the attacker's DLL)
  ▶ How it works: when the victim clicks the icon, the legitimate App.exe runs and looks for its DLL
    first in CustomFolder (the current working directory), loading it from there.

docs.title: Recent behaviour and constraints
docs.text:
1. DLL search order and SafeDllSearchMode: Since Windows XP SP2, all modern Win 10/11 have SafeDllSearchMode on by default. In this mode the current working directory (StartIn) is searched after the system folder (System32) — it's 5th in the order. So the StartIn trick only works if the target program tries to load a uniquely named DLL that does not exist in System32 (NAME NOT FOUND).
  2. Direct side-loading of %LocalAppData%-based apps (Teams, OneDrive, Slack, Discord): Many enterprise apps now install to user-writable paths like %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\OneDrive or %LOCALAPPDATA%\Discord so they can update without admin rights. Here you don't even need to touch the .lnk — just drop a proxied malicious DLL inside the real install folder, and it loads from the 1st search path (the application folder) every time the user opens the app.

docs.title: Core idea
docs.text:
IFEO is a Windows kernel/loader feature originally built so developers could tune an app's heap settings or attach a debugger at launch. (Local admin required.)

  1. Basic Debugger hooking: Create a string value Debugger under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\notepad.exe and set it to a payload path; when the user runs Notepad (notepad.exe), the kernel intercepts and runs the payload instead. (Notepad itself won't open, so the victim may notice — the payload has to re-launch Notepad.)
  2. Advanced SilentProcessExit: A stealthier technique that runs the payload in the background via the Windows Error Reporting system (werfault.exe) not when the program starts, but when the user finishes and closes it (on exit).
[SilentProcessExit architecture and required registry settings]

[Setup: two registry keys (admin rights)]
  ① HKLM\...\Image File Execution Options\notepad.exe
     └─ GlobalFlag (DWORD) = 0x00000200 (enables the FLG_MONITOR_SILENT_PROCESS_EXIT bitmask)
  ② HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit\notepad.exe
     ├─ ReportingMode (DWORD) = 1 (enables LAUNCH_MONITORPROCESS)
     └─ MonitorProcess (REG_SZ) = "C:\ProgramData\LegitUpdater\updater.exe"

[Trigger flow]
[Victim opens Notepad (notepad.exe) and works normally]
       │
       ▼
[Victim closes the Notepad window (ExitProcess / NtTerminateProcess)]
       │
       ▼
[Kernel checks GlobalFlag (0x200) and signals WerSvc (Windows Error Reporting service)]
       │
       ▼
[werfault.exe runs] ──> [reads the SilentProcessExit registry] ──> [quietly runs the payload in MonitorProcess]

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
• Abnormal process lineage: When SilentProcessExit fires, the parent is recorded as svchost.exe (WerSvc) or werfault.exe with the attacker's binary as a child. Modern EDR (CrowdStrike, MDE) treats the error-reporting utility werfault.exe spawning a non-standard-path executable or shell as an immediate IoC.
  • DFIR rule: Monitor Debugger/GlobalFlag changes under Image File Execution Options and SilentProcessExit key creation via Sysmon Event ID 12, 13.

docs.title: 4.3 Winlogon Helper and the death of legacy techniques (AppInit_DLLs)
Winlogon Helper (Shell, Userinit, Notify)
docs.text:
The registry (HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon) that winlogon.exe references to initialise the session at login. (Local admin required.)

  • Userinit: Append an executable path after the default C:\Windows\system32\userinit.exe, (comma-separated) to run it in sequence at logon.
  • Shell: Specify a program to run alongside the default explorer.exe.
  • Notify (dead — version note ❌): The famous old technique of registering a DLL under Winlogon\Notify to intercept logon events worked on Windows XP/Server 2003, but since Windows Vista/7 and on all current Win 10/11 the architecture changed and the Notify key was removed entirely — it never works.

docs.title: [Essential update] Why AppInit_DLLs no longer works on current Win 10/11
docs.text:
AppInit_DLLs, introduced as a persistence technique in many older security texts, was a powerful feature: write a DLL path to the registry (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\AppInit_DLLs) and that DLL is force-injected into nearly every process that loads user32.dll.

Why it fails today (tied to UEFI Secure Boot): To stop indiscriminate DLL injection, from Windows 8 and Win 10/11 Microsoft patched it so that if UEFI Secure Boot is enabled, the OS kernel unconditionally ignores and disables AppInit_DLLs even when LoadAppInit_DLLs is set to 1. Since Windows 11 requires UEFI Secure Boot as a minimum install requirement, the AppInit_DLLs technique is effectively dead in a modern enterprise environment.

docs.title: 4.4 Modifying existing Windows services and svchost.exe ServiceDll hijacking
docs.text: Part 2 covered creating a new service. But creating one leaves a System Event ID 7045 log and is easily caught, so an operator with local-admin rights prefers to modify an existing service.

docs.title: Mechanism 1: Altering the ImagePath of an inactive default service
docs.text: Find a service that ships with Windows but is normally stopped (Disabled/Manual) — e.g. Fax, Spooler, or an old third-party service — switch its start type to Auto, and replace its registry ImagePath with the attacker's service binary. This avoids the new-service-creation log (ID 7045).

docs.title: Mechanism 2: ServiceDll hijacking of svchost.exe-based services (advanced stealth ⭐)
docs.text:
Many default Windows services exist as .dlls hosted inside the system process svchost.exe -k <group> rather than as individual .exes.

  • Registry structure:
    • HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<service>\ImagePath → %SystemRoot%\System32\svchost.exe -k netsvcs
    • HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<service>\Parameters\ServiceDll → this defines the actual DLL to load
  • Stealth effect: If the attacker builds a malicious DLL implementing the service entry (ServiceMain) and swaps an existing service's Parameters\ServiceDll for it, no suspicious separate .exe process appears in Task Manager or the process list — it runs hidden as a thread inside the legitimate system process svchost.exe.
  • Win 10/11 mitigation (signature): Microsoft has started applying a "Microsoft Signed Only" mitigation to major system svchost.exe processes. Putting an unsigned ServiceDll into a core security group's svchost can be blocked (Event ID 7023 and CodeIntegrity logs), so targeting must shift to ordinary service groups or third-party services without the signing policy.

docs.title: 4.5 Application and modern dev-environment persistence (2025~2026 trends)
docs.text: Techniques that, without admin rights, tamper with the config files of business/dev apps that security tools rarely watch.

docs.title: ① Microsoft Office persistence (Word, Excel, COM Add-ins)
docs.text: Technique Target path / registry (standard user) Mechanism and constraints Excel XLSTART %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Excel\XLSTART\ Auto-loads .xlam, .xll in the folder when Excel starts. Word STARTUP %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Word\STARTUP\ Auto-loads a global template (.dotm) or Word add-in (.wll — essentially a DLL) in the folder without warning when Word starts. Office COM Add-in registry HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Office\<ver>\<app>\Addins\<CLSID> Set LoadBehavior to 3 (auto-load at startup) to attach a COM DLL. (Note: if an add-in takes ~1s+ to load, Office flags it as a "slow add-in", notifies the user, and moves it to Resiliency\DisabledItems — so the payload must return immediately on an async thread.)

docs.title: ② PowerShell profile ($PROFILE) injection
docs.text:
An init script that runs automatically whenever an admin or developer launches PowerShell. The file doesn't exist by default, but creating it at the path makes it work immediately.

Profile Variable Filesystem path Privilege Current user / current host $PROFILE.CurrentUserCurrentHost %USERPROFILE%\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1 (PowerShell 7+: \Documents\PowerShell\...) Standard user Current user / all hosts $PROFILE.CurrentUserAllHosts %USERPROFILE%\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\profile.ps1 Standard user All users / all hosts $PROFILE.AllUsersAllHosts $PSHOME\profile.ps1 (C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\profile.ps1) Admin
  • Constraint: In an enterprise where PowerShell is forced into Constrained Language Mode (CLM) via WDAC/AppLocker, or the ExecutionPolicy is pinned to AllSigned by GPO, profile-script execution is blocked.

docs.title: ③ Modern dev tools: Windows Terminal & VS Code (current trend ⭐)
docs.text:
A popular user-land technique when targeting IT/cloud-engineer/developer machines.

  • Windows Terminal (settings.json): The settings file of Windows 11's default terminal (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\Microsoft.WindowsTerminal_...\LocalState\settings.json) is standard-user writable. Appending a background-payload argument to a profile's "commandline": "powershell.exe" runs it each time the user opens the terminal.
  • Visual Studio Code (tasks.json & extensions): Putting "runOptions": { "runOn": "folderOpen" } with a shell command in a project's .vscode\tasks.json auto-runs a background task the moment the developer opens that folder in VS Code. (Recent VS Code patches prompt for "allow automatic tasks" on first open, but it works smoothly in an already-trusted workspace.)

docs.title: 4.6 Account manipulation (RID Hijacking) and SDDL backdoors
RID Hijacking
docs.text:
Running net user hacker /add and net localgroup administrators hacker /add from the command line raises Windows Security Event ID 4720 and 4732 and is caught by the SOC 100% of the time. To avoid this, the attacker (SYSTEM rights needed) overwrites the byte that defines the RID inside the binary F value of the registry HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\Users\000001F5 (1F5 = decimal 501, i.e. the built-in Guest account) — changing F5 01 to F4 01 (decimal 500 = built-in Administrator).

  • Effect: net user guest or Control Panel still shows a plain, unprivileged Guest account, but when you actually log in with it, the kernel recognises the RID as 500 and grants a full local Administrator token.

docs.title: Service and registry SDDL (security descriptor) backdoor
docs.text: When admin rights are held briefly, instead of planting a malicious file now, modify the ACL/SDDL of a specific system service (e.g. the Remote Registry service) or registry key to grant "Full Control" to a standard-user account too. Even if the admin password changes later and access is lost, logging in as the standard user and manipulating the now-open service acts as a "privilege backdoor" to recover SYSTEM at any time.

docs.title: [Final summary] Blue Team / DFIR persistence hunting checklist
docs.text:
Layer Techniques addressed Actionable detection Registry & startup Run/RunOnce keys, Startup folder, COM hijacking, Office add-ins, IFEO Monitor writes to CurrentVersion\Run, HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID\...\InprocServer32, Image File Execution Options (Debugger/GlobalFlag), SilentProcessExit (Sysmon ID 12/13). Alert on file creation in Startup / XLSTART / Word\STARTUP (Sysmon ID 11). Scheduled tasks & WMI Scheduled Tasks, WMI event subscription Security Event ID 4698 + TaskScheduler ID 106 for task creation. Sysmon ID 19/20/21 for WMI subscriptions; periodically enumerate root\subscription consumers. Services & accounts New/modified services, ServiceDll hijacking, RID hijacking, SDDL backdoor System Event ID 7045 (new service) / 7023 + CodeIntegrity (blocked unsigned ServiceDll). Watch Services\...\Parameters\ServiceDll changes. Audit SAM F-value edits and service/registry ACL (SDDL) changes. Dev-tool / user-land LNK tampering, PowerShell profile, Windows Terminal, VS Code Baseline and monitor .lnk StartIn/working-directory changes, $PROFILE script creation, settings.json/.vscode\tasks.json edits on engineer workstations.

This page is a personal reference re-organised from CRTO study notes, for Blue Team / DFIR learning (detection and defence).

docs.title: Post-Exploitation
docs.text:
Learn to connect what a command returns with what happens inside the operating system. This collection covers Beacon architecture, situational awareness, session and file management, collection, and execution models.

The 19 sections are organized into five learning pages, with command explanations, comparison tables and execution diagrams.

Scope and provenance

Independently written explanations based on the supplied “7 - Post-Exploitation” chapter. Original course files and screenshots are not redistributed. Examples assume an authorized lab. This site does not execute the commands. Product behavior depends on version and configuration; official supplements were reviewed on 2026-10-27.

docs.text:
Order Page Original sections 1 3.1 Architecture and command behavior 1–3 2 3.2 Sessions and file systems 4–6 3 3.3 Processes and collection 7–11 4 3.4 Execution and external tools 12–17 5 3.5 Modern defense and review 18–19

docs.title: Four questions
docs.text: Question Inspect Example Where does it run? Beacon, temporary process, existing process BOF vs fork & run Whose authority? User, token, integrity, session spawn vs spawnas What changes? Files, processes, clipboard, network printscreen affects clipboard Where do results go? Console, result tab, server, Client download vs Sync Files

docs.title: Common confusions
docs.text:
Assumption Correction Memory-only means no evidence Disk, memory, process and network visibility are separate Administrator account always has elevated rights Inspect the current token and UAC state Another Beacon means more privilege Session creation and elevation are different PID and JID are interchangeable Process identity and Beacon job identity differ A download is immediately local Team Server receives it before Client synchronization PowerShell requires powershell.exe Another process can host the engine

Start with Architecture and command behavior, or return to Red Team.

docs.title: 3.4 Execution and external tools
docs.text: Post-Exploitation index · Reviewed 2026-10-27

docs.title: 12. shell versus run
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S["shell whoami /user"] --> C["cmd.exe /c"]
    C --> W["whoami.exe"]
    R["run whoami /user"] --> W
    W --> O["Account name and SID"]
    D["shell dir"] --> I["cmd.exe built-in dir"]
shell whoami /user
run whoami /user
shell dir

Both whoami examples return the account and SID, but shell passes through cmd.exe /c while run executes the program directly. SID is Windows' security identifier, distinct from the display name.

Property shell run Uses cmd.exe Yes No Standalone executable Supported Supported cmd built-in such as dir Supported Not directly Shell syntax Interpreted by cmd Not automatically interpreted

The source suggests ls instead of dir and getuid for identity checks. Learn the behavioral difference rather than assuming that one command is invisible.

docs.title: 13. External tools
docs.text:
Tool Purpose described in the chapter Seatbelt Local system and security configuration reconnaissance PowerView Active Directory reconnaissance Certipy / Certify AD CS security assessment Rubeus Kerberos assessment Impacket Windows network protocol testing

Determine whether a tool is PowerShell, a .NET Framework assembly, native code or Python, and whether it runs on-host or over the network. These tools are not interchangeable execute-assembly inputs. Network-side operation is deferred to the source's Pivoting chapter.

docs.title: 14. Three PowerShell execution paths
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    P["PowerShell command"] --> E["powershell"]
    P --> K["powerpick"]
    P --> I["psinject"]
    E --> EX["powershell.exe"]
    K --> T["Temporary process"]
    I --> X["Existing process"]
    EX --> N["PowerShell engine"]
    T --> N
    X --> N
    N --> O["Command output"]
    N -.-> L["Logging / AMSI depend on version and configuration"]
Command Host in the source model powershell powershell.exe powerpick Engine hosted in a temporary process psinject Engine hosted in a selected existing process 
powershell [commandlet] [arguments]
powershell $env:computername
powerpick [commandlet] [arguments]
psinject [pid] [arch] [commandlet] [arguments]
psinject 3020 x64 $PID

The computername environment variable returns the host name. The source describes powershell execution with -nop, -exec bypass and -EncodedCommand: skip profiles, set execution-policy behavior, and pass encoded text. Base64 is encoding, not encryption; execution-policy Bypass is neither elevation nor disabling endpoint security. Execution policies

Powerpick uses unmanaged hosting of the PowerShell engine and a fork-and-run DLL, retrieving output over a named pipe. “Unmanaged” does not mean the engine disappeared. PsInject uses the same idea in an existing process. $PID reports the host process: 3020 proves execution location, not privilege escalation.

The source help also lists optional PATCHES arguments for powerpick and execute-assembly. These describe advanced in-memory function modifications; the chapter supplies no concrete patch rules, and they are not required to understand basic execution.

docs.title: 15. Importing PowerShell scripts
docs.text:
powershell-import [/path/to/local/script.ps1]
powershell-import C:\Tools\PowerSploit\Recon\PowerView.ps1
powerpick Get-Domain

The script path is on the operator Client, not a requirement for the same file to exist on the lab host. The source describes loading imported content into later powershell, powerpick and psinject executions using an internal web server. One imported script is retained at a time; this is not a persistent interactive PowerShell session.

Get-Domain is supplied by PowerView in this example, not built into PowerShell.

Output Meaning Forest Containing forest DomainControllers Domain controllers Children / Parent Domain hierarchy DomainMode / DomainModeLevel Functional-level representation PdcRoleOwner PDC Emulator RidRoleOwner RID Master InfrastructureRoleOwner Infrastructure Master Name Domain name

Unknown DomainMode may reflect an older library not recognizing a level, rather than a broken domain.

docs.title: 16. .NET assemblies
docs.text:
execute-assembly [/path/to/file.exe] [arguments]
execute-assembly C:\Tools\Seatbelt\Seatbelt\bin\Release\Seatbelt.exe AntiVirus

The source describes a temporary process hosting the CLR and loading a .NET assembly from memory. CLR means Common Language Runtime, correcting the source's “Command Language Runtime.”

This mechanism is described for .NET Framework assemblies, not arbitrary modern .NET/.NET Core applications or native EXEs. The filename extension alone does not prove compatibility.

Seatbelt's AntiVirus argument requests the relevant inventory. Engine, ProductEXE and ReportingEXE are product registration/reporting information; they do not prove every protection component is active. The data-store help reference concerns reuse of already loaded content, rather than necessarily rereading the same file every time.

docs.title: 17. BOFs and Aggressor Script
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Command alias: ipconfig"] --> S["Aggressor Script"]
    S --> O["Read architecture-compatible BOF"]
    O --> B["Beacon loader"]
    B --> G["Entry point: go"]
    G --> W["Windows API calls"]
    W --> R["Results"]
inline-execute [/path/to/file.o] [args]
ipconfig

In the chapter, ipconfig is a command alias supplied by TrustedSec's Situational Awareness BOF tooling. It is distinct from shell ipconfig, which runs the Windows executable through cmd.

beacon_inline_execute(
    $1,
    readbof($1, "ipconfig", $null, "T1016"),
    "go",
    $null
);
Part Meaning in this context beacon_inline_execute Execute the BOF $1 Target Beacon identifier readbof The tooling's BOF-reading helper ipconfig BOF selection go Entry function Final $null No additional argument buffer T1016 Network configuration discovery identifier

An alias can wrap a BOF, so a familiar command name does not prove the implementation. Review loaded scripts and version-specific help.
