docs.title: Lesson 1.7 — Selecting Only the Packets You Need with BPF
Lesson 1.7 — Selecting Only the Packets You Need with BPF
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

The 'host ... and port 80' at the end of the tcpdump command in lesson 1.6 is a BPF filter. This lesson covers that filter language from the ground up.

  • What BPF is, and why it's the means of filtering "earliest and cheapest"
  • Protocol, address and port primitives, and the src and dst direction qualifiers
  • and, or, not and parentheses, and the commonly mistaken operator precedence
  • vlan, portrange, gateway, and byte- and bit-level conditions
  • What filters silently miss with IPv6, VLANs and fragmented packets
  • Reducing a large pcap with BPF, and testing and recording filters

Lab material and notation

(Actual output) in this lesson was produced with tcpdump 4.99.4 (libpcap 1.10.4) in this work environment. IPv6 is disabled in this environment, so IPv6 traffic couldn't be generated for real; instead the filter practice pcap (lab.pcap, 13 packets) was assembled by hand in Python. Only private and documentation ranges are used (10.10.0.0/16, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24, 2001:db8::/32). Each packet's makeup is in the table in section 2.

docs.title: 1. One PC's traffic on a 1 Gbps link
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) Right after lesson 1.4's incident, it's decided to watch whether suspicious traffic recurs from research-segment PC 10.10.6.14. The tapped link carries an average of several hundred Mbps. Storing it all piles up several TB a day, but all that's needed is that one PC's traffic.

"Store everything and filter later" isn't the answer. The disk runs short, and if the capture machine's CPU and storage can't keep up, as in lesson 1.6, you may miss even the packets you need. You must take only what you need from the start. That's the job of BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter).

BPF decides "is this packet of interest?" at a very low level, as packets enter the OS kernel. Uninteresting packets are never even passed up to the user program (tcpdump, etc.), so every later step, whether on screen, to disk or handed to another tool, gets lighter. And almost every libpcap-based tool uses BPF, so once learned it applies everywhere: tcpdump, tshark's capture filters, Zeek, Arkime and more.

docs.title: 2. An analogy: the airport's first X-ray
docs.text:
Picture bags going through the X-ray machine at airport security. The screener judges each bag quickly against very simple rules ("pull out anything with liquids"). Only bags that pass on go to detailed inspection.

BPF is exactly this first X-ray: simple rules, but very fast, applied to every packet. But the analogy hides one of BPF's most important properties. The screener judges each bag on its own, without remembering "that passenger's other bag". BPF is the same: after judging one packet it forgets everything it saw and judges the next packet from scratch. So BPF can't express connection-level conditions such as "the rest of the packets of connections that started with a SYN", and this property also explains why src host, which we'll see later, catches only one side of a conversation.

The 13 practice packets in this lesson look like this:

# Content Notes 1–4 10.10.6.14 ↔ 203.0.113.50 port 80 HTTP: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, GET IPv4 5 10.10.6.14 → 10.10.4.53 UDP 53 DNS query IPv4 6 10.10.6.14 → 10.10.4.53 TCP 53 SYN DNS over TCP 7 10.10.6.14 → 198.51.100.7 ICMP echo ping 8 2001:db8:6::14 → 2001:db8:ff::50 TCP 80 SYN IPv6 9 2001:db8:6::14 → 2001:db8:4::53 UDP 53 IPv6 10 10.10.6.14 → 203.0.113.60 TCP 443 SYN IPv4 11 10.10.6.14 → 224.0.0.251 UDP 5353 Multicast 12 10.10.6.14 → 203.0.113.50 TCP 80 SYN 802.1Q VLAN 20 tag 13 203.0.113.60 → 10.10.6.14 TCP 443 RST+ACK Reply from a closed port

docs.title: 3. How it works: BPF is a tiny program
docs.text:
The filter text we write is for people; the kernel turns it into a very small machine-code program and runs it on every packet. tcpdump -d shows that program (actual output):

$ tcpdump -d -y EN10MB 'udp port 53'
(000) ldh      [12]
(001) jeq      #0x86dd          jt 2    jf 8
(002) ldb      [20]
(003) jeq      #0x11            jt 4    jf 19
(004) ldh      [54]
(005) jeq      #0x35            jt 18   jf 6
(006) ldh      [56]
(007) jeq      #0x35            jt 18   jf 19
(008) jeq      #0x800           jt 9    jf 19
(009) ldb      [23]
(010) jeq      #0x11            jt 11   jf 19
(011) ldh      [20]
(012) jset     #0x1fff          jt 19   jf 13
(013) ldxb     4*([14]&0xf)
(014) ldh      [x + 14]
(015) jeq      #0x35            jt 18   jf 16
(016) ldh      [x + 16]
(017) jeq      #0x35            jt 18   jf 19
(018) ret      #262144
(019) ret      #0

-d means "don't apply the filter, show the compiled result", and -y EN10MB means "assume an Ethernet link". It looks like code at first, but reading a few lines reveals the principle.

  • ldh [12]: load 2 bytes from byte 12 of the packet (load half-word). In the Ethernet header, that's the EtherType field.
  • jeq #0x86dd jt 2 jf 8: if that value is 0x86dd (IPv6), go to line 2, otherwise line 8 (jump if equal; jt if true, jf if false).
  • The IPv6 side (lines 2–7): ldb [20] is the IPv6 header's "next header" field, 0x11 (17) is UDP, [54] and [56] are the UDP source and destination ports, and 0x35 is 53.
  • The IPv4 side (lines 8–17): 0x800 means IPv4, [23] is IPv4's protocol field, jset #0x1fff is the line that rejects the packet if the fragment offset is non-zero, and ldxb 4*([14]&0xf) computes the IPv4 header length to skip over it.
  • ret #262144: accept (pass up to 262,144 bytes). ret #0: reject.

This short program already shows two important facts. First, udp port 53 checks both IPv4 and IPv6. Second, because of line 12, IPv4 fragments other than the first never match a port condition. When a large UDP packet is split into several fragments, the second fragment onwards has no UDP header, so the port can't be known. Section 7 comes back to this.

docs.title: 4. Primitives: the basic units of a filter
docs.text: BPF expressions are built from small conditions called primitives. For each packet, each primitive is judged true or false.

docs.title: 4.1 Protocols
docs.text:
The simplest are protocol names: ip, ip6, tcp, udp, icmp and others. If the packet is that protocol it's "of interest" and evaluation continues; if not, libpcap stops processing that packet and waits for the next. The packet itself carries on its way; BPF isn't a blocking device, it selects copies.

Results against the practice file (actual output):

Filter Packets matched Interpretation (no filter) 13 Everything ip 10 IPv4 only. The two IPv6 packets (8, 9) and the VLAN-tagged packet (12) are excluded ip6 2 IPv6 only (8, 9) ip or ip6 12 Both IPv4 and IPv6. The VLAN-tagged packet (12) is still excluded tcp 8 Both IPv4 TCP and IPv6 TCP (8). The VLAN-tagged packet is excluded udp 3 5, 9, 11 icmp 1 7

Here's the first trap. ip means IPv4 only. If you wanted "all IP traffic", write ip or ip6. With IPv6 increasingly common, writing just ip and missing all IPv6 traffic happens more often than you'd think. The second trap (VLANs) is in section 6.1.

docs.title: 4.2 Addresses and ports
docs.text:
Primitive Meaning Example ether host Packets where the layer 2 MAC address is the source or destination ether host 00:50:56:0a:04:53 host Packets where the layer 3 IP address is the source or destination host 10.10.4.53 net Packets where an IP address is in that network range (CIDR) net 203.0.113.0/24 port Packets where the layer 4 port is the source or destination (TCP and UDP alike) port 53

The results (actual output):

Filter Matched Interpretation host 10.10.4.53 2 5, 6 (the DNS server's IPv4 address) net 203.0.113.0/24 6 1–4, 10, 13. The VLAN-tagged packet (12) is excluded ether host 00:50:56:0a:04:53 3 5, 6, 9 sent to the DNS server's MAC (including IPv6) port 53 3 UDP 5, TCP 6, IPv6 UDP 9 udp port 53 2 5, 9 tcp port 53 1 6

port ignores protocol. port 53 catches both UDP 53 and TCP 53. DNS is usually UDP, but uses TCP for large responses or zone transfers. To see all DNS, port 53 is right; for UDP only, put the protocol in front, as in udp port 53.

Note also that the IPv6 packet (9) appears in the ether host result. A MAC address is layer 2, so it doesn't matter whether IPv4 or IPv6 sits above it. You can use it to catch the same device's IPv4 and IPv6 traffic together. But MAC addresses only mean something within one segment. They change across a router, so depending on the tap position (lesson 1.1 section 10), what you see may be "the router's MAC" rather than "that device's MAC".

docs.title: 4.3 Direction: src and dst
docs.text:
All the primitives above ignore direction. host 10.10.4.53 matches whether that address is source or destination. To set a direction, put a direction qualifier, src (source) or dst (destination), in front (actual output):

Filter Matched Interpretation src host 10.10.6.14 8 Only IPv4 packets that PC sent dst host 10.10.6.14 2 Only IPv4 packets that PC received (2, 13)

To see both sides of the conversations that PC is part of, just use host 10.10.6.14. Remember section 2's analogy: BPF judges each packet separately, so src host looks only at that packet's source field and has no idea a reply to it comes separately.

Oddly, only MAC addresses use different syntax. For IP the qualifier comes before, as in src host, src net, src port, but for MAC it comes after ether and host is dropped, as in ether src and ether dst. Both directions is ether host. Annoying to memorise, but getting it wrong is a syntax error, so you'll soon get used to it.

docs.title: 5. Combining with logic
docs.text:
Primitives are simple, but combining them with and (or &&), or (||) and not (!) builds elaborate conditions, and parentheses set the order.

'tcp and (port 80 or port 443 or port 8080) and (not dst host 203.0.113.1)'

That means "TCP packets on one of ports 80, 443 or 8080, whose destination isn't 203.0.113.1". As lesson 1.6 said, parentheses and spaces are special to the shell, so wrapping the whole filter in quotes is essential.

docs.title: 5.1 [Caution] and and or have equal precedence
docs.text:
Many people get this wrong. In maths and most programming languages, "and" is evaluated before "or". BPF is different. Per the libpcap documentation, not comes first, and and and or have equal precedence and associate left to right. Compare directly (actual output):

Filter Matched tcp port 80 or udp port 53 and host 10.10.4.53 1 tcp port 80 or (udp port 53 and host 10.10.4.53) 6

If you wrote the first line meaning "all HTTP, or UDP DNS to the DNS server", you're in trouble. BPF groups it from the left as (tcp port 80 or udp port 53) and host 10.10.4.53, leaving only the one packet involving the DNS server (5). All five HTTP packets are dropped. As a capture filter, the HTTP would never have been stored. So when mixing and and or, always state your intent with parentheses.

One more: libpcap has a rule that "if a keyword is omitted, the most recent keyword is assumed". not host 10.10.4.53 and 10.10.4.54 is read as not host 10.10.4.53 and host 10.10.4.54, which means something completely different from not (host 10.10.4.53 or host 10.10.4.54). It's safer not to abbreviate and to write the keyword for every primitive.

docs.title: 5.2 Identical to the computer, different to people
docs.text:
Look at these two filters:

'ip and (tcp port 80 or udp port 53)'
'(ip and tcp port 80) or (ip and udp port 53)'

Drawn as a picture, one packet passes through the first filter in this order:

flowchart TD
    P["One packet arrives"] --> A{"IPv4?"}
    A -->|"no"| R["Reject"]
    A -->|"yes"| B{"TCP 80?"}
    B -->|"yes"| K["Accept (store · show)"]
    B -->|"no"| C{"UDP 53?"}
    C -->|"yes"| K
    C -->|"no"| R

How to read the diagram: each diamond is one decision, asked in turn from top to bottom. Once a decision reaches a conclusion (accept or reject), that packet's evaluation ends, and the next packet starts again from the top. Section 2's "each bag on its own" property is right there in the picture.

They mean the same. Both matched 5 packets in the practice file, and comparing the compiled output from tcpdump -d showed exactly the same 21-line program (actual output):

$ tcpdump -d -y EN10MB 'ip and (tcp port 80 or udp port 53)' > a.bpf
$ tcpdump -d -y EN10MB '(ip and tcp port 80) or (ip and udp port 53)' > b.bpf
$ cmp -s a.bpf b.bpf && echo "IDENTICAL compiled code"
IDENTICAL compiled code

Tools like tcpdump optimise filters before running them, so expressions with the same meaning often become the same program however a person wrote them. But the logical flow a person reads differs. The first reads "among IPv4, HTTP or DNS"; the second "IPv4 HTTP, or IPv4 DNS".

As the source material stresses, whether a person can understand and explain the filter matters as much as computational efficiency, perhaps more. Filters get written into reports, reused by colleagues, and become the answer in court to "under what conditions was this evidence collected?" The more complex a filter, the more room for syntax mistakes and the harder to explain, so pick the most readable form.

docs.title: 6.1 vlan: tagged traffic
docs.text:
A VLAN (virtual LAN) logically splits one switch into several segments, and when switches carry several VLANs over one link, a 4-byte 802.1Q tag is inserted into the Ethernet header. Such a link is called a trunk. If a tap or mirror is on a trunk, captured packets carry this tag.

The problem is that the 4-byte tag shifts every later position by 4 bytes. Fixed positions like [12] and [23] in section 3's compiled output no longer line up. So the practice file's VLAN-tagged packet (12, a TCP 80 SYN on VLAN 20) did this (actual output):

Filter Matched Interpretation tcp port 80 5 1–4 and the IPv6 packet 8. The VLAN-tagged packet 12 is excluded vlan and tcp port 80 1 Only 12 vlan 20 1 Packets with VLAN number 20

With the vlan keyword, libpcap computes the conditions after it at positions shifted by the tag. So for a file captured on a trunk, write vlan and tcp port 80. If tagged and untagged packets are mixed, write both, as in tcp port 80 or (vlan and tcp port 80) (6 matches, actual output). Order matters: putting vlan first and the untagged condition after can make the later condition use shifted positions too, contrary to intent. As the source material puts it, this "can get tricky", so always test filters for trunk links against real files.

The lesson for investigations: when a filter returns "nothing matched", first check whether the capture point was a trunk. The tags may have made the filter silently miss.

docs.title: 6.2 portrange
docs.text: Matches a contiguous range of ports rather than one port. portrange 50000-50002 matched 5 in the practice file (port 50000 in 1–4 and port 50002 in 8; actual output). Direction qualifiers work too, as in src portrange and dst portrange. It's handy for services using dynamic ports, or malware using source ports in a particular range.

docs.title: 6.3 gateway
docs.text:
gateway host matches packets whose layer 2 MAC address is that host's but whose layer 3 IP address is not that host's, i.e. packets that passed through that host. The libpcap documentation describes it as equivalent to ether host <MAC> and not host <IP>. Normally the default gateway (router) plays this role, so if a device that isn't the gateway matches, you might suspect a fake gateway intercepting traffic in the middle (a man-in-the-middle, MITM).

But per the documentation, gateway must be followed by a name, and that name must resolve on the analysis machine both to an IP address (hosts file, DNS, etc.) and to a MAC address (/etc/ethers, etc.). In practice it's simpler to write the equivalent ether host ... and not host ... directly, which also avoids creating OPSEC problems through name lookups.

docs.title: 6.4 Byte- and bit-level conditions
docs.text:
The most cryptic but most powerful feature. The form is protocol[offset:size], with size 1, 2 or 4 bytes (1 if omitted). You can use comparisons (=, !=, >, <) and bitwise operations (& and, | or).

[Correction] Offsets count from the start of that protocol's header. The source material says "the offset is zero-based and calculated from the first byte of the IP header", which is true for ip[...]. Per the libpcap documentation, tcp[...] counts from the start of the TCP header and ether[...] from the start of the Ethernet header.

Some examples (actual output):

Filter Meaning Matched ip[9] == 6 Byte 9 of the IPv4 header (protocol field) is 6 (TCP) 7 tcp[13] & 0x02 != 0 In byte 13 of the TCP header (flags), the SYN bit (0x02) is set 4 tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0 The same meaning, written with names 4 tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn Only SYN is set in the flags 3

Unpacking tcp[13] & 0x02 != 0: bitwise-AND byte 13 with 0x02 (binary 00000010); if the result isn't 0, i.e. the SYN bit is set, it matches. libpcap provides names for these positions such as tcpflags, tcp-syn, tcp-ack, tcp-rst and tcp-fin, which read more easily than numbers.

The difference between the last two lines matters. & tcp-syn != 0 means "if SYN is set (even with other flags)", catching both SYN and SYN-ACK (1, 2, 6, 10), while == tcp-syn means "exactly SYN", catching only the first packets of new connections (1, 6, 10). To see "who started the connection", the latter is right.

Now we can unpack the puzzling filter from lesson 1.6:

'tcp[((tcp[12]&0xf0)>>2):4] = 0x47455420'
  • tcp[12]: byte 12 of the TCP header. Its upper 4 bits are the TCP header length (in 4-byte units).
  • & 0xf0: keep only those upper 4 bits.
  • >> 2: shift right 2 bits. The upper-4-bit value sits at 16× its value, so dividing by 4 (>>2) gives "header length × 4", i.e. the header length in bytes. A header length field of 5 is 0x50 → 0x14 = 20 bytes.
  • tcp[that value:4]: the 4 bytes right after the TCP header, i.e. the first 4 bytes of data.
  • = 0x47455420: are those 4 bytes G (0x47) E (0x45) T (0x54) space (0x20), i.e. GET?

In the practice file only packet 4 matched. It finds HTTP GET requests on any port, so you can use it to find lesson 1.2's "HTTP bypassing the proxy out on an odd port".

These conditions look complex but run very fast, close to the kernel. If this is the surest way to pick out the traffic of interest, filtering with BPF before handing it to CPU-heavy back-end processing is the right call.

docs.title: 7. [Caution] What filters silently miss
docs.text:
Here are the traps seen so far. None produces an error; they just silently catch less, which makes them more dangerous.

Byte conditions don't match IPv6. Packet 8 in the practice file is an IPv6 TCP SYN, yet none of section 6.4's SYN filters caught it. Checking (actual output):

Filter Matched ip6 and tcp[13] & 0x02 != 0 0 ip6 and ip6[6] == 6 1

The libpcap documentation still states (both the 1.10 branch and the current development documentation) that byte access for upper-layer protocols such as tcp[...] and udp[...] doesn't match IPv6 packets (checked 2026-11-05). For IPv6, count directly from the IPv6 header with ip6[...]. ip6[6] == 6 checks whether byte 6 of the IPv6 header (the next header field) is 6 (TCP). But this too only works when there are no extension headers, because extension headers push the TCP header further back. If you use byte-level filters in an environment with a lot of IPv6, always test against real files and record the limits. Distinguish this from named primitives like tcp and tcp port 80, which did catch IPv6 (section 4).

VLAN tags throw off fixed positions, as section 6.1 showed.

IPv4 fragments from the second onwards don't match port conditions, because of the jset #0x1fff in section 3's compiled output. If an attacker deliberately splits packets into small fragments, the later fragments can be missing from a capture using a port filter. To be sure of seeing fragmented traffic, capture on address conditions (host) only and judge ports later, after reassembly.

ip is IPv4 only, the trap from section 4.1.

docs.title: 8. Reducing large files
docs.text:
Another key use of tcpdump is reducing an existing pcap with BPF. Leave the original untouched, and make a new file by extracting what's relevant or removing what isn't (actual output):

$ cat reduce.bpf
not port 443
and not net 224.0.0.0/4
and not port 53
$ tcpdump -n -r lab.pcap -F reduce.bpf -w reduced.pcap
reading from file lab.pcap, link-type EN10MB (Ethernet), snapshot length 262144
$ capinfos -c -s lab.pcap reduced.pcap
File name:           lab.pcap
Number of packets:   13
File size:           1078 bytes
File name:           reduced.pcap
Number of packets:   7
File size:           587 bytes

It reads the original with -r, uses a filter written in a file with -F, and writes a new file with -w. -F lets you manage complex filters as files, so a team can keep its filters in a git repository and everyone uses the same ones. Inside a filter file you can split lines, and there are no shell quoting issues.

This filter removed port 443 (usually HTTPS, content not visible), 224.0.0.0/4 (multicast, usually noise) and port 53 (DNS, assumed to be in other logs already). 13 packets became 7, and 1,078 bytes became 587. On real large files you can cut size substantially this way too. Wireshark takes a long time to open large pcaps and may not open files beyond several hundred MB at all, so reducing before opening is especially important.

[Caution] Check the "it's elsewhere" assumption. If DNS was removed "because it's in the DNS server logs", confirm those logs really exist and cover the incident window. And because you're making a new file, not editing the original, you can always go back to the original to look at what was removed. Always keep the original.

docs.title: 9. How to interpret it in a real investigation
docs.text:
Capture filters are permanent. Packets dropped by a BPF applied at capture time can never be seen again. Wireshark's display filters, covered in lesson 1.9, only choose which already-stored packets to show, so they can always be undone. Hence the principle: keep capture filters conservative, i.e. generous, and do fine selection after storing. For section 1's case, it's safer to apply just host 10.10.6.14 and not filter by port or protocol, which is less exposed to section 7's traps (fragments, VLANs, IPv6).

Test filters and record them. The more elaborate a filter, the more chance of a syntax mistake. Before using one in operations, ① count matches against known traffic in the lab, ② check it compiles with tcpdump -d, and ③ confirm it doesn't drop packets under real load. And in reports, write the filter used verbatim. With pcapng, as lesson 1.6 showed, it's also kept in the file.

Don't read "the filter caught nothing" as "there was nothing". This is the BPF version of the principle repeated since lesson 1.1. If the result is 0, first check for IPv6, a VLAN trunk, fragments, or a precedence mistake.

docs.title: 10. Summary
docs.text:
• BPF is a filter language that judges "is this of interest?" for each packet close to the kernel, and almost every libpcap-based tool uses it. Filtering at capture reduces load and storage.
  • BPF judges each packet separately and doesn't remember earlier packets. So src host catches only one side of a conversation.
  • The basic primitives are protocols (ip, ip6, tcp, udp, icmp), addresses (ether host, host, net), port, and direction (src, dst, and for MAC ether src/ether dst). ip is IPv4 only, and port doesn't distinguish TCP from UDP.
  • and and or have equal precedence and group from the left. Always use parentheses when mixing them. Computers optimise equivalent meanings into the same code, but choosing a form people can read matters.
  • vlan, portrange, gateway and byte/bit conditions (ip[9], tcp[tcpflags]) are powerful, but offsets count from each protocol header's start, and they can silently miss VLAN-tagged packets, IPv6, and later IPv4 fragments.
  • Reduce large files with tcpdump -r original -F filterfile -w newfile, and keep the original.
  • Capture filters can't be undone, so keep them generous, and test and record the filters you use verbatim.

In the next lesson (1.8) we cover tcpdump's practical options (splitting, rotating and limiting files) and reading the Wireshark window.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. To capture "all IP traffic that PC exchanged", you wrote ip and host 10.10.6.14. The PC has both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. What do you miss, and how should you fix it?

Answer and explanation

ip means IPv4 only, and host 10.10.6.14 is an IPv4 address too. So you miss all of the PC's IPv6 traffic. Writing the PC's IPv6 address (e.g. 2001:db8:6::14) as well, as host 10.10.6.14 or host 2001:db8:6::14, is right; you can drop ip and entirely. You could exploit both addresses being the same device and write ether host 00:50:56:0a:06:14, but MAC addresses only mean something within one segment, so if the tap is across a router, the PC's MAC won't be visible. Choose according to the capture point.

Question 2. (Precedence) How many packets does this filter match in the practice file? Explain why, and rewrite it to mean what the author probably wanted.

'host 203.0.113.50 or host 203.0.113.60 and tcp port 443'
Answer and explanation

BPF groups and and or at equal precedence from the left, so this filter is (host 203.0.113.50 or host 203.0.113.60) and tcp port 443. In the practice file, only packets 10 (SYN to 203.0.113.60) and 13 (RST from 203.0.113.60) involve port 443, both involving .60, so 2 match. The HTTP packets with 203.0.113.50 (1–4) are on port 80 and all drop out. If the author wanted "all traffic with 203.0.113.50, plus HTTPS with 203.0.113.60", write host 203.0.113.50 or (host 203.0.113.60 and tcp port 443). That matches 6: 1–4, 10 and 13 (the VLAN-tagged packet 12 still drops out). The results of 2 and 6 for the two filters were confirmed by running them against the practice file.

Question 3. Explain the difference between tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0 and tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn, and say which is right for building "a list of internal PCs that started new connections outward".

Answer and explanation

The former means "if the SYN bit is set, even with other bits", catching both connection requests (SYN) and their replies (SYN-ACK). The latter catches only packets where SYN alone is set, i.e. the first packet that starts a connection. To find who started connections, == tcp-syn is right; with the former, external servers that sent SYN-ACKs get mixed into the list. Adding and src net 10.10.0.0/16 makes it "first SYNs sent by internal addresses". And this condition doesn't match IPv6 packets (section 7), so in an environment using IPv6, look at the IPv6 side separately by other means (ip6[...], or Wireshark filters after storage).

Question 4. (Common misconception) A colleague applied tcp port 80 to a pcap captured from a tap on a trunk link, got 0 results, and says "there was no HTTP on this segment". How would you check?

Answer and explanation

On a trunk link every packet carries an 802.1Q VLAN tag, shifting later positions by its 4 bytes. tcp port 80 then silently misses tagged packets (confirmed directly in section 6.1). First check with tcpdump -n -e -r file -c 5 whether packets show vlan, and if so, count again with vlan and tcp port 80 or tcp port 80 or (vlan and tcp port 80). If it's still 0, then you can say "within this file's scope, no HTTP on port 80 is visible", and check HTTP on other ports separately by a port-independent method such as section 6.4's GET byte condition.

Question 5. (Byte calculation) Byte 12 of a TCP header is 0x80. How many bytes is the TCP header, and where does section 6.4's GET filter look for the start of data in this packet?

Answer and explanation

0x80 & 0xf0 = 0x80, 0x80 >> 2 = 0x20 = 32, so the TCP header is 32 bytes, the same as the upper-4-bit value 8 times 4 (8 × 4 = 32). That's the common case of the basic 20-byte header plus 12 bytes of options (e.g. the timestamp option). So the filter compares tcp[32:4], the 4 bytes 32 bytes after the start of the TCP header, with 0x47455420. Had you assumed a fixed header length of 20 and written tcp[20:4], it would miss on most real packets with options. That's why the expression computes the length per packet.

Question 6. (IPv6) On an IPv6-only segment you want to capture "new TCP connection requests (packets with only SYN set)" with BPF. What happens with tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn, and what's the alternative?

Answer and explanation

Per the libpcap documentation, tcp[...] byte access doesn't match IPv6 packets, so nothing is captured (the same reason the IPv6 SYN got 0 in section 7). The alternative is to count directly from the IPv6 header. The basic IPv6 header is 40 bytes, and with no extension headers the TCP header follows immediately, so the TCP flags byte is ip6[40+13] = ip6[53]. You can write ip6 and ip6[6] == 6 and ip6[53] == 0x02 (or the expression form ip6[40+13]); in the practice file both forms matched only packet 8, the IPv6 SYN (actual output). ip6[6] == 6 checks "next header is TCP". But this approach misses when there are extension headers. So rather than a capture filter with such limits, it's safer to capture generously with something like ip6 and tcp and pick out SYNs afterwards with Wireshark or tshark display filters (lesson 1.9).

Question 7. (Data reduction) Before viewing a 5 GB pcap in Wireshark, you reduced it with not port 53 and not port 443 to 800 MB. What goes in the report, and what do you do if the hypothesis "C2 over DNS" comes up later?

Answer and explanation

The report gives the original file and its hash, the command and filter used to reduce it verbatim (tcpdump -n -r original.pcap -w reduced.pcap 'not port 53 and not port 443'), the reduced file's hash and packet count, and the limitation "this analysis used a file with ports 53 and 443 removed". If a DNS C2 hypothesis comes up later, the reduced file has no port 53, so go back to the original and extract with port 53 this time to analyse separately. That's possible because you kept the original. Had you written "no DNS anomalies" from the reduced file alone, you'd have said something wasn't there that you could never have seen.

Question 8. (Design) In section 1's case, a colleague proposes the capture filter host 10.10.6.14 and (tcp port 80 or tcp port 443) and not ip6. Give at least three risks of this filter, and propose a better capture filter.

Answer and explanation
  1. It permanently misses traffic outside 80 and 443. Attackers can run C2 on other ports (53, 8080, arbitrary high ports).
  2. It misses UDP. DNS tunnels and QUIC (UDP 443) traffic drop out.
  3. It explicitly excludes IPv6. If the PC has an IPv6 address, all that traffic drops out; and host 10.10.6.14 is an IPv4 address, so IPv6 was excluded anyway.
  4. It can miss later IPv4 fragments and VLAN-tagged packets. The port conditions drop fragments from the second onwards, and on a trunk, tagged packets drop out.

A better proposal: apply only the PC's addresses, as in host 10.10.6.14 or host 2001:db8:6::14 (considering vlan if it's a trunk), and do port and protocol selection with display filters after storage. The principle: capture filters generous, analysis filters fine-grained. If storage is a concern, manage it with lesson 1.8's file rotation options rather than narrowing the filter.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• The Tcpdump Group, libpcap 1.10 branch pcap-filter documentation source (checked 2026-11-05). Primitives and qualifiers; the rule that not comes first and and/or have equal precedence grouping from the left; the omitted-keyword rule; the definition of gateway and its name resolution requirement; offsets in proto[expr:size] being relative to that protocol layer; names such as tcpflags.
  • The Tcpdump Group, libpcap development branch pcap-filter documentation source (checked 2026-11-05). The current statement that upper-layer byte access doesn't match IPv6 packets.
  • IEEE 802.1Q (VLAN tags), RFC 8200 (IPv6 header and extension headers) and RFC 791 (the IPv4 fragment offset) are the basis for the header structures used in this lesson's offset calculations.

About this page

Personal study notes rewritten in my own words from a range of study material. The practice packets were assembled by hand for explanation.

docs.title: 1.12 — Challenges and Opportunities in Network Investigations
1.12 — Challenges and Opportunities in Network Investigations
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Change is inevitable: a network diagram starts going stale the moment it's drawn
  • NAT: mapping one "address and port" reported from outside back to an inside PC (a correlation done by hand)
  • Encryption: [Changed] TLS you can decrypt with the server's private key has become rare (tested directly: only TLS 1.2 RSA decrypted)
  • Tunnels: BPF can't see traffic inside GRE and 6in4 (tested directly), DoH, and [Changed] ECH (RFC 9849)
  • VPNs, WAN optimisation, wireless, cloud: the challenges and opportunities of each
  • Traffic volumes grow, and malware still depends on the network

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) comes from this environment's tshark 4.2.2, tcpdump 4.99.4 and OpenSSL 3.0.13. The TLS experiment captured real connections made on loopback with openssl s_server and s_client, using a self-signed certificate I created (files.lab.example). The pcaps for the NAT and tunnel experiments were assembled in Python (private and documentation addresses only). Assembled pcaps are for showing the principle, and may differ in detail from traffic produced by real equipment.

docs.title: 1. Change: inevitable, and usually hard
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) In an incident response meeting, the network engineer puts up the diagram. "The lab is behind this firewall, and all web traffic goes to the proxy." But when you actually capture packets, some traffic is leaving by a completely different path because of a device installed three months ago. It isn't on the diagram.

Network investigation is a field of constant change. Every new technology, every new design approach (sometimes just a buzzword) brings something to add to analysis toolkits and response plans. Nobody wants to tell the executives that "a device installed a few months ago made the whole response procedure useless". If the security team is involved from the moment a new technology is adopted, though, you can make use of the opportunities it brings.

This isn't only about new technology. Most organisations have detailed diagrams and operating documents, but they're never 100% accurate; they start going stale as soon as they're written. In the end, success depends less on pressing a fixed sequence of buttons than on adapting to the unexpected and seizing unexpected opportunities.

This lesson goes through the structures that most often trouble investigators, and for each one sums up the challenge it brings and, at the same time, the opportunity.

docs.title: 2. NAT: who on the inside is that one outside address?
2.1 What NAT is
docs.text:
When RFC 760 (later superseded by RFC 791) set IP addresses at 32 bits in 1980, hardly anyone imagined more than four billion devices on the Internet. Today IPv4 exhaustion is real, and one response is NAT (Network Address Translation). A NAT device maps one or more inside addresses to one or more outside addresses, remembers the mapping per connection, and rewrites the addresses on returning packets. Each end sees only addresses consistent with its own place on the network.

NAT is commonly used between private ranges (RFC 1918) and public addresses, but also between private and private, or public and public. A typical case is after one company acquires another and the two networks' addresses overlap. NAT is often inserted as a workaround instead of proper network integration.

What matters to the investigator is the observation point. The same connection appears as 10.10.6.14:51000 inside the NAT and 203.0.113.5:61022 outside. Depending on which side a pcap was captured or a log was written, the "source" differs.

docs.title: 2.2 Opportunity: devices that record both, and correlation
docs.text:
Some enterprise devices record NAT translations. Many flow deployments store both the pre- and post-translation addresses for each connection (the nfdump 1.7.3 used in lesson 1.11's lab also showed translated-address columns such as X-Src IP Addr the first time it printed in its default format; they were empty as 0.0.0.0 because softflowd doesn't do NAT). Then, when an outside party reports "your public address talked to a known C2 server", finding the connection in the flows gives you the inside address immediately.

Without such records, all is not lost. You can correlate several pieces of evidence; it just takes longer. I tried it.

(Hypothetical) The outside party's notification: "Around 2026-11-02 09:02:00 UTC, there was a connection from your 203.0.113.5, source port 61022, to 198.51.100.66:443." We have inside.pcap captured inside the NAT and outside.pcap captured outside.

① Inside, find every connection start (SYN) to that destination at that time

tshark -n -r inside.pcap -Y 'ip.dst == 198.51.100.66 && tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0' \
  -T fields -e frame.time_utc -e ip.src -e tcp.srcport -e tcp.seq_raw

(Actual output)

Nov  2, 2026 09:02:00.200000000 UTC 10.10.7.11  50110   3492838502
Nov  2, 2026 09:02:00.900000000 UTC 10.10.6.14  51000   3340291515
Nov  2, 2026 09:02:01.300000000 UTC 10.10.7.15  49822   1388325221
Nov  2, 2026 09:02:01.600000000 UTC 10.10.6.11  53001   3794726010
Nov  2, 2026 09:02:02.400000000 UTC 10.10.6.14  51001   1337529987

Five connections to the same C2 within three seconds, from four PCs. "Around 09:02:00" alone can't pick one, and the outside party's clock may be a few seconds off. The inside port was changed by NAT, so you can't search for 61022 either.

② Outside, find the connection on the reported port and look at its TCP sequence number

tshark -n -r outside.pcap -Y 'tcp.srcport == 61022 && tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0' \
  -T fields -e frame.time_utc -e ip.src -e tcp.srcport -e tcp.seq_raw

(Actual output)

Nov  2, 2026 09:02:00.900000000 UTC 203.0.113.5 61022   3340291515

tcp.seq_raw is the sequence number actually written in the packet, not the relative number Wireshark renumbers from 0 for readability. Ordinary NAT changes addresses and ports and leaves this value alone.

③ Search for that sequence number inside

tshark -n -r inside.pcap -Y 'tcp.seq_raw == 3340291515' -T fields -e ip.src -e tcp.srcport

(Actual output) 10.10.6.14 51000. The time (09:02:00.9) matches exactly too. When time, destination and sequence number all line up, that's fairly strong support.

[Caution] When this method fails

  • Devices that rewrite sequence numbers: some firewalls randomise the TCP initial sequence number for security (e.g. Cisco ASA's sequence number randomisation). Step ③ then fails, and you must match on other characteristics such as time, packet sizes and connection duration.
  • No outside capture: the time and source port in the notification alone can be matched against the NAT device's translation log. If even that is missing, narrow the candidates as in step ① and choose with other evidence.
  • Proxy logs: if the C2 used HTTP or HTTPS, the proxy logs (lesson 1.3) contain the inside address, host name and URL. If the connection seen from outside belongs to the proxy, the proxy log points directly to the inside PC.
  • The two pcaps in this lab were assembled to show the principle and assume a NAT that leaves sequence numbers unchanged.

docs.title: 3. Encryption: the biggest wall, and what remains
3.1 The challenge
docs.text:
The biggest wall in network investigation is encryption. There's no easy way to "crack" strong, properly deployed encryption, and plaintext services are disappearing fast. If your analytic methods are built on being able to see the content, their effectiveness drops immediately.

Still, encryption ultimately rests on trust, and trust is complicated. In enterprise environments, the TLS interception from lesson 1.2 (the proxy re-issues certificates from the organisation's CA) lets you inspect and capture most TLS in plaintext.

docs.title: 3.2 [Changed] "Capture now, decrypt later with the key" rarely works any more
docs.text:
The source material explains, from a law enforcement perspective, that "if you might acquire the private key later (e.g. by a search warrant), capturing the encrypted traffic now is useful, and with the key, tools like Wireshark can decrypt it". I tested how true this is for today's TLS.

With the same server certificate and private key, I made three kinds of connection and sent a GET /secret-report.txt request in each. Then I gave tshark ① no key, ② the server's private key, and ③ a key log of session secrets written by the client, and checked whether the request path became visible.

# ② decrypt with the server private key
tshark -n -r t13.pcap -d tcp.port==8444,tls -o 'uat:rsa_keys:"srv.key",""' -Y http.request -T fields -e http.request.uri
# ③ decrypt with the key log
tshark -n -r t13.pcap -d tcp.port==8444,tls -o 'tls.keylog_file:t13.keys' -Y http.request -T fields -e http.request.uri
  • -d tcp.port==8444,tls: "Decode As": dissect this port as TLS (lesson 1.9).
  • -o 'uat:rsa_keys:...': puts the server's private key file in Wireshark's RSA keys list.
  • -o 'tls.keylog_file:...': points to the file recording the keys created for each session. Browsers, curl and OpenSSL can write this file via the SSLKEYLOGFILE environment variable or the -keylogfile option.

(Actual output)

Connection Key exchange No key Server private key Key log TLS 1.2, AES128-GCM-SHA256 RSA not visible visible visible TLS 1.2, ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256 ECDHE not visible not visible visible TLS 1.3, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 (EC)DHE not visible not visible visible

Why the difference? In RSA key exchange, the client sends the material for the session key encrypted with the server's public key. So with the server's private key you can recover that material, even later, and rebuild the session key. (EC)DHE key exchange such as ECDHE builds the session key from temporary keys that both sides use for that connection only and then discard. The server's private key is used only to sign "this server is genuine", not to build the session key. So obtaining the private key later doesn't decrypt past connections. This property is called forward secrecy.

And TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) removed RSA key exchange altogether; every key exchange is designed to provide forward secrecy. Most TLS connections today are TLS 1.3 or TLS 1.2 with ECDHE, so assume that seizing the server's private key will almost never decrypt traffic you've already captured.

So what does work?

  • Key logs. All three connections in the table decrypted. That's possible if you prepared endpoints or proxies to write key logs in advance. But obtaining such a log after the fact for an attacker's connections is hard.
  • Devices that are one end of the connection. TLS-intercepting proxies and decryption appliances can see or record plaintext (lessons 1.2 and 1.11).
  • So a "capture now, decrypt later" plan is only possible after checking which key exchange the connections use. You can see it in the pcap from the Server Hello's tls.handshake.ciphersuite: in the experiment above, 0x009c (RSA), 0xc02f (ECDHE) and 0x1302 (TLS 1.3).

[Supplement] SSH and other protocols

The source material notes that decrypted SSHv2 content isn't accessible at this time. SSHv2's key exchange is also Diffie-Hellman based, so after-the-fact decryption is effectively hard for the same reason. There is research and tooling for extracting keys from endpoints, but that belongs to endpoint forensics.

docs.title: 3.3 Opportunity: flow analysis works the same on encrypted traffic
docs.text: If you can't see the content, do analysis that doesn't need content: flow analysis. Addresses and ports, and also packet sizes and timing, are enough to generate leads and build hypotheses, just as lesson 1.11 found five-minute-interval connections of identical size (717 bytes) and a 20 MB upload without any content. And even with TLS 1.3, the Client Hello is still mostly plaintext, so unless ECH is used, the server name being contacted (SNI) is visible (lesson 1.2).

docs.title: 4.1 What a tunnel is
docs.text:
In a tunnel, one stream of traffic becomes the payload of another. Some protocols are designed for tunnelling, such as GRE (IP protocol 47); others, such as HTTP, DNS and ICMP, are repurposed as tunnels. There's also 6in4 (IP protocol 41), joining two IPv6 enclaves across an IPv4 network, SOCKS, somewhere between a proxy and a tunnel, and SSH tunnels.

The challenge: many tools aren't tunnel-aware, and there are so many tunnel types that detecting, let alone managing, them is hard. Investigators must first notice that a tunnel exists and decide how to strip it before content analysis can begin.

docs.title: 4.2 Tested: BPF can't see inside a tunnel
docs.text:
I built a pcap containing the same HTTP request in three shapes: ① plain TCP 80 over IPv4, ② IPv4 TCP 80 inside GRE, ③ IPv6 TCP 80 inside 6in4.

(Actual output)

Filter Tool Matching packets tcp port 80 tcpdump (BPF) 1 ip proto 47 tcpdump (BPF) 1 (the GRE packet) ip proto 41 tcpdump (BPF) 1 (the 6in4 packet) host 10.20.1.5 (inner GRE address) tcpdump (BPF) 0 tcp.port == 80 tshark (display filter) 3 ip.addr == 10.20.1.5 tshark (display filter) 1 http.request tshark (display filter) 3

BPF's tcp port 80 looks only at the outer header (lesson 1.7). The GRE packet's outside is "IP protocol 47" and the 6in4 packet's outside is "IP protocol 41", so neither looks like TCP. Had tcp port 80 been the capture filter, the web traffic inside the tunnels wouldn't even have been saved. Wireshark's dissectors, on the other hand, strip tunnels and dissect what's inside, so the display filter found all three.

One more thing: printing ip.src for the GRE packet gave two values, 192.0.2.1,10.20.1.5 (actual output), because both the outer and inner IP headers are present. The "multi-value fields" of lesson 1.9 appear in tunnels even for an ordinary field like ip.src. A filter like ip.src != 10.20.1.5 may behave unexpectedly on such packets.

The opportunity: for engineered tunnels such as GRE or 6in4, the points of encapsulation and decapsulation are fixed. Identify them and place the capture platform after decapsulation, and you receive traffic in its original shape without messy preprocessing.

docs.title: 4.3 Everything over HTTPS: DoH and ECH
docs.text:
There's a strong recent trend towards repurposing HTTPS for all sorts of new uses. Visibility into network behaviour falls, and the importance of intercepting encrypted communication rises.

  • DoH (DNS over HTTPS, RFC 8484) puts DNS queries inside HTTPS. From outside it's an ordinary web connection on 443, so the premise from lesson 1.11, "force every endpoint to use the internal DNS servers and you see all DNS in one place", breaks down. There's also DoT (DNS over TLS, RFC 7858, usually port 853) and DoQ (DNS over QUIC, RFC 9250) for the same purpose. DoT uses a dedicated port, so it's easy to block or spot; DoH blends in with normal web traffic. Organisations therefore usually disable DoH or allow only an internal DoH server through endpoint and browser policy, and check proxies and firewalls for connections to known public DoH servers.
  • [Changed] ECH (Encrypted Client Hello) encrypts even the server name in the Client Hello. When lesson 1.2 was written it was treated mainly as a technology trend, but it was published as RFC 9849 in March 2026. As ECH spreads, the "server name from SNI" mentioned in section 3.3 also disappears from packet sensors. That's why records kept at one end of the connection, such as an explicit proxy's CONNECT log, matter even more.

docs.title: 5. VPNs: an opportunity, if placement is right
docs.text:
A VPN is a special case of tunnelling, used in nearly every network. Remote users send all their traffic into the corporate network inside an encrypted tunnel.

The challenge: place the capture platform outside the VPN endpoint and you see only the encrypted tunnel. That shows who connected, when and how much, so it isn't useless, but most investigations need the traffic after decryption, flowing "natively" inside the network. So understand the VPN architecture fully before choosing a capture location.

The opportunity: clear that small hurdle, and a VPN lets you watch and capture most of your scattered remote users' traffic in one place. Cross-check with the VPN authentication logs, and it becomes easy to tie traffic of interest to a source device, a user account, and sometimes a location.

[Supplement] Not all traffic may go through the VPN

Modern VPNs commonly use split tunnelling: only corporate destinations go through the tunnel, and other Internet traffic goes straight out over the user's own connection. In that case remote users' web activity won't appear in the corporate proxy or in capture behind the VPN. Check first whether the VPN is full tunnel or split tunnel.

docs.title: 6. WAN optimisation: flows that don't match the diagram
docs.text:
Devices that improve network speed and efficiency also change the flow. The most common is the web proxy: identical content is fetched from the remote server once and served to many inside users over the fast LAN (the cache in lessons 1.2 and 1.5). Extending that idea beyond HTTP gives WAN optimisation appliances. The source material cites commercial products such as Riverbed SteelHead and F5 BIG-IP, which act transparently like proxies for email, web applications, file sharing, video and more.

The challenge: the client thinks it connected to the remote server, but the optimiser in the middle may answer from its own cache. The remote server (and every segment outside the optimiser) may not even know the request happened, or who made it. From outside, every connection appears to come from the optimiser. In short, the actual flows differ from what the diagram leads you to expect. "Not in the outside pcap" doesn't mean no request was made inside.

The opportunity: these devices generally log very well, which is valuable for correlating activity seen on either side of the optimiser. And since they usually sit at the edge of large networks, that position itself may be a good place for capture or monitoring.

docs.title: 7. Wireless: it doesn't stop at the wall
docs.text:
Wireless is now a major part of networks. Not long ago many enterprises refused to deploy it, but user demand, mobile devices, security-conscious deployment options and convenience made it spread fast.

The challenges:

  • The network is everywhere. A wireless network's reach depends not only on the infrastructure but also on the client's equipment. Transmit power is regulated, but people with bad intent aren't guaranteed to comply, and large or highly directional receive antennas often aren't regulated. So even physically "controlled" wireless networks reach well beyond their designed area. As the source slide's picture shows, the perceived coverage (inside the office) and the actual coverage differ.
  • Legal requirements change a lot. Laws on capturing wireless signals vary by jurisdiction and are often stricter than for wired networks. Always get legal advice first. The source material cites, as a warning, the case of a mapping service's street-imagery vehicles collecting wireless data, which caused major trouble.

The opportunities:

  • One big shared medium. Unlike wired networks, where switches separate traffic per port, radio is shared by every device on that channel, so the capture constraints of lesson 1.11's mirror ports don't apply.
  • Location can be estimated. Commercial and free tools use signal strength and known location data (GPS, or points on a map) to find the approximate physical location of a device of interest.
  • Good logs. Large wireless deployments usually have controllers that record associations, authentication and roaming well.

[Caution] What's different in today's wireless networks

  • A shared medium, but the content is encrypted. Even capturing frames in monitor mode (lesson 1.11, section 3.1), data frames encrypted with WPA2 or WPA3 can't be read without keys. WPA2-Personal can be decrypted if you have the passphrase and also capture the 4-way handshake at connection start, but WPA3-Personal (SAE) is designed so that knowing the password doesn't let you passively decrypt traffic already captured. So controller logs and capture on the wired side have become more important in wireless investigations too.
  • MAC addresses change. Today's phone and laptop operating systems use randomised MAC addresses by default, per network (or periodically). Lesson 1.11 called DHCP logs "the key for mapping an IP back to a device", but with random MACs that key may not point to a single device. Look at it together with the wireless controller's user authentication records (802.1X accounts and so on).

docs.title: 8. The cloud: activity beyond the perimeter
docs.text:
"Cloud" became a buzzword quickly, but the shift back to centralised, remote computing is real: hosted applications, remote storage, elastic compute. The enterprise no longer ends at its traditional perimeter, and since these services' core functions depend on network connectivity, investigations must cover them.

The challenges:

  • Lack of visibility and control. For example: "How many failed logins came before the successful one that exported the whole customer database? From which IPs?" Depending on the service, that record may not exist at all, and if it does, the provider may not hand it over without legal process.
  • New and changing fast. Each service can be completely different, so be ready to "start from zero" when a new service comes into scope. The Azure NSG flow log retirement seen in lesson 1.11 is a good example.

The opportunity: most cloud services expose data and functions through structured HTTP requests: APIs. HTTP(S) can be proxied, so requests and responses can be intercepted and logged, and since providers publish their API documentation, you can use it to interpret, or reconstruct as a transcript, what happened in the service.

[Supplement] Check the cloud-side records first

Major cloud and SaaS providers today offer audit logs recording administrative actions and logins. But what's on by default, how long it's kept, and which items are recorded at which subscription tier varies by service and changes often. For any incident involving the cloud, check whether that service's audit logs were enabled and how long they're kept first, alongside the network evidence.

docs.title: 9. Trend 1: everything over the network
docs.text:
The once underused office LAN is now a high-speed switched fabric divided into VLANs, and it still never seems fast enough. Voice (VoIP), storage (SAN, iSCSI), backups, remote synchronisation, video and security cameras have all moved onto the network.

The challenge: new data brings new analytic challenges, and the volume is enormous. Links of tens of Gbps carrying several GB per second are common, so separating out the relevant data takes a lot of work. That's why this course spends so much time on flow analysis and data reduction: use flows to characterise large volumes of traffic quickly and find the time windows worth a deep look, then use data reduction (tcpdump and BPF from lesson 1.10, section 8) to pull out just that window's traffic and dig in.

The opportunity: as the source material jokes, more work means job security.

docs.title: 10. Trend 2: malware depends on the network
docs.text:
Malware's basic nature is to take commands from its master and return something. Spy films aside, malware almost always communicates over the network. There are clever ways to "hide" from host-based detection tools, but the network path involves many devices and fairly strict protocols, so hiding there is much harder. That's why finding and analysing malware from the network is sometimes faster and more fruitful than starting from the host and working up.

Attackers use encryption, obfuscation and more to make discovery and analysis harder, but the data is on the wire and can be found in a properly instrumented environment. This work is always an arms race: when we gain a new capability, attackers find a way around it, and round it goes.

Right now, the network is malware's weakness: malware relies on the network for its core functions, but can't control or manipulate the network extensively. We should seize on that weakness while it lasts.

[Supplement] Today's C2 tries to look ordinary

Recent malware often uses legitimate services everyone uses (cloud storage, collaboration tools, well-known CDNs) as its command channel instead of unfamiliar attacker-owned servers. Destination addresses or names alone make it hard to tell apart from normal traffic. That makes the size and timing patterns this course keeps stressing (the 900-second interval in lesson 1.10, the repeated identical sizes in lesson 1.11) and deviation from normal, such as "does that PC normally use that service?", even more important.

docs.title: 11. How to use this in real investigations
docs.text:
1. Trust the diagram, but verify. Check it against the actual paths in captured traffic (which device's address appears as the source, what tunnels exist).
  2. At every NAT boundary, note "which side's address is this?" When you get an outside notification, always obtain the time, public address and source port, then correlate in the order: translation logs, captures on both sides, proxy logs.
  3. For encrypted traffic, look at the key exchange first. Judge whether after-the-fact decryption is possible from the Server Hello's cipher suite; if not, turn to flow analysis and records from devices at the connection's ends.
  4. Make capture filters tunnel-aware. BPF like tcp port 80 can't see inside tunnels. On segments with tunnels, keep capture filters generous, or capture after decapsulation.
  5. State the scope of "nothing". Check for paths that bypass your observation (DoH, split tunnels, WAN optimisation, QUIC) and qualify conclusions with "from this observation point".

docs.title: 12. Summary
docs.text:
• Networks keep changing and diagrams are always out of date. Adapting and seizing opportunities decides the outcome more than fixed procedures.
  • NAT makes the source depend on the observation point. Flows or translation logs recording both sides are easiest; otherwise you can match on time, port and TCP sequence number (done by hand here; fails on devices that rewrite sequence numbers).
  • [Changed] The only TLS the server's private key decrypted was TLS 1.2 with RSA key exchange. ECDHE and TLS 1.3 needed a key log (tested directly). "Capture now, decrypt later with the key" rarely works now.
  • When content can't be seen, flow analysis (addresses, ports, sizes, timing) works regardless of encryption.
  • BPF can't see traffic inside tunnels (tcp port 80 caught 1 of 3). Display filters see inside, but fields like ip.src become multi-valued.
  • DoH undermines visibility centred on internal DNS servers, and [Changed] ECH, published as RFC 9849 (March 2026), hides even SNI. Records from devices at the connection's ends matter more.
  • With the right capture placement, a VPN lets you see remote users' traffic in one place, and authentication logs tie it to people. Watch out for split tunnelling.
  • WAN optimisers change flows but offer good logs and good capture positions.
  • Wireless doesn't stop at the wall and has heavy legal constraints, but offers a shared medium, location estimation and controller logs. Today, factor in encryption and random MACs too.
  • The cloud lacks visibility and changes fast, but APIs and audit logs are opportunities.
  • Traffic keeps growing, and malware still depends on the network. Exploiting that weakness is the job of this field.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Application) An outside party reports only "around 2026-11-02 09:02:02 UTC there was a connection from your 203.0.113.5 to 198.51.100.66:443". No port number. Can you tell which PC it was from the inside.pcap results in section 2.2 alone? What would you ask for?

Answer and explanation

No. Between 09:02:00 and 09:02:03 there were five connections to the same destination from four PCs, and around 09:02:02 both 10.10.6.11 (09:02:01.6) and 10.10.6.14 (09:02:02.4) are candidates. The outside party's clock may be a few seconds off too. Ask the outside party for the source port, and if possible the exact time (milliseconds) and packet sizes or byte counts; on your side, look for the NAT device's translation logs, outside captures or flows, and proxy logs. Until then, the report says "two candidates".

Question 2. (Changed conditions) In the situation of section 2.2, if the NAT firewall had TCP initial sequence number randomisation enabled, what happens to steps ②–③, and what could you match on instead?

Answer and explanation

The outside SYN's sequence number differs from the inside one, so the tcp.seq_raw search in step ③ finds nothing. Don't read "not found" as "not inside". Instead, match on ① time (down to milliseconds, if both capture boxes' clocks are right), ② the size of the first data packet and the sequence of subsequent packet sizes, ③ connection duration and bytes exchanged, and ④ the NAT device's translation logs. In this lab, four of the five candidates had the same size (517 bytes), so one size alone isn't enough; use several characteristics together. Whether both capture boxes' clocks are synchronised by NTP is decisive (lesson 1.11, section 10.2).

Question 3. (Common misconception) "We've secured the incident server's TLS private key, so we can decrypt all of that server's HTTPS traffic we captured last month." What condition must hold for this to be true?

Answer and explanation

Those connections must be TLS 1.2 or earlier using RSA key exchange. In section 3.2's experiment, only the AES128-GCM-SHA256 (RSA key exchange) connection decrypted with the server's private key; ECDHE-RSA-... and TLS 1.3 did not. Those build session keys from per-connection temporary keys (forward secrecy), so the server's private key isn't used in computing them. Most servers today use TLS 1.3 or ECDHE, so first check the cipher suite in the Server Hello in the pcap. The alternatives are key logs, or records from the proxy or load balancer that terminates TLS.

Question 4. (Interpretation) After seeing section 4.2's experiment, a colleague says, "Then it's better never to use capture filters at all." How would you respond?

Answer and explanation

The direction is right, but the conclusion goes too far. The experiment showed that BPF conditions that look only at the outer header (tcp port 80, the inner address) miss what's inside tunnels. Capture filters are still often needed for storage and throughput reasons (lessons 1.7 and 1.11). The realistic answer is: ① first find out what tunnels exist on that segment; ② set filters generously so tunnel protocols (ip proto 47, ip proto 41, etc.) aren't excluded; ③ where possible, capture after decapsulation; ④ record the capture filter used in the capture notes.

Question 5. (Changed conditions) Lesson 1.11 said "force every endpoint to use only the internal DNS servers and you can see DNS in one place". Give three cases where this premise breaks, and how you'd check each.

Answer and explanation

① DoH: a browser or malware puts DNS inside HTTPS and sends it to a public DoH server. Check proxy logs or firewalls for port 443 connections to known DoH servers, and the browser and endpoint policy settings. ② DoT: goes directly to an external DNS server on port 853. Look for outbound port 853 connections at the firewall. ③ Direct port 53 queries: an endpoint asks an external DNS server on 53 directly instead of the internal one. Look in firewall or flow records for outbound port 53 from sources other than the internal DNS servers. Others include DoQ (QUIC) and queries that leave directly over the user's own connection through a VPN split tunnel. Qualify conclusions with "based on internal DNS logs".

Question 6. (Calculation) In section 2.2's inside.pcap, the five SYNs were at 09:02:00.2, 00.9, 01.3, 01.6 and 02.4. If the outside party's clock may differ from ours by up to ±1 second and the reported time is 09:02:00.0, how many candidates are there? How many after finding the outside sequence number by port?

Answer and explanation

09:02:00.0 ± 1 s is 09:01:59.0 to 09:02:01.0. The SYNs in that range are 00.2 (10.10.7.11) and 00.9 (10.10.6.14): two. Finding the SYN on port 61022 outside and searching the inside for sequence number 3340291515 reduced it to one (10.10.6.14:51000). The calculation shows that time only narrows candidates; a value unique to each connection (port, sequence number) is what pins down one.

Question 7. (Application) A remote worker's laptop appears to be infected. There's a tap at the perimeter outside the VPN appliance, and no capture inside it. The VPN uses split tunnelling. What do you secure, and where?

Answer and explanation

① VPN authentication logs: when the user connected, from which public address, and which internal address they were given. ② The outside tap: the user's VPN tunnel is encrypted so the content isn't visible, but connection times and volumes are. ③ Traffic to and from that internal address inside the VPN appliance: internal server logs, firewalls, flows. If needed, place a temporary capture box behind the VPN (lesson 1.11's standby kit). ④ With split tunnelling, Internet traffic may have gone straight out over the user's own connection, so that part isn't in corporate records. Separately secure the endpoint's own records (browser, DNS cache, security product logs) or records from any cloud security service the endpoint uses.

Question 8. (Interpretation) At a branch office with a WAN optimiser, the head office file server's access log has no record of branch employee A opening a file. Yet the file was found on A's PC. What explanations are possible, and what should you check?

Answer and explanation

The most likely explanation is that the optimiser served the file from its own cache. If someone else had opened it first and it was cached, A's request may never have reached the head office server, and even if it did, the source would be recorded as the optimiser. So check ① the optimiser's logs (which client was served which object), ② capture or flows on the branch LAN (traffic between A's PC and the optimiser), and ③ head office server log entries recorded under the optimiser's address. Of course, keep other routes such as email or USB open as well.

Question 9. (Common misconception) "Wireless is one big shared medium, so one monitor-mode capture box lets you see all the communication content of everyone on that floor." Point out what's wrong.

Answer and explanation

① Monitor mode sees one channel at a time (lesson 1.11, section 3.1). If the APs use several channels and bands (2.4/5/6 GHz), you see only part. ② Data frames are encrypted with WPA2 or WPA3. WPA2-Personal needs the passphrase plus the 4-way handshake, and WPA3-Personal (SAE) is designed so that knowing the password still doesn't allow passive decryption. ③ The capture box's wireless chip must support the standard and channel width the network uses. ④ Wireless capture carries heavy legal constraints, so get legal advice first. In practice, wireless controller logs and capture on the wired side behind the APs are the more realistic evidence sources.

docs.text:

  • IETF, RFC 8446: TLS 1.3, section 1.2. Static RSA and static DH cipher suites removed; all public-key-based key exchange provides forward secrecy.
  • IETF, RFC 9849: TLS Encrypted Client Hello (published March 2026; checked through search results on 2026-11-05).
  • IETF, RFC 8484: DNS Queries over HTTPS, RFC 7858: DNS over TLS, RFC 9250: DNS over Dedicated QUIC Connections.
  • IETF, RFC 2784: GRE, RFC 4213: Basic Transition Mechanisms for IPv6 (IPv6 over IPv4 tunnels), RFC 1918: private addresses, RFC 791: IP.
