docs.title: Lesson 1.6 — The Container for Packets: libpcap, tcpdump, and the pcap/pcapng File Format
Lesson 1.6 — The Container for Packets: libpcap, tcpdump, and the pcap/pcapng File Format
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

At the end of lesson 1.5 we said "if you can't extract a commercial cache, go to the data that crossed the wire: packets". This lesson covers the container those packets come in.

  • What libpcap is, and why tcpdump, Wireshark and tshark all run on top of it
  • Reading the pcap file header (24 bytes) and the per-packet record header (16 bytes) byte by byte
  • Snapshot length (snaplen) and truncated packets
  • What pcapng adds, its standardisation status, and what you lose converting to pcap
  • The basic tcpdump capture command, and what the statistics at the end mean

BPF filter syntax is lesson 1.7; practical tcpdump options and the Wireshark window are lesson 1.8.

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) in this lesson comes from Ubuntu packages tcpdump 4.99.4 (libpcap 1.10.4) and tshark 4.2.2 installed in this work environment, really capturing traffic exchanged with a test web server (127.0.0.1:8082) on the loopback interface (lo) of the same machine. As of 2026-11-05 the latest tags of each project are tcpdump 4.99.7, libpcap 1.11.0 and Wireshark stable 4.6.16 (checked from repository tags). Versions keep moving, so "latest" means as of that date.

docs.title: 1. A pcap file someone hands you
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) The day after lesson 1.4's incident, the network team hands over research-1014.pcap: "packets captured on the research segment tap during the incident window". You'll want to open it in Wireshark straight away, but first there are questions to ask.

  • What time zone are the times in this file in?
  • Are the packets whole, or only their first part?
  • What kind of link (Ethernet, wireless, etc.) was it captured on?
  • How many interfaces was it captured on, and were packets missed during capture?

Some of these answers are written in the file itself. Knowing the container's structure lets you judge, before even opening it, "what this evidence can and can't do".

docs.title: 2. An analogy: a recording tape and its label
docs.text:
Think of a packet capture file as a recording tape. At the very front is a label: "this tape was recorded this way, at this quality, with this camera". And each scene on the tape has the time it was recorded and its length.

A pcap file is the same. The file header at the front is the label (format, the most bytes stored per packet, the kind of link), and the record header in front of each packet is the per-scene time and length.

There are differences from the analogy too. The old pcap format's label has no "which camera (interface) recorded it", and you can't put several cameras' footage on one tape. pcapng was created to fill this gap (section 6). Also, the tape's times follow the recording machine's clock. If that machine's clock was wrong, every scene's time is wrong together.

docs.title: 3. libpcap: the foundation under almost every packet tool
docs.text:
The most fundamental tool in network forensics is tcpdump. It captures packets from the network, then either shows as much of each packet's information as you want on screen or writes the whole packet (or part of it) to disk. It's a command-line tool, so it works on your own PC or a remote server, typed by a person or automated in a script. It started in the Unix world but has been ported to other operating systems, and is a staple for Windows and Unix-like administrators and investigators alike.

tcpdump's core features actually come from the libpcap library underneath it. Four of them matter most:

  1. The BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) language. A simple filter language that decides "capture only packets like this". It builds elaborate filters by combining defined basic units (primitives) with logic (lesson 1.7).
  2. Showing on screen or saving to a pcap file. pcap is a standardised format for storing packets on disk. Most of the data in this series is pcap files.
  3. Reading from a live network, or from a saved pcap file. As the reverse of saving, libpcap lets you read a saved file just as if it were arriving from the network now. From a forensic perspective this is huge: capture once, and years later you can analyse perfect copies of the original with many tools.
  4. Deciding how much to keep (snaplen). Keeping every byte is ideal, but legal or practical reasons sometimes prevent it. You can then keep only the first so many bytes of each packet, for example just the headers (section 5).

Because these features live in the library, not in tcpdump, other tools use exactly the same features. In fact the overwhelming majority of network analysis tools run on libpcap (or Npcap, its compatible implementation on Windows).

flowchart TD
    N["Network card"] --> K["OS kernel<br/>first-pass selection by BPF filter"]
    K --> L["libpcap"]
    L --> T["tcpdump · Wireshark · tshark<br/>dumpcap · Zeek · Arkime etc."]
    T --> F[("pcap / pcapng file")]
    F -->|"read again"| L

How to read the diagram: packets flow from top to bottom. The BPF filter in the kernel screens them first, and libpcap passes the result to the various tools. A file a tool writes is read back through libpcap, as the arrow looping back up shows, so any tool can analyse it again.

docs.title: 3.1 Wireshark and tshark
docs.text:
tcpdump is great for capture but doesn't offer much for deep interpretation of packet content. Wireshark takes over there. It's a graphical program for visually examining network traffic and doing useful high-level analysis. Its biggest strength is hundreds of protocol parsers (dissectors, decoders). Because they show what each field in a packet means, you get productive much faster than reading protocol standards (RFCs) from scratch. The community often contributes dissectors even for proprietary protocols without published standards, and you can write your own.

Wireshark ships with tshark, the same features on the command line. You can work out an analysis approach in the GUI, then carry it over to tshark to apply across many files at once. That's a workflow we'll use often in this series.

Wireshark can capture too, but its GUI and dissectors do a lot behind the scenes, so it doesn't suit high-volume capture. It's fine in a lab, but when traffic picks up you need a dedicated capture tool like tcpdump. Modern Wireshark hands capture itself to a separate program, dumpcap, which can also be used on its own without the GUI (lesson 1.9).

docs.title: 4. Dissecting a pcap file
docs.text:
Let's open the container. I captured traffic with the test web server on loopback using tcpdump to make full.pcap (actual output):

$ file full.pcap
full.pcap: pcap capture file, microsecond ts (little-endian) - version 2.4 (Ethernet, capture length 262144)
$ hexdump -C full.pcap | head -3
00000000  d4 c3 b2 a1 02 00 04 00  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  |................|
00000010  00 00 04 00 01 00 00 00  6f ec eb 6a d4 fe 04 00  |........o..j....|
00000020  4a 00 00 00 4a 00 00 00  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  |J...J...........|

docs.title: 4.1 The file header: the first 24 bytes
docs.text:
The first 24 bytes (0x00–0x17) are the file header. Read them four bytes at a time.

Offset Bytes Value Meaning 0x00 d4 c3 b2 a1 0xa1b2c3d4 Magic number: "this is a pcap file, times in microseconds" 0x04 02 00 · 04 00 2 · 4 Format version 2.4 0x08 00 00 00 00 0 The field older documents called "time zone offset" 0x0C 00 00 00 00 0 The field older documents called "timestamp accuracy" 0x10 00 00 04 00 262,144 Snapshot length (maximum bytes stored per packet) 0x14 01 00 00 00 1 Link-layer type. 1 = Ethernet

Magic number and byte order. Notice that the "Bytes" and "Value" columns are reversed? Computers store multi-byte numbers either smallest part first (little-endian) or largest part first (big-endian). Today's Intel and AMD x86 and x86-64 are little-endian, so the value 0xa1b2c3d4 is written d4 c3 b2 a1 in the file. That's why the first four bytes of the most common pcap files are d4 c3 b2 a1. A file made on a very old big-endian machine shows a1 b2 c3 d4. These four bytes also tell a program "in which order to read the numbers in this file". That's why file reported (little-endian).

Also, if the magic number is 0xa1b23c4d (4d 3c b2 a1 in the file), the format is the same but the fractional part of packet times is nanoseconds rather than microseconds. Even within pcap, interpret the times according to the magic number.

[Changed] The time zone and accuracy fields. The source material describes these two fields as "time zone always 0 because it's always UTC, accuracy also 0". Today's libpcap file format documentation defines both as "not used": writers should fill them with 0, readers must ignore them, and it notes that some older writers stored non-zero values (checked 2026-11-05 in the pcap-savefile documentation on the libpcap 1.10 branch). The practical conclusion is the same: pcap packet times are counted from 1 January 1970 UTC, so they have no time zone, and whatever value is in these fields must not be used to adjust times.

Snapshot length. The most bytes stored per packet. 262,144 is tcpdump 4.99's default (confirmed in the tcpdump documentation). The source material's example is a good one: if every packet in an IPv4 pcap file is 40 bytes or less, were they truncated by a network error, or did someone capture with only 40 bytes? This field gives the answer. Defaults varied widely across tool versions and operating systems (old tcpdump defaulted to 68 or 96 bytes at times), so test and confirm tools before using them.

Link-layer type. The kind of medium it was captured from. 1 is Ethernet; there are many other values, such as wireless (802.11), Linux's "any" pseudo-interface (LINUX_SLL) and raw IP. The full list is in the pcap-linktype documentation. If this value is wrong, programs misinterpret a packet's first bytes. This lab used loopback yet showed 1 (Ethernet), because Linux presents loopback in Ethernet form.

docs.title: 4.2 The record header: 16 bytes per packet
docs.text:
After the file header come zero or more packets, each preceded by a 16-byte record header. In the hexdump above, the first packet's record header starts at 0x18.

Offset Bytes Value Meaning 0x18 6f ec eb 6a 0x6aebec6f = 1,793,846,383 Capture time, seconds (Unix time) 0x1C d4 fe 04 00 0x0004fed4 = 327,380 Microseconds after that second 0x20 4a 00 00 00 74 Bytes stored in the file (caplen) 0x24 4a 00 00 00 74 Bytes originally on the wire (len)

The calculation (actual output):

$ date -u -d @$((0x6aebec6f))
Thu Nov  5 02:39:43 UTC 2026
$ echo $((0x0004fed4))
327380

$((0x6aebec6f)) asks the shell to turn hex into decimal. The first packet was captured at 02:39:43.327380 UTC on 2026-11-05. capinfos on the same file confirms it (actual output, partial):

$ capinfos -M full.pcap
File name:           full.pcap
File type:           pcap
File encapsulation:  ether
File timestamp precision:  microseconds (6)
Packet size limit:   file hdr: 262144 bytes
Number of packets:   36
...
First packet time:   2026-11-05 02:39:43.327380
...
SHA256:              f734f65f4e69efec6bc4daa9b3bba40c9d379d61835aab27f45e09eded9f8957
Strict time order:   True

capinfos, included with Wireshark, summarises a capture file (-M shows large numbers in full instead of abbreviating them as 1k, 1M). It's the first command to run when someone hands you a file: file type, snapshot length, packet count, first and last packet times and even hashes, all at once. Strict time order: True means the packets are in time order; a result of merging several files may show False.

[Caution] Packet times are "the capturing machine's clock". The record header's time isn't an objective time the packet crossed the wire; it's what the machine that captured it stamped with its own clock. If the capture device's clock was five minutes fast, every packet is stamped five minutes fast. So check whether the capture device was synchronised with NTP (network time synchronisation), and align a few points with other evidence (e.g. lesson 1.3's proxy logs) for the same events, recording the offset.

docs.title: 5. Truncated packets: reducing the snapshot length
docs.text:
I also captured the same traffic with -s 96 (only 96 bytes per packet) for comparison (actual output):

$ capinfos -M snap96.pcap | grep "Packet size"
Packet size limit:   file hdr: 96 bytes
Packet size limit:   inferred: 96 bytes
$ tshark -r snap96.pcap -T fields -e frame.number -e frame.cap_len -e frame.len | awk '$2!=$3' | head -4
4   96  143
6   96  252
8   96  98
16  96  153

The second command extracts each packet's number, stored length (frame.cap_len, the record header's caplen) and original length (frame.len, len), then uses awk to keep only packets where they differ. Packet 4 was originally 143 bytes but only 96 were stored. Its content shows where it was cut (actual output, partial):

$ tcpdump -n -r snap96.pcap -A -c 4
...
.V7....(GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.

-A shows packet content as text. The HTTP request breaks off at Host: 127.0.0.. The IP and TCP headers (who talked to whom, on which port, when) are intact, but the content after them survives only up to 96 bytes.

That's the two sides of snapshot length:

  • Why reduce it: it saves a lot of storage, and keeps only headers when law or privacy policy forbids storing content. It also reduces processing load.
  • What you lose: content is cut, so file carving (lesson 1.5) and payload analysis are impossible. You can't answer "what was exchanged", only "who talked to whom, when and how much". On lesson 1.1's spectrum, this evidence sits somewhere between full packets and flows.

So when packets are truncated, check the file header's snapshot length first. If it's 96, they were captured that way on purpose; if it's 262144 and they're still cut, look for another cause (a problem with the capture device, etc.).

docs.title: 6. pcapng: the next-generation format
docs.text:
The old pcap format has limits. A file holds only one interface and one link type, you can't choose timestamp precision, and there's nowhere to leave notes or capture information. pcapng (pcap next generation) was created to fix this. Its structure is completely different from the old format: an extensible structure that chains units called blocks. Commonly cited benefits:

  • Packets from several interfaces (even of different types) in one file
  • Better timestamp precision options
  • Rich metadata such as comments, capture statistics and name resolution (DNS) records

Capturing the same traffic with tshark to make a pcapng file shows the difference (actual output, partial):

$ file capture.pcapng
capture.pcapng: pcapng capture file - version 1.0
$ capinfos -M capture.pcapng
...
Capture hardware:    Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz (with SSE4.2)
Capture oper-sys:    Linux 6.18.44-fc-v236
Capture application: Dumpcap (Wireshark) 4.2.2 (Git v4.2.2 packaged as 4.2.2-1.1build3)
Number of interfaces in file: 1
Interface #0 info:
                     Name = lo
                     Encapsulation = Ethernet (1 - ether)
                     Capture length = 262144
                     Time precision = nanoseconds (9)
                     Filter string = tcp port 8082

Information pcap didn't have is visible: which interface (lo), which filter (tcp port 8082), which program, OS and hardware captured it, and that times are at nanosecond precision. For an investigator, that's a valuable record of "how this evidence was made". A preserved capture filter in particular tells you "what was missing from this file from the start". Captured with tcp port 8082, it's normal that other traffic such as DNS isn't there at all.

docs.title: 6.1 [Changed] Standardisation and compatibility
docs.text:
The source material says pcapng "was proposed in the IETF in 2004 but is still a draft, and critical tools don't fully support it, so convert to legacy pcap wherever possible". Status as checked on 2026-11-05:

  • Standardisation: pcapng is still an IETF Internet-Draft. The latest revision is draft-ietf-opsawg-pcapng-05 from March 2026. A separate draft describing the old pcap format (draft-ietf-opsawg-pcap-08, May 2026) targets "Historic" status and states that pcapng replaces that format.

  • Support: Wireshark, tshark and dumpcap use pcapng as their default save format. libpcap can read pcapng files too, but its documentation says "not all pcapng files can be read". For example, a file mixing several interfaces with different link types may not be read correctly by libpcap-based tools. In this lab, tcpdump 4.99.4 read the simple file without problems (actual output):

    $ tcpdump -n -r capture.pcapng | head -2
reading from file capture.pcapng, link-type EN10MB (Ethernet), snapshot length 262144
02:39:43.327380 IP 127.0.0.1.36314 > 127.0.0.1.8082: Flags [S], seq 833062265, ...

docs.title: 6.2 Converting to pcap, and what you lose
docs.text:
When you must feed pcapng to an untested tool, Wireshark's command-line tool editcap converts it to legacy pcap (actual output):

$ editcap -F pcap capture.pcapng converted.pcap
$ file converted.pcap
converted.pcap: pcap capture file, microsecond ts (little-endian) - version 2.4 (Ethernet, capture length 262144)
$ capinfos -M converted.pcap | grep -i precision
File timestamp precision:  microseconds (6)

-F pcap means "output format pcap". The conversion worked, but the converted file lacks the interface name, capture filter and capture program, OS and hardware information seen in section 6, and timestamp precision dropped from nanoseconds to microseconds. pcap has nowhere to hold that information.

So it's better to apply the source material's "convert to pcap wherever possible" with an adjustment:

  1. Preserve the original pcapng as evidence and record its hash.
  2. Convert only a working copy for the tool that needs it, and record when and with what command you converted it.
  3. Interpret results from the converted copy alongside the original's metadata (interface, filter, precision).

docs.title: 7. Capturing with tcpdump
docs.text:
Now the capture command. Its basic form:

sudo tcpdump -n -s 0 -i ens33 -w out.pcap 'host 203.0.113.5 and port 80'
Part Meaning Why sudo Run with administrator rights Capturing directly from an interface usually needs administrator rights -n Don't turn addresses into names or ports into service names Generates no name lookup traffic (OPSEC), and is faster -s 0 Snapshot length 0 = the default maximum (262,144 bytes) Keep whole packets. Defaults varied across versions, so say it explicitly -i ens33 Capture on interface ens33 tcpdump -D lists usable interfaces -w out.pcap Save to a file instead of the screen Analyse again later with any tool 'host 203.0.113.5 and port 80' BPF filter Only packets involving that address and port 80 (lesson 1.7)

Almost always add -n. Without it, tcpdump does a DNS lookup for every IP it sees. Besides slowing things down, if the attacker watches their own DNS server, they learn "someone looked up my address". That's the OPSEC issue we've discussed since lesson 1.2.

Wrap BPF filters in quotes. If the shell interprets characters in the filter such as spaces and parentheses first, you get a different filter from what you meant. Single or double quotes are the best habit.

tcpdump -D lists interfaces (actual output, partial):

$ tcpdump -D
1.eth0 [Up, Running, Connected]
2.any (Pseudo-device that captures on all interfaces) [Up, Running]
3.lo [Up, Running, Loopback]
...

Promiscuous mode. A network card normally accepts only packets addressed to itself. For capture, the card is switched to promiscuous mode to accept packets not addressed to it, which needs administrator rights. tcpdump turns promiscuous mode on by default. But on a switched network promiscuous mode alone doesn't show other people's traffic, because the switch never sends their packets to that port in the first place. That's why taps or switch mirroring are needed, covered in lesson 1.11. Note that capturing on Linux's any interface doesn't use promiscuous mode.

[Supplement] The user that writes the file. For security, tcpdump on many Linux distributions drops administrator rights after starting capture and writes the file as an ordinary user such as tcpdump. So saving with -w to a folder that user can't write may give a permission error. In this lab I used -Z root to stop it switching users. In practice it's better to set up permissions on a dedicated capture folder.

docs.title: 7.1 The three numbers at the end
docs.text:
When capture stops, tcpdump shows statistics (actual output):

tcpdump: listening on lo, link-type EN10MB (Ethernet), snapshot length 262144 bytes
36 packets captured
72 packets received by filter
0 packets dropped by kernel
Line Meaning (per tcpdump documentation) packets captured Packets tcpdump actually received and processed packets received by filter Meaning varies by OS. It may count packets regardless of the filter, or include packets that matched but haven't been processed yet packets dropped by kernel Packets the OS capture mechanism discarded for lack of buffer space. 0 if the OS doesn't report it

In this lab, 72 "received" versus 36 "captured" looks odd, but as documented, the meaning of this number depends on the OS and configuration. The reason it was exactly double here is a property of the loopback interface, confirmed from the libpcap source in lesson 1.10, section 5.1. The important point is not to read it as "36 were missed". To see missed packets, look at the last line, dropped by kernel.

And 0 dropped doesn't guarantee nothing was missed. It counts only what was discarded inside the capturing machine. Packets discarded before that, for example by an overflowing switch mirror port, are invisible to this machine. And even with -s 0 to keep whole packets, packets are lost if the capture machine's CPU can't keep up, or if the storage can't write as fast as the link delivers. So test capture equipment at real speed and scale before relying on it in operations.

docs.title: 7.2 Reading a captured file
docs.text:
Read a saved file back with -r (actual output, partial):

$ tcpdump -n -r full.pcap -A 'tcp[((tcp[12]&0xf0)>>2):4] = 0x47455420' | head -4
02:39:43.327455 IP 127.0.0.1.36314 > 127.0.0.1.8082: Flags [P.], seq 833062266:833062343, ack 1449026129, win 64, options [nop,nop,TS val 3495311331 ecr 3503756584], length 77
E...H.@.@...............1..zV^bQ...@.u.....
.V7....(GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8082

The filter at the end is BPF meaning "packets whose TCP data starts with the four bytes GET". It looks daunting now, but lesson 1.7 unpacks it piece by piece. In full.pcap the same request is visible intact up to Host: 127.0.0.1:8082. Compare with section 5's truncated file.

docs.title: 8. How to interpret it in a real investigation
docs.text:
Given section 1's research-1014.pcap, before opening it:

  1. Make a copy and record a hash. Leave the original untouched and analyse the copy (sha256sum, or capinfos's SHA256).
  2. Check the container with capinfos. Format (pcap/pcapng), snapshot length (is the content intact?), link type, first and last packet times (does it cover the incident window?), packet count, time order.
  3. If it's pcapng, record the metadata. Interface name, capture filter (what was left out from the start), capture program, comments.
  4. Ask about capture conditions. At which tap or mirror point (lesson 1.1 section 10's tap positions), which direction, with what equipment. Are there statistics on packets dropped during capture? Was the capture device's clock right?
  5. From that, write down "what this file can do". E.g. "snapshot length 96, so no file carving; only connection records and header analysis possible", or "capture filter was tcp, so no DNS (mostly UDP)".

These five lines become the "evidence description" part of the report. Later, when someone says "X isn't in this file, so X didn't happen", they're also the basis for telling whether that's a limit of the evidence or X really didn't happen.

docs.title: 9. Summary
docs.text:
• Most tools, such as tcpdump, Wireshark, tshark and Zeek, run on libpcap. BPF filters, pcap saving and reading, and snapshot length are all libpcap features, so the same principles hold across tools.
  • Capture once into pcap, and years later you can re-analyse perfect copies of the original with many tools.
  • A pcap file consists of a 24-byte file header (magic number, version, two unused fields, snapshot length, link type) and a 16-byte record header per packet (seconds, microseconds or nanoseconds, stored length, original length).
  • Magic d4 c3 b2 a1 is little-endian microseconds; 4d 3c b2 a1 is nanoseconds. Packet times are UTC Unix time and follow the capturing machine's clock.
  • If the stored length is shorter than the original length, the packet is truncated. Check the file header's snapshot length to see whether that was intended.
  • pcapng holds several interfaces, nanosecond precision, and metadata such as interface names, capture filters and capture environment. As of 2026 it's still an IETF draft but is the default format for the Wireshark family. Converting to pcap loses this information, so preserve the original.
  • When capturing, add -n, quote the filter, and check dropped by kernel at the end. Even 0 can't tell you what was missed outside the capture machine.

In the next lesson (1.7) we unpack the BPF filters glimpsed here step by step, from primitives to byte-level conditions.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. A capture file's first four bytes are 4d 3c b2 a1. What does that tell you? What happens if you interpret this file's packet times as microseconds?

Answer and explanation

As a value it's 0xa1b23c4d: a nanosecond-precision pcap file stored little-endian. The record header's second field is nanoseconds, not microseconds. Misread as microseconds, 0.327380123 seconds (327,380,123 ns), say, becomes 327,380,123 microseconds, i.e. a little over 327 seconds, giving a nonsensical time far past the next second. Most tools handle this from the magic number, but when writing a script that reads bytes directly, check the magic number first.

Question 2. (Calculation) The first 8 bytes of a pcap record header are 00 e1 f5 05 40 42 0f 00 (little-endian, microsecond format). When was this packet captured? Is anything odd about the second value?

Answer and explanation

The first four bytes 00 e1 f5 05, read backwards, are 0x05f5e100 = 100,000,000 seconds. date -u -d @100000000 gives 1973-03-03 09:46:40 UTC. The second four bytes 40 42 0f 00 are 0x000f4240 = 1,000,000, but the microsecond field must be 0–999,999. 1,000,000 should have rolled over into "the next second", so it's not valid for the format. Such a value signals that the file is corrupt, that it's really nanosecond format and the magic number was misread, or that the tool that made the file has a problem. The 1973 time itself also suggests the capture device's clock may have been in a reset state. Don't ignore such anomalies; record them in the evidence description.

Question 3. (Interpretation) Every packet in a pcap a colleague handed over is 68 bytes or less. The colleague says "there were only small packets on the network". How do you check?

Answer and explanation

Look at the file header's snapshot length (capinfos's "Packet size limit"). If it's 68, the packets weren't small; it was captured storing only up to 68 bytes. Some old tcpdump versions defaulted to 68, so this is common in files from old equipment or scripts. More definitively, compare each packet's stored length (caplen) with its original length (len) (tshark -T fields -e frame.cap_len -e frame.len). If many packets have an original length above 68, there were big packets but they were truncated. Then record the limitation that this file can't support content analysis or file carving.

Question 4. (Common misconception) After capture you see 1520 packets captured, 3040 packets received by filter, 0 packets dropped by kernel. A colleague wants to report "1,520 packets were missed". Right?

Answer and explanation

Wrong. Per the tcpdump documentation, the meaning of received by filter varies by OS, and may count regardless of the filter. Packets discarded by the capture machine are dropped by kernel, which is 0. So the correct reading is "no packets were discarded inside the capture machine". Even that doesn't mean "nothing at all was missed". Packets discarded before the capture machine, by a mirror port or tap, don't appear in this number, so check those devices' statistics too.

Question 5. (Conversion) To feed evidence.pcapng, received as incident evidence, into an old analysis tool, you converted it with editcap -F pcap. What should go in the report, and what's the problem with keeping only the converted copy instead of the original?

Answer and explanation

The report should give the original file and its hash, the conversion date, command (editcap -F pcap evidence.pcapng work.pcap) and tool version, and the converted copy's hash, and state that the converted copy was used for analysis. Keeping only the converted copy permanently loses information that existed only in pcapng. As section 6.2 showed, the interface name, capture filter, capture program, OS and hardware, comments and nanosecond precision disappear. If the file mixed several interfaces, you may lose which packet came from which. Then you can no longer answer questions like "which tap did this packet come from?" or "was anything excluded by the capture filter?" Preserve the original pcapng as it is.

Question 6. (Reading a command) Find what's wrong or risky in this command and fix it.

sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w case.pcap host 198.51.100.20 and (port 80 or port 443)
Answer and explanation
  1. No -n. When writing to a file, names aren't shown on screen, so the impact may be small, but add it out of habit. Run the same command without -w to view on screen, and tcpdump looks up every IP in DNS: an OPSEC problem.
  2. The BPF isn't quoted. The shell treats ( and ) as special characters, so this command either fails with a syntax error or behaves differently from what was meant.
  3. No -s 0. tcpdump 4.99 defaults to 262,144 bytes so it's fine, but older versions and other tools had small defaults, so stating it is a good habit.

Fixed: sudo tcpdump -n -s 0 -i eth0 -w case.pcap 'host 198.51.100.20 and (port 80 or port 443)'

Question 7. (pcapng metadata) A pcapng file's capinfos output shows Filter string = not port 22. What does this mean for an investigation?

Answer and explanation

This file was captured excluding port 22 (mostly SSH) traffic from the start. So SSH traffic not appearing in this file doesn't mean "there was no SSH traffic"; it means it was outside the collection scope. If the attacker came in over SSH or tunnelled through SSH, this file can't tell you, and you need other evidence such as flow records or the server's authentication logs. Also record why the capture administrator excluded SSH (to cut management traffic, etc.). In the old pcap format this information wouldn't be in the file, and you couldn't know without asking whoever captured it.

Question 8. (Time) The first packet time in a pcap from the capture device is 2026-10-14 15:02:10, and the proxy log (lesson 1.4) recording the same moment says 15:07:10. Both are UTC. What do you suspect, and how should you handle it?

Answer and explanation

The pcap's time is the capture device's clock; the proxy log's time is the proxy server's clock. Five minutes apart for the same event means one (or both) clocks are likely wrong. As lesson 1.3 showed, Squid records when a request finished, but for a short request that doesn't explain five minutes. Check: both devices' NTP configuration and sync records, and the times in a third record of the same event (firewall, DNS server). Handling: don't alter the original times; record with evidence which device was off and by how much, and when building the timeline, apply that correction explicitly. Don't assume one side is "right" without evidence.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• The Tcpdump Group, libpcap 1.10 branch pcap-savefile documentation source (checked 2026-11-05). Magic numbers 0xa1b2c3d4 and 0xa1b23c4d, the definition of two fields as "not used (writers 0, readers ignore)", the snapshot length and link-type fields, and the record header structure.
  • The Tcpdump Group, libpcap 1.10 pcap_open_offline documentation source (checked 2026-11-05). pcapng can be read, but not all pcapng files can be.
  • The Tcpdump Group, tcpdump 4.99 branch tcpdump.1 documentation source (checked 2026-11-05). Default snapshot length 262,144 bytes, -r reads pcapng files too, promiscuous mode and the any interface, and the meaning of the end-of-capture statistics.
  • IETF, draft-ietf-opsawg-pcapng (revision -05, March 2026, confirmed by search 2026-11-05) and draft-ietf-opsawg-pcap (revision -08, May 2026, targeting Historic status).
  • tcpdump, libpcap and Wireshark repository tags (checked 2026-11-05 with git ls-remote --tags): tcpdump-4.99.7, libpcap-1.11.0, Wireshark v4.6.16.

About this page

docs.title: Lesson 1.5 — Commercial Proxy Logs, and Pulling Responses Out of the Proxy Cache
Lesson 1.5 — Commercial Proxy Logs, and Pulling Responses Out of the Proxy Cache
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

The last lesson of the web proxy unit:

  • Reading commercial proxy logs: find the field definitions first, and check whether more detailed logs already exist
  • What a proxy cache keeps and doesn't keep (refresh_pattern and response headers)
  • The folder layout of a Squid cache, and the internal structure of one cache file
  • Finding cache objects of interest (grep, strings) and turning them back into original files (carving)
  • Checking the extracted file: identifying its type, comparing hashes, decompressing, opening it safely
  • Why commercial proxy caches are hard, and what to turn to instead

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) in this lesson comes from installing the Ubuntu package Squid 6.14 in this work environment, running a test web server I wrote (127.0.0.1:8081, with the example domains mapped to that address), fetching files through the proxy, and examining the real cache files that resulted. Times show the lab date (2026-11-05 UTC). Squid 6 is out of support upstream but still common as a distribution package, and for what this lesson covers its cache file structure matches the Squid 7 documentation. The commercial log example is a sample I made.

docs.title: 1. Commercial proxy logs: "find the rules first"
docs.text:
Lesson 1.4's investigation could go straight to shell commands because the Squid log was plain text. What about the commercial proxies common in enterprises? As lesson 1.2 said, the data is there, but getting it out and reading it takes more effort.

Appliances such as Broadcom's Edge SWG (ProxySG), for example, accumulate logs on the device and export them in batches (e.g. over FTP), or send them through SIEM connectors. The logs you receive are usually in the W3C Extended Log File Format (ELFF). Its distinguishing feature is a header at the top of the file with lines starting #, among which the #Fields: line gives the name of each column in order. Here's a sample I made:

#Software: ExampleProxy 1.0
#Version: 1.0
#Date: 2026-10-14 15:00:00
#Fields: date time time-taken c-ip sc-status s-action sc-bytes cs-bytes cs-method cs-uri-scheme cs-host cs-uri-port cs-uri-path cs-uri-query cs-username cs-auth-group s-hierarchy s-supplier-name rs(Content-Type) cs(Referer) cs(User-Agent) sc-filter-result cs-categories x-virus-id s-ip
2026-10-14 15:48:26 212 10.10.6.14 302 TCP_NC_MISS 727 664912 POST https paste.example 443 /post - jdoe LAB\research DIRECT 198.51.100.40 text/html "https://paste.example/" "Mozilla/5.0 (...) Firefox/144.0" OBSERVED "Pastebins" - 10.10.4.3

Field names follow a rule. The leading letters give the direction. c is the client, s the proxy itself (server), r the origin server (remote); cs- means "sent by the client to the proxy", sc- "sent by the proxy to the client", and rs() "a header sent by the origin server". So cs-bytes is how much the client uploaded, and sc-bytes how much the client received.

Here's an important connection to lesson 1.4. There, Squid's default log had no upload size, so we couldn't tell how much went to the paste site. This sample line shows cs-bytes as 664,912 bytes. The commercial appliance's example format shown in the source material includes cs-bytes too. It depends on the device and configuration, so always check, but it means commercial logs may hold more than plain Squid logs. Fields like cs-categories (URL category) and sc-filter-result (policy verdict) aren't in Squid's default log either.

docs.title: 1.1 A shell command that finds fields by name
docs.text:
ELFF column order varies with device configuration, so memorising column numbers breaks on another device. Instead, read the #Fields: line to build a "name → number" table and extract fields by name, and the same command works under any configuration. Some fields (User-Agent and others) are quoted and contain spaces, so the script also keeps quoted values together as one field.

# Build a "field name -> number" table from the #Fields header, then extract fields by name.
/^#Fields:/ { for (i = 2; i <= NF; i++) col[$i] = i - 1; next }
/^#/ { next }
{
  n = 0; line = $0
  while (length(line) > 0) {
    sub(/^ +/, "", line)
    if (substr(line, 1, 1) == "\"") { m = index(substr(line, 2), "\""); f[++n] = substr(line, 2, m - 1); line = substr(line, m + 2) }
    else { m = index(line, " "); if (m == 0) { f[++n] = line; line = "" } else { f[++n] = substr(line, 1, m - 1); line = substr(line, m + 1) } }
  }
  print f[col["date"]], f[col["time"]], f[col["c-ip"]], f[col["cs-username"]], f[col["cs-method"]], f[col["cs-host"]] f[col["cs-uri-path"]], f[col["sc-status"]], "out=" f[col["cs-bytes"]], "cat=" f[col["cs-categories"]]
}

col[$i] = i - 1 subtracts 1 because #Fields: itself is the first field, so the real names start from the second. Run against a three-line sample (actual output):

$ awk -f elff.awk elff.log
2026-10-14 15:48:26 10.10.6.14 jdoe POST paste.example/post 302 out=664912 cat=Pastebins
2026-10-14 15:55:48 10.10.6.14 jdoe GET customs.example/files/form-cm105.pdf 200 out=512 cat=Government
2026-10-14 15:56:02 10.10.7.15 - GET c2.example.net/gate 403 out=389 cat=Malicious Sources

docs.title: 1.2 What to check before interpreting commercial logs
docs.text:
• Find the rules (field definitions) first. Fields with the same name can mean slightly different things across vendors and versions. Interpret only after checking the vendor's field documentation (e.g. Broadcom's Edge SWG access log fields article) and that device's actual log format configuration. In particular, don't assume s-action values (TCP_HIT, TCP_NC_MISS, TCP_DENIED, etc.) are defined the same as Squid's cache statuses just because the names look similar.
  • Check the time zone. ELFF date and time are usually UTC, but device settings can make them local time. Look at the #Date: header together with the device configuration.
  • Check whether more detailed logs already exist. Commercial devices may keep several logs besides the access log: policy verdict logs, malware scan logs, authentication logs. What operations normally send to the SIEM may be a subset of fields. The originals on the device may be richer, so ask first what exists and how far back.

docs.title: 2. The proxy cache: what's kept and what isn't
docs.text: Now to the cache. Back to lesson 1.2's analogy, the cache is the purchasing desk's storeroom. Its original purpose was keeping copies of frequently requested content to save slow links. For investigators, those copies can be important clues, such as malware delivered to victims and material sent outside. To use them, you need to know two things: which responses the proxy decides to keep, and in what form it stores them.

docs.title: 2.1 Who decides whether to keep it?
docs.text:
A proxy that receives a response weighs three things.

  1. Did the server say it may be kept? The response headers Cache-Control and Expires give instructions. Cache-Control: max-age=1209600 means "fresh for 1,209,600 seconds (14 days); use it without asking again until then", no-store means "don't store this at all", and private means "this is personal; don't store it in a shared cache (a proxy)".
  2. What if the server said nothing? Then the proxy's refresh_pattern rules estimate "how long to treat it as fresh".
  3. Other conditions. Size limits, objects excluded from caching by ACL, responses with cookies and more.

refresh_pattern looks like this, the final line found in lesson 1.2's example and most configurations:

refresh_pattern .               0       20%     4320
Position Value Meaning (per Squid 7 documentation) Regular expression . Pattern applied to URLs. . means "any character", so it matches every URL min 0 Minimum minutes an object without a server-given expiry is treated as fresh. 0 means "never assume fresh by default" percent 20% When there's a Last-Modified header but no max-age or Expires, the percentage of (response time − last modified time) used as the freshness period max 4320 Maximum minutes an object without a server-given expiry is treated as fresh (4,320 minutes = 3 days)

A worked example. If an image response has neither max-age nor Expires, and Last-Modified is 10 days before the response time, the freshness period is 10 days × 20% = 2 days. That's between min (0 minutes) and max (3 days), so for 2 days the cached copy is served without asking the server. If Last-Modified were 100 days earlier, 20% would be 20 days, but max caps it at 3 days. And if there's no Last-Modified at all, there's no basis for percent, so min applies, 0 minutes: "not fresh" as soon as it arrives.

The source material continues from here to "min is 0, so nothing is cached unless the server instructs it, which is why the pastes weren't in the cache". But testing it myself showed something slightly different.

docs.title: 2.2 [Correction] What testing showed: "not fresh" is not "not stored"
docs.text:
I prepared four responses on the test web server differing only in headers, fetched each once through Squid 6.14, and checked the cache folder (actual output):

Test response Cache-related headers Stored as a cache file? PDF form Cache-Control: max-age=1209600, Last-Modified present Stored. A repeat request gave TCP_MEM_HIT Script (gzip-compressed) Cache-Control: public, max-age=7200 Stored Paste ① No cache-related headers Stored. A repeat request was logged TCP_REFRESH_MODIFIED (fetched anew from the server), and the cache file changed to a new number Paste ② Cache-Control: no-store Not stored Paste ③ Cache-Control: private + Set-Cookie Not stored

The third row is the key. The response with no instructions was judged "not fresh", so it wasn't served as-is on the next request, but it was stored on disk. And until a new response replaced it on the next request, that copy stayed in the cache folder.

So the right summary for investigators:

  • If the server sent no-store or private, there's almost no chance of finding it in the cache. Pages after login and web apps that serve different content per person use these headers a lot.
  • If there were no instructions, it may have been stored. But a repeat request for the same URL replaces it with a new copy, and when the cache fills, the oldest objects are deleted.
  • So don't conclude "this site isn't cached" from zero cache search hits. Conversely, if something turns up, you were lucky, and you must check when that copy was stored (the Date header, section 4).

Why the pastes in the source material's case weren't in the cache can only be known by checking the headers the real site sent (cookies, private, etc.). Note too that this test was one version, Squid 6.14, against a simple test server, so other versions or settings (refresh_pattern options such as store-stale or ignore-private) may behave differently. If an administrator used options like ignore-private or ignore-no-store to cache more than the standard allows, there's more evidence, but correspondingly bigger privacy issues. That too is something to check in the config first, as in lesson 1.2.

docs.title: 3. The folder layout of a Squid cache
docs.text:
To secure the cache, first know where it is. The starting point is always the config file:

cache_dir ufs /var/spool/squid 100 16 256

You read this line in lesson 1.2. It gives the storage type (ufs), location, maximum size (MB), number of first-level folders (16) and second-level folders (256). The source material describes the default size as 100 MB, which is closer to the example value distributions put in their default config; in practice most administrators make it much larger. And as lesson 1.2 showed, per the Squid 7 documentation, with no cache_dir line at all there's no disk cache.

Two things to watch when securing it:

  • There may be several cache_dir lines. Squid then spreads cache objects across several folders. Copy one folder and you miss part of it, so secure every path in the config.
  • The storage type may differ. Besides ufs, aufs and diskd use the same family of folder layout, but rock is a completely different structure that packs objects into one large file. If you see a non-default type, learn that type's structure first.

ufs cache files appear at paths like these (actual output):

$ find /var/tmp/squid-lab/spool -type f -name '0*' | sort
/var/tmp/squid-lab/spool/00/00/00000000
/var/tmp/squid-lab/spool/00/00/00000001
/var/tmp/squid-lab/spool/00/00/00000002

That's two hex digits / two hex digits / eight hex digits, like 00/00/00000000. Unfortunately these names tell you nothing about the original URL, file type, size or time; they're just numbers assigned in storage order. So you have to open them.

docs.title: 4. Inside one cache file
docs.text:
Run file on a cache file and it usually just says "data" (binary). But there's plenty of readable text mixed in, so a handful can be taken apart by eye. Here's the start of the cache file holding the PDF, with hexdump -C (actual output, partial):

$ hexdump -C 00/00/00000000 | head -26
00000000  03 90 00 00 00 03 10 00  00 00 60 e8 f8 2b d1 ab  |..........`..+..|
...
00000050  68 74 74 70 3a 2f 2f 66  69 6c 65 73 2e 65 78 61  |http://files.exa|
00000060  6d 70 6c 65 2e 6e 65 74  3a 38 30 38 31 2f 66 69  |mple.net:8081/fi|
00000070  6c 65 73 2f 66 6f 72 6d  2d 63 6d 31 30 35 2e 70  |les/form-cm105.p|
00000080  64 66 00 0a 08 00 00 00  71 02 00 00 00 00 00 00  |df......q.......|
00000090  48 54 54 50 2f 31 2e 30  20 32 30 30 20 4f 4b 0d  |HTTP/1.0 200 OK.|
000000a0  0a 53 65 72 76 65 72 3a  20 42 61 73 65 48 54 54  |.Server: BaseHTT|
...
00000120  61 63 68 65 2d 43 6f 6e  74 72 6f 6c 3a 20 6d 61  |ache-Control: ma|
00000130  78 2d 61 67 65 3d 31 32  30 39 36 30 30 0d 0a 4c  |x-age=1209600..L|
...
00000160  33 3a 30 30 3a 30 30 20  47 4d 54 0d 0a 0d 0a 25  |3:00:00 GMT....%|
00000170  50 44 46 2d 31 2e 34 0a  31 20 30 20 6f 62 6a 3c  |PDF-1.4.1 0 obj<|

Each hexdump -C line has three parts. The left is the position in the file (hex byte offset), the middle the values of 16 bytes from that position (in hex), and the right, inside | |, the same bytes shown as characters, with unprintable values shown as ..

The file has four parts:

flowchart TD
    A["① Squid metadata<br/>0x00~ (binary)"] --> B["② Original URL<br/>0x50~ http://files.example.net..."]
    B --> C["③ HTTP response headers from the server<br/>0x90~ HTTP/1.0 200 OK ..."]
    C --> D["Separator 0d 0a 0d 0a<br/>(blank line)"]
    D --> E["④ Data: the body exactly as the server sent it<br/>0x16f~ %PDF-1.4 ..."]

How to read the diagram: top to bottom is front to back of the file. The 0x.. in each box is where that part starts in the hexdump above.

  1. Squid metadata. The binary values at the very start are information Squid attaches for its own management (the object's identifying key, timing information, etc.). Hard for a person to read.
  2. Original URL. Starting with the protocol marker (http://), the first readable text you notice.
  3. HTTP response headers. The headers the server originally sent, stored as-is: Date (when the server responded), Content-Type, Content-Length, Cache-Control, Last-Modified and so on.
  4. Data. The body starts after the blank line that ends the headers. From the start of the headers to the end of the file is exactly the response the server sent for the original request.

The separator 0d 0a 0d 0a between headers and body is set by the HTTP standard. 0d is carriage return (CR, back to the start of the line) and 0a line feed (LF, next line), so 0d 0a 0d 0a is "end the line, then end another with nothing on it": a blank line. HTTP places one blank line after the header lines before the body begins. In the hexdump above, 0d 0a 0d 0a sits at 0x16b–0x16e, and right after it, at 0x16f, 25 is %, the first character of %PDF.

[Supplement] Use the Date header to check "when is this copy from". Cache file names carry no time, but the stored response's Date header is when the server produced that response. This lab's file contained Date: Thu, 05 Nov 2026 02:30:45 GMT. It's the first clue for telling whether the file you found in the cache is the one received at the time of the incident, or a replaced copy from someone fetching the same URL later. Align this time with the matching request time in the proxy log.

docs.title: 5.1 Cast a wide net: grep -rail
docs.text:
Cache files contain the URL and headers as text, so grep can sweep the whole folder for files containing a name of interest (actual output):

$ cd /var/tmp/squid-lab/spool
$ grep -rail form-cm105 .
./00/00/00000000

The options one by one:

Option Meaning Why -r Search everything under the folder (recursive) The cache is spread across several folder levels -a Treat binary files as text Cache files are detected as binary, and otherwise their contents aren't shown -i Ignore case URLs and headers may mix case -l Print only file names, not matching lines So binary content doesn't clutter the screen -F Search literally, not as a regular expression Finds symbols like . as text, and is much faster

The first four together are often called "railgrep" (grep -rail). On a large cache, adding -F too, as in grep -railF 'files.example.net' ., is a good idea. But for objects whose body is stored compressed (gzip etc.), the text inside the body is compressed, so you can't find them by body content. URLs and headers aren't compressed, so searching by URL or file name is reliable.

docs.title: 5.2 A quick look at what it is: strings
docs.text:
strings shows quickly what a found file is. It extracts only runs of consecutive printable characters from a file, and -n 10 means "only runs of 10 or more", which filters out short accidental fragments in the binary (actual output):

$ strings -n 10 00/00/00000000 | head -8
http://files.example.net:8081/files/form-cm105.pdf
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Server: BaseHTTP/0.6 Python/3.13.18
Date: Thu, 05 Nov 2026 02:30:45 GMT
Content-Type: application/pdf
Content-Length: 402
Cache-Control: max-age=1209600
Last-Modified: Wed, 01 Oct 2025 03:00:00 GMT

The URL, result code, content type, size and even why it was cached (max-age) are visible at a glance. The headers themselves explain what this object is and why it stayed in the cache.

docs.title: 5.3 What's in the cache: listing URLs
docs.text:
To see many files at once, extract just the first line starting with http (= the original URL) from each (actual output):

$ for file in $(grep -rail 'example' .); do strings -n 10 "$file" | grep '^http' | head -n 1; done
http://cdn.example.net:8081/js/app.js
http://files.example.net:8081/files/form-cm105.pdf
http://paste.example:8081/k7Qm2x

for file in $( ... ); do ... done is shell syntax for running the inner command once per file name produced by the command in the parentheses. Inside, strings extracts the text runs, grep '^http' keeps only lines starting with http (^ means "start of line"), and head -n 1 takes the first. The result is "the list of URLs in the cache". The paste k7Qm2x, with the same name as in lesson 1.4, appears here because of section 2.2's test.

docs.title: 6. Pulling the original file out of the cache (carving)
docs.text: Now let's restore the PDF to its original file. Cutting just the wanted file out of a larger lump of data like this is called carving. The principle is simple: delete the separator 0d 0a 0d 0a and every byte before it, and what's left is the body the server sent, i.e. the original file.

docs.title: 6.1 By hand: a hex editor
docs.text: With only a few files, open a copy of the cache file in a hex editor (ghex or bless on Linux, HxD on Windows, etc.), find 0d 0a 0d 0a, delete it and everything before it, and save under a new name. Leave the original cache file untouched.

docs.title: 6.2 By command: the same job, repeatably
docs.text:
Doing it by hand is error-prone and hard to apply to many files. A small Python script that does the same job lets you reproduce the same result any time, which is also better for evidence handling.

import sys, hashlib
src, dst = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
data = open(src, "rb").read()
start = data.index(b"HTTP/")              # beginning of the stored response headers
sep = data.index(b"\r\n\r\n", start)       # end of headers (the blank line)
body = data[sep + 4:]
open(dst, "wb").write(body)
print(f"headers at 0x{start:x}, separator at 0x{sep:x}, body {len(body)} bytes")
print("sha256", hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest())

There's a reason the separator is searched for after HTTP/ rather than from the start of the file: the binary metadata at the front might happen to contain the same bytes as 0d 0a 0d 0a. The real separator is the first blank line after the headers begin. \r\n is how Python writes 0d 0a. The result (actual output):

$ python3 carve.py 00/00/00000000 out/carved.pdf
headers at 0x90, separator at 0x16b, body 402 bytes
sha256 120db0f4998cb4d20d6238a3a92d254a61b32e5f46175a91837c7f2ce9f0bbfb

The positions the script found (headers 0x90, separator 0x16b) match what we saw by eye in section 4's hexdump, and the 402-byte body matches the header's Content-Length: 402.

docs.title: 7.1 Identify the type: file
docs.text:
file compares the bytes at the start of a file against known file formats to tell you its type (actual output):

$ file out/carved.pdf
out/carved.pdf: PDF document, version 1.4, 1 page(s)

The header's Content-Type: application/pdf matches the actual content. Lesson 1.3 said the MIME type is only the server's claim; file is a quick, reasonable cross-check of that claim against the real content. If the server said PDF and file says executable, that is itself an important finding.

docs.title: 7.2 Compare hashes
docs.text:
In this lab the original file is on the test server, so the hashes can be compared directly (actual output):

$ sha256sum www/form-cm105.pdf
120db0f4998cb4d20d6238a3a92d254a61b32e5f46175a91837c7f2ce9f0bbfb  www/form-cm105.pdf

Exactly the same as the carved file's hash: the cache copy is byte-for-byte identical to the server's original. In real cases you usually can't have the original, but recording the carved file's hash lets you ① reproduce the same result later, and ② look up whether a known malicious file with that hash exists in threat intelligence services. (That's different from uploading the file itself to a public service; remember lesson 1.2's OPSEC.)

docs.title: 7.3 If it's compressed: decompress and check again
docs.text:
Not every object opens straight away. Carving the script file the same way gives (actual output):

$ python3 carve.py 00/00/00000001 out/carved-js
headers at 0x83, separator at 0x14c, body 84 bytes
$ file out/carved-js
out/carved-js: gzip compressed data, last modified: Thu Nov  5 02:30:45 2026, max compression, original size modulo 2^32 1264
$ strings -n 10 00/00/00000001 | grep -i content-encoding
Content-Encoding: gzip
$ gunzip -c < out/carved-js > out/app.js
$ file out/app.js
out/app.js: ASCII text

The server sent it compressed with Content-Encoding: gzip, and the cache stored it compressed. So the carved result is a gzip file, and gunzip is needed to get the original script back. Besides gzip there are br (Brotli), deflate and others, and sometimes decompressing reveals another encoding (e.g. Base64). Check the headers and decode as many times as needed until you reach the original form. file is your guide at every step.

[Caution] Other cases where the result may differ from the original. If the response was 206 (partial), the cache may hold only part of it; and if you see Transfer-Encoding: chunked in the headers, the body may have chunk length markers mixed in that need removing. If the carved size differs from Content-Length, don't move on; find out why.

docs.title: 7.4 Open it safely
docs.text: To see the content you eventually have to open the file. This PDF was made by hand for the test and is safe, but in a real case a file carved from the cache is an untrusted file. A malicious PDF or document can attack the analysis PC the moment it's opened. So open such files in a throwaway analysis environment that can break without consequence (a virtual machine isolated from the network, etc.). Opening it straight on your main forensic workstation can contaminate the workstation itself, casting doubt on every analysis result after that.

docs.title: 8. Back to the case, and the remaining questions
docs.text:
Applying this to lesson 1.4's case:

  • The currency declaration form PDF: the log had TCP_MEM_HIT, so it likely entered the cache. Using this lesson's method, find it by URL, check the headers' Cache-Control and Date, carve it, confirm with file and a hash, and open it in a throwaway environment to confirm it really is "a currency declaration form". This turns lesson 1.4 section 7's "PDF that appears to be a form" into "the form".
  • The three pastes: try grep -railF k7Qm2x with the paste IDs. If it turns up, that's a big win; if not, weigh which of section 2.2's reasons applies (headers, replacement on re-request, deletion for lack of space). In the source material's case, nothing turned up. Even then, the conclusion "the paste content could not be confirmed from proxy evidence alone" stands.

Before wrapping up, ask these questions of the evidence not yet fully reviewed:

  • Were there other exfiltration attempts? (other upload sites, cloud storage, large POSTs)
  • Was there suspicious activity leading up to the events we examined?
  • Are there other "artifacts of communication" (lesson 1.1's goal 2)? (DNS queries, firewall records, mail server records)
  • What further evidence would explain better what happened?

At the same time, beware of the "rabbit hole" from the end of lesson 1.4. These questions are for setting priorities within the question and time given, not an invitation to dig endlessly.

docs.title: 9. Commercial proxy caches: "it's complicated"
docs.text:
Extracting content from a Squid cache is fairly easy like this, and can be automated. Commercial products are different. If their log analysis is complicated, cache extraction is often all but impossible. The cache format isn't published, so you need proprietary knowledge, or reverse engineering to learn the structure, or both. Some devices also encrypt the cache.

In that case it may be easier to reach the root truth through other evidence sources. The most certain root is the data that actually crossed the wire: packets. Skip the complex, undocumented cache format and look at the data that passed over the network itself. That doesn't mean giving up on the commercial device's data; as section 1 showed, use whatever usable format there is. But working with packets requires knowing how network data is stored, analysed and replayed. That's the subject from the next lesson on.

docs.title: 10. Summary
docs.text:
• Commercial proxy logs like ELFF define their columns in a #Fields: header. Find the rules (field definitions) first, extract fields by name, and check whether more detailed logs already exist. They may hold information Squid's default log lacks, such as cs-bytes.
  • Whether to cache is decided by the server's Cache-Control and Expires, and the proxy's refresh_pattern (min, percent, max).
  • [Correction] In Squid 6.14 as tested, responses with no cache instructions were still stored on disk (just judged not fresh). no-store and private responses were not stored. Don't conclude "not cacheable" from zero cache search hits.
  • A ufs cache consists of files named hex2/hex2/hex8, and the names tell you nothing. With several cache_dir lines, secure them all.
  • A cache file runs metadata → URL → response headers → 0d 0a 0d 0a → body, and from the headers to the end it's exactly the server's response. Use the headers' Date to establish when the copy is from.
  • Find with grep -railF, look with strings -n 10, and carve by deleting the separator and everything before it. A repeatable script beats manual work.
  • Confirm the type with file and identity with a hash, and decompress as many times as needed. Open untrusted files in a throwaway environment.
  • Commercial caches are very hard to extract from; then turn to the data that crossed the wire (packets).

In the next lesson (1.6) we cover libpcap and tcpdump, the basic tools for handling those packets, and the structure of pcap and pcapng files.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. An ELFF log's #Fields: line has cs-bytes and sc-bytes. To judge the amount exfiltrated in lesson 1.4's paste site case, which field should you look at, and why?

Answer and explanation

cs-bytes. The leading letters of ELFF field names give the direction: cs- is client → proxy, sc- is proxy → client. The amount uploaded to the paste site is what the client sent, so it's cs-bytes. sc-bytes is the size of the response the site returned (a short 302 redirect in this case), unrelated to the amount exfiltrated. But confirm the field's exact definition (whether headers are included, etc.) from that device's field documentation.

Question 2. (Calculation) With refresh_pattern . 0 20% 4320, how long is each of the following responses treated as fresh? None has Cache-Control: max-age or Expires. (a) Last-Modified 5 days before the response time (b) 40 days before (c) no Last-Modified

Answer and explanation

The server gave no expiry, so refresh_pattern applies.

  • (a) 5 days × 20% = 1 day. Between min (0 minutes) and max (4,320 minutes = 3 days), so 1 day as computed.
  • (b) 40 days × 20% = 8 days, but max caps it at 3 days.
  • (c) With no Last-Modified there's no basis for percent, so min applies: 0 minutes, not fresh as soon as it arrives.

(c) is the common case for dynamic pages like pastes. And as section 2.2 showed, not fresh is not the same as not stored.

Question 3. (Common misconception) A colleague says: "refresh_pattern's min is 0, so this proxy never stores responses the server didn't give instructions for. No point searching the cache." How would you respond?

Answer and explanation

min 0 means "the minimum period treated as fresh is 0", not "don't store". In this lesson's Squid 6.14 test, a response with no cache instructions was stored on disk and only replaced with a new copy on the next request. So searching the cache is worthwhile. But also point out that no-store and private responses weren't stored, that re-requesting the same URL or the cache filling up removes copies, and that behaviour can differ by version and configuration. Search, and if nothing turns up, work out why: that's the right order.

Question 4. Searching the cache folder with grep -raiF 'invoice-2026' . returns 0 hits. But the proxy log records http://files.example.net/docs/invoice-2026.zip fetched with TCP_MISS/200. Give at least three possible reasons.

Answer and explanation
  1. The server said not to store it: with no-store or private in the response, it isn't stored.
  2. It was stored and then disappeared: the same URL may have been fetched again later, replacing it with a new copy (the file number changes), or the cache filled and the oldest objects were deleted.
  3. It's in another cache_dir: with several cache_dir lines, it may be stored under another path.
  4. There's no disk cache: with no cache_dir, it was only in memory and may have vanished on restart.
  5. It was excluded by a size limit or ACL: it may have hit a maximum object size setting or a no-cache rule.
  6. A search problem: check you didn't drop -l or give the wrong path. URLs aren't compressed, so searching by URL text is itself a sound approach.

Narrow it down with the config file and cache.log.

Question 5. (Reading structure) Below is part of a cache file's hexdump. Where does the body (data) start, and what do the first bytes 4d 5a most likely mean?

000001a0  36 0d 0a 43 6f 6e 6e 65  63 74 69 6f 6e 3a 20 63  |6..Connection: c|
000001b0  6c 6f 73 65 0d 0a 0d 0a  4d 5a 90 00 03 00 00 00  |lose....MZ......|
Answer and explanation

The 0d 0a 0d 0a on the second line is at 0x1b4–0x1b7 (the fifth to eighth bytes from the line's start at 0x1b0), so the body starts right after, at 0x1b8. 4d 5a is MZ as text, the unique two bytes (magic bytes) that start a Windows executable (EXE, DLL). So this cache object is most likely a Windows executable. If the headers' Content-Type claims another format such as image/png, the server disguised the content, which is an important finding. Carve it, confirm with file, record a hash, and handle it only in a throwaway environment.

Question 6. (Changed conditions) file on a carved file says gzip compressed data. The headers have Content-Type: text/html and Content-Encoding: gzip. What do you do next, and how do you interpret the result?

Answer and explanation

The server sent the HTML compressed with gzip, and the cache stored it compressed. Decompress with gunzip -c and check again with file. If the result is HTML text, it's normal and matches the headers' claim. If decompressing reveals yet another format (e.g. a Base64 blob, another compression), repeat as many steps as needed. Also remember that in its compressed state, a grep for text inside the body didn't work; objects like this must be found by URL.

Question 7. (Interpreting a hash) You looked up the carved file's SHA-256 in a threat intelligence service and found no match. Can you conclude "this file isn't malicious"?

Answer and explanation

No. "No lookup result" only means that service doesn't know this hash. Files attackers tweak per target have a different hash each time, so having no record anywhere is normal. No result is the same problem as lesson 1.1's "no result ≠ nothing". Judge it together with the file type (file), its content, behavioural analysis in a throwaway environment, and the communication from that PC after receiving it (proxy and flow records). And uploading the file itself to a public analysis service to check may alert the attacker (OPSEC), so follow your organisation's policy.

Question 8. (Judgement) You need to extract a particular malicious file from the cache of your organisation's commercial proxy, but the vendor doesn't publish the cache format. What alternatives are there?

Answer and explanation
  • Packet capture: if there's full packet capture for that segment at that time, you can reassemble the HTTP response from the packets and extract the file (covered from the next lesson). On a proxy doing TLS interception, the proxy–PC segment is encrypted with the internal CA, so which segment the packets come from matters.
  • Endpoint evidence: the file may remain in the receiving PC's browser cache, downloads folder or antivirus quarantine.
  • The device's own features: some commercial devices keep files separately for malware scanning, or have records of passing them to a sandbox. Ask operations or vendor support.
  • Other victims or intelligence: the same URL or hash may have been obtained elsewhere (look it up with OPSEC in mind).

The key is not "can't extract from the cache, so that's it", but finding other evidence sources that reach the same fact: lesson 1.1's "many witnesses" principle.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Squid project, Squid 7 branch src/cf.data.pre (checked 2026-11-05). Definitions of refresh_pattern min, percent and max, options such as ignore-private, ignore-no-store and store-stale, and the cache_dir format and storage types.
  • RFC 9111, HTTP Caching. Cache-Control max-age, no-store and private, and heuristic freshness.
  • RFC 9112, HTTP/1.1: section 2.1 message format (the blank line after headers) and section 7.1 chunked transfer coding.
  • W3C, Extended Log File Format (Working Draft). The #Fields header and the meaning of the c, s, r, cs and sc prefixes.
  • Broadcom, Edge SWG (ProxySG) access log fields, article 240610 (title confirmed by search 2026-11-05). An example of a primary source for a commercial device's field definitions.

About this page

Personal study notes rewritten in my own words from a range of study material. The lab server, cache files and logs were made up for explanation.

docs.title: Lesson 1.4 — Reconstructing an Incident from Proxy Logs Alone: Investigation Walkthrough
Lesson 1.4 — Reconstructing an Incident from Proxy Logs Alone: Investigation Walkthrough
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

We put everything from lesson 1.2 and lesson 1.3 to work on one case.

  • The order of an investigation: plan → collect evidence → hypothesise → analyse → support, refute or refine → repeat until stable
  • Getting the overall picture with shell commands when automated tools fail
  • Following the characters a user typed through search autocomplete requests
  • Reading webmail traces, and the "test it and compare" method
  • Interpreting requests logged several times in the same second, redirects and 404s
  • Traces suggesting exfiltration via a paste site, and their limits
  • Weaving scattered findings into one timeline, and reporting facts, hypotheses and open questions separately

About the lab material

The case, people, organisation and domains in this lesson are all hypothetical. The sample log (combined format, 144 lines) was built for this case, and command output marked (Actual output) was produced by really running the commands against that sample log. Long output is trimmed with .... All times are UTC.

docs.title: 1. The case: a researcher disappears
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) At lesson 1.1's research institute, an employee who uses research-segment PC 10.10.6.14 abruptly leaves one afternoon and doesn't come to work the next day. This employee had already been suspected of passing research results to a competitor. The next day word comes that the employee was stopped at the airport while boarding an overseas flight, carrying a large undeclared sum of cash. The employee had no company material on them, and no electronic devices such as USB drives or laptops.

Management asks: "Determine whether this employee leaked company material." The employee's PC has already had a first-pass analysis (triage), which found no access to material outside their duties and no obvious signs of wrongdoing. A detailed PC analysis is under way, and we look at network evidence in parallel.

The organisation's environment:

  • All internal web traffic goes through a Squid proxy, and the firewall prevents bypass.
  • The proxy uses TLS interception (generating certificates on the fly) and logs query strings, User-Agent and Referer.
  • Staff sign an acceptable use policy on joining stating that "use of the company network is logged and may be reviewed". That notice and approval are what make an investigation like this possible.

docs.title: 2. The order of an investigation
docs.text:
You'll want to open the logs straight away, but first set the order.

flowchart TD
    P["① Plan<br/>question · time · resources · existing analysis"] --> C["② Collect evidence<br/>config · logs"]
    C --> H["③ Form hypotheses<br/>(broad at first)"]
    H --> A["④ Analyse evidence"]
    A --> R["⑤ Support · refute · refine"]
    R -->|"still shifting"| A
    R -->|"stable"| D["Report: facts · hypotheses · open questions"]

How to read the diagram: it runs top to bottom, but ④ and ⑤ loop until the hypotheses stop shifting. The key is asking, with every new finding, "does this support, refute or require refining my hypothesis?"

① Plan. Make the question clear. What's needed now isn't "the ultimate truth" but "enough to give a well-founded opinion on whether this employee leaked material". Time is short, so scope the work to that. Also check what analysis is already done (the PC triage result). The fact that it found "no traces" is itself information.

② Collect evidence. What we secured this time:

  • The proxy config file /etc/squid/squid.conf: tells us log locations, format and behaviour
  • Proxy logs: access.log, and cache.log (the error log)

The logs were received reduced to this employee's PC address only. That's also good practice for handling personal data minimally, since there's no reason to look at other staff's records unrelated to the investigation. The trade-off, which we record, is that this data can't show whether the same thing happened from other PCs.

The key points from the config, read with lesson 1.2's method: the main changes from defaults are an enabled disk cache, TLS interception, query string logging (strip_query_terms off), and the combined format with User-Agent and Referer. So we can expect HTTPS requests to be logged with full URLs too.

[Supplement] Older Squid installations sometimes wrote Referer and User-Agent not into access.log but into separate files such as referer.log and useragent.log. Squid 7 still has built-in referrer and useragent formats, so the same setup is possible. If the config has access_log lines like that, secure those files too.

③ Form hypotheses. Start broad, for example:

  • Hypothesis A: this employee sent company material out via the web.
  • Hypothesis B: this employee planned the departure and carrying the cash in advance.
  • Hypothesis C: this employee's web activity was no different from normal work (there's nothing to support the leak suspicion).

Include a "nothing happened" hypothesis like C on purpose. As lesson 1.1 taught, having something to look for contradicting evidence against keeps you from drifting to one side.

docs.title: 3. First attempt: an automated tool
docs.text: First, run an automated summary tool. But what lesson 1.3 warned about actually happens. Many Squid summary tools can only read the default log format, so given a log switched to combined like this proxy's, they stop with "I don't know this input format". With open source you could change the code to read the new format, but there's no time now. Drop the easy option and go to the shell.

docs.title: 4. The overall picture: which sites were visited
docs.text:
In the combined format, split on whitespace, the seventh field is the URL (IP - - [date +0000] "method URL HTTP/1.1" ...). So we use lesson 1.3's command with just the field number changed (actual output):

$ grep -v '"CONNECT ' access.log | awk '{print $7}' | awk -F/ '{print $3}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
     82 search.example
     14 news.example
     10 intranet.lab.example
     10 cdn.news.example
      8 paste.example
      6 weather.example
      5 customs.example
      3 mx3.webmail.example
      2 webmail.example
      2 login.webmail.example
      1 travel-rules.example

grep -v '"CONNECT ' means drop the CONNECT lines (-v means "only non-matching lines"). On a proxy with TLS interception, each HTTPS connection first produces a CONNECT line, and the real requests inside are logged separately as https:// URLs. CONNECT lines have host:443 in the URL field, which doesn't fit the next step of extracting hostnames, so they're dropped.

This list is the first material for hypotheses. Search requests dominate, and the intranet, news and weather look like ordinary work and life. Three things stand out: a paste site (paste.example), webmail (the webmail.example family), and customs.example, which looks customs-related. Let's follow each.

docs.title: 5. Search autocomplete: exactly what the user typed
docs.text:
There are 82 search requests. Did a person really search 82 times in a day? Opening them up, most are to a /complete address (actual output):

$ grep -c 'search.example' access.log
83
$ grep 'search.example' access.log | grep -c '/complete'
81

grep -c counts only the number of matching lines. 81 of the 83 lines are /complete. What is this?

It's autocomplete, the feature that shows suggested searches under the box as you type. Every time a key is pressed, the browser sends the characters typed so far to the server and gets suggestions back. Requests like this, exchanged in the background without reloading the page, are commonly called AJAX (asynchronous requests). The result is that the proxy log holds requests growing one character at a time, a record close to a keylogger. Extracting just the time and the value after q= (actual output, partial):

$ grep -F 'search.example/complete' access.log | awk '{split($7,a,"q="); print substr($4,14), a[2]}'
15:02:10 o
15:02:11 or
15:02:12 orc
15:02:13 orch
...
15:02:26 orchid%20alloy%20test
...

Breaking the command down: split($7,a,"q=") splits the URL (seventh field) in two at q= into array a, and a[2] is the second part, the typed characters. substr($4,14) takes the fourth field [14/Oct/2026:15:02:10 from the 14th character on, i.e. just the time. %20 is how a space is written inside a URL (percent-encoding).

There's no need to read every line as characters accumulate. Just extract where typing ended, i.e. where the next line isn't a continuation of the previous one (actual output):

$ grep -F 'search.example/complete' access.log | awk '{split($7,a,"q="); t=substr($4,14); q=a[2]; if (prev!="" && index(q,prev)!=1) print pt, prev; prev=q; pt=t} END{print pt, prev}'
15:02:26 orchid%20alloy%20test
15:06:52 orchid%20patent
15:10:21 flight%20711%20status
15:10:53 connecting%20482
15:53:03 currency%20declaration

index(q,prev)!=1 is the condition "this value does not start with the previous value". That's the moment the previous input ended, so it prints the previous value (prev) and its time (pt). The last input has no following line, so END prints it separately.

Now we can read what this employee typed. Let's say orchid is the name of one of the institute's sensitive research projects. The employee looked up that project's test results and patent, then flight status and a connecting flight, and much later currency declaration.

docs.title: 5.1 [Caution] Reading autocomplete records
docs.text:
This record is powerful, but interpret it with care.

  • "Typed" and "searched" are different. An autocomplete request records that the user typed characters into the search box. Whether they actually pressed search and saw results needs a separate search request (/search?q=). In the sample log there's an actual search request only for orchid patent (actual output):

    $ grep -F 'search.example/search' access.log | awk '{print substr($4,14), $7}'
15:07:02 https://search.example/search?q=orchid%20patent

    For the rest, the user may have clicked a suggestion, the results page may have opened by another path, or they may have just deleted it. Reports must distinguish "typed X into the search box" from "searched for X". - Who typed it is a separate question. This record is about "this PC".
