Who was using that PC at that time is confirmed by other evidence such as logon records. - Every search site works differently. Many browsers also send suggestion requests for characters typed into the address bar, and the request shape (path, parameter names, GET/POST) varies by site and browser and changes often. In a real case, test the behaviour at that time before interpreting (section 6.1). - Without TLS interception, this record doesn't exist. A non-intercepting proxy has just one CONNECT search.example:443 line. Autocomplete is visible in this case purely because of the configuration.

docs.title: 5.2 So why didn't the PC analysis find it?
docs.text: If the employee searched like this in a browser, why didn't the PC triage find search or browsing history? Possible explanations: they browsed in private mode (an incognito window), or cleared the browser history and cache afterwards. Those traces may or may not be partly recoverable in the detailed PC analysis. But from the proxy, the record is plain to see. It even shows characters accumulating one at a time, so it's more detailed than a perfect PC analysis would be. This is lesson 1.1's advantage that "evidence accumulates apart from the target (here, the employee's PC)" in action.

docs.title: 6. Webmail
docs.text:
The host list included a webmail service. It's one of countless free webmail providers, and a sign the employee may have sent a message (actual output):

$ grep -F 'webmail.example' access.log | awk '{print substr($4,14), $6, $7, $9, $10}'
15:18:30 "GET https://webmail.example/ 200 16120
15:19:27 "POST https://login.webmail.example/login 302 507
15:46:12 "POST https://login.webmail.example/login 302 507
15:46:28 "POST https://mx3.webmail.example/mail/compose;sid=9f2c?action=autosave 200 967
15:46:58 "POST https://mx3.webmail.example/mail/compose;sid=9f2c?action=autosave 200 967
15:50:14 "GET https://mx3.webmail.example/mail/sentconfirm;sid=9f2c?view=SHOW_CONFIRM 200 7161
15:50:23 "GET https://webmail.example/logout 200 15169

Line by line:

  • 15:18:30 Opened the webmail front page.
  • 15:19:27, 15:46:12 Sent a POST to the login page and got 302 (moved elsewhere). That's the common shape of submitting a login form and, on success, being sent on to the inbox. The two logins are about 27 minutes apart.
  • 15:46:28, 15:46:58 Right after the second login, two POSTs to the compose address with action=autosave, 30 seconds apart. These look like the web app autosaving in the background while a message is written.
  • 15:50:14 An address containing sentconfirm and SHOW_CONFIRM. By its name, a "sent confirmation" screen.
  • 15:50:23 Logout.

There's a very important limit here. The message content, recipients and attachments are not in the log. They travelled in the body of the POST requests, and the proxy log records the URL and some headers, not the body. They're not in the cache either. The cache keeps only reusable responses the server returned, and there's no reason to cache an outgoing request body.

docs.title: 6.1 Does "sent confirmation" really mean it was sent? Test it and compare
docs.text:
Seeing the name sentconfirm and guessing "a message was sent" is a reasonable hypothesis. But it's a guess, not confirmation. A good way to confirm is to do the same thing yourself and compare what the proxy records.

  1. Use a separate account created for the investigation to access the same webmail service. Never use the subject's account.
  2. Under the same conditions (same proxy, same kind of browser), log in, write a message, send it and log out, one step at a time, noting the time of each action.
  3. Extract your test records from the proxy log and match which URLs appeared for each action.
  4. Compare with the subject's records. If you confirm "pressing send produces sentconfirm, and saving alone doesn't", the 15:50:14 record strongly supports sent.

Logout can be confirmed the same way. But web services change constantly, so test as close to the incident as possible and record the test date and environment in the report. Also note that the test only tells you "this is how it behaves today"; there's no guarantee it behaved identically at the time.

docs.title: 7. Related activity: a PDF fetched three times in one second
docs.text:
The last autocomplete input was currency declaration. Check what was viewed around it. There's a blog post reached from the search results (travel-rules.example/blog/carrying-cash, with the search site as Referer), and right after it, records from a customs site (actual output):

$ grep -F 'customs.example' access.log | awk '{print substr($4,14), $7, $9, $10, $NF}'
15:54:17 http://customs.example/forms/declare-currency.pdf 301 444 TCP_MISS:HIER_DIRECT
15:54:19 https://customs.example/forms/declare-currency.pdf 404 16211 TCP_MISS:HIER_DIRECT
15:55:48 https://customs.example/files/form-cm105.pdf 200 237248 TCP_MISS:HIER_DIRECT
15:55:48 https://customs.example/files/form-cm105.pdf 200 237247 TCP_MISS:HIER_NONE
15:55:48 https://customs.example/files/form-cm105.pdf 206 40701 TCP_MEM_HIT:HIER_NONE

$NF in awk means "the last field on the line", here the cache and hierarchy status.

  • 15:54:17 Requested a PDF over http:// and got 301 (moved permanently), the common shape of a server sending you back with "come again over https://".
  • 15:54:19 Requested again over https://, but got 404 (not found). The file was no longer at that address; perhaps an old link was followed.
  • 15:55:48 A PDF at another path fetched three times in the same second. Twice 200 (sizes 237,248 and 237,247, a one-byte difference), once 206 (partial, 40,701 bytes, from memory cache).

Three lines in one second looks odd, but it's common with PDFs. A browser's PDF viewer often doesn't fetch the file in one go; it requests only the ranges it needs (HTTP Range requests), or requests a preview and the full download separately. The 206 is that trace. The exact cause of the one-byte difference can't be known from this log. The size field includes headers, so it could be a one-character header difference. Don't assert anything here; leave it as "cause not determined". The important observed fact is "the employee downloaded what appears to be a currency declaration form PDF".

[Caution] Why not just fetch the PDF again now? Be careful about visiting that URL now to check the content, for three reasons. First, OPSEC: if the target is an attacker's server, connecting from the organisation's address announces the investigation (the risk is small for a government site as in this case, but the habit matters). Second, it may already have changed: the file may have been deleted or altered. Third, servers can serve different content to different requesters: some return different content depending on the requesting IP, cookies or settings. So where possible, prefer a copy from the time, pulled from the proxy cache (lesson 1.5) or packets. This PDF even shows signs of having entered the cache (TCP_MEM_HIT), so there's a good chance it can be extracted.

docs.title: 8. The paste site: material walking out the door?
docs.text:
paste.example in the host list is a paste site, where anyone can paste text and share it by link. It's handy for parking text briefly, so it comes up often in data leaks (actual output):

$ grep -F 'paste.example' access.log | awk '{print substr($4,14), $6, $7, $9, $10}'
15:35:01 "GET http://paste.example/ 301 585
15:35:05 "CONNECT paste.example:443 200 0
15:35:05 "GET https://paste.example/ 200 8925
15:48:26 "POST https://paste.example/post 302 727
15:48:30 "GET https://paste.example/k7Qm2x 200 664841
15:49:12 "POST https://paste.example/post 302 727
15:49:14 "GET https://paste.example/Zp81Lr 200 635510
15:49:46 "POST https://paste.example/post 302 727
15:49:48 "GET https://paste.example/R4tw9B 200 281017

The first three lines are the first visit to the site: http://, then 301 to https://, the CONNECT line from lesson 1.2, and, thanks to interception, the https:// URL.

The key is the three pairs that follow. A POST to /post gets a 302, and within seconds a GET fetches a never-before-seen short address like /k7Qm2x. Sites like this commonly redirect you to the new paste's short unique address after you post. So this shape fits the interpretation "a paste was posted, and the site sent the user to the new paste's address". Testing as in section 6.1 would confirm it. Three paste IDs (k7Qm2x, Zp81Lr, R4tw9B) and their response sizes (about 650 KB, 620 KB and 270 KB) remain. That's a lot for text.

So what was posted? Here we hit the wall again.

  • The posted content (the POST body) isn't in the log, for the same reason as the webmail in section 6.
  • The response from fetching the paste address is probably not in the cache either. Sites like this often don't include "you may cache this" instructions in their responses, and then Squid's default settings don't keep them (lesson 1.5 explains why).
  • Opening it on the site now may show nothing. Sites like this can set pastes to expire; suppose checking shows they're already gone.

The remaining hope is the site operator's cooperation. The paste IDs survive exactly, so if the operator keeps expired pastes, they might be found. But that usually requires a legal request through law enforcement, with no guarantee of success.

[Supplement] To at least record how much was uploaded. The default log's size field from lesson 1.3 (%<st) is the size of the response sent to the client, so it doesn't tell you how much the employee uploaded. That's why all three POSTs above show 727 bytes: it's the size of the short redirect response the server returned. To prepare for exfiltration investigations, add %>st, the size of the request received from the client, to logformat. Then even without the content you can say "about 650 KB went out in this POST". But it's only recorded from the moment you add that field, so set it up before an incident.

docs.title: 9. Weaving a timeline
docs.text:
So far the findings are scattered by site. Put back in time order (2026-10-14, UTC):

Time Event Basis 15:02:26 Typed orchid alloy test into search box Autocomplete requests 15:06:52 · 15:07:02 Typed orchid patent, actually ran the search Autocomplete + /search request 15:10:21 Typed flight 711 status Autocomplete requests 15:10:53 Typed connecting 482 Autocomplete requests 15:18:30 First visit to webmail GET 15:19:27 First webmail login POST → 302 15:35:05 First visit to paste site 301 → CONNECT → GET 15:46:12 Second webmail login POST → 302 15:46:28 Started writing a message (autosave) compose POST 15:48:30 Paste ① k7Qm2x created POST → 302 → new ID 15:49:14 Paste ② Zp81Lr created Same shape 15:49:48 Paste ③ R4tw9B created Same shape 15:50:14 Message sent (apparently) sentconfirm 15:50:23 Webmail logout logout 15:53:03 Typed currency declaration into search box Autocomplete requests 15:53:55 Read a blog post on carrying cash GET, Referer = search site 15:55:48 Downloaded currency declaration form PDF 200 · 200 · 206

In order, a flow emerges that wasn't visible site by site. The employee looked up the sensitive project, checked flights, logged into webmail, opened the paste site, logged in again and started a message, posted three pastes in the meantime, sent the message and logged out immediately, then looked up the rules for carrying cash.

docs.title: 10. Summing up: facts, hypotheses and open questions
docs.text:
Now separate them as in lesson 1.1.

Observed facts (directly in the log).

  • The sensitive project's name and related words were typed into the search box on this PC, and one of them was actually searched.
  • The same day, flight-related words and, later, currency-declaration-related words were typed, and a PDF that appears to be a currency declaration form was downloaded.
  • There were two webmail logins, autosave requests from the compose screen, what appears to be a "sent confirmation" screen, and a logout.
  • There were three POSTs to the paste site, each followed by a request that appears to be a new paste address, leaving three paste IDs.

Hypotheses those facts support.

  • Hypothesis B (planned the departure and carrying the cash in advance) is strongly supported, and fits the actual arrest.
  • Hypothesis A (leaked material via the web) is supported but not established, because the content of the three pastes and the sent message is unknown.
  • Hypothesis C (no different from normal) fits this record poorly.

What needs further evidence.

  • The content of the pastes and the message: legal requests to the site and mail service operators (with law enforcement cooperation), the proxy cache (lesson 1.5), and packets if there's packet capture.
  • Who was using the PC at the time: logon records, physical access records.
  • On the PC, traces of private browsing or history clearing, and paste content left in the clipboard or temporary files: detailed PC analysis.
  • Whether the sensitive project's material was actually accessed: file server access logs (SMB, Part 3).

The recommendation to management can read: "The proxy records strongly indicate the departure was planned in advance, and support the possibility that a substantial amount of data left via webmail and a paste site. However, what left has not yet been confirmed; confirming it requires the following steps." This is lesson 1.1's report that withstands challenge: it doesn't claim content it doesn't have, yet says clearly what the current evidence points to.

The investigation isn't over. To reach a judgement in a short time, we picked the lines essential to the question; we didn't review the whole log and cache. Reviewing everything might reveal more. But to avoid falling down the "rabbit hole" of endless aimless review, the investigator must always set priorities against the question and time given.

docs.title: 11. Summary
docs.text:
• An investigation is a loop: plan → collect → hypothesise → analyse → support, refute or refine. Include a "nothing happened" hypothesis too.
  • Automated tools often can't read custom-format logs. Match the field numbers and shell commands give you the overall picture right away.
  • On a proxy with TLS interception and query string logging, search autocomplete is recorded one character at a time. But "typed" and "searched" are different.
  • POST bodies are in neither the log nor the cache. What was sent via webmail or a paste site can't be known from the proxy alone; to record even the upload size, log %>st in advance.
  • Don't infer behaviour from URL names alone; test with a separate account and compare.
  • Several lines in the same second (200, 206) can be normal behaviour such as PDF viewing. Leave unexplained causes as "not determined".
  • Revisiting the URL now carries OPSEC risk and the problem of changed content, so prefer a copy from the time.
  • Weave scattered findings into a timeline, and report facts, hypotheses and open questions separately.

In the next lesson (1.5) we cover reading commercial proxy logs, and actually extracting from the proxy cache the responses we said this time "might be in the cache".

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. In section 4's host list, search.example dominates with 82 entries. What's wrong with reporting from this number alone that "the employee searched 82 times that day"?

Answer and explanation

81 of the 82 are autocomplete requests (/complete). The browser sends a request per key press, so 82 is closer to the number of characters typed than the number of searches. Five search phrases were actually completed, and only one went as far as a results page (/search). Before reporting a number, open up the requests that make it up and see what kind they are.

Question 2. (Common misconception) A colleague's draft report says "the employee searched for flight 711 status". What needs fixing, and how can you check?

Answer and explanation

The log only has autocomplete requests showing those characters were typed into the search box; there's no actual search results request (/search?q=flight%20711%20status). So the accurate wording is "typed flight 711 status into the search box". Whether results were actually seen can be checked by /search requests near that time, the request shape produced by clicking a suggestion (confirmed by testing), and any following visit to an airline site. Without the distinction, you can't answer the other side's challenge that "they may have typed it and deleted it".

Question 3. (Changed conditions) If this proxy didn't use TLS interception, what parts of the analysis in sections 5–8 would still be possible, and what would not?

Answer and explanation

Every HTTPS connection would leave just one CONNECT host:443 line.

  • Possible: which sites were visited and when (the CONNECT times for search.example, webmail.example, paste.example and customs.example). Requests over plain HTTP, like the first http:// visit to the paste site, remain visible.
  • Not possible: the characters typed via autocomplete, the webmail login, compose and sent-confirmation paths, the paste IDs, the PDF paths and the 206 distinction. If a tunnel stays open a long time, many requests inside it are still one line, so timing is known only in lumps.

You could still say "these sites were visited in this time window", but most of this case's conclusions would lose their basis. It shows how much the strength of conclusions about the same incident depends on collection settings.

Question 4. (Reading a command) In section 5's awk command that "extracts only where typing ended", what happens if you change index(q,prev)!=1 to q!=prev?

Answer and explanation

q!=prev means "this value differs from the previous one", and in autocomplete growing one character at a time, almost every line differs from the previous one (o and or differ). So every intermediate step of typing is printed, which is almost the same as reading all 81 lines. index(q,prev)!=1 catches only when "this value doesn't start with the previous value", i.e. the moment something new was typed rather than continuing the previous input, giving the final shape of each input. Note, though, that backspacing a few characters and retyping (orchid pat → orchid pa → orchid patent) can also register as "new input", so check the original lines around the extracted results once more.

Question 5. (Interpreting results) In section 9's timeline, the three pastes were created between starting the message (15:46:28) and the sent confirmation (15:50:14). Name one hypothesis this order supports, and explain what's needed to confirm it.

Answer and explanation

Hypothesis: the pastes were posted and their links put into the message that was sent. It fits the order of starting a message, posting pastes, and sending right after. But the order fits other explanations too: the message and pastes may be unrelated, or the paste links may have been passed on another channel (a messenger, etc.). Confirming it requires the message content: obtaining the sent message through a legal request to the mail service operator, or finding clipboard or browser traces in the detailed PC analysis. The proxy log doesn't keep POST bodies, so it can't establish this hypothesis.

Question 6. (Judgement) Of section 7's three PDF lines, the two 200s differ in size by one byte. A colleague says "it's a sign someone swapped the file". How would you respond?

Answer and explanation

That conclusion lacks grounds. The observed fact is only "the same URL was logged twice with 200 within the same second, one byte different in size". The size field includes response headers, so a single character of header difference (e.g. the number of digits in a date or length value) could account for one byte. One was handled from the server (HIER_DIRECT) and the other without contacting the server (HIER_NONE), so the header makeup may have differed. To check, extract the actual responses from the cache and compare (lesson 1.5), or test under the same conditions. Until then, "cause not determined" is the accurate wording.

Question 7. (OPSEC) To check whether a paste really expired, a colleague wants to open https://paste.example/k7Qm2x in the browser on their office PC. What's the problem, and what's better?

Answer and explanation

Three problems. ① The office PC goes out through the organisation's address and proxy, which can signal to the site operator or whoever is watching the paste (an accomplice, say) that "this organisation is looking for this paste". ② That visit mixes into the evidence logs, later confusing "is this request the subject's or the investigator's?" ③ If the paste still exists, it can change the site's view counts or access records. If checking is truly necessary, do it from an environment separated for investigation (a network not linked to the organisation, investigation equipment), and record the time and method. And where possible, rather than visiting the site directly, asking the operator through legal process to preserve and provide it is also safer as evidence. This OPSEC habit is covered in detail in Part 5.

Question 8. (Design) After this incident, the security team wants to change the proxy config because "next time we want to know better what was uploaded". Suggest one change based on this lesson, and state its limits.

Answer and explanation

Suggestion: add %>st, the size of the request received from the client, to logformat. Then each POST records how much data left, so you can find by size the moments large data went out via a paste site or webmail, as in this case. You can also put paste and file-sharing sites under a separate condition to log them in more detail (splitting logs, lesson 1.3).

Limits: you still know only the size, not the content. And it's only recorded from when the setting is changed. Recording content needs other means such as data loss prevention (DLP) equipment or packet capture, and since that stores staff uploads, privacy and legal review and staff notification must come with it.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Squid project, Squid 7 branch src/cf.data.pre (checked 2026-11-05). The %>st (total size of request received from client) and %<st (size of reply sent to client) format codes, and the built-in referrer and useragent formats.
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: section 14 Range requests, 15.3.7 206 Partial Content, 15.4.2 301, 15.4.3 302.

About this page

Personal study notes rewritten in my own words from a range of study material. The organisation, people, domains and logs in the case are all made up for explanation.

docs.title: Lesson 1.3 — Reading Proxy Logs: The Ten Default Fields, Custom Formats, and Unix Time
Lesson 1.3 — Reading Proxy Logs: The Ten Default Fields, Custom Formats, and Unix Time
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

In lesson 1.2 the config file told us "where the logs are and in what format". This time we read the logs themselves.

  • What each of the ten fields in Squid's default log format means, and what it tells an investigator
  • Reading "what happened" from cache status codes and HTTP status codes
  • What the default format leaves out (User-Agent, Referer, readable time), and building a custom format with logformat
  • Automated analysis tools, and analysing directly with shell commands
  • Turning Unix time into human-readable time, one line at a time or all at once

Notation

Command output marked (Actual output) in this lesson was produced by really running the commands against a 12-line sample log I built. All addresses and domains in the sample log are hypothetical, and its date is 2025-10-12 (UTC). This work environment's system time zone is UTC.

docs.title: 1. One line of numbers
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) A colleague copies this line from the proxy server and asks: "Looks like this PC downloaded something. What does it mean?"

1760231140.004    388 10.10.7.15 TCP_MISS/200 1843200 GET http://files.example.net/update.bin - HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.50 application/octet-stream

At first it's a lump of numbers and symbols. But the line is a form with set information in set fields. Once you know the fields, this one line tells you "when, which PC, with what result, how big, what, and from where". By the end of this lesson you'll read it fluently.

docs.title: 2. An analogy: a parcel waybill
docs.text:
Think of a parcel waybill. It has set fields for sender, recipient, weight and drop-off time, so you can read a waybill you've never seen once you know the fields. A proxy log line is like one waybill, and one is added every time a request finishes.

But just as each courier has its own waybill layout, proxy logs change which fields appear and in what order depending on configuration. That's why lesson 1.2 started with the config's access_log and logformat lines. One way this analogy differs from reality: a waybill is filled in before shipping, but Squid writes the log line after the request finishes. That difference affects how you read the time, as section 3.2 explains.

docs.title: 3. The ten fields of the default format
docs.text:
Squid's default log format is named squid, and Squid 7's documentation defines it as:

logformat squid      %ts.%03tu %6tr %>a %Ss/%03>Hs %<st %rm %ru %[un %Sh/%<a %mt

Each item starting with % is a format code, replaced by the value of one field. The 03 in %03tu means "three digits, padding with zeros", and the 6 in %6tr means "at least six characters wide". That's why there were several spaces before the second field in the log. Now let's split section 1's line by this definition.

# Format code Value in section 1 Meaning What to watch in an investigation 1 %ts.%03tu 1760231140.004 Unix time (seconds.milliseconds) UTC. The time the request finished (section 3.2) 2 %6tr 388 Response time (milliseconds) Used to compute the start time 3 %>a 10.10.7.15 Requesting client IP May be another proxy's address if it came through one 4 %Ss/%03>Hs TCP_MISS/200 Cache status / HTTP status code sent to the client The heart of "what happened" (section 3.3) 5 %<st 1843200 Size of reply sent to the client (bytes) Includes headers. May not equal the file size exactly 6 %rm GET Request method POST is a request that uploads data 7 %ru http://files.example.net/update.bin Request URL By default query strings are stripped 8 %[un - User name Only has a value with proxy authentication. - otherwise 9 %Sh/%<a HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.50 How it was fetched / IP of the server actually contacted Records the DNS result at that moment 10 %mt application/octet-stream Content type declared by the server (MIME type) Only what the server claims; may not match the actual content

Now you can put section 1's line into words: "At about 01:05:40 UTC on 2025-10-12, PC 10.10.7.15 requested http://files.example.net/update.bin with GET. It wasn't in the cache (MISS), so the proxy went directly to 203.0.113.50 to fetch it; the result was 200 (success), the size 1,843,200 bytes, and the server declared it a generic binary (application/octet-stream). Processing took 0.388 seconds. No proxy authentication was used."

docs.title: 3.1 More about each field
docs.text:
Requesting IP (field 3). Usually the address of the device that connected to the proxy, i.e. the network-layer (layer 3) source address. But if another proxy or load balancer sits between the client and this proxy, the intermediate device's address appears here. The real client address may then be in a header the intermediate device adds, such as X-Forwarded-For. With follow_x_forwarded_for enabled, Squid reflects that header's address in its records. But clients can invent this header freely, so confirm in the config that the value comes from a trusted intermediate device.

Reply size (field 5). %<st is the total sent by the proxy to the client, so it includes the HTTP response headers. So even a 1,843,200-byte file usually shows a value a few hundred bytes larger. Allow for this when matching files by size. On CONNECT lines it's the number of bytes passed through the tunnel.

URL (field 7). As seen in lesson 1.2, if strip_query_terms is at its default on, everything after ? is stripped before logging. If you see no query strings, check the config to tell whether it's that setting or there simply weren't any.

Hierarchy status and server IP (field 9). HIER_DIRECT means the proxy went straight to the origin server; HIER_NONE means it didn't contact a server (served from cache or denied). Going through an upstream proxy gives values like PARENT_HIT. The IP after it is the address the proxy actually connected to at that moment. A domain's IP changes over time, so this record is closer to the facts at that time than a DNS lookup today.

MIME type (field 10). The value the server declared in its response header, such as "this is an image". Malicious servers sometimes send executables labelled image/png, so read this field only as the server's claim, and confirm the real content from a file pulled from the cache or packets (lesson 1.5).

docs.title: 3.2 Is that time the start or the end?
docs.text:
So is the time in the first field when the request started, or when it finished? Squid 7's source code takes this value from the current time at the moment the log line is written. Squid writes the log when request processing ends, so it's the finish time. You can estimate the start time as "timestamp − response time".

Most requests take under a second, so it makes little difference. Long-lived connections are different. Here's the calculation for the sample log's CONNECT line (actual output):

01:03:32  start~01:02:32  mail.example:443

The recorded time is 01:03:32, but the response time is 60,412 ms (about 60 seconds), so the tunnel actually opened around 01:02:32. For a tunnel open for hours, the difference is hours. When aligning with other evidence (firewall connection start times, the first SYN in packets), not knowing this can lead to the wrong conclusion that "the proxy records are a minute late".

docs.title: 3.3 What happened: cache status and HTTP status codes
docs.text:
The fourth field has two parts. The first is how Squid handled this request (cache status); the second is what result it returned to the client (HTTP status code). Investigators should read the HTTP status code in particular as the field telling them "what happened".

Common cache statuses, checked against the status name list in Squid 7's source:

Cache status Meaning What it means for an investigation TCP_MISS Not in cache, fetched from the server There really was communication with the external server at that moment TCP_HIT / TCP_MEM_HIT Served straight from disk / memory cache No external communication. Also means someone fetched the same thing earlier TCP_REFRESH_UNMODIFIED Asked the server whether the cached copy was still valid; told it hadn't changed Brief contact with the server. Content is the cached copy TCP_REFRESH_MODIFIED Asked, found it had changed, fetched it again Contact with the server, new content TCP_DENIED Denied by access control (http_access) Block policy or authentication failure. The attempt still happened TCP_TUNNEL Opened a CONNECT tunnel and relayed as-is Uninspected HTTPS, etc. Content unknown NONE family Ended before processing, e.g. by an error Malformed request, connection failure, etc.

Statuses sometimes carry a suffix such as _ABORTED (cut off midway) or _TIMEDOUT. For example, TCP_MISS_ABORTED/200 means "was fetching from the server and got cut off", so the size may not be the whole file.

[Changed] The source material's example log shows TCP_REFRESH_HIT/304. That name isn't in Squid 7's status name list; the same case is logged as TCP_REFRESH_UNMODIFIED (checked 2026-11-05 in Squid 7 source src/LogTags.cc). When reading logs from older servers, recognise both the old and current names. Also, depending on the Squid version, CONNECT lines appear as TCP_MISS/200 or TCP_TUNNEL/200, so when looking for CONNECT it's safer to filter on the method field (field 6) than on the status name.

Common HTTP status codes only; see the HTTP status codes reference for the full list.

Code Meaning What it means for an investigation 200 Success Got what was requested (doesn't mean it was executed) 206 Partial content Downloading a big file in pieces or resuming. Combine several lines for the same URL 301 / 302 Moved elsewhere Redirect. Find the real destination in the next line 304 Not modified Use the copy you already have. No content transferred 403 Forbidden Blocked by the proxy or server 407 Proxy authentication required Requested without credentials. Malware that can't authenticate sometimes leaves these repeatedly 404 Not found No such path on the server. Could be a scanner or an old C2 address 5xx Server-side error A problem with the server or the upstream path

docs.title: 3.4 A small example: same site, three lines
docs.text:
Look at the first three lines of the sample log (the sample log as written):

1760230869.433    531 10.10.7.11 TCP_MISS/200 17746 GET http://news.example/ - HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.20 text/html
1760230895.705    246 10.10.7.11 TCP_REFRESH_UNMODIFIED/304 303 GET http://news.example/ - HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.20 -
1760230901.112     12 10.10.7.11 TCP_MEM_HIT/200 5120 GET http://news.example/static/logo.png - HIER_NONE/- image/png

The first line is the PC requesting the news front page for the first time, which the proxy fetched from the server (MISS, 200, about 17 KB). The second line, about 26 seconds later, is the same page requested again. This time the browser asked "is my copy still valid?", the proxy checked with the server and learned it hadn't changed (TCP_REFRESH_UNMODIFIED), and returned only a short 303-byte "use what you have" (304). The logo image in the third line came straight from memory cache, so the server IP is - and the response took only 12 ms.

This gives an interpretation useful in investigations. The 303 bytes in the second line are not "the size of the page this PC received". The page the PC actually displayed was the copy in its browser cache, the roughly 17 KB from the first line. Judging "it received a small response" from the size field alone is wrong.

docs.title: 3.5 Examples with changed conditions: denial, authentication and repetition
docs.text:
Other lines from the sample log:

1760231141.920      0 10.10.7.15 TCP_DENIED/403 3870 GET http://c2.example.net/gate - HIER_NONE/- text/html
1760231260.002      1 10.10.5.25 TCP_DENIED/407 3995 GET http://news.example/ - HIER_NONE/- text/html
1760231300.551    174 10.10.7.11 TCP_MISS/200 2211 POST http://api-telemetry-sync.example/gate - HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.77 text/html
1760231600.549    169 10.10.7.11 TCP_MISS/200 2211 POST http://api-telemetry-sync.example/gate - HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.77 text/html
1760231900.553    171 10.10.7.11 TCP_MISS/200 2211 POST http://api-telemetry-sync.example/gate - HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.77 text/html
  • The 403 line: 10.10.7.15 requested c2.example.net but the proxy blocked it. The 3,870-byte reply is the size of the proxy's "blocked" page, and the server IP is -, so there was no external communication. Observed fact: that PC sent a request to a blocked domain. Hypothesis: something on that PC is trying to reach the C2. This is the very PC that fetched update.bin two seconds earlier (section 1). Linking the two lines strengthens the hypothesis, but to conclude you need to check which process on the endpoint made the request.
  • The 407 line: the security analyst's PC requested without authentication and was told "proxy authentication required". A browser used by a person normally gets this reply and immediately retries with credentials. So one or two 407s are normal. But hundreds of 407s in a row from the same PC may signal a program that doesn't know the proxy authentication (possibly malware) repeatedly trying to get out.
  • The three POST lines: the same PC sent same-size (2,211-byte) POSTs to the same address at 5-minute (300-second) intervals. That regularity is hard for a human to produce by hand, and it's the typical shape of lesson 1.1's "program that periodically talks to the outside". Legitimate telemetry programs look like this too, so check domain reputation and the endpoint's processes together.

docs.title: 4. What the default format leaves out
docs.text:
The default format is useful, but investigators miss three things.

There's no User-Agent. The User-Agent is a string the requesting program declares about itself, like a name tag. A browser used by a person sends something like Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ..., a command-line tool sends curl/8.5.0, and malware may send nothing or a clumsy imitation of a browser. It's a clue to whether section 3.5's POSTs came from a browser or another program. But this value is also a claim the program can set freely. User-Agent analysis is covered in depth in the Blue Team Essentials User-Agent and cookies lesson.

There's no Referer. The Referer header (the misspelling became part of the standard) tells you "which page led to this one". Click a link in search results and the request for the new page carries the search results page's address as the Referer. If the user clicked a link in a mail program, typed the address or used a bookmark, it's usually empty. With this value you can piece the user's path through the web back together. Malware infections often go through several redirects and hops, and without Referer it's hard to get the order right. Users themselves don't remember where they went once time has passed.

[Supplement] For privacy, today's browsers by default send only the origin (domain) instead of the full URL in the Referer when moving to another site (the strict-origin-when-cross-origin policy; the web standard made this the default in November 2020). So in today's logs the Referer often appears without a path, like https://search.example/. Don't expect to read search terms from the Referer as in older examples.

The time isn't human-readable. The first field is Unix time, which is hard to read directly. Section 6 shows how to convert it.

docs.title: 5. Building a custom format with logformat
docs.text:
To fill these gaps, Squid lets administrators define the log format themselves, using the logformat directive. Squid 7 already defines several common formats, and using combined adds User-Agent, Referer and readable time all at once.

logformat combined   %>a - %[un [%tl] "%rm %ru HTTP/%rv" %>Hs %<st "%{Referer}>h" "%{User-Agent}>h" %Ss:%Sh
access_log daemon:/var/log/squid/access.log logformat=combined

The first line is a definition already built into Squid 7, so you don't need to write it; just name it as in the second line. The new format codes mean:

Code Meaning %tl Human-readable server local time (default shape 12/Oct/2025:01:05:40 +0000) %tg Human-readable GMT (UTC) time %rv The request's HTTP version %{Referer}>h The Referer header the client sent %{User-Agent}>h The User-Agent header the client sent %Ss:%Sh Cache status and hierarchy status

A line in this format looks like this (illustrative output):

10.10.6.11 - - [12/Oct/2025:01:06:43 +0000] "GET http://parcel-redelivery.example/dl/label.zip HTTP/1.1" 200 98211 "http://parcel-redelivery.example/track" "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:144.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/144.0" TCP_MISS:HIER_DIRECT

Now you can read "the user downloaded this ZIP with Firefox via the track page", information the default format couldn't give.

[Caution] %tl is the server's local time. The source material's example shows +0000, so it looks like "human-readable UTC", but that's only because that server's time zone was UTC. If the server is in Sydney time, the same moment is written [12/Oct/2025:12:06:43 +1100]. Always read the trailing +1100 (11 hours ahead of UTC) and convert to UTC to align with other evidence. If you want UTC from the start, %tg is safer.

[Changed] The source material's custom format won't even start in Squid 7. The source material defines combined itself with %[ui (the user name obtained via the ident protocol) in the second field. Squid 7 removed ident support entirely, and configurations containing the %ui format code are rejected, so Squid fails to start. Instead, the built-in common and combined formats always put a - in that position (checked 2026-11-05 in the Squid 7 release notes). For investigators this means two things. First, that field always being - in Squid 7 logs is normal. Second, if that field has a value in an older server's logs, it's a name obtained through ident, an untrustworthy mechanism. Ident simply accepts a value reported from the client side, so don't use that name as evidence of a user's identity.

docs.title: 5.1 Splitting logs into several files
docs.text:
Squid can have several access_log lines, each with its own format and condition (ACL). That's very useful in network forensics. During a response, you can agree with the proxy administrator to log only requests matching known-malicious patterns separately, in a more detailed format (example config):

acl suspect_dst dstdomain .c2.example.net .api-telemetry-sync.example
access_log daemon:/var/log/squid/access.log logformat=squid
access_log daemon:/var/log/squid/suspect.log logformat=combined suspect_dst

dstdomain is an ACL that matches on destination domain, and the leading dot (.) includes subdomains. Because the third line ends with the ACL name, only requests matching that condition are additionally written to suspect.log in combined format. The original log on the second line still records every request. Turned around: if the server under investigation already has a line like this, there's another log file someone else created. This is exactly lesson 1.2's "read the config first to find evidence you'd otherwise miss".

docs.title: 6.1 What Unix time is
docs.text: Unix time (epoch time) is the number of seconds elapsed since 00:00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970. It just counts seconds, with no time zones or daylight saving, so it's very convenient for computers to store and calculate with. The difference between two times is a single subtraction. Section 3.5's POST interval came straight out as 1760231600.549 − 1760231300.551 ≈ 300 seconds. People, though, need it converted.

docs.title: 6.2 One line at a time: date
docs.text:
The Linux date command converts it directly (actual output):

$ date -d @1760230869.433
Sun Oct 12 01:01:09 UTC 2025
$ date -u -d @1760230869.433
Sun Oct 12 01:01:09 UTC 2025
$ TZ=Australia/Sydney date -d @1760230869.433
Sun Oct 12 12:01:09 AEDT 2025

-d means "show this time", and the @ before the number marks it as Unix time. -u shows it in UTC. The first two lines match above only because this work environment's time zone is already UTC. On an analysis PC in another time zone, the result without -u comes out in that PC's local time. The third line temporarily changes the time zone with the TZ= environment variable, showing the same moment is 12:01 midday in Sydney (AEDT, daylight saving applied). Get into the habit of always adding -u to standardise on UTC when analysing, so you can align with other evidence straight away.

date -d @ is a feature of the GNU version used on Linux. macOS's date has different syntax and doesn't accept a decimal point, so give it only the integer part:

$ date -j -u -r 1760230869

Other tools do the same. In Python, datetime.fromtimestamp(1760230869.433, tz=timezone.utc) gave 2025-10-12T01:01:09.433000+00:00 (actual output), and in PowerShell you can convert at millisecond precision with something like [DateTimeOffset]::FromUnixTimeMilliseconds(1760230869433).UtcDateTime.

docs.title: 6.3 All at once: awk
docs.text:
Converting one line at a time is a neat trick, but useless for tens of thousands of lines. Use awk to change only the first field and leave the rest (actual output):

$ awk '{$1=strftime("%F %T", $1, 1); print $0}' access.log | head -3
2025-10-12 01:01:09 531 10.10.7.11 TCP_MISS/200 17746 GET http://news.example/ - HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.20 text/html
2025-10-12 01:01:35 246 10.10.7.11 TCP_REFRESH_UNMODIFIED/304 303 GET http://news.example/ - HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.20 -
2025-10-12 01:01:41 12 10.10.7.11 TCP_MEM_HIT/200 5120 GET http://news.example/static/logo.png - HIER_NONE/- image/png

Breaking the command down:

  • awk '{ ... }' access.log: reads the log line by line and does what's inside the braces. awk splits each line into fields on whitespace, calling the first $1, the second $2, and the whole line $0.
  • strftime("%F %T", $1, 1): turns the Unix time in the first field into text shaped like %F %T (2025-10-12 01:01:09). The third argument 1 means "convert to UTC". Leave it out and you get the analysis PC's local time.
  • $1=...; print $0: puts the converted value back in the first field and prints the whole line.
  • | head -3: shows only the first three lines.

The reason for the %F %T shape (year-month-day hour:minute:second) is that it writes the largest unit first, so sorting it as text also sorts it chronologically. Merge and sort several files and the time order stays intact.

Three things to know about this method:

  1. Milliseconds disappear. strftime only goes to whole seconds. If event order matters down to milliseconds, append the decimal part like this (actual output):

    $ awk '{ms=substr($1, index($1,".")); $1=strftime("%F %T", int($1), 1) ms; print}' access.log | head -2
2025-10-12 01:01:09.433 531 10.10.7.11 TCP_MISS/200 17746 GET http://news.example/ - HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.20 text/html
2025-10-12 01:01:35.705 246 10.10.7.11 TCP_REFRESH_UNMODIFIED/304 303 GET http://news.example/ - HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.20 -

    index($1,".") finds the position of the dot, substr takes from the dot to the end (.433), and that's appended after the converted time.

  2. Spaces between fields collapse to one. When awk changes a field it rebuilds the line with single spaces between fields. Losing the original log's alignment spaces is harmless, but leave the original untouched and save the converted result to a new file. Never modify original evidence.

  3. Some awks lack strftime. strftime started as a GNU awk (gawk) extension. In this work environment the default awk, mawk 1.3.4, ran the commands above, but older versions such as mawk 1.3.3 don't have it. If you get an error like "function strftime never defined", run it with gawk.

You can chain this with other commands such as grep, e.g. grep -F 'c2.example.net' access.log | awk '{$1=strftime("%F %T", $1, 1); print}': filter first, then convert. If you use it often, a shell alias is handy:

alias squidtime='awk '\''{$1=strftime("%F %T", $1, 1); print}'\'''

To put single quotes inside single quotes, it uses '\'' (close the quote, one escaped quote, reopen). With this you can write grep -F 'c2.example.net' access.log | squidtime (tested in this work environment).

docs.title: 7.1 Automated analysis tools
docs.text: Squid is so widely used that there are countless tools to summarise its logs and show them as graphs. The source material cites calamaris and squidview, and the Squid project maintains a list of log analysis tools. But most were built for proxy administrators. They're good for questions like "which sites use the most bandwidth?" or "what's the cache hit rate?", which may not be the investigator's questions. Many also only read the default format and can't parse custom-format logs; you'll run into exactly this in lesson 1.4's walkthrough. With open-source tools you can modify the code to read new formats, so weigh what each tool offers and pick or adapt what suits the situation.

docs.title: 7.2 Plain-text logs mean a shell is all you need
docs.text:
The biggest strength of Squid logs is that they're plain text. A proprietary binary or database format needs converting first, but plain text can be cut, counted and sorted with familiar tools straight away.

flowchart TD
    M["Meaning and value<br/>(investigation findings)"]
    T2["bash · PowerShell · python · jq · Grok"] --> M
    T1["grep · awk · sed · perl"] --> T2
    L["access.log (plain text)"] --> T1

How to read the diagram: it stacks from bottom to top. On top of the plain-text log are line tools (grep, awk, etc.), and above them the scripting languages and structuring tools that combine them. The "meaning" at the top isn't a tool; it's what a person gets by interpreting. Grok is a pattern language that splits a log line into named fields; it comes back in Part 2's log aggregation.

Automated tools and shell commands reduce vast data so outliers are easy to find. The machine points "look here", and the person looks there to find the data that answers the questions. A few examples run directly against the sample log (actual output):

Which sites got the most requests?

$ awk '$6!="CONNECT"{print $7}' access.log | awk -F/ '{print $3}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
      4 news.example
      3 api-telemetry-sync.example
      2 parcel-redelivery.example
      1 files.example.net
      1 c2.example.net
  • awk '$6!="CONNECT"{print $7}': keeps only lines whose sixth field (method) isn't CONNECT, and prints the seventh field (URL). CONNECT lines have host:443 in the URL field, which doesn't fit the next step, so they're excluded.
  • awk -F/ '{print $3}': this time uses / as the field separator to split the URL. http://news.example/a splits into http:, empty, news.example, a, so the third field is the hostname.
  • sort | uniq -c: groups identical values (sort) and counts how many times each appears (uniq -c). uniq only merges adjacent identical lines, so the sort before it is essential.
  • sort -rn: sorts by the count (-n), largest first (-r).

What were the results?

$ awk '{print $4}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
      6 TCP_MISS/200
      1 TCP_TUNNEL/200
      1 TCP_REFRESH_UNMODIFIED/304
      1 TCP_MISS/302
      1 TCP_MEM_HIT/200
      1 TCP_DENIED/407
      1 TCP_DENIED/403

Which PC received the most?

$ awk '{b[$3]+=$5} END{for(c in b) print b[c], c}' access.log | sort -rn
1847070 10.10.7.15
98823 10.10.6.11
48213 10.10.6.14
29802 10.10.7.11
3995 10.10.5.25

b[$3]+=$5 means "keep adding the reply size (field 5) per client address (field 3)", and END{...} means print the accumulated totals after reading the whole file.

Taking the three results together gives an interpretation. 10.10.7.15 received by far the most because of the single update.bin file, and the same PC also requested the blocked C2 domain. 10.10.7.11 received little but has regular POSTs. The key point is that receiving little doesn't mean safe. Beacons are small by nature. So "which PC received the most" and "which PC sends regularly" are different questions, and you must ask both. These numbers are only a starting point, though; conclusions come after cross-checking endpoint, DNS and firewall records in the order from lesson 1.1.

docs.title: 8. How to interpret it in a real investigation
docs.text:
Common mistakes when reading proxy logs:

  • "200, so it's infected" is wrong. 200 only means it was received, not executed. Confirm execution with endpoint records.
  • Size isn't exactly the received file's size. Headers are included; 206 means only part, _ABORTED means the amount before it was cut off. 304 is a "no change" answer with no content.
  • The time is the finish time, and you must check the time zone. The default format's Unix time is UTC, but custom formats using %tl are in the server's local time. The server clock itself may be wrong, so where possible align a few times against other records the same event left (firewall, packets) and record the offset.
  • The requesting IP may not be the real client. If another proxy or load balancer sits in between, its address is recorded.
  • Some things aren't in the log. Traffic that bypassed the proxy, stripped query strings, paths of uninspected HTTPS, and POST request bodies (what was uploaded) aren't in the log. The missing POST body matters especially in exfiltration investigations, and you'll hit it head-on in lesson 1.4.

docs.title: 9. Summary
docs.text:
• A proxy log line is a form with information in set fields, and which fields appear and in what order is set by the config's logformat.
  • The ten fields of Squid's default format are time, response time, client IP, cache status/HTTP code, size, method, URL, user name, hierarchy status/server IP and MIME type.
  • The time is UTC Unix time when the request finished; estimate the start as "time − response time".
  • The HTTP status code tells you "what happened", and the cache status tells you whether there was real external communication. In Squid 7, TCP_REFRESH_UNMODIFIED replaces TCP_REFRESH_HIT, and CONNECT is logged as TCP_TUNNEL.
  • The default format lacks User-Agent, Referer and readable time. The built-in combined format fills them in, but %tl is server local time. Squid 7 removed ident (%ui).
  • Convert Unix time one line at a time with date -u -d @number, or all at once with awk's strftime. Leave the original untouched and save results to a new file.
  • Automated tools and shell commands only point at outliers; a person finds the meaning by aligning them with other evidence.

In the next lesson (1.4) we use all of these skills to reconstruct one employee's day from proxy logs alone.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. Put this default-format log line into words, with the time in UTC.

1760231203.910    455 10.10.6.11 TCP_MISS/200 98211 GET http://parcel-redelivery.example/dl/label.zip - HIER_DIRECT/198.51.100.77 application/zip
Answer and explanation

At about 01:06:43 UTC on 2025-10-12 (date -u -d @1760231203.910), PC 10.10.6.11 requested http://parcel-redelivery.example/dl/label.zip with GET. It wasn't in the cache (TCP_MISS), so the proxy went directly (HIER_DIRECT) to server 198.51.100.77 to fetch it; the result was 200 (success), the size sent to the client was 98,211 bytes including headers, and the server declared it a ZIP file (application/zip). Processing took 0.455 seconds and there's no user name (-). But "it's a ZIP file" is the server's claim, and "the user opened it" can't be known from this line.

Question 2. A CONNECT line has a recorded time of 1760231012.880 and a response time of 60412. The firewall log records the same connection as starting at 01:02:32 UTC. How do you explain the one-minute difference?

Answer and explanation

Squid's timestamp is when the request finished. 1760231012.880 is 01:03:32 UTC, and with a response time of 60,412 ms (about 60 seconds), the tunnel opened at about 01:03:32 − 60 s = 01:02:32, exactly matching the firewall's connection start time. So no clock is wrong; the two devices recorded different moments (start and finish). Not knowing this and "correcting" the proxy clock by a minute would shift every other time wrongly.

Question 3. (Common misconception) A PC's log has TCP_REFRESH_UNMODIFIED/304 303. A colleague says "this PC only received 303 bytes, so it barely saw that page". Right?

Answer and explanation

Wrong. A 304 to the client means "the copy the browser already has is still valid; use it". The 303 bytes are just the size of that short answer, and the user most likely saw the whole page on screen from the browser cache's copy. The TCP_REFRESH_UNMODIFIED in front means the proxy, too, checked with the server and found its cached copy unchanged. The real content size is in the earlier TCP_MISS/200 line for the same URL (17,746 bytes in section 3.4).

Question 4. (Changed conditions) The proxy server's time zone is Australia/Sydney and the log format is combined. The log shows [12/Oct/2025:12:06:43 +1100]. What's that in UTC, and if the same server also logged in the default squid format, what would the first field contain?

Answer and explanation

+1100 means 11 hours ahead of UTC, so in UTC it's 12:06:43 − 11 h = 2025-10-12 01:06:43. The default format's first field is Unix time, independent of time zone, so it's 1760231203.xxx, the same as question 1 (the milliseconds are unknown because the combined format doesn't carry them). Unix time not changing with the server's time zone is a strength of the default format; with %tl formats you must read the trailing zone. Logging with %tg (GMT) from the start avoids this conversion.

Question 5. (Reading a command) Explain step by step what this command does, and how the result changes if you remove the first sort.

awk '{print $3}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
Answer and explanation
  1. awk '{print $3}': extracts the third field of each line, the client IP.
  2. sort: sorts so identical IPs are adjacent.
  3. uniq -c: merges adjacent identical lines and counts them.
  4. sort -rn: sorts by count, largest first.
  5. head -5: shows the top five only.

The result is "the five clients that sent the most requests". Without the first sort, uniq -c only merges consecutive identical IPs, so an IP scattered through the log gets counted as several separate lines. The PC that actually made the most requests then drops in the ranking, giving a wrong result.

Question 6. (Today's environment) You want to upgrade an old Squid server to Squid 7, but its config has a line like the source material's logformat combined %>a %[ui %[un [%tl] .... What happens, and from an investigation standpoint how should the second field of that server's old logs be treated?

Answer and explanation

Squid 7 removed ident support and rejects configurations containing the %ui format code, so Squid won't start. To upgrade, remove that line and use the built-in combined, or a format without %ui. After the upgrade that field is always -. If the second field in old logs has a value, it's a name obtained via ident. Ident is an old, insecure mechanism that simply accepts what the client side reports, so don't use that value as evidence that "this person did it". Confirm user identity from trustworthy sources such as proxy authentication (%ul) or domain logon records.

Question 7. (Interpreting results) Looking at section 7.2's results, a colleague says "10.10.7.11 received about the least, so let's drop it from the priority list". How would you respond?

Answer and explanation

Don't drop it. 10.10.7.11 is the PC that sent same-size (2,211-byte) POSTs to the same address at exactly 5-minute intervals. Beacons and C2 traffic are small and regular by nature, so they don't show in totals received. "How much was received" and "how regularly was something sent" are different questions, and you must ask both. And a POST is a request that uploads data, yet the default log doesn't record what was uploaded (the body). So this PC is, if anything, a priority target for checking endpoint records, DNS and domain reputation together.

Question 8. (Reading config) In the proxy under investigation you find a line like section 5.1's access_log ... suspect.log logformat=combined suspect_dst. But the administrator says "our proxy log is just access.log". What do you check, and what possibilities should you consider?

Answer and explanation

Per the config, requests matching suspect_dst are additionally written to suspect.log, so check whether that file exists and since when it's been written (file creation and modification times, config change history). There are several possibilities. Someone may have created it during an earlier incident and forgotten, or the administrator may simply not know. Because it's in combined format, that file holds User-Agent and Referer values missing from the default log, making it richer evidence for those domains. Conversely, if nobody knows who added this setting or why, the config change itself may be something to investigate. Either way, what the config file actually instructs takes priority over what the administrator says.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Squid project, Squid 7 branch src/cf.data.pre (checked 2026-11-05). Definitions of the built-in squid, common, combined, referrer and useragent log formats, meanings of format codes, and the recommended access_log syntax (logformat= option and ACLs).
  • Squid project, Squid 7 src/LogTags.cc and src/format/Format.cc (checked 2026-11-05). The list of cache status names; %ts comes from the current time when the log line is written, and %tr is request processing time.
  • Squid project, Squid 7 release notes source (checked 2026-11-05). Ident support removed, configurations with %ui fail to start, and that field in common/combined is always -.
  • MDN Web Docs, Referrer-Policy (checked in the source repository 2026-11-05). With no policy specified, strict-origin-when-cross-origin is the default; before the November 2020 Fetch standard revision (whatwg/fetch#1066) it was no-referrer-when-downgrade.

About this page

Personal study notes rewritten in my own words from a range of study material. The sample log and configuration were made up for explanation.

docs.title: Lesson 1.8 — Practical tcpdump Options and Reading the Wireshark Window
Lesson 1.8 — Practical tcpdump Options and Reading the Wireshark Window
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • tcpdump options for long captures: splitting files by size and time (-C, -G), limiting their number (-W), filter files (-F), and post-rotation processing (-z)
  • Reading four common capture and conversion commands piece by piece
  • The five parts of the Wireshark window (filter bar, packet list, packet details, packet bytes, status bar) and how they relate
  • Name resolution settings and OPSEC: what's safe to turn on and what to turn off
  • Adding columns and time display formats

Display filter syntax and following streams are the next lesson (1.9).

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) was produced with tcpdump 4.99.4 and tshark 4.2.2 in this work environment. This environment has no display (GUI), so the Wireshark window itself couldn't be opened. The window is therefore described by its menu names and structure, and the same features (detail view, byte view, name resolution, time formats, custom columns) were actually run with tshark, which uses the same engine. Wireshark menu names may vary slightly between versions.

docs.title: 1. Capturing only DNS for two weeks
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) After lesson 1.4's incident, the security team decides "let's capture all of the organisation's DNS traffic for the next two weeks". As lesson 1.7 taught, port 53 will do for the capture filter, but problems remain.

  • Two weeks in one file is too big to open, and if the file gets corrupted midway you lose everything.
  • When the disk fills, capture may stop or the system may stall.
  • Later, when you want only "the afternoon of 20 October", you need to find that part straight away.

That's why tcpdump has options to split files, name them and limit their number. And the captured files eventually get opened in Wireshark, which has a setting you mustn't leave as it is. This lesson covers both.

docs.title: 2. tcpdump options for long captures
docs.text:
On top of lesson 1.6's basic options (-r, -w, -i, -n, -s), these are commonly used in practice:

Option Meaning Remember -r file Read from a pcap file instead of the network -w file Write to a pcap file instead of the screen -i interface Interface to capture on On Linux and others, any captures all interfaces at once -n No name lookups Almost always add it. Prevents slowdowns and OPSEC problems -C size Start a new file when the file exceeds that size Unit is 1,000,000 bytes (a million bytes, not MiB) -G seconds Start a new file every that many seconds The file name must include a time format -W count With -C, rotate through that many files; with -G, create that many and exit -F file Read the filter from a file instead of the command line For a team to share filters (lesson 1.7) -z command Run a command on each file as it's closed e.g. -z gzip to compress -c count Capture that many packets and exit -A Show content as text Lesson 1.6

Now the results of testing each option. Tests ran on the loopback interface while sending continuous requests to the test web server.

docs.title: 2.1 -G: splitting by time
docs.text:
$ tcpdump -n -i lo -G 2 -W 3 -w 'dns-%F_%H%M%S.pcap' 'tcp port 8082'
$ echo $?
0
$ ls -1 dns-*
dns-2026-11-05_025710.pcap
dns-2026-11-05_025712.pcap
dns-2026-11-05_025714.pcap

(Actual output. In reality -Z root was also added; see lesson 1.6 section 7.) -G 2 means a new file every 2 seconds and -W 3 means make three and exit; it really made three files and exited normally (0). The %F (year-month-day) and %H%M%S (hours, minutes, seconds) in the file name are strftime, the standard time format syntax, the same one you saw in lesson 1.3's awk. So you can tell from the file name alone when each file is from.

Testing revealed three things.

① Without a time format in the name, files keep getting overwritten. Capturing for 5 seconds with -G 1 -w same.pcap left only one file, same.pcap (actual output). The tcpdump documentation also warns that "if no time format is specified, each new file will overwrite the previous". Each new file made every second has the same name, so only the last second survives. For the same reason, a time format coarser than the rotation interval (e.g. rotating every second with only minutes in the name) also overwrites.

② The time in the file name is the capture machine's local time zone. Capturing with the time zone set to Sydney, a file made at 02:58 UTC was named tz-2026-11-05_135818.pcap, i.e. 13:58 (actual output). The times inside the packets are UTC (lesson 1.6) but the file names are local time, so looking for "the files from the 03:00 UTC hour" later, you might open the wrong file. Running capture scripts in UTC, as in TZ=UTC tcpdump ..., removes this confusion.

③ New files are only created when packets arrive. On the first test the traffic stopped partway, and even after waiting 20 seconds there were only two files and tcpdump hadn't exited (actual output). tcpdump checks "is it time to rotate?" when it receives a packet, so on a quiet link a file may not change even after the set time has passed. So don't assume "rotated every 2 hours, so each file is exactly 2 hours"; check each file's first and last packet times with capinfos.

docs.title: 2.2 -C and -W: splitting by size and rotating
docs.text:
$ tcpdump -n -i lo -C 1 -W 3 -w ring.pcap 'tcp port 8082'
$ ls -l ring.pcap*
1000021 ring.pcap0
1000021 ring.pcap1
589919 ring.pcap2

(Actual output, sizes and names only.) -C 1 means a new file every 1,000,000 bytes and -W 3 means rotate through three files (a ring buffer). The file names got 0, 1 and 2 appended. Per the documentation, with -W it pads names with leading zeros to fit the file count (e.g. from 00 for a count of 100) so they sort in order, and once the set number is used it overwrites from the first file. This test only filled up to the third file, so I didn't observe the overwriting itself.

The file size being 1,000,021 bytes rather than exactly 1,000,000 has a reason too. tcpdump checks "is the file now bigger than this size?" before writing each packet, so it overshoots by the last packet. And the documentation states that the unit is 1,000,000 bytes, not 1,048,576 (MiB).

[Changed] Unit suffixes depend on the version. The latest tcpdump documentation says you can add k, m or g suffixes, as in -C 20k or -C 500m, to change the unit. But -C 20k on this work environment's 4.99.4 gave the error tcpdump: invalid file size 20k (actual output). The repository's documentation and change log show this feature arrived in 4.99.6 (checked 2026-11-05). Distribution packages often lag the latest, so test on the capture device's tcpdump version first.

A ring buffer with -C and -W keeps the disk from overflowing, but old data silently disappears. Lesson 1.1 section 8.1's "retention" calculation applies directly. Work out in advance how many hours one ring buffer holds, and when an incident occurs, copy the files you need before they're overwritten.

docs.title: 2.3 -z: processing each file as it's closed
docs.text:
-z gzip runs gzip on each file as it's closed, compressing it. Put a small script that records a hash there instead of compressing, and you keep each file's hash from the moment it's created, which helps evidence management. In this lab environment no rotation happened within the test window, so I didn't directly confirm the -z result.

[Supplement] dumpcap's ring buffer. dumpcap, included with Wireshark, does the same job. It splits and rotates with -b duration:seconds, -b filesize:kilobytes and -b files:count, and its default save format is pcapng, so each file keeps the interface and filter information from lesson 1.6. Whichever you use, testing on the capture device under real load comes first.

docs.title: 2.4 Four common commands
docs.text:
The source material's examples, adapted to this series' hypothetical organisation and read piece by piece.

① A quick look on screen

sudo tcpdump -n -s 100 -A -i ens33 -c 1000

Captures the first 1,000 packets (-c 1000) on interface ens33, shows the first 100 bytes of each (-s 100) including content as text (-A), and exits. Good for getting a feel for what's on a link. Without -n it looks up a name for every IP and is much slower.

② Extracting one host from a large file

tcpdump -n -r input.pcap -w output.pcap 'host 10.10.6.14'

Reads input.pcap and writes only packets involving 10.10.6.14 to output.pcap: lesson 1.7's "data reduction". It only reads a file, so no administrator rights are needed.

③ 14 days of DNS, one file per day

sudo TZ=UTC tcpdump -n -i ens33 -w 'dns-%F_%H%M%S.pcap' -G 86400 -W 14 'port 53'

A new file every 86,400 seconds (24 hours × 60 minutes × 60 seconds), exiting after 14 files. The source material writes the filter as '(tcp or udp) and port 53', but as lesson 1.7 showed, port already catches both TCP and UDP, so it's effectively the same as 'port 53' (the original form is better if you need to exclude other transports such as SCTP precisely). TZ=UTC in front makes the file names UTC too (section 2.1 ②). But as in section 2.1 ③, files only change when packets arrive, so don't assume each file breaks exactly at midnight.

④ A suspicious host, 100 MB at a time, indefinitely

sudo tcpdump -n -i ens33 -w suspect.pcap -C 100 'host 203.0.113.77'

Writes traffic with 203.0.113.77 to a new file (suspect.pcap, suspect.pcap1, suspect.pcap2 …) every 100,000,000 bytes (100 × 1,000,000), without end. With no -W it doesn't rotate and just keeps growing, so watch the disk. This shape is for when you expect little volume, since it's just one suspicious host.

docs.title: 3. Reading the Wireshark window
docs.text:
Now open the captured files in Wireshark, the window you'll stare at longest in this series. From top to bottom it has five parts.

flowchart TD
    F["① Display filter bar<br/>choose packets to show"]
    L["② Packet list<br/>one row per packet · configurable columns"]
    D["③ Packet details<br/>frame → Ethernet → IP → TCP → HTTP"]
    B["④ Packet bytes<br/>hex + text"]
    S["⑤ Status bar<br/>field name · length · packet counts"]
    F --> L
    L -->|"select a row"| D
    D <-->|"highlight each other"| B
    B ~~~ S
    D -.->|"selected field name"| S

How to read the diagram: top to bottom is the actual layout of the window. Selecting a row in the packet list shows that packet in the details and bytes panes, and fields in the details pane and bytes in the bytes pane highlight each other (two-way arrow). Selecting a field in the details pane shows its name in the status bar (dotted line).

② Packet list. One row per packet, with configurable columns. The default "Time" column is seconds since the capture started, handy for intervals between packets but not the actual time. As lesson 1.6 showed, pcap has a UTC time for each packet, so you can switch to a human-readable time (section 5). The "Info" column is the dissector's one-line summary of the packet, good for scanning many packets for interesting ones.

③ Packet details. Where the dissectors show their real power. It unfolds every field in the packet by layer, from the IP, TCP and UDP headers up to the application data at the top. Even unfamiliar protocols are shown with human-readable field names and values, so start here when exploring a protocol you don't know. tshark's -V shows the same content as text (actual output, partial):

$ tshark -r nameres.pcap -n -Y 'frame.number==6' -V
Frame 6: 201 bytes on wire (1608 bits), 201 bytes captured (1608 bits)
    Arrival Time: Oct 14, 2026 17:46:40.600000000 UTC
    ...
Ethernet II, Src: 00:50:56:0a:06:14, Dst: 00:50:56:0a:00:01
    ...
Internet Protocol Version 4, Src: 10.10.6.14, Dst: 203.0.113.50
    ...
    Time to Live: 64
    Protocol: TCP (6)
    ...
Transmission Control Protocol, Src Port: 50010, Dst Port: 80, Seq: 1, Ack: 1, Len: 147

"Frame" at the top isn't data from the wire but metadata Wireshark attaches (capture time, stored length, etc.: lesson 1.6's record header). Below it are the real headers stacked as Ethernet, IP, TCP.

④ Packet bytes. A hex dump of every byte of the packet as stored in the pcap file (= as it crossed the wire). tshark's -x gives the same shape (actual output, partial):

$ tshark -r nameres.pcap -n -Y 'frame.number==6' -x
0000  00 50 56 0a 00 01 00 50 56 0a 06 14 08 00 45 00   .PV....PV.....E.
0010  00 bb 12 34 40 00 40 06 db be 0a 0a 06 0e cb 00   ...4@.@.........
0020  71 32 c3 5a 00 50 00 00 03 e9 00 00 1b 59 50 18   q2.Z.P.......YP.
0030  fa f0 00 00 00 00 47 45 54 20 2f 75 70 64 61 74   ......GET /updat

At first it seems unnecessary next to the details pane, but the raw bytes often reveal interesting parts the details pane passed over. So Wireshark links the two panes. Click a byte in the bytes pane and the field that byte decodes into is highlighted in the details pane; click a field in the details pane and its bytes are highlighted. For example, clicking the 06 at offset 0x17 in the dump above highlights "Protocol: TCP (6)" in the details pane. It does the byte-offset arithmetic you did by hand in lessons 1.6 and 1.7, and understanding this link is critical for an analyst.

① Display filter bar. At the top of the window, where you choose which packets to show. Lesson 1.9 covers it in detail.

⑤ Status bar. At the bottom, giving a quick frame of reference. On the left it shows the dissector field name and byte length of the field selected in the details pane (e.g. ip.proto), which is essential information for building display filters. In the middle it shows the total packet count and how many packets the current filter displays. If capturing with Wireshark directly, it also shows values such as how many packets libpcap dropped for lack of resources.

Changing the layout. Under Edit → Preferences → Appearance → Layout you can pick one of six pane layouts and what each pane shows. Only cosmetic, but on an odd screen ratio or a large shared screen it can make a big difference to usability.

docs.title: 4. Name resolution and OPSEC
docs.text:
Wireshark has several name resolution settings that show addresses and numbers as human-readable names (Edit → Preferences → Name Resolution). Some are safe to turn on; some can ruin an investigation.

Setting What it changes Where it looks OPSEC MAC address resolution First 3 bytes of a MAC → vendor name Wireshark's built-in vendor table Safe (no outbound traffic) Transport name resolution Port number → service name (80 → http) Wireshark's built-in service table Safe Network address resolution IP address → hostname The two methods below Depends on the method ├ Use captured DNS packets Name addresses from DNS responses in the file The pcap you opened Safe, and the name as of that time └ Use an external name resolver The analysis PC really asks a DNS server Today's DNS Dangerous

docs.title: 4.1 Testing it
docs.text:
I built a test pcap with a DNS query and response plus an HTTP request to that address, and ran it through tshark (actual output, partial):

$ tshark -r nameres.pcap -n
    2   0.120000   10.10.4.53 → 10.10.6.14   DNS 93 Standard query response 0xabcd A files.example.net A 203.0.113.50
    3   0.240000   10.10.6.14 → 203.0.113.50 TCP 54 50010 → 80 [SYN] Seq=0 Win=64240 Len=0
$ tshark -r nameres.pcap -N dn
    3   0.240000   10.10.6.14 → files.example.net TCP 54 50010 → 80 [SYN] Seq=0 Win=64240 Len=0
$ tshark -r nameres.pcap -N mt -T fields -e eth.src_resolved -e _ws.col.Info
VMware_0a:06:14 50010 → 80 [SYN] Seq=0 Win=64240 Len=0
VMware_0a:00:01 http(80) → 50010 [SYN, ACK] Seq=0 Ack=1 Win=64240 Len=0

-n turns off all name resolution. The letters after -N are the kinds of resolution to turn on; per the tshark documentation, d is use captured DNS packets, n network address resolution, N use external resolvers, m MAC, and t transport (ports). With -N dn, 203.0.113.50 became files.example.net based on the DNS response in the file; with -N mt, the MAC prefix 00:50:56 showed as VMware and port 80 as http(80).

So did the analysis PC send anything out? I ran it again watching the network operations tshark requested from the OS with a tool called strace (actual output):

tshark option Times the analysis PC tried to connect to a DNS server (port 53) -N dn (captured DNS + network address resolution) 0 -N dnN (plus external resolver) 2 (to the system DNS server 8.8.8.8) -o nameres.network_name:TRUE (only the setting equivalent to ticking "Resolve network addresses" in the GUI) 2

The third row is the key. In this version's (4.2.2) default preferences, the external resolver is already on and only network address resolution is off (checked with tshark -G defaultprefs). So the moment you tick "Resolve network addresses" in the GUI, the analysis PC starts sending real DNS queries for every IP in the pcap. The latest documentation (as of 4.6) also gives the default with no settings as -N dmN, i.e. with the external resolver on.

docs.title: 4.2 Why external resolution is dangerous
docs.text:
The source material gives three reasons.

  1. OPSEC. Attackers who run their own DNS servers often watch queries for their IPs and domains. A query from an unfamiliar source can tell them "someone has found my infrastructure". It sounds paranoid, but it has happened in the wild, and attackers react fast. And if the query goes out through the organisation's DNS server, the investigator's queries get mixed into the DNS logs from lesson 1.3, causing confusion later.
  2. Time differs. DNS records change often. The answer you get now may differ from the answer when the evidence was collected weeks ago. If the attacker changed the domain's address, you'll see the wrong name on screen.
  3. Location differs. DNS responses can vary with the network location of the querier (regional responses, internal-only names, etc.). The answer at the analysis PC may differ from the one the victim PC got.

So the rule is to almost never turn this setting on. Instead, the use captured DNS packets feature the Wireshark team added is a good alternative. It names addresses only from DNS responses inside the packets, so there's no outbound traffic and, above all, it shows the names as of when the evidence was collected: a kind of passive DNS. But remember that addresses with no DNS response in the file get no name (e.g. a capture filter that excluded DNS, lesson 1.7), and that the DNS response itself may have been forged.

MAC and transport name resolution are a matter of personal preference and create no outbound traffic, so there's no OPSEC worry. But transport names are a convenience feature attached from the port number alone, so http(80) doesn't mean the connection really is HTTP. Don't miss cases where an attacker uses a different protocol on port 80.

[Changed] Where the vendor and service tables live. The source material says these tables are in the files /usr/share/wireshark/manuf and services. Since Wireshark 4.2.0, these files (manuf, services, enterprises) were compiled into the program for faster start-up and are no longer shipped as separate files.
