docs.title: Lesson 1.1 — Evidence Beyond the Disk: Why Network Forensics, and the Investigator's Mindset
Lesson 1.1 — Evidence Beyond the Disk: Why Network Forensics, and the Investigator's Mindset
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

This is the first lesson of Part 1. It answers these questions:

  • When does disk forensics hit a wall?
  • What evidence does the network keep when that happens?
  • What can each kind of evidence tell you, and what can't it?
  • What attitude should an investigator bring to the evidence?

It also introduces how threat hunting and threat intelligence link security operations (the SOC) with incident response, the time, scope and scale pressures on a response team, the hypothetical organisation network used throughout the series, and the series goals. There are almost no commands or tools yet. This lesson is about why we will spend the next lessons on proxy logs, pcap and flows.

Notation

(Hypothetical) = a story made up to aid understanding, (Illustrative output) = output that shows the shape only and was not actually run, [Changed] = something that differs from older material, [Supplement] = a practical addition. External addresses use documentation ranges (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24) and example domains. Internal addresses use the private 10.0.0.0/8 range so they cannot collide with any real network.

docs.title: 1. A phone call on a Friday afternoon
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) At four o'clock on a Friday afternoon, the security team gets a call from an outside agency: "An address in your range has been talking to an attack server we're tracking, 203.0.113.50, for the past few weeks." All you have is that one external address and a rough "a few weeks ago".

If you were the responder, where would you start? The first idea is probably "find that PC and image the disk". Disk forensics is powerful. Deleted files leave traces, and trying to wipe them leaves more traces. But this route is blocked more often than you might expect.

  • You don't know which PC it is. The agency gave you one of your public IPs, and behind it thousands of machines hide behind NAT (address translation).
  • The PC may already be gone. It may have been rebuilt, the laptop lost, or it was a cloud instance that has since been deleted.
  • Touching it may tip off the attacker. If the attacker is still inside, suddenly seizing a PC or running security tools signals "an investigation has started". The attacker may wipe traces or hide through another path. Acting so that the investigation doesn't leak to the adversary is called OPSEC (operational security). It comes up throughout this series.
  • It may not be just one machine. Attackers don't stop at the first PC; they move on to other systems inside. This is lateral movement. In an organisation with tens of thousands of staff, answering "how far did it spread?" by imaging one disk at a time is simply not realistic.

To be fair, the disk side still has chances. Even disk encryption can sometimes be defeated with keys left in memory (RAM) or the page file, if the system that did the encrypting wasn't carefully sanitised. The catch is that you have to be able to touch that system.

The network side, on the other hand, has two advantages the disk doesn't.

  • The evidence may already be collected. Packet sensors, flow collectors and proxy and firewall logs that were running before the incident may already hold records of that moment. Unlike disk forensics, where you image a PC after the fact, you don't have to "create" the evidence; you just have to pull it out.
  • You can look for attackers you don't yet know exist. Going out to look for "is there an attacker already inside?" before any alert fires is called threat hunting. Network data, which carries the whole organisation's communication, is an excellent place to hunt. You can't look at tens of thousands of disks, but you can see those machines' outbound traffic all at once at a few points.

And the skills you learn here aren't only for incident response. The same skills apply to alert analysis in security operations (the SOC), detection rule development and hunting. Section 7 returns to this link.

So what do you look at when you can't look at the disk? The answer is the path the communication took. For a PC to talk to an external server, data must pass through switches, proxies, firewalls and routers. Some of those devices record the conversation in their own way. Network forensics is collecting those records, reading them, and fitting them together.

docs.title: 2. An analogy: one incident, many witnesses
docs.text:
Picture something going missing from a building. If you can't search the suspect's home (= the disk), what would you check?

  • Corridor CCTV footage: you see who went past, when, and what they carried. But it takes a lot of storage, so it isn't kept for long.
  • Access-card records: only "card X passed door Y at time Z". You don't know what they carried, but months of records cost little to keep.
  • The guard's log book: only what the guard judged important, such as "door alarm, 3rd-floor store room, 14:02".

The network has the same structure. CCTV is full packet capture (every byte exchanged, stored in full). Access-card records are flow records (only who talked to whom, when, and how much; NetFlow is the best-known form). The guard's log book is the device logs written by proxies, firewalls, DNS servers and intrusion detection systems. Several witnesses saw the same communication from different angles, so by fitting them together you get a picture no single witness can give.

There is one way this analogy differs from reality, and it matters a lot. A human witness remembers even without a recording device. A network cable remembers nothing. Packets vanish once they pass, and unless someone attached a recorder beforehand, that moment can never be seen again. A disk keeps what happened before we arrived; the network only shows what happened after collection started. That is why one of the biggest tasks in network forensics is "install and run collection before you need it".

Fortunately, even an organisation that prepared nothing is not empty-handed. Firewalls and proxies already log for operational reasons, and DNS servers, VPN appliances and cloud services often keep records of their own. A skilled investigator doesn't say "no packets, so we're done"; they find every remaining witness and fill as many gaps in their hypotheses as they can.

docs.title: 3. The evidence spectrum: from summaries to a complete copy
docs.text:
Network evidence can be lined up by "how summarised it is". At one end are heavily summarised sources: statistics, graphs, flow records, host logs. At the other end is full packet capture, a bit-for-bit copy of everything that crossed the wire. Dozens of evidence sources sit in between.

flowchart TD
    A["Statistics · graphs<br/>(most summarised)"] --> B["Flow records<br/>NetFlow etc."]
    B --> C["Device · server logs<br/>proxy · firewall · DNS"]
    C --> D["Full packets<br/>pcap (complete copy)"]

How to read the diagram: moving top to bottom, detail increases. In exchange, storage grows, retention shrinks and analysis takes longer. Moving up, you can see further back and wider, but "what was exchanged" disappears.

"So isn't full packet capture all we need?" is the natural question. In theory yes, but in practice two things hold it back. First, volume. A 1 Gbps link at an average of 30% utilisation produces about 3.2 TB a day (1,000,000,000 bit/s × 0.3 ÷ 8 = 37.5 MB/s, × 86,400 s ≈ 3.24 TB). Second, encryption. Most traffic today is TLS-encrypted, so even with every packet you often can't read the content. In practice, organisations run several layers together, such as "months of flows + days of packets + assorted logs".

Here is what each source answers, side by side. Retention varies a lot between organisations, so treat that column as a rough feel only.

Source Questions it answers well Questions it can't answer Size · retention tendency Full packets (pcap) Exactly what was exchanged, which file crossed the wire Encrypted content, traffic outside the collection point Very large, usually days to weeks Flows (NetFlow etc.) Who talked to whom, when, for how long, how much Content, URLs, file names Small, months to a year or more possible Web proxy logs Which endpoint requested which URL, the result code, sometimes the username Traffic that bypassed the proxy, request bodies Medium, weeks to months Firewall logs Which connections were allowed or denied What was inside the connection Can be large depending on settings DNS logs Which name was looked up, when, by whom What was actually done with that name Medium Host logs Which process or account on that system communicated Other systems, records that were deleted Varies per system

docs.title: 3.1 A small example: the traces one web request leaves
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) Internal PC 10.10.5.21 downloads http://files.example.net/update.bin with a browser. The request takes this path:

flowchart TD
    PC["Internal PC<br/>10.10.5.21"] --> SW["Switch"]
    SW --> PX["Web proxy"]
    PX --> FW["Firewall"]
    FW --> RT["Internet router"]
    RT --> SV["External server<br/>203.0.113.50"]
    TAP(["Tap/sensor<br/>stores packets"]) -.copy.- FW
    PX -.log.-> L1[("Proxy log")]
    FW -.log.-> L2[("Firewall log")]
    RT -.summary.-> L3[("Flow records")]

How to read the diagram: solid arrows are the direction the request actually travels (inside → Internet). Dotted lines show each device recording the request in its own way. The response comes back along the same path in reverse.

Each witness records the same moment like this (illustrative output, formats simplified):

[proxy log]     2026-10-12 01:14:09 10.10.5.21 GET http://files.example.net/update.bin 200 1843200
[firewall log]  2026-10-12 01:14:09 allow tcp 10.0.0.3:50122 -> 203.0.113.50:80
[flow record]   2026-10-12 01:14:09 tcp 203.0.113.50:80 -> 10.0.0.3:50122 packets 1290 bytes 1901544
[packet capture] GET /update.bin HTTP/1.1 / Host: files.example.net ... (entire file content)

Notice something here. In the firewall log and the flow record, the source is 10.0.0.3, not the PC's address 10.10.5.21. Why? Because the PC asks the proxy, and the proxy makes the outbound connection on its behalf. So from the firewall or the router's outside, every web request looks like it came from one proxy. The question "which PC was it?" can only be answered from the proxy log. The byte counts differing slightly is also normal. The proxy log counts the HTTP response size; the flow counts bytes including IP and TCP headers. Remember that each witness counts by a different rule.

docs.title: 3.2 Changing the conditions
docs.text:
Condition 1: what if it was HTTPS? Say the same download was https://. If the proxy doesn't use TLS inspection (decryption), its log keeps only a CONNECT files.example.net:443 line, not which file was fetched. The packet capture shows the server name inside the TLS handshake (SNI) plus sizes and timing, but the file content is ciphertext. The flow tells you size and time, exactly as with HTTP. So you can say "something of about 1.8 MB was received", but to say "a malicious file named update.bin was received" you need records from the endpoint or other evidence. Part 5 covers TLS in depth.

Condition 2: what if the attacker cleared the PC's logs? Even with the browser history and event logs wiped, the proxy, firewall and flow records sit on other devices, so they survive, unless the attacker controlled those too. This is a big advantage of network evidence: it accumulates physically apart from the target.

Condition 3: what if there was no collection at all? With no tap or sensor, there are no packets, ever. Then the first job is to find out which logs the devices were already writing and how long they keep them. If the firewall overwrites the oldest logs when space runs out, every day of delay costs a day of evidence. That is why, early in a response, securing the logs that still exist often comes before analysis.

docs.title: 3.3 How to interpret it in a real investigation
docs.text: In the example above, what the one proxy log line directly shows is "10.10.5.21 requested that URL and the server returned 200 (success) with 1,843,200 bytes". Concluding "that PC is infected" is premature. The file may have been downloaded but never run, or blocked by antivirus. To judge infection, you then check whether new outbound communication appeared from that PC (flows, proxy) and whether the file executed (endpoint records). Section 6 below formalises this "fact → hypothesis → further checks" flow.

docs.title: 4. Finding ten machines among tens of thousands: narrowing the scope
docs.text:
Now a harder situation. (Hypothetical) During the investigation you find that the attacker obtained a domain admin account's credentials and tried to use it to log on to other systems. The organisation has 30,000 endpoints, most of them not configured to log enough. Time to update your CV?

No. Lateral movement is still network communication. In a Windows environment, remote logon, file sharing and remote command execution use protocols such as SMB (port 445), RDP (3389) and WinRM (5985/5986). Which internal systems received such connections from the first infected PC is largely visible from internal flow records alone. That's how you cut 30,000 machines down to dozens, and then perform detailed disk and memory analysis on only the dozen or so that are genuinely suspicious.

flowchart TD
    A["All endpoints: 30,000"] -->|"Flows: systems that talked to the infected PC"| B["~300"]
    B -->|"SMB · RDP · WinRM + suspicious time window"| C["~40"]
    C -->|"Proxy · DNS: same C2 address"| D["12 for detailed analysis"]
    D --> E["Disk · memory forensics"]

How to read the diagram: moving down, the set of systems shrinks. The text by each arrow is the network evidence used at that step. The numbers are made up for illustration.

This shows one of network forensics' key roles. Network evidence sometimes reaches conclusions on its own, but more often it acts as a lead generator that tells you which systems to examine closely. It doesn't compete with disk forensics; it's the map that tells disk forensics where to dig.

A common misconception. Don't jump to "there was a connection on port 445, so it's lateral movement". Port 445 connections to file servers and domain controllers are countless and normal every day. Meaning appears only with unusual combinations: a user PC connecting to another user PC on 445, a connection at 3 a.m. outside working hours, a connection right after the suspected infection time. That's why knowing "what normal looks like" (a baseline) is where analysis starts.

docs.title: 5. The strengths and limits of network evidence
docs.text:
Network evidence alone usually struggles to prove criminal liability in court. The reason is simple: an IP address is not a person. Several people can share one address (NAT, shared PCs), and an endpoint may have been remotely controlled. Turning "this request came from this address" into "this person did it" needs other evidence alongside, such as account logs, physical access records and endpoint forensics.

That doesn't make it low-value. Inside an organisation, it is very persuasive as grounds for isolating an infected PC, suspending an account, or deciding where to spend budget and people. And as shown above, its value as a lead to other forensic evidence is huge. The same holds when an attack fails. The tools and techniques the attacker used, and what they were after, remain on the network. These are the attacker's TTPs (tactics, techniques and procedures). TTPs from a failed attack become intelligence for predicting the attacker's motives, capabilities and next moves.

docs.title: 6. The investigator's mindset: separating facts, hypotheses and conclusions
docs.text: Network evidence is voluminous and open to interpretation. So the attitude an investigator brings has a big effect on the result.

docs.title: 6.1 Be wary of tidy stories
docs.text:
Occam's razor, "the simplest explanation is usually right", is a fine everyday principle. In incident investigation it doesn't always hold, for two reasons.

First, skilled attackers deliberately mislead us. They plant tool strings used by other groups, generate eye-catching decoy traffic to draw attention away, or use covert channels that look like normal services. The first simple explanation you spot may be the one the attacker intended.

Second, inexperienced users leave unexpected traces too. They install odd software without understanding it, or misconfigure something so it produces traffic that looks like an attack. If you expect all the evidence to fit one neat story, you end up ignoring evidence that doesn't fit.

docs.title: 6.2 Investigate like a scientist
docs.text:
What an investigator needs, then, is a scientist's attitude. When gathering data, be disinterested, impartial and objective, with no stake in either conclusion. When an observation contradicts your hypothesis, abandon the hypothesis. Never believe in or rule out an idea dogmatically, and never use rhetorical exaggeration to push it or knock it down.

The best way to actually keep to this is to write down, from the start and separately, the facts you observed, the hypotheses those facts support, and the conclusions that need further evidence. Applied to the download example:

Category Content Basis · what's needed Observed fact 10.10.5.21 requested update.bin and received about 1.8 MB with a 200 response One proxy log line Observed fact From 01:20 the same day, small connections from that PC to 203.0.113.77 every 5 minutes Flow records Hypothesis The downloaded file ran and installed malware that calls out periodically Fits both facts, but a legitimate updater could look the same Conclusion needing more evidence The PC is infected and remotely controlled by the attacker Endpoint execution records, file analysis, content and destination reputation of the periodic traffic

The further down the table, the stronger the claim and the more evidence it needs. If you want to write "infected" in a report, you have to fill the right-hand cell of the bottom row. If you can't, the accurate report says "infection is suspected" and lists what still needs checking.

flowchart TD
    O["Observe<br/>(facts seen in evidence)"] --> H["Form hypothesis"]
    H --> T["Look for evidence to test it"]
    T -->|"supports"| R["Refine hypothesis"]
    T -->|"contradicts"| X["Abandon hypothesis"]
    R --> O
    X --> H

How to read the diagram: an investigation isn't a one-way task; it's a loop. When new evidence supports a hypothesis, you make it more specific and go back to observing. When it contradicts, you drop it and form a new one. The key is that the "contradicts → abandon" arrow exists at all.

docs.title: 6.3 Who receives the findings
docs.text:
The people who use a network forensic investigation's results, its "customers", are more varied than you might think. Even for the same incident, each asks different questions.

Who receives the findings What they mainly ask Incident response team How far has it spread, what do we block, what do we isolate Management How bad is the damage, do we stop operations, where do we spend budget Legal · HR Who broke which rule, does this support discipline or litigation Law enforcement · regulators Was there a crime or a breach of reporting duty, is the evidence legally usable SOC · intelligence team Which indicators and TTPs should become detection rules

Missions and priorities differ, but they all share one need: to know what actually happened. So the investigator must keep strictly to process and doggedly pull threads even when current tools don't handle them well. The work product must rest on data that withstands challenge, not on conjecture or unfounded opinion. When legal, or the other side's expert, asks "how do you know that?", you must be able to answer with evidence and process.

docs.title: 6.4 Be careful when there are no results, too
docs.text:
"I searched the proxy logs for that C2 address and found nothing" is not the same as "there was no communication with that address". First check:

  • Collection scope: was that PC's traffic really supposed to pass through that proxy? Was there a path that bypassed it?
  • Retention: are logs for the suspected period still there?
  • Encryption and logging behaviour: was it HTTPS, leaving only a CONNECT line instead of a URL? Did the proxy strip query strings before logging?
  • Tool settings: did you get the case sensitivity or the log format wrong?

Only after checking these can you say "no trace of communication within the scope examined", and even then you say it with that "within the scope examined" qualifier.

docs.title: 7. DFIR is not an island
docs.text:
DFIR (Digital Forensics and Incident Response) doesn't run on its own. It sits inside a cycle spanning the whole security organisation.

flowchart TD
    M["SOC · continuous monitoring"] --> DET["SOC · detection<br/>probable adversary behaviour"]
    DET -->|"alert"| IR["DFIR · incident response<br/>host · network"]
    IR --> TG["DFIR · intelligence generation"]
    TG -->|"CTI: behavioural signatures · TTPs"| SC["SOC · intelligence consumption<br/>SIEM analysis"]
    SC --> M
    TG --> HU["DFIR · threat hunting"]
    HU --> IR

How to read the diagram: "SOC" and "DFIR" at the start of each box name the function that does that work. The SOC (security operations centre) monitors and, when it detects probable adversary behaviour, hands an alert to DFIR. DFIR responds to and analyses incidents and generates intelligence about the attacker. That intelligence is used two ways. One is CTI (cyber threat intelligence) passed to the SOC, where it becomes detection signatures and feeds back into monitoring (the big outer loop). The other is reused inside DFIR as the starting point for threat hunting, and what hunting finds leads back into incident response (the small inner loop). Threat intelligence ties the SOC and DFIR into one cycle. There's no fixed starting point. An incident may start from a SOC detection alert, or from internally or externally generated threat intelligence (like the phone call in section 1).

Findings from network forensics flow around this cycle. For example, a C2 address and traffic pattern found during analysis are written up as threat intelligence, which becomes a detection rule in the SIEM (a system that collects many logs for search and alerting) or a firewall block policy. With the same information, the hunting team looks for "does any other PC show this pattern?" The next time the same attacker shows up, they're detected sooner.

Note the phrase "behavioural signatures". Attackers change IP addresses and domains easily, but rarely change how they work (their TTPs). So a rule that catches behaviour, such as "alert on same-size POSTs to the outside every 5 minutes", stays useful far longer than "alert on this address".

DFIR itself has several specialities: host, network, memory, malware analysis, mobile and more. No one person knows them all in depth, but they overlap a lot. The network knowledge in this series is useful when looking at network-related artifacts left on Windows, Linux, macOS or mobile devices, and when adding context to SIEM alerts. Conversely, someone who knows Windows file system artifacts will understand SMB (the Windows file-sharing protocol, covered in Part 3) traffic far faster. Building a broad bench of knowledge, alone or as a team, pays off.

docs.title: 8. How late is detection? The reality in numbers
docs.text:
The time an attacker stays inside before being discovered is called dwell time. This number ties directly to the question "how long do we need to keep evidence?"

[Changed] Older material on this topic cited the 2022 edition of the M-Trends report: a global median dwell time of 21 days, 14 days when the victim found it themselves, and 47% of victims first learning of the breach from an outside party. M-Trends 2026 (covering 2025 investigations), published on 23 March 2026, reports the following (checked 2026-11-05, Google Cloud blog summary).

Item Older material (2022 report) M-Trends 2026 Global median dwell time 21 days 14 days (up again from 11 in the previous report) Share first detected internally 53% (47% external notification) 52% (up from 43% the year before) Notable detail 8% undetected for over a year Median of 122 days for cyber espionage and North Korean IT worker cases

The year-by-year trend from the same report cited in the older material shows the direction more clearly (values are the median for that year's investigations, in days).

Investigation year 2011 2013 2015 2017 2019 2020 2021 All 416 229 146 101 56 24 21 Found via external notification — — 320 186 141 73 28 Found internally — — 56 57.5 30 12 18

In ten years the median dropped from over a year to about three weeks, which says the industry's detection and response improved that much. And in every year, cases learned of through outside notification had stayed hidden longer than those found internally. Outside notification comes from law enforcement, security researchers or regulators, and by the time they notice, the intrusion is often long under way.

A few cautions when reading these tables.

First, a median is "the middle value when the cases are lined up". A median of 14 days means half were found faster than 14 days and half were found later. Because it isn't a mean, cases that hid for months or years (the long tail) barely show in it. The 122 days for espionage cases shows how long that tail can be.

Next, year-to-year movement partly reflects changes in the mix of cases investigated. Lots of ransomware cases, which announce themselves, shorten dwell time; lots of espionage cases lengthen it. Don't read "14 days this year" as "an attacker is always caught within two weeks".

Finally, cases learned of through outside notification usually come with little detail, like the call in section 1: one address, one rough timeframe. That makes the network evidence you've stored internally even more important.

docs.title: 8.1 Do the maths: when retention is shorter than dwell time
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) An organisation keeps full packets for 7 days, proxy logs for 30 days and flows for 180 days. What if an attack is discovered 14 days after it began?

  • Full packets: 7 days < 14 days, so the first 7 days of the intrusion are already gone. You can't see the packets from the moment of entry.
  • Proxy logs: 30 days > 14 days, so the initial access is still recorded.
  • Flows: 180 days, so you can compare not just the start but also the "normal" picture before it (the baseline).

For an espionage-style case with 122 days of dwell time, the proxy logs (30 days) lose the start too, and only flows (180 days) cover it. That's why the more summarised the evidence, the more it's worth keeping for longer, and why layered retention makes sense. Retention isn't just a cost question, though; it interacts with privacy law and internal policy, so set it together with legal and privacy staff.

docs.title: 9. Three pressures on a response team: time, scope and scale
docs.text:
A response team ready to deploy doesn't mean things will go smoothly. A vague trigger like "some servers are dropping out oddly" doesn't tell you what to follow first. In many organisations, response teams name three big challenges.

Time. Response is almost always against a deadline. Yet DFIR doesn't allow guesses or unfounded claims, so you must be fast and accurate to the point of pedantry. Balancing deadlines against accuracy takes training and discipline.

Scope. Even if only 10–15 systems were really involved, picking those out of hundreds of thousands is very hard. Even with perfect knowledge of the environment and good tools, it can take days or weeks.

Scale. Many tools simply don't work at that size. So the team splits the environment into manageable chunks, and complexity grows with the number of chunks.

These three boil down to two questions. "How do we know we've found every affected system?" and "If hundreds are affected, how do we remediate them at scale?" Miss even one, and the attacker comes back through it. That's why remediation is often done all at once after scoping is complete, and until then it matters to investigate without the attacker noticing (the OPSEC from section 1).

Network data eases this pressure. The key is to start with the data that's most readily accessible right now. This series groups that data into three kinds:

Label Kind Example P Full-packet capture stores pcap saved by taps and sensors F Flow-based traffic summaries NetFlow exported by routers and firewalls L Infrastructure and endpoint logs Proxy, firewall, DNS, event logs

These show many systems at once from one place, so they directly reduce the scope and scale problems. The scoping in section 4 is exactly that. How much it helps, though, depends on how well this data is woven into the investigative process. And the investigator's most important skill is balance: adapting the method to the situation while sticking to established process and policy.

[Supplement] What to check on day one. Later lessons cover these in detail, but here's what's worth checking as soon as a response starts:

  1. Make a list of which evidence sources exist right now (proxy, firewall, DNS, VPN, flows, packet sensors, cloud logs).
  2. Check each source's retention and overwrite settings, and copy the periods you need before they disappear.
  3. Secure the devices' configuration files. The config tells you where logs are written and in what format (you'll see this first-hand with the proxy in the next lesson).
  4. Record each device's time zone and clock accuracy. If devices are minutes apart, the timeline tangles.
  5. Confirm that collection and analysis are within authorised scope. Network data contains individual employees' activity verbatim, so looking without authority is a problem in itself.

docs.title: 10. The hypothetical organisation used in this series
docs.text:
Many lessons will use the same hypothetical organisation as their stage. (Hypothetical) It's a government-funded institute researching specialised alloys and bioengineering. Recently the industry's information-sharing body (an ISAC, where organisations in the same sector share threat information) circulated a warning that activity by a state-backed group targeting the sector had risen sharply. This group is known to move freely once inside, and to use both freely available public tools and custom-built ones.

Then the mail server started dropping out intermittently, after similar odd behaviour on the Internet-facing web server. In other words, anomalies on DMZ servers were the first clue. While looking for the cause, IT suspected malicious activity and a full incident response began. Another team is running host forensics across the whole organisation; we investigate using only the collected network data.

flowchart TD
    NET(("Internet")) ---|"Tap A"| FW["Firewall"]
    VPN["VPN users"] --- FW
    FW ---|"Tap B"| DMZ["DMZ<br/>mail relay · DNS<br/>FTP · web"]
    FW ---|"Tap C"| CR["Core router"]
    CR ---|"Tap D"| SV["Services segment<br/>DC · file · mail<br/>collaboration · proxy"]
    CR --- MG["Management segment<br/>sensors · log collection"]
    CR --- PC["Research segment<br/>User segment"]

How to read the diagram: lines are real connections, and "Tap A–D" on a line means a tap (a device placed in a link that copies the traffic passing through) sits on that link. DC is the domain controller (the server that handles account authentication). The management segment holds two sensors, an AV server, an event log collector, a log aggregator, and the admin and security analyst PCs. The proxy has TLS inspection enabled. The tap positions in a table:

Tap Where it sits Traffic it sees Sensor that stores it A Between the Internet and the firewall The whole organisation's Internet traffic (seen as the firewall's outside address) Sensor 1 B Between the firewall and the DMZ Traffic to and from DMZ servers, from the Internet and from inside Sensor 1 C Between the firewall and the core router All internal segments to and from the firewall (internal addresses as-is) Sensor 2 D Between the core router and the services segment User and research PCs talking to servers (domain controller, file, mail, proxy) Sensor 2

Packets copied by the taps are stored on the two sensors in the management segment. The firewall and core router summarise traffic through all their interfaces as NetFlow, and server and device logs are gathered on the log aggregator in the management segment. Note also that the web proxy has TLS inspection enabled. From lesson 1.2 you'll read this proxy's logs directly.

One question worth asking straight away: "Which tap would see traffic between two PCs inside the user segment?" The answer is "none". Traffic within one segment goes straight through that segment's switch and never reaches the core router. Traffic moving sideways inside the organisation is called east-west traffic; traffic between inside and outside is north-south traffic. Thanks to tap D, this organisation sees some east-west traffic in the "PC → server" direction, but "PC → PC" is still a blind spot. The lateral movement from section 4 can pass right through it. How to fill this gap (switch mirroring, endpoint logs, etc.) is covered in the evidence-collection lesson later in Part 1.

The organisation's key users and endpoints are below. These addresses come back in later lessons.

Role Hostname Address Notes CEO hq-wkstn-01 10.10.7.11 User segment Senior manager hq-wkstn-05 10.10.7.15 User segment, out-of-support legacy OS Senior researcher hq-rd-01 10.10.6.11 Research segment, access to sensitive material Programme manager hq-rd-04 10.10.6.14 Research segment IT administrator (separate normal and domain admin accounts) hq-admin 10.10.5.26 Management segment Security analyst (separate normal and security admin accounts) hq-hunt 10.10.5.25 Management segment

Notice that the administrators use separate normal and admin accounts. That's good security practice, and in an investigation "when and where was the admin account used?" becomes an important lead. If an admin account logs on from a PC where it's never normally used, that's a reason to suspect the lateral movement from section 4.

docs.title: 11. Goals of this series
docs.text:
Finally, here's what you should be able to do by the end of this series. Every lesson that follows serves at least one of these five.

  1. Apply forensic methods to network investigations. Evidence preservation, separating facts from hypotheses, and repeatable procedures apply to network data just the same.
  2. Find and use evidence containing artifacts of communication. Treat every place that records "who talked to whom" as an evidence source: not only packets, but proxy, DNS, flow and device logs.
  3. Carve payloads when needed. Extract the files and data that actually crossed the wire from packets or caches (carving). You'll do this hands-on in the lab at the end of Part 1.
  4. Build sound OPSEC habits. Habits that avoid signalling the attacker while you investigate, starting with small settings such as turning off name lookups in your tools.
  5. Build an activity timeline. Aligning the times from several evidence sources into one timeline is how you understand the whole incident.

docs.title: 12. Summary
docs.text:
• Disk forensics hits a wall when the system is gone, when touching it tips off the attacker, or when there are too many systems. Even then, the path the traffic took keeps records.
  • Network evidence forms a spectrum from summaries (statistics, flows, logs) to a complete copy (full packets). Each source answers different questions, so you need to fit several witnesses together.
  • The cable remembers nothing. Collection must start before you need it; if nothing was prepared, rush to secure the logs devices were already writing.
  • Network evidence sometimes reaches conclusions on its own, but more often it acts as the lead that picks which systems to examine closely.
  • The network may already hold collected evidence, and because it shows the whole organisation at once, it suits threat hunting for attackers you don't yet know exist.
  • Threat intelligence ties SOC detection and DFIR response and hunting into one cycle. Rules that catch behaviour (TTPs) outlast rules that catch addresses.
  • Reduce scope and scale problems by starting with the most readily accessible data: packets (P), flows (F) and logs (L).
  • Write observed facts, hypotheses and conclusions needing more evidence separately, and drop a hypothesis when contradicting evidence appears. When there are no results, first suspect collection scope, retention, encryption and tool settings.
  • Median dwell time is 14 days per the 2026 report, but espionage-type cases run far longer. Design retention against these numbers.

In the next lesson (1.2) we start with the witness that answered "which PC was it?" this time: what a web proxy is, and why it matters so much to an investigator.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. Why couldn't you find the PC straight away from the address the outside agency gave in section 1? What evidence would you need to find it?

Answer and explanation

What the agency saw was the organisation's outside address. Internal PCs go out through NAT or a proxy, so from outside many PCs look like one address. To find the actual PC behind it, you need records from the device that translated the address. For web traffic, the proxy log (which internal PC requested that destination); for other traffic, firewall/NAT translation logs or internal flow records. It's the same principle as in section 3.1, where the firewall only showed the proxy's address.

Question 2. Evaluate the claim "if we have packet capture, we don't need flow records".

Answer and explanation

The claim is wrong. Packets carry the most detail but are large, so they're usually kept only for days to weeks. As in the section 8.1 calculation, if dwell time exceeds retention, the packets from the start of the intrusion are already gone. Flows have no content but are small enough to keep for months, so they show the starting point and the normal baseline. Also, in segments with no tap (east-west traffic in section 10) there may be no packets at all, while flows from routers or firewalls may still exist. The two complement each other rather than substitute.

Question 3. (Changed conditions) The download in section 3.1 was HTTPS and the proxy does not do TLS inspection. What can and can't you learn from each witness?

Answer and explanation
  • Proxy log: a line like CONNECT files.example.net:443 tells you which PC connected to which host and when. It doesn't tell you which path (/update.bin) was fetched.
  • Packet capture: you see the server name in the TLS handshake, certificate information (depending on TLS version), and sizes and timing. The file content is ciphertext and unreadable.
  • Flow: as with HTTP, only addresses, ports, times and byte counts.

So you can say "about 1.8 MB was received", but to say "that file is malicious" you need other evidence, such as the file left on the endpoint or execution records.

Question 4. (Interpreting results) A colleague wants to write in the report: "We searched the proxy logs for the C2 domain and got 0 hits, so no PC in our organisation communicated with that C2." What would you advise?

Answer and explanation

"0 hits" only means no trace within the scope examined. Before it goes in the report, advise checking:

  1. Whether every PC's web traffic really passes through that proxy (bypass paths, home-working PCs, server segments).
  2. Whether logs for the suspected period are within retention.
  3. Whether the malware uses a protocol or port other than HTTP/HTTPS. That traffic doesn't pass the proxy, so look at firewall, flow and DNS logs as well.
  4. Whether it connected directly by IP address instead of the domain.
  5. Whether the search conditions (case, subdomains, log format) are right.

Even after checking these, the report should state its scope, e.g. "no trace of communication was found within the evidence sources and time period examined".

Question 5. (Common misconception) Flow records show user PC 10.10.7.11 made hundreds of connections to the file server on port 445. Is this evidence of lateral movement?

Answer and explanation

Not by itself. A user PC connecting to a file server on 445 (SMB) is everyday normal work with shared folders. The observed fact is "hundreds of 445 connections", which fits both normal work and lateral movement. It becomes meaningful only with something unusual: is the destination another user PC rather than the file server, a system this PC never normally talks to, at an odd hour such as 3 a.m., starting suddenly right after the suspected infection time? To judge, compare with the baseline (the same PC's flows over previous weeks) and cross-check host evidence such as that system's logon records.

Question 6. (Calculation) An organisation keeps packets for 10 days, proxy logs for 45 days and flows for 90 days. For an incident with dwell time of (a) 14 days and (b) 122 days, which sources can show the first day of the intrusion? Assume preservation happened immediately on discovery.

Answer and explanation

Dwell time is how far back from discovery you must reach to get to day one. Retention must be at least that long for day one to survive.

  • (a) 14 days: packets 10 < 14, no. Proxy 45 ≥ 14, yes. Flows 90 ≥ 14, yes.
  • (b) 122 days: packets no, proxy 45 < 122 no, flows 90 < 122 no. None of the three covers day one.

In (b), it's hard to establish the entry path from network evidence alone; you rely more on endpoint traces or outside information. Given the long dwell times of espionage-style attacks, this is a reason to consider keeping summarised evidence (flows, DNS logs) for longer.

Question 7. (Application) In the section 10 organisation, (a) research-segment PC 10.10.6.14 connects via RDP to 10.10.6.11 in the same research segment. (b) The same PC 10.10.6.14 connects via SMB to the file server in the services segment. Which tap sees each? If no tap does, what evidence should you look for?

Answer and explanation
  • (a) No tap sees it. Traffic between PCs in the same research segment goes straight through the research switch and never crosses the core router. Tap C (firewall–core router) and tap D (core router–services segment) aren't on that path, and it won't appear in the core router's NetFlow either. Look for endpoint-side evidence such as the research switch's logs or mirroring settings, and both PCs' Windows event logs (RDP logon records).
  • (b) Going from the research segment to the services segment crosses the core router into the services segment, so tap D sees it. The core router's NetFlow records it too.

Internal traffic from the same PC can be visible or invisible depending on its destination. So before investigating, check "where, and in which direction" each tap sits, and never conclude "it's not on the tap, so it didn't happen".

Question 8. (Concept) How does threat hunting differ from incident response? Why is network data especially well suited to hunting?

Answer and explanation

Incident response starts from an already known event, such as an alert or an outside notification. Threat hunting starts with no alert, forms the hypothesis "is there an attacker already inside that we haven't found?", and goes looking first. As in the section 7 diagram, hunting hypotheses mostly come from threat intelligence (TTPs from other incidents), and once hunting finds something, it becomes incident response. Network data fits well because although you can't look at tens of thousands of disks one by one, you can see those endpoints' communication all at once at a few collection points (the taps in section 10, firewall and router NetFlow, proxy logs). For example, you can search the whole organisation in one go for "endpoints sending same-size POSTs every 5 minutes".

Question 9. (Mindset) During analysis you find, in the packets, a string from a tool known to be used by a particular state-backed group. Can you conclude "this is that group's attack"?

Answer and explanation

Not yet. The observed fact is "that string was in the packets"; "that group's attack" is a hypothesis. As in section 6.1, skilled attackers sometimes plant other groups' traces to send investigators the wrong way. Tools are also often public or leaked and used by several groups. Judging who is behind it means checking whether infrastructure (addresses, domain registration), timing, targeted information and TTPs across several stages all fit, and cross-checking with the threat intelligence team. The accurate report states the observation as is, e.g. "a tool string reported to be associated with group X was observed".

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Google Cloud Threat Intelligence, M-Trends 2026: Data, Insights, and Strategies From the Frontlines (published 2026-03-23, checked 2026-11-05). Median dwell time 14 days (previously 11), 52% detected internally (previously 43%), 122-day median for espionage and North Korean IT worker cases.
  • MITRE ATT&CK, Lateral Movement (TA0008) (checked 2026-11-05). The lateral movement tactic and its techniques.

About this page

Personal study notes rewritten in my own words from a range of study material. The organisation, people and addresses in the hypothetical cases are all invented.

docs.title: Lesson 1.9 — Wireshark Display Filters and Following Streams
Lesson 1.9 — Wireshark Display Filters and Following Streams
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • How display filters differ from BPF (where, how fast, and what they know when filtering)
  • Comparisons, sets, substrings, regular expressions and functions, and operator precedence that's the opposite of BPF's
  • Finding field names, and "Apply as Filter" vs "Prepare as Filter"
  • The syntax checker's green, red and yellow, and what it doesn't tell you
  • Multi-value fields and !=: the difference between the source material's explanation and today's behaviour (since 3.6)
  • Following TCP streams, "Decode As", and capturing directly in Wireshark

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) was produced with tshark 4.2.2 in this work environment. tshark's -Y uses the same filter engine as the display filter bar in the Wireshark window. The filter practice pcap was assembled by hand in Python (private and documentation addresses only), and stream following used the file actually captured on loopback in lesson 1.6. With no GUI in this environment, I couldn't see the syntax checker's colours directly; instead I checked the error messages tshark gives for the same filters.

docs.title: 1. You want "this value in this protocol" from stored packets
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) You have the file captured generously with host 10.10.6.14 in lesson 1.7. Now the questions get specific: "Which DNS responses this PC received had more than five answers?", "Which HTTP requests had a username in the cookie?", "Which HTTP on ports other than 80 and 8080 contained the word stolen?"

Doing this with lesson 1.7's BPF means computing every byte position: where in a DNS response the answer count sits, where the HTTP headers start. There are hundreds or thousands of protocols, and even the most brilliant investigator can't do all of that with offsets and bit masks. So the Wireshark developers made the dissectors (the ones that fill lesson 1.8's packet details pane) usable directly as filters. These are display filters. Any field Wireshark dissects can be used in a filter.

'dns.flags.response == 1 and dns.count.answers > 5 and dns.qry.name contains "example.net"'

"DNS responses with more than five answers whose queried name contains example.net." Not a single byte offset.

docs.title: 2. An analogy: the X-ray at the entrance and the librarian in the stacks
docs.text:
Lesson 1.7 compared BPF to the first X-ray at airport security. A display filter is more like a librarian finding books in the stacks. The librarian opens a book, reads the contents and text, and judges "this book has that content". That's slower than an X-ray, but answers far more complex questions.

There are two important differences in this analogy.

  • The timing differs. A bag that doesn't pass the X-ray (a BPF capture filter) never gets on the plane; it's gone for good. The librarian (a display filter) picks which to show among books already in the stacks. Ask another question and you get other books; clear the filter and every book is visible again. The originals are untouched.
  • What's read differs. The librarian reads a book's content. A display filter likewise doesn't look at the packet's bytes directly; it applies to the logical content the dissector has already decoded. For example, DNS saves bytes when the same name appears several times by replacing it with a short "that name from earlier" marker, a compression scheme. Reading a DNS packet's raw bytes is therefore fairly painful, but Wireshark decodes first and filters second, so you can compare the whole name directly with dns.qry.name.
BPF (capture filter) Display filter When applied At capture (also when reading a file) After capture and storage, when displaying Speed Very fast (close to the kernel) Slow (decides after decoding everything) Undo What a capture filter dropped is gone for good Clear it and everything shows again What it knows Fixed header positions and a few protocols Every field Wireshark dissects Syntax host 10.10.6.14 and tcp port 80 ip.addr == 10.10.6.14 and tcp.port == 80

Drawn as a picture, here's where each filter sits in the processing order:

flowchart TD
    W["Packets on the wire"] --> BPF{"BPF capture filter"}
    BPF -->|"reject"| X["Gone for good"]
    BPF -->|"accept"| P[("Stored pcap")]
    P --> DS["Dissectors decode every field"]
    DS --> DF{"Display filter"}
    DF -->|"match"| SH["Shown on screen"]
    DF -->|"no match"| HD["Hidden (still in the file)"]

How to read the diagram: top to bottom is the order packets pass through. BPF sits before storage, so what it rejects can't be seen again; the display filter sits after storage and dissection, so what it hides stays in the file.

Wireshark dissects IP, TCP and UDP too, so there are display filters that do the same job as BPF, such as tcp.port == 80 or ip.src == 203.0.113.50. But for the same condition BPF is much faster, so the rule is to reduce with BPF first wherever possible (lesson 1.7 section 8). Wireshark is mostly used on traffic already stored, and there trading a bit of speed for expressiveness is a good deal.

docs.title: 3.1 Comparison and logic
docs.text:
Kind Operators Example Equal / not equal ==, != http.request.method == "POST" Magnitude <, >, <=, >= dns.count.answers > 5 Set membership in { } http.response.code in {200, 301, 302, 404} Logic and (&&), or (||), not (!), parentheses http and not tcp.port == 80 Substring contains http.host contains "example" Regular expression matches (~) http.user_agent matches "curl|wget"

[Caution] Precedence is the opposite of BPF's. Lesson 1.7 said BPF gives and and or equal precedence and groups from the left. Display filters, like most programming languages, group and before or. The Wireshark 4.0.0 release notes announced this change, and the current documentation's order is not > and > xor > or (checked 2026-11-05). Checking with the practice file (actual output):

Filter Packets matched http.response.code == 404 or http.response.code == 301 and ip.src == 10.10.6.14 1 (packet 6, the 404 response) (http.response.code == 404 or http.response.code == 301) and ip.src == 10.10.6.14 0

The first line reads as 404 or (301 and source is that PC), so the server's 404 response (packet 6) matched. The same shape in BPF would have read the opposite way. Switching between the two languages, this difference is easy to forget, so the safest habit is parentheses whenever you mix them, in either language.

docs.title: 3.2 [Changed] Sets use commas
docs.text:
To check whether a value is one of several, use a set instead of a long chain of ors. The source material separates elements with spaces, as in http.response.code in { 200 301 302 404 }, but since Wireshark 3.6 set elements must be separated by commas, and space separation became syntax "to be removed in a future version". Testing in 4.2.2, it really was an error (actual output):

Filter Result http.response.code in {200, 301, 302, 404} 3 (packets 5, 6, 7) http.response.code in {200 301 302 404} Error: "301" was unexpected in this context.

Pasting filters from old material or scripts into the current version can fail like this. Failing is the lucky case; it's more dangerous when the meaning changes silently, like != in section 6.

docs.title: 3.3 Case: contains, matches, lower()
docs.text:
The practice HTTP request's cookie is Cookie: theme=dark; UserName=jdoe (capital U and N). The results (actual output):

Filter Matched Interpretation http.cookie contains "username" 0 contains is case-sensitive http.cookie matches "(?i)username" 1 The source material's method. (?i) means "ignore case" http.cookie matches "username" 1 Today's matches ignores case by default http.cookie matches "(?-i)username" 0 (?-i) makes it case-sensitive lower(http.cookie) contains "username" 1 Lowercase the field, then compare

The source material says to add (?i) to make matches ignore case, but the current Wireshark documentation describes matches as a PCRE2 regular expression that is case-insensitive by default, and 4.2.2 behaved that way. (?i) is harmless but unnecessary; it's when you want case sensitivity that you add (?-i). contains, on the other hand, is still case-sensitive, so when you don't know the case, wrap the field in lower() or use matches. Besides lower(), the current documentation lists more functions such as upper(), len() and count().

docs.title: 3.4 It only matches if the dissector knows it
docs.text:
Let's test one of the source material's examples: "HTTP on ports other than 80 and 8080 containing stolen". Packet 8 in the practice file POSTs stolen=orchid-007 to port 4444 (actual output):

Filter Matched (not tcp.port == 80 and not tcp.port == 8080) and http contains "stolen" 1 not tcp.port in {80, 8080} and http contains "stolen" 1 tcp.payload contains "stolen" 1 frame contains "stolen" 1

For http contains to match, Wireshark must dissect the packet as HTTP. Port 4444 isn't an HTTP port, but this version recognised it through its content-guessing feature (heuristics). Had the dissector not recognised it, http contains would return 0. So to find "packets containing this text in any protocol", filters that don't rely on dissection, such as frame contains or tcp.payload contains, are more reliable. These look only at one packet's bytes, though, so remember they can miss text split across two packets (use section 7's stream following for that).

docs.title: 3.5 BPF syntax doesn't work
docs.text: Writing BPF syntax such as host 203.0.113.80 where a display filter goes is an error (actual output: "203.0.113.80" was unexpected in this context.). As a display filter it must be ip.addr == 203.0.113.80. Conversely, Wireshark's capture filter box (on the capture start screen) takes BPF. Always remember that one program contains two languages.

docs.title: 4. Finding field names
docs.text:
With so many protocols, how do you know the field names to use in filters? Back to the GUI.

The answer is the status bar from lesson 1.8. Select the Name line of a DNS query in the packet details pane, and the left side of the status bar shows:

Query Name (dns.qry.name), 19 bytes

The dns.qry.name in parentheses is the field name, and 19 bytes is the field's length. Packet 2 in the practice file queried files.example.net; it has 17 characters (5 + 1 + 7 + 1 + 3), and why it's 19 bytes is interesting. DNS stores a name by putting a one-byte length in front of each dot-separated piece (label) and a 0 byte at the end. files (5), example (7) and net (3), so 3 length bytes + 15 characters + 1 terminator = 19 bytes. The dots aren't stored; the length bytes do their job. A display filter doesn't need to know this storage scheme; write it as a person reads it, as in dns.qry.name == "files.example.net". That's section 2's "decode first, filter second" in action.

Once you know the field name you can type it, but building it in the GUI is faster and avoids typos. Right-click a field in the details pane and there are two menus:

  • Apply as Filter: builds a new filter and applies it immediately.
  • Prepare as Filter: only puts it in the filter bar without applying it.

Both have submenus such as "Selected", "Not Selected", "…and Selected" and "…or Selected", so you can also add conditions to the current filter. The difference seems subtle, but once you've experienced how very long applying a filter to a large file can take, you'll value "Prepare". Refining several conditions and then applying once saves a lot of time watching the progress bar.

[Supplement] Finding field names on the command line. tshark -G fields prints a list of every field Wireshark knows. Filtering it, as in tshark -G fields | awk -F'\t' '$3=="dns.qry.name"', gives that field's description and type (here Name | dns.qry.name | FT_STRING, actual output). Handy when writing scripts.

docs.title: 5. The syntax checker and its limits
docs.text:
Display filters can get complex, so Wireshark checks the syntax as you type, using the filter bar's background colour, in three stoplight colours:

  • Green: the syntax is valid.
  • Red: an unknown field name or a syntax error. The status bar shows why.
  • Yellow: the syntax is valid, but a warning that results may not be what you expect.

Putting typical red cases into tshark gives the same reasons as error messages (actual output):

Filter tshark 4.2.2 error message Reason some.made.up.field == "x" Constant expression is invalid. Field name doesn't exist http.host == "intranet.lab.example The final quote was missing from a quoted string. Quote not closed host 203.0.113.80 "203.0.113.80" was unexpected in this context. BPF syntax used http.response.code in {200 301 302 404} "301" was unexpected in this context. No commas in the set (section 3.2)

The source material's typical yellow example is !=. In older versions, using != raised a yellow warning that "results may not be what you expect". Why, and how it has changed now, is the subject of the next section. With no GUI in this environment, I couldn't confirm directly whether today's version still shows yellow for !=.

And the most important limit: the syntax checker checks syntax only, not logic. Green doesn't mean it selects the packets you want. In section 3.1's precedence example, the filter without parentheses had perfectly valid syntax too. So test filters against known packets to confirm the results are right.

docs.title: 6. [Changed] Multi-value fields and !=
docs.text: Some fields appear several times in one packet. A DNS response's address (dns.a) appears several times if there are several answers; ip.addr appears twice (source and destination), and so does tcp.port. Asking "not equal" of such fields is trickier than it sounds. Does it mean "all values are not equal" or "at least one value is not equal"?

docs.title: 6.1 The source material's explanation (old behaviour)
docs.text: The source material explains it like this: filtering with dns.a != X matched a packet whose response clearly contained X, because that response also had another dns.a that wasn't X. So the old != was true "if any value is not equal". To find "responses that don't contain X", it said to write dns.a && !(dns.a == X): among packets with dns.a, exclude those where any value equals X.

docs.title: 6.2 Today's behaviour
docs.text:
Since Wireshark 3.6, a != b always means the same as !(a == b). The release notes explain that with this change, ip.addr != 1.1.1.1 works "as expected", giving the same result as ip.src != 1.1.1.1 and ip.dst != 1.1.1.1, and it removes the contradiction of a == b and a != b both being true (checked 2026-11-05). A separate operator was introduced for the old meaning: ~= in 3.6, then in 4.0.0 ~= was deprecated in favour of !==. The current documentation summarises:

Operator Aliases Meaning == any_eq, eq True if any value is equal != all_ne, ne True if all values are not equal (= no value is equal) === all_eq True if all values are equal !== any_ne True if any value is not equal (the old != meaning)

You can also prefix any or all, as in any dns.a != X.

docs.title: 6.3 Checking it
docs.text:
The practice file has three DNS responses. Packet 1 has two answers (203.0.113.70, 198.51.100.71), packet 2 has just 198.51.100.71, and packet 3 just 203.0.113.70 (actual output):

Filter Packets matched Interpretation dns.a == 203.0.113.70 1, 3 Responses with that address at least once dns.a != 203.0.113.70 2 Responses with that address not at all dns.a && !(dns.a == 203.0.113.70) 2 The source material's workaround; now the same as the line above dns.a !== 203.0.113.70 1, 2 Responses with at least one other address (the old !=) any dns.a != 203.0.113.70 1, 2 Same as above dns.a === 203.0.113.70 3 Responses where every answer is that address all dns.a == 203.0.113.70 3 Same as above dns.a ~= 203.0.113.70 Error ~= is no longer accepted in 4.2.2 ip.addr != 10.10.6.14 0 Every packet has that PC as source or destination

With the != of the source material's era, packet 1 would have matched too. Now only packet 2 does. The last row is interesting as well: under the old behaviour, ip.addr != 10.10.6.14 would have matched almost every packet (one of source or destination is always another address), but now it has the intuitive meaning "packets not involving that PC", and matched 0.

Why does this matter for investigations? Because the same filter string selects different packets depending on the Wireshark version. Rerun a report's or script's != filter written for a version before 3.6 on today's version, and it gives a different result silently, with no error. So reports must record the tool version alongside the filters used, and when reusing someone else's filters, check which version's meaning they were written for. And when asking "not" of a multi-value field, choose explicitly the meaning you want: != (none equal) or !== (at least one different). Running filters on large data sets without understanding these nuances produces grossly inaccurate results.

docs.title: 7. Following TCP streams
docs.text:
Looking at packets one at a time doesn't show the flow of a conversation well, because HTTP requests and responses are split across several packets. Follow TCP Stream stitches together just the data portion of one TCP connection in order, showing the whole conversation in one view. It's one of the features you'll use most in this series and in real cases.

Select a packet, right-click (or use the Analyze menu), then Follow → TCP Stream, and a window opens. Client → server is coloured red, server → client blue. For a text protocol like HTTP you can see the whole exchange at a glance. tshark's -z follow does the same (the real capture from lesson 1.6, actual output):

$ tshark -r full.pcap -n -q -z follow,tcp,ascii,0
===================================================================
Follow: tcp,ascii
Filter: tcp.stream eq 0
Node 0: 127.0.0.1:36314
Node 1: 127.0.0.1:8082
77
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8082
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
Accept: */*


    186
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Server: SimpleHTTP/0.6 Python/3.13.18
Date: Thu, 05 Nov 2026 02:39:43 GMT
Content-type: text/html
Content-Length: 32
Last-Modified: Thu, 05 Nov 2026 02:39:39 GMT


    32
<html><body>hello</body></html>

===================================================================

follow,tcp,ascii,0 means "the TCP stream, as text (ascii), stream number 0". Wireshark numbers each connection from 0 (tcp.stream), and following a stream automatically puts a filter like tcp.stream eq 0 in the filter bar. The numbers in the output (77, 186, 32) are each chunk's byte count, and chunks preceded by a tab are server → client (blue in the GUI). The connection list from -z conv,tcp shows how many streams there are.

Two features of the stream window to know:

  • Choosing a direction: the "Entire conversation" list at the bottom lets you pick just one direction. Especially useful for protocols where requests and responses don't fall into neat chunks the way HTTP's do.
  • Save as: saves just the data portion of the selected direction to disk, exactly as it was. Like lesson 1.5's cache carving, saving the response direction is a starting point for restoring a file the server sent (you still need to strip the headers). You'll do this hands-on in the lab at the end of Part 1.

The same feature exists for UDP, TLS and HTTP streams, and newer versions add streams such as HTTP/2 and QUIC.

[Caution] What stream following can't show. It stitches together only the captured packets. If packets were missed during capture, those spots are empty (Wireshark may mark the number of missing bytes), and if packets were cut by snapshot length as in lesson 1.6, you see only what was kept. TLS-encrypted connections show only ciphertext without keys (Part 5). And only data is shown, so check header timing and size information separately in the packet list.

docs.title: 8.1 Decode As
docs.text:
Wireshark usually decides the protocol by port number and content guessing (heuristics). But attackers often send a protocol over an unexpected port to evade detection. Wireshark may then fail to recognise it or decode it as the wrong protocol. In that case, right-click the packet, choose "Decode As", and specify the dissector you want, forcing that connection to be decoded as that protocol. In tshark, write it as -d tcp.port==443,http.

I tried three cases: HTTP on port 4444, DNS on UDP 5300, and unencrypted HTTP on port 443 (actual output). 4.2.2 recognised all three without being told. Even HTTP on 443 was caught as http.request, not tls, with the same result as giving -d tcp.port==443,http. That's how good the latest Wireshark heuristics have become. That doesn't make the feature obsolete. For proprietary protocols built by attackers, or when heuristics guess wrong (e.g. data that happens to look like another protocol), you must specify it yourself; and when you doubt a label Wireshark attached, you can switch dissectors to check. It's the same principle as not trusting labels like http(80) at face value (lesson 1.8).

docs.title: 8.2 Capturing directly in Wireshark
docs.text: Capturing and analysing in one step is sometimes convenient, so Wireshark can capture. The GUI exposes all the same functionality as tcpdump. But don't forget the heavy processing load of the GUI and dissectors. Never capture important data through the Wireshark GUI, because dropped packets add up quickly. In a suitable environment such as a lab, skipping the separate capture step can save time. Modern Wireshark hands the actual capture to a separate program, dumpcap, which can be used on its own without the GUI and may be a good option in some cases (lesson 1.8 section 2.3). Whatever you use, test it before relying on it in operations.

docs.title: 9. How to use this in a real investigation
docs.text:
1. Reduce first with BPF, then look in detail with display filters. Applying display filters straight to large files is slow.
  2. Build filters from fields in the details pane with "Prepare as Filter", refine, then apply.
  3. Precedence is the opposite of BPF's, so use parentheses.
  4. When asking "not" of multi-value fields (ip.addr, tcp.port, dns.a, etc.), choose the meaning you want: != (none equal) or !== (at least one different).
  5. When you don't know the case, use matches or lower() instead of contains.
  6. When you must search without relying on dissectors, use frame contains.
  7. Test filters against known packets, and record the filter string together with the tool version in reports.
  8. Apply filters settled in the GUI to many files with tshark -Y (connecting to lesson 1.3's shell analysis).

docs.title: 10. Summary
docs.text:
• A display filter is a language that filters on every field Wireshark dissects. Slower than BPF, it's used after storage, can always be undone, and applies to logical content rather than bytes.
  • Use comparisons (==, !=, < etc.), sets (in {a, b}, commas required), contains (case-sensitive), matches (PCRE2, case-insensitive by default) and functions such as lower(). BPF syntax is an error.
  • Precedence is not > and > xor > or, unlike BPF. Use parentheses when mixing.
  • Find field names in the status bar; "Apply as Filter" applies immediately, "Prepare as Filter" only fills the bar. tshark -G fields finds them too.
  • The syntax checker checks syntax only, in green, red and yellow. Test logic yourself.
  • Since 3.6, != means "no value is equal", and the old meaning ("at least one different") is !== (any_ne). The same filter gives different results across versions, so record the tool version with filters.
  • Following a TCP stream stitches one connection's data together to show the whole conversation (client → server red, server → client blue), and lets you save one direction exactly as it was. Uncaptured parts and encrypted content aren't visible.
  • "Decode As" forces a protocol on an unexpected port to be decoded. Don't do important captures through the Wireshark GUI.

In the next lesson (1.10) we cover a lab guide for getting hands-on with the tcpdump and Wireshark skills learned so far.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. Explain how the following is read as BPF (tcpdump) and as a display filter (Wireshark). Why does the same shape mean different things?

A or B and C
Answer and explanation

BPF gives and and or equal precedence and groups from the left, so it reads (A or B) and C (lesson 1.7). Display filters, since 4.0.0, group and before or, so it reads A or (B and C) (confirmed directly in section 3.1). The two languages use different rules, so the same shape can be read the opposite way. It's a common mistake for analysts who switch between them, so parentheses whenever you mix and and or, in either language, is the safest approach.

Question 2. (Changes) An internal investigation procedure written in 2021 says "to find DNS responses from somewhere other than the internal DNS server 198.51.100.53, use ip.src != 198.51.100.53 and dns.flags.response == 1". Does this filter give the same result in Wireshark 4.x as it did then?

Answer and explanation

ip.src appears only once per packet, so it's unaffected by the change in !='s meaning; with one value, "all values differ" and "at least one differs" are the same. So this filter gives the same result before and after 3.6. The meaning changes when != is used on fields that appear several times, like ip.addr, tcp.port and dns.a. Even so, it's good to note in the procedure "which Wireshark version" the filter is written for, and to remember results may differ for packets where ip.src appears twice, such as tunnels (IP inside IP).

Question 3. (Calculation) For section 6.3's three practice DNS responses (1: .70 and .71, 2: .71, 3: .70), give the packet numbers each filter matches. (a) dns.a == 198.51.100.71 (b) dns.a != 198.51.100.71 (c) dns.a !== 198.51.100.71 (d) dns.a === 198.51.100.71

Answer and explanation

.71 is 198.51.100.71 and .70 is 203.0.113.70.

  • (a) Responses with .71 at least once: 1, 2
  • (b) Responses with no .71 at all: 3
  • (c) Responses with at least one value other than .71: packet 1 has .70 so yes, packet 2 has only .71 so no, packet 3 has only .70 so yes: 1, 3
  • (d) Responses where every answer is .71: 2

All four results were confirmed by running them against the practice file with tshark 4.2.2. The difference between (b) and (c) is the difference in !='s meaning before and after 3.6; the old != behaved like today's !==, giving (c)'s result.

Question 4. (Case) To find requests with curl in the User-Agent you used http.user_agent contains "curl", but requests sending CURL/8.5.0 or Curl/7.88 were missed. Explain why and fix it two ways.

Answer and explanation

contains is case-sensitive, so it treats curl, CURL and Curl as different text. Fix it by ① lowercasing the field before comparing, as in lower(http.user_agent) contains "curl", or ② using matches, which ignores case by default, as in http.user_agent matches "curl". Writing matches "(?i)curl" as in the source material works too, but today's version ignores case even without (?i). And remember the User-Agent is a value the program sets freely (lesson 1.3), so no curl doesn't mean it isn't a command-line tool.

Question 5. (Dissector dependence) A colleague searched a whole pcap with http contains "password", got 0 hits, and concluded "no password was ever sent in plaintext". When could this conclusion be wrong? Suggest a broader filter too.

Answer and explanation

① If Wireshark didn't dissect the traffic as HTTP (unusual port, heuristic failure), http contains won't match. ② If it went over another plaintext protocol (FTP, POP3, Telnet, etc.) rather than HTTP, it's obviously excluded. ③ If the text is split across two packets, a per-packet search can miss it. ④ If the case differs (Password, PASSWORD), contains misses it. ⑤ If the body is compressed (gzip) or encoded (Base64), the text isn't visible as-is. ⑥ If it was encrypted with TLS, it's not visible at all. More broadly, use a filter that doesn't rely on dissectors and ignores case, such as frame matches "pass(word)?", and check splitting and compression separately with stream following or HTTP object export. And write the conclusion with the qualifier "within the scope examined".

Question 6. Give an example where the syntax checker is green but the packets you want don't appear, and explain how you'd discover it.

Answer and explanation

Example: tcp.port == 80 or tcp.port == 443 and ip.src == 10.10.6.14. The syntax is perfect, so it's green, but and groups first, making it tcp.port == 80 or (443 and that PC), so other PCs' port 80 traffic all shows too. The author probably wanted "that PC's 80 and 443". Another example: using != on a multi-value field expecting the old meaning is also green but gives different results. Discover it by testing against packets with known answers. For instance, find one port-80 packet from another PC beforehand and see whether it disappears when the filter is applied. A "displayed packets" count in the status bar larger or smaller than expected is a signal to be suspicious. The syntax checker checks syntax; people check logic.

Question 7. (Streams) Following the stream of an HTTP download, you see a marker like "[345 bytes missing in capture file]" in the middle of the response body. What can you do with a file saved from this stream with "Save as", and what must you watch out for?

Answer and explanation

The marker means packets were missed during capture, leaving that many bytes empty. The saved file's bytes differ from the original file, so its hash won't match the original's (e.g. a known hash from threat intelligence), and depending on the format it may not open or may be partly corrupt. You can still get information such as the file type (file), its opening content and strings. Watch out to ① record that the file is incomplete, ② not conclude things like "the hash differs from the known malicious file, so it isn't malicious", and ③ look for an intact copy of the same file from other evidence sources (the proxy cache, lesson 1.5; the endpoint). Also record in the evidence description why packets were missed (capture device load, etc., lesson 1.6 section 7.1).

Question 8. (Application) Referring to section 2's table, choose BPF or display filter for each of the following, and explain why. (a) Extracting one IP's traffic from a month's 50 TB of pcaps (b) Finding, in the extracted file, "DNS responses with a TTL under 60 seconds and three or more answers" (c) Capturing only a particular subnet's traffic for the next week

Answer and explanation
  • (a) BPF. BPF, as in tcpdump -r ... -w ... 'host address', is very fast and suits reducing large files. Filtering 50 TB with a display filter means dissecting every packet, which is enormously slow.
  • (b) Display filter. You can name DNS internal fields, as in dns.flags.response == 1 and dns.resp.ttl < 60 and dns.count.answers >= 3. With BPF you'd have to compute byte positions for the TTL and answer count inside DNS responses, which is practically impossible. The file is already reduced by (a), so speed isn't an issue. But remember dns.resp.ttl is a multi-value field appearing once per answer. < means "at least one", so if you want "every answer under 60 seconds", state it explicitly, as in all dns.resp.ttl < 60. This field name and the all syntax were confirmed working in tshark 4.2.2.
  • (c) BPF. Only BPF can be used as a filter at the capture stage. Following lesson 1.7's principle, capture generously (net 10.10.6.0/24) and do fine selection with display filters after storage.

  • RFC 1035, Domain Names - Implementation and Specification, section 3.1 (label length representation of names) and section 4.1.4 (message compression).

About this page

Personal study notes rewritten in my own words from a range of study material. The practice packets were assembled by hand for explanation; the case is hypothetical.

Part 2 — Core Protocols and Log Aggregation/Analysis
docs.text:
What Part 2 covers

It starts with reading the two protocols that appear in almost every case, HTTP and DNS, through an investigator's eyes. After the parts of requests and responses, web server logs, and DNS structure and abuse (fast flux, domain generation algorithms, encrypted DNS), it turns packets into logs with Zeek and works with them in jq. Finally, it covers log aggregation that brings syslog and Windows event logs into one place, and an analysis environment built on the Elastic Stack.
