docs.title: 2.6 — DNS Structure: Records, Messages, Compression, Hierarchy, Vantage Points
2.6 — DNS Structure: Records, Messages, Compression, Hierarchy, Vantage Points
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Why DNS matters to an investigation: almost every connection starts with a DNS lookup
  • Record types: A, AAAA, NS, CNAME, MX, PTR, SRV, TXT, NULL, SSHFP, plus [Supplement] the HTTPS (SVCB) record you now see everywhere
  • Building a "normal" from record-type ratios
  • Message structure: transaction ID, flags, response codes (NXDOMAIN)
  • UDP, TCP and EDNS: the 512-byte limit and [Changed] the post-2020 1232-byte default
  • Name compression: reading 0xC0.. pointers byte by byte
  • Hierarchy, recursion and caching, and how what you see depends on where you look ([Changed] QNAME minimisation)
  • CNAMEs: stitching queries and responses together, and why their TTLs drift apart

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) came from a small practice DNS hierarchy built inside this environment. I ran five instances of Unbound 1.19.2 (Ubuntu package) as a root (127.0.0.11), the TLDs com, net, org and arpa (127.0.0.12), the authoritative server for example.com and example.net (127.0.0.13), the authoritative server for example.org (127.0.0.14), and an in-house recursive resolver (127.0.0.10). It is not the real Internet root; it imitates the same structure on loopback addresses. Clients queried with dig 9.18.39 from 127.0.0.101 and 127.0.0.102; captures used tcpdump, and decoding used TShark 4.2.2 and dnspython 2.9.2. All record addresses are documentation addresses (192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24, 2001:db8::/32), and the domains are example domains (example.com/net/org).

docs.title: 1. DNS is the glue between people and the network
docs.text:
Nobody types 192.168.24.102 to reach the timecard system or 172.30.41.216 for webmail. We type names like timecard.example.com and webmail.example.com. Turning names into addresses is the job of DNS (the Domain Name System). We use it countless times a day, usually without noticing.

A phone book is a fair analogy: look up a name, get a number. It breaks in three places. ① A phone book is one volume, but DNS is split across a huge number of servers, each responsible for its own part (section 7). ② A phone number stays put for years, but every DNS answer carries a lifetime (TTL) and can change at any time. Attackers exploit exactly that (lesson 2.7). ③ DNS answers many kinds of questions, not just name → address: mail servers, service locations, even arbitrary text (section 2).

DNS matters to investigators for a simple reason. Web, mail, remote access, and malware calling its command server almost all begin with a DNS lookup. Read DNS records well and you can take the pulse of nearly everything happening on the network. That is why DNS is also a foundation for threat hunting and real-time alerting.

docs.title: 2. Record types
docs.text:
Some terms first.

  • Resource record (RR): one line of information that DNS stores and returns: name, TTL, class (almost always IN), type and value.
  • Forward lookup: asking for an address by name. The most common kind, especially where people work.
  • Reverse lookup: asking for a name by address (PTR).
Type Number Name What it does A 1 Address Name → IPv4 address AAAA 28 IPv6 address Name → IPv6 address (128-bit) NS 2 Name server The authoritative servers for a domain or subdomain CNAME 5 Canonical name An alias: "look up that name instead" (section 8) MX 15 Mail exchange The servers that receive a domain's mail, with priorities PTR 12 Pointer Reverse lookup. 192.0.2.25 is queried as 25.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa SRV 33 Service locator Location of any service (priority, weight, port, host). A generalised MX TXT 16 Text Arbitrary text, these days mostly machine-read data such as SPF and DKIM NULL 10 Null Arbitrary content (up to 65,535 bytes). Experimental; it should almost never appear in production SSHFP 44 SSH fingerprint Host-key fingerprints of SSH servers, to help confirm you reached the right server HTTPS 65 HTTPS binding [Supplement] see below

This is only part of the full list, which lives in the IANA registry (references).

I asked the practice authoritative server for a few of these. +norec means "don't ask for recursion" (section 7), and +noall +answer means "show only the answer section".

(Actual output)

$ dig @127.0.0.13 _sip._tcp.example.com SRV +norec +noall +answer
_sip._tcp.example.com.  300 IN  SRV 10 60 5060 sip.example.com.

$ dig @127.0.0.13 -x 192.0.2.25 +norec +noall +answer
25.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa. 3600   IN  PTR mail.example.com.

$ dig @127.0.0.13 ssh.example.com SSHFP +norec +noall +answer
ssh.example.com.    300 IN  SSHFP   4 2 0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF01234567 89ABCDEF

$ dig @127.0.0.13 www.example.com HTTPS +norec +noall +answer
www.example.com.    300 IN  HTTPS   1 . alpn="h2,h3"

How to read them:

  • SRV 10 60 5060 sip.example.com.: priority 10, weight 60, port 5060, host sip.example.com. The _sip._tcp prefix means "the SIP service over TCP".
  • dig -x 192.0.2.25 has dig reverse the address and ask for PTR at 25.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa. The leftmost octet of an address is the largest unit, so it is flipped to sit at the right-hand (largest) end of the name.
  • SSHFP 4 2 …: key algorithm 4 (Ed25519), fingerprint type 2 (SHA-256), then the fingerprint. This one is a fake value made for practice. dig merely breaks long values with a space; there's no space in the data itself.
  • HTTPS 1 . alpn="h2,h3": priority 1, target . (this same name), and a hint that HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are supported.

[Supplement] HTTPS and SVCB records (standardised in 2023)

They're not on the book's list, but capture a user segment today and you'll see type 65 (HTTPS) queries pouring out alongside A and AAAA. RFC 9460 (November 2023) defines SVCB and its HTTPS-specific form. Before connecting, a browser can learn from DNS that "this site speaks HTTP/3" (what lesson 2.3's Alt-Svc used to do), an alternate port, or Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) settings. For investigations, know that ① a large share of HTTPS queries in a user segment's type ratio is normal, and ② HTTPS queries with NODATA answers, or without a matching A query, are common. The alpn="h2,h3" here is a practice value I added.

[Correction] TXT isn't limited to \"255 characters per record\"

The book describes TXT as "limited to 255 characters per record". More precisely, a TXT value is made of one or more character-strings, and each string is at most 255 bytes, because its length is stored in a single byte. One record can hold several strings, so the full value can be far longer than 255 bytes (the limit for the whole value is 65,535 bytes). Long SPF records and DKIM keys are split across strings this way.

(Actual output) I fetched a two-string TXT record with dnspython and counted.

strings: 2 [243, 244]

One record holds strings of 243 and 244 bytes, 487 bytes together. The practice zone also has big.example.com, a TXT of seven strings totalling about 1.4 KB, which section 5 uses. For investigations, this connects to the idea that long TXT answers can be a sign of DNS tunnelling or of data being brought in (lesson 2.7).

docs.title: 3. Building "normal" from type ratios
docs.text:
A useful metric to track is the ratio of record types at each vantage point. Once you know the usual ratio (the baseline), a swing beyond some threshold is a starting point for spotting suspicious activity. The key is to build baselines separately for each point, because what counts as normal varies greatly from segment to segment.

  • Mail (SMTP) server segments do a reverse lookup for every new TCP connection, so PTR queries dominate.
  • Segments where people work are mostly web browsing, so A and AAAA (and nowadays HTTPS) take the biggest share.

To check the commands, I deliberately generated queries from two "segments": 127.0.0.101 acted like a web user, 127.0.0.102 like a mail server.

(Actual output; the query mix was constructed for practice)

$ tshark -r mix.pcap -Y 'dns.flags.response == 0' -T fields -e ip.src -e dns.qry.type \
    | sort | uniq -c | sort -k2,2 -k1,1nr
     18 127.0.0.101 1
     18 127.0.0.101 28
      6 127.0.0.101 65
     12 127.0.0.102 12
      3 127.0.0.102 15
      3 127.0.0.102 16

Piece by piece:

  • -Y 'dns.flags.response == 0': queries only. Counting responses too would count each question twice.
  • -T fields -e ip.src -e dns.qry.type: print only the source address and the query type number, tab-separated.
  • sort | uniq -c: group identical lines and prefix a count.
  • sort -k2,2 -k1,1nr: group by the second column (address), then by count, descending.

Read the type numbers from the table in section 2: 1=A, 28=AAAA, 65=HTTPS, 12=PTR, 15=MX, 16=TXT. The user segment shows only A, AAAA and HTTPS; in the mail segment, PTR is over half. On a real network you'd accumulate these numbers daily and by hour to form a baseline, then look closer when, say, TXT or NULL suddenly rises from user PCs, or MX lookups pour out of something that isn't a mail server (a spam bot).

Count response codes too. Every response carries a status code, and most are success (NOERROR). NXDOMAIN means "no such name". Large volumes of it can signal certain malicious activity (DGAs, lesson 2.7).

(Actual output)

$ dig @127.0.0.13 nosuch.example.com A +norec
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NXDOMAIN, id: 30504
;; flags: qr aa; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 0, AUTHORITY: 1, ADDITIONAL: 1

There are zero answers, and the AUTHORITY section holds the zone's SOA record. It tells the asker how long it may remember the "doesn't exist" answer (negative caching).

docs.title: 4. Message structure: query and response
docs.text:
At its core, DNS is a simple protocol. A client sends a query to a server and the server sends back a response. The response repeats the question and appends the answers.

It normally uses UDP port 53. UDP keeps no connection state, so when a client has dozens of queries outstanding it needs a way to match each response to its query. That's the transaction ID, a 2-byte field that DNS software should randomise.

Here are the first bytes of the first query sent to the practice resolver (tshark -x prints a packet in hex).

(Actual output, excerpt)

0020  00 0a d4 c8 00 35 00 40 fe c0 bd 70 01 20 00 01   .....5.@...p. ..
0030  00 00 00 00 00 01 03 77 77 77 07 65 78 61 6d 70   .......www.examp
0040  6c 65 03 63 6f 6d 00 00 01 00 01 00 00 29 04 d0   le.com.......)..

After the UDP header (d4 c8 = source port 54472, 00 35 = destination 53) come the 12 bytes of the DNS header.

Bytes Value Meaning 1–2 bd 70 Transaction ID 0xbd70 3–4 01 20 Flags. 0x0100 = RD (recursion desired), 0x0020 = AD (tell me the validation result). dig sets AD by default 5–6 00 01 1 question 7–8 00 00 0 answers 9–10 00 00 0 authority records 11–12 00 01 1 additional record (the EDNS OPT record, section 5)

The question follows: 03 77 77 77 (length 3, www), 07 … (length 7, example), 03 63 6f 6d (length 3, com), 00 (end). Then type 00 01 (A) and class 00 01 (IN). The trailing 00 00 29 04 d0 is EDNS: 0x29 = 41 (OPT type) and 0x04d0 = 1232 (the size the client can accept).

The response flags were 0x8180: QR (response), RD (echoed from the query) and RA (recursion available). The transaction ID was the same 0xbd70, and the destination port was the query's source port (54472). Those two values are how the client pairs response with query.

[Supplement] A 2-byte ID wasn't enough: source-port randomisation

With only 65,536 possible IDs, an attacker who floods forged responses can guess right. After a cache-poisoning attack built on this became widely known in 2008, resolvers began randomising the source port as well (RFC 5452). The 11 queries this lab's resolver sent to authoritative servers all used different source ports (actual output). Conversely, if a client floods queries from one fixed port with sequentially increasing IDs, consider that it may be a custom tool rather than an ordinary OS resolver. That is a hypothesis to weigh with other evidence.

docs.title: 5. UDP, TCP and EDNS
docs.text:
DNS normally uses UDP, but in certain cases it falls back to TCP.

  • The original limit: 512 bytes. The 1987 DNS standard (RFC 1035) capped UDP messages at 512 bytes. If an answer doesn't fit, the server sends what fits and sets the TC (truncated) flag, and the client re-asks over TCP.
  • Zone transfers. When DNS servers replicate a whole zone (AXFR), they use TCP from the start.
  • EDNS (Extension Mechanisms for DNS). As IPv6 and DNSSEC spread, answers over 512 bytes became common, and opening a TCP connection each time was costly. EDNS was the answer. The query carries an OPT record saying "I can receive UDP up to this size", in a way that remains compatible with old clients that don't understand EDNS (current standard: RFC 6891).

I asked the practice authoritative server for an approximately 1.4 KB TXT (big.example.com) under varying conditions.

(Actual output)

--- A: no EDNS (+noedns)
;; Truncated, retrying in TCP mode.
;; SERVER: 127.0.0.13#53(127.0.0.13) (TCP)
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 1480
--- B: EDNS, accept up to 1232 bytes (+bufsize=1232)
;; Truncated, retrying in TCP mode.
; EDNS: version: 0, flags:; udp: 1232
;; SERVER: 127.0.0.13#53(127.0.0.13) (TCP)
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 1491
--- C: EDNS, accept up to 4096 bytes (+bufsize=4096)
;; Truncated, retrying in TCP mode.
; EDNS: version: 0, flags:; udp: 1232
;; SERVER: 127.0.0.13#53(127.0.0.13) (TCP)
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 1491
--- D: keep the truncated reply (+noedns +ignore)
;; flags: qr aa tc; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 0, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 0
;; SERVER: 127.0.0.13#53(127.0.0.13) (UDP)
;; MSG SIZE  rcvd: 33

Interpretation:

  • A: over 512 bytes, so truncated → re-asked over TCP and received 1,480 bytes.
  • D: with +ignore blocking the TCP retry, the truncated UDP reply had the tc flag, zero answers and 33 bytes. This server doesn't half-fill an overflowing reply; it returns just the question, meaning "come back over TCP".
  • C is the interesting one. The client offered to accept 4,096 bytes, yet the server answered udp: 1232 and truncated. That's because this server (Unbound 1.19.2) caps its own UDP replies at 1232 bytes, which the next box explains.

In packets, case A went: UDP query → UDP reply (TC=1, 0 answers) → TCP three-way handshake → query over TCP → reply over TCP (1 answer) → connection close (packets 1–12 of tc.pcap).

[Changed] Since 2020: UDP up to about 1232 bytes, and TCP is mandatory

The book's statement ("EDNS allows larger UDP packets") still holds, but operational defaults have moved.

  • On DNS Flag Day 2020 (effective 2020-10-01), major DNS software vendors and operators lowered the default EDNS buffer size to 1232 bytes. The aim was to avoid IP fragmentation of large UDP replies, which get lost or abused in spoofing attacks. 1232 is the IPv6 minimum MTU of 1280 minus 48 bytes of IPv6 and UDP headers. BIND, Unbound and others changed their defaults; case C above shows the result.
  • TCP is required, not optional. RFC 7766 (2016) requires DNS implementations to support TCP, and RFC 9210 (2022) tells operators not to block TCP 53 either.

What this means for investigations: ① Large answers (DNSSEC, long TXT, many addresses) now show up on TCP 53 more often. A capture filter of udp port 53, chosen because "DNS is just UDP", misses these answers entirely. Use port 53. ② Conversely, heavy outbound TCP 53 from user PCs is worth checking for zone-transfer attempts or DNS tunnelling (lesson 2.7).

docs.title: 6. Name compression: say the shared tail once
docs.text:
To fit many names into 512 bytes, the DNS designers invented a clever compression scheme. It exploits how often DNS data repeats the same tail (for example example.com).

Basic encoding: each dot-separated piece of a name (a label) is written as one length byte plus the characters, ending with a zero length (00). Section 4's 03 www 07 example 03 com 00 has this shape.

Compression pointer: if the top two bits of a length byte are 11, it isn't a length but a pointer. In those two bytes, the remaining 14 bits after the top two give a zero-based offset from the start of the DNS message. The rest of the name is whatever is already written at that offset, read until its terminating 00. Top bits 00 mean an ordinary length byte, which is why a label can be at most 63 (0x3F) bytes.

Following the book's idea, I encoded five names with dnspython, uncompressed and compressed. A 12-byte placeholder header comes first so the offsets match a real message.

(Actual output)

uncompressed total name bytes: 99
  off 0x0C www.example.com.               17B  03 77 77 77 07 65 78 61 6D 70 6C 65 03 63 6F 6D 00
  off 0x1D mail.example.com.              18B  04 6D 61 69 6C 07 65 78 61 6D 70 6C 65 03 63 6F 6D 00
  off 0x2F mail2.example.com.             19B  05 6D 61 69 6C 32 07 65 78 61 6D 70 6C 65 03 63 6F 6D 00
  off 0x42 superlong.mail2.example.com.   29B  09 73 75 70 65 72 6C 6F 6E 67 05 6D 61 69 6C 32 07 65 78 61 6D 70 6C 65 03 63 6F 6D 00
  off 0x5F mx.example.net.                16B  02 6D 78 07 65 78 61 6D 70 6C 65 03 6E 65 74 00
compressed total name bytes: 60
  off 0x0C www.example.com.               17B  03 77 77 77 07 65 78 61 6D 70 6C 65 03 63 6F 6D 00
  off 0x1D mail.example.com.               7B  04 6D 61 69 6C C0 10
  off 0x24 mail2.example.com.              8B  05 6D 61 69 6C 32 C0 10
  off 0x2C superlong.mail2.example.com.   12B  09 73 75 70 65 72 6C 6F 6E 67 C0 24
  off 0x38 mx.example.net.                16B  02 6D 78 07 65 78 61 6D 70 6C 65 03 6E 65 74 00

Decoding the pointer C0 10

  C0 10  =  1100 0000  0001 0000
            ^^                     top two bits 11 → pointer
              00 0000  0001 0000   remaining 14 bits = 0x010 = 16

What's at offset 16 (0x10)? The first name starts at 0x0C, and right after 03 77 77 77 (4 bytes), at 0x10, comes 07 example 03 com 00. So 04 mail C0 10 means "mail + example.com (read from offset 16)" = mail.example.com.

superlong.mail2.example.com is 09 superlong C0 24. 0x24 is where the second name, mail2.example.com, begins. Following it gives 05 mail2 and then another pointer, C0 10, which leads on to example.com. Pointers can lead to more pointers.

mx.example.net was not compressed. The label example appeared earlier, but compression can only point at a matching tail from the right-hand end. No earlier name ended in example.net, so it has to be written out in full.

Result: name bytes dropped from 99 to 60, about 39% (the book's example went 82 → 57, about 30%; different names give different numbers).

When investigators need to understand compression

  • When looking at raw bytes: a plain string search (grep, Wireshark's "find string") for mail.example.com can fail inside a response, because the packet contains only mail and a pointer. Search with decoded fields such as Wireshark's dns.qry.name and dns.resp.name.
  • Malformed pointers: pointers to themselves (infinite loops) or outside the message have long been used to break parsers. Bugs in DNS compression handling have led to remote code execution in several DNS implementations and embedded TCP/IP stacks. A packet with strange compression is evidence in its own right.

docs.title: 7. Hierarchy, recursion, caching and vantage points
7.1 Terms
docs.text:
• Authoritative server: a server that holds a zone's records itself. Only example.com's authoritative servers can give the definitive answer for example.com.
  • Recursive resolver: a server that chases answers all the way on a client's behalf. In-house DNS, ISP DNS and public DNS services are all resolvers.
  • Recursive query: "find me the final answer" (RD=1). Client → resolver.
  • Iterative query: "tell me what you know" (RD=0). Resolver → authoritative servers. A server that doesn't know returns a referral ("ask that server").
  • Cache and TTL: a resolver remembers answers for their TTL (in seconds), and until then serves the same question from memory without asking outside.

As an analogy, a recursive resolver is an errand runner for paperwork. I ask once, "please get me this certificate" (recursion), and the runner goes from city hall's front desk (root) to the district office (TLD) to the responsible department (authoritative server), one after another (iteration). Asked for the same document again, they hand over the copy they kept (cache). Where it breaks: an errand runner would write my name on the request form, but a DNS resolver does not put my address on the queries it sends outside. That is the heart of this section.

docs.title: 7.2 One query, many round trips
docs.text:
In the practice hierarchy, with the resolver's cache empty, two clients asked for the same name (www.example.com) two seconds apart.

Figure 7-1. The round trips caused by one query, and two vantage points (top to bottom in time order; each boxed group is what one vantage point can see)

flowchart TD
    subgraph IN["Inside vantage point: clients ↔ resolver"]
        C1["Client 1 (127.0.0.101)<br/>www.example.com A? RD=1"]
        C2["2 s later, client 2 (127.0.0.102)<br/>same question"]
    end
    R["In-house recursive resolver (127.0.0.10)<br/>cache"]
    subgraph OUT["Outside vantage point: resolver ↔ Internet DNS"]
        ROOT["Root (127.0.0.11)<br/>asked: com A? → referral: com is at ns.gtld"]
        TLD["com server (127.0.0.12)<br/>asked: example.com A? → referral: ns1.example.com"]
        AUTH["example.com authoritative (127.0.0.13)<br/>asked: www.example.com A? → answer: 192.0.2.10"]
    end
    C1 --> R
    R -->|"① iterative queries, RD=0"| ROOT
    ROOT --> TLD
    TLD --> AUTH
    AUTH -->|"② answer, TTL 60"| R
    R -->|"③ answer"| C1
    C2 -->|"④ answered straight from cache (TTL 58)"| R

How to read it: the upper "inside" box is what a sensor between users and the resolver sees; the lower "outside" box is what a sensor at the perimeter (Internet egress) sees. ①–③ are the first client's lookup; ④ is the second client's.

Splitting the actual capture by vantage point:

(Actual output, summary of vantage.pcap)

Inside (clients ↔ resolver) — 4 packets
  0.000 s  127.0.0.101 → 127.0.0.10  query  www.example.com A   RD=1
  0.004 s  127.0.0.10 → 127.0.0.101  answer www.example.com A 192.0.2.10 (TTL 60)
  2.029 s  127.0.0.102 → 127.0.0.10  query  www.example.com A   RD=1
  2.030 s  127.0.0.10 → 127.0.0.102  answer www.example.com A 192.0.2.10 (TTL 58)

Outside (resolver ↔ authoritative servers) — 22 packets (11 queries), all within 0.000–0.005 s
  127.0.0.1 → root        . NS        (checking the root server list, "priming")
  127.0.0.1 → root        com A       ← not www.example.com
  127.0.0.1 → com server  example.com A
  127.0.0.1 → auth server www.example.com A   ← the full name only here
  (plus 7 queries for the A/AAAA of the name servers themselves)
  For client 2's query 2 s later: 0

Three things to take away.

  1. The outside vantage point has no client addresses. Every outbound query came from the resolver (here it left as 127.0.0.1). Nothing in the packets shows which PC asked. With only a perimeter sensor, you can't tell "who".
  2. The outside vantage point sees only the first query. The second client got its answer from cache, so there were zero outbound queries. Counted at the perimeter, "the name was looked up once"; in fact two PCs looked it up. The longer the TTL, the bigger the gap. The second answer's TTL of 58 rather than 60 marks it as a cached answer, two seconds older.
  3. Outside, even the name may be only partly visible. See the next box.

[Changed] QNAME minimisation: root and TLD servers don't get the full name

The book's diagram shows the traditional behaviour, where the resolver sends the full name (www.example.com) to root and TLD servers too. Today's resolvers usually use QNAME minimisation (RFC 9156, 2021; first proposed as RFC 7816 in 2016): each server is asked only as much as it needs to answer. Above, the root was asked only com, the com server only example.com, and only the final authoritative server saw the full name. Unbound's manual documents this feature as on (yes) by default (in this lab I set qname-minimisation: yes explicitly in the config and confirmed the behaviour), and the other major resolvers support it too. Minimised queries may also go out as type A rather than the original type (AAAA, MX and so on).

What this means for investigations: in perimeter captures, depending on resolver configuration, one event can appear as name fragments split across stages, and query types may differ from what the client really asked. Don't conclude "the full name isn't in the outside DNS log, so nobody looked it up". In perimeter data, look for the query that reached the final authoritative server. Better still, get the inside (in front of the resolver) records.

[Supplement] There can be a clue about the client outside: EDNS Client Subnet

The book says there is no way to determine the original client's address from the perimeter. By default that's right. But a resolver with EDNS Client Subnet (ECS, RFC 7871) enabled sends the leading part of the client's address (e.g. a /24) to authoritative servers such as CDNs, so they can pick the nearest server. When you see it, you can narrow things to "someone in this range". It's still not an individual address, and it's often off by default, as with this lab's resolver. And if users bypass the in-house resolver with DNS over HTTPS (DoH), nothing lands in the inside DNS records either. Lesson 2.7 covers this.

docs.title: 7.3 The "13 root servers"
docs.text:
A resolver starts with a list of root servers (root hints). The book calls them "the 13 root DNS servers". More precisely:

[Supplement] 13 is the number of names (addresses); there are roughly 2,000 actual servers

The root servers are defined as 13 names and addresses, a.root-servers.net through m.root-servers.net, run by 12 organisations. Each address is served by anycast (the same address announced from many places worldwide), so there are about 2,000 actual server instances; a post to the RIPE DNS Working Group list on 30 October 2025 reported that 2,000 had been passed. root-servers.org wasn't reachable from this environment, so the figure was checked through search results (2026-11-05). For investigations, what helps is that the 13 root addresses don't change. A workstation querying them directly instead of going through the resolver is unusual.

As this lab showed, a resolver with an empty cache first asks the root for . NS to confirm the list (priming), and makes extra queries to find the addresses of the name servers themselves (ns.gtld.test, ns1.example.com). That's why one client question produced 11 outbound queries. A real Internet resolver already has most of this cached and asks far less.

docs.title: 8. CNAMEs: stitching responses together
docs.text:
A CNAME response is a kind of hand-off. Instead of an address it returns another name: "look this one up instead". A CNAME's value must be a name. Responses take one of two forms.

  • If the responding server can also answer for the target name, it returns the CNAME together with the target's answer (an A record, say).
  • If not, it returns only the CNAME, and the client (usually a resolver) sends a completely separate query for the new name.

I asked the authoritative server directly to see both cases. 127.0.0.13 serves both example.com and example.net, but not example.org.

(Actual output)

$ dig @127.0.0.13 alias.example.com +norec +noall +answer
alias.example.com.  300 IN  CNAME   www.example.com.
www.example.com.    60  IN  A   192.0.2.10

$ dig @127.0.0.13 ext.example.com +norec +noall +answer
ext.example.com.    300 IN  CNAME   host.example.org.

In the first case the same server also serves www.example.com, so both came back. In the second, it doesn't serve example.org, so only the CNAME came back. When ext.example.com was asked via the resolver, the outside records show the resolver asking 127.0.0.13 for ext.example.com (getting just the CNAME), then going via the org server and sending a new query for host.example.org to 127.0.0.14. The client received one combined answer from the resolver.

So an analyst sometimes has to stitch query/response pairs together to see the full result. In outside-vantage or authoritative-side records especially, ext.example.com and host.example.org are logged as separate queries.

docs.title: 8.1 [Caution] CNAME and A records have separate TTLs and cache states
docs.text:
A CNAME record and its target's A record are fully independent records, with different TTLs and different cache lifetimes. I checked with cdn.example.com (CNAME, TTL 300) → edge.example.net (A, TTL 30): one query to a resolver with an empty cache, then another client asking 33 seconds later.

(Actual output)

First query (0 s)
cdn.example.com.    300 IN  CNAME   edge.example.net.
edge.example.net.   30  IN  A   198.51.100.80

Another client 33 s later
cdn.example.com.    267 IN  CNAME   edge.example.net.
edge.example.net.   30  IN  A   198.51.100.80

Outbound queries from the resolver at that point: just one, edge.example.net A

Interpretation: the CNAME was still cached (300 − 33 = 267), so the resolver didn't ask outside for it. The A record had expired after 30 seconds, so the resolver re-asked only for edge.example.net (a fresh answer, hence TTL 30 again). At the outside vantage point at the 33-second mark, the name cdn.example.com never appears; there's only the edge.example.net query. Yet cdn.example.com was the name the user actually wanted.

What this means for investigations: CDNs and cloud services stack CNAMEs several deep and keep the final A record's TTL very short. Looking only at outside records, or a short window, it can seem "this PC only looked up some unfamiliar edge… name". Following the CNAME chain backwards to the original name is the analyst's job. Attackers use CNAMEs for the same reason: keep an innocuous-looking name and just swap its target.

docs.title: 9. How this is used in real investigations
docs.text:
1. Write down the vantage point first. Is this DNS record between clients and the resolver (you can see who asked) or outside the resolver (you can't, and the cache hides some lookups)? Record it in the report.
  2. Capture filter: port 53. udp port 53 misses large answers that moved to TCP (section 5).
  3. Baseline types and response codes per vantage point. Don't mix user and server segments. Watch for rises in NXDOMAIN, TXT and NULL.
  4. Search decoded fields. Compression makes byte-string searches miss names (section 6).
  5. Stitch CNAME chains together. Outside, they appear as separate queries with independent TTLs (section 8).
  6. Read the cache from TTLs. If a resolver's answer has a smaller TTL than the original, it came from cache. That's a clue for working back to the first lookup (original TTL − remaining TTL = time since the first lookup). It's only an estimate, because resolvers may cap, floor or refresh TTLs.
  7. Collect the resolver's configuration. QNAME minimisation, ECS and forwarding settings change what's visible outside.

docs.title: 10. Summary
docs.text:
• DNS is a distributed system that turns names into addresses and more. Almost every connection starts with a DNS lookup, which makes it a great starting point for investigations.
  • Main records: A, AAAA, NS, CNAME, MX, PTR (reversed into in-addr.arpa), SRV, TXT, NULL, SSHFP, and [Supplement] HTTPS (type 65), now common in user segments. [Correction] TXT's 255-byte limit applies to each string, not each record.
  • Baseline type ratios per vantage point: PTR for mail servers; A, AAAA and HTTPS for users. Mass NXDOMAIN is a signal.
  • Header: a random 2-byte transaction ID, flags (QR, RD, RA, TC, AA…) and per-section counts. Resolvers randomise source ports too.
  • UDP is the default, but a truncated (TC) answer is re-asked over TCP. [Changed] Since 2020 UDP replies are often capped near 1232 bytes, so TCP 53 shows up more often.
  • Name compression: top bits 11 mark a pointer, and the remaining 14 bits give an offset. In my own encoding, 99 bytes shrank to 60, and a name with a different tail (example.net) wasn't compressed.
  • Recursion (RD=1) versus iteration (RD=0), caching and TTLs. What I confirmed: the outside vantage point has no client addresses and doesn't see the second lookup, and [Changed] with QNAME minimisation the root and TLD servers received only part of the name.
  • A CNAME comes with its target's answer if the same server serves both, separately otherwise, and CNAME and A records have independent TTLs and cache states (a CNAME with 267 s left beside a freshly fetched 30 s A record).

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Basics) Explain each line of this dig output, and say what you can infer about the server that gave it.

shop.example.com.   300 IN  CNAME   shop.cdn.example.net.
shop.cdn.example.net.   20  IN  A   198.51.100.31
Answer and explanation

Line 1: shop.example.com is an alias whose canonical name is shop.cdn.example.net, and this may be cached for 300 seconds. Line 2: shop.cdn.example.net has IPv4 address 198.51.100.31, valid for only 20 seconds. Inference: if this response came straight from an authoritative server, that server serves both zones; if it came from a recursive resolver, the resolver may have made two lookups and combined them (section 8). The flags: line in dig's output helps: aa means an authoritative answer, ra means recursion available. A very short TTL on the A record is typical of CDNs.

Question 2. (Vantage points) You captured a month of DNS with a sensor just outside the perimeter firewall. The incident lead asks for "a list of internal PCs that looked up the malicious domain bad.example.org". What can and can't you do with this data?

Answer and explanation

Can't: produce the PC list. Every outbound query comes from the internal resolver, and nothing in the packets shows which PC asked (section 7.2). Because of caching, repeat lookups within the TTL never leave the network, so you can't get counts either. Can: the times the resolver first asked outside for the name (once each time the cache expired), the addresses it got back (a lead for finding later connections to them), and CNAME chains. Next steps: obtain the internal resolver's query records (or a capture in front of it, or the logs from lesson 2.7), and use the resolved addresses to find which PCs actually connected, via firewall, proxy or NetFlow records. Also remember that if the resolver uses QNAME minimisation, the full name bad.example.org may never have gone to the org server in the perimeter data.

Question 3. (Changed conditions) In question 2's situation, what changes if the internal resolver had EDNS Client Subnet enabled? What limits remain?

Answer and explanation

Queries from the resolver to authoritative servers may carry the leading part of the client's address (e.g. a /24), so reading that option in the perimeter capture narrows things to "a client in this range" (the [Supplement] in section 7.2). Remaining limits: ① It's a range, not an individual PC. ② ECS is usually configured for specific authoritative servers (CDNs and the like), so it may not have gone to the attacker's domain. ③ Lookups answered from cache still don't appear outside. ④ Private-range addresses are usually not sent via ECS. It doesn't replace inside records.

Question 4. (Common misconception) "DNS only uses UDP 53, so to save disk I set the DNS capture filter to udp port 53." What could you miss?

Answer and explanation

You'd miss entire large answers that are re-fetched over TCP after a truncated (TC) reply (section 5's experiment: over UDP only the question came back with zero answers; the real 1,480-byte answer came over TCP). Since 2020 UDP replies are often capped near 1232 bytes, so answers with DNSSEC signatures, long TXT records or many addresses increasingly arrive over TCP. You'd also miss zone transfer (AXFR) attempts and DNS tunnelling over TCP. Use port 53. Port 853 (DNS over TLS) and DoH on 443 aren't caught by that filter either; that's lesson 2.7.

Question 5. (Reading compression) Part of a response packet's bytes is shown below. The first name starts at offset 0x0C. Read the name at offset 0x1D.

0x0C: 03 61 70 69 07 65 78 61 6D 70 6C 65 03 63 6F 6D 00
...
0x1D: 03 64 65 76 C0 0C
Answer and explanation

The name at 0x0C is 03 api 07 example 03 com 00 = api.example.com. At 0x1D, 03 64 65 76 is a 3-byte label dev; then C0 0C has top bits 11, so it's a pointer, and its remaining 14 bits are 0x00C = 12. Reading from offset 12 (0x0C) gives api.example.com, so the full name is dev.api.example.com. A pointer to the start of a name (0x0C) appends that whole name as the tail; a pointer into the middle, like section 6's C0 10, appends just the remainder.

Question 6. (Interpretation) A capture in front of the internal resolver shows one PC asking for www.example.com three seconds apart, receiving TTLs of 3600, 3597 and 3594. Another PC asked for the same name the same day and got TTL 1205. What can you infer?

Answer and explanation

The first PC's first answer (3600) was freshly fetched by the resolver (the original TTL appears to be 3600), and 3597 and 3594 were served from cache, dropping 3 seconds each time. The second PC's 1205 means the answer had been in the cache for about 3600 − 1205 = 2395 seconds (about 40 minutes). So you can estimate that someone — the first PC, or another PC not in this record — first looked up the name about 40 minutes before the second PC asked. Resolvers that cap or floor TTLs, or prefetch, throw this calculation off, so record it as an estimate and confirm with resolver logs or an outside capture.

Question 7. (Common misconception) "TXT records are limited to 255 characters, so you can't smuggle larger data out over DNS." Refute this on two grounds.

Answer and explanation

① [Correction] 255 bytes is the limit for each string within a TXT record, and one record can hold several strings (section 2's experiment: 243 + 244 bytes; the practice big record is seven strings, about 1.4 KB). A single response can also carry multiple TXT records. ② More fundamentally, size limits don't matter if the data is chopped up and sent many times. Real DNS tunnelling encodes outbound data into query names (subdomains) across thousands of lookups and receives commands in TXT, NULL or CNAME answers (lesson 2.7). That's why the baseline (section 3) watches TXT and NULL ratios and the number of unique subdomains under one domain.

Question 8. (Interpretation) In a perimeter capture, the internal resolver asks a root server address for com A and a com server for example.com A. A colleague concludes "someone was only interested in the name example.com". What did they miss?

Answer and explanation

QNAME minimisation (the [Changed] box in section 7.2). The resolver asks each server only as much as that server can answer, so the root gets com and the com server gets example.com. The client's real question might have been www.example.com or x7f3.data.example.com, and the original type might have been AAAA or TXT (minimised queries may go out as A). Look for the real name in the next stage, the query to example.com's authoritative server; the most reliable source is the record in front of the resolver. If that next-stage query is missing, consider whether the resolver already had example.com's delegation cached.

Question 9. (Application) You're asked to reshape your organisation's DNS architecture to help investigations. What principles from this lesson would you propose?

Answer and explanation

For example: ① Run a small number of internal resolvers and make every client use them (distributed via DHCP). ② At the perimeter firewall, allow only those resolvers to reach outside DNS (53, and 853 too), and block clients from going to outside DNS directly. Then "who asked" is concentrated in one place. ③ Log both queries and responses at the resolver, or put a sensor in front of it on the client side (section 7.2: outside, clients and cached lookups are invisible). ④ Capture with port 53 (section 5). ⑤ Build per-vantage-point baselines of types and response codes (section 3). ⑥ Document resolver settings (QNAME minimisation, ECS, forwarding). The book likewise advises against outsourcing such a critical function and recommends internal resolvers. The remaining gap, DoH (DNS leaving on 443), is covered in lesson 2.7.

docs.text:
• Tools used in this environment: Unbound 1.19.2 (a practice hierarchy of four authoritative servers and one recursive resolver), dig 9.18.39 (BIND), tcpdump, TShark 4.2.2, dnspython 2.9.2, Python 3.13. Results obtained on 2026-11-05.
  • IETF, RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 (1987: record formats, header, 512-byte UDP limit, name compression, TXT character-strings).
  • IETF, RFC 6891 (EDNS(0)), RFC 7766 (TCP support required), RFC 9210 (operational requirements for TCP, 2022).
  • DNS Flag Day 2020 (1232-byte default EDNS buffer recommendation; checked via search results on 2026-11-05).
  • IETF, RFC 9156 (QNAME minimisation, 2021), RFC 7871 (EDNS Client Subnet), RFC 5452 (resilience against forged answers: source-port randomisation).
  • IETF, RFC 9460 (SVCB and HTTPS records, 2023), RFC 4255 (SSHFP), RFC 2782 (SRV).
  • IANA, DNS Parameters (full list of record type numbers).
  • Root server instance count: root-servers.org (not reachable from this environment) and the RIPE DNS Working Group list post of 30 October 2025 (2,000 passed). Checked via search results on 2026-11-05.
  • rfc-editor.org couldn't be opened directly from this environment, so RFC content was checked through search results and the published standards' known text.

About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The practice DNS hierarchy, records and queries are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.1 — Reading HTTP Requests: Methods, URIs and Request Headers
2.1 — Reading HTTP Requests: Methods, URIs and Request Headers
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Why HTTP: traces gone from the disk remain on the wire
  • HTTP's nature (text-based, stateless) and version history. [Changed] the current standards for HTTP/1.1, 2 and 3
  • The four parts of a request: request line, headers, blank line, body
  • Methods: [Correction] the methods a server must support are GET and HEAD, and the difference between "safe" and "idempotent"
  • The request target (URI), query strings and percent-encoding
  • Request headers one by one: Host, User-Agent, the Accept family, Cookie, Authorization, X-Forwarded-For, Referer
  • [Changed] What browsers send today: Referer policy, Client Hints, Sec-Fetch-* (checked with Chromium requests captured directly)

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) was produced in this environment. Browser requests were actually sent by the built-in Chromium (headless, version 153.0.8010.12), driven with Playwright, to a practice web server (Python http.server) on loopback; the server recorded the headers it received verbatim while tcpdump captured the traffic. Command-line requests were sent with curl 8.5.0. People and accounts in the scenarios are hypothetical, and external addresses use documentation ranges only.

docs.title: 1. Not on the disk, but on the wire
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) Another employee at lesson 1.4's research institute comes under investigation. This time the laptop is locked with full-disk encryption, and the employee reportedly used the browser only in private mode, possibly a portable browser carried on USB. Recovering web activity by disk forensics looks hard.

What remains in such cases is the path the activity took (lesson 1.1). Web activity almost all travels over HTTP, and its records end up in proxy logs (lesson 1.3), full packets (lesson 1.6), and the web server logs and Zeek logs covered in coming lessons. Reading HTTP is almost unavoidable in investigations.

  • People's web activity: which pages were viewed and what was downloaded. A frequent question in employee misconduct and criminal cases.
  • Programs talking to each other (APIs): HTTP today is as much the channel for APIs, through which programs exchange data with other services, as for web pages people look at. Knowing which software used which APIs can paint a fairly detailed picture of what happened on a system.
  • Malware command channels (C2): much malware talks to its master over HTTP or HTTPS. Working with a malware analyst, you can learn what commands were exchanged and what was taken.
  • Web server compromise: looking at the traffic itself, in addition to server logs and disk analysis, gives a more complete picture even if the attacker covered their tracks.

docs.title: 2. What kind of protocol is HTTP?
2.1 Letters written in text, letters that don't know each other
docs.text:
HTTP is a protocol of requests and responses. A letter analogy helps: the client writes "please send me this document" (the request), and the server writes back "here it is" (the response).

HTTP/1.x letters have two properties.

  • They're written in text. The head of each request and response is readable letters and digits, exactly as seen when following a stream in lesson 1.9. So you can read a lot without tools.
  • Letters don't know about each other (stateless). Each request and response stands on its own; the protocol itself doesn't remember earlier requests. When continuing state is needed, such as "logged-in user", a separate mechanism such as cookies is required (section 6.4).

Where the analogy differs: opening one web page actually involves not one letter but tens to hundreds. The page body, images, style sheets and scripts are each requested separately, from several servers. So behind the single sentence "they visited this site" lie hundreds of request lines, and sorting out which were things the person actually did is the investigator's job (section 6.7, lesson 2.4).

Traditionally HTTP uses TCP port 80 and HTTPS TCP port 443. But as lessons 1.9 and 1.12 showed, port numbers are just conventions; HTTP can travel on any port.

docs.title: 2.2 [Changed] Version history and today's standards
docs.text:
Version First appeared Characteristics Current standard HTTP/0.9 1991 a single request line, no headers should essentially never be seen HTTP/1.0 1996 headers and status codes appear RFC 1945 (informational) HTTP/1.1 1997 Host required, connection reuse RFC 9110 (semantics), RFC 9112 (message syntax), 2022 HTTP/2 2015 binary framing, multiplexing, header compression RFC 9113, 2022 (replaces RFC 7540) HTTP/3 2022 runs over QUIC (UDP), TLS mandatory RFC 9114, 2022

The source material cites RFC 2616 as the reference for HTTP/1.1; it was replaced by RFC 7230–7235 in 2014 and again by RFC 9110–9112 in 2022. The source material also dates HTTP/3 to "2016" and describes it as "still in development", but HTTP/3 became a standard as RFC 9114 in June 2022, and QUIC beneath it is RFC 9000 (2021). As lesson 1.2 showed, HTTP/3 (QUIC) uses UDP 443 and can therefore bypass proxies, which matters for investigations. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 get their own treatment in lesson 2.3. This lesson and the next are based on HTTP/1.1. Methods, status codes and the meaning of headers stay the same across versions, so what you learn here carries over.

docs.title: 3. The four parts of a request
docs.text:
Take a real request. This is what the server received when the built-in Chromium opened the practice server's /start page and clicked a link on it.

(Actual output, exactly as the server received it)

GET /next?q=orchid+results HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8201
Connection: keep-alive
sec-ch-ua: "HeadlessChrome";v="153", "Not_A Brand";v="8", "Chromium";v="153"
sec-ch-ua-mobile: ?0
sec-ch-ua-platform: "Linux"
Upgrade-Insecure-Requests: 1
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) HeadlessChrome/153.0.8010.12 Safari/537.36
Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,image/avif,image/webp,image/apng,*/*;q=0.8,application/signed-exchange;v=b3;q=0.7
Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin
Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate
Sec-Fetch-User: ?1
Sec-Fetch-Dest: document
Referer: http://127.0.0.1:8201/start
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd

flowchart TD
    A["Request line<br/>method · target · version"] --> B["Headers<br/>Name: value (one per line)"]
    B --> C["Blank line<br/>end of headers"]
    C --> D["Body<br/>only for POST etc."]

How to read it: top to bottom, in the order the request goes on the wire. Every line ends in \r\n, and one blank line marks the end of the headers. That's why lesson 1.13 looked for \r\n\r\n to cut off the body.

  • Request line (required): GET (method), /next?q=orchid+results (request target), HTTP/1.1 (version), separated by single spaces.
  • Headers: one Name: value per line. In HTTP/1.1 only Host is required; the rest are mostly optional. That is, the sender can add, omit or fabricate them at will. Keep this in mind throughout the lesson.
  • Blank line: the end of the headers.
  • Body: usually absent on GET requests. Present on requests that send data, such as POST or PUT (the multipart body in lesson 1.13).

docs.title: 4.1 Common methods
docs.text:
Method Meaning What to note in investigations GET give me the resource The most common. Also sends values in the query string POST here's data, please process it Form submissions, uploads, API calls. Content is in the body (usually not in logs, lesson 1.4) HEAD same as GET, headers only Checks whether a file changed or how big it is. Also used by reconnaissance tools PUT create (replace) this location with this content Can be used to upload files to a server. Notable if seen on a web server DELETE remove the resource at this location Normal for APIs; odd on a static web server OPTIONS tell me what you support Browser preflight (CORS) requests, scanners TRACE echo back the request you received Diagnostic; mostly disabled. If seen, suspect a scan CONNECT open a tunnel Used when a proxy relays HTTPS (lesson 1.2)

Protocols that extend HTTP, such as WebDAV, use their own methods: PROPFIND, PROPPATCH, MKCOL, COPY, MOVE, LOCK, UNLOCK. WebDAV, used like file sharing, can become an exfiltration channel, so when unfamiliar methods appear, first work out what protocol it is.

[Correction] The methods a server must support are GET and HEAD

The source material says "the only methods a server is required to support are GET and POST". The current standard, RFC 9110 section 9.1, states that "all general-purpose servers MUST support the methods GET and HEAD; all other methods are OPTIONAL" (RFC 7231 before it said the same). Many static web servers don't accept POST at all. This difference rarely matters in investigations, but a server responding oddly to HEAD can itself be a clue.

docs.title: 4.2 [Correction] "Safe" and "idempotent" are different
docs.text:
The source material describes GET as "idempotent", meaning the same request at a later time yields the same result without changing content on the server. The standard splits this into two concepts.

  • Safe: the request does not intend to change server state. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE.
  • Idempotent: sending the same request several times has the same effect as sending it once. All safe methods plus PUT and DELETE, since PUTting the same file twice or DELETEing the same resource twice leaves the same result.
  • POST is neither. POSTing the same order twice can create two orders.

What this means for investigations: these are promises only. As the source material notes, web apps that change state via GET, like GET /delete.php?id=17, are common, and attackers deliberately send commands by GET (most of the attack traces in web server logs in lesson 2.5 are GETs). So don't conclude "it was a GET, so nothing changed". The method is a starting point for guessing intent; confirm the actual effect from the response and server-side records.

docs.title: 5. The request target (URI) and query strings
docs.text:
The middle of the request line is the request target, pointing to the resource the client wants. It's commonly called the URI, and logs also call it the "request string" or "URL".

/next?q=orchid+results
└─┬─┘ └──────┬───────┘
 path    query string
  • Path: once it pointed directly to folders and file names on the server's disk, but today a web app usually interprets the path and generates content. /questions/34476646/forensic-... looks like folders, but no such folders necessarily exist on the server.
  • Query string: name=value pairs after ?, joined with &. It's how a GET request passes values to the server: search terms, page numbers, tracking identifiers.
  • Percent-encoding: characters not allowed in addresses become % plus two hex digits. Space is %20, / is %2F, and the Korean character "가" is three UTF-8 bytes, %EA%B0%80. In queries coming from forms, spaces may become +, as in orchid+results in the request above (lesson 1.13, question 2).

[Supplement] The URI in logs may not be \"what a person read\"

Logs and packets keep the encoded form (%EA%B0%80). Decode it to read search terms, and conversely, when searching by keyword, also search for the encoded form. Remember that the same character may appear with upper-case hex (%2F) or lower-case (%2f). Attackers also use double encoding (%252F) on purpose to evade filters.

docs.title: 6.1 Host
docs.text: The only required header in an HTTP/1.1 request. In virtual hosting, where one server (one IP address) runs many sites under different names, it says which site the request is for. So you can't say "they went to such-and-such site" from the IP address alone: one IP can host hundreds of sites (CDNs are the typical case), and Host (or SNI for HTTPS, lesson 1.2) tells you which. In HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, the :authority pseudo-header plays the same role (lesson 2.3).

docs.title: 6.2 User-Agent: a self-declared name
docs.text:
The name the sending software declares for itself. It often contains the browser type and version and the operating system, which makes it good material for sketching a user's environment. But remember three things.

  • It can be changed at will. It's an optional header by the standard, and a browser extension or a command-line option (curl -A) can put anything in it. The upload in lesson 1.13 claimed to be Firefox but was actually curl.
  • Mozilla/5.0 means nothing. It's a compatibility leftover from the days when old web sites chose features based on that string, so Chrome, Safari, Edge and Firefox all start with it.
  • Defaults are clues too. In this lab, the request curl sent had only three headers.

(Actual output)

GET /api/status HTTP/1.1
Host: 127.0.0.1:8201
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
Accept: */*

The request Chromium sent to the same server (section 3) had fourteen headers. The number, order and combination of headers are more tedious to fake than the User-Agent string, so they're a supporting clue for judging whether a request came from a person's browser or an automated tool (lesson 2.4). Also, the headless Chromium in this lab put the word HeadlessChrome right into its User-Agent (actual output): a trace that gives an automation tool away if it doesn't change it.

[Changed] The User-Agent has shrunk, and Client Hints have appeared

In the source material's era, the User-Agent carried detailed OS versions and full browser versions. Since 2022 (Chrome 101), Chromium-based browsers have phased in User-Agent reduction, freezing the minor version numbers at 0.0.0 and sending a fixed OS version. More detail moved to Client Hints (Sec-CH-UA-* headers), sent only when the server asks; by default just three go out: sec-ch-ua, sec-ch-ua-mobile and sec-ch-ua-platform, as in the request above. So reading "the User-Agent says Windows 10, so it's Windows 10" can now be wrong (Windows 11 can send the same value). Note that this lab's headless Chromium sent its full version (153.0.8010.12). It may behave differently from ordinary desktop browsers, so in real cases test that version of that browser yourself before interpreting.

docs.title: 6.3 Accept, Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding
docs.text:
These announce what responses the client wants: Accept for content types (MIME types), Accept-Language for languages, Accept-Encoding for compression. A trailing q=0.9 is a preference weight (0–1).

In investigations, these too are profile material. For example, Accept-Language: ko-KR,ko;q=0.9,en-US;q=0.8 suggests a user environment that prefers Korean. This lab's headless Chromium sent no Accept-Language at all, and its Accept-Encoding included zstd, which didn't exist in the source material's era (actual output). If requests with a different combination suddenly appear from the same PC, that can signal a different program has started using HTTP.

docs.title: 6.4 Cookie: memory attached to a stateless protocol
docs.text:
As section 2.1 said, HTTP itself doesn't remember earlier requests. So the server leaves a small value with the client via the response's Set-Cookie, and the client returns it in a Cookie header on every later request. That's how logged-in state, shopping carts and user identification are maintained.

  • Session cookies: have no expiry and disappear when the browser closes.
  • Persistent cookies: stay on disk until a set expiry time.

In investigations, cookies are the thread linking the same person (strictly, the same browser storage) across requests and days. If the same cookie value keeps appearing as addresses change, it's probably the same browser. Advertising and analytics trackers' cookies even carry past information such as the time of the first visit, covered separately in lesson 2.3. Conversely, don't forget that a session cookie is itself a login key. Mishandling session cookies left in pcaps or logs is like walking into someone else's account.

docs.title: 6.5 Authorization and Proxy-Authorization: Base64 isn't encryption
docs.text:
Authentication through a login box the browser pops up (not a login form within the page) is called HTTP authentication, and its simplest scheme, Basic, puts username:password converted to Base64 in a header. The request sent in this lab with curl -u "jdoe:Spring2026!" went out like this.

(Actual output)

Authorization: Basic amRvZTpTcHJpbmcyMDI2IQ==

echo 'amRvZTpTcHJpbmcyMDI2IQ==' | base64 -d

(Actual output) jdoe:Spring2026!

Base64 is a notation, not encryption, so anyone can reverse it immediately (lesson 1.13). And Basic authentication sends this header with every request, so over plain HTTP the account is visible in any packet while the site is being used. In investigations it's a strong clue to the user's identity, and also very sensitive information, so mask it in reports.

  • The Digest scheme doesn't send the password itself, but is rarely used today.
  • [Supplement] Bearer tokens: today's APIs commonly send a token obtained at login, as in Authorization: Bearer eyJ.... If the token is a JWT, Base64-decoding the middle part reveals the issuer, user and expiry. Tokens, like session cookies, are keys in themselves.
  • Proxy-Authorization: a header of the same form exchanged only between the client and the first proxy when a proxy requires authentication. This is how user names end up in the proxy logs of lesson 1.3.

docs.title: 6.6 X-Forwarded-For: an "original address" anyone can write
docs.text:
A header that proxies and load balancers add when relaying a request, to convey the original client's address. Through several hops, addresses accumulate as original client, first proxy, ....

The problem is that the client can put it in from the start. In this lab, sending curl -H "X-Forwarded-For: 10.10.4.3", the server received the header as-is, even though the address that actually connected was 127.0.0.1 (actual output).

X-Forwarded-For: 10.10.4.3

10.10.4.3 is the internal proxy address from lesson 1.1. If a web app trusts this header, as in "allow the admin screen for requests from the internal proxy", an attacker can get past that control with one header line, exactly as the source material warns.

Investigative principle: when you see X-Forwarded-For in logs, ask who added it. A value added by your own proxy or load balancer (the rightmost value, nearest your equipment) is trustworthy, but values already present to its left may have been written by the client. And whether that equipment strips and rewrites client-supplied values or appends to them depends on configuration, so check.

[Supplement] Headers starting with X-, and the standard Forwarded

X- was a convention for non-standard extension headers, but RFC 6648 (2012) recommended against using the prefix for new headers. The already widespread X-Forwarded-For remained a de facto standard, and there's a formal standard header for the same purpose, Forwarded (RFC 7239, 2014). You may see both in logs. Other X- headers vary wildly by program, so an unusual X- header can become a fingerprint of a particular program.

docs.title: 6.7 Referer: where did they come from, and [Changed] how much does it say today?
docs.text:
Referer (a spelling mistake in the original standard that stuck; the English word is referrer) is the address of the previous page that led to this request: the page holding the clicked link, or the page that loaded an image or script. Chaining requests by Referer lets you reconstruct the path a user took between pages. Of course, it's optional too and may be missing or faked.

The source material explains that "it shouldn't be sent when going from HTTPS to HTTP, but in practice a truncated value may go". Today's browsers additionally follow a Referrer-Policy, whose default when nothing is specified is strict-origin-when-cross-origin (in Chrome from 2020 and Firefox from around 2021, lesson 1.3). I tested three cases directly.

(Actual output)

Navigation Referer received by the server Same origin: http://127.0.0.1:8201/start → /next?q=... http://127.0.0.1:8201/start (full path) Cross origin: http://127.0.0.1:8201/start → http://localhost:8202/landing http://127.0.0.1:8201/ (origin only, no path) HTTPS → HTTP: https://127.0.0.1:8443/secure → http://127.0.0.1:8202/plain none

An "origin" is the combination of scheme, host name and port. 127.0.0.1 and localhost are the same computer but different names, so they were treated as different origins. In short, under today's default policy:

  • Within the same site, the previous page's full address (including the query) is sent.
  • When going to another site, only the origin is sent. If the visitor came from a search engine, as in the source material's example, you'll see only Referer: https://search-engine/, and not what the search terms were.
  • When going down from HTTPS to HTTP, nothing is sent at all, matching the requirement in RFC 9110 section 10.1.3.

So don't conclude "they typed the address directly" just because Referer is missing. It may have been a link on an HTTPS page, or the page may have set its policy to no-referrer.

[Supplement] Sec-Fetch-*: browsers telling you the circumstances of a request

Today's browsers use Sec-Fetch-Site, Sec-Fetch-Mode, Sec-Fetch-User and Sec-Fetch-Dest to say in what situation a request arose (W3C Fetch Metadata). In this lab, Sec-Fetch-Site was none when an address was opened directly, same-origin for a same-origin link and cross-site for a cross-origin link, and navigations made by clicking a link carried Sec-Fetch-User: ?1 (actual output). They also distinguish a page body (Sec-Fetch-Dest: document) from images and scripts. With Referer reduced, these headers are a good supporting clue for "was this navigation clicked by a person, or a resource the page loaded by itself?" But they're added by browsers, so non-browser tools may omit or fake them.

[Supplement] The DNT: 1 in the source material's example

The DNT ("do not track") header effectively died out because sites didn't honour it, and MDN marks it deprecated. If you see it in old logs, don't read much into it.

docs.title: 7. How to use this in real investigations
docs.text:
1. Start with the request line. Method, request target, version. Note PUT or DELETE on a static site, diagnostic TRACE, or unfamiliar WebDAV methods.
  2. Decode query strings before reading them. Search terms and identifiers live there. Search for keywords in their encoded form too.
  3. Name the site by Host, the server by IP. Don't mix different sites on the same IP.
  4. Read optional headers as "self-declared". User-Agent, X-Forwarded-For and Referer can be faked. Ask who added them and whether they agree with other evidence.
  5. Build profiles from header combinations. Requests whose combination differs from a PC's usual one may come from a different program.
  6. Mask the keys. Authorization, session cookies and tokens are the accounts themselves. Mask them in reports and shared material, and confirm legal authority before using them.

docs.title: 8. Summary
docs.text:
• HTTP is text-based, stateless requests and responses. Web activity gone from the disk still remains on the wire and in logs.
  • [Changed] The reference for HTTP/1.1 is RFC 9110 and 9112 (2022), not RFC 2616; HTTP/2 is RFC 9113, and HTTP/3 became a standard as RFC 9114 in 2022.
  • A request consists of the request line, headers, a blank line and the body; the only required header is Host. Everything else is up to the sender.
  • [Correction] The methods that must be supported are GET and HEAD. "Safe" (no intent to change state) and "idempotent" (same effect when repeated) differ, and both are only promises; confirm actual effects separately.
  • Decode query strings and percent-encoding before reading them.
  • The User-Agent is a self-declared name, and [Changed] has shrunk, with some detail moved to Client Hints. Header combinations (three from curl, fourteen from the browser) are a supporting clue.
  • Basic authentication's Base64 decodes instantly. X-Forwarded-For can be written by anyone (confirmed directly).
  • [Changed] Under today's default Referer policy: full address for the same origin, origin only for cross-origin, nothing for HTTPS→HTTP (confirmed directly). Sec-Fetch-* tells you the circumstances of a request.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Structure) Split the request line of the following request into its three parts, and pick out all headers that aren't required.

POST /api/v2/sync?device=7f3a HTTP/1.1
Host: files.example.net
User-Agent: SyncAgent/4.2
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 58
Answer and explanation

Method POST, request target /api/v2/sync?device=7f3a (path /api/v2/sync and query device=7f3a), version HTTP/1.1. Only Host is required, so User-Agent, Content-Type and Content-Length are all optional. But a request with a body needs Content-Length (or chunked transfer, lesson 1.13, question 6) for the server to read the body correctly. "Not a required header" and "not needed in this request" are different things. This request sent 58 bytes of JSON to an API; SyncAgent/4.2 is a self-declared name, so confirm the actual program on the endpoint.

Question 2. (Corrected content) A colleague says, "This web server returned 405 (method not allowed) to a HEAD request. HEAD is optional, so nothing odd there." Right?

Answer and explanation

The standard (RFC 9110 section 9.1) says general-purpose servers must support GET and HEAD. So a general-purpose web server rejecting HEAD is unusual behaviour that doesn't match the standard. It might be a deliberate security setting, a characteristic of a particular web app or device, or a clumsy implementation in an attacker's fake server (C2). As lesson 2.2 shows, such "slight deviations from the standard" can become fingerprints identifying a server. So it's not "nothing odd" but "a characteristic worth recording".

Question 3. (Common misconception) "The log has only GET /admin/user.php?action=remove&id=42 and no POST, so this user didn't change anything." Explain the problem with this conclusion.

Answer and explanation

GET being "safe" is only a promise set by the standard; whether the web app keeps it is another matter. This request's query is action=remove, and by its name alone it looks like a function deleting account 42. Whether it was actually deleted must be confirmed from ① the response status code and size (lesson 2.2), ② the web app's and database's records, and ③ whether that account had any later activity. The method lets you guess intent, but not conclude the effect.

Question 4. (Decoding) A proxy log has the request GET /search?q=%EC%9C%A0%EC%B6%9C+%EB%B0%A9%EB%B2%95. What's the search term, and what string should you search for to find this value in logs?

Answer and explanation

%EC%9C%A0 is "유", %EC%B6%9C is "출", + is a space, %EB%B0%A9 is "방" and %EB%B2%95 is "법", so the search term is "유출 방법" ("how to leak"), in UTF-8 (decode with something like Python's urllib.parse.unquote_plus). Searching logs for the Korean text won't match; you must search for %EC%9C%A0%EC%B6%9C. Records may also be written with lower-case hex (%ec%9c%a0...), so a case-insensitive search is safer.

Question 5. (Interpretation) In section 6.2, curl's request had 3 headers and Chromium's had 14. A PC sends a request every five minutes with User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ... Chrome/... but only three headers: Host, User-Agent and Accept: */*. What can you suspect, and what can't you conclude?

Answer and explanation

What you can suspect: a real Chrome browser opening a page normally also sends headers like Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding, sec-ch-ua and Sec-Fetch-*, and this request isn't that combination. So it may be a non-browser program borrowing Chrome's name, and combined with the five-minute regularity (lesson 1.10), it looks like automated communication. What you can't conclude: that it's malware. Update tools, monitoring agents and in-house scripts can send requests like this too. Check the destination, the response content and the process that opened the connection on the endpoint. Also, requests a browser makes for images or APIs (where Sec-Fetch-Dest isn't document) can have different header combinations, so compare against the same kind of request from the same browser.

Question 6. (Changed conditions) An investigation procedure based on 2016 material says "for visitors arriving from search engines, find the search terms from the q= value in Referer". Does this still work? Explain with the results tested directly.

Answer and explanation

Hardly ever. Under today's default Referrer-Policy, strict-origin-when-cross-origin, only the origin is sent when navigating to another origin. In section 6.7's experiment, moving from 127.0.0.1:8201/start to localhost:8202 gave Referer: http://127.0.0.1:8201/, without path or query. Moreover, search engines are mostly HTTPS, and going from HTTPS to an HTTP site sent no Referer at all. Search engines often have their own policies not to pass search terms either. So find search terms in the requests to the search engine itself (/search?q= in proxy logs, the autocomplete requests of lesson 1.4).

Question 7. (Application) A web server log shows access to the admin page from an external address, recorded together with X-Forwarded-For: 10.10.4.3, 192.0.2.10. In front of the server is our organisation's load balancer, which appends the connecting address to whatever value it receives. Who most likely actually connected, and what is 10.10.4.3?

Answer and explanation

If our load balancer appends, the rightmost 192.0.2.10 is the connection address the device actually saw: the trustworthy client address. 10.10.4.3 to its left was already in the header before the request reached the device. Another proxy in between may have added it, but the external client may also have written it in directly. That it happens to be the internal proxy address suggests a test of whether the web app uses this header to decide "request from inside" (section 6.6). So check ① which value the web app trusts, ② whether the response to that request was a success, and ③ other activity from 192.0.2.10.

Question 8. (Common misconception) "The Authorization header's value is encrypted, so sharing the pcap won't expose the account." What's wrong?

Answer and explanation

The Basic value is just Base64-converted, so as in section 6.5, one base64 -d gives username:password. Over plain HTTP, anyone receiving the pcap can read the account. Bearer tokens and session cookies are keys in themselves too, reusable to get in while still valid. So when sharing pcaps or logs, make copies with these headers masked or removed, and restrict access to the originals. Logging in with accounts learned during an investigation must not be done without legal authority.

Question 9. (Interpretation) From a day of requests from one PC, you want only the pages the user actually opened by clicking a link. Which headers from this lesson can you use, and what are the limits?

Answer and explanation

With today's browsers, requests carrying both Sec-Fetch-Dest: document (a page-body request) and Sec-Fetch-User: ?1 (navigation started by user activation) are good candidates; in section 6.7's experiment, both were attached to the navigations made by clicking links. Sec-Fetch-Site can also separate directly opened addresses (none) from those reached by link. The limits: ① these headers are visible only where headers can be seen, such as plain HTTP or a TLS-intercepting proxy (not if you only have HTTPS packets); ② the default proxy log format doesn't record headers (lesson 1.3); ③ older browsers and non-browser tools don't send them; ④ they can be faked. Without these headers, estimate human navigation from request timing and Referer chains, as in lesson 2.4.

About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The experiment server and requests are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.2 — Reading HTTP Responses: Status Codes, Response Headers and Investigative Use
2.2 — Reading HTTP Responses: Status Codes, Response Headers and Investigative Use
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • The three parts of the status line: version, status code, reason phrase. One byte of reason phrase can fingerprint a server (tested directly)
  • The five families of status codes and the ones common in investigations. [Correction] the name of 400, and 302 versus 307/308
  • Reading attacker intent from the flow of status codes: a storm of 404s, a 200 after 500s
  • Response headers: Connection ([Correction] HTTP/1.1 keeps connections alive by default), Server, content information and compression, Date (measuring clock skew), cache directives, Location
  • Typical investigative uses of HTTP: paste sites, User-Agent profiles, Basic authentication, URI records

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) was produced in this environment. Responses came from a practice server on loopback (written in Python for this lesson), deliberately built to run its clock 437 seconds slow and to return two redirects, a gzip-compressed body, and a response with one extra space after the reason phrase. Requests were sent with curl 8.5.0, captured with tcpdump 4.99.4 and read with tshark 4.2.2. Addresses and scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 1. Responses tell you "what happened on the server side"
docs.text:
The requests of lesson 2.1 tell you what the client wanted. The response tells you how that request was actually handled. Writing "they accessed the admin page" from request logs alone is half the story. Whether the request got a 200 (success), a 403 (refused) or a 302 back to the login screen changes everything.

As an analogy, the request is an application form handed in at a service counter, and the response is the notice of outcome the counter returns. The notice carries a result number (the status code), a short description (the reason phrase), notes about the handling (response headers), and possibly an attached document (the body). Where the analogy differs: the server can write most of that description and those notes however it likes, just like request headers in lesson 2.1.

docs.title: 2. The status line: version, code, reason phrase
docs.text:
The first line of a response is the status line.

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
  • Version (HTTP/1.1): usually matches the request's version.
  • Status code (301): a three-digit number. Programs decide what to do from this number alone.
  • Reason phrase (Moved Permanently): a short description for humans. The standard recommends phrases, but clients must ignore it and servers can write anything.

docs.title: 2.1 One byte of reason phrase becomes a fingerprint
docs.text:
The source material describes a researcher who found the servers of a popular attack and penetration-testing framework by a single space after the reason phrase. Those servers sent HTTP/1.1 200 OK with an extra space after OK, and scanning the Internet for this quirk turned up thousands of them (it has since been fixed). Clients ignore the reason phrase, so nothing breaks, but an implementation that deviates slightly from the standard becomes a fingerprint of that program.

I tested this principle. The practice server returns OK (with the space) only for /beacon requests.

tshark -n -r resp.pcap -Y 'http.response.phrase == "OK "' -T fields -e tcp.stream

(Actual output) 9. Of twelve responses, only the one with the space (stream 9) matched. The table below lists all responses; by eye, the difference between OK and OK is barely visible.

(Actual output, some columns trimmed)

tcp.stream  code  phrase             location            content_encoding  content_length
0           301   Moved Permanently  /promo                                0
0           302   Found              /landing?cid=8812                     0
0           200   OK                                     gzip              78
1           404   Not Found                                                12
...         ...   ...
8           404   Not Found                                                12
9           200   OK                                                       48

What it means for investigations: when threat intelligence reports "this C2 server sends this unusual response", one display filter can find the same server across all your past pcaps. Conversely, remember that such fingerprints vanish the moment the attacker fixes them. Don't conclude from one characteristic alone; use it alongside other evidence such as the destination, timing patterns and content.

[Changed] HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 have no reason phrase

HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) and HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) send only the status code, in the :status pseudo-header, and don't carry the version or reason phrase at all. So reason-phrase fingerprints work only on HTTP/1.x responses. If a logging tool shows a reason phrase for an HTTP/2 response, it's a standard phrase filled in by the tool to match the code.

docs.title: 3.1 The five families
docs.text:
Family Meaning One-line summary 1xx Informational still working, carry on 2xx Success the request was received and handled 3xx Redirection go elsewhere, or use what you already have 4xx Client error something is wrong with the request 5xx Server error the request was fine, but the server couldn't handle it

Even for an unfamiliar code, the first digit gives the broad meaning. The standard says to treat an unknown code as the x00 of its family.

docs.title: 3.2 Codes commonly seen in investigations
docs.text:
Code Standard name How to read it in investigations 100 Continue confirmation before sending a body (Expect: 100-continue). A precursor of large uploads 200 OK handled successfully.
