Read together with body size 204 No Content success, no body. Common as a beacon's "nothing to do" reply 206 Partial Content sent part only (Range request). The PDF fetched three times in the same second in lesson 1.4 301 Moved Permanently permanent move. Follow the Location header 302 Found temporary move. Return after login, the new post's address after an upload (lessons 1.4 and 1.13) 304 Not Modified use the copy you have. No body: no content was exchanged at that moment 307 · 308 Temporary · Permanent Redirect like 302 and 301, but resend without changing the method and body 400 Bad Request malformed request. Fuzzing, sloppy tools 401 Unauthorized authentication required. Look at subsequent Authorization attempts 403 Forbidden refused regardless of authentication 404 Not Found nonexistent resource. Many at once suggests reconnaissance (section 3.3) 405 Method Not Allowed that method isn't allowed. Traces of trying method after method 407 Proxy Authentication Required proxy authentication required (the proxy version of 401) 429 Too Many Requests requesting too often. Brute forcing or scraping hitting a limit 500 Internal Server Error internal server error. A web app falling over on strange input 502 · 504 Bad Gateway · Gateway Timeout front-end equipment got no answer from the back-end server 503 Service Unavailable overloaded or under maintenance 511 Network Authentication Required the login screen of places like public Wi-Fi (captive portals)

[Correction] The name of 400 and the meaning of 302

  • The source material calls 400 "Bad Syntax", but the standard name is Bad Request (RFC 9110 section 15.5.1).
  • The source material describes 302 as "in practice a temporary relocation, though not strictly in compliance with the standard". The background: 302 originally meant "repeat the request with the same method", but browsers turned a POST answered with 302 into a GET. Today's standard (RFC 9110 section 15.4.3) accepts that reality and allows the method to change to GET after a 302, and provides 307 (temporary) and 308 (permanent) for when the method must be kept. So in logs, POST → 302 → GET is a normal shape, while POST → 307 → POST means the same body was sent once more. It makes a difference when you count upload volume.

[Supplement] 304 means \"no content was exchanged\"

A 304 response has no body. It tells the client to use the copy it already has (the browser cache, lesson 1.5). So writing "they received that file at that time" from a 304 record is wrong. The file was received some time earlier; at that moment only the question "is it still valid?" was exchanged. To find when it was first received, search back for a 200 response to the same address.

docs.title: 3.3 Reading intent from the flow of codes
docs.text:
Status codes say more as a flow than one at a time. I requested common admin pages and config file names from the practice server one after another, like a reconnaissance tool.

(Actual output, requests joined with their response codes)

/phpmyadmin/      404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/pma/             404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/admin/setup.php  404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/wp-login.php     404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/.env             404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/.git/config      404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/backup.zip       404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x
/server-status    404   Mozilla/5.0 zgrab/0.x

Eight requests all got 404 within 0.06 seconds; no person with a browser could do that. This is the source material's "long bout of 400-series codes from a single address", the classic shape of reconnaissance. The names requested also show what was being looked for (a database admin tool, WordPress login, config files holding passwords, source repositories, backups). Lesson 2.5 shows the same shape in real web server log formats.

Another flow the source material describes is 500-series codes against a search form, then a 200, followed by many POSTs. Input with broken SQL syntax causes an error between the web app and the database, so it usually comes back as a 500. If an attacker kept adjusting input and getting 500s and finally got a 200, that may be the moment the injection succeeded, and the POSTs after it may be post-compromise operations. The server's error log often holds database error messages in such cases, so secure it too.

[Caution] A pile of 404s doesn't mean \"it failed, so we're fine\"

If a reconnaissance run ended all in 404s, that only means nothing was found from that list. Check whether even one request from the same address got a 200, and whether that address came back days later in another way. Also, as lesson 1.10, section 6.3 showed, an exported file named backup.zip may contain a 404 page. In this lab too, the file exported under the name backup.zip was a 12-byte <h1>404</h1> (actual output).

docs.title: 4.1 Connection: [Correction] HTTP/1.1 keeps connections alive by default
docs.text:
The source material says HTTP/1.1 gained the ability to carry several request/response pairs over one TCP connection, and that when the client signals support with Connection: Keep-Alive, the server answers with the same header. More precisely, persistent connections are the default in HTTP/1.1 (RFC 9112 section 9.3). The connection stays open without any announcement, and the side wanting to close sends Connection: close. Stating Keep-Alive explicitly is the HTTP/1.0-era extension.

What it means for investigations: one TCP connection (one stream, as in lesson 1.9) can contain several requests. In this lab, the three requests curl -L made following redirects (/go, /promo, /landing) all travelled in stream 0 (actual output). So don't count "one stream = one request", and remember that one connection in flow records (lesson 1.11) can hold several requests. Zeek, covered in lesson 2.8, distinguishes them with trans_depth.

docs.title: 4.2 Server: the name the server declares for itself
docs.text: The server-side counterpart of lesson 2.1's User-Agent. Values like Apache/2.4.29 (Ubuntu), nginx and Microsoft-IIS/10.0 are common and useful for guessing the server type and version. But it can also be written freely. This lab's server was written in Python yet declared Server: Apache/2.4.29 (Ubuntu) (actual output), because I made it so. Many operators remove versions or write misleading names for security, and front-end CDNs or proxies may replace it with their own. Headers such as Via, X-Cache and X-Served-By are clues that a cache or CDN sits in between.

docs.title: 4.3 Content information: length, type, compression
docs.text:
• Content-Length: the number of bytes in the body. This is the size on the wire.
  • Content-Type: the body's type (MIME type) and character set. Only what the server claims; confirm the actual content by its magic number (lesson 1.13).
  • Content-Encoding: compression applied to the body: gzip, br (Brotli), and zstd seen in lesson 2.1, among others.

With compression, there are two "sizes". In this lab, the /landing response had Content-Length: 78, but the file tshark exported was 1,106 bytes of HTML (actual output), because Wireshark decompressed the gzip on export. The same response can appear in proxy logs with its on-the-wire size (around 78 bytes) and in Zeek's http.log with its decompressed size (response_body_len in lesson 2.8). When matching sizes across sources, first establish which size it is. And when carving directly from packets (lesson 1.13), decompression adds another layer.

docs.title: 4.4 Date: another clock
docs.text:
The time the server generated the response. Caches use it to calculate freshness (lesson 1.5), but for investigators it's another independent clock. Comparing the capture box's time (the packet time) with the server's Date shows whether one of the clocks is off.

(Actual output)

frame.time_epoch: 1793861118.334450000   → Thu Nov  5 06:45:18 UTC 2026
http.date:        Thu, 05 Nov 2026 06:38:01 GMT

date -u -d @1793861118

The capture time and the server's Date differed by 437 seconds (7 minutes 17 seconds), exactly as expected since I set the practice server's clock that far back. In a real case, a difference like this means checking ① the capture box's NTP status (lesson 1.11) and ② that server's clock, then correcting all of that server's log times by the same amount before matching them with other evidence. Conversely, in a pcap captured on a user's PC, if many servers' Date values are all off in the same direction, the PC's clock is likely wrong. The source material also mentions malware that used the Date value of an ordinary web request as the seed for its domain generation algorithm (lesson 2.7): a clock is useful to malware too.

docs.title: 4.5 Cache directives: Cache-Control, Expires, ETag, Vary
docs.text:
These are the headers seen with the proxy cache in lesson 1.5. Briefly:

  • Cache-Control: max-age=1800 means fresh for 30 minutes; no-store means don't store; private means don't store in a shared cache.
  • Expires is an absolute time when freshness ends (the older approach).
  • ETag is an identifier for that content. If the client sends it back in If-None-Match on the next request, the server answers 304 when it hasn't changed.
  • Vary: Accept-Encoding means "store separate copies by compression method".

ETag is surprisingly useful in investigations. The same ETag is the server's indication of the same content, so it can be used to compare whether requests at different times or from different PCs received the same file. But how ETags are generated varies by server (some build them from file size and modification time), and they can be faked, so they don't replace hashes.

docs.title: 4.6 Location: chains of redirects
docs.text:
3xx responses carry a Location header giving the next address. One request in this lab (/go) continued like this.

flowchart TD
    A["GET /go"] -->|"301 · Location: /promo"| B["GET /promo"]
    B -->|"302 · Location: /landing?cid=8812"| C["GET /landing?cid=8812"]
    C -->|"200 · gzip body"| D["Final page"]

How to read it: top to bottom, the order in which the browser (here curl -L) followed automatically. The text on each arrow is that step's response code and Location value.

The user clicked once, yet three requests went out. Such chains are very common, and mostly normal, with URL shorteners, ad tracking and login flows. But malicious delivery networks love chains too: multiple hops make it easier to hide the final server and evade blocking. In investigations, find both the start of the chain (the link the user actually clicked, and where it came from) and the end (the content actually received), and put the intermediate addresses into block lists and threat intelligence. The query in a Location (cid=8812) can, like a campaign identifier, tell you who sent the link.

docs.title: 5. Typical investigative uses of HTTP
docs.text:
The source material lists four. Tying them to earlier lessons:

  • Exfiltration to paste and file-sharing sites. Attackers open a browser on a remotely accessed PC and upload data to a paste site, or build the site's published API into malware to upload automatically. Lessons 1.4 (the shape seen in logs) and 1.13 (the content carved from packets) were this case. A 302 and short Location after a POST are the typical traces.
  • Profiles built from User-Agents. A well-managed organisation knows its permitted User-Agent values, so unfamiliar ones signal unauthorised software. Some malware puts its own version in the User-Agent, so collecting User-Agents at the perimeter quickly sketches the extent of an infection and its version distribution. Remember, as lesson 2.1 showed, that they can be faked.
  • Basic authentication. Every request carries the account in Base64 (lesson 2.1, section 6.5), so over plain HTTP the account can be obtained at any point while the subject uses the site. A strong identity clue, and sensitive information.
  • URI records. Search terms, clicked results, form submissions and API calls show up in URIs. For malware, a network analyst and a malware analyst working together can learn which commands were exchanged.

And the starting point of lesson 2.1 was that all of this remains on the wire and in logs even after private mode, portable apps and disk encryption have wiped it from the endpoint. The Date header becomes an independent clock for refining the sequence of events.

docs.title: 6. How to use this in real investigations
docs.text:
1. Pair every request with its response. Write not "they accessed it" but "they accessed it and got a 200 (or a 403)".
  2. Read status codes as a flow. Look for a storm of 404s from one address, a 200 after 500s, success after 401s.
  3. Read 304 and 206 carefully. 304 means no content was exchanged at that moment; 206 means only part was.
  4. State which layer a size belongs to. Compressed on-the-wire size, or decompressed size.
  5. Align clocks with Date. Measure the differences between the capture box, servers and endpoints, and record the corrected values and the method in the report.
  6. Find the start and end of redirect chains. Intermediate addresses are material for blocking and threat intelligence.
  7. Save unusual responses as fingerprints. Reason phrases, header order, unfamiliar X- headers. But don't conclude from one fingerprint alone.

docs.title: 7. Summary
docs.text:
• The response tells you how a request was actually handled. The status line is version, code and reason phrase.
  • The reason phrase is up to the server, so even one byte (a space after OK) becomes a fingerprint (tested: one display filter matched only that response). [Changed] HTTP/2 and 3 have no reason phrase.
  • Status codes come in five families. [Correction] 400 is Bad Request; after a 302 the method may change to GET, and 307/308 keep it. 304 means no content was exchanged at that moment.
  • A storm of 404s from one address suggests reconnaissance; a 200 after 500s can signal successful injection (a hand-made reconnaissance flow: eight 404s in 0.06 seconds).
  • [Correction] HTTP/1.1 keeps connections alive by default, so one stream can carry several requests (confirmed: three redirect requests in one stream).
  • Server is also a self-declared name. Content-Length is the on-the-wire size, so with compression it differs from the decompressed size (78 bytes versus 1,106).
  • Date is an independent clock; comparing it with packet times measured a 437-second skew.
  • Find both the start and the end of Location chains.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Status line) A response's first line is HTTP/1.1 200 Everything is fine, nothing to see here. How does a browser handle it, and what might an investigator consider?

Answer and explanation

The browser ignores the reason phrase and treats it as a normal response from the 200 alone. The standard says clients must ignore the reason phrase and servers can write anything, so nothing is formally wrong. For the investigator, the unusual reason phrase is the clue. Common web server software uses the standard phrase (OK), so this may be the trace of a hand-built server or a particular tool. Search past pcaps with a display filter (http.response.phrase contains "nothing to see") for other servers returning the same phrase, and look for what they have in common (address ranges, certificates, timing patterns).

Question 2. (Common misconception) A proxy log has GET /reports/q3-financials.xlsx 304 at 2026-11-03 14:10. Can you write "this employee downloaded this file at 14:10"?

Answer and explanation

No. A 304 (Not Modified) has no body. At 14:10 only "is my copy still valid?" was exchanged, and the server answered "it hasn't changed, use what you have". So the employee's browser had already received the file some time before 14:10 and held it in cache. To find when it was first received, search back for a 200 response to the same address, and check the endpoint's browser cache too. Use 14:10 only as grounds for "they probably reopened the file (from cache) at that time".

Question 3. (Corrected content) A web app log shows POST /upload 307 followed by POST /storage/upload 201. How many times did the client's uploaded file probably cross the wire, and how would it differ with a 302?

Answer and explanation

307 means "resend to another address keeping the method and body", so the client most likely sent the POST containing the same file to /storage/upload once more: the same body crossed the wire twice. Be careful not to double-count upload volume (the actual data is one copy). With a 302, most real browsers would change the method to GET and re-request without the body, so the second request wouldn't have carried the file. Clients can differ, though, so confirm from the second request's method and size.

Question 4. (Interpretation) In three minutes, one external address sent 1,200 GETs to the same web server: 1,196 got 404, 3 got 403 and 1 got 200. What do you check first?

Answer and explanation

The 1,196 404s are the classic shape of reconnaissance trying name after name (section 3.3). But the most important are the single 200 and the three 403s. ① The URI and response size of the request that got 200: did the attacker actually find what they were looking for (a config file, a backup, an admin screen)? ② The URIs of the 403s: resources that exist but are blocked, which told the attacker "there's something here". ③ Whether that address later came back and re-requested the resource that got 200, and whether other addresses requested the same resource. Use the 404 list itself as material showing what the attacker was after (which software, which files).

Question 5. (Calculation) In a pcap captured on a user's PC, the Date headers of three unrelated web servers are ahead of the packet times by exactly 3 min 2 s, 3 min 1 s and 3 min 3 s respectively. Which clock is probably wrong, and how should other evidence from this PC be handled?

Answer and explanation

If three unrelated servers are all consistently about three minutes ahead, the wrong clock is most likely not the servers but the PC that stamped the packet times: its clock is about 3 min 2 s slow (servers are usually NTP-synchronised). So when matching this PC's evidence (this pcap's times, its event logs, file times) with other evidence, correct by about +182 seconds. In the report, record the original times, the correction and its basis (the comparison with three servers' Date values). Differences of about a second are natural, given the gap between when the server generated the response and when the packet was stamped, and Date's one-second resolution.

Question 6. (Application) A proxy log records a response as 2,048 bytes, while Zeek's http.log records the same response's body as 15,320 bytes. Is one of them wrong?

Answer and explanation

Not necessarily. If the response was compressed (Content-Encoding: gzip etc.), the proxy log records the on-the-wire size sent to the client (possibly including headers, lesson 1.3), while Zeek's response_body_len records the decompressed body size (lesson 2.8). In this lab, a response with Content-Length: 78 was 1,106 bytes decompressed. Text compresses well, so a sevenfold difference isn't strange. First confirm the two records are the same response by time and URI, check the response's Content-Encoding header, and state in the report which layer's size you're quoting.

Question 7. (Interpretation) An employee's PC opened an unfamiliar short link, and at the end of a 301 → 302 → 302 → 200 chain an executable was downloaded. What goes on the block list, and what do you investigate further?

Answer and explanation

Record the hosts of every step of the chain, and put the intermediate steps and the final delivery server into block lists and threat intelligence. The URL-shortening service at the start may be a legitimate service, so block that short link, not the whole service. Investigate further: ① the start of the chain: where did the employee get the short link (email, messenger, another page's Referer)? ② query values in intermediate steps (like campaign identifiers, they may reveal who sent the link); ③ the final file's hash and content (the methods of lesson 1.13); ④ other PCs that opened addresses in the same chain (scoping, lesson 1.11).

Question 8. (Common misconception) "The response says Server: Microsoft-IIS/10.0, so this C2 server is a Windows server." Explain the problem with this judgement.

Answer and explanation

The Server header is a value the server declares for itself, and anything can be written there. This lab's server was written in Python but declared Apache/2.4.29 (Ubuntu). An attacker may imitate a common value to look like a normal server, or a front-end CDN or proxy may have changed it. To estimate the real server, look at several characteristics together: ① the order of its response headers and its combination of default headers, ② the look of its error pages, ③ its TLS certificate and TLS handshake fingerprints (Part 5), ④ other services at the same address. Even then, keep open the conclusion "it may be a server imitating IIS".

Question 9. (Changed conditions) You put the "reason-phrase fingerprint" detection rule from section 2.1 on the organisation's packet sensors, and it hasn't fired once in a year. Can you conclude the attacker is gone? Give possible reasons.

Answer and explanation

No. ① The attack tool may have fixed the quirk (the source material's example was fixed). ② If the traffic is HTTPS, sensors can't see the status line. ③ With HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, there's no reason phrase at all (the [Changed] box in section 2.1). ④ The sensors may not sit where that traffic passes (lesson 1.11). Fingerprint-based detection is "a strong clue when it fires, silent when it doesn't", so don't conclude absence from its silence. Record each detection rule's creation date, basis and applicable conditions (plain HTTP/1.x) alongside it.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Tools used in this environment: a practice server written in Python 3, curl 8.5.0, tcpdump 4.99.4, tshark 4.2.2. Outputs were obtained on 2026-11-05.
  • IETF, RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics. Section 15 (status codes; 15.4.3 for 302 and method change; 15.4.8–15.4.9 for 307 and 308; 15.5.1 for 400 Bad Request), section 6.6.1 (Date), section 8.8.3 (ETag), section 10.2.2 (Location), section 10.2.4 (Server).
  • IETF, RFC 9112: HTTP/1.1, section 4 (status line and reason phrase), section 9.3 (persistent connections by default).
  • IETF, RFC 9113: HTTP/2, section 8.3.2 (the :status response pseudo-header; no reason phrase).
  • IETF, RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes (429, 511, etc.), RFC 9111: HTTP Caching.

About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The practice server and requests are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.4 — Lab Guide: HTTP Profiling
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Strategies for collecting useful HTTP artifacts: which fields, grouped by what
  • Finding what stands out (outliers): the User-Agent inventory, header counts, hours of activity
  • Forming hypotheses about human versus program: regularity of intervals, working hours, sub-resource requests
  • Seeing beyond the evidence with advertising cookies: finding a first visit seven months earlier in one day of pcap
  • Writing results up as facts, hypotheses and evidence still needed

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) was produced with this environment's tshark 4.2.2 and GNU awk. The lab pcap day.pcap was assembled in Python to imitate one day (2026-11-02, UTC) of HTTP on an office segment (9,162 packets, private and documentation addresses and example domains only). It mixes human web use, a legitimate updater and a deliberately hidden automated channel. Being assembled, it shows a simplified version of human behaviour; real traffic is much messier.

docs.title: 1. When you must find "what's odd on this segment" with no leads
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) The day after lesson 1.11's "something seems off in the research lab" case. The capture box in front of the research segment holds a day of pcap, and there are proxy logs. But the proxy logs are in lesson 1.3's default format, with no User-Agent, only URLs and sizes. As the source material's lab takeaways put it, the data formats available are not always ideal. This time the pcap, with headers, is more flexible, so we build the profile from it.

Profiling means summarising "what normally travels on this segment" so you can find what deviates from it. Think of a door guard who knows the faces and arrival times of the staff, and so can spot a stranger or someone coming in at dawn. Where the analogy differs: we know even faces (User-Agents) can be forged (lesson 2.1). So we look not at one face but also at gait (header combinations), hours of movement (time of day) and rhythm of steps (intervals).

docs.title: 2. How this lab is organised
docs.text:
Objectives

  1. Form strategies for collecting useful HTTP artifacts (which fields, grouped by what).
  2. Identify outliers that warrant further investigation.
  3. Form hypotheses separating human activity from program activity.
  4. Use advertising cookies to see beyond the period of the evidence you have.

Preparation

  • tshark, awk, sort, uniq, date
  • The lab pcap day.pcap. There's no starting lead, only "the research segment seems odd".

Record a hash first, as soon as you receive it.

sha256sum day.pcap
capinfos -c -a -e day.pcap

(Actual output)

2cc699cf6bd7d49b69f8dd12b8589cbe052fc65255efcca74ebb69c58fc03bf6  day.pcap
Number of packets:   9162
First packet time:   2026-11-02 00:02:17.000000
Last packet time:    2026-11-02 23:55:02.382120

A full day. Note first that there are packets from just after midnight to just before midnight. If HTTP is moving on an office segment in the small hours, who (or what) is sending it?

flowchart TD
    A["User-Agent inventory<br/>faces"] --> B["Header counts<br/>gait"]
    B --> C["Hours of activity<br/>when they move"]
    C --> D["Intervals<br/>rhythm of steps"]
    D --> E["Cookies<br/>the past"]
    E --> F["Facts · hypotheses · evidence needed"]

How to read it: top to bottom, the order of this lab. Each step looks again, from another angle, at what the previous steps didn't filter out.

docs.title: 3. Step 1: the User-Agent inventory, this segment's "faces"
docs.text:
tshark -n -r day.pcap -Y http.request -T fields -e http.user_agent | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

(Actual output)

   2823 Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/141.0.0.0 Safari/537.36
    951 Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:144.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/144.0
    777 Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/141.0.0.0 Safari/537.36 Edg/141.0.0.0
     30 VendorUpdate/5.3 (Windows)

As the source material's lab takeaways note, tshark's -T fields output makes such reports quick (lesson 1.10). There are only four faces: Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and an updater called VendorUpdate/5.3. No unfamiliar faces. By User-Agent alone, this segment looks clean. Stop here and the lab fails.

Whether VendorUpdate/5.3 really is that company's updater is checked against the administrators' allow list (lesson 2.2, section 5). In this lab we assume it's an allowed program.

docs.title: 4. Step 2: header counts, this segment's "gait"
docs.text:
Remember from lesson 2.1 that curl sent three headers and the browser fourteen? A User-Agent can be faked in one line, but not many programs imitate the whole combination of headers. Count the header lines per request, by source and site. The sub-resource host cdn.example.net is excluded because it's too numerous.

tshark -n -r day.pcap -Y 'http.request && http.host != "cdn.example.net"' -T fields -E aggregator='|' \
  -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.request.line \
  | awk -F'\t' '{n=split($3,a,"|"); print $1, $2, n}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -k2,2 -k3,3
  • -e http.request.line: the header lines after the request line. There are several, so one cell holds several values (lesson 1.10, section 7.2).
  • -E aggregator='|': joins those values with | instead of commas. Header values contain commas (like Accept's value), so joining with commas gives the wrong count. My first count with commas came out too high, which is why I switched.
  • awk ... split($3,a,"|"): the number of |-separated pieces is the number of header lines.

(Actual output, the 10.10.6.14 part and one other PC)

    144 10.10.6.14 cdn-sync.example 3
     31 10.10.6.14 docs.example.com 10
     24 10.10.6.14 intranet.lab.example 10
     19 10.10.6.14 jobs.rival.example 10
     18 10.10.6.14 mail.example.org 10
     26 10.10.6.14 news.example 10
      6 10.10.6.14 update.vendor.example 3
     ...
     36 10.10.7.11 docs.example.com 10
     29 10.10.7.11 intranet.lab.example 10
     30 10.10.7.11 mail.example.org 10
     31 10.10.7.11 news.example 10
      6 10.10.7.11 update.vendor.example 3

Two things show.

  • Browser requests from every PC have 10 header lines and the updater 3. That's this segment's "normal gait".
  • Only 10.10.6.14 (hq-rd-04) sent 3-line requests to cdn-sync.example, 144 times. No other PC has this site at all.

So what User-Agent did those 3-line requests use? Step 1's inventory had no unfamiliar faces, so it must have borrowed one of the existing ones.

tshark -n -r day.pcap -Y 'http.host == "cdn-sync.example"' -T fields -e http.user_agent | sort | uniq -c

(Actual output) 144 Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/141.0.0.0 Safari/537.36

A User-Agent identical, character for character, to the real Chrome. These 144 were hiding among the 2,823 Chrome requests of step 1. Same face, different gait: none of the Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding, Sec-Fetch-* or cookies Chrome sends when opening a page (lesson 2.1, section 6.2, question 5).

docs.title: 5. Step 3: hours of activity, when this segment "moves"
docs.text:
People arrive, work, eat lunch and go home. Look at the earliest and latest hour (UTC) at which requests appear, by source and site.

tshark -n -r day.pcap -Y 'http.request && http.host != "cdn.example.net"' -T fields -e ip.src -e http.host -e frame.time_epoch \
  | awk -F'\t' '{h=strftime("%H",$3,1); k=$1" "$2; c[k]++;
                 if(!(k in mn)||h<mn[k])mn[k]=h; if(!(k in mx)||h>mx[k])mx[k]=h}
                END{for(k in c) print k, c[k], mn[k]"-"mx[k]}' | sort
  • strftime("%H",$3,1): turns Unix time into the UTC hour; the final argument 1 means UTC (GNU awk). Fixed to UTC to avoid the time-zone trap from lesson 1.10.
  • mn[k], mx[k]: remember the earliest and latest hour for each group.

(Actual output, the 10.10.6.14 part)

10.10.6.14 cdn-sync.example 144 00-23
10.10.6.14 docs.example.com 31 08-17
10.10.6.14 intranet.lab.example 24 08-17
10.10.6.14 jobs.rival.example 19 09-17
10.10.6.14 mail.example.org 18 08-17
10.10.6.14 news.example 26 08-17
10.10.6.14 update.vendor.example 6 00-20

Browser requests from the other PCs were all between 08 and 17 as well (actual output). So human web use on this segment is concentrated in working hours, and only two things appear all day (00–23): update.vendor.example (every PC) and cdn-sync.example (10.10.6.14 only). The small-hours packets came from these two programs.

[Supplement] When there are no logon/logoff records

The source material's lab takeaways say "with no logon/logoff data, human activity is difficult to characterise, so we turn to other clues". This lab is exactly that case. With the endpoint's logon records (lesson 1.11, section 2.2) you could tell directly who was at the keyboard; without them you estimate from hours of activity, intervals, sub-resource requests and human irregularity. It's an estimate, so the report says so.

docs.title: 6. Step 4: intervals, this segment's "rhythm of steps"
docs.text:
Measure the intervals between requests from the same source to the same site, and compute the mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum. Human browsing is irregular; programs are often regular (the 900 seconds of lesson 1.10, the five minutes of lesson 1.11).

for h in cdn-sync.example update.vendor.example jobs.rival.example; do
  tshark -n -r day.pcap -Y "http.request && http.host == \"$h\" && ip.src == 10.10.6.14" -T fields -e frame.time_epoch \
  | awk -v h=$h 'NR>1{d=$1-p; s+=d; ss+=d*d; n++; if(n==1||d<mn)mn=d; if(n==1||d>mx)mx=d} {p=$1}
                 END{m=s/n; printf "%-22s n=%d mean=%.1f sd=%.1f min=%.1f max=%.1f\n", h, n+1, m, sqrt(ss/n-m*m), mn, mx}'
done

(Actual output)

cdn-sync.example       n=144 mean=600.0 sd=2.5 min=594.3 max=605.7
update.vendor.example  n=6 mean=14400.0 sd=0.0 min=14400.0 max=14400.0
jobs.rival.example     n=19 mean=1601.6 sd=1663.5 min=4.8 max=5652.3
  • cdn-sync.example: mean 600 seconds (10 minutes), standard deviation 2.5 seconds, barely wavering between 594 and 606 seconds. 144 a day = 24 hours × 6. A machine's rhythm. The few seconds of wobble may be deliberate "jitter": many tools shake their intervals slightly to evade detection.
  • update.vendor.example: exactly every four hours (14,400 seconds). Also a machine's rhythm, but it appears identically on every PC and is an allowed program.
  • jobs.rival.example: intervals range wildly from 5 seconds to an hour and a half; the standard deviation is as large as the mean. Closer to a human rhythm. Looking at the request lines, each page carries Sec-Fetch-User: ?1, followed by a cluster of sub-resource requests (lesson 2.1, section 6.7).

By now cdn-sync.example has narrowed to "something pretending to be Chrome, sending requests every ten minutes all day that get no content back (204)". Look at the request paths too.

(Actual output, beginning)

1793577902.857440000    198.51.100.66   /api/ping?id=7f3a&n=0
1793578501.155126000    198.51.100.66   /api/ping?id=7f3a&n=1
1793579101.926539000    198.51.100.66   /api/ping?id=7f3a&n=2
1793579698.945641000    198.51.100.66   /api/ping?id=7f3a&n=3

id=7f3a looks like an identifier for the infected device, and n= like an incrementing counter. The response is a bodyless 204 No Content every time, the shape lesson 2.2's table described as "common as a beacon's nothing-to-do reply".

docs.title: 7. Step 5: seeing the past through cookies
docs.text:
Now to the human side. The user of 10.10.6.14 opened the competitor's recruitment site jobs.rival.example 19 times during working hours. Since when have they been looking at it? We have only one day of pcap, but we look at the cookies using lesson 2.3's method.

tshark -n -r day.pcap -Y 'http.request && ip.src == 10.10.6.14 && http.cookie && http.host != "cdn.example.net"' \
  -T fields -e http.host -e http.cookie | sort -u

(Actual output)

docs.example.com    _ga=GA1.1.16400249.1783036800
intranet.lab.example    _ga=GA1.1.19789581.1773446400
jobs.rival.example  _ga=GA1.1.18205781.1773792000
mail.example.org    _ga=GA1.1.16424006.1782777600
news.example    _ga=GA1.1.13668194.1785715200

There's one _ga value per site: the same browser store kept sending the cookie it received from each site. Convert the last number to a date.

date -u -d @1773792000 +%F

(Actual output)

Site Last number of _ga Date (UTC) jobs.rival.example 1773792000 2026-03-18 intranet.lab.example 1773446400 2026-03-14 mail.example.org 1782777600 2026-06-30 docs.example.com 1783036800 2026-07-03 news.example 1785715200 2026-08-03

Following lesson 2.3, section 3's interpretation (last number = the time the cookie was first created), this browser store first received the competitor's recruitment-site cookie on 18 March 2026. One day of pcap reached back seven and a half months. The internal intranet cookie dating from 14 March is interesting too. This browser store may have come into use in mid-March (a new PC, a new browser profile, cookies cleared). If so, 18 March is "four days after the store came into being", and the possibility remains that the site was visited before that from another store. That's what lesson 2.3, section 4's "a user is a store" means.

[Caution] The cookies in this lab are invented values

The _ga values in the lab pcap were made to show the structure. With real evidence, ① check the value format and the basis of the interpretation as lesson 2.3 cautions, ② bound it with browser cookie-lifetime caps (Chrome 400 days, Safari 7 days), and ③ check it against the endpoint's cookie database and past proxy-log records.

docs.title: 8. Writing it up
docs.text:
• Observations (facts):
    • On 2026-11-02, at this capture point, HTTP requests showed four User-Agent values.
    • Only 10.10.6.14 sent requests to cdn-sync.example (198.51.100.66): 144 of them, at a mean interval of 600 seconds (standard deviation 2.5 seconds), continuing from 00:00 to 23:00.
    • Those requests used the same User-Agent as genuine Chrome but carried three header lines (the same PC's browser requests carried ten). Every response was 204.
    • The same PC opened jobs.rival.example 19 times during working hours (09:00–17:00). The last value of the _ga cookie on requests to that site corresponds to 2026-03-18.
  • Interpretation (hypotheses):
    • The cdn-sync.example traffic appears to be periodic check-ins (beaconing) by an automated program imitating Chrome, not a person's browser.
    • The recruitment-site visits appear to be human browsing, and by this browser store may have continued since mid-March at the latest.
    • Whether the two activities are related isn't yet known.
  • Evidence still needed:
    • The process that opened the 198.51.100.66 connections on the endpoint.
    • DNS records for cdn-sync.example (lessons 2.6–2.7) and when it first appeared.
    • Pcaps and proxy logs from other days (when did the ten-minute rhythm start?).
    • Whether the same rhythm appears on PCs in other segments (scoping).
    • For the recruitment-site visits, whether HR or legal needs to make a judgement.
  • Limits of the observation:
    • One day, plain HTTP only. This method can't see headers of HTTPS traffic.
    • The cookie interpretation relies on a widely used interpretation, not official documentation.

As the last item suggests, the recruitment-site visits may be an HR matter, not a security incident. The investigator records the facts accurately and leaves it to the authorised departments to decide how to handle them.

docs.title: 9. Summary
docs.text:
• The data formats you have aren't always ideal. A pcap with headers is often more flexible for profiling than proxy logs without them.
  • The User-Agent inventory alone found nothing (no unfamiliar faces). Header counts (3 lines versus 10) found the 144 requests hiding inside the same User-Agent.
  • Human web use clustered in working hours (08–17), and only two programs appeared all day.
  • The standard deviation of intervals separated people from machines: 10 minutes ± 2.5 seconds (machine), exactly 4 hours (the allowed updater), 5 seconds to 1.5 hours (human).
  • Cookies let one day of pcap read a first visit seven and a half months earlier (2026-03-18), with the "store" caveat attached.
  • Write results up as facts, hypotheses, evidence needed and limits.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Strategy) In section 3 the User-Agent inventory looked clean, yet we didn't stop. Besides this lab's method, give at least two other ways to find a program hiding inside the same User-Agent.

Answer and explanation

① The number and order of headers (this lab); ② combinations of header values: for the same browser, the values of Accept, Accept-Language and Accept-Encoding are nearly identical across PCs; ③ presence of Client Hints and Sec-Fetch-* (lesson 2.1): claiming to be Chrome without sec-ch-ua is odd; ④ presence of cookies: browsers used by people send cookies for sites they visit often; ⑤ hours and intervals (sections 5–6); ⑥ for HTTPS, TLS handshake fingerprints (Part 5): the same User-Agent with a different TLS library gives a different fingerprint. Whatever the method, don't conclude from one alone; look at several characteristics together.

Question 2. (Reading a command) What goes wrong if you count section 4's command without -E aggregator='|', joining with commas?

Answer and explanation

-T fields joins several values in one cell with commas by default (lesson 1.10, section 7.2). But header lines themselves contain commas: Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,... or Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br, zstd is one line with several commas. So splitting on commas gives a count larger than the number of header lines, and the more commas a browser's values contain, the more wrong it is. In this lab too, my first comma-based count came out too high. Using a separator that doesn't appear in header values (|) gives the right count.

Question 3. (Calculation) In section 6, the 144 requests to cdn-sync.example spanned the day. If the interval were exactly 600 seconds, how many should there be in a day (86,400 seconds), and does it match?

Answer and explanation

86,400 ÷ 600 = 144, exactly matching the lab's 144. "Requests per day = day ÷ interval" fitting this neatly is itself a sign of a program that never stops: people sleep, turn PCs off and leave their desks. Conversely, if the number falls short, the PC was off, the network dropped, or capture missed a period, and looking for those gaps can reveal the PC's usage pattern (lesson 1.10, question 5).

Question 4. (Interpretation) update.vendor.example also appeared all day, exactly every four hours. Why didn't we suspect it like cdn-sync.example? What should still be checked?

Answer and explanation

① It appeared with the same rhythm on every PC (the shape of a program deployed organisation-wide). ② Its User-Agent is its own name, and its header combination is the same on every PC. ③ We assumed it's on the allow list. cdn-sync.example, by contrast, went from one PC only, under someone else's name (Chrome), to a destination not on the allow list. Still check that update.vendor.example's destination address (203.0.113.120) really belongs to that company, that response sizes are as usual, and the program file's signature: supply-chain attacks can abuse legitimate update paths.

Question 5. (Common misconception) "cdn-sync.example has CDN in its name and the responses were 204, so no content was exchanged and it's harmless." What's wrong?

Answer and explanation

① Anyone can choose a name; cdn and sync are common words used to look normal. ② 204 may mean the server had no command to send at that moment. A beacon gets "nothing to do" most of the time, then a different response (200 with a body) the moment the attacker queues a command. ③ The requests carry information too: id=7f3a looks like a device identifier, n= like a counter, and the request itself signals "this device is alive". ④ Above all, imitating Chrome is not how legitimate programs behave. So look in other days' records for non-204 responses, and at what happened on the PC right after them.

Question 6. (Changed conditions) You have to do the same investigation, but this time with no pcap, only Squid logs in lesson 1.3's default format (no User-Agent). Which steps of this lab can you do, and which can't you?

Answer and explanation

Can do: section 5's hours (the log's times and source addresses), section 6's intervals (time differences between the same address and destination), response codes and sizes (204 and 0 bytes), request URLs (/api/ping?id=7f3a&n=...). In fact, these alone are enough to expose the all-day ten-minute rhythm. Can't do: section 3's User-Agent inventory, section 4's header counts and section 7's cookies. So the fact that it "imitated Chrome" and the recruitment site's first-visit time can't be known. As the source material's lab takeaways suggest, when the available format isn't ideal, do what the fields you have allow first, and recommend adding User-Agent to the log format for the future (lesson 1.3).

Question 7. (Interpretation) In section 7, the intranet cookie dated from 14 March and the recruitment-site cookie from 18 March. Give two interpretations of these two dates, and say how you'd check each.

Answer and explanation

Interpretation ①: this browser store came into being around 14 March (a new PC, a new profile, all cookies cleared). Then the cookie for the intranet the employee uses daily was recreated that day, and the recruitment site may have been viewed earlier. Check: PC issue or reinstall records, the creation time of the endpoint's browser profile, and proxy logs before 14 March for the same PC's intranet and recruitment-site access. Interpretation ②: the store existed earlier and only the intranet cookie changed that day (e.g. a change to the intranet's analytics setup). Then 18 March is more likely the recruitment site's first visit. Check: whether other PCs' intranet cookie dates also cluster around 14 March. If they do, it's a change on the site's side.

Question 8. (Application) You want to turn this lab's method into organisation-wide continuous detection. What rules would you make, and what would you watch out for?

Answer and explanation

For example: ① "the same source requests the same destination more than 50 times a day with an interval standard deviation under 5% of the mean" (rhythm); ② "a browser User-Agent with far fewer headers than that browser normally sends" (gait); ③ "browser-shaped requests outside working hours" (hours); ④ "regular requests to a never-before-seen destination" (novelty). Watch out that ① legitimate programs (updaters, monitoring, messengers) are regular too, so maintain an allow list alongside; ② tools with large jitter can evade standard-deviation thresholds; ③ HTTPS hides headers, so flow- and TLS-fingerprint-based rules are needed. Record each rule's basis, creation date and false-positive cases.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Tools used in this environment: tshark 4.2.2, GNU awk (strftime with the UTC option), coreutils sort, uniq, date and sha256sum, capinfos. The lab pcap was assembled in Python, and outputs were obtained on 2026-11-05.
  • This lab uses lessons 2.1 (request headers), 2.2 (response codes), 2.3 (tracking cookies) and 1.10 (building tables with tshark). See each lesson's references too.
  • GNU, Gawk manual: time functions. strftime([format [, timestamp [, utc-flag]]]).

About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The lab procedure and practice pcap are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.3 — Seeing the Past Through Tracking Cookies, and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
2.3 — Seeing the Past Through Tracking Cookies, and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Why advertising and analytics cookies are useful to investigators: they contain times from a past you have no other evidence for
  • The structure and reading of the classic analytics cookies (__utma, __utmb, __utmz). [Changed] today it's _ga and _ga_<ID>
  • A "user" is not a person but a cookie store: browsers, private mode, deletion
  • Marketing cookies (__hstc, hubspotutk, hsfirstvisit) and millisecond timestamps
  • [Changed] Browsers cap cookie lifetimes: Chrome 400 days, Safari 7 days
  • HTTP/2: binary framing, header compression, multiplexing (confirmed by decrypting HTTP/2 traffic captured directly, using session keys). [Changed] server push has been removed from browsers
  • HTTP/3: HTTP over QUIC, and what changes for investigations

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) was produced in this environment. HTTP/2 traffic came from nghttp2 1.59.0's nghttpd server on loopback, run both over TLS (with a self-signed certificate I created) and in cleartext (h2c), with requests sent by curl 8.5.0 (built with nghttp2) and captured with tcpdump. TLS session keys were written with SSLKEYLOGFILE and used to decrypt with tshark 4.2.2. All cookie values are invented for illustration, and time conversions were computed directly with date.

docs.title: 1. A window onto a past you have no evidence for
docs.text:
(Hypothetical) The pcap captured from the employee's PC under investigation covers only one week from 1 November 2026. But the question is "when did this employee first look at that competitor's recruitment site?" Even if the week's packets contain visits to the site, that only shows they visited that week, not when the first time was.

What unexpectedly helps here are advertising and analytics cookies. These companies make money by recording as precisely as possible when visitors first came, how often, and from where, so they often store that information inside the cookie value. The cookie travels in the Cookie header with every request (lesson 2.1, section 6.4), so a single line of today's packets can yield a first-visit time months ago.

As an analogy, it's a café loyalty card. Look at a customer's card today and you see the date it was issued, the date of the last visit and the number of stamps so far. The café's CCTV may hold only a week, but the card tells an older story. The analogy differs in two ways. First, the card belongs not to a person but to a wallet (the browser's cookie store). Second, the café (the company) designs the card format and often doesn't publish it, so interpretation always carries caveats.

docs.title: 2. The classic analytics cookies: __utma, __utmb, __utmz
docs.text:
The source material covers in detail three old cookies of what was long the most widely used web analytics service. They're no longer used (section 3), but you can still meet them in old evidence (pcaps from years ago, old cookie files on disk), and they're a good example for learning "how to read the numbers inside a cookie", so here is their structure. The utm in the names comes from Urchin Tracking Module, on which the service was based.

All are dot-separated (.), and the first value is a hash of the site (domain): it's the same across cookies of the same site.

Cookie Lifetime Composition of the value __utma 2 years domain hash . visitor identifier . first visit . previous visit . current visit . visit count __utmb 30 minutes domain hash . pages this session . outbound link countdown (from 10) . current visit time __utmz 6 months domain hash . time . visit count . source count . source information (utmcsr=source|utmccn=campaign|utmcmd=medium|utmctr=term)

(Hypothetical) Here's an __utma value invented for this lesson.

__utma=111872281.1938459823.1767225600.1793000000.1793512345.14

The time values are Unix time (seconds since 1970, lesson 1.3), so convert with date.

date -u -d @1767225600
date -u -d @1793000000
date -u -d @1793512345

(Actual output)

1767225600 → 2026-01-01 00:00:00 UTC   (first visit)
1793000000 → 2026-10-26 07:33:20 UTC   (previous visit)
1793512345 → 2026-11-01 05:52:25 UTC   (current visit)

The final 14 is the visit count. One line of packets from 1 November tells the story "this browser first came to this site on 1 January 2026, this is its 14th visit, and the previous visit was 26 October", a past a week of pcap could never show. This is exactly one of the objectives of the lab in lesson 2.4: using advertising cookies to see beyond the evidence you have.

__utmz's source information tells you how the visitor arrived at the site. utmcsr=search-engine|utmcmd=organic|utmctr=... means via search, utmcmd=referral via a link on another site, and utmcsr=(direct) via a typed address or bookmark. As lesson 2.1 showed, Referer now often gives only the origin, so such source information, where it survives, is valuable (especially in old evidence).

docs.title: 3. [Changed] Today's analytics cookies: _ga and _ga_<ID>
docs.text:
The old tracking code that set the __utm* cookies fell out of use long ago, and the generation that replaced it (Universal Analytics) stopped processing data for standard properties on 1 July 2023 (per Google's help centre). The official cookie documentation for the generation widely used today (GA4) lists these two:

Cookie Default lifetime Official description _ga 2 years used to distinguish users _ga_<container ID> 2 years used to persist session state

The official documentation doesn't describe the internal structure of the values. But a widely used interpretation is that _ga looks like GA1.1.<random number>.<Unix time>, with the last number being the time the cookie was first created. With the invented value placed in this lab's HTTP/2 requests:

_ga=GA1.1.1234567890.1793500000

date -u -d @1793500000

(Actual output) 2026-11-01 02:26:40 UTC. If the interpretation holds, that's "when this browser store first got that site's _ga cookie".

_ga_<ID> is known to hold values such as the session start time, session number and last activity time, and several sources reported around 2025 that its format changed from GS1.1.… to $-separated GS2.1.…. This change was confirmed from third-party analyses, not the vendor's official documentation, so when interpreting real evidence, look at the values as they were at the time, and open the same site in a test browser to see how the cookie changes before relying on it.

[Caution] Using undocumented values as evidence

Analytics vendors have no obligation to publish cookie formats, and change them without notice. So in the report, record ① on what basis you read a number as a time (official documentation, public analysis, or your own test), and ② whether it agrees with other evidence (as in the source material's example, compare with the browser history or the creation time in the cookie database). If there's only one interpretation, write "appears to be".

docs.title: 4. A "user" is a cookie store
docs.text:
The "user" a cookie identifies is not a person but one cookie store. Confusing the two badly skews conclusions.

  • Each browser is different. If one person uses Chrome and Firefox, there are two cookie stores and so two "users". The same goes for different profiles in the same browser.
  • Private mode is a new store each time. Every private window starts from an empty store, so by cookies it's a "new user arriving for the first time" every time. In private mode, __utma's first-visit time is just a time after that private window was opened.
  • Deleting starts over. If the user deleted cookies, the first-visit time resets to after that.
  • Several people can share one store. Shared PCs, shared accounts.

So read a cookie's first-visit time not as "when this person first visited" but as "when this store first received that site's cookie, and it hasn't been deleted since". Still, the same cookie value appearing on several days and from several addresses is a strong thread linking the same browser store, which other evidence (logon records, the endpoint) can tie to a person.

docs.title: 5. Marketing cookies: __hstc, hubspotutk, hsfirstvisit
docs.text:
Analytics services aren't the only ones using such cookies. Seeing cookies from several different trackers in one case is common, and each vendor's format has to be looked up and interpreted. The source material's example is a marketing automation service's cookies.

  • __hstc: the main visitor-tracking cookie. domain hash . visitor identifier . first visit . previous visit . current visit . visit count, almost the same structure as __utma, but with times in milliseconds (13 digits).
  • hubspotutk: the visitor identifier. The same as __hstc's second value, used to link the same person across several sites using that service.
  • hsfirstvisit: a cookie present in the source material's era that held the address through which the visitor first entered the domain and a millisecond time.

Convert millisecond times by dropping the last three digits or dividing by 1000.

date -u -d @1793512345    # first 10 digits of 1793512345678

(Actual output) 2026-11-01 05:52:25 UTC (the trailing 678 is 0.678 seconds).

[Changed] Lifetimes have changed, and official values need checking

The source material gives __hstc two years and hubspotutk and hsfirstvisit ten years. Many sites' published cookie lists now give __hstc and hubspotutk 13 months, but some say six months, so they disagree (search results, 2026-11-05). The vendor has changed lifetimes and its cookie list to meet privacy regulations. In real cases, check the vendor's current official documentation and the expiry of cookies actually received in a test browser.

docs.title: 6. [Changed] Browsers cap cookie lifetimes
docs.text:
Even if a vendor sets "two years" or "ten years", the browser may cut it shorter. GA4's official cookie documentation itself notes browser limits such as "a maximum of 400 days for Chrome and 7 days for Safari if a user doesn't return". Safari limits the lifetime of cookies set by script, and Chrome caps cookies at 400 days.

What it means for investigations: a first-visit time three weeks ago in a cookie doesn't mean "first came three weeks ago". A Safari user may have come earlier, with the cookie disappearing every seven days. Conversely, a first visit two years ago also means the browser didn't delete cookies in that time. You need the browser type and version (lesson 2.1's User-Agent and Client Hints) to know the upper bound of a cookie's times.

docs.title: 7. Where cookies are visible
docs.text:
• Plain HTTP packets: the Cookie header is visible as-is. Rare today.
  • HTTPS: not visible from packets alone. You need records from a TLS-intercepting proxy (lesson 1.2) or session keys (lesson 1.12, section 8).
  • Proxy logs: the default format doesn't record headers (lesson 1.3). They can be configured to record cookies, but session cookies are login keys in themselves, so store them with care.
  • The endpoint's cookie database: the domain of disk forensics. Not kept in private mode.

And today's analytics cookies mostly attach to the visited site's own domain (first party). So the _ga cookie appears in the Cookie header of requests to that site, not to the analytics vendor. In this lab too, the _ga value travelled on both requests to the site (127.0.0.1:8445) (actual output).

docs.title: 8. HTTP/2: a completely different shape, the same meaning
8.1 What changed
docs.text:
HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) keeps the meaning of methods, status codes and headers from HTTP/1.1, but its shape on the wire is completely different.

  • Binary framing: traffic moves in binary units called frames instead of text. Following the stream as in lesson 1.9 shows almost nothing readable.
  • Header compression (HPACK, RFC 7541): headers are compressed, and frequent ones are sent as index numbers. It's a stateful compression that remembers headers sent earlier in the same connection, so missing the beginning of a connection can make later headers undecodable.
  • Pseudo-headers: :method, :path, :authority (HTTP/1.1's Host) and :scheme replace the request line, and :status replaces the status line (lesson 2.2: no reason phrase).
  • Multiplexing: several streams (numbered request/response pairs) travel simultaneously in one TCP connection. Streams opened by the client have odd numbers (1, 3, 5, …).
  • TLS: not mandatory by the standard, but browsers use HTTP/2 only over TLS. Cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c) appears only between servers or in tools.

docs.title: 8.2 Seeing it: zero lines without keys, a table with them
docs.text:
I requested two files from nghttpd over HTTPS. curl put both requests on one TCP connection.

SSLKEYLOGFILE=$PWD/keys.log curl -s -k --http2 -A "Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64; rv:140.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/140.0" \
  -H "Cookie: _ga=GA1.1.1234567890.1793500000" https://127.0.0.1:8445/index.html https://127.0.0.1:8445/report.txt

Applying http2 in tshark without session keys gave zero lines: everything was encrypted with TLS. Given the keys written via SSLKEYLOGFILE:

tshark -n -r h2.pcap -o tls.keylog_file:keys.log -Y 'http2.type == 1' -T fields \
  -e tcp.stream -e http2.streamid -e http2.headers.method -e http2.headers.path \
  -e http2.headers.authority -e http2.headers.user_agent -e http2.headers.status

(Actual output, User-Agent column partly trimmed)

0   1   GET /index.html 127.0.0.1:8445  Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64; rv:140.0) ...
0   1,1                 200
0   3   GET /report.txt 127.0.0.1:8445  Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64; rv:140.0) ...
0   3,3                 200
  • http2.type == 1 selects only HEADERS frames (frames carrying headers).
  • The first column is 0 throughout: one TCP stream. Inside it, HTTP/2 streams 1 and 3 each carried one request. Lesson 1.9's "TCP stream" and HTTP/2's "stream" are different concepts; don't mix them.
  • Wireshark shows decompressed headers by name, as in http2.headers.user_agent and http2.headers.path. Only the field names differ from HTTP/1.1's http.user_agent; the meaning is the same, so the filters and tables of lessons 1.9 and 1.10 carry over directly.

Following the stream of a request sent in cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c), only the very beginning was text and the rest was binary.

(Actual output, beginning)

PRI * HTTP/2.0

SM

..............d.....................>...

PRI * HTTP/2.0\r\n\r\nSM\r\n\r\n is the fixed opening string (connection preface) with which a client starts HTTP/2. If you see it, it's a cleartext HTTP/2 connection, and the headers after it are HPACK-compressed and unreadable. To have Wireshark dissect it, designate the port as HTTP/2 (-d tcp.port==8446,http2); doing so immediately showed GET /index.html and 200 (actual output).

[Supplement] HTTP/2 in browser developer tools

The source material also shows viewing HTTP/2 requests in a browser's developer tools (network tab). The browser is the TLS endpoint, so it shows headers such as :authority and :path regardless of encryption, and marks h2 (HTTP/2) or h3 (HTTP/3) in the protocol column. In investigations, use it to learn by opening the same site in a test browser what requests go out and in what shape. It's rarely possible to do this on the subject's own browser.

docs.title: 8.3 [Changed] Server push is gone from browsers
docs.text: The source material warns about HTTP/2 server push, where a server pushes objects nobody requested into the browser cache. A file in the cache can't be told apart as user-requested or server-pushed, so endpoint cache analysis could be wrong. This feature was disabled by default in Chrome 106 (2022) for lack of real benefit, and Firefox announced in 2024 that it would disable it, then removed it. So in today's browser caches this concern has largely gone, but keep it in mind for evidence from before 2022. Its suggested replacement, the 103 Early Hints response, only sends a hint to preload a resource; the browser makes the actual request.

docs.title: 9. HTTP/3: HTTP over QUIC
docs.text:
HTTP/3 (RFC 9114, 2022) moves the ideas of HTTP/2 onto QUIC (RFC 9000). What changes for investigations:

  • It uses UDP 443. Not TCP, so as lesson 1.2 showed, it can bypass proxies that handle only TCP. That's why you need to look separately at UDP 443 in firewall records.
  • Almost everything is encrypted. QUIC builds in TLS 1.3 and encrypts not only HTTP headers but most of the transport-layer information that would be visible with TCP (sequence numbers, acknowledgements). From packets alone you can see little more than addresses, ports, sizes, timing and connection identifiers, plus the SNI in the Client Hello of the first Initial packet (unless ECH is used, lesson 1.12).
  • Header compression is QPACK (RFC 9204): a similar idea to HPACK, but a different mechanism.
  • Decrypting it still needs session keys. Wireshark documents decrypting QUIC with keys in SSLKEYLOGFILE format. The curl in this environment was built without HTTP/3 support, so I couldn't test HTTP/3 directly.

In the end, for both HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, investigators need records from one end of the connection (the browser, a TLS-intercepting proxy, server logs) or session keys to see content. With packets alone, turn to lesson 1.12's flow analysis (size and timing patterns).

docs.title: 10. How to use this in real investigations
docs.text:
1. Identify the vendor from the cookie name. Names like _ga, __utma and __hstc tell you the vendor and format. For unknown names, look for the vendor's public documentation and published cookie lists.
  2. Try converting numbers to times. Ten digits are often seconds, thirteen milliseconds. Check that the converted time falls in a plausible range (the last few years).
  3. Read the "user" as a store. Allow for browsers, profiles, private mode and deletion, and bound the times with the browser's cookie-lifetime caps.
  4. Record the level of documentation. Note whether the basis is official documentation, public analysis or your own test.
  5. For HTTP/2 and 3, look for keys or endpoint records first. Without them, use the TLS version, SNI, and size and timing patterns.
  6. Distinguish TCP streams from HTTP/2 streams. One TCP connection carries several requests simultaneously.

docs.title: 11. Summary
docs.text:
• Advertising and analytics cookies contain past information such as first visit, previous visit, visit count and traffic source, showing beyond the period of your evidence. From an invented __utma value we read the first visit (2026-01-01), the previous visit and the visit count (14).
  • [Changed] __utm* is an old generation, and the next one stopped processing on 2023-07-01. Today it's _ga and _ga_<ID> (official default lifetime two years); their structure isn't in official documentation, and the format has changed before.
  • A cookie's "user" is a cookie store, varying with browser, private mode and deletion.
  • Marketing cookies use millisecond times. [Changed] Lifetimes differ from the source material, and published lists disagree, so check.
  • [Changed] Browsers cap cookie lifetimes (Chrome 400 days, Safari 7 days). The upper bound on first-visit times depends on the browser.
  • HTTP/2 is binary framing, HPACK, pseudo-headers and multiplexing. Without keys, zero lines; with session keys, HTTP/2 streams 1 and 3 appeared inside one TCP connection. Cleartext starts with PRI * HTTP/2.0.
  • [Changed] Server push has been removed from Chrome 106 and Firefox.
  • HTTP/3 encrypts almost everything over QUIC on UDP 443. Content is visible only through endpoint records or session keys.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
Question 1. (Calculation) A pcap from 4 November 2026 shows __utma=48210377.551902814.1735689600.1792800000.1793750400.37. Find the dates of the first, previous and current visits, and the visit count.

Answer and explanation

date -u -d @1735689600 is 2025-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, @1792800000 is 2026-10-24 00:00:00 UTC, and @1793750400 is 2026-11-04 00:00:00 UTC (you can verify by dividing the seconds by 86,400 per day). The visit count is the last value, 37. So this browser store first received this site's cookie on 1 January 2025, 4 November 2026 is the 37th visit, and the previous visit was 24 October. Note that the first visit means "this store first received it then and hasn't deleted it since" (section 4).

Question 2. (Common misconception) "The last number of the competitor site's _ga cookie on the employee's PC is three days ago, so the employee first visited that site three days ago." Give at least three cases where this conclusion could be wrong.

Answer and explanation

① In private mode, each window is a new store, so it's just a cookie first received in a private window opened three days ago. ② If cookies were deleted, it resets from then. ③ The employee may have visited earlier with another browser or profile. ④ A browser lifetime cap (e.g. Safari's short limit) may have removed an older cookie and created a new one. ⑤ Reading that number as "first creation time" is itself an interpretation not in official documentation. So the sentence you can write is "this browser store's _ga cookie for that site appears to have been created three days ago", and the first visit is traced back through other evidence (proxy logs, browser history).

Question 3. (Calculation) A marketing cookie contains the value 1793598745123. What time is it? What happens if you feed it as-is to date -u -d @1793598745123?

Answer and explanation

With 13 digits, treat it as milliseconds and convert the first 10 digits, 1793598745: 2026-11-02 05:52:25 UTC, with the trailing 123 being 0.123 seconds (1793512345 was 05:52:25 on 1 November; adding 86,400 seconds gives 1793598745, exactly one day later). Fed as-is, date takes the 13 digits as seconds and gives an absurd date tens of thousands of years in the future, or a range error. When an implausible year comes out, first suspect the unit (seconds, milliseconds, microseconds).

Question 4. (Interpretation) The same hubspotutk value appears in requests to three different companies' web sites. What can you tell, and what can't you?

Answer and explanation

What you can tell: the same browser store visited three sites that use that marketing service. The value is an identifier the service gave the visitor, so it links the same person (strictly, the same store) across different sites. What you can't: who the person using the store was (it may be a shared PC), and how the value was generated (the source material also says its composition is undocumented). How the value is shared across sites can also depend on the vendor and the browser's cookie policy (first-party, third-party restrictions), so confirm the behaviour at the time before writing it up.

Question 5. (Changed conditions) A procedure written in 2016 says "treat files in the endpoint's browser cache as requested by the user, but note the possibility of HTTP/2 server push". For a Chrome cache in a 2026 case, how should this caveat change?

Answer and explanation

Chrome disabled HTTP/2 server push by default from 106 (2022), so a cache from later Chrome versions is very unlikely to contain server-pushed objects. For a 2026 case, write "server push disabled since Chrome 106" with its basis, and instead note that files may be in the cache for other reasons the user didn't directly request: images and scripts the page loaded itself, prefetching, resources the browser fetched early due to 103 Early Hints. The principle of not reading a single cache file as "something the user chose to open" stays.

Question 6. (Structure) In section 8.2's results, tcp.stream is always 0 but http2.streamid is 1 and 3. Explain the difference, and say how the same requests would have looked over HTTP/1.1.

Answer and explanation

tcp.stream is the number Wireshark assigns per TCP connection; http2.streamid is the number HTTP/2 assigns per request/response pair within one connection. The two requests were multiplexed as HTTP/2 streams 1 and 3 inside one TCP connection (client-opened streams are odd). Over HTTP/1.1, persistent connections (lesson 2.2, section 4.1) could also put them on one TCP connection, but requests would go one after another (the next only after the previous response finished), with no stream numbers. Sending two requests at the same time often means opening two TCP connections. So in HTTP/2 environments there are fewer connections, and counting "one connection = one request" in flow records is even more wrong.

Question 7. (Application) UDP 443 traffic on the packet sensors has grown sharply, but the number of web requests in the proxy logs is unchanged. What has most likely happened, and what do you check?

Answer and explanation

Browsers or apps are most likely going out directly over HTTP/3 (QUIC), bypassing a proxy that handles only TCP (lesson 1.2). Check ① the sources and destinations of outbound UDP 443 at the firewall (which PCs, which services), ② browser policy (e.g. whether QUIC is allowed) and when it changed, ③ destination names from the SNI in QUIC Initial packets (unless ECH), ④ whether proxy-log requests from the same PCs to the same services decreased. Remedies include blocking UDP 443 so browsers fall back to TCP, or disabling QUIC by policy; record the decision and its basis.

Question 8. (Common misconception) "HTTP/2 headers are compressed, so with the session keys you can read all headers from any point in the pcap." What's missing?

Answer and explanation

HPACK is stateful compression: it remembers headers sent earlier in the same connection in a dynamic table and later refers to them by number. So if capture began in the middle of a connection, or early packets are missing, some later headers may point to entries you don't know and can't be fully decoded, even with session keys. The TLS session keys themselves also need to be matched with the handshake at the start of the connection. So analysing HTTP/2 needs a pcap captured from the start of the connection, and the capture notes should record the start time.

Question 9. (Interpretation) In an old pcap (2014), you find __utmz=...utmcsr=search-engine|utmccn=(organic)|utmcmd=organic|utmctr=orchid%20alloy%20formula. What can you tell?

Answer and explanation

__utmz records how the visitor arrived at the site. utmcmd=organic means they came by clicking a (non-advertising) search result, and decoding utmctr gives "orchid alloy formula", the search term used at the time. Back then, search terms were sometimes passed along when going from a search engine to another site, which is why such values survived. Today Referer passes only the origin (lesson 2.1) and search engines often don't pass search terms, so such information is especially valuable in old evidence. But note that the cookie records the store's most recent source (as of when the cookie was updated), and which visit it belonged to must be read together with the other values.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Tools used in this environment: nghttp2 1.59.0 (nghttpd), curl 8.5.0 (built with nghttp2, SSLKEYLOGFILE), tcpdump 4.99.4, tshark 4.2.2, GNU date. Outputs were obtained on 2026-11-05.
  • Google, GA4 cookie usage (checked through search results on 2026-11-05). _ga and _ga_<container-id> default two years; browser lifetime caps (Chrome 400 days, Safari 7 days).
  • Google, Universal Analytics shutdown notice (checked through search results on 2026-11-05). Standard properties stopped processing on 2023-07-01.
  • Chrome Developers blog, Removing HTTP/2 Server Push from Chrome (checked through search results on 2026-11-05). Disabled by default in Chrome 106; 103 Early Hints recommended.
  • IETF, RFC 9113: HTTP/2 (section 3.4 connection preface, section 5 streams), RFC 7541: HPACK, RFC 9114: HTTP/3, RFC 9204: QPACK, RFC 9000: QUIC, RFC 8297: 103 Early Hints.
  • Marketing cookie lifetimes disagreed between published cookie lists on several sites (13 months versus 6 months, search on 2026-11-05). Check the vendor's current official documentation.

About this page

A personal study note, rewritten in my own words from several learning resources. The cookie values and experiment traffic are my own, and the scenarios are hypothetical.

docs.title: 2.5 — Web Server Logs: Formats, Reading Them, Traces of Attacks
2.5 — Web Server Logs: Formats, Reading Them, Traces of Attacks
docs.text:
Scope of this lesson

  • Why web server logs are special in investigations: even for HTTPS, server logs are plaintext
  • Common formats: NCSA Common, Common+VHost, Combined, Apache mod_log_forensic, IIS's formats
  • Reading the fields one by one, and the pitfalls confirmed by running Apache 2.4.58: the time is when the request was received, so lines appear out of order; the size field means different things per distribution; the virtual-host field isn't the requested name; failed logins still record the username
  • [Correction] "W3C Extended" and "Combined" are different formats, and non-printable characters are written as \xhh, not +
  • Analysing with the shell: the source material's four commands run on real logs
  • Traces of attacks: reconnaissance, SQL injection attempts, remote administration tools

Lab environment and notation

(Actual output) came from Apache 2.4.58 (Ubuntu package) installed in this environment. I created a practice virtual host (www.lab.example, alias portal.lab.example) on port 8080 and configured it to write the same requests in several log formats at once. The search CGI is a practice script made to return 500 deliberately when it sees a quote; there's no real database. All requests were sent with curl from the same computer, so the source appears as 127.0.0.1. IIS couldn't be run here and was checked through documentation only.

docs.title: 1. Why web server logs are special
docs.text:
Web server logs are as old as web servers. Their original purpose is unchanged: usage reports (how much was transferred, how many pages served) and records for fixing server and content errors. Yet in incidents involving a web server, these logs often become the most important evidence, because they record line by line everything from automated and manual reconnaissance, to the attack itself, to the moment of compromise (SQL injection, say), to post-compromise operations. With attacks using remote administration tools (RATs), every one of the attacker's commands may be recorded as a request line.

Compared with lesson 1.3's proxy logs: proxy logs record our staff going out, and web server logs record outsiders coming in to our server. The same HTTP, seen from the other side.

And web server logs have one big advantage: HTTPS requests are recorded in plaintext too. The web server is the TLS endpoint, so it writes the log after decrypting the request and knows the result before encrypting the response ("one end of the connection" from lesson 1.12). Even when packet sensors saw only encrypted bytes, the server log has the method, path, query and status code. Such logs are often the investigator's only window onto web activity: logs from web servers, caching proxies, and network security monitoring tools like lesson 2.8's Zeek. Those logs are all created from network communication, so what lessons 2.1–2.4 taught with packets carries straight over to log analysis.

docs.title: 2. Common formats
docs.text:
There are many web server programs, but log formats converge on a few. Most servers offer standard formats as options, plus a way to define your own (templates).

Server Main formats Apache NCSA Common, Common+VHost, Combined, separate Referer and User-Agent logs, custom definitions via format strings, mod_log_forensic IIS W3C extended format (default), IIS format, NCSA Common, centralised binary logging (CBL), ODBC (database) nginx combined (a predefined format), custom definitions via log_format

nginx isn't in the source material, but it's very widely used today, so it's included. nginx's predefined combined format uses the same field order as Apache's Combined.

docs.title: 3. NCSA Common: the basic seven fields
docs.text:
The most basic format is Common, defined by NCSA (the US National Center for Supercomputing Applications), which created much of early web technology. As an Apache format string it's %h %l %u %t "%r" %>s %b. Here's a line written by the lab server.

(Actual output)

127.0.0.1 - jdoe [05/Nov/2026:07:03:23 +0000] "GET /admin/ HTTP/1.1" 200 11
Field Format string Value in this line Meaning 1 %h 127.0.0.1 the requester's address (or host name, depending on configuration) 2 %l - remote user name (identd). Almost always - today 3 %u jdoe user name from HTTP authentication (Basic etc.). Form logins don't count 4 %t [05/Nov/2026:07:03:23 +0000] the time the request was received, with time zone 5 "%r" "GET /admin/ HTTP/1.1" the request line as-is: method, request target (including query, no host name), version 6 %>s 200 the final status code (after internal redirects) 7 %b 11 bytes in the response body (excluding headers); - if zero

Missing values are filled with -. Like lesson 1.3's Squid logs, it can be read by field position, which suits awk. Now let's confirm the pitfalls hidden in these seven fields.
