Lesson 16: Windows services and diagnostic findings · Course overview

docs.title: Lesson 1 — C2 Fundamentals
docs.text: Goal: Explain what C2 does and why a connection does not automatically grant administrator privileges.

docs.title: Where the lecture starts
docs.text:
Lecture: The workshop uses an assumed-breach model. We begin with the ability to run a program on a lab workstation and study what happens afterward. Initial access is assumed rather than reproduced in this lesson.

Supplement: Running a program and having administrator rights are different capabilities. A program launched as an ordinary user generally starts with that user's permissions. Using Sliver does not itself remove those limits.

docs.title: What C2 means
docs.text:
C2 means Command and Control: a system for delivering tasks, managing remote communication, and collecting results. The two words beginning with C give the abbreviation its name.

Imagine asking a remote lab PC for the current user's name. A program on that PC must receive the request, perform the task, and return the answer. C2 organizes that exchange.

flowchart LR
    O["Operator"] -->|"Request a task"| S["C2 Server"]
    S -->|"Deliver task"| I["Implant on lab PC"]
    I -->|"Return result"| S
    S -->|"Display result"| O

The arrows show the logical task flow. They do not specify who initiates a network connection. An implant can contact the server first and receive tasks through that communication.

Term Meaning Analogy Operator Person assigning tasks and reading results Work coordinator C2 server System managing communication, tasks, and results Operations office Implant Software running on the lab PC and performing tasks Field worker

An implant here is software, not a physical device. C2 is a general capability; Sliver is one framework implementing it. Bishop Fox describes Sliver as an open-source, cross-platform framework for authorized adversary emulation and red-team testing. Official repository

docs.title: Why use a framework instead of only a reverse shell?
docs.text:
A shell is an interface for issuing commands and receiving output. In a reverse shell, the target side initiates a connection toward the operator's side to provide remote command input and output.

One short-lived connection may be manageable by hand. With multiple computers, an operator also needs to identify hosts, track tasks, distinguish results, and handle interruptions. A C2 framework provides structure for those activities.

Aspect Simple reverse shell C2 framework Main purpose Remote command input/output Organized remote task and connection management Multiple hosts Often managed separately Host identification and selection features Task handling Commonly tied to a direct interaction Can include interactive and queued tasking Additional capabilities Depend on the implementation and extra tools Built-in features and extensions

Supplement — correction: A reverse shell is not inherently unencrypted. Encryption depends on its implementation and transport. The useful distinction is the breadth of management and tasking features, not a universal encrypted/unencrypted split.

docs.title: Four separate questions
docs.text:
What has been established? What does not automatically follow? C2 communication Administrator privileges Code execution on one PC Access to another PC A currently running implant Automatic execution after a reboot

Keep these concepts separate: connectivity, privilege, reachability/access, and persistence. For example, a browser can contact a server while running as an ordinary user; outbound communication is not proof of administrator rights.

docs.title: The defender's view
docs.text:
An external connection alone does not prove malicious C2. Updaters, messengers, and legitimate remote-management tools also contact servers and receive instructions.

Look at the surrounding evidence:

  • Which process made the connection, and how did it start?
  • Which user account was involved?
  • What destination was contacted?
  • What actions happened before and after the communication?

An unfamiliar program contacting a new destination and then accessing sensitive files provides a different evidential picture from an approved updater performing a scheduled update. The conclusion comes from correlated evidence, not the word “C2” or the presence of traffic alone.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. An implant running as an ordinary user contacts the C2 server. Has it automatically gained administrator rights?
  2. A program periodically contacts an external server. Is that fact sufficient to classify it as malicious C2?
Answers and reasoning

1. No. Network communication may be available to ordinary user programs. A successful connection does not demonstrate a change of privilege.

2. No. Normal applications also communicate externally. Investigate the process, destination, execution context, and associated activity.

Continue to Lesson 2 — Components and commands

docs.title: Lesson 10 — Web Server to Internal SSH: A Virtual Lab
Lesson 10 — Web Server to Internal SSH: A Virtual Lab
docs.text:
Goal: Use a web-server VM's existing Sliver session to reach an internal SSH service, then distinguish tunnel operation, server identity, user authentication, and account permissions.

Supplement / illustrative lab: These are worked command examples for learner-owned VMs. They describe expected observations; they are not a report of commands executed on your machines.

docs.title: Scenario and starting point
docs.text:
An externally reachable web server can be an intermediate host when it also has a permitted connection to an internal service. This is a realistic architecture to model, but web-server access to internal SSH is an explicit lab condition, not a property of every web server.

We start after an authorized Linux implant has established a working Sliver Session on the web VM. Having a web-administration login alone would not establish that condition. No additional implant on the internal SSH VM is required for these forwarding exercises.

The web VM uses Linux in this lesson. The Windows executable used earlier does not run natively on this Linux VM. The identity of its implant process may be a low-privilege web-service account; that does not become root simply because forwarding works.

docs.title: Three VMs and two virtual networks
docs.text:
All three machines belong to the isolated lab. “External” describes the operator's role relative to the internal network; the web server does not need public Internet exposure.

VM OS / hostname Network A Network B Role Operator Linux / operator-lab 192.168.56.10/24 None Sliver Client and Server, SSH client Web server Ubuntu / web-lab 192.168.56.20/24 10.20.0.20/24 Existing Linux implant Session; intermediate host Internal SSH Ubuntu / ssh-lab None 10.20.0.15/24 OpenSSH on TCP 22; ordinary lab account labuser

Use two separate virtual switches. Attach the operator only to A, the internal SSH VM only to B, and the web VM to both. Configure the listed addresses inside the guests. Keep the operator without a separate route into B. Hypervisor or host routing must not accidentally provide another direct path.

flowchart LR
    O["Operator VM<br/>192.168.56.10<br/>Sliver Client + Server"]
    W["Web VM<br/>192.168.56.20 / 10.20.0.20<br/>Existing Sliver Session"]
    I["Internal SSH VM<br/>10.20.0.15:22<br/>labuser"]
    W -->|"Existing C2 connection on network A"| O
    W -->|"Permitted TCP 22 on network B"| I
    O -.->|"No direct route to network B"| I

This layout gives the web VM its own connection to each network. Application forwarding makes an outbound connection from the implant; enabling kernel IP forwarding on the web VM is not required for this exercise. If your lab instead uses a router or firewall, it must allow the web VM to reach 10.20.0.15:22 and allow the existing C2 connection.

Before starting, OpenSSH must be running on the internal VM. The learner must already have a valid labuser login permitted by that server's policy. The examples below assume a lab password is permitted; enter it at the prompt. Key-based authentication is also shown below for a lab key that has already been provisioned.

The operator and web VMs use the OpenBSD implementation of nc, available as netcat-openbsd on Ubuntu. Other programs named nc can have different options.

docs.title: Establish a baseline from each VM
docs.text:
On the internal SSH VM's own console, record its hostname and host-key fingerprint:

hostname
ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub

The expected hostname is ssh-lab if you assigned it during setup. Keep the displayed SHA256:... fingerprint for comparison at first SSH connection. This assumes the server has an Ed25519 host key. If it uses another host-key type, record that actual public host key instead. The fingerprint identifies the SSH server; it is separate from the user's password or login key. OpenSSH fingerprint options

On the operator VM's Linux terminal, attempt the direct connection:

nc -vz -w 3 10.20.0.15 22

With the intended separation, this direct attempt fails. The exact message can be a routing error or a timeout, depending on the lab. Failure alone does not prove that a firewall blocked it; it establishes that this attempt did not connect.

On the web VM's own Linux console, run the same check:

nc -vz -w 3 10.20.0.15 22

A success message supports a TCP connection from the web VM to that address and port. The -z option performs a connection check; it does not log in or verify the server's SSH identity. These two baseline checks are run from the VM consoles to make the different network paths easy to see. OpenBSD nc options

docs.title: Select the web VM's Session
docs.text:
In the Sliver console on the operator VM:

sessions
sessions --interact <Web_Session_ID>
info
help portfwd
help socks5

Replace <Web_Session_ID> with the actual session ID shown by your console, without angle brackets. Check that the selected host is the web VM. Both methods below use this live Session. If you currently have only a Beacon, follow Lesson 9's interactive-session steps and wait for the additional Session before continuing.

docs.title: Method A: a fixed forward to SSH
docs.text:
The mapping is operator loopback port 2222 → internal SSH port 22. These two port numbers do not need to match.

flowchart LR
    A["Operator: ssh<br/>labuser@127.0.0.1:2222"] --> B["Operator loopback<br/>127.0.0.1:2222"]
    B --> C["Sliver C2 channel"]
    C --> D["Web VM implant"]
    D --> E["Internal SSH<br/>10.20.0.15:22"]

In the Sliver console with the web Session selected:

portfwd add --bind 127.0.0.1:2222 --remote 10.20.0.15:22
portfwd

--bind creates the local listening address on the operator's console machine. --remote fixes the destination that the web implant will contact. The forward does not require an SSH login to the web VM: its already established implant Session carries the connection. Sliver port-forward flags, client-side forwarding implementation

In a separate operator Linux terminal:

ssh -o ConnectTimeout=10 -p 2222 labuser@127.0.0.1
Part Meaning ssh Start the SSH client on the operator VM -o ConnectTimeout=10 Bound connection establishment and the initial SSH handshake; this does not limit the whole login session -p 2222 Connect to the local forwarded port labuser@127.0.0.1 Request the internal server's labuser account through that local endpoint

At the first connection, compare the host-key fingerprint with the one recorded on the internal VM. Accept it only when it matches. Although the client addresses 127.0.0.1:2222, the SSH server answering through this mapping is the internal VM. OpenSSH can record it under [127.0.0.1]:2222 in known_hosts. OpenSSH client behavior

Then enter the password for the internal VM's lab account when prompted. The network path and user authentication are separate steps. A valid password or accepted user key is still required. SSH authentication protocol

If your lab instead provisioned a user key, the operator-side command can be:

ssh -i ./labuser_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o ConnectTimeout=10 -p 2222 labuser@127.0.0.1

Here ./labuser_ed25519 is your pre-provisioned user private key on the operator VM. It is not the server's public host-key file, and the forwarding command does not create it.

After successful login, run these commands in the SSH shell now open on the internal VM:

hostname
whoami
id

Illustrative results are ssh-lab, labuser, and that account's UID/group information. This supports successful login and command execution as that account. It does not establish root access or permission to modify every file. End the SSH shell with:

exit

docs.title: Method B: SSH through SOCKS5
docs.text:
This method uses the same web Session, but a SOCKS5-aware helper supplies the final destination for each connection.

flowchart LR
    A["Operator: ssh"] --> B["ProxyCommand: nc<br/>SOCKS5 CONNECT 10.20.0.15:22"]
    B --> C["Operator SOCKS5<br/>127.0.0.1:1080"]
    C --> D["Sliver C2 channel"]
    D --> E["Web VM implant"]
    E --> F["Internal SSH<br/>10.20.0.15:22"]

In the Sliver console, with the web Session selected:

socks5 start --host 127.0.0.1 --port 1080
socks5

This creates a local SOCKS5 listener on the operator VM. Its destination is supplied by the client connection rather than the socks5 start command. Sliver SOCKS5 flags, listener implementation

In a separate operator Linux terminal using OpenBSD nc:

ssh -o 'ProxyCommand=nc -X 5 -x 127.0.0.1:1080 %h %p' labuser@10.20.0.15
Part Meaning ProxyCommand=... Have SSH use this helper for its connection stream nc -X 5 Use SOCKS version 5 -x 127.0.0.1:1080 Contact the operator's local SOCKS5 listener %h OpenSSH substitutes the destination hostname/IP: 10.20.0.15 here %p OpenSSH substitutes the SSH destination port: 22 here labuser@10.20.0.15 Request the internal server and its lab account

The single quotes preserve the complete helper command as one SSH option. The %h and %p tokens are expanded by OpenSSH; you do not manually replace them. This syntax assumes the stated OpenBSD nc implementation. OpenSSH ProxyCommand, OpenBSD nc SOCKS options

Verify the internal server's host-key fingerprint and authenticate with its lab account as in Method A. Because this command names 10.20.0.15 rather than [127.0.0.1]:2222, OpenSSH may ask to confirm that address's host key separately even when the server is the same.

After login, use hostname, whoami, and id, then exit. The key-based alternative is:

ssh -i ./labuser_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -o 'ProxyCommand=nc -X 5 -x 127.0.0.1:1080 %h %p' labuser@10.20.0.15

Starting SOCKS5 alone does not change an ordinary ssh labuser@10.20.0.15 into a proxied connection. The explicit ProxyCommand provides that behavior in this example.

docs.title: Compare what the client connects to
docs.text:
Observation Fixed forward SOCKS5 Address in the SSH command 127.0.0.1, port 2222 10.20.0.15, default port 22 Local listener 127.0.0.1:2222 127.0.0.1:1080 Who chooses the internal destination? Sliver forwarding configuration SSH destination passed through the helper Actual SSH server Internal VM Internal VM Account being authenticated Internal VM's labuser Internal VM's labuser

Neither method automatically opens an SSH session on the web VM first. The web implant relays the connection, while SSH authentication remains between the operator's SSH client and the internal SSH service.

docs.title: Diagnose the stage that failed
docs.text:
Result Interpretation and next check Direct operator connection fails Expected for this layout; verify the baseline rather than assuming a specific blocking cause Web VM cannot connect to internal TCP 22 Check guest addresses, virtual adapters, route, service, and firewall; a tunnel cannot repair this missing path Sliver reports a bind/listen error Inspect whether the chosen operator-side port is already in use SSH reports connection refused on local port 2222 Check that the forward is active on this operator machine; do not assume the internal server refused it SSH times out through a forward Inspect the Session, intermediate-to-internal path, and service; the timeout alone does not locate the fault SSH displays a host-key prompt Key exchange reached an SSH-speaking endpoint; compare its fingerprint before trusting its identity SSH displays Permission denied (publickey,password) User authentication was not accepted; inspect the account, permitted methods, and provided credentials Login succeeds but a later file operation is denied Check that account's rights for that operation and object

The authentication error is illustrative; the method list depends on the server. It is different from proving that the entire tunnel failed.

For defensive observation on the internal Ubuntu VM's administrative console, inspect recent SSH service records:

sudo journalctl -u ssh.service --since "10 minutes ago" --no-pager

Depending on the Ubuntu installation, authentication records can also appear in /var/log/auth.log. With this two-network layout and no NAT between the web and internal VM, the internal service normally sees the connection from the web VM's internal address, 10.20.0.20. Correlate timestamps, accepted or failed authentication, and the actual logged source. A source address alone does not identify the person controlling the connection. Ubuntu OpenSSH logging guidance

docs.title: Finish and remove the exercise listeners
docs.text:
Exit any SSH shell first. In the Sliver console, list the two sets of entries and remove only those created in this exercise:

portfwd
portfwd rm --id <Forward_ID>
socks5
socks5 stop --id <Proxy_ID>

Use the actual IDs from the corresponding lists. Keep the entry IDs distinct from Session IDs. Removing these local listeners ends their use for new connections; it does not delete a lab account or uninstall the internal SSH service.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. In Method A, why does labuser@127.0.0.1 authenticate to the internal VM rather than the operator VM?
  2. Does a web VM's successful TCP 22 check prove that its implant knows a valid SSH password?
  3. With Sliver SOCKS5 running, what is missing from an ordinary ssh labuser@10.20.0.15 command in this lab?
  4. You log in successfully as labuser. Has administrator access been established?
Answers and reasoning

1. The local port is mapped to the internal service. SSH connects to loopback port 2222, and Sliver carries that stream to 10.20.0.15:22 through the web implant. The internal SSH service supplies the host key and authenticates the user.

2. No. That check establishes a TCP path from the web VM. The internal service still requires valid authentication. The lab deliberately supplies a known account; the tunnel supplies connectivity.

3. Explicit proxy use. The shown ProxyCommand asks nc to negotiate a SOCKS5 connection for the SSH stream. Simply starting a listener does not redirect an ordinary client.

4. No. It establishes the accepted account and, after successful commands, execution in that login context. Its permissions on each resource remain a separate question.

Previous: Port forwarding and SOCKS5 · Next: Pivot connections and SSH evidence

docs.title: Lesson 11 — Pivot Connections and SSH Evidence
Lesson 11 — Pivot Connections and SSH Evidence
docs.text:
Goal: Read an internal server's SSH records without confusing a network peer, a human operator, TCP connectivity, and successful authentication.

Supplement: Continue the three-VM exercise from Lesson 10. All outputs below are illustrative rather than measurements from the reader's machines.

docs.title: Keep the lab connection open
docs.text:
Role Address Operator 192.168.56.10 Web VM, external side 192.168.56.20 Web VM, internal side 10.20.0.20 Internal SSH server 10.20.0.15:22

With the web VM's Session selected, the Sliver console creates the forward:

portfwd add --bind 127.0.0.1:2222 --remote 10.20.0.15:22

In a separate operator Linux terminal, connect and authenticate with the pre-provisioned internal lab account. Verify the server host key as explained in Lesson 10:

ssh -p 2222 labuser@127.0.0.1

Keep this connection open while observing it from the internal VM's separate administrative console.

docs.title: Which source does the internal server see?
docs.text:
The web implant creates a new TCP connection to the internal server. In this topology, without intervening NAT or another proxy, the server normally sees the web VM's internal address, not the operator's address.

flowchart LR
    A["Operator SSH client"] --> B["Operator loopback<br/>127.0.0.1:2222"]
    B --> C["Sliver channel"]
    C --> D["Web VM implant"]
    D -->|"New TCP connection<br/>10.20.0.20:51534 to 10.20.0.15:22"| E["Internal SSH server"]

51534 is an illustrative temporary source port. Its actual value changes. The SOCKS5 method has the same internal-facing principle: the web implant connects to the requested internal service. An additional NAT or proxy could change the source address observed by the server.

docs.title: Read SSH authentication records
docs.text:
On the internal Ubuntu VM's administrative console:

sudo journalctl -u ssh.service --since "10 minutes ago" --no-pager

journalctl reads the journal; -u selects the service, --since sets the time window, and --no-pager prints directly. Administrative log access here does not imply that the ordinary SSH account labuser has administrator rights. Depending on installation, authentication records can also appear in /var/log/auth.log. Ubuntu OpenSSH guidance

An illustrative record is:

Oct 24 11:30:05 ssh-lab sshd[2401]: Accepted password for labuser from 10.20.0.20 port 51534 ssh2
Field Interpretation ssh-lab Server recording the event sshd[2401] Logging process name and PID; names vary by OpenSSH version Accepted password Password authentication was accepted for labuser Account authenticated from 10.20.0.20 Peer source address observed by the server port 51534 Peer source port, not the server's listening port ssh2 SSH protocol-version information

The supported conclusion is: this server accepted password authentication for labuser on a connection it observed from 10.20.0.20. This alone does not identify the person controlling it, prove Sliver was involved, establish administrator rights, or record later commands. Accepted authentication also does not by itself establish that a requested interactive shell opened successfully.

docs.title: Why the port is not 2222 or 1080
docs.text:
Port Role in this exercise 2222 Operator-side fixed-forward listener 1080 Operator-side SOCKS5 listener in the alternative method 51534 Example source port for the web VM's outbound connection 22 Internal SSH server's listening port

Reading port 51534 in the authentication record does not mean the SSH service is listening on 51534. Always identify which side the field describes.

docs.title: Observe a current connection
docs.text:
On the internal VM's administrative console, while the SSH connection is open:

sudo ss -tnp '( sport = :22 )'

-t selects TCP, -n keeps numeric addresses, -p requests process information, and the filter selects local port 22. Listening sockets are omitted by default. ss manual

Simplified illustrative output:

State  Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
ESTAB  10.20.0.15:22       10.20.0.20:51534

Local is the machine where this command runs: the internal server. Peer is the other endpoint. ESTAB describes an established TCP connection. It does not by itself establish SSH user authentication. After the connection ends, its absence from this current view does not erase historical login evidence.

docs.title: Detailed answer 1: source address versus human action
docs.text:
Question: Does the accepted-password record prove that a person using the web VM directly typed the SSH command there?

Answer: No. These situations can produce the same observed source address:

Situation Source the internal server may see A person runs SSH in the web VM's terminal 10.20.0.20 An automated job on the web VM runs SSH 10.20.0.20 An operator elsewhere uses the web implant to relay SSH 10.20.0.20

The host making the final TCP connection and the place where a person directs the action can differ. Inspect the web VM's associated process, its execution history, relevant external connections, and timestamps. Attributing a connection to a program still differs from identifying the human responsible.

Authentication acceptance is also separate from a shell request or a particular command succeeding. Record those later stages only when their own evidence supports them.

docs.title: Detailed answer 2: ESTAB versus login success
docs.text:
Question: A connection is ESTAB, but no matching authentication success has been found. Can labuser login be declared successful?

Answer: No. A usual sequence is:

TCP connection established
    -> SSH negotiation and key exchange
    -> User authentication
    -> Shell or command request
    -> Requested operation

TCP can be established while the client awaits host-key approval, waits for a password, or retries an incorrect password. It can also remain established after successful login. ESTAB alone cannot distinguish those states.

Observation What it supports TCP ESTAB TCP connection establishment SSH host-key prompt Progress to SSH key exchange; verify the fingerprint Matching Accepted password record Password authentication acceptance Confirmed command result in the intended context Success of that command

Not finding success is different from finding failure. The query window, log location, collection coverage, and permissions can limit evidence. The careful conclusion is “TCP established; SSH authentication not yet confirmed,” rather than asserting either login success or failure. Match a later record to this connection using time, source address and port, account, and process context; yesterday's accepted login does not prove today's login succeeded.

docs.title: Commands and encrypted content need separate evidence
docs.text:
Ordinary SSH authentication records are not a complete command-execution audit. A record accepting labuser authentication does not show which later commands ran. Process-execution or other appropriately collected audit records may be needed. Shell history can help but is not a guaranteed complete execution record.

SSH protects its transport content with encryption. Seeing addresses and ports in a normal network capture does not imply that the observer can read the commands inside that connection. SSH transport specification

docs.title: Correlate evidence across hosts
docs.text:
Location Evidence to compare Operator VM Lab SSH command and its time Web VM Outbound internal connection and associated process Internal SSH server Observed peer, account, and authentication result Additional internal audit data Subsequent actions, when collected

Normal web-access logs describe web requests and may not explain an outbound SSH connection. Compare operating-system process and network evidence as well. Align timestamps and time zones, addresses, ports, accounts, and processes; similar times alone do not prove two records belong to one event.

Previous: Virtual SSH lab · Next: Network interfaces and sockets

docs.title: Lesson 12 — Network Interfaces, Sockets, and Reachability
Lesson 12 — Network Interfaces, Sockets, and Reachability
docs.text:
Goal: Use Sliver's ifconfig and netstat to inspect the selected host, then distinguish interface addresses, listening sockets, connectivity, and application success.

Supplement: Expand the course's situational-awareness topic using the established virtual lab. Outputs are illustrative. The detailed answers include the follow-up question about causes other than firewall blocking.

docs.title: Select the host before interpreting Local
docs.text:
Host or interface Address Operator 192.168.56.10 Web VM, external side 192.168.56.20 Web VM, internal side 10.20.0.20 Internal SSH VM 10.20.0.15

In the operator's Sliver console, select the web Session using its real ID:

sessions
sessions --interact <Web_Session_ID>
info
Where a command is entered Host being inspected Sliver console with the web Session selected Web VM Operator's ordinary Linux terminal Operator VM SSH shell on the internal server Internal SSH VM

Sliver's built-in commands query the selected target. Their names do not change the importance of input location.

docs.title: Inspect interface addresses
docs.text:
In the Sliver console:

help ifconfig
ifconfig
ifconfig --all

The built-in command retrieves interface configuration. Default display can omit some adapters or addresses; --all requests the fuller display. Absence from the default view does not establish absence from the host. Sliver ifconfig implementation

Simplified example; interface names depend on guest configuration:

Interface Address Lab role lo 127.0.0.1/8 Loopback ens33 192.168.56.20/24 Operator-facing network ens34 10.20.0.20/24 Internal network 
flowchart LR
    A["Operator VM<br/>192.168.56.10"] --- B["Web VM: ens33<br/>192.168.56.20/24"]
    B --- C["Web VM: ens34<br/>10.20.0.20/24"]
    C --- D["Internal SSH VM<br/>10.20.0.15/24"]

The two middle interfaces belong to the same VM. An interface is a network communication attachment; a VM's virtual network card provides one. Finding the internal address supports “this address is configured,” not “every internal service is reachable.” Link state, routing, filtering, and the destination service still matter.

docs.title: Inspect current connections
docs.text:
With the same web Session selected:

help netstat
netstat --numeric

--numeric avoids reverse-name display, making IP comparison easier. The checked defaults select IPv4 and TCP; do not interpret them as an inspection of all UDP and IPv6 activity. Sliver network flags

While the forwarded SSH connection is active, an illustrative entry is:

Protocol  Local Address       Foreign Address  State        PID/Program name
tcp       10.20.0.20:51534     10.20.0.15:22    ESTABLISHED  2030/lab-implant
Field Meaning Local Address Selected web VM's endpoint Foreign Address Other endpoint of this connection ESTABLISHED Established TCP connection PID/Program name Associated process information when available

OS and permissions can limit process attribution. The example shows an implant-related connection; it does not establish SSH authentication or later command success. Sliver netstat implementation

docs.title: The same connection from opposite ends
docs.text:
Observation point Local Other endpoint Web VM 10.20.0.20:51534 10.20.0.15:22 Internal SSH server 10.20.0.15:22 10.20.0.20:51534

Local means the host being inspected. It does not always mean the connection initiator. Foreign does not inherently identify an attacker. This is why the learner's answer “Local is the web VM” is correct when the web Session is selected.

docs.title: Listening is a different observation
docs.text:
In Sliver:

netstat --listen --numeric

This requests listening-socket information. An illustrative web-service entry is:

Local Address   State
0.0.0.0:80      LISTEN

It describes an IPv4 socket bound to the wildcard local address on port 80 in that network environment. It does not configure a firewall allowance or prove remote access. 127.0.0.1:8000 LISTEN would instead describe a loopback binding, with different direct-access conditions. Linux IPv4 socket semantics

Observation What it supports LISTEN Socket waiting for connections at that binding ESTABLISHED A particular TCP connection is established Expected application response That request received the expected response Matching authentication acceptance The service accepted the account's authentication

docs.title: A snapshot has a collection time
docs.text:
An absent SSH entry does not establish that no connection ever existed, that the server is off, or that a firewall blocked it. The connection may have ended, filters may exclude it, or collection may be limited. A Beacon task can run later than the time the operator typed it; consider check-in and actual collection time.

The basic inspection sequence is:

info
ifconfig --all
netstat --numeric
netstat --listen --numeric

docs.title: Detailed answer 1: does LISTEN prove remote web access?
docs.text:
Question: The web VM shows 0.0.0.0:80 LISTEN. Can the operator necessarily use the web service?

Learner answer: “No. A firewall could block it. Please explain other possibilities.”

Correct. A successful request needs the right destination, a working path to the server, TCP establishment, request processing, and a response path. A listener is one part of that chain. The following cases explain the remaining possibilities.

docs.title: Separate virtual networks or a disconnected adapter
docs.text: The operator can have 192.168.56.10/24 and the web VM 192.168.56.20/24, yet be attached to separate, unconnected virtual switches. Matching address ranges do not connect the switches. A disconnected virtual NIC or an address configured on the wrong adapter can also break the path. Check both guest addresses and actual virtual-network attachments.

docs.title: Wrong destination, name resolution, port, or address family
docs.text: A request to 192.168.56.30 does not test a listener on .20. A hostname can resolve to an old or different address. Port 80 is different from 8080, and HTTP is different from HTTPS. 0.0.0.0:80 describes IPv4 listening; that entry alone establishes nothing about an IPv6 connection attempt.

docs.title: The request or response lacks a working route
docs.text:
TCP requires communication in both directions. A request may reach a server while its response follows a wrong route. However, the operator .10/24 and web VM .20/24 in our directly connected subnet do not require a default gateway simply to communicate with each other.

In the operator Linux terminal, inspect the selected route:

ip route get 192.168.56.20

In the web VM's own Linux terminal, inspect the return choice:

ip route get 192.168.56.10

These commands read routing decisions; they do not test successful delivery or alter routes. ip route manual

docs.title: A container listener differs from a published VM port
docs.text:
In a typical Docker bridge setup, a container's 0.0.0.0:80 LISTEN concerns its own network environment. If its port is published as VM port 8080, the mapping is:

Web VM port 8080 -> Container port 80
Operator URL: http://192.168.56.20:8080/

Do not infer a VM listener on port 80 from a container listener on port 80. Confirm the mapping and access conditions. This is a supplementary topology, not a claim that our earlier VM necessarily uses Docker. Docker port publishing

docs.title: Service state changed or processing is overloaded
docs.text:
11:00:00  Listener observed on port 80
11:00:02  Web-server process exits
11:00:05  Operator attempts a connection

The earlier observation can be correct while the later attempt fails. A live process can also delay accepting connections or handling requests under resource pressure. A listener alone does not prove overall application health.

docs.title: TCP works but the web request is not successful
docs.text:
Result Interpretation TCP connection fails HTTP processing was not reached through that attempt HTTP 403 An HTTP response refused access HTTP 500 An HTTP response reported a server processing error An unexpected site appears A different virtual-host configuration may have handled the request

A web server can select among sites using the HTTP Host header. An IP-based request may show a default site while the intended domain shows the desired one. Receiving 403 or 500 differs from complete network failure; still confirm the actual responder. nginx request processing

docs.title: Diagnose with one explicit HTTP request
docs.text:
In the operator's ordinary Linux terminal:

curl --noproxy "*" -v --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 10 http://192.168.56.20/
Option Purpose --noproxy "*" Make this request directly rather than through an environment-configured proxy -v Display connection and request/response details --connect-timeout 5 Bound connection establishment --max-time 10 Bound the complete attempt

An explicitly configured browser or client proxy can otherwise change the actual path. curl option reference

Observation Careful interpretation Connection timeout Inspect path, filtering, and service state; this does not locate the cause by itself Connection refused A refusal occurred; a missing listener or explicit rejection can cause it Connected, then waiting TCP connected; HTTP processing and response need further investigation HTTP status and body received Inspect status, body, and responder to judge the request outcome

docs.title: Detailed answer 2: which host is Local?
docs.text:
Question: In the web Session's Sliver output, Local is 10.20.0.20:51534 and Foreign is 10.20.0.15:22. Is Local the operator or the web VM?

Learner answer: “The web VM.” Correct. The selected target supplies these socket records. Typing the command at the operator's keyboard does not make the operator the Local endpoint of every reported connection. Looking at the same connection on the internal server reverses the endpoint columns.

Previous: SSH evidence · Next: Armory and BOF basics

docs.title: Lesson 13 — Built-in Commands, Armory, and BOFs
Lesson 13 — Built-in Commands, Armory, and BOFs
docs.text: Goal: Separate Sliver's included features, package preparation on the Client, and code execution on a selected target.

docs.title: Different roles, not competing names
docs.text:
Term Role Analogy Built-in command Functionality already included in Sliver Basic tool Armory Find, install, and manage additional tool packages Tool catalogue and installer BOF Compiled task code following a supported execution convention Additional working attachment

Armory itself is not a BOF, and not every Armory package is a BOF. The official index distributes aliases and extensions. Official Armory

docs.title: Start with built-in functionality
docs.text:
Examples already used in the Sliver console include:

pwd
ifconfig
netstat --numeric

When included functionality answers the question, an additional tool is unnecessary. Other questions can require a more specialized tool, such as a detailed inspection of account groups and privileges. Armory helps prepare additional commands for such tasks.

docs.title: Installation happens before target execution
docs.text:
Prepare a tool package on the operator side
    -> Register its command in the Sliver Client
    -> Request execution on a selected target
    -> Target performs the task
    -> Result returns

Installation does not establish execution. Packages are installed and registered on the Sliver Client machine. If the Client and Server are separate, do not treat the Server's filesystem as the Client's. The installation implementation downloads package assets and registers commands; target execution is a separate action. Armory installation implementation

Earlier distinction Corresponding tool distinction Implant generation versus execution Tool installation versus target execution Listener startup versus implant connection Command registration versus task success Task request versus task completion BOF request versus a valid returned result

docs.title: Find and inspect a package
docs.text:
These examples are entered in the Sliver console, not an ordinary OS shell:

help armory
armory
armory search whoami
armory info sa-whoami

In the checked command version, armory displays available packages, search searches command names using a regular expression, and info retrieves configured armory or package details. Match syntax to the installed help rather than guessing from an older demonstration. Current Armory command definitions

sa-whoami is present in the official index as an example. Actual results depend on configured repositories, available metadata, and version. Searching and inspecting it do not run its account query on a target. Official package index

docs.title: Install and check command registration
docs.text:
An illustrative package-installation sequence is:

armory install sa-whoami
help sa-whoami
Observation What it establishes Package appears in search Matching metadata was found Installation reports success Client-side installation was reported complete Help appears Command is registered in the current console Expected task result returns from the intended target Evidence of that task's execution outcome

Registered help does not establish target compatibility. OS, implant-process architecture, supported executor, and dependencies must match. The extension implementation selects artifacts by target OS and architecture. The Linux web VM used earlier cannot be assumed compatible with a Windows tool. Extension target selection

docs.title: Aliases and extensions
docs.text:
Package mechanism Introductory meaning Alias Configuration and assets that expose an external tool as a Sliver command Extension A mechanism for integrating additional executable functionality

A Sliver alias is more than an ordinary shell nickname: it connects a tool and execution arguments to a command. Extensions can include BOF-related execution configurations. Ask what the package runs, which target environments it supports, and which execution mechanism it requires. The label alone does not answer all three questions.

docs.title: What a BOF contributes
docs.text:
BOF means Beacon Object File. A typical Windows BOF is compiled task code, commonly written in C/C++, prepared as a COFF object file and following a compatible execution convention. An object file is not an ordinary finished EXE; it needs an appropriate loader or executor.

flowchart LR
    A["Sliver command"] --> B["Existing C2 channel"]
    B --> C["Implant process"]
    subgraph T["Target host"]
        C --> D["BOF loader / executor"]
        D --> E["BOF code"]
        E --> F["Task result"]
    end
    F --> G["Operator console"]

COFFLoader is one implementation. Current Sliver code also supports a built-in BOF executor path; the exact loader choice depends on version and package configuration. Do not assume every package needs the same manually installed loader. COFFLoader project, Sliver execution paths

The word Beacon in BOF's name does not mean the tool format is restricted to Sliver Beacon mode. BOF format and Session/Beacon communication modes are separate concepts.

docs.title: Memory execution describes only part of the behavior
docs.text:
A usual BOF execution model prepares code inside the existing implant process. This differs from starting a separate complete EXE. However, the BOF's own actions determine further effects:

Incorrect generalization More accurate interpretation A BOF never creates another process Its task code could create one Memory execution means no file activity The task could read or write files Memory execution cannot be detected Memory and runtime behavior can be observed A BOF automatically grants administrator rights Execution mechanism alone does not elevate privileges

A file-reading BOF still performs file access; a network-querying BOF still communicates. Consider both the execution mechanism and the task's behavior. For the simplest explanation and object-file questions, continue to the BOF, COFF, and OBJ questions.

docs.title: Detailed answer 1: help is not a target result
docs.text:
Question: Installation succeeds and help sa-whoami appears. Has the selected target performed the user-information query?

Learner answer: “Displaying help does not guarantee target OS compatibility or execution success.”

Correct. The preceding stage distinction makes this even more precise: installation and help do not themselves request that target query. No target result has been established. Even after an execution request, the task may await a Beacon check-in or fail, so request and successful completion remain distinct.

docs.title: Detailed answer 2: in-process does not mean invisible
docs.text:
Question: A BOF ran in the existing implant. Does that establish no file activity, no network traffic, and no possible detection?

Learner answer: “No.” Correct. Where code runs and what it does are different questions. File inspection can access files, a server query can open a connection, a setting change can modify a file or registry entry, and a program-launching task can create a child process. Security tools may observe behavior or memory activity; actual visibility depends on their configuration and capabilities. Neither guaranteed invisibility nor guaranteed detection follows from the term BOF.

Previous: Network interfaces and sockets · Continue: BOF, COFF, and OBJ questions

docs.title: Lesson 14 — EXE, .NET Assembly, and BOF Execution
Lesson 14 — EXE, .NET Assembly, and BOF Execution
docs.text:
Goal: Compare execution mechanisms using the harmless task “report the current account.” Separate code format, file location, runtime, process placement, and successful results.

These are lab command examples, not a report of executions performed for the reader. Use a compatible Windows target for the Windows examples, not the Linux web Session from the earlier SSH scenario.

docs.title: Three ways to perform a similar task
docs.text:
Mechanism Prepared code Execution model Launch a program with execute A program available on the target Start a program process Execute a .NET Assembly Compatible .NET code and metadata Use a suitable .NET execution environment Execute a BOF Compatible task object code Usually prepare and run it inside the existing implant

These are comparisons of mechanisms, not mutually exclusive filename categories. In particular, a .NET program can also be launched normally when the target has the file and required runtime.

docs.title: Launch an existing Windows program
docs.text:
Windows provides whoami.exe to report identity information. With a Windows lab Session selected in the Sliver console:

help execute
execute --output whoami.exe

execute requests a program launch on the target, --output captures its output, and whoami.exe is the target program. This assumes the Windows program can be located on that target. The command does not automatically upload an executable from the operator's machine. Sliver execute implementation

Target Windows host
    Implant process
    Separate whoami.exe program process

Compare the built-in Sliver command with the explicit program launch:

whoami
execute --output whoami.exe

They concern similar information but do not establish identical internal behavior. The second explicitly starts a target-side program. Similar names or output do not prove identical execution paths.

docs.title: A .NET Assembly is a code unit, not assembly language
docs.text:
Here, Assembly does not mean assembly language. It is a .NET unit containing code and related information. Imagine a simple C# console program that prints its Windows account identity. A compatible .NET Framework build might be named LabWhoAmI.exe.

Assemblies can be EXE or DLL files. An EXE suffix alone does not identify whether its code is native or managed .NET code. Microsoft assembly explanation

For the ordinary managed .NET Framework example used here:

C# source
    -> Build a .NET Assembly
    -> .NET runtime prepares the code
    -> CPU executes the required instructions

The CLR, Common Language Runtime, supplies the execution environment. Managed compilation commonly produces intermediate code; the runtime can translate needed code into CPU instructions and supply services such as memory management. This is an introductory model, not a claim that every modern C# build uses the same deployment/runtime model. Microsoft managed execution process

docs.title: execute-assembly reads a Client-side file
docs.text:
In the Sliver console:

help execute-assembly

An illustrative command shape is:

execute-assembly /home/student/lab/LabWhoAmI.exe

LabWhoAmI.exe is an illustrative filename, not an included Sliver tool. A compatible harmless assembly must actually exist at that path on the Sliver Client machine. Not every C# or EXE file satisfies that requirement. The Client reads its bytes for target execution. execute-assembly implementation

Example Where the named file is located execute --output whoami.exe Target machine execute-assembly /home/student/lab/LabWhoAmI.exe Client machine

The operator-side Linux path does not make the assembly a Linux target program. Source-file location and target compatibility are separate properties.

docs.title: Memory loading and process placement are different questions
docs.text:
In the checked Sliver version, default execute-assembly loads and executes the assembly in a child hosting process on Windows. An in-process option also exists. Therefore memory execution does not automatically mean execution inside the existing implant. Sliver command definitions

Target Windows host
    Implant process
    Separate hosting process
        .NET runtime
            Supplied assembly code

A hosting process supplies a place for the code to run. Keep two dimensions separate:

Question Dimension How is code prepared and run? Loading/execution mechanism In which process does it run? Process placement

The actual behavior depends on the selected implementation and options. Inspect the installed help and observed process evidence rather than inferring it from the words “in memory.”

docs.title: BOF execution uses the object-file model
docs.text:
The same account-query task could be implemented as a BOF:

Account-query source
    -> Compile for compatible target
    -> BOF object file
    -> Loader prepares execution
    -> Task runs inside the existing implant

Target Windows host
    Implant process
        BOF executor / loader
            Account-query BOF

An additional tool such as sa-whoami illustrates this package model. Installation, target compatibility, and required execution support must be in place. A BOF can itself start another program if its task does so; the diagram describes usual placement of the BOF's own code, not a guarantee about every subsequent action.

docs.title: Compare evidence, not just returned names
docs.text:
Point Program launch .NET Assembly mechanism Usual BOF mechanism Code artifact Finished program image .NET code and metadata Task object code Preparation OS loading and needed runtime support Hosting model and .NET environment BOF executor/loader Placement discussed here New program process Separate host by default Existing implant Automatically gains administrator rights? No No No

Similar account-name output does not establish the same execution mechanism. Different effective contexts can also produce different identities. A result must be tied to the intended target, task, and context; request, execution, and successful completion remain separate stages.

docs.title: Detailed answer 1: can every Tool.exe use execute-assembly?
docs.text:
Question: The file is named Tool.exe. Is that enough to choose execute-assembly?

Learner answer: “No. It could be an ordinary executable.”

Correct. It could be a native executable or a .NET assembly. The suffix does not distinguish them, and renaming a file does not turn it into compatible .NET code. Check the actual format and runtime requirements.

The additional clarification is important: a compatible .NET EXE can also be started as an ordinary program with execute when it is present on the target and that target has the necessary environment. Artifact type and requested execution mechanism are different classifications.

docs.title: Detailed answer 2: does memory execution exclude a new host?
docs.text:
Question: An assembly was loaded into memory. Can we conclude no new process was created?

Learner answer: “No. A hosting process might have been started.”

Correct. Both of these descriptions involve memory loading:

Model A
Existing implant process
    -> Load and run code in that process

Model B
Existing implant process
    -> Create separate hosting process
        -> Load and run code in its memory

Ask both how the code was executed and where it executed. Process creation and identity need their own evidence; memory execution alone does not answer either question.

Previous: BOF, COFF, and OBJ questions · Next: Windows tokens and privileges · Course overview

docs.title: Lesson 15 — Windows Tokens, Deny Only, and Privileges
Lesson 15 — Windows Tokens, Deny Only, and Privileges
docs.text:
Goal: Read account, group, privilege, and integrity information without confusing group membership, a program's current permissions, and evidence that an action occurred.

Use a Windows lab VM for these examples. Outputs are illustrative, not measurements of the reader's machines. This lesson includes the follow-up questions, detailed answers, and the simpler permission-card explanation.

docs.title: One account, two programs
docs.text:
Two programs started by the same person can use different permissions.

Suppose student belongs to local Administrators. The user opens an ordinary PowerShell, then another with Run as administrator and normal UAC approval. In a typical administrator-approval configuration:

flowchart TD
    A["Same account: student<br/>Member of Administrators"]
    A --> B["Ordinary PowerShell"]
    A --> C["PowerShell started with<br/>administrator approval"]
    B --> D["Filtered permission card<br/>Administrators: Deny only<br/>Integrity: Medium"]
    C --> E["Administrative permission card<br/>Administrators: Enabled<br/>Integrity: High"]

The username can match while the permission card differs. This card is the access token. UAC can use a filtered token for ordinary applications and an administrative token for approved elevated applications. Microsoft UAC explanation

Opening an elevated PowerShell does not automatically elevate an already running implant. Inspect the program and context actually performing the action.

docs.title: What is on the permission card?
docs.text:
An access token describes a process or thread's security context. Windows consults the relevant token along with the resource's rules and other controls. Microsoft access tokens

Information Plain question User identity Which account is this? Groups and attributes How can these group identities participate in access checks? Privileges and states Which system-operation privileges are present and active? Integrity level Which integrity protection level applies?

These statements need different evidence:

The student account belongs to Administrators.
The implant is running with an administrative token.

The first does not establish the second. A username does not describe every token property. A token also does not list the outcome of every possible resource-access request.

docs.title: Read a Windows execution context
docs.text:
In PowerShell on the Windows lab VM:

whoami.exe /all

Or inspect the parts separately:

whoami.exe /user
whoami.exe /groups
whoami.exe /priv
Option Information /user Account name and SID /groups Groups and attributes /priv Privileges and states /all Combined current-token information

A SID is a Windows security identifier. These commands inspect the context of the whoami.exe instance started from that terminal. Matching usernames do not prove a separate implant uses the same token. Microsoft whoami reference

docs.title: Query the implant with getprivs
docs.text:
In the Sliver console, select the actual Windows Session:

sessions
sessions --interact <Windows_Session_ID>
info
help getprivs
getprivs

Replace the placeholder without brackets. getprivs is built-in and Windows-specific; it needs no Armory package. The checked implementation displays process privileges and integrity level. This privilege list does not replace a separate inspection of group attributes. Sliver getprivs implementation

Simplified illustrative output:

Privilege Information for lab-implant.exe (PID: 2030)

Process Integrity Level: Medium

Name                       Attributes
SeChangeNotifyPrivilege    Enabled
SeShutdownPrivilege        Disabled

Actual lists and formatting vary. Read incomplete-information or collection errors. A Beacon task may require waiting for check-in and the returned result.

Query Context described Terminal: whoami.exe /all That program's execution context Selected implant: getprivs Implant process privilege and integrity information

docs.title: What does Deny only mean?
docs.text:
The learner asked: “No, but what does Deny only mean?”

Group: Administrators
Attribute: Deny only

This group identity participates in denial checks, but does not obtain access through rules allowing that group.

Resource rule Treatment of Deny-only Administrators Allow Administrators to read Do not use this group identity to obtain that allowance Deny Administrators modification Consider this identity when checking the denial

An analogy: the administrator badge cannot claim administrator benefits, but restrictions applying to that badge can still matter. Microsoft token SID attributes

This is a property of the current token. It does not mean the account was deleted or removed from the group. It does not itself create a new deny rule on every file.

docs.title: Does Deny only prohibit every file operation?
docs.text:
No. Other identities in the token can still provide access. To isolate this idea, assume no other grants or restrictions in this simplified example:

File Read allowance notes.txt Granted directly to user student admin.txt Granted only to Administrators

The ordinary program's token is:

User: student
Administrators: Deny only
File Interpretation in this example notes.txt The user's own identity supplies read allowance admin.txt The Deny-only group identity cannot supply that allowance

Deny only specifies how one group identity is used. Another active group or the user identity can matter. Actual access also depends on other rules and controls; this illustration is not a complete ACL-evaluation algorithm.

docs.title: Group attributes and privilege states differ
docs.text:
Example Describes Administrators — Deny only Group identity attribute SeShutdownPrivilege — Disabled State of a particular privilege

A privilege concerns a system operation, such as local shutdown or changing system time. File read/write permissions concern operations on an object. The same domain account can have different privileges on different computers. Microsoft privileges

State Meaning Enabled Present and currently active in the queried token Disabled Present in the queried token but currently inactive

Disabled does not mean absent. Enabled does not mean used or guarantee every condition for success.

docs.title: A state is not an action record
docs.text:
Suppose the observation is:

SeShutdownPrivilege    Enabled

It establishes an active privilege in the inspected token. It does not establish a shutdown request, request success, or actual shutdown.

flowchart LR
    A["Privilege present"] --> B["Privilege enabled"]
    B --> C["Operation requested"]
    C --> D["Operation succeeds"]

These are stages for a privilege-requiring operation, not instructions to perform shutdown. Each later claim needs separate evidence.

Question Answered by Enabled alone? Is the privilege active? Yes Was shutdown requested? No Did the request succeed? No Did the machine shut down? No

docs.title: Integrity level is another protection property
docs.text:
Level Introductory example Low Restricted execution environment Medium Ordinary user program High Commonly seen in elevated programs System Commonly seen in system services

Integrity control operates alongside object access rules. A default protection principle restricts lower-integrity code from writing to higher-integrity objects. High is not unrestricted file access or administrator access to another server. Microsoft integrity control

In our example, ordinary PowerShell uses Medium and the approved elevated program uses High. Inspect actual process information; account membership alone is insufficient.

docs.title: Read a complete example
docs.text:
This is a teaching note combining observations, not the literal output of one command:

Account: student
Account membership: Administrators

Current implant:
    Administrators: Deny only
    Integrity: Medium
    SeShutdownPrivilege: Disabled
Question Supported answer Which account? student Does membership alone prove elevation? No Can this Administrators entry supply group allowances? No; it is Deny only Observed integrity? Medium Is the shown shutdown privilege active? No; Disabled Can every file be read or modified? Not established; inspect the relevant operation and resource rules

This illustrates an administrator-group account using a filtered token for an implant. Identity, current token, resource permissions, and performed actions are separate observations.

docs.title: Review answers and learner reasoning
docs.text:
Question 1: Administrators appears, but it is Deny only and integrity is Medium. Does the group name establish an elevated process?

Learner answer: “No. What does Deny only mean?”

Correct. Read the attribute as well as the group name. The group entry supplies no access from its allow rules, while matching denial rules can still matter. The two-file example explains why this is not a blanket prohibition on all actions.

Question 2: SeShutdownPrivilege is Enabled. Does that prove actual shutdown?

Learner answer: “No. The privilege exists, but whether it was used is unknown.”

Correct, with one refinement: it is present and currently enabled in the queried token. Whether it was requested, used, or resulted in shutdown needs separate evidence, just as HTTP 200, TCP ESTABLISHED, or package installation has a limited evidential meaning.

Previous: EXE, .NET, and BOF execution · Next: Windows services and diagnostic findings · Course coverage · Course overview

docs.title: Lesson 16 — Windows Services, Permissions, and Diagnostic Findings
Lesson 16 — Windows Services, Permissions, and Diagnostic Findings
docs.text:
Learning goal: Separate a service's execution identity, your rights to manage the service, your rights over its files, and evidence that a particular action actually happened.

Use your own isolated Windows lab VM. The names, paths, process IDs, and outputs below are illustrative. They are not measurements from the learner's computer. The commands shown here query information.

docs.title: What is a Windows service?
docs.text:
A Windows service performs background work such as printing, updates, or backups. Depending on its configuration, it can run while no user is signed in. The Service Control Manager (SCM) manages services.

Windows component Company analogy Service An employee doing an assigned job Service executable The program used to perform the job Service execution account The employee's identity and permission card Service Control Manager The office that manages starting and stopping jobs

A service can have its own process or share a host process with other services. This lesson assumes a service with its own process to keep the example simple. Microsoft: service programs

Our fictional example is:

Service name:  LabReportService
Program:       C:\LabApps\ReportService\report-service.exe
Run as:        LocalSystem

This means Windows is configured to start the service program under LocalSystem, an account with extensive privileges on the local computer. Processes running in that context commonly show the identity NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. Microsoft: LocalSystem

docs.title: Two processes, two permission cards
docs.text:
Finding a service configured for SYSTEM does not change your implant's token.

flowchart TD
    W["Windows VM"]
    W --> I["Sliver implant<br/>Account: student<br/>Integrity: Medium"]
    W --> M["Service Control Manager"]
    M --> S["Report service process<br/>Account: SYSTEM"]
    I -. "Queries service information" .-> M

The service process and implant are separate processes. Reading information about another employee's position does not change your own permission card.

Observation Supported interpretation Service StartName is LocalSystem The configured service execution account Service State is Running The service reports that it is running at the observation time Implant identity is student The identity observed for the implant Implant integrity is Medium The integrity level observed for the implant

StartName is a configuration property. To establish the actual token of a particular running process, inspect that process separately. A service listing is not proof that your implant is SYSTEM. Microsoft: Win32_Service

docs.title: Query services from Windows PowerShell
docs.text:
Input location: PowerShell inside the Windows VM you want to inspect. These are not commands to paste directly into the Sliver command prompt.

First list services:

Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Service |
    Select-Object Name, State, StartName
Element Meaning Get-CimInstance Query Windows management information Win32_Service Select service information Select-Object Choose the properties to display Name Service name State Reported current state StartName Configured execution account

Without a remote computer or CIM session, this command queries the local Windows VM where it runs. Microsoft: Get-CimInstance

Inspect one service:

Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Service -Filter "Name='LabReportService'" |
    Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, StartName, PathName, ProcessId |
    Format-List

LabReportService is a fictional example, not a service installed by this lesson. If it does not exist in your VM, use an actual service name from the first query.

Illustrative output:

Name      : LabReportService
State     : Running
StartMode : Auto
StartName : LocalSystem
PathName  : C:\LabApps\ReportService\report-service.exe
ProcessId : 4120

Read it as: the service reports running, is configured for automatic startup under LocalSystem, and lists the program path and current process ID. Auto is a startup setting; Running is a reported current state. An automatically started service can still be stopped or fail to start.

docs.title: Three different permission questions
docs.text:
What you inspect Question Example Service process Under whose authority does this process execute? SYSTEM Service object Which management operations may my current context request? Query, change configuration, start, or stop Executable and directory Which file operations may my current context perform? Read, execute, write, or delete

Service management operations have separate rights:

Service right Operation SERVICE_QUERY_CONFIG Query configuration SERVICE_QUERY_STATUS Query status SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG Change configuration SERVICE_START Start the service SERVICE_STOP Stop the service

A successful query does not establish configuration-change or start/stop permission. File permissions are also separate from service-object permissions. Reading a service's status may be allowed while changing its executable is forbidden; a directory may be writable while service start/stop is forbidden. Microsoft: service security and access rights

docs.title: Inspect executable and directory permissions
docs.text:
For the fictional path, run these queries in the Windows VM's PowerShell. Use a real path from your own service query when following along.

icacls "C:\LabApps\ReportService\report-service.exe"

icacls "C:\LabApps\ReportService"

An illustrative file entry might be:

BUILTIN\Users:(I)(RX)
Mark Meaning BUILTIN\Users Group to which this entry applies I Inherited entry R Read RX Read and execute W Write M Modify, including deletion F Full access

This entry grants Users read and execute rights; it does not itself grant write rights. It is one entry, not a complete effective-access decision. Other entries, the current token, parent-directory permissions, and other applicable controls can affect a particular operation. Microsoft: icacls

Recall Lesson 15: a group listed in a token may be Deny only, so its name alone is insufficient to establish an allow grant.

docs.title: What does a diagnostic warning mean?
docs.text:
A fictional tool reports:

Service: LabReportService
Runs as: LocalSystem
Warning: Service executable may be writable by ordinary users

In plain language:

An ordinary user might be able to change a program file that a service is configured to run with SYSTEM authority.

That is an important lead. If a less-privileged user can control code that later runs under a more-privileged account, the user may be able to influence privileged behavior. But the warning does not establish that the file was changed, that changed code ran, or that an implant's token changed.

Treat the tool's “Runs as” field as a reported observation. Check whether it represents configuration or an actual process-token measurement.

flowchart TD
    A["Tool reports a possible weakness"]
    --> B["Check the exact file or service setting"]
    --> C["Check permissions for the current token"]
    --> D["Check when changes could affect execution"]
    --> E["Observe actual execution and its security context"]

Check the path against the service configuration; inspect rights for the current token; consider file locking and other controls; establish when a change could take effect; and collect evidence about the process that actually executes.

docs.title: A simpler analogy: the manager's instructions
docs.text:
Imagine an ordinary employee who cannot change important company systems. A manager can change them and follows a written instruction sheet.

If the ordinary employee can edit the instructions, and the manager later follows the edited version, the employee can influence work performed with the manager's authority.

Company analogy Service example Ordinary employee Less-privileged user Instructions that influence the manager's work Service executable Manager with greater authority Service process running as SYSTEM Ability to edit instructions Ability to modify the executable

The instruction sheet is an analogy for executable code, not a claim that an EXE is a text document.

The concern is the combination: a less-privileged person may control what a more-privileged process executes.

docs.title: Three checks between a warning and a result
docs.text:
First: can the current context really perform the required modification? The tool may have identified a suspicious permission entry. Confirm the exact file, the current user's token and applicable rights, and whether the intended file operation is allowed. A file in use or another control can affect that operation.

Second: will the changed content actually be executed? Even if an on-disk change were possible, the existing process does not automatically become a new version. Establish when the relevant program would load and execute the changed content.

Third: what ran, and under which token? A service-start message does not by itself prove that the expected changed file ran, that a particular action happened, or that the process had the expected token. Correlate the actual process, loaded program, observed behavior, and security context.

These checks separate a possible weakness, a confirmed permission, and an observed outcome.

docs.title: Disk file versus a running process
docs.text:
Suppose a service starts at 09:00 and an on-disk file could be changed at 10:00. You cannot conclude that the process already running since 09:00 instantly changes to execute the new content.

flowchart LR
    A["Program file on disk<br/>Original content"] -->|"Program starts"| B["Running process<br/>Original program"]
    A -->|"Assume a file change is possible"| C["Program file on disk<br/>Changed content"]
    C -. "Does not establish an automatic<br/>change to the existing process" .-> B

In the company analogy, the manager takes a copy of the instructions at 09:00. Someone changes the original in the cabinet at 10:00. The manager may still be following the earlier copy.

This is a conceptual distinction between a stored artifact and a running process, not a complete description of Windows executable loading. Inspect when the relevant changed content would actually be loaded and used.

docs.title: What each observation proves
docs.text:
Observation Supported conclusion A tool displays a warning A possible weakness was reported The required file modification is confirmed for the current token That particular file operation is permitted under the checked conditions A disk file changes The stored file changed The service reports a successful start A service-start outcome was reported The changed program's execution and SYSTEM token are observed Changed code executed under that observed token

Each row requires its own evidence. Do not use one earlier observation as proof of all later events.

A service error also does not, by itself, settle whether any process or code executed. Status reporting and code execution are separate observations.

Even when a separate process is observed running changed code as SYSTEM, an existing student implant does not automatically receive that process's token. Check each process individually.

A precise finding would be: “A configuration that could permit privileged execution was reported. Current permissions, execution conditions, and the actual outcome still require verification.”

docs.title: Question 1: a SYSTEM service was found
docs.text:
Question: The implant is running as student at Medium integrity. A service query shows a service configured for LocalSystem. Is the implant now SYSTEM?

Answer: no. The query describes another service. It does not change the implant's account or token. Reading an employee's senior job title does not upgrade your own permission card.

StartName describes a configured service account. To establish the actual token of a running service process, inspect that process. To establish the implant's current authority, inspect the implant itself.

The supported conclusion is: “A service configured for LocalSystem was found; the observed implant remains student at Medium integrity.”

docs.title: Question 2: a Users RX entry was found
docs.text:
Question: The service executable has a BUILTIN\Users:(RX) entry. Does this entry prove that an ordinary user can modify the file?

Answer: no. RX grants read and execute rights through that entry. Executing an existing program and changing its file are different operations.

Do not reverse this into a blanket claim that the user can never modify the file. Another applicable entry might grant modification:

BUILTIN\Users:(RX)
LAB\student:(M)

Here the user has a separate Modify grant. Assuming no other applicable restrictions, the direct user entry can grant modification even though the Users entry grants only read and execute.

Read the full relevant permissions, current token, and parent-directory rights. This is not a complete ACL-ordering algorithm.
